p.seg: B The Commentary
B1 The principal wife of Huì Gōng was Mèng Zǐ.
When Mèng Zǐ died,
Shēng Zǐ became the successor wife
and gave birth to Yǐn Gōng.
Sòng Wǔ Gōng had a daughter, Zhòng Zǐ.
When Zhòng Zǐ was born, there were characters on her hand
that said she would be a Lady of Lǔ;
therefore, Zhòng Zǐ came to our state in marriage.
She gave birth to Huán Gōng, and then Huì Gōng passed away;
for this reason, Yǐn Gōng was established to support him.
A1.1 The Annals: The First Year of Yǐn Gōng
A1.1.1 In the spring of the first year, the King’s first month.
A1.1.2 In the third month,
the Duke and Yí Fù of Zhū made a covenant at Miè.
A1.1.3 In the summer, the fifth month,
Zhèng Bó defeated Duàn at Yān.
A1.1.4 In the autumn, the seventh month,
the Heavenly King sent Zǎi Xuǎn to come and deliver funeral gifts for Huì Gōng
and Zhòng Zǐ.
A1.1.5 In the ninth month,
there was a covenant with the people of Sòng at Sù.
A1.1.6 In the winter, the twelfth month,
Zhài Bó came.
A1.1.7 Gōngzǐ Yì Shī died.
B1.1 The Commentary: The First Year of Yǐn Gōng
B1.1.1 In the spring of the first year,
the King's Zhōu first month,
the accession to the throne is not recorded
because he was acting as regent.
B1.1.2 In the third month,
the Duke and Yí Fù of Zhū made a covenant at Miè.
This was Kè, the Viscount of Zhū.
Since he had not yet received the King’s appointment,
his title was not recorded.
Calling him "Yí Fù"
was to honor him.
The Duke held the regency and wished to seek good relations with Zhū;
therefore, they held the covenant at Miè.
B1.1.3 In the summer, the fourth month,
Bì Bó led an army to build walls at Láng.
This is not recorded
because it was not the Duke's command.
B1.1.4 Previously,
Zhèng Wǔ Gōng took a wife from Shēn,
called Wǔ Jiāng,
who gave birth to Zhuāng Gōng and Gòng Shū Duàn.
Zhuāng Gōng was born feet-first,
which startled Jiāng Shì;
therefore, he was named Wù Shēng,
and she subsequently disliked him.
She loved Gòng Shū Duàn
and wished to establish him as heir.
She repeatedly requested this of Wǔ Gōng,
but the Duke would not permit it.
When Zhuāng Gōng ascended the throne,
she requested Zhì for him.
The Duke said:
"Zhì
is a precipitous city;
Guó Shū died there.
Any other city is yours to command."
She then requested Jīng.
He had him reside there,
and he was called Jīngchéng Tàishū.
Zhài Zhòng said:
"A capital city
with a wall exceeding one hundred zhì
is a harm to the state.
According to the system of the former kings:
a large city
should not exceed one-third of the state capital;
a medium one,
one-fifth;
and a small one,
one-ninth.
Now Jīng does not conform to the measure;
it is not the system,
and you, my lord, will find it unbearable."
The Duke said:
"Jiāng Shì desired it,
so how can I avoid the harm?"
He replied:
"What satisfaction does Jiāng Shì have?
It would be better to arrange a place for him early,
so as not to let it spread like a creeping vine!
A creeping vine
is difficult to deal with.
Even creeping weeds cannot be removed,
how much more so your lord’s favored brother?"
The Duke said:
"One who commits many injustices will surely bring about his own ruin;
you should just wait for it."
Soon after, Tàishū ordered the western and northern borderlands to give their primary allegiance to him as well.
Gōngzǐ Lǚ said:
"The state cannot endure a divided allegiance;
what will you do about it?
If you wish to give the state to Tàishū,
I request to serve him;
if you will not give it,
then I request to remove him,
so as not to give rise to ideas among the people."
The Duke said:
"There is no need;
he will bring it upon himself."
Tàishū then took those borderlands of divided allegiance and made them his own cities,
extending as far as Lǐnyán.
Zǐ Fēng said:
"It is time!
As his territory grows thick, he will gain the masses."
The Duke said:
"Being unjust,
he will not have closeness.
Though his power is thick, he will collapse."
Tàishū completed his preparations and gathered resources;
he repaired his armor and weapons,
and prepared his infantry and chariots,
intending to surprise Zhèng.
The Lady was going to open the gates for him.
The Duke heard the date set for it,
and said:
"Now is the time."
He ordered Zǐ Fēng to lead two hundred chariots to attack Jīng.
Jīng rebelled against Tàishū Duàn.
Duàn entered Yān.
The Duke attacked him at Yān.
On the day xīnchǒu of the fifth month,
Tàishū fled to Gòng.
The Annals record:
"Zhèng Bó defeated Duàn at Yān."
Duàn did not act like a younger brother;
therefore, the word "brother" is not used.
They were like two rulers;
therefore, the word "defeated" is used.
He is called "Zhèng Bó"
to criticize his failure to instruct his brother;
this is called the "Intent of Zhèng."
That his flight is not mentioned
is because it was a difficult matter for the Duke.
Subsequently, he settled Jiāng Shì at Chéngyǐng
and swore an oath to her, saying:
"Until we reach the Yellow Springs,
we shall not see each other!"
Soon after, he regretted this.
Yǐng Kǎo Shū was the border official of Yǐnggǔ;
hearing of this,
he made an offering to the Duke.
The Duke bestowed a meal upon him.
While eating, he set aside the meat.
The Duke asked him about it.
He replied:
"Your servant has a mother;
she has tasted all of your servant's food,
but she has never tasted the Lord's broth.
I request to leave it for her."
The Duke said:
"You have a mother to give things to,
but I alone have none!"
Yǐng Kǎo Shū said:
"May I venture to ask what you mean by that?"
The Duke told him the reason
and informed him of his regret.
He replied:
"What worry does the Lord have?
If you tunnel into the earth until you reach the springs
and meet through the tunnel,
who could say it was not so?"
The Duke followed his advice.
The Duke entered and chanted:
"Within the great tunnel,
how harmonious is the joy!"
Jiāng came out and chanted:
"Outside the great tunnel,
how overflowing is the joy!"
Consequently, they became mother and son as before.
The noble man says:
"Yǐng Kǎo Shū
was a man of pure filial piety;
he loved his mother,
and this extended to Zhuāng Gōng.
The Classic of Poetry says:
'A filial son's devotion is never exhausted;
forever it is granted to your kind.'
Does it not refer to this!"
B1.1.5 In the autumn, the seventh month,
the Heavenly King sent Zǎi Xuǎn to come and deliver funeral gifts for Huì Gōng
and Zhòng Zǐ.
This was late;
moreover, Lady Zǐ had not yet passed away;
therefore, their names were used.
The Son of Heaven is buried seven months after death,
and those with common carriage axles all arrive;
a feudal lord is buried after five months,
and those of the same alliance arrive;
a Great Officer is buried after three months,
and those of the same rank arrive;
an officer is buried after the passing of a month,
and relatives by marriage arrive.
To present funeral gifts when they cannot reach the corpse,
to offer condolences to the living when the peak of grief has passed,
or to prepare for inauspicious events in advance,
are not in accordance with ritual.
B1.1.6 In the eighth month,
the people of *Jì* attacked *Yí*.
*Yí* did not report it,
so it was not recorded.
B1.1.7 There were *fěi* insects.
They did not cause a disaster,
so they were also not recorded.
B1.1.8 In the final years of *Huì Gōng*,
he defeated the army of *Sòng* at *Huáng*.
When the Duke was established, he sought peace with them.
In the ninth month,
he made a covenant with the people of *Sòng* at *Sù*,
and relations began to be opened.
B1.1.9 In winter, the tenth month, on the day *gēngshēn*,
*Huì Gōng* was reburied.
The Duke did not preside over the ceremony,
so it was not recorded.
When *Huì Gōng* passed away,
there was the war with the *Sòng* army,
and the Crown Prince was young;
because the burial had deficiencies,
he was therefore reburied.
B1.1.10 The Marquis of *Wèi* came to attend the burial
but did not see the Duke,
so this was also not recorded.
B1.1.11 Regarding the rebellion of *Gòng Shū* of *Zhèng*,
*Gōngsūn Huá* fled to *Wèi*.
The people of *Wèi* attacked *Zhèng* on his behalf
and took *Lǐnyán*.
The people of *Zhèng* used the King’s army
and the army of *Guó* to attack the southern border of *Wèi*.
They requested troops from *Zhū*;
the Viscount of *Zhū* sent a private message to *Gōngzǐ Yù*.
*Yù* requested to go,
the Duke did not permit it,
but he went nonetheless,
and with the people of *Zhū*
and the people of *Zhèng*, he made a covenant at *Yì*.
This was not recorded
because it was not by the Duke’s command.
B1.1.12 The South Gate was newly built;
it was not recorded,
also because it was not by the Duke’s command.
B1.1.13 In the twelfth month,
*Zhài Bó* came,
but not by the King’s command.
B1.1.14 *Zhòngfù* died;
the Duke did not participate in the minor enshrouding,
so the day was not recorded.
A1.2 The Annals of *Yǐn Gōng*, Second Year
A1.2.1 In the spring of the second year,
the Duke met with the *Róng* at *Qián*.
A1.2.2 In summer, the fifth month,
the people of *Jǔ* entered *Xiàng*.
A1.2.3 *Wúhài* led an army and entered *Jí*.
A1.2.4 In autumn, the eighth month, on the day *gēngchén*,
the Duke and the *Róng* made a covenant at *Táng*.
A1.2.5 In the ninth month,
*Jì Lièxū* came to fetch the bride.
A1.2.6 In winter, the tenth month,
*Bó Jī* went to her home in *Jì*.
A1.2.7 *Jì Zǐbó*
and the Viscount of *Jǔ* made a covenant at *Mì*.
A1.2.8 In the twelfth month, on the day *yǐmǎo*,
the Lady, of the *Zǐ* clan, passed away.
A1.2.9 The people of *Zhèng* attacked *Wèi*.
B1.2 The Commentary on *Yǐn Gōng*, Second Year
B1.2.1 In the spring of the second year,
the Duke met with the *Róng* at *Qián*
to renew the friendship of *Huì Gōng*.
The *Róng* requested a covenant,
but the Duke declined.
B1.2.2 The Viscount of *Jǔ* married a woman from *Xiàng*,
but *Jiāng* of *Xiàng* was not at ease in *Jǔ* and returned home.
In summer,
the people of *Jǔ* entered *Xiàng*
and returned with Lady *Jiāng*.
B1.2.3 The Minister of Works *Wúhài* entered *Jí*,
and *Fèi Qínfù* conquered it.
B1.2.4 The *Róng* requested a covenant.
In autumn,
they made a covenant at *Táng*,
again renewing the friendship with the *Róng*.
B1.2.5 In the ninth month,
*Jì Lièxū* came to fetch the bride;
a high minister fetching a bride for his ruler.
B1.2.6 In winter,
*Jì Zǐbó*
and the Viscount of *Jǔ*
made a covenant at *Mì*
for the sake of *Lǔ*.
B1.2.7 The people of *Zhèng* attacked *Wèi*
to punish the rebellion of *Gōngsūn Huá*.
A1.3 The Annals of *Yǐn Gōng*, Third Year
A1.3.1 In the spring of the third year, in the King’s second month,
on the day *jǐsì*,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A1.3.2 In the third month, on the day *gēngxū*,
the Heavenly King passed away.
A1.3.3 In summer, the fourth month, on the day *xīnmǎo*,
the Lady of the ruler's house died.
A1.3.4 In autumn,
the son of the *Wǔ* clan came to request funeral contributions.
A1.3.5 In the eighth month, on the day *gēngchén*,
*Hé*, Duke of *Sòng*, passed away.
A1.3.6 In winter, the twelfth month,
the Marquis of *Qí*
and the Earl of *Zhèng* made a covenant at *Shímén*.
A1.3.7 On the day *guǐwèi*,
*Mù Gōng* of *Sòng* was buried.
B1.3 The Commentary on *Yǐn Gōng*, Third Year
B1.3.1 In the spring of the third year,
in the King’s third month,
on the day *rénxū*,
King *Píng* passed away.
The death notice gave the day as *gēngxū*,
so it was recorded as such.
B1.3.2 In summer,
the Lady of the ruler's house died.
She was *Shēng Zǐ*.
Because no death notice was sent to the feudal lords,
no wailing was performed upon returning to the bedchamber,
and she was not enshrined with her mother-in-law,
she was not said
to have "passed away."
She was not called "Lady,"
so her burial was not mentioned,
and her surname was not recorded.
For the sake of the Duke,
she was called
"*Jūn Shì*."
B1.3.3 Duke *Wǔ* and Duke *Zhuāng* of *Zhèng*
served as high ministers to King *Píng*.
The King was double-minded in favor of *Guó*.
The Earl of *Zhèng* resented the King.
The King said,
"It is not so."
Therefore, *Zhōu* and *Zhèng* exchanged hostages.
Prince *Hú* became a hostage in *Zhèng*,
and *Gōngzǐ Hū* of *Zhèng* became a hostage in *Zhōu*.
When the King passed away,
the people of *Zhōu* were about to give the administration to the Duke of *Guó*.
In the fourth month,
*Zhài Zú* of *Zhèng* led an army and took the wheat of *Wēn*.
In autumn,
they also took the grain of *Chéngzhōu*.
Relations between *Zhōu* and *Zhèng* soured.
The gentleman says:
"If sincerity does not come from within,
hostages are of no use.
If one acts with enlightened reciprocity
and binds it with ritual,
even without hostages,
who could come between them?
If there is enlightened good faith,
the weeds of the mountain streams and brooks,
and the ponds and islets,
and the vegetables like duckweed, white mugwort,
and water-starwort..."
Square baskets and round baskets,
three-legged pots and cauldrons;
water from pools and puddles,
and road-ditches;
these may be presented to ghosts and spirits,
and offered to Wáng and Gōng.
How much more so when a Jūnzǐ cements the trust between two states,
conducting it with Lǐ,
what need then for a hostage?
The "Fēng" contains "Cǎi Fán"
and "Cǎi Píng";
the "Yǎ" contains "Xíng Wěi"
and "Jiòng Zhuó"—
these illuminate loyalty and trust."
B1.3.4 A son of the Wǔ clan came to request funeral contributions,
as the Wáng had not yet been buried.
B1.3.5 When Sòng Mù Gōng was ill,
he summoned the Dàsīmǎ Kǒngfù
and entrusted Shāng Gōng to him,
saying:
"The late ruler passed over Yǔyí and established me;
I dare not forget this.
If, by your grace,
I am able to preserve my head and neck until death;
if the late ruler asks about Yǔyí,
what words shall I use to respond?
I request that you support him
to preside over the Shèjì.
Even if I die,
I shall have no regrets."
He replied:
"The ministers wish to support Féng."
The Gōng said:
"That cannot be.
The late ruler considered me worthy
and made me preside over the Shèjì.
If I were to abandon virtue and not yield,
that would be to nullify the late ruler's choice;
how could I be called worthy?
To glorify the late ruler’s illustrious virtue,
can we not strive for this?
Sir, do not nullify the late ruler's achievement!"
He sent Gōngzǐ Féng to go out and reside in Zhèng.
In the eighth month, on the day Gēngchén,
Sòng Mù Gōng died,
and Shāng Gōng ascended the throne.
The Jūnzǐ says:
"Sòng Xuān Gōng can be called one who knows people.
He established Mù Gōng,
and his own son enjoyed the benefit of it;
he commanded based on righteousness!
The "Shāng Sòng" says:
'Yīn received the mandate, and all was fitting;
they bore a hundred blessings.'
This is what that means!"
B1.3.6 In winter,
Qí and Zhèng held a covenant at Shímén,
renewing the covenant of Lú.
On the day Gēngxū,
the chariot of Zhèng Bó overturned in the Jì River.
B1.3.7 Wèi Zhuāng Gōng married the sister of Qí Dōnggōng Déchén,
called Zhuāng Jiāng.
She was beautiful but had no children;
the people of Wèi composed "Shuò Rén" for her.
He also married from Chén,
a lady called Lì Guī,
who gave birth to Xiàobó,
who died early.
Her younger sister Dài Guī
gave birth to Huán Gōng;
Zhuāng Jiāng took him as her own son.
Gōngzǐ Zhōuyú
was the son of a favored concubine.
He was favored and loved military affairs;
the Gōng did not forbid him.
Zhuāng Jiāng detested him.
Shí Què remonstrated, saying:
"I have heard that if one loves a child,
one teaches him with righteousness
and does not let him enter into evil.
Arrogance, extravagance, debauchery, and excess
are the sources of evil.
These four things come
from excessive favor and emoluments.
If you intend to establish Zhōuyú,
then settle it now;
if not yet,
it will serve as a ladder to disaster.
For one to be favored but not arrogant,
arrogant but able to be humble,
humble but without resentment,
and resentful but able to restrain himself—
such cases are rare.
Moreover, the lowly obstructing the noble,
the young encroaching on the old,
the distant coming between the near,
the new coming between the old,
the small being placed above the great,
and debauchery undermining righteousness—
these are called the six rebellions.
The ruler being righteous,
the minister acting accordingly,
the father being kind,
the son being filial,
the elder brother being loving,
and the younger brother being respectful—
these are called the six accords.
To abandon the accords and follow the rebellions
is to hasten disaster.
One who rules people
should strive to remove disaster;
to hasten it
is surely not permissible?"
The Gōng did not listen.
His son Hòu socialized with Zhōuyú;
Shí Què forbade him,
but he would not stop.
When Huán Gōng ascended the throne,
Shí Què then retired.
A1.4 "Yǐn Gōng's Fourth Year Annals"
A1.4.1 In the fourth year, in spring,
the Wáng's second month,
the people of Jǔ attacked Qǐ
and took Móulóu.
A1.4.2 On the day Wùshēn,
Zhōuyú of Wèi assassinated his ruler, Wán.
A1.4.3 In summer,
the Gōng and Sòng Gōng met at Qīng.
A1.4.4 Sòng Gōng,
Chén Hóu,
the people of Cài,
and the people of Wèi attacked Zhèng.
A1.4.5 In autumn,
Huī led an army to meet Sòng Gōng,
Chén Hóu,
the people of Cài,
and the people of Wèi to attack Zhèng.
A1.4.6 In the ninth month,
the people of Wèi killed Zhōuyú at Pú.
A1.4.7 In winter, the twelfth month,
the people of Wèi established Jìn.
B1.4 "Yǐn Gōng's Fourth Year Commentary"
B1.4.1 In the fourth year, in spring,
Zhōuyú of Wèi assassinated Huán Gōng and established himself.
B1.4.2 The Gōng and Sòng Gōng held a meeting
to renew the covenant of Sù.
Before the appointed time,
the people of Wèi came to report the rebellion.
In summer,
the Gōng and Sòng Gōng met at Qīng.
B1.4.3 When Sòng Shāng Gōng ascended the throne,
Gōngzǐ Féng fled to Zhèng.
The people of Zhèng wished to restore him.
When Wèi Zhōuyú was established,
he wished to settle the old grievances of the late ruler against Zhèng,
and seek favor from the feudal lords
to harmonize his own people.
He sent word to Sòng, saying:
"If you, my lord, attack Zhèng
to remove your harm,
and you act as the leader,
my humble state will provide troops along with Chén
and Cài to follow you,
then this would be the wish of the state of Wèi."
The people of Sòng agreed to this.
At that time, Chén
and Cài were on friendly terms with Wèi;
therefore, Sòng Gōng,
Chén Hóu,
the people of Cài,
and the people of Wèi attacked Zhèng,
besieged its East Gate,
and returned after five days.
The Gōng asked Zhòng Zhòng:
"Will Wèi Zhōuyú succeed?"
He replied:
"I have heard of harmonizing the people through virtue,
but never of doing so through chaos."
By means of disorder,
it is like trying to untangle silk but only tangling it further.
As for Zhōu Xū,
he relies on military force and is cruel.
Relying on force, he lacks the support of the masses;
being cruel, he lacks close kin.
When the masses rebel
and his kin desert him,
it will be difficult for him to succeed.
Military force
is like fire;
if not restrained,
it will incinerate itself.
Zhōu Xū murdered his lord
and oppressed his people.
Furthermore, he does not strive for fine virtue
but wishes to succeed through disorder;
he will surely not escape."
B1.4.4 In autumn,
the feudal lords again attacked Zhèng.
The Duke of Sòng sent an envoy to request troops;
the Duke declined.
Yǔfù requested to join them with troops,
but the Duke did not permit it.
He requested persistently and then went.
Therefore the record says,
"Huī led the army,"
which was to criticize him.
The armies of the feudal lords defeated the foot soldiers of Zhèng,
took their grain, and returned.
B1.4.5 Zhōu Xū was unable to harmonize his people,
so Shí Hòu asked Shí Zǐ about how to stabilize the ruler's position.
Shí Zǐ said,
"An audience with the King would do it."
He asked,
"How can he obtain an audience?"
He said,
"Duke Huán of Chén is currently in favor with the King.
Chén and Wèi are currently on friendly terms;
if you pay court to Chén and have them request it,
it can surely be obtained."
Shí Hòu followed Zhōu Xū to Chén.
Shí Què sent word to Chén, saying,
"The state of Wèi is narrow and small,
and I, an old man, am aged and senile,
unable to do anything.
These two men
actually murdered my ruler;
I venture to ask that you deal with them."
The people of Chén seized them
and requested that Wèi come to handle it.
In the ninth month,
the people of Wèi sent the Right Minister Chǒu to supervise the execution of Zhōu Xū at Pú.
Shí Què sent his steward Nòuyáng Jiān to supervise the execution of Shí Hòu in Chén.
The Noble Man said,
"Shí Què
was a pure minister.
He hated Zhōu Xū, and Hòu was involved therein.
'Placing great righteousness above family ties,'
this must be what that refers to!"
B1.4.6 The people of Wèi welcomed Prince Jìn from Xíng.
In winter, the twelfth month, Duke Xuān ascended the throne.
The record says,
"The people of Wèi established Jìn,"
to show it was the will of the masses.
A1.5 The Classic of Year 5 of Duke Yǐn
A1.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
the Duke shot fish at Táng.
A1.5.2 In the summer, the fourth month,
Duke Huán of Wèi was buried.
A1.5.3 In autumn,
the army of Wèi entered Chéng.
A1.5.4 In the ninth month,
the temple of Zhòngzǐ was completed.
Six plumes were first offered.
The people of Zhū and
the people of Zhèng attacked Sòng.
A1.5.6 There was an infestation of crop-destroying insects.
A1.5.7 In winter, the twelfth month, on the day Xīnsì,
Prince Kōu died.
A1.5.8 The people of Sòng attacked Zhèng and besieged Chánggě.
B1.5 The Commentary on Year 5 of Duke Yǐn
B1.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
the Duke was about to go to Táng to observe those fishing.
Zāng Xībó remonstrated, saying,
"Whatever thing is insufficient for practicing the great affairs,
or whose materials are insufficient for providing ritual implements,
then the ruler does not take it up.
The ruler
is one who brings the people into the tracks of order and
standards.
Therefore, practicing affairs
to measure tracks and quantities is called 'the track';
taking materials to display standards and colors is called 'the standard'.
If it is neither according to the track nor the standard,
it is called disordered government.
If disordered government is practiced frequently,
that is how the state is ruined.
Therefore, the spring hunt,
the summer weeding hunt,
the autumn selection hunt,
and the winter hunt
all take place during the intervals of agricultural work to practice these affairs.
Every three years there is a military review,
and upon return, the troops are reorganized.
Returning, they drink at the arrival ceremony
to count the military spoils.
This illustrates patterns and insignia,
makes clear the noble and the base,
distinguishes ranks and orders,
arranges the young and the old,
and practices the rituals of authority.
As for birds and beasts, if their meat
is not presented on the sacrificial platters,
or if their skins, teeth, bones, horns, fur, and feathers are not presented for ritual implements,
then the Duke does not shoot them; this is the ancient regulation.
As for the produce of mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes,
and the resources for daily utensils,
these are the business of the menials and servants,
and the duties of the minor officials;
they are not what the ruler should concern himself with."
The Duke said,
"I am going to inspect the border territory there."
He then went,
spread out the fish and observed them;
Xībó claimed illness and did not follow.
The record says,
"The Duke shot fish at Táng,"
to show it was contrary to ritual,
and to say it was a distant place.
B1.5.2 Zhuāngbó of Qūwò, with the people of Zhèng and
the people of Xíng, attacked Yì;
the King sent the Yǐn clan and
the Wǔ clan to assist him.
The Marquis of Yì fled to Suí.
B1.5.3 In summer,
Duke Huán of Wèi was buried.
Because of the disorder in Wèi,
it was delayed.
B1.5.4 In the fourth month,
the people of Zhèng invaded the pasturage of Wèi,
to take revenge for the campaign at the East Gate.
The people of Wèi, with the army of Yàn, attacked Zhèng.
Jì Zú of Zhèng,
Yuán Fán,
and Xiè Jià
with three armies encamped in their front,
while sending Mànbó and Zǐyuán to secretly encamp their armies in their rear.
The people of Yàn feared the three armies of Zhèng
but did not prepare for the men of Zhì.
In the sixth month,
the two princes of Zhèng, with the men of Zhì, defeated the army of Yàn at Běizhì.
The Noble Man said,
"Without preparation against the unexpected,
one cannot lead an army."
B1.5.5 Qūwò rebelled against the King.
In autumn,
the King ordered the Duke of Guó to attack Qūwò,
and established Marquis Āi at Yì.
B1.5.6 During the disorder in Wèi,
the people of Chéng invaded Wèi,
therefore the army of Wèi entered Chéng.
B1.5.7 In the ninth month,
the temple of Zhòngzǐ was completed,
and the Wàn dance was about to be performed there.
The Duke asked Zhòng Zhòng about the number of plumes.
He replied,
"The Son of Heaven uses eight,
the feudal lords use six,
the grandees four,
and the officers two.
As for the dance,
it is how the eight sounds are modulated
and the eight winds are set in motion;
therefore it starts from eight downward."
The Duke followed this.
Thereupon, six plumes were first offered,
using six rows of dancers for the first time.
B1.5.8 The people of Sòng took the fields of Zhū.
The people of Zhū reported to Zhèng, saying,
"We request that the Ruler release his resentment against Sòng,
and our humble state will serve as the guide."
The people of Zhèng joined them with the King's army,
attacked Sòng,
entered its outer walls,
to take revenge for the campaign at the East Gate.
The people of Sòng sent an envoy to announce the situation.
The Gōng heard that they had entered the outer city walls;
he was about to rescue them,
and asked the envoy,
“How far has the army reached?”
He replied,
“It has not yet reached the capital.”
The Gōng was angry
and so he stopped.
He dismissed the envoy, saying,
“Your ruler commanded me to share the concern for the hardships of the state.
Now I asked the envoy,
and he said,
‘The army has not yet reached the capital.’
This is not something I dare to concern myself with.”
B1.5.9 In winter, in the twelfth month on the day Xīnsì,
Zāng Xībó died.
The Gōng said,
“My uncle had a grievance against me;
I dare not forget it.”
He buried him with honors one rank higher than his status.
B1.5.10 The people of Sòng attacked Zhèng
and besieged Zhǎnggé
in retaliation for the campaign of entering the outer walls.
A1.6 Classic of the Sixth Year of Yǐn Gōng
A1.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
the people of Zhèng came to renew the peace.
A1.6.2 In the summer, in the fifth month on the day Xīnyǒu,
the Gōng met with the Qí Hóu
and made a covenant at Ài.
A1.6.3 In the autumn, in the seventh month.
A1.6.4 In the winter,
the people of Sòng took Zhǎnggé.
B1.6 Commentary on the Sixth Year of Yǐn Gōng
B1.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
the people of Zhèng came to renew the peace;
it was to change the terms of the settlement.
B1.6.2 The Nine Clans and Five Officials of Yì,
and Jiāfù, the son of Qǐngfù,
welcomed the Jìn Hóu at Suí
and brought him into È;
the people of Jìn called him È Hóu.
B1.6.3 In the summer,
they made a covenant at Ài;
this was the beginning of peace with Qí.
B1.6.4 In the fifth month on the day Gēngshēn,
the Zhèng Bó invaded Chén
and achieved a great capture.
In the previous year,
the Zhèng Bó had requested peace from Chén,
but the Chén Hóu did not grant it.
Wǔfù remonstrated, saying,
“Cherishing the benevolent
and being friendly to neighbors
are the treasures of a state.
My lord, please grant Zhèng’s request!”
The Chén Hóu said,
“Sòng
and Wèi are the real troubles;
what can Zhèng do?”
Consequently, he did not grant it.
The Noble Man said,
“Good must not be lost,
and evil must not be allowed to grow;
does this not refer to Chén Huán Gōng?
Allowing evil to grow without repenting
only brings it upon oneself.
Even if one wishes to save it,
how will it be possible?
The Shāngshū says:
‘The spreading of evil
is like a fire blazing on the plains;
it cannot be approached,
how then can it be extinguished?’
Zhōu Rèn had a saying:
‘Those who govern states,
upon seeing evil,
must be like a farmer dedicated to removing weeds,
cutting them down, weeding them out, and piling them up,
severing their roots,
and not letting them multiply;
then the good will truly flourish.’”
B1.6.5 In the autumn,
the people of Sòng took Zhǎnggé.
B1.6.6 In the winter,
the capital came to report a famine;
the Gōng, on their behalf, requested to buy grain from Sòng,
Wèi, Qí,
and Zhèng;
this was in accordance with ritual.
B1.6.7 The Zhèng Bó went to Zhōu,
having his first audience with Huán Wáng.
The King did not treat him with courtesy.
Zhōu Huán Gōng said to the King,
“When our Zhōu moved to the east,
we relied on Jìn and Zhèng.
Treat Zhèng well to encourage those who come;
even then one fears they will not arrive;
how much more so if you are discourteous?
Zhèng will not come again.”
A1.7 Classic of the Seventh Year of Yǐn Gōng
A1.7.1 In the spring of the seventh year,
in the royal third month,
Shū Jī went to Jì to be married.
A1.7.2 The Téng Hóu died.
A1.7.3 In the summer,
they walled Zhōngqiū.
A1.7.4 The Qí Hóu sent his younger brother Nián on a mission of friendly inquiry.
A1.7.5 In the autumn,
the Gōng attacked Zhū.
A1.7.6 In the winter,
the Heavenly King sent Fán Bó on a mission of friendly inquiry.
The Róng attacked Fán Bó at Chǔqiū and took him back with them.
B1.7 Commentary on the Seventh Year of Yǐn Gōng
B1.7.1 In the spring of the seventh year,
the Téng Hóu died.
His personal name was not recorded
because he had not joined the covenant.
In all cases where feudal lords have joined a covenant,
they are referred to by name;
therefore, when they die,
the announcement of death is made with the name
to report the end and designate the successor,
so as to continue friendship and give rest to the people;
this is called a standard rule of ritual.
B1.7.2 In the summer,
they walled Zhōngqiū.
It was recorded because it was not at the proper time.
B1.7.3 The Qí Hóu sent Yí Zhòngnián on a mission of friendly inquiry
to solidify the covenant of Ài.
B1.7.4 In the autumn,
Sòng and Zhèng made peace.
In the seventh month on the day Gēngshēn,
they made a covenant at Sù.
The Gōng attacked Zhū
to punish them on behalf of Sòng.
B1.7.5 Initially,
the Róng had an audience at Zhōu
and distributed gifts to the dukes and ministers,
but Fán Bó did not treat them as guests.
In the winter,
the King sent Fán Bó on a mission of friendly inquiry.
On his way back,
the Róng attacked him at Chǔqiū and took him back with them.
B1.7.6 Chén and Zhèng made peace.
In the twelfth month,
Chén Wǔfù went to Zhèng to preside over the covenant.
On the day Rénshēn,
he made a covenant with the Zhèng Bó,
but his smearing of blood was done as if he were oblivious.
Xièbó said,
“Wǔfù will certainly not escape calamity;
he does not rely on the covenant.”
Zhèng Liáng Zuǒ went to Chén to preside over the covenant;
on the day Xīnsì,
he made a covenant with the Chén Hóu,
for he also knew that Chén was about to fall into disorder.
B1.7.7 Prince Hū of Zhèng was at the King's place,
and therefore the Chén Hóu requested to give him a wife;
the Zhèng Bó granted it,
and so the marriage was concluded.
A1.8 Classic of the Eighth Year of Yǐn Gōng
A1.8.1 In the spring of the eighth year,
the Sòng Gōng
and the Wèi Hóu met at Chuí.
In the third month,
the Zhèng Bó sent Wǎn to return Bàng.
On the day Gēngyín,
we entered Bàng.
A1.8.3 In the summer, in the sixth month on the day Jǐhài,
Cài Hóu Kǎofù died.
On the day Xīnhài,
the Sù Nán died.
In the autumn, in the seventh month on the day Gēngwǔ,
the Sòng Gōng,
the Qí Hóu,
and the Wèi Hóu made a covenant at Wǎwū.
A1.8.6 In the eighth month,
Lord Xuān of Cài was buried.
A1.8.7 In the ninth month on the xīnmǎo day,
the Duke and the people of Jǔ made a covenant at Fúlái.
A1.8.8 Armyworms.
A1.8.9 In winter, the twelfth month,
Wúhài died.
B1.8 The Commentary on the Eighth Year of Duke Yǐn
B1.8.1 In the spring of the eighth year,
the Lord of Qí was about to reconcile Sòng and Wèi.
A date was set for a meeting.
The Lord of Sòng used silks as gifts to request of Wèi
to meet beforehand.
The Lord of Wèi granted it,
and so they had an informal meeting at Quǎnqiū.
B1.8.2 The Earl of Zhèng requested to cease the sacrifices to Mount Tài
and instead sacrifice to the Duke of Zhōu,
exchanging the ritual lands of Bàng at Mount Tài for Xǔtián.
In the third month,
the Earl of Zhèng sent Wǎn to return Bàng,
and no longer sacrificed to Mount Tài.
B1.8.3 In the summer,
Jìfù, Lord of Guó, began to serve as a High Minister in Zhōu.
B1.8.4 In the fourth month on the jiǎchén day,
Prince Hū of Zhèng went to Chén to meet his bride Guī.
On the xīnhài day,
he returned with Lady Guī.
On the jiǎyín day,
they entered Zhèng.
Zhēnzǐ of Chén escorted the lady.
They consummated the marriage before presenting her to the ancestors.
Zhēnzǐ said:
"This is not making a husband and wife;
it is to deceive their ancestors.
This is a violation of ritual;
how can they produce offspring?"
B1.8.5 The people of Qí finally reconciled Sòng
and Wèi with Zhèng.
In autumn,
they met at Wēn
and made a covenant at Wǎwū
to set aside the grievances of the campaign at Dōngmén;
this was ritual.
B1.8.6 In the eighth month on the bǐngxū day,
the Earl of Zhèng led the people of Qí to have an audience with the King;
this was ritual.
B1.8.7 The Duke and the people of Jǔ made a covenant at Fúlái
to establish friendship with Jǐ.
B1.8.8 In winter,
the Lord of Qí sent an envoy
to report the peace between the three states.
The Duke had Zhòngzhòng reply, saying:
"That your Lordship has set aside the designs of the three states
in order to bring peace to their people
is your Lordship's benevolence.
My ruler has received the command
and how would he dare not receive your Lordship's brilliant virtue?"
B1.8.9 Wúhài died;
Yǔfù requested a posthumous title and a lineage name.
The Duke asked Zhòngzhòng about lineage names.
Zhòngzhòng replied:
"The Son of Heaven establishes virtue;
he bestows a surname based on birth,
grants them land
and names their lineage.
The feudal lords use the courtesy name as a posthumous title
and subsequently take it as their lineage name.
When an office has merit for generations,
then there is an official lineage.
This is also the case for cities."
The Duke ordered that the courtesy name be used as the Zhǎn lineage.
A1.9 The Annals of the Ninth Year of Duke Yǐn
A1.9.1 In the spring of the ninth year,
the Heavenly King sent Nánjì on a mission of inquiry.
A1.9.2 In the third month on the guǐyǒu day,
there was great rain
with thunder and lightning.
On the gēngchén day,
there was a great fall of rain and snow.
A1.9.3 Xié died.
A1.9.4 In the summer,
the walls of Láng were built.
A1.9.5 Autumn, the seventh month.
A1.9.6 In winter,
the Duke met the Lord of Qí at Fáng.
B1.9 The Commentary on the Ninth Year of Duke Yǐn
B1.9.1 In the ninth year, in the spring, the King's third month, on the guǐyǒu day,
there was a great soaking rain with thunder;
this was recorded as the beginning of the rain.
On the gēngchén day,
there was a great fall of rain and snow;
it was also recorded thus.
These were recorded
because they were unseasonable.
Generally, for rain,
from the third day onward it is called soaking;
a foot of snow on level ground is called a great snow.
B1.9.2 In the summer,
the walls of Láng were built.
This was recorded
because it was unseasonable.
B1.9.3 The Lord of Sòng did not acknowledge the King's authority.
The Earl of Zhèng, as the King's Left High Minister,
used the King's command to punish him.
He attacked Sòng.
Sòng was resentful toward the Duke because of the campaign that entered their outer walls,
so they did not announce the command.
The Duke was angry
and broke off relations with Sòng's envoys.
B1.9.4 In autumn,
the people of Zhèng used the King's command to report the attack on Sòng.
B1.9.5 In winter,
the Duke met the Lord of Qí at Fáng
to plan the attack on Sòng.
B1.9.6 The Northern Róng invaded Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng resisted them.
He was worried about the Róng army,
saying:
"They are on foot and we are in chariots;
I fear they will overrun us."
Prince Tū said:
"Order those who are brave but lack steadfastness
to engage the enemy and then quickly retreat.
Your Lordship should set three ambushes to wait for them.
The Róng are light and disorganized,
greedy and without kinship.
When they win, they do not yield to each other;
when they lose, they do not save each other.
Those in front, seeing captures,
will certainly strive to advance.
Advancing and meeting an ambush,
they will surely flee quickly.
Those behind will not save them,
so there will be no succession.
Thus we can have our way with them."
He followed this.
The Róng people in the front, meeting the ambush, fled.
Zhù Dān pursued them,
cutting through the middle of the Róng army
and attacking them from front and back,
killing them all.
The Róng army fled in a great rout.
In the eleventh month on the jiǎyín day,
the people of Zhèng greatly defeated the Róng army.
A1.10 The Annals of the Tenth Year of Duke Yǐn
A1.10.1 In the tenth year, in the spring, the King's second month,
the Duke met the Lord of Qí
and the Earl of Zhèng at Zhōngqiū.
A1.10.2 In the summer,
Huī led the army to meet the people of Qí
and the people of Zhèng to attack Sòng.
A1.10.3 In the sixth month on the rénxū day,
the Duke defeated the Sòng army at Jiān.
On the xīnwèi day,
he took Gào.
On the xīnsì day,
he took Fáng.
A1.10.4 In autumn,
the people of Sòng
and the people of Wèi entered Zhèng.
The people of Sòng,
the people of Cài,
and the people of Wèi attacked Dài.
The Earl of Zhèng attacked and took it.
A1.10.5 In winter, the tenth month, on the rénwǔ day,
the people of Qí
and the people of Zhèng entered Chéng.
B1.10 The Commentary on the Tenth Year of Duke Yǐn
B1.10.1 In the tenth year, in the spring, the King's first month,
the Duke met the Lord of Qí
and the Earl of Zhèng at Zhōngqiū.
On the guǐchǒu day,
they made a covenant at Dèng
to set the date for the army.
B1.10.2 In the summer, the fifth month,
Yǔfù first met the Lord of Qí and the Earl of Zhèng to attack Sòng.
B1.10.3 In the sixth month on the wùshēn day,
the Duke met the Lord of Qí and the Earl of Zhèng at Lǎotáo.
On the rénxū day,
the Duke defeated the Sòng army at Jiān.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
the army of Zhèng entered Gào.
On the day Xīnwèi,
it was returned to us.
On the day Gēngchén,
the army of Zhèng entered Fáng.
On the day Xīnsì,
it was returned to us.
The gentleman said of Gōng Zhuāng of Zhèng,
"In this, he may be called correct.
He punished the non-compliant by the King's command,
did not covet their land,
and credited the King's rank with the effort;
this is the substance of correctness."
B1.10.4 The people of Cài, Wèi, and Chéng
did not comply with the King's command.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Gēngyín,
the army of Zhèng entered Jiāo,
and remained there.
The people of Sòng and
Wèi entered Zhèng,
and the people of Cài followed them to attack Dài.
In the eighth month, on the day Rénxū,
the Bó of Zhèng surrounded Dài.
On the day Guǐhài,
he conquered it
and captured the three armies there.
Sòng and
Wèi had already entered Zhèng,
and then summoned the people of Cài to attack Dài;
the people of Cài were angry,
therefore they were not in harmony and were defeated.
B1.10.5 In the ninth month, on the day Wùyín,
the Bó of Zhèng entered Sòng.
B1.10.6 In winter,
the people of Qí and
Zhèng entered Chéng,
to punish them for disobeying the King's command.
A1.11 The Annals of Yǐn Gōng, Year Eleven
A1.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
the Hóu of Téng and
the Hóu of Xuē came for an audience.
A1.11.2 In summer,
the Gōng met with the Bó of Zhèng at Shílái.
A1.11.3 In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Rénwǔ,
the Gōng together with the Hóu of Qí and
the Bó of Zhèng entered Xǔ.
A1.11.4 In winter, the eleventh month, on the day Rénchén,
the Gōng passed away.
B1.11 The Commentary on Yǐn Gōng, Year Eleven
B1.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
the Hóu of Téng and
the Hóu of Xuē came for an audience
and disputed over precedence.
The Hóu of Xuē said,
"I was enfeoffed first."
The Hóu of Téng said,
"I
am the Bǔzhèng of Zhōu;
Xuē is of a common surname;
I cannot take a position behind him."
The Gōng sent Yǔfù to request of the Hóu of Xuē, saying,
"You, My Lord, and the Lord of Téng have deigned to visit me.
A Zhōu proverb has it:
'The mountains have trees,
and the carpenter measures them;
guests have rituals,
and the host chooses them.'
In the ancestral alliances of Zhōu,
those of different surnames follow behind.
If I were to pay court to Xuē,
I would not dare to rank myself with those of the Rèn surname.
If you, My Lord, would deign to grant me this favor,
then I would request it for the sake of the Lord of Téng."
The Hóu of Xuē agreed,
and thus precedence was given to the Hóu of Téng.
B1.11.2 In summer,
the Gōng met with the Bó of Zhèng at Lái
to plan the attack on Xǔ.
The Bó of Zhèng was about to attack Xǔ.
In the fifth month, on the day Jiǎchén,
weapons were distributed at the Dàgōng.
Gōngsūn È and Yǐng Kǎoshù disputed over a chariot;
Yǐng Kǎoshù tucked the chariot pole under his arm and ran,
and Zǐdū snatched a halberd to pursue him.
Reaching the great thoroughfare,
he could not catch him;
Zǐdū was angry.
B1.11.3 In autumn, the seventh month,
the Gōng met with the Hóu of Qí and
the Bó of Zhèng to attack Xǔ.
On the day Gēngchén,
they reached the walls of Xǔ.
Yǐng Kǎoshù took the Bó of Zhèng's Máohú flag
to be the first to mount the wall;
Zǐdū shot him from below,
and he fell.
Xiá Shūyíng also took the Máohú and mounted,
waving the flag and shouting,
"Our Lord has ascended!"
The army of Zhèng all ascended.
On the day Rénwǔ,
they finally entered Xǔ.
Xǔ Zhuāng Gōng fled to Wèi.
The Hóu of Qí offered Xǔ to the Gōng.
The Gōng said,
"You, My Lord, said Xǔ was not submissive,
so I followed you to punish it.
Since Xǔ has already submitted to its crime,
even if you have a command,
I do not dare to hear of it."
It was then given to the Zhèng people.
The Bó of Zhèng sent the Xǔ Grand Master Bǎilǐ to escort Xǔshū
to reside in the eastern border of Xǔ,
saying,
"Heaven has brought calamity upon the state of Xǔ,
and the ghosts and spirits were indeed not pleased with the Lord of Xǔ,
and so used my hand.
I cannot even keep my own few brothers in harmony,
how could I dare to take Xǔ as my own achievement?
I have a brother
whom I could not harmonize with,
and who was made to seek his food in the four quarters;
how much less could I long possess Xǔ?
You, Sir, should escort Xǔshū
to comfort and soothe these people.
I will send Huò to assist you.
If I am fortunate enough to die and be buried,
and if Heaven uses ritual to regret the calamity upon Xǔ,
would it not be better for the Lord of Xǔ to again support his altars?
If only my state of Zhèng has requests or petitions,
like the old marriage alliances,
he might be able to condescend and comply.
Do not let other clans come to dwell here and press close,
to dispute this land with my state of Zhèng.
My descendants will have no leisure even to save themselves from ruin,
how much less could they perform the pure sacrifices to Xǔ?
My making you, Sir, reside here
is not only for the sake of the state of Xǔ,
but also to temporarily secure my borders."
He then sent Gōngsūn Huò to reside in the western border of Xǔ,
saying,
"As for your vessels and goods,
do not store them in Xǔ.
When I die,
leave it quickly!
My former lord newly founded this city,
the Royal House has already become low,
and the descendants of Zhōu lose their order daily.
As for Xǔ,
it is the descendant of Dàyuè.
Since Heaven has already tired of the virtue of Zhōu,
how can I compete with Xǔ?"
The gentleman said of Gōng Zhuāng of Zhèng,
"In this, he possessed ritual.
Ritual
governs the state,
stabilizes the altars of land and grain,
orders the people,
and benefits descendants.
Xǔ
was lawless so he attacked it;
it submitted so he spared it.
He measured virtue in managing it
and measured strength in acting.
He acted according to the time,
and did not burden his successors.
This may be called knowing ritual."
B1.11.4 The Bó of Zhèng ordered the soldiers to bring out boars
and the units to bring out dogs
and chickens
to curse the one who shot Yǐng Kǎoshù.
The gentleman said of Gōng Zhuāng of Zhèng,
"He failed in government and punishment.
Government is to govern the people;
punishment is to correct evil.
Since there was no virtuous government,
and no majestic punishment,
it reached the point of evil.
If there is evil and one curses it,
what benefit will there be!"
B1.11.5 The King took the fields of Wù,
Liú, Wèi,
and Yú from Zhèng,
and gave the Zhèng people the fields of Sū Fènshēng:
Wēn, Yuán,
Chī, Fán,
Shíchéng,
Cuánmáo,
Xiàng, Méng,
Zhōu, Xíng,
Tuí, and Huái.
The superior man thereby knew
Huán Wáng’s loss of Zhèng.
To act with reciprocity
is the rule of virtue
and the constant principle of ritual.
If one cannot possess it oneself
yet uses it to give to others,
and others do not come to him,
is that not appropriate?
B1.11.6 Zhèng and
Xī had a disagreement in words.
Xī Hóu attacked Zhèng,
and the Earl of Zhèng fought him at the border.
The army of Xī was greatly defeated and returned.
The superior man thereby knew that Xī was about to perish:
“He does not estimate virtue,
does not measure strength,
does not treat relatives with affection,
does not verify words,
and does not examine where guilt lies.
Committing these five errors
and using them to attack others,
that he should lose his army,
is it not appropriate?”
B1.11.7 In winter, the tenth month,
the Earl of Zhèng used the army of Guó to attack Sòng.
On Rénxū,
they greatly defeated the Sòng army
in order to retaliate for their invasion of Zhèng.
Sòng did not report the event,
so it was not recorded.
Whenever the feudal lords have an event,
if they report it, it is recorded;
otherwise, it is not.
Whether the army’s departure is good or bad
is also like this.
Even in the case of a state being destroyed,
if the defeated do not report defeat
and the victors do not report conquest,
it is not recorded in the bamboo tablets.
B1.11.8 Yǔfù requested to kill Duke Yǐn,
intending to seek the position of Dàzǎi.
The Duke said:
“Because he was young,
I intended to hand it over to him.
I have had Tùqiú prepared,
and I shall retire there.”
Yǔfù was afraid,
so he instead slandered the Duke to Huán Gōng and requested to assassinate him.
When the Duke was a prince,
he fought with the people of Zhèng at Húruàng
and was captured there.
The people of Zhèng imprisoned him with the Yǐn clan.
He bribed the Yǐn clan
and prayed to their deity Zhōngwū.
He then returned with the Yǐn clan
and established their deity.
In the eleventh month,
the Duke sacrificed to Zhōngwū,
purified himself at Shèpǔ,
and stayed at the residence of the Wěi clan.
On Rénchén,
Yǔfù sent an assassin to murder the Duke at the Wěi residence,
established Huán Gōng,
and punished the Wěi clan,
among whom some died.
The burial is not recorded
because the mourning was not properly completed.
A2.1 The Classic of the First Year of Huán Gōng
A2.1.1 In the first year, spring,
the King’s first month,
the Duke ascended the throne.
A2.1.2 In the third month,
the Duke met the Earl of Zhèng at Chuí.
The Earl of Zhèng used a jade disc to borrow the Xǔ fields.
A2.1.3 In summer, the fourth month, on Dīngwèi,
the Duke and the Earl of Zhèng made a covenant at Yuè.
A2.1.4 In autumn,
there was a great flood.
A2.1.5 In winter, the tenth month.
B2.1 The Commentary of the First Year of Huán Gōng
B2.1.1 In the first year, spring,
the Duke ascended the throne
and cultivated good relations with Zhèng.
The people of Zhèng requested to resume sacrifices to Zhōu Gōng
and finally exchanged the Bàng fields.
The Duke granted it.
In the third month,
the Earl of Zhèng used a jade disc to borrow the Xǔ fields,
for the sake of Zhōu Gōng
and the matter of Bàng.
B2.1.2 In summer, the fourth month, on Dīngwèi,
the Duke and the Earl of Zhèng made a covenant at Yuè,
concluding the Bàng agreement.
The covenant said:
“If one violates the covenant,
may they not enjoy their state!”
B2.1.3 In autumn,
there was a great flood.
Whenever water emerges onto level plains, it is called a great flood.
B2.1.4 In winter,
the Earl of Zhèng paid respects for the covenant.
B2.1.5 Huá Fù Dū of Sòng saw the wife of Kǒng Fù on the road;
his eyes followed her as she came and went,
and he said:
“Beautiful and alluring!”
A2.2 The Classic of the Second Year of Huán Gōng
A2.2.1 In the second year, spring,
the King’s first month, on Wùshēn,
Dū of Sòng murdered his ruler Yǔyí and his high official Kǒng Fù.
A2.2.2 The Viscount of Téng came to court.
A2.2.3 In the third month,
the Duke met the Marquis of Qí,
the Marquis of Chén,
and the Earl of Zhèng at Jì,
to settle the disorder in Sòng.
A2.2.4 In summer, the fourth month,
the great tripod of Gào was taken from Sòng.
On Wùshēn,
it was placed in the Grand Ancestral Temple.
A2.2.5 In autumn, the seventh month,
the Marquis of Qǐ came to court.
A2.2.6 The Marquis of Cài
and the Earl of Zhèng met at Dèng.
A2.2.7 In the ninth month,
they entered Qǐ.
A2.2.8 The Duke and the Róng made a covenant at Táng.
A2.2.9 In winter,
the Duke arrived from Táng.
B2.2 The Commentary of the Second Year of Huán Gōng
B2.2.1 In the second year, spring,
Dū of Sòng attacked the Kǒng clan,
killed Kǒng Fù and took his wife.
Duke Shāng was angry,
Dū was afraid,
and thus he murdered Duke Shāng.
The superior man considers that Dū first had the heart of having no ruler
and afterwards moved toward evil;
therefore, it first records the murder of his ruler.
They met at Jì
to settle the disorder in Sòng
for the sake of bribes,
and to establish the Huá clan.
Since Duke Shāng of Sòng ascended the throne,
in ten years there were eleven battles,
and the people could not bear his commands.
Kǒng Fù Jiā was the Sīmǎ
and Dū was the Dàzǎi;
therefore, taking advantage of the people’s inability to bear the commands,
Dū first spread the word, saying:
“It is the Sīmǎ who causes this.”
Having killed Kǒng Fù and murdered Duke Shāng,
he summoned Duke Zhuāng from Zhèng
and established him,
in order to be close to Zhèng.
He bribed the Duke with the great tripod of Gào;
Qí, Chén,
and Zhèng all received bribes;
therefore, he subsequently became the prime minister for the Duke of Sòng.
B2.2.2 In summer, the fourth month,
the great tripod of Gào was taken from Sòng.
On Wùshēn,
it was placed in the Grand Ancestral Temple,
which was contrary to ritual.
Zāng Āi Bó remonstrated, saying:
“One who is a ruler of men
should make virtue manifest and block transgressions
so as to look down upon and enlighten the hundred officials.
Even then he fears he may lose it.
Therefore he makes manifest bright virtue
to show to his descendants.
Thus the Pure Temple has a thatched roof,
the Great Carriage has grass mats,
the great sacrificial soup is not seasoned,
and the grain offerings are not finely milled—
to make manifest his frugality.
The robes, the crown, the knee-covers, the jade tablets,
the sash, the skirt, the leggings, the shoes,
the crown-weights, the ear-plugs, the chin-straps, and the crown-covers
make manifest his regulation of degrees.”
The waterweed patterns, the colored cords, the scabbard ornaments,
the scabbard covers, the girdles, the sash ends, the streamers, and the bridle tassels
make clear the degrees of rank.
The fire, the dragons,
the fǔ-ax patterns, and the fú-bow patterns
make clear the decorative patterns.
The five colors arranged in images
make clear the material objects.
The bridle bells, the yoke bells, the carriage bells, and the handheld bells
make clear the sounds.
The sun, moon, and stars upon the banners
make clear the brightness.
Now, virtue
is frugal and yet has regulation,
with fixed numbers for ascending and descending.
Decorative patterns and material objects are used to record it,
sounds and brightness are used to manifest it,
in order to appear before and illuminate the hundred officials.
The hundred officials are thereby cautioned and made fearful,
and do not dare to violate the regulations and laws.
Now you have extinguished virtue
and established defiance,
and placed a bribe-vessel in the Grand Temple
to display it clearly to the hundred officials.
If the hundred officials take it as a model,
whom can you then punish?
The ruin of a state
comes from the corruption of the officials.
The loss of virtue by officials
is because favor and bribes are made manifest.
With the Gào Dǐng in the temple,
what could manifest this more?
When Wǔ Wáng overcame Shāng,
he moved the nine dǐng to Luòyì,
and yet righteous men still criticized him;
how much more so when you are about to display a bribe-vessel of defiance and disorder in the Grand Temple—
what will you do about it?"
The Gōng did not listen.
The Royal Scribe of Zhōu heard of it
and said,
"Will Zāng Sūn Dá have descendants in Lǔ!
Even when the ruler defies what is right,
he does not forget to admonish him with virtue."
B2.2.3 In autumn, the seventh month,
the Hóu of Qǐ came to court
and was disrespectful.
When the Hóu of Qǐ returned,
[the Gōng] then planned to attack him.
B2.2.4 The Hóu of Cài and
the Bó of Zhèng met at Dèng,
beginning to fear Chǔ.
B2.2.5 In the ninth month,
[the Gōng] entered Qǐ,
to punish the disrespect.
B2.2.6 The Gōng and the Róng made a covenant at Táng,
to cultivate old friendship.
B2.2.7 In winter,
the Gōng arrived from Táng,
and made a report in the temple.
Whenever the Gōng goes out,
he reports in the ancestral temple;
when he returns from a journey,
he drinks the toast of arrival, offers the cup, and records the merit there;
this is ritual.
When he meets with only one other party,
the departure and return mention the place;
this is an act of yielding.
When there are three or more parties,
then the departure mentions the place,
and the return mentions the meeting;
this is a completed matter.
B2.2.8 Formerly,
the wife of Mù Hóu of Jìn, Jiāng Shì,
gave birth to the Crown Prince during the campaign of Tiáo;
he named him Chóu.
His younger brother was born during the battle of Qiānmǔ;
he named him Chéng Shī.
Shī Fú said,
"How strange
the ruler names his sons!
Names are used to establish righteousness,
righteousness is used to produce ritual,
ritual is used to embody government,
and government is used to rectify the people;
thus government is successful and the people listen.
If they are changed, then disorder arises.
A good match is called a spouse,
a resentful match is called an enemy (chóu);
such were the namings of old.
Now the ruler names the Crown Prince 'Enemy'
and the younger brother 'Successful Army' (Chéng Shī);
this is the first omen of disorder.
Will the elder brother be replaced!"
In the twenty-fourth year of Huì [of Zhōu],
Jìn first experienced disorder,
therefore Huán Shū was enfeoffed at Qū Wò.
Luán Bīn, the grandson of Jìng Hóu, served as his tutor.
Shī Fú said,
"I have heard that when a state is established,
the root should be large and the branches small;
thus it can be firm.
Therefore the Tiān Zǐ establishes states,
the Zhū Hóu establish houses,
the Qīng set up side chambers,
the Dà Fū have secondary lineages,
the Shì have subordinate younger brothers,
and commoners, artisans, and merchants
each have their related kin,
all having their grades and ranks.
Thus the people serve their superiors,
and those below have no ambitious designs.
Now Jìn
is a marcher marquisate,
yet it is establishing a state within itself.
Since the root is already weak,
how can it last long?"
In the thirtieth year of Huì,
Pān Fù of Jìn assassinated Zhāo Hóu
and tried to set up Huán Shū,
but did not succeed.
The people of Jìn set up Xiào Hóu.
In the forty-fifth year of Huì,
Zhuāng Bó of Qū Wò attacked Yì
and assassinated Xiào Hóu.
The people of Yì set up his younger brother, È Hóu.
È Hóu fathered Āi Hóu.
Āi Hóu encroached upon the fields of Xíngtíng.
The southern border of Xíngtíng guided Qū Wò to attack Yì.
A2.3 The Annals of the Third Year of Huán Gōng.
A2.3.1 In the third year, spring, the first month,
the Gōng met with the Hóu of Qí at Yíng.
A2.3.2 In summer,
the Hóu of Qí and
the Hóu of Wèi exchanged commands at Pú.
A2.3.3 In the sixth month,
the Gōng met with the Hóu of Qǐ at Chéng.
A2.3.4 In autumn, the seventh month, on the day rénchén, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun;
it was total.
A2.3.5 Gōngzǐ Huī went to Qí to meet the bride.
A2.3.6 In the ninth month,
the Hóu of Qí escorted Jiāng Shì to Huān.
A2.3.7 The Gōng met with the Hóu of Qí at Huān.
A2.3.8 The Lady Jiāng Shì arrived from Qí.
A2.3.9 In winter,
the Hóu of Qí sent his younger brother Nián to pay a friendly visit.
A2.3.10 There was a good harvest.
B2.3 The Commentary for the Third Year of Huán Gōng.
B2.3.1 In the spring of the third year,
Wǔ Gōng of Qū Wò attacked Yì
and halted at Xíngtíng.
Hán Wàn drove the chariot,
and Liáng Hóng was the spearman on the right.
They pursued the Hóu of Yì to the marsh of Fén.
His outside trace-horse became entangled and he stopped;
at night they captured him,
along with Luán Gòng Shū.
B2.3.2 The meeting at Yíng
was to conclude the marriage with Qí.
B2.3.3 In summer,
the Hóu of Qí and
the Hóu of Wèi exchanged commands at Pú,
they did not make a covenant.
B2.3.4 The Gōng met with the Hóu of Qǐ at Chéng,
as Qǐ sought a settlement.
B2.3.5 In autumn,
Gōngzǐ Huī went to Qí to meet the bride.
He was cultivating the friendship of the late ruler;
therefore it says
"Gōngzǐ."
B2.3.6 The Hóu of Qí escorting Jiāng Shì to Huān
was contrary to ritual.
Whenever a daughter of a Gōng
is married to a state of equal rank,
if she is a sister,
then a high-ranking minister (Shàng Qīng) escorts her
out of respect for the late ruler;
if she is a daughter (Gōngzǐ),
then a lower-ranking minister (Xià Qīng) escorts her.
For a great state,
even if she is a daughter (Gōngzǐ),
a high-ranking minister also escorts her.
For the Tiān Zǐ,
then all the ministers go,
but the Gōng does not escort her himself.
For a small state,
then a high-ranking Grand Master (Shàng Dà Fū) escorts her.
B2.3.7 In winter,
Qí Zhòngnián came on a mission of state
to escort the lady.
B2.3.8 Ruì Jiāng, the mother of Ruì Bó Wàn, detested Ruì Bó’s many favorites;
therefore, she expelled him,
and he went to live in Wèi.
A2.4 Annals of the Fourth Year of Duke Huán
A2.4.1 In the fourth year, in spring, in the first month,
the Duke hunted in Láng.
A2.4.2 In summer,
the Heavenly King sent the Steward Qū Bójiǔ on a mission of state.
B2.4 Commentary on the Fourth Year of Duke Huán
B2.4.1 In the fourth year, in spring, in the first month,
the Duke hunted in Láng.
It was recorded
because it was at the proper time,
which is according to ritual.
B2.4.2 In summer,
Zǎi Qū Bójiǔ of Zhōu came on a mission of state.
Since his father was still alive,
he was recorded by his personal name.
B2.4.3 In autumn,
the army of Qín invaded Ruì
but was defeated there,
because they had made light of the enemy.
B2.4.4 In winter,
the King’s army and
the Qín army besieged Wèi
and seized Ruì Bó to return with him.
A2.5 Annals of the Fifth Year of Duke Huán
A2.5.1 In the fifth year, in spring, in the first month,
on the day jiǎxū
and the day jǐchǒu,
Marquis Bào of Chén died.
A2.5.2 In summer,
the Marquis of Qí and
the Earl of Zhèng went to Jǐ.
A2.5.3 The Heavenly King sent the son of Réng Shū on a mission of state.
A2.5.4 Duke Huán of Chén was buried.
A2.5.5 Zhùqiū was walled.
A2.5.6 In autumn,
the people of Cài,
the people of Wèi,
and the people of Chén followed the King to attack Zhèng.
A2.5.7 The Great Rain Sacrifice was performed.
A2.5.8 There were migratory locusts.
A2.5.9 In winter,
the Duke of Zhōu went to Cáo.
B2.5 Commentary on the Fifth Year of Duke Huán
B2.5.1 In the fifth year, in spring, in the first month,
on the day jiǎxū
and the day jǐchǒu,
Marquis Bào of Chén died.
This was because there were two announcements of the death.
At that time, Chén was in disorder;
Tuó, the son of Duke Wén, had killed Crown Prince Miǎn
and taken his place.
Because the Marquis was critically ill and disorder broke out,
the people of the state were scattered and divided,
hence the two announcements.
B2.5.2 In summer,
the Marquis of Qí and
the Earl of Zhèng went to court in Jǐ,
wishing to take it by surprise.
The people of Jǐ became aware of this.
B2.5.3 The King stripped the Earl of Zhèng of his administrative duties,
and the Earl of Zhèng stopped attending court.
In autumn,
the King led the feudal lords to attack Zhèng,
and the Earl of Zhèng resisted him.
The King commanded the central army;
Duke Línfù of Guó commanded the right army,
with the people of Cài
and Wèi attached to it;
Duke Hēijiān of Zhōu commanded the left army,
with the people of Chén attached to it.
Zǐyuán of Zhèng requested to form a left wing
to oppose the people of Cài
and Wèi,
and a right wing
to oppose the people of Chén,
saying:
"Chén is in disorder,
and its people have no heart for fighting.
If we attack them first,
they will surely flee.
When the King’s troops see this,
they will surely be thrown into confusion.
Cài and Wèi will not hold firm
and are bound to flee first.
Afterward, we can concentrate our forces on the King’s troops,
and we can achieve our objective."
This advice was followed.
Mànbó formed the right wing
and Zhài Zhòngzú formed the left wing;
Yuán Fán
and Gāo Qūmí accompanied the Duke with the central army,
adopting the "Fish-Scale" formation.
The chariots were in front and the five-man squads behind,
with the squads following to fill the gaps.
They fought at Xúgé.
The order was given to the two wings:
"When the signal flag moves, beat the drums!"
The people of Cài, Wèi,
and Chén all fled,
the King’s troops fell into disorder,
and the Zhèng army converged to attack them.
The King’s troops were soundly defeated.
Zhù Dān shot the King and hit his shoulder;
the King was unable to keep his army in order.
Zhù Dān requested to pursue him,
but the Duke said:
"A gentleman does not wish to assert himself overmuch over others,
how much less would he dare to insult the Son of Heaven?
If we can only save ourselves
and ensure our altars are not lost,
that is enough."
That night,
the Earl of Zhèng sent Zhài Zú to comfort the King
and inquire after his attendants.
B2.5.4 As for the son of Réng Shū,
he was mentioned because of his youth.
B2.5.5 In autumn,
the Great Rain Sacrifice was performed.
It was recorded
because it was at the wrong time.
In all cases of sacrifice,
the suburb sacrifice is performed when the insects first stir,
the rain sacrifice when the Dragon constellation appears,
the tasting sacrifice when the first frost begins,
and the winter sacrifice when insects hibernate.
If these times are exceeded, it is recorded.
B2.5.6 In winter,
the Duke of Chúnyú went to Cáo.
Estimating that his state was in danger,
he ultimately did not return.
A2.6 Annals of the Sixth Year of Duke Huán
A2.6.1 In the sixth year, in spring, in the first month,
Shí arrived.
A2.6.2 In summer, in the fourth month,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Jǐ at Chéng.
A2.6.3 In autumn, in the eighth month, on the day rénwǔ,
there was a grand review of the troops.
A2.6.4 The people of Cài killed Chén Tuó.
A2.6.5 In the ninth month, on the day dīngmǎo,
the son Tóng was born.
A2.6.6 In winter,
the Marquis of Jǐ came to court.
B2.6 Commentary on the Sixth Year of Duke Huán
B2.6.1 In the sixth year, in spring,
he came from Cáo to court.
The record says
"Shí arrived,"
because he did not return to his own state.
B2.6.2 King Wǔ of Chǔ invaded Suí
and sent Wěi Zhāng to seek peace,
stationing the army at Xiá to wait for him.
The people of Suí sent the Shǎoshī to negotiate the peace.
Dòu Bóbǐ said to the Viscount of Chǔ:
"That we have not achieved our ambitions east of the Hàn River
is due to our own actions.
We display our three armies
and don our armor and weapons
to approach them with martial force;
they then become afraid and coordinate to plan against us,
so it is difficult to find an opening.
Among the states east of the Hàn,
Suí is the largest.
If Suí becomes arrogant,
it will surely abandon the small states.
If the small states are alienated,
it will be to the advantage of Chǔ.
The Shǎoshī is conceited;
please weaken our army's appearance to make him more arrogant."
Xióng Shuàiqiěbǐ said:
"Jì Liáng is there;
what good will it do?"
Dòu Bóbǐ said:
“In order to make plans for the future,
let Shǎoshī gain the favor of his lord.”
The King disordered his army
and received Shǎoshī.
When Shǎoshī returned,
he requested to pursue the Chǔ army.
The Marquis of Suí was about to grant it.
Jì Liáng stopped him,
saying:
“Heaven is just now bestowing favor upon Chǔ.
Chǔ’s appearance of weakness
is but a lure for us.
Why are you in such a hurry, my lord?
I have heard that for a small state to be able to resist a large one,
the small must follow the Way
while the large is licentious.
What is called ‘the Way’
is being loyal to the people
and being trustworthy toward the spirits.
When those above think of benefiting the people,
that is loyalty;
when the invocators and scribes use truthful words,
that is trustworthiness.
Now the people are starving
while the lord indulges his desires,
and the invocators and scribes make false claims in their sacrifices;
I do not know how this can be acceptable.”
The Duke said:
“My sacrificial animals are whole and fat,
the millet offerings are abundant and complete;
why then should there be a lack of trustworthiness?”
He replied:
“The people
are the masters of the spirits.
Therefore, the Sage Kings first brought the people to fulfillment
and only afterward applied their efforts to the spirits.
Thus, when presenting sacrificial animals, they announced,
‘They are large, magnificent, and fat,’
meaning that the people’s strength is pervasive,
meaning that their livestock are large and prolific,
meaning that they are free from disease and scabs,
and meaning that all varieties are fully fattened and available.
When presenting grain, they announced,
‘The millet is pure and abundant,’
meaning that the three seasons were not harmed
and that the people are in harmony and the harvest is rich.
When presenting wine and spirits, they announced,
‘Excellent, pure, and delicious wine,’
meaning that those above and below all possess excellent virtue
and have no contrary hearts.
What is called fragrance
is the absence of slander and evil.
Therefore, they attended to the three seasons,
cultivated the five teachings,
showed affection to the nine grades of kin,
and then performed the pure sacrifices.
In this way, the people were in harmony
and the spirits descended blessings upon them;
thus, every action met with success.
Now the people each have their own hearts,
and the ghosts and spirits lack a master;
although you alone have abundance,
what blessings can there be?
You should for now cultivate your government
and befriend the brotherly states;
then perhaps you will escape disaster.”
The Marquis of Suí was afraid and cultivated his government,
and Chǔ did not dare to attack.
B2.6.3 In summer,
there was a meeting at Chéng;
Jǐ came to consult and plan concerning the difficulties with Qí.
B2.6.4 The Běiróng attacked Qí.
The Marquis of Qí sent an envoy to request an army from Zhèng.
Zhèng Crown Prince Hū led an army to rescue Qí.
In the sixth month,
he greatly defeated the Róng army,
capturing their two commanders, Dàliáng
and Shǎoliáng,
and three hundred armored heads,
which he presented to Qí.
Thereupon, the grandees of the feudal lords guarded Qí.
The people of Qí provided them with provisions
and had Lǔ determine their order of precedence.
Zhèng was placed last.
Zhèng Hū, because of his merit,
was angry;
therefore, the battle of Láng occurred.
Before the Duke had married into Qí,
the Marquis of Qí wished to marry Wén Jiāng to the Zhèng Crown Prince Hū.
Crown Prince Hū declined.
People asked him the reason.
The Crown Prince said:
“Every person has their own match.
Qí is great;
it is not my match.
The *Shī* says,
‘Seek many blessings for oneself.’
It depends on me alone;
what does a great state have to do with it?”
The noble man said:
“He was good at planning for himself.”
When he defeated the Róng army,
the Marquis of Qí again requested to marry her to him.
He firmly declined.
People asked him the reason.
The Crown Prince said:
“When there was no trouble in Qí,
I still did not dare.
Now, having rushed to Qí’s emergency by my lord’s command,
if I were to take a wife and return,
it would be using the army to get a marriage.
What would the people say of me?”
He then declined the offer to the Earl of Zhèng.
B2.6.5 In autumn,
there was a great military review
to inspect the chariots and horses.
B2.6.6 In the ninth month, on the day Dìngmǎo,
Zǐ Tóng was born.
He was raised according to the rites for the birth of a crown prince:
he was welcomed with the dàláo,
a divined officer carried him on his back,
an officer's wife suckled him,
and the Duke, together with Wén Jiāng
and the women of the clan, named him.
The Duke asked Shēn Xú about naming.
He replied:
“Names are of five kinds:
there is truth,
there is righteousness,
there is resemblance,
there is borrowing,
and there is category.
Naming by something at birth is truth;
naming by a virtuous command is righteousness;
naming by likeness
is resemblance;
taking from an object is borrowing;
taking from the father
is category.
One does not name by a state,
one does not name by an office,
one does not name by mountains or rivers,
one does not name by hidden ailments,
one does not name by livestock,
one does not name by vessels or silks.
The people of Zhōu use taboos to serve the spirits;
the name
will eventually be tabooed.
Thus, naming by a state would abolish its name;
naming by an office would abolish the post;
naming by mountains or rivers would abolish its master;
naming by livestock would abolish sacrifices;
naming by vessels or silks would abolish the rites.
Jìn, because of Xī Hóu,
abolished the office of Sītú;
Sòng, because of Wǔ Gōng,
abolished the office of Sīkōng;
the late lords Xiàn
and Wǔ
abolished the names of two mountains;
thus, great things
cannot be used for naming.”
The Duke said:
“This child, at his birth,
had the same physical mark as I.
Let us name him Tóng.”
B2.6.7 In winter,
the Marquis of Jǐ came to court
to request a royal command to seek peace with Qí.
The Duke announced he was unable.
A2.7 *The Annals of Huán Gōng, Year 7*
A2.7.1 In the seventh year, in spring, in the second month on the day Jǐhài,
there was a fire at Xiánqiū.
A2.7.2 In summer,
the Earl of Gǔ, Suí, came to court.
The Marquis of Dèng, Wúlǐ, came to court.
B2.7 *The Commentary of Huán Gōng, Year 7*
B2.7.1 In the spring of the seventh year,
the Earl of Gǔ
and the Marquis of Dèng came to court.
Recording their personal names
was to show slight toward them.
B2.7.2 In summer,
Méng and Xiàng sought peace with Zhèng,
but later went back on it.
B2.7.3 In autumn,
the people of Zhèng, Qí, and Wèi
attacked Méng and Xiàng.
The King moved the people of Méng and Xiàng to Jiǎ.
B2.7.4 In winter,
the Earl of Qǔwò enticed the young Marquis of Jìn,
and killed him.
A2.8 *The Annals of Huán Gōng, Year 8*
A2.8.1 In the eighth year, in spring, in the first month, on the day jǐmǎo,
the zhēng sacrifice was performed.
A2.8.2 The King of Heaven sent Jiāfù to come on a mission of friendly inquiry.
A2.8.3 In summer, in the fifth month, on the day dīngchǒu,
the zhēng sacrifice was performed.
A2.8.4 In autumn,
we attacked Zhū.
A2.8.5 In winter, in the tenth month,
it rained and snowed.
A2.8.6 Zhìgōng came,
and then went to Jǐ to meet the royal queen.
B2.8 《Duke Huán, Eighth Year, Zuǒ Zhuàn Commentary》
B2.8.1 In the spring of the eighth year,
Yì was destroyed.
B2.8.2 In Suí, Shǎoshī was in favor.
Dòubópǐ of Chǔ said:
"It is possible now.
Our enemy has a rift,
which must not be missed."
In summer,
the Viscount of Chǔ assembled the feudal lords at Shěnlù.
The lords of Huáng and Suí did not attend.
He sent Wěizhāng to reprimand Huáng.
The Viscount of Chǔ attacked Suí.
He encamped between the Hàn
and the Huái.
Jìliáng requested to submit to him, saying:
"If he does not grant it and we then fight,
that is how to rouse our men and make the enemy lax."
Shǎoshī said to the Marquis of Suí:
"We must fight quickly.
Otherwise,
we will lose the Chǔ army."
The Marquis of Suí resisted them.
He looked out at the Chǔ army.
Jìliáng said:
"The Chǔ people value the left;
my lord must face their left,
and do not encounter the King.
Moreover, attack their right.
There are no good troops on the right,
so they will surely be defeated.
Once the flank is defeated,
the multitude will then fall apart."
Shǎoshī said:
"If we do not face the King,
he is not a worthy opponent."
The Marquis did not follow the advice.
They fought at Sùqǐ.
The Suí army was utterly defeated.
The Marquis of Suí escaped.
Dòudān captured his war chariot
along with his chariot-right, Shǎoshī.
In autumn,
Suí made peace with Chǔ;
the Viscount of Chǔ was about to refuse.
Dòubópǐ said:
"Heaven has removed their sickness;
Suí cannot yet be conquered."
Then they made a covenant and returned.
B2.8.3 In winter,
the King ordered Guózhòng to establish Mín, the younger brother of Marquis Āi of Jìn, in Jìn.
B2.8.4 Zhìgōng came,
and then went to meet the royal queen in Jǐ,
which was in accordance with ritual.
A2.9 《Duke Huán, Ninth Year, Classic of the Spring and Autumn Annals》
A2.9.1 In the ninth year, in spring,
Jìjiāng of Jǐ went to the capital to be married.
A2.9.2 In summer, the fourth month.
A2.9.3 In autumn, the seventh month.
A2.9.4 In winter,
the Earl of Cáo sent his heir apparent Shègū to come for an audience.
B2.9 《Duke Huán, Ninth Year, Zuǒ Zhuàn Commentary》
B2.9.1 In the spring of the ninth year,
Jìjiāng of Jǐ went to the capital.
Whenever the daughter of a feudal lord goes to be married,
only for a royal queen is it recorded.
B2.9.2 The Viscount of Bā sent Hánfú to report to Chǔ,
requesting to establish good relations with Dèng.
The Viscount of Chǔ sent Dàoshuò to lead the Bā guests
on a mission to Dèng;
the people of Yōu on the southern border of Dèng attacked
and seized their silks
and killed Dàoshuò and the Bā envoy.
The Viscount of Chǔ sent Wěizhāng to reprimand Dèng.
The Dèng people did not accept it.
In summer,
Chǔ sent Dòulián to lead an army along with the Bā army to besiege Yōu.
Dèngyǎngshēng
and Dānshēng led an army to rescue Yōu.
Thrice they drove back the Bā army,
but did not overcome it.
Dòulián drew up his army in a transverse formation within the Bā army
to fight
and then retreated.
The Dèng people pursued them,
turning their backs to the Bā army;
then they were attacked from both sides.
The Dèng army was greatly defeated.
The people of Yōu collapsed at night.
B2.9.3 In autumn,
Guózhòng, Ruìbó, Liángbó, the Marquis of Xún, and Jiǎbó attacked Qūwò.
B2.9.4 In winter,
the heir apparent of Cáo came for an audience.
He was treated as an upper minister,
which was in accordance with ritual.
A feast was held for the heir apparent of Cáo.
During the first offering,
the music was played and he sighed.
Shīfù said:
"Does the heir apparent of Cáo have some sorrow?
This is not the place for sighing."
A2.10 《Duke Huán, Tenth Year, Classic of the Spring and Autumn Annals》
A2.10.1 In the tenth year, in spring,
the King's first month, on the day gēngshēn,
Zhōngshēng, the Earl of Cáo, died.
A2.10.2 In summer, the fifth month,
they buried Duke Huán of Cáo.
A2.10.3 In autumn,
the Duke met the Marquis of Wèi at Táochiū,
but they did not meet.
A2.10.4 In winter, the twelfth month, on the day bǐngwǔ,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Marquis of Wèi,
and the Earl of Zhèng came to fight at Láng.
B2.10 《Duke Huán, Tenth Year, Zuǒ Zhuàn Commentary》
B2.10.1 In the spring of the tenth year,
Duke Huán of Cáo died.
B2.10.2 Guózhòng slandered his Grand Master Zhānfù to the King.
Zhānfù had a defense
and with the King's army attacked Guó.
In summer,
the Lord of Guó fled to Yú.
B2.10.3 In autumn,
the people of Qín restored Ruìbó Wàn to Ruì.
B2.10.4 Previously,
Yúshū had a piece of jade
which the Lord of Yú requested.
He did not present it.
Later he regretted it,
saying:
"A Zhōu proverb says:
'A common man is without guilt,
but possessing a jade disc is his crime.'
Why should I use this
to invite harm?"
Thereupon he presented it.
The Lord requested his precious sword again.
Shū said:
"This is insatiable.
Being insatiable,
he will eventually reach me."
Thereupon he attacked the Lord of Yú.
Therefore the Lord of Yú fled to Gòngchí.
B2.10.5 In winter,
Qí, Wèi,
and Zhèng came to fight at Láng,
because we were in the right.
Previously,
the Northern Róng distressed Qí;
the feudal lords rescued it,
and Prince Hū of Zhèng performed meritorious deeds there.
The people of Qí provided provisions to the feudal lords
and had Lǔ determine the order of precedence.
Lǔ placed Zhèng after others according to the Zhōu court rank.
The people of Zhèng were angry
and requested troops from Qí.
The people of Qí used the Wèi army to assist them;
therefore it is not called an invasion or an attack.
Qí and Wèi are written first
because of their royal ranks.
A2.11 《Duke Huán, Eleventh Year, Classic of the Spring and Autumn Annals》
A2.11.1 In the eleventh year, in spring, the first month,
the people of Qí,
the people of Wèi,
and the people of Zhèng made a covenant at Ècáo.
A2.11.2 In summer, the fifth month, on the day guǐwèi,
Wùshēng, the Earl of Zhèng, died.
A2.11.3 In the autumn, the seventh month,
Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng was buried.
A2.11.4 In the ninth month,
the people of Sòng seized Jì Zhòng of Zhèng.
Tū returned to Zhèng.
Hū of Zhèng fled to Wèi.
A2.11.5 Róu met with the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
and Shū of Cài to form a covenant at Zhé.
A2.11.6 The Duke met with the Duke of Sòng at Fūzhōng.
A2.11.7 In the winter, the twelfth month,
the Duke met with the Duke of Sòng at Kàn.
B2.11 *The Commentary on the Eleventh Year of Duke Huán*
B2.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
Qí, Wèi,
Zhèng, and Sòng formed a covenant at Ècáo.
B2.11.2 Qū Xiá of Chǔ was about to form a covenant with Èr and Zhěn.
The people of Yún encamped at Púsāo,
intending to attack the Chǔ army along with Suí, Jiǎo, Zhōu, and Liào.
The Mò'áo was worried about this.
Dòu Lián said:
“The people of Yún have encamped in their suburbs;
they will surely not be on guard.
Moreover, they expect the arrival of the four cities daily.
You, My Lord, should halt in the suburbs of Yǐng
to resist the four cities,
and I will use elite troops to launch a night attack on Yún.
The people of Yún are apprehensive
but rely on their walls;
none will have the will to fight.
If we defeat the Yún army,
the four cities will surely disperse.”
The Mò'áo said:
“Why not request reinforcement troops from the King?”
He replied:
“Victory for an army lies in harmony,
not in numbers.
That Shāng and Zhōu were not equals
is something you have heard.
An army has been formed and sent out;
why seek reinforcements?”
The Mò'áo said:
“Shall we divine it?”
He replied:
“Divination is to resolve doubts.
When there is no doubt,
why divine?”
Subsequently, they defeated the Yún army at Púsāo,
and finally concluded the covenant and returned.
B2.11.3 When Duke Zhāo of Zhèng defeated the Běiróng,
the people of Qí wished to give him a wife.
Duke Zhāo declined.
Jì Zhòng said:
“You must take her.
The Lord has many favorites in the inner palace;
you have no great support,
and will not be established.
The three sons of the Lord are all potential rulers.”
He did not follow the advice.
In the summer,
Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng died.
Previously,
Jì Zhòngzú, the warden of the border,
was favored by Duke Zhuāng,
and Duke Zhuāng made him a high minister.
He had married Dèng Màn for the Duke,
who gave birth to Duke Zhāo.
Therefore, Jì Zhòng established him.
The Yōng clan of Sòng gave a daughter to Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng;
she was called Yōng Jí,
and she gave birth to Duke Lì.
The head of the Yōng clan
was favored by Duke Zhuāng of Sòng;
therefore, he lured Jì Zhòng and seized him,
saying:
“If you do not establish Tū,
you shall die.”
They also seized Duke Lì
and sought a bribe from him.
Jì Zhòng formed a covenant with the people of Sòng,
