and the masses return to it.
These six aspects do not change;
they combine and can be firm,
they are at peace and can strike.
This is the hexagram of dukes and marquises.
The descendants of dukes and marquises
will surely return to their original status."
A4.2 The Classic of the Second Year of Duke Mǐn.
A4.2.1 In the second year, in spring,
in the royal first month,
the people of Qí moved the people of Yáng.
A4.2.2 In summer, in the fifth month, on the day yǐyǒu,
an auspicious Dì sacrifice was performed for Zhuāng Gōng.
A4.2.3 In autumn, in the eighth month, on the day xīinchǒu,
the Gōng passed away.
A4.2.4 In the ninth month,
the lady Jiāng Shì fled to Zhū.
A4.2.5 Gōngzǐ Qìngfù fled to Jǔ.
A4.2.6 In winter,
Gāo Zǐ of Qí came to make a covenant.
A4.2.7 In the twelfth month,
the Dí entered Wèi.
A4.2.8 Zhèng abandoned its army.
B4.2 The Commentary on the Second Year of Mǐn Gōng.
B4.2.1 In the second year, in spring,
Guó Gōng defeated the Quǎnróng at Wèiruì.
Zhōu Zhīqiáo said:
"To have emolument without virtue
is a calamity.
Calamity is about to arrive."
He then fled to Jìn.
B4.2.2 In summer,
the auspicious Dì sacrifice was performed for Zhuāng Gōng;
it was premature.
B4.2.3 Previously,
the Gōng's tutor seized the fields of Bǔ Yǐ,
and the Gōng did not stop him.
In autumn, in the eighth month, on the day xīinchǒu,
Gòngzhòng sent Bǔ Yǐ to assassinate the Gōng at Wǔguī.
Chéng Jì went to Zhū with Xī Gōng.
Gòngzhòng fled to Jǔ.
Then he entered
and established him.
He sought Gòngzhòng from Jǔ with bribes;
the people of Jǔ returned him.
When they reached Mì,
he sent Gōngzǐ Yú to plead.
It was not granted;
he went away weeping.
Gòngzhòng said:
"That is the voice of Xī Sī."
He then hanged himself.
Mǐn Gōng
was the son of Shūjiāng, the younger sister of Āijiāng;
therefore the people of Qí established him.
Gòngzhòng had an illicit affair with Āijiāng,
and Āijiāng wanted to establish him.
Regarding the death of Mǐn Gōng,
Āijiāng was complicit in the knowledge of it,
therefore she fled to Zhū.
The people of Qí took her and killed her at Yí,
returning with her corpse;
Xī Gōng requested to bury her.
B4.2.4 When Chéng Jì was about to be born,
Huán Gōng sent the father of Bǔ Chǔqiū
to divine it by tortoise shell,
and he said:
"It will be a boy;
his name shall be Yǒu,
and he will be at the Gōng's right;
he will be between the two altars of the land,
serving as a pillar for the Ducal House.
If the Jì Shì perishes,
then Lǔ will not flourish."
He also divined it by stalks,
and encountered Dàyǒu changing into Qián,
which said:
"The companion returns to the father;
respected as if in the ruler's place."
When he was born,
there were characters on his hand saying 'Yǒu,'
so they named him accordingly.
B4.2.5 In winter, in the twelfth month,
the Dí people attacked Wèi.
Yì Gōng of Wèi loved cranes;
there were cranes that rode in carriages.
When they were about to fight,
those among the people of the state who received armor all said:
"Employ the cranes!
The cranes actually have emoluments and positions;
how can we fight?"
The Gōng gave Shí Qízǐ a jade ring,
and gave Nìng Zhuāngzǐ arrows,
sending them to defend,
saying:
"Use these to assist the state,
and choose what is advantageous to do."
He gave his wife embroidered clothing
and said:
"Listen to these two gentlemen!"
Qú Kǒng drove the war chariot,
Zǐbó was the charioteer on the right;
Huáng Yí was the vanguard,
and Kǒng Yīngqí was the rearguard.
They fought with the Dí people at Yíngzé;
the army of Wèi was utterly defeated,
and consequently Wèi was destroyed.
The Hóu of Wèi would not lower his flags,
and because of this, he was severely defeated.
The Dí people captured Shǐ Huà Lónghuá and Lǐ Kǒng
to pursue the people of Wèi.
The two men said:
"We
are the Grand Shǐ;
we actually manage the sacrifices.
If we do not go first,
the state cannot be obtained."
So they were sent ahead.
When they arrived,
they told the defenders:
"It is impossible to wait."
At night, they left with the people of the state.
The Dí entered Wèi,
then followed them,
and defeated them again at the River.
Previously,
when Huì Gōng ascended the throne, he was young.
The people of Qí sent Zhāobó to have an incestuous relationship with Xuānjiāng;
he would not,
but they forced him.
They gave birth to Qízǐ, Dài Gōng, Wén Gōng, Sòng Huán Fūrén, and Xǔ Mù Fūrén.
Because Wèi had many troubles, Wén Gōng
first went to Qí.
When the defeat occurred,
Sòng Huán Gōng met them at the River
and crossed during the night.
The remaining people of Wèi, seven hundred and thirty men and women,
were supplemented by the people of Gòng
and Téng
to make five thousand people.
They established Dài Gōng to reside in Cáo.
Xǔ Mù Fūrén composed the poem 'Zàichí.'
The Hóu of Qí sent Gōngzǐ Wúkuī to lead three hundred chariots
and three thousand armored soldiers to garrison Cáo.
He presented the Gōng with a carriage and horses, five sets of sacrificial robes, and cows, sheep, pigs, chickens, and dogs, three hundred of each, along with timber for gates.
He presented the lady with a carriage decorated with fish skins and thirty pairs of heavy silk.
B4.2.6 The people of Zhèng disliked Gāo Kè,
and sent him to lead the army to camp on the River bank;
after a long time without recalling him,
the army collapsed and returned,
Gāo Kè fled to Chén.
The people of Zhèng composed the poem 'Qīngrén' about it.
B4.2.7 The Hóu of Jìn sent Tàizǐ Shēnshēng to attack Dōngshān Gāoluò Shì.
Lǐ Kè remonstrated, saying:
"The Tàizǐ upholds the ancestral sacrifices
and the grain offerings for the Altars of Earth and Grain,
and oversees the ruler's meals morning and evening;
therefore he is called the Eldest Son.
When the ruler travels, he stays to guard;
if there is a guard, he follows.
Following is called 'Soothing the Army,'
and guarding is called 'Supervising the State.'
This is the ancient regulation.
As for leading an army,
it is to act with sole authority in planning;
administering oaths to the military
is what the ruler and the state's government deliberate upon.
It is not the business of the Tàizǐ.
When the army is in the field, it is only a matter of establishing commands;
to receive commands is to lack majesty,
while to act with sole authority in commands is to be unfilial.
Therefore, the ruler's legitimate heir should not lead an army.
If the ruler neglects his officials,
and the leader of the army has no majesty,
what use will it be?
Furthermore, I have heard that Gāoluò Shì is about to fight.
May the ruler set aside this plan!"
The Hóu said:
"I have sons,
and do not yet know who will be established!"
He did not respond and withdrew.
He saw the Tàizǐ.
The Tàizǐ said:
"Am I about to be discarded?"
He replied:
"Instructing you with presiding over the people
and teaching you with the military—
only fear not being reverent;
for what reason should you be discarded?
Moreover, you should fear being unfilial
and not fear not being established.
If you cultivate yourself and do not blame others, then you will escape calamity."
Dàzǐ led the army;
the Duke dressed him in split clothing
and bestowed a gold slit-ring upon him.
Hú Tū drove the chariot,
and Xiān Yǒu served as the spearman on the right.
Liáng Yú Zǐ Yǎng drove the chariot for Hǎn Yí,
and Xiān Dān Mù served as the spearman on the right.
Yáng Shé Dà Fū served as the marshal.
Xiān Yǒu said:
"Dressing the person in split colors,
and grasping the essentials of military power,
are for this expedition;
you should exert yourself!
If one’s own person is without fault,
and military power keeps away disaster,
if one remains close to others without calamity,
what then is there to worry about?"
Hú Tū sighed and said:
"The timing
is the omen of an affair;
the clothing
is the insignia of the person;
the pendant
is the flag of one's inner intent.
Therefore, when one respects an affair,
the command is given at the beginning of a season;
to clothe the person,
one uses clothing of a uniform color;
to employ one's inner intent,
the pendant follows proper measure.
Now, giving the command at the end of the season
is to shut down the affair;
dressing him in variegated clothing
is to distance him from oneself;
bestowing a gold slit-ring
is to abandon the inner intent.
Clothing is used to distance him,
and timing is used to shut it down;
variegated and desolate,
winter
and killing,
metal
and cold,
the slit-ring
and separation;
how can one rely on these?
Even if you wish to exert yourself,
can the Dí be completely eliminated?"
Liáng Yú Zǐ Yǎng said:
"He who leads an army
receives his command in the ancestral temple
and receives the sacrificial meat at the altar of the soil;
there are fixed garments for this.
When he does not receive those but gets variegated dress,
the nature of the command can be known.
To die and be unfilial
is not as good as fleeing."
Hǎn Yí said:
"The variegated is strange and lacks constancy;
the gold slit-ring means there is no returning.
Even if he returns, what is there to do?
The Ruler has already made up his mind."
Xiān Dān Mù said:
"With this kind of dress,
even a madman would be deterred by it.
He says
'Eliminate the enemy and then return,'
but can the enemy be eliminated?
Even if the enemy is eliminated,
there will still be internal slanders;
it would be better to disobey."
Hú Tū wished to proceed.
Yáng Shé Dà Fū said:
"That is not possible.
To disobey a command is unfilial;
to abandon one's duty is disloyal.
Although we know it is cold,
evil should not be chosen.
You should die for it!"
Dàzǐ was about to go to battle;
Hú Tū remonstrated, saying:
"It is not possible.
Formerly, Xīn Bó advised Zhōu Huán Gōng, saying:
'When internal favorites are equal to the Queen,
external favorites hold the two powers of government,
concubines' sons are matched with the legitimate heir,
and great cities are equal to the capital,
these are the roots of disorder.'
Zhōu Gōng did not follow this,
and so he met with disaster.
Now the roots of disorder are established;
can your succession be certain?
To be filial and bring peace to the people—
you should consider this!
Rather than endangering your person
to hasten your own guilt."
B4.2.8 Chéng Fēng heard the prophecy concerning Chéng Jì,
so she served him
and entrusted Xī Gōng to him;
therefore Chéng Jì established him.
B4.2.9 In the first year of Xī Gōng,
Qí Huán Gōng moved Xíng to Yí Yí.
In the second year,
he enfeoffed Wèi at Chǔ Qiū.
The move of Xíng was like returning home;
the state of Wèi forgot its destruction.
B4.2.10 Wén Gōng of Wèi wore clothing of coarse cloth
and a cap of coarse silk;
he applied himself to materials and trained in agriculture,
opened trade and benefited the artisans,
respected education and encouraged learning,
and assigned duties and employed the capable.
In his first year,
there were thirty war chariots;
in his final year,
there were reached three hundred chariots.
A5.1 *Xī Gōng Yuán Nián Jīng*
A5.1.1 The first year, spring,
the King's first month.
A5.1.2 The armies of Qí,
the armies of Sòng,
and the armies of Cáo halted at Niè Běi,
to rescue Xíng.
A5.1.3 Summer, the sixth month,
Xíng moved to Yí Yí.
A5.1.4 The armies of Qí,
the armies of Sòng,
and the armies of Cáo walled Xíng.
A5.1.5 Autumn, the seventh month, on the day wùchén,
the Lady Jiāng Shì died at Yí;
the people of Qí took her remains back.
A5.1.6 The people of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
A5.1.7 The eighth month,
the Duke met the Qí Hóu,
the Sòng Gōng,
the Zhèng Bó,
the Cáo Bó,
and the people of Zhū at Chéng.
A5.1.8 The ninth month,
the Duke defeated the army of Zhū at Yǎn.
A5.1.9 Winter, the tenth month, on the day rénwǔ,
Gōng Zǐ Yǒu led an army and defeated the army of Jǔ at Lì,
capturing Ná of Jǔ.
A5.1.10 The twelfth month, on the day dīngsì,
the funeral of the Lady Shì arrived from Qí.
B5.1 *Xī Gōng Yuán Nián Zhuàn*
B5.1.1 The first year, spring,
the accession is not mentioned
because the Duke had gone abroad.
That the Duke left and returned
is not recorded,
in order to conceal it.
To conceal the state's disgrace
is in accordance with ritual.
B5.1.2 The feudal lords rescued Xíng.
The people of Xíng collapsed
and fled to the armies.
The armies then pursued the Dí people,
prepared the utensils and implements of Xíng
and moved them;
the armies took nothing for themselves.
B5.1.3 In the summer,
Xíng moved to Yí Yí,
and the feudal lords built its walls,
to rescue it from distress.
Whenever a Hóu Bó
rescues from distress,
shares in disaster,
and punishes crimes,
it is in accordance with ritual.
B5.1.4 In the autumn,
the people of Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
because Zhèng had sided with Qí.
The meeting at Luò
was to plan the rescue of Zhèng.
B5.1.5 In the ninth month,
the Duke defeated the army of Zhū at Yǎn;
these were the guards of Xū Qiū who were about to return.
B5.1.6 In the winter,
the people of Jǔ came to demand bribes;
Gōng Zǐ Yǒu defeated them at Lì,
capturing Ná, the younger brother of the Jǔ Zǐ.
— — He was not a high minister,
but his capture was commended.
The Duke bestowed upon Jì Yǒu the fields of Wèn Yáng and the city of Fèi.
The remains of the Lady of the Shì clan arrived from Qí.
The noble man considered the Qí people’s killing of Āijiāng to be excessive;
a woman
is one who follows others.
A5.2 The Annals of the Second Year of Duke Xī
A5.2.1 In the spring of the second year, in the King’s first month,
the walls of Chǔqiū were built.
A5.2.2 In summer, the fifth month, on the xīnsì day,
we buried our Little Lord Āijiāng.
A5.2.3 The army of Yú
and the army of Jìn extinguished Xiàyáng.
A5.2.4 In autumn, the ninth month,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the people of Jiāng,
and the people of Huáng made a covenant at Guàn.
A5.2.5 In winter, the tenth month,
it did not rain.
A5.2.6 The people of Chǔ invaded Zhèng.
B5.2 The Commentary of the Second Year of Duke Xī
B5.2.1 In the spring of the second year,
the feudal lords walled Chǔqiū and enfeoffed the state of Wèi there.
It does not record who met there,
because they were late.
B5.2.2 Xún Xī of Jìn requested to use the team of horses from Qūchǎn and the jade disk of Chuíjí to borrow a way through Yú
in order to attack Guó.
The Duke said:
“These are my treasures.”
He replied:
“If you obtain the way through Yú,
it is like an external treasury.”
The Duke said:
“Gōngzhī Qí is there.”
He replied:
“As for Gōngzhī Qí’s character,
he is weak and unable to remonstrate forcefully;
moreover, having grown up with the ruler since youth,
the ruler is intimate with him;
even if he remonstrates,
[the ruler] will not listen.”
Thereupon he sent Xún Xī to borrow a way from Yú,
saying:
“Jì acted without principle;
they entered from Diānlíng,
and attacked the three gates of Míng.
Since Jì has already been distressed,
it was also only for the sake of your Lordship.
Now Guó acts without principle;
they take refuge in their fortifications,
to invade the southern borders of our humble state.
We venture to request a way
to seek punishment upon Guó.”
The Duke of Yú granted it,
and furthermore requested to attack Guó first.
Gōngzhī Qí remonstrated,
but was not listened to,
and so they raised the army.
In summer,
Lǐ Kè and Xún Xī of Jìn led the army
to meet with the army of Yú,
attacked Guó,
and extinguished Xiàyáng.
Recording Yú first
was because of the bribery.
B5.2.3 In autumn,
they made a covenant at Guàn,
to bring to submission Jiāng
and Huáng.
B5.2.4 Eunuch Diāo of Qí first
leaked the army’s position at Duōyú.
B5.2.5 The Duke of Guó defeated the Róng at Sāngtián.
Bǔ Yǎn of Jìn said:
“Guó will surely perish.
Losing Xiàyáng, he is not afraid,
and moreover, he has achieved success;
this is Heaven depriving him of insight
and increasing his malady.
He will surely treat Jìn lightly
and fail to cherish his people.
He cannot last five harvests.”
B5.2.6 In winter,
the people of Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
and Dòu Zhāng took Dān Bó of Zhèng prisoner.
A5.3 The Annals of the Third Year of Duke Xī
A5.3.1 In the spring of the third year,
the King’s first month,
it did not rain.
A5.3.2 In summer, the fourth month, it did not rain.
A5.3.3 The people of Xú took Shū.
A5.3.4 In the sixth month, it rained.
A5.3.5 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the people of Jiāng,
and the people of Huáng met at Yánggǔ.
A5.3.6 In winter,
Gōngzǐ Yǒu went to Qí to attend the covenant.
A5.3.7 The people of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
B5.3 The Commentary of the Third Year of Duke Xī
B5.3.1 In the spring of the third year,
it did not rain.
In summer, the sixth month,
it rained.
From the tenth month
it did not rain until the fifth month.
It is not called a “drought”
because it did not become a disaster.
B5.3.2 In autumn,
they met at Yánggǔ,
planning to attack Chǔ.
B5.3.3 The Marquis of Qí, because of the meeting at Yánggǔ, came to renew the covenant.
In winter,
Gōngzǐ Yǒu went to Qí to attend the covenant.
B5.3.4 The people of Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
and the Earl of Zhèng wished to make peace.
Kǒng Shū did not agree,
saying:
“Qí is just now toiling for us;
to abandon their virtue
is inauspicious.”
B5.3.5 The Marquis of Qí and Cài Jī were in a boat in the park;
she rocked the Duke.
The Duke was afraid
and changed color;
he forbade it,
but she would not stop.
The Duke was angry,
sent her back,
but had not yet broken with her.
The people of Cài married her off.
A5.4 The Annals of the Fourth Year of Duke Xī
A5.4.1 In the spring of the fourth year,
the King’s first month,
the Duke met the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Baron of Xǔ,
and the Earl of Cáo to invade Cài.
Cài collapsed,
and then they attacked Chǔ,
halting at Xíng.
A5.4.2 In summer,
Xīn Chén, the Baron of Xǔ, died.
A5.4.3 Qū Wán of Chǔ came to make a covenant with the army;
they covenanted at Zhàolíng.
A5.4.4 The people of Qí seized Yuán Tāotú of Chén.
A5.4.5 In autumn,
together with the people of Jiāng
and the people of Huáng, they attacked Chén.
A5.4.6 In the eighth month,
the Duke arrived from the attack on Chǔ.
A5.4.7 We buried Duke Mù of Xǔ.
A5.4.8 In winter, the twelfth month,
Gōngsūn Zī led the army to meet with the people of Qí,
the people of Sòng,
the people of Wèi,
the people of Zhèng,
the people of Xǔ,
and the people of Cáo to invade Chén.
B5.4 The Commentary of the Fourth Year of Duke Xī
B5.4.1 In the spring of the fourth year,
the Marquis of Qí, with the armies of the feudal lords,
invaded Cài.
Cài collapsed,
and then they attacked Chǔ.
The Viscount of Chǔ sent a messenger to speak to the army, saying:
“Your Lordship resides at the Northern Sea,
and I reside at the Southern Sea;
even when our horses and cattle are in heat, they would not reach one another.
I did not expect Your Lordship would tread upon my land.
For what reason?”
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"In the past, Zhào Kāng Gōng commanded our late Jūn Tàigōng, saying:
'The Wǔ Hóu
and Jiǔ Bó,
you shall punish them,
so as to assist and support the Zhōu Shì!'
He granted our late Jūn territory,
extending east to the Hǎi,
west to the Hé,
south to Mùlíng,
and north to Wúdì.
Your tribute of bundled couch grass has not arrived,
and the Wáng's sacrifices are not supplied,
leaving nothing with which to strain the wine;
for this, Guǎ Rén has come to collect.
Zhāo Wáng went on a southern expedition and did not return;
regarding this, Guǎ Rén has come to inquire."
[Qū Wán] replied:
"The failure of the tribute to arrive
is indeed our Guǎ Jūn's fault;
how would we dare not provide it?
As for Zhāo Wáng's failure to return,
your Jūn should inquire about that at the riverbanks!"
The army advanced
and halted at Xíng.
In summer,
Chǔ Zǐ sent Qū Wán to the army.
The army retreated
and halted at Shàolíng.
Qí Hóu arrayed the forces of the Zhū Hóu
and rode with Qū Wán to observe them.
Qí Hóu said:
"How could it be for the sake of Bùgǔ alone?
It is to continue the friendship of the late Jūn;
what would you think of sharing the same friendship with Bùgǔ?"
[Qū Wán] replied:
"Your Jūn's kindness in seeking blessings for the Shèjì of our humble state,
and deigning to accept our Guǎ Jūn,
is our Guǎ Jūn's wish."
Qí Hóu said:
"If I use these masses to fight,
who can resist them?
If I use them to attack cities,
what city will not be overcome?"
[Qū Wán] replied:
"If your Jūn uses virtue to soothe the Zhū Hóu,
who would dare not submit?
If your Jūn uses force,
Chǔ Guó will use Fāngchéng as its city walls
and the Hàn as its moat;
although your Jūn's masses are numerous,
they will have no use there."
Qū Wán made a covenant with the Zhū Hóu.
B5.4.2 Chén Yuán Tāotú said to Zhèng Shēn Hóu:
"If the army passes between Chén
and Zhèng,
the states will certainly suffer greatly.
If it goes through the eastern region,
demonstrating military power among the Dōngyí,
and returns along the Hǎi,
that would be acceptable."
Shēn Hóu said:
"Excellent."
Tāotú informed him,
and Qí Hóu
agreed to it.
Shēn Hóu had an audience and
said:
"The army is weary;
if it goes through the eastern region and encounters enemies,
I fear it cannot be used.
If it passes between Chén
and Zhèng,
they will supply provisions
and footwear;
that would be acceptable."
Qí Hóu was pleased
and granted him Hǔláo.
He arrested Yuán Tāotú.
B5.4.3 In autumn,
they attacked Chén,
to punish its disloyalty.
B5.4.4 Xǔ Mù Gōng died in the army;
he was buried as a Hóu,
which was in accordance with Lǐ.
Whenever Zhū Hóu die at the court of another
or at a meeting,
their rank is raised by one level;
if they die on the Wáng's business,
it is raised by two levels.
Thus, he was shrouded in Gǔn.
B5.4.5 In winter,
Shūsūn Dàibó led an army
to meet the armies of the Zhū Hóu to invade Chén.
Chén made peace,
and Yuán Tāotú was returned.
B5.4.6 Earlier,
Jìn Xiàn Gōng wanted to make Líjī his Fūrén;
he divined by turtle shell,
and it was inauspicious;
he divined by milfoil stalks,
and it was auspicious.
The Gōng said:
"Follow the stalks."
The diviner said:
"Stalks are short while the turtle is long;
it is better to follow the long.
Furthermore, the omen said:
'A singular focus leads to change,
usurping the Gōng's ram.
One bit of Xūn and one bit of Yóu,
after ten years there will still be a stench.'
It must not be done!"
He did not listen
and established her.
She gave birth to Xīqí,
and her younger sister gave birth to Zhuózǐ.
When he was about to establish Xīqí,
and had already completed the plan with the Zhōng Dàfū,
Jī said to the Dàzǐ:
"The Jūn dreamed of Qí Jiāng;
you must quickly offer sacrifices to her!"
The Dàzǐ sacrificed at Qūwò
and returned the sacrificial meat to the Gōng.
The Gōng was hunting;
Jī placed it in the palace for six days.
The Gōng arrived,
and she poisoned it and presented it.
The Gōng poured a libation on the ground,
and the ground swelled up.
He gave it to a dog,
and the dog died.
He gave it to a Xiǎochén,
and the Xiǎochén also died.
Jī wept and said:
"The assassin is the Dàzǐ."
The Dàzǐ fled to Xīnchéng.
The Gōng killed his tutor Dù Yuánkuǎn.
Someone said to the Dàzǐ:
"If you defend yourself,
the Jūn will surely investigate."
The Dàzǐ said:
"Without the Jī Shì, the Jūn
will not rest comfortably
and will not eat his fill.
If I defend myself,
Jī will surely be found guilty.
The Jūn is old,
and I would not be happy."
The person said:
"Will you leave then?"
The Dàzǐ said:
"The Jūn has not truly examined the crime;
if I leave bearing this reputation,
who will receive me?"
In the twelfth month, on the day Wùshēn,
he hanged himself at Xīnchéng.
Jī then slandered the Èr Gōngzǐ,
saying:
"They both knew of it."
Zhòng'ěr fled to Pú,
and Yíwú fled to Qū.
A5.5 The Jīng of Xī Gōng Wǔ Nián
A5.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
Jìn Hóu killed his Shìzǐ Shēnshēng.
A5.5.2 Qǐ Bójī came to present her son at court.
A5.5.3 Gōngsūn Zī went to Móu.
A5.5.4 The Gōng and Qí Hóu,
Sòng Gōng,
Chén Hóu,
Wèi Hóu,
Zhèng Bó,
Xǔ Nán,
and Cáo Bó met the Wáng Shìzǐ at Shǒuzhǐ.
In autumn, in the eighth month,
the Zhū Hóu made a covenant at Shǒuzhǐ.
Zhèng Bó fled home and did not join the covenant.
A5.5.7 The people of Chǔ destroyed Xián;
Xián Zǐ fled to Huáng.
In the ninth month, on the day Wùshēn, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A5.5.9 In winter,
the people of Jìn captured Yú Gōng.
B5.5 The Zhuàn of Xī Gōng Wǔ Nián
B5.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year, in the first month of the King’s calendar, on the day of Xīnhài, the first day of the month,
the sun reached its southern limit.
After the Lord had observed the new moon,
he then ascended the observation tower to gaze
and record;
this was the ritual.
Whenever there was an equinox,
a solstice, the beginning,
or the close of a season,
one must record the celestial phenomena
for the purpose of making preparations.
B5.5.2 The Marquis of Jìn sent an envoy to announce the reason for killing the Crown Prince Shēnshēng.
Previously,
the Marquis of Jìn had sent Shì Wěi
to build the cities of Pú and Qū for the two young lords;
he was not careful
and placed firewood within the walls.
Yíwú complained of this.
The Marquis sent a reprimand.
Shì Wěi bowed his head and replied:
“Your servant has heard:
‘To grieve without a loss,
sorrow will surely find an enemy;
to fortify without an army,
the enemy will surely hold the position.’
If it is to be held by an enemy,
why be careful?
To neglect the duties of office
is irreverent;
to strengthen what an enemy will hold
is disloyal.
Having lost loyalty and reverence,
how can one serve a ruler?
The *Shī* says:
‘Cherishing virtue is peace;
the clan sons are the wall.’
If my Lord cultivates virtue
and strengthens the clan sons,
what wall can compare to that?
Within three years, troops will be gathered there;
what use is there for care?”
He retired and recited a poem:
“The fox-fur is shaggy and worn;
in one state there are three lords;
whom shall I follow?”
When the trouble occurred,
the Marquis sent the eunuch Pī to attack Pú.
Zhòng’ěr said:
“The commands of one’s lord and father must not be resisted.”
He then proclaimed:
“He who resists
is my enemy.”
He climbed over the wall and fled.
Pī cut off his sleeve.
He then fled to the Dí.
B5.5.3 In the summer,
Gōngsūn Zī went to Móu
and took a wife there.
B5.5.4 A meeting was held at Shǒuzhǐ,
where they met with the King’s Crown Prince Zhèng
to plan for the peace of Zhōu.
B5.5.5 Yuán Xuānzhòng of Chén
resented Shēn Hóu of Zhèng for turning against him at Zhàolíng;
therefore, he encouraged him to fortify his granted city,
saying:
“Make the walls beautiful;
it will be a great reputation
that your descendants will not forget.
I will help you request it.”
He then requested it from the feudal lords
and fortified it;
it was beautiful.
He then slandered him to the Earl of Zhèng,
saying:
“He has made the walls of his granted city beautiful;
he intends to use it to rebel.”
Shēn Hóu thus fell into disfavor.
B5.5.6 In the autumn,
the feudal lords made a covenant.
The King sent Zhōu Gōng Zhào to call upon the Earl of Zhèng,
saying:
“I will comfort you if you follow Chǔ,
and support you with Jìn;
you can then have a little peace.”
The Earl of Zhèng was pleased with the King’s command
yet feared not attending the court of Qí;
therefore, he fled back and did not join the covenant.
Kǒng Shū stopped him,
saying:
“A ruler of a state must not act lightly;
acting lightly, he loses his kin;
losing his kin,
disaster will surely arrive.
To beg for a covenant after suffering
will result in great loss.
My Lord will surely regret it.”
He did not listen
and fled from his army to return home.
B5.5.7 Dòugǔ Yútù of Chǔ destroyed Xián;
the Master of Xián fled to Huáng.
At this time, Jiāng, Huáng, Dào, and Bǎi were in harmony with Qí,
and all were relatives of Xián by marriage.
The Master of Xián relied on them
and did not serve Chǔ,
nor did he make preparations;
thus he was destroyed.
B5.5.8 The Marquis of Jìn again requested passage through Yú
to attack Guó.
Gōng Zhī Qí remonstrated, saying:
“Guó
is the outer protection of Yú.
If Guó is destroyed,
Yú will surely follow it.
Jìn should not be given an opening,
and the enemy should not be treated lightly.
Once is already too much;
how can it be done a second time?
The proverb says:
‘The cheek and the jawbone rely on each other;
when the lips are gone, the teeth are cold.’
This
refers to Yú
and Guó.”
The Duke said:
“Jìn
is of my own clan;
how would they harm me?”
He replied:
“Tàibó
and Yúzhòng
were the luminous sons of Dàwáng;
Tàibó did not follow the succession,
so he did not inherit.
Guózhòng
and Guóshū
were the sons of Wángjì;
they were ministers to Wénwáng,
their merit was in the royal house,
and it is stored in the covenant office.
If they would destroy Guó,
what love would they have for Yú?
Moreover, can Yú be closer than the lineages of Huán and Zhuāng?
As for their love for them,
what crime did the families of Huán and Zhuāng commit
that they were slaughtered?
Was it not because they were a threat?
When close kin become a threat due to favor,
he still harms them;
how much more so with a whole state?”
The Duke said:
“My sacrifices are abundant and pure;
the spirits will surely support me.”
He replied:
“Your servant has heard
that ghosts and spirits are not truly close to people
but rely only on virtue.
Thus the *Zhōu Shū* says:
‘Great Heaven has no favorites;
it assists only the virtuous.’
It also says:
‘The grains are not the fragrance;
bright virtue is the fragrance.’
It also says:
‘The people do not change the offerings,
but it is virtue that makes the offerings.’
If it is so,
then without virtue,
the people will not be in harmony
and the spirits will not accept the offerings.
That which the spirits rely upon
resides in virtue.
If Jìn takes Yú
and uses bright virtue
to present fragrant offerings,
will the spirits spit them out?”
The Duke did not listen
and granted the Jìn envoy’s request.
Gōng Zhī Qí left with his clan,
saying:
“Yú will not survive to perform the year-end sacrifice.
On this campaign,
Jìn will not need to raise an army again.”
In the eighth month, on the day Jiǎwǔ,
the Marquis of Jìn besieged Shàngyáng.
He asked the diviner Yǎn:
“Shall I succeed?”
He replied:
“You will overcome it.”
The Marquis said:
“When?”
He replied:
“A children’s rhyme says:
‘On the morning of the Bǐng day,
the Dragon’s Tail hides the star;
the uniforms are grand and numerous,
as the banners of Guó are taken.
The Quail-fire is bright,
the Heavenly Spear is shining,
the army is formed under the Fire star,
and the Lord of Guó will flee.’”
It must have been during the transition between the ninth
and tenth months!
On the morning of the day Bǐngzǐ,
the sun was in the mansion Wěi,
the moon was in Cè,
and Chūnhuǒ was at the meridian;
it was surely at this time."
In winter, the twelfth month, on the day Bǐngzǐ,
the first day of the month,
Jìn destroyed Guó.
Chǒu, the Lord of Guó, fled to the royal capital.
When the army returned,
it lodged in Yú,
and subsequently surprise-attacked Yú,
destroying it.
They captured the Duke of Yú and his Grand Master Jǐng Bó,
using them as dowry servants for Mù Jī of Qín,
but they maintained the sacrifices of Yú
and sent its professional tributes to the King.
Therefore, the record says:
"The people of Jìn captured the Duke of Yú,"
to place the blame on Yú
and to indicate that it was easy.
A5.6 The Classic of the Sixth Year of Duke Xī.
A5.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
the King's first month.
A5.6.2 In the summer,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Wèi,
and the Count of Cáo to attack Zhèng,
and they besieged Xīnchéng.
A5.6.3 In the autumn,
the people of Chǔ besieged Xǔ,
and the regional lords then rescued Xǔ.
A5.6.4 In the winter,
the Duke arrived from the attack on Zhèng.
B5.6 The Commentary of the Sixth Year of Duke Xī.
B5.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Jiǎ Huá to attack Qū.
Yíwú could not defend it,
so he made a covenant and departed.
As he was about to flee to the Dí,
Xì Ruì said:
"To leave later and flee to the same place
is a crime;
it is better to go to Liáng.
Liáng is near Qín and is favored by it."
He then went to Liáng.
B5.6.2 In the summer,
the regional lords attacked Zhèng
because it had fled from the Covenant of Shǒuzhǐ.
They besieged Xīnmì;
this was why Zhèng had not fortified its walls in time.
B5.6.3 In the autumn,
the Viscount of Chǔ besieged Xǔ to rescue Zhèng;
the regional lords rescued Xǔ
and then returned.
B5.6.4 In the winter,
Marquis Mù of Cài led Duke Xī of Xǔ
to see the Viscount of Chǔ at Wǔchéng.
The Baron of Xǔ had his hands bound behind his back,
held a jade bi in his mouth,
his Grand Masters wore mourning garments,
and the officers carried a coffin.
The Viscount of Chǔ asked Féng Bó about this.
He replied:
"In the past, when King Wǔ overcame Yīn,
Wēizǐ Qǐ acted like this.
King Wǔ personally released his bonds,
received his jade bi and performed a purification ritual over him,
burned his coffin,
treated him with ritual and gave him his charge,
and sent him back to his place."
The Viscount of Chǔ followed this advice.
A5.7 The Classic of the Seventh Year of Duke Xī.
A5.7.1 In the spring of the seventh year,
the people of Qí attacked Zhèng.
A5.7.2 In the summer,
the Viscount of Xiǎo Zhū came for an audience.
A5.7.3 Zhèng killed its Grand Master Shēn Hóu.
A5.7.4 In the autumn, the seventh month,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
Kuǎn the Heir Apparent of Chén,
and Huá the Heir Apparent of Zhèng,
to covenant at Nìngmǔ.
A5.7.5 Bān, the Count of Cáo, died.
A5.7.6 Young Lord Yǒu went to Qí.
A5.7.7 In the winter,
they buried Duke Zhāo of Cáo.
B5.7 The Commentary of the Seventh Year of Duke Xī.
B5.7.1 In the spring of the seventh year,
the people of Qí attacked Zhèng.
Kǒng Shū said to the Count of Zhèng:
"The proverb has it:
'If the heart is not competitive,
why fear distress?'
Since we can neither be strong
nor be weak,
that is why we face ruin.
The state is in danger;
I request that we submit to Qí to save the state."
The Duke said:
"I know how this came about;
wait for me just a little while."
He replied:
"The morning does not wait for the evening;
how can you wait, my lord?"
B5.7.2 In the summer,
Zhèng killed Shēn Hóu to please Qí,
and also because of the slander of Yuán Tāotú of Chén.
Initially,
Shēn Hóu
was born in Shēn
and was favored by King Wén of Chǔ.
When King Wén was about to die,
he gave him a jade bi
and sent him away,
saying:
"Only I know you.
You are greedy for profit and never satisfied;
I gave what you took and what you sought,
and did not find fault with you.
Later people will demand much from you,
and you will surely not escape.
When I die,
you must leave quickly;
do not go to a small state,
for it will not tolerate you."
After the burial,
he fled to Zhèng,
where he was also favored by Duke Lì.
Zǐwén heard of his death
and said:
"The ancients had a saying:
'No one knows a minister like his ruler,'
and it truly cannot be changed."
B5.7.3 In the autumn,
they covenanted at Nìngmǔ,
which was to plan concerning Zhèng.
Guǎn Zhòng said to the Marquis of Qí:
"I have heard:
Recruit those who are estranged through ritual,
and cherish those who are distant through virtue.
If virtue and ritual are not changed,
there is no one who will not be cherished."
The Marquis of Qí practiced ritual toward the regional lords,
and the officials of the regional lords received their regional products.
The Count of Zhèng sent Heir Apparent Huá
to receive orders at the meeting,
and he said to the Marquis of Qí:
"The three clans of Xiè,
Kǒng,
and Zǐrén
actually went against your commands, my lord.
If you, my lord, remove them to achieve peace,
I will make Zhèng an internal subject,
and you, my lord, will have nothing but benefit from it."
The Marquis of Qí was about to grant this.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"You, my lord, associate with the regional lords through ritual and good faith,
yet to end it with wickedness,
would that not be unacceptable?
A son not acting wickedly toward his father is called ritual;
keeping commands and being punctual is called good faith.
To violate these two
is the greatest wickedness."
The Duke said:
"The regional lords had a punitive expedition against Zhèng
but have not yet succeeded;
now if there is a crack
and we follow it,
is that not also acceptable?"
He replied:
"If you, my lord, soothe them with virtue,
add to it with instruction,
use persuasive words,
and lead the regional lords to punish Zhèng,
Zhèng will not even have time to worry about its own destruction,
how would they dare not be afraid?"
If you assemble these criminals to confront them,
Zhèng will have a justification for defense.
Why should they be afraid?
Furthermore, the meeting of the feudal lords
is for the purpose of exalting virtue.
If you meet and give rank to the treacherous,
how will you show the way to future descendants?
At the meetings of the feudal lords,
their virtue,
punishments, rituals,
and righteousness
are recorded by every state.
If you record the rank of the treacherous,
your lordship's leadership of the covenants will perish.
To act and not have it recorded
is not a sign of abundant virtue.
May your lordship not grant his request!
Zhèng will certainly accept the covenant.
As for Zǐ Huá, since he is already the heir
yet seeks assistance from a great state to weaken his own country,
he will surely not escape disaster.
Zhèng has three good men—Shū Zhān,
Dǔ Shū,
and Shī Shū—governing,
and there is as yet no opening to exploit."
The Marquis of Qí declined the request.
Because of this, Zǐ Huá incurred guilt in Zhèng.
B5.7.4 In winter,
the Earl of Zhèng sent an envoy to request a covenant with Qí.
B5.7.5 In the leap month,
King Huì died.
King Xiāng dreaded the trouble caused by Tàishū Dài.
Fearing that he might not be established,
he did not announce the death
but reported the trouble to Qí.
A5.8 Annals of the Eighth Year of Duke Xī.
A5.8.1 In the spring of the eighth year,
the King's first month,
the Duke met with the King's representative,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Baron of Xǔ,
the Earl of Cáo,
and the Heir of Chén, Kuǎn,
and covenanted at Táo.
The Earl of Zhèng begged to join the covenant.
A5.8.2 In summer,
the Dí invaded Jìn.
A5.8.3 In autumn, the seventh month,
the Dì sacrifice was performed in the Great Ancestral Temple
to introduce the late Consort.
A5.8.4 In winter, the twelfth month, on the day Dīngwèi,
the Heavenly King died.
B5.8 Commentary on the Eighth Year of Duke Xī.
B5.8.1 In the spring of the eighth year,
they covenanted at Táo
to deliberate on the affairs of the Royal House.
The Earl of Zhèng begged to join the covenant
to request submission.
King Xiāng secured his position
and only then announced the death.
B5.8.2 Lǐ Kè of Jìn led the army,
Liáng Yóumǐ drove the chariot,
and Guō Shè served as the chariot-right
when they defeated the Dí at Cǎisāng.
Liáng Yóumǐ said:
"The Dí have no sense of shame;
if we pursue them,
we will surely achieve a great victory."
Lǐ Kè said:
"It is enough to frighten them;
let us not provoke the masses of the Dí."
Guō Shè said:
"Within a year, the Dí will surely come;
we have shown them weakness."
In summer,
the Dí invaded Jìn
to retaliate for the campaign at Cǎisāng.
It was exactly one year later.
B5.8.3 In autumn,
the Dì sacrifice was held
and the spirit of Āi Jiāng was introduced;
this was contrary to ritual.
In general, for a consort,
if she does not die in her chamber,
is not laid in state in the temple,
is not announced to peer states,
and is not joined in the temple to her mother-in-law,
then she should not be 'introduced.'
B5.8.4 In winter,
the King's representative came to announce the death;
because of the trouble,
it was delayed.
B5.8.5 The Duke of Sòng was ill;
the Heir Zīfǔ firmly requested,
saying:
"Mùyí is elder and benevolent,
may your lordship establish him!"
The Duke gave the command to Zǐyú.
Zǐyú declined,
saying:
"If one can yield the state,
what benevolence could be greater?
I am not his equal,
and furthermore, it would not be in the proper order of succession."
He then hurried away and retired.
A5.9 Annals of the Ninth Year of Duke Xī.
A5.9.1 In the spring of the ninth year,
the King's third month, on the day Dīngchǒu,
Yùshuō, the Duke of Sòng, died.
A5.9.2 In summer,
the Duke met the Prime Minister Duke of Zhōu,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Son of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Baron of Xǔ,
and the Earl of Cáo at Kuíqiū.
A5.9.3 In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Yǐyǒu,
Bó Jī died.
A5.9.4 In the ninth month, on the day Wùchén,
the feudal lords covenanted at Kuíqiū.
A5.9.5 On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Guǐzhū, the Marquis of Jìn, died.
A5.9.6 In winter,
Lǐ Kè of Jìn killed Xīqí, the son of his ruler.
B5.9 Commentary on the Ninth Year of Duke Xī.
B5.9.1 In the spring of the ninth year,
Duke Huán of Sòng died.
Before he was buried, Duke Xiāng met with the feudal lords;
therefore, the text calls him
"Son."
In general, while in mourning,
the King is called
"Small Child,"
while Dukes and Marquises are called
"Son."
B5.9.2 In summer,
they met at Kuíqiū
to renew the covenant
and to cultivate good relations;
this was ritual.
The King sent Zǎi Kǒng
to grant the Marquis of Qí sacrificial meat from the ancestral sacrifice,
saying:
"The Son of Heaven has performed sacrifices to King Wén
and King Wǔ,
and has sent Kǒng to grant the Elder Uncle the sacrificial meat."
The Marquis of Qí was about to go down and bow.
Kǒng said:
"There is also a subsequent command.
The Son of Heaven has sent Kǒng to say:
'Since the Elder Uncle is of an advanced age,
and to add an honor for his labors,
I grant him a rank of distinction:
he need not go down to bow!'"
The Marquis replied:
"The majesty of Heaven is not even a foot away from one's face.
How could Xiǎobái
dare to presume upon the Son of Heaven's command
and not go down to bow?
I fear I might fall and stumble below,
thereby bringing shame upon the Son of Heaven.
How could I dare not to go down and bow?"
He went down
and bowed;
then he ascended
and received the gift.
B5.9.3 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí covenanted with the feudal lords at Kuíqiū,
saying:
"All of us who have joined this covenant,
after the covenant is made,
let us return to friendly relations."
Zǎi Kǒng returned first,
and meeting the Marquis of Jìn,
he said:
"You need not attend the meeting.
The Marquis of Qí does not focus on virtue
but exerts himself in distant strategies;
thus he campaigned against the Shānróng in the north,
against Chǔ in the south,
and now has held this meeting in the west.
"I do not know about the strategy in the east;
as for the west, that is not the case.
It is in a state of chaos!
Your Lordship should focus on settling the chaos
and not weary yourself with travel."
The Jìn Hóu then returned.
5.9.4 In the ninth month,
Jìn Xiàn Gōng died.
Lǐ Kè and Pī Zhèng wished to bring in Wén Gōng,
so they used the followers of the Sān Gōngzǐ to start a rebellion.
Earlier,
Xiàn Gōng had appointed Xún Xī as tutor to Xī Qí.
When the Gōng was ill,
he summoned him
and said:
"With this small orphan, whom I humbly leave to the Dàfū,
what shall be done?"
Xún Xī bowed his head to the ground and replied:
"Your servant will exhaust the strength of his limbs
and add to it loyalty
and integrity.
If it succeeds,
it is your Lordship’s spiritual power;
if it does not succeed,
then I will follow it with my death."
The Gōng said:
"What is meant by loyalty
and integrity?"
He replied:
"To know what is in the interest of the Gōng house and do it without fail
is loyalty;
to see off the departed and serve the living,
so that both parties are without suspicion,
is integrity."
When Lǐ Kè was about to kill Xī Qí,
he first told Xún Xī:
"The three resentments are about to arise,
and Qín and Jìn will assist them;
what will you do, sir?"
Xún Xī said:
"I shall die for him."
Lǐ Kè said:
"It will be of no benefit."
Xún Shū said:
"I have given my word to the late lord;
I cannot deviate from it.
Could I wish to go back on my words because I love my own life?
Though it may be of no benefit,
how can I avoid it?
Moreover, as for people's desire to be good,
who is not like me?
I wish to have no duplicity;
can I then tell others to stop?"
In winter, the tenth month,
Lǐ Kè killed Xī Qí in the mourning shed.
The record says
"killed the son of his lord,"
because he had not yet been buried.
Xún Xī was about to die for him, but
someone said:
"It would be better to install Zhuōzǐ
and support him."
Xún Xī installed Gōngzǐ Zhuō
to perform the burial.
In the eleventh month,
Lǐ Kè killed Gōngzǐ Zhuō in the court.
Xún Xī died for him.
The Jūnzǐ said:
"What the Shī says,
'A flaw in a white jade tablet
may still be ground away;
but for a flaw in these words,
nothing can be done,'
applies to Xún Xī."
5.9.5 The Qí Hóu led the armies of the Zhūhóu to attack Jìn,
reaching Gāoliáng and then returning,
to punish the rebellion in Jìn.
The command did not reach Lǔ,
so it was not recorded.
5.9.6 Xì Ruì of Jìn made Yíwú offer heavy bribes to Qín
to seek entry,
saying:
"Others will actually possess the state;
why should I be stingy with it?
If I enter and can win the people,
what does land matter?"
He followed this.
Xí Péng of Qí led an army to join the Qín army
to install Jìn Huì Gōng.
The Qín Bó said to Xì Ruì:
"Whom does the Gōngzǐ rely on?"
He replied:
"Your servant has heard
that an exile has no faction;
if he has a faction, he must have enemies.
Yíwú, when young, did not like play;
he could fight but not excessively;
and as he grew up, he did not change.
I know nothing else."
The Gōng said to Gōngsūn Zhī:
"Will Yíwú be established securely?"
He replied:
"Your servant has heard:
'Only through principle is a state settled.'
The Shī says:
'Without awareness, without knowledge,
he follows the principles of the Dì.'
This refers to Wén Wáng.
It also says:
'Neither overstepping nor being cruel,
few fail to follow the principle.'
This refers to being without personal likes or dislikes,
without jealousy or competitiveness.
Now his words are full of jealousy and competitiveness;
it will be difficult!"
The Gōng said:
"If he is jealous, he will have many resentments;
how then can he be successful?
This is to our advantage."
5.9.7 Sòng Xiāng Gōng took the throne.
Regarding Gōngzǐ Mùyí as benevolent,
he made him Zuǒshī to handle the government;
thus Sòng was well-governed.
Therefore, the Yú clan served as Zuǒshī for generations.
A5.10 Xī Gōng Tenth Year Jīng
5.10.1 In the tenth year, in spring,
the Wáng's first month,
the Gōng went to Qí.
5.10.2 The Dí destroyed Wēn;
the Wēn Zǐ fled to Wèi.
5.10.3 Lǐ Kè of Jìn assassinated his lord Zhuō and his Dàfū Xún Xī.
5.10.4 In summer,
the Qí Hóu
and the Xǔ Nán attacked the Běi Róng.
5.10.5 Jìn killed its Dàfū Lǐ Kè.
5.10.6 Autumn, seventh month.
5.10.7 In winter,
there was a great fall of rain and snow.
B5.10 Xī Gōng Tenth Year Zhuàn
5.10.1 In the tenth year, in spring,
the Dí destroyed Wēn
because the Sū Zǐ was untrustworthy.
The Sū Zǐ rebelled against the Wáng and joined the Dí,
yet he could not get along with the Dí.
The Dí people attacked him;
the Wáng did not save him,
so he was destroyed.
The Sū Zǐ fled to Wèi.
5.10.2 In summer, the fourth month,
Zhōu Gōng Jìfù
and Wángzǐ Dǎng met Xí Péng of Qí
to install the Jìn Hóu.
The Jìn Hóu killed Lǐ Kè
to please the people.
When he was about to kill Lǐ Kè,
the Gōng sent someone to say to him:
"Without you,
I would not have reached this position.
Although this is so,
you killed two lords and one Dàfū;
to be your lord,
is it not also difficult?"
He replied:
"Without the removal of the others,
how could your Lordship have risen?
If you wish to impose a crime,
can you not find a pretext?
Your servant has heard your command."
He fell upon his sword and died.
At this time, Pī Zhèng went on a mission to Qín
and to apologize for the delay in the bribes,
so he was not caught up in it.
5.10.3 The Jìn Hóu reburied Gòng Tàizǐ.
In autumn,
Hú Tū went to Xiàguó
and encountered the Tàizǐ.
The Tàizǐ made him climb into the carriage
to act as driver
and told him:
"Yíwú is without ritual.
I have obtained a request from the Dì;
I shall give Jìn to Qín,
and Qín will sacrifice to me."
He replied:
"Your servant has heard:
'Spirits do not enjoy the offerings of those not of their kind,
and the people do not sacrifice to those not of their lineage.'
Would your Lordship's sacrifices not then be cut off?"
"Moreover, what is the crime of the people?
Forfeiting punishments and
lacking sacrifices—
may my Lord consider it!"
The Lord said:
"Agreed.
I shall request it again.
In seven days,
on the western side of Xīnchéng, there will be a medium
through whom I shall see you."
He agreed to it,
and then the Lord was seen no more.
When the appointed time came, he went,
and the ghost told him:
"The Emperor has granted me permission to punish the guilty;
they will be defeated at Hán."
When Pī Zhèng went to Qín,
he said to the Earl of Qín:
"Lǚ Shēng,
Xì Chēng,
and Jì Ruì
are actually not compliant.
If you send heavy gifts and inquiries to summon them,
I will drive out the Jìn ruler,
and you can bring in Chóng'ěr;
there is no way it will not succeed."
In winter,
the Earl of Qín sent Lìng Zhì to return the report
and inquire,
and also to summon the three men.
Xì Ruì said:
"The gifts are heavy and the words are sweet;
they are enticing us."
Consequently, they killed Pī Zhèng,
Qí Jǔ, and the seven Chariot Grand Masters:
Zuǒháng Gònghuá,
Yòuháng Jiǎhuá,
Shū Jiān,
Zhuī Chuān,
Lěi Hǔ,
Tè Gōng,
and Shān Qí;
all were of the factions of Lǐ
and Pī.
Pī Bào fled to Qín
and said to the Earl of Qín:
"The Marquis of Jìn has turned his back on his great patron
and holds onto petty grudges;
the people do not support him.
If you attack him,
he will certainly be expelled."
The Duke said:
"If he has lost the masses,
how could he kill them?
Since he has avoided calamity,
who could expel the ruler?"
A5.11 *The Annals of Duke Xī, Eleventh Year*
A5.11.1 In the eleventh year, in spring,
Jìn killed its Grand Master Pī Zhèngfù.
A5.11.2 In summer,
the Duke and his wife, Lady Jiāng, met the Marquis of Qí at Yánggǔ.
A5.11.3 In autumn, in the eighth month,
there was a great rain sacrifice.
A5.11.4 In winter,
the people of Chǔ attacked Huáng.
B5.11 *The Commentary of Duke Xī, Eleventh Year*
B5.11.1 In the eleventh year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn sent word to announce the rebellion of Pī Zhèng.
B5.11.2 The King of Heaven sent Zhào Wǔgōng
and Interior Scribe Guò
to confer a mandate upon the Marquis of Jìn;
he was disrespectful when receiving the jade.
When Guò returned,
he told the King:
"The Marquis of Jìn will likely have no heirs!
Your Majesty conferred a mandate upon him,
but he was disrespectful in receiving the auspicious jade;
he has already abandoned himself.
How can there be a succession?
Ritual
is the trunk of the state;
respect
is the carriage of ritual.
Without respect,
ritual cannot be carried out;
if ritual is not carried out,
then those above and below will be in confusion.
How can the state long endure?"
B5.11.3 In summer,
the Róng of Yáng, Jù,
Quán, Gāo,
Yī, and Luò together attacked the capital.
They entered the Royal City,
burned the East Gate;
Prince Dài had summoned them.
Qín and Jìn attacked the Róng to rescue Zhōu.
In autumn,
the Marquis of Jìn settled the Róng for the King.
B5.11.4 The people of Huáng did not send their tribute to Chǔ.
In winter,
the people of Chǔ attacked Huáng.
A5.12 *The Annals of Duke Xī, Twelfth Year*
A5.12.1 In the twelfth year, in spring,
in the King's third month, on the day gēngwǔ,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A5.12.2 In summer,
the people of Chǔ destroyed Huáng.
A5.12.3 In autumn, in the seventh month.
A5.12.4 In winter, in the twelfth month, on the day dīngchǒu,
Chǔjiǔ, the Marquis of Chén, died.
B5.12 *The Commentary of Duke Xī, Twelfth Year*
B5.12.1 In the twelfth year, in spring,
the feudal lords walled the outer city of Chǔqiū in Wèi,
fearing trouble from the Dí.
B5.12.2 The people of Huáng relied on the harmony of the feudal lords with Qí
and did not perform their duties to Chǔ,
saying:
"From Yǐng to us is nine hundred lǐ;
how can they harm us?"
In summer,
Chǔ destroyed Huáng.
B5.12.3 Because of the trouble with the Róng, the King
punished Prince Dài.
In autumn,
Prince Dài fled to Qí.
B5.12.4 In winter,
the Marquis of Qí sent Guǎn Yíwú to settle the Róng for the King
and sent Xí Péng to settle the Róng for Jìn.
The King entertained Guǎn Zhòng with the rites of a High Minister.
Guǎn Zhòng declined, saying:
"Your servant
is a lowly official.
There are the Son of Heaven's two guardians, Guó
and Gāo, present.
If they should come according to the seasonal rites
to receive the King's commands,
what rites would be used for them?
A servant of a feudal lord dares to decline."
The King said:
"Uncle!
I commend your merits!
In response to your admirable virtue,
I say I shall not forget.
Go and perform your duties,
and do not disobey my command!"
Guǎn Zhòng finally accepted the rites of a Lower Minister
and returned.
The noble man said:
"How appropriate it is that the sacrifices of the Guǎn family have lasted for generations!
In yielding, he did not forget his superior.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'The joyful and easy-going noble man,
is the one whom the spirits reward.'"
A5.13 *The Annals of Duke Xī, Thirteenth Year*
A5.13.1 In the thirteenth year, in spring,
the Dí invaded Wèi.
A5.13.2 In summer, in the fourth month,
Duke Xuān of Chén was buried.
A5.13.3 The Duke met with the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Baron of Xǔ,
and the Earl of Cáo at Xián.
A5.13.4 In autumn, in the ninth month,
there was a great rain sacrifice.
In winter,
Nobleman Yǒu went to Qí.
B5.13 *The Commentary of Duke Xī, Thirteenth Year*
B5.13.1 In the thirteenth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Qí sent Zhòngxì Qiū on a mission to Zhōu
and also to speak of Prince Dài.
When the business was finished,
he did not speak with the King.
On returning,
He returned and reported, saying:
"It is not yet possible.
The King’s anger has not yet subsided.
Will it be ten years?
If ten years have not passed,
the King will not summon you."
B5.13.2 In the summer,
there was a meeting at Xián.
This was because the Huái Yí were distressing Qǐ,
and also to plan for the Royal House.
B5.13.3 In the autumn,
because of the troubles with the Róng,
the feudal lords garrisoned Zhōu.
Zhòngsūn Qiū of Qí delivered them.
B5.13.4 In the winter,
Jìn suffered from a repeated famine
and sent an envoy to beg to buy grain from Qín.
The Earl of Qín said to Zǐsāng:
"Should we give it to them?"
He replied:
"If we bestow a favor again and they return it,
what more could my Lord seek?
If we bestow a favor again and they do not return it,
their people will surely be alienated;
if they are alienated and you then punish them,
they will have no following,
and they will certainly be defeated."
He said to Bǎilǐ:
"Should we give it to them?"
He replied:
"Natural disasters occur everywhere,
and states take turns having them.
To relieve disasters
and take pity on neighbors
is the Way.
By following the Way,
there will be blessings."
Bào, the son of Pī Zhèng, was in Qín,
and requested to attack Jìn.
The Earl of Qín said:
"It is their ruler who is wicked;
what crime have their people committed?"
Thereupon Qín transported grain to Jìn;
from Yōng to Jiàng, the shipments followed one after another.
It was called "The Service of the Drifting Boats."
A5.14 The Classic of the Fourteenth Year of Duke Xī
A5.14.1 In the spring of the fourteenth year,
the feudal lords walled Yuánlíng.
A5.14.2 In the summer, in the sixth month,
Jì Jī and the Viscount of Zēng met at Fáng.
She made the Viscount of Zēng come to court.
A5.14.3 In the autumn, in the eighth month, on the day Xīnmǎo,
Shālù collapsed.
A5.14.4 The Dí invaded Zhèng.
A5.14.5 In the winter,
Xì, the Marquis of Cài, died.
B5.14 The Commentary of the Fourteenth Year of Duke Xī
B5.14.1 In the spring of the fourteenth year,
the feudal lords walled Yuánlíng and moved Qǐ there;
that the names of the participants are not recorded
is because there was an omission.
Jì Jī of Zēng came to inquire about the Duke's health;
the Duke was angry
and detained her,
because the Viscount of Zēng had not come to court.
In the summer,
they met at Fáng,
and she made him come to court.
B5.14.3 In the autumn, in the eighth month, on the day Xīnmǎo,
Shālù collapsed.
Bǔ Yǎn of Jìn said:
"Within a year there will be a great calamity;
the state will nearly perish."
B5.14.4 In the winter,
Qín suffered from famine
and sent an envoy to beg to buy grain from Jìn,
but the people of Jìn did not give it.
Qìng Zhèng said:
"To turn your back on a favor
is to be without affection;
to take pleasure in a disaster
is to be unkind;
to be greedy for what one loves
is inauspicious;
to anger a neighbor
is unrighteous.
If these four virtues are all lost,
how can the state be maintained?"
Guó Shè said:
"When the skin no longer exists,
where can the hair be attached?"
Qìng Zhèng said:
"If we discard good faith
and turn our backs on our neighbor,
who will pity us in our distress?
Without good faith,
troubles will arise;
losing support,
we will surely perish.
This is how it will be."
Guó Shè said:
"It will not diminish their resentment,
and it will only strengthen our enemy;
it is better not to give."
Qìng Zhèng said:
"Turning one's back on a favor
and taking pleasure in a disaster
are things that the people will reject.
Even those close to us would treat us as enemies,
how much more so our resentful foe?"
He did not listen.
Qìng Zhèng withdrew and said:
"The ruler will surely regret this!"
A5.15 The Classic of the Fifteenth Year of Duke Xī
A5.15.1 In the spring of the fifteenth year,
in the Royal first month,
the Duke went to Qí.
A5.15.2 The people of Chǔ attacked Xú.
A5.15.3 In the third month,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Baron of Xǔ,
and the Earl of Cáo,
and made a covenant at Mǔqiū;
they then halted at Kuāng.
Gōngsūn Áo led an army along with the Grand Masters of the feudal lords to rescue Xú.
A5.15.4 In the summer, in the fifth month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A5.15.5 In the autumn, in the seventh month,
the army of Qí
and the army of Cáo attacked Lì.
A5.15.6 In the eighth month,
there was a plague of locusts.
A5.15.7 In the ninth month,
the Duke arrived from the meeting.
A5.15.8 Jì Jī returned to Zēng.
On the last day of the month, the day Jǐmǎo,
thunder struck the ancestral temple of Yí Bó.
A5.15.10 In the winter,
the people of Sòng attacked Cáo.
A5.15.11 The people of Chǔ defeated Xú at Lóulín.
A5.15.12 In the eleventh month, on the day Rénxū,
the Marquis of Jìn and the Earl of Qín fought at Hán,
and the Marquis of Jìn was captured.
B5.15 The Commentary of the Fifteenth Year of Duke Xī
B5.15.1 In the spring of the fifteenth year,
the people of Chǔ attacked Xú
because Xú had aligned with the various Zhōu states.
In the third month,
they made a covenant at Mǔqiū,
renewing the covenant of Kuíqiū
and also to rescue Xú.
Mèng Mùbó led an army along with the armies of the feudal lords to rescue Xú,
and the feudal lords halted at Kuāng to wait for him.
B5.15.2 In the summer, in the fifth month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
That the first day of the month and the day were not recorded
was because the officials lost the record.
B5.15.3 In the autumn,
they attacked Lì
in order to rescue Xú.
B5.15.4 When the Marquis of Jìn entered his state,
Mù Jī of Qín had entrusted Lady Jiǎ to him,
and also said:
"You must return all the other sons of the former Duke."
The Marquis of Jìn committed incest with Lady Jiǎ,
and also did not return the other sons of the former Duke;
for this reason, Mù Jī bore a grudge against him.
The Marquis of Jìn had promised bribes to the Middle Grand Masters,
but later went back on all of them.
He promised the Earl of Qín five cities beyond the River,
extending east to the territory of Guó,
south to Huà Shān,
and inward as far as the city of Jiěliáng,
but later did not give them.
Jìn suffered a famine,
and Qín sent them grain;
when Qín suffered a famine,
Jìn refused them the purchase of grain,
and therefore the Qín Bó attacked Jìn.
Bǔtúfù performed a divination by milfoil regarding it,
and the result was auspicious:
"Crossing the Hé,
the Hóu's chariot is defeated."
They questioned him about it.
He replied,
"Indeed, it is greatly auspicious.
After three defeats,
you will certainly capture the Jìn Jūn.
The hexagram encountered was Gǔ
䷑, which says:
'A thousand chariots depart thrice;
after the three departures,
its male fox is captured.'
Now, the fox in Gǔ
must be their ruler.
The Zhēn of Gǔ
is Wind;
its Huǐ
is Mountain.
The year is now in autumn;
we shake down its fruit
and take its timber—
that is how we will conquer.
When the fruit has fallen
and the timber is lost,
if they are not defeated,
what are we waiting for?"
After three defeats, they reached Hán.
The Jìn Hóu said to Qìng Zhèng,
"The enemy has penetrated deep;
what should be done?"
He replied,
"It was you, My Lord, who let them penetrate so deep;
what can be done now!"
The Gōng said,
"Insolent!"
They divined to choose the right-hand attendant,
and the lot for Qìng Zhèng was auspicious.
Yet the Gōng did not employ him.
Bù Yáng drove the war-chariot,
and Jiāpútú acted as the right-hand attendant.
They rode a team of small horses,
presented by Zhèng.
Qìng Zhèng said,
"In ancient times, during great affairs,
one must ride horses bred in one's own land,
born of its water and soil,
and thus knowing the people's hearts;
they are at ease with their training
and accustomed to its ways;
wherever you direct them,
they will not fail to follow your will.
Now you ride a foreign breed
to engage in military affairs;
when they become frightened and change,
they will act contrary to their driver.
Their disordered spirit will become fierce and agitated;
their internal blood will be aroused everywhere;
their veins will swell and rise;
they will be strong on the outside but exhausted within.
Advancing or retreating will become impossible,
and maneuvering will be out of their power;
My Lord will surely regret this."
The Gōng did not listen.
In the ninth month,
the Jìn Hóu encountered the Qín army
and sent Hán Jiǎn to inspect the forces.
He returned and said,
"Their army is fewer than ours,
but their warriors are double ours."
The Gōng said,
"For what reason?"
He replied,
"They left their state because of your reliance on their resources;
they entered your state because of your use of their favor;
and when starving, they ate their grain.
Three favors were granted without repayment,
and that is why they have come.
Now you attack them again;
we are sluggish
while Qín is roused—
to say they are 'double' is still not enough."
The Gōng said,
"Even one man cannot be treated lightly,
how much more so a state?"
He then sent a messenger to request battle,
saying,
"I, a man of little virtue,
have been able to assemble my multitude but cannot disperse them.
If you, My Lord, do not return,
I have no place to escape your command."
The Qín Bó sent Gōngsūn Zhī to reply,
saying,
"Before you, My Lord, had returned to your state,
I feared for you;
when you returned but had not yet settled your ranks,
it was still my worry.
If your ranks are now settled,
how would I dare not accept your command?"
Hán Jiǎn withdrew
and said,
"I shall be fortunate if I am only taken prisoner."
On the day of Rénxū,
they fought at Hányuán.
The Jìn war-horses turned into the mud and stopped.
The Gōng called out to Qìng Zhèng.
Qìng Zhèng said,
"You stubbornly refused remonstrance
and disobeyed the divination;
you certainly sought this defeat,
so why try to escape it now?"
And so he left him.
Liáng Yóumǐ was driving for Hán Jiǎn,
and Guó Shè was the right-hand attendant;
they intercepted the Qín Bó
and were about to capture him.
Qìng Zhèng, on account of saving the Gōng, interfered with them,
and consequently they lost the Qín Bó.
Qín captured the Jìn Hóu and returned.
The Jìn Dàfū, with their hair unbound and having struck their tents,
followed him.
The Qín Bó sent a message to decline their following,
saying,
"Why are you sirs so sorrowful?
My following your lord to the west
is merely to fulfill the ominous dream of Jìn;
how would I dare to go to extremes?"
The Jìn Dàfū bowed thrice and prostrated themselves, saying,
"You, My Lord, tread upon Hòutǔ
and carry Huángtiān on your head;
Huángtiān and Hòutǔ
truly hear your words;
we, your servants, venture to remain in submission."
Mù Jī heard that the Jìn Hóu was about to arrive;
taking the Dàzǐ Yīng,
Hóng, and her daughter Jiǎnbì, she ascended a platform
and trod upon firewood.
She sent a messenger in mourning garments with unpinned hair to meet them,
and announced,
"High Heaven has sent down calamity,
causing our two rulers to meet not with jade and silk,
but by raising arms.
If the Jìn Jūn enters in the morning,
then I, your handmaid, shall die by the evening;
if he enters in the evening,
then I shall die by the morning.
Only you, My Lord, may decide this!"
Thereupon the Qín Bó lodged him at Língtái.
The Dàfū requested to let him enter the capital.
The Gōng said,
"In capturing the Jìn Hóu,
I returned with great gain;
but if a death follows the return,
what would be the use of it?
What would you Dàfū have then?
Furthermore, the people of Jìn are grieved and worried,
which moves me,
and Heaven and Earth constrain me.
If I do not care for Jìn's sorrow,
I double their anger;
if I eat my words,
I turn my back on Heaven and Earth.
Doubled anger
is difficult to bear;
turning one's back on Heaven
is inauspicious;
I must return the Jìn Jūn."
Gōngzǐ Zhí said,
"It is better to kill him,
so as not to accumulate more grievances."
Zǐsāng said,
"Return him and take his Dàzǐ as a hostage;
you will certainly achieve a great settlement.
Jìn cannot yet be destroyed,
and killing its ruler
only serves to complete the enmity.
Furthermore, Shǐ Yì has a saying:
'Do not start calamity,
do not rely on disorder,
do not double anger.'
Doubled anger
is difficult to bear;
oppressing others
is inauspicious."
Thereupon he granted peace to Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn sent Xì Qǐ
to inform Xiá Lǚ Yíshēng
and to summon him.
Zǐ Jīn taught him what to say,
saying:
"Assemble the people of the state at court
and grant rewards in the name of the ruler.
Also tell them:
'Although I, the lonely one, return,
I have brought shame to the altars of soil and grain;
let the divination be to replace me with Yǔ.' "
The multitude all wept,
and Jìn then established the *yuántián* (allotted fields).
Lǚ Shēng said:
"The ruler does not worry about his own exile,
but makes his ministers his concern;
this is the height of kindness.
What shall we do for the ruler?"
The multitude said:
"What can be done that would be right?"
He replied:
"Levy taxes and repair armor
to support the young prince.
When the feudal lords hear of this—
that having lost a ruler we have another ruler,
that the ministers are harmonious,
and that armored soldiers have increased—
those who love us will be encouraged,
and those who hate us will be afraid.
Perhaps this will be beneficial!"
The multitude was pleased,
and Jìn thereupon established the *zhōubīng* (district troops).
Previously,
Marquis Xiàn of Jìn divined by milfoil about marrying Bó Jī to Qín
and encountered *Guī Mèi*
changing to *Kuí*.
Shǐ Sū interpreted it,
saying:
"It is inauspicious.
Its omen says:
'The man stabs the sheep,
yet there is no blood;
the woman holds the basket,
yet there is no gift.
The western neighbor's words of reproach
cannot be compensated for.'
*Guī Mèi* changing to *Kuí*
is like having no assistance.
*Zhèn* changing to *Lí*
is also *Lí* changing to *Zhèn*.
'Becoming thunder and becoming fire,
it is Yíng defeating Jī.
The carriage loses its axle strap,
fire burns its banner;
it is unfavorable for leading an army,
which will be defeated at Zōngqiū.
*Guī Mèi* and *Kuí* are solitary;
the enemy draws his bow.
The nephew follows his paternal aunt;
in six years he will flee,
escaping back to his own state
and abandoning his family;
in the following year he will die in the ruins of Gāoliáng.' "
When Marquis Huì was in Qín,
he said:
"If the former ruler had followed Shǐ Sū's divination,
I would not have come to this!"
Hán Jiǎn was in attendance
and said:
"The tortoise shell
provides images;
the milfoil stalks
provide numbers.
Once things are born, then there are images;
once there are images, then there is growth;
once there is growth, then there are numbers.
The former ruler's loss of virtue—
can it even be counted?
Since Shǐ Sū made this divination,
what benefit would there have been in not following it?
The *Book of Songs* says:
'The calamities of the common people
do not descend from Heaven.
Flattery to the face and hatred behind the back—
their rivalry comes from men.' "
Thunder struck the temple of Yí Bó;
this was to punish him,
as the Zhǎn clan had hidden evils there.
In winter,
the people of Sòng attacked Cáo,
punishing an old grievance.
Chǔ defeated Xú at Lóulín,
as Xú had relied on rescue.
In the tenth month,
Yīn Yíshēng of Jìn met with the Earl of Qín,
and they formed an alliance at Wángchéng.
The Earl of Qín said:
"Is the state of Jìn in harmony?"
He replied:
"It is not in harmony.
The commoners feel the shame of losing their ruler
and mourn the loss of their kin;
they do not shrink from taxes and repairs
in order to establish Yǔ,
saying:
'We must seek revenge,
rather would we serve the Róng or Dí.'
The superior men love their ruler
and acknowledge his guilt;
they do not shrink from taxes and repairs
in order to await Qín's commands,
saying:
'We must repay the kindness,
even unto death without a second heart.'
Because of this, they are not in harmony."
The Earl of Qín said:
"What does the state say of the ruler?"
He replied:
"The commoners are anxious,
saying he will not be released;
the superior men are forgiving,
believing he will surely return.
The commoners say:
'We have been toxic to Qín;
how could Qín return our ruler?'
The superior men say:
'We have acknowledged our guilt;
Qín will surely return our ruler.
Because he was double-hearted, they captured him;
because he has submitted, they will release him.
No kindness is greater than this;
no punishment is more awe-inspiring than this.
Those who submit will cherish the kindness;
those who are double-hearted will fear the punishment.
Through this one campaign,
Qín can become a hegemon.
If they brought him in but did not stabilize him,
or if they deposed him and did not re-establish him,
they would be turning kindness into resentment;
Qín will not do that.' "
The Earl of Qín said:
"This is my heart's thought as well."
He changed the Marquis of Jìn's lodging
and presented him with seven sets of sacrificial animals.
É Xī said to Qìng Zhèng:
"Why not flee?"
He replied:
"I led the ruler into defeat;
the defeat happened and I did not die,
and I further caused him to fail in his punishment;
this is not the way of a minister.
To be a minister and not act like a minister—
where could I go?"
In the eleventh month,
the Marquis of Jìn returned.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
he executed Qìng Zhèng and then entered.
In this year,
Jìn again suffered a famine.
The Earl of Qín again sent them grain,
saying:
"I resent their ruler,
but I pity their people.
Furthermore, I have heard that when Táng Shú was enfeoffed,
Jī Zǐ said:
'His descendants will surely be great.'
Can Jìn then be disregarded?
For now, I shall plant virtue there
to await a capable person."
Thereupon Qín first collected taxes from Jìn's Hédōng
and established officials there.
A5.16 The Annals of the Sixteenth Year of Duke Xī
A5.16.1 In the spring of the sixteenth year, in the Royal first month, on the new moon of Wùshēn, five stones fell in Sòng. In this month, six *yì*-birds flew backward, passing the capital of Sòng.
A5.16.2 In the third month, on Rénshēn, Prince Jì Yǒu died.
A5.16.3 In the summer, the fourth month, on Bǐngshēn, Jì Jī of Zēng died.
A5.16.4 In the autumn, the seventh month, on Jiǎzǐ, Gōngsūn Zī died.
A5.16.5 In the winter, the twelfth month,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Baron of Xǔ,
the Marquis of Xíng,
and the Earl of Cáo at Huái.
B5.16 Commentary on the Sixteenth Year of Duke Xī
B5.16.1 In the spring of the sixteenth year,
five meteorites fell in Sòng;
they were falling stars.
Six ospreys flew backward
past the capital of Sòng;
it was the wind.
Shū Xīng, the Internal Scribe of Zhōu, came to Sòng on a mission of state.
Duke Xiāng of Sòng questioned him,
saying:
“What sort of omen is this?
Where do good and bad fortune reside?”
He replied:
“In this year, there will be many great funerals in Lǔ.
Next year, there will be chaos in Qí.
You, my lord, will gain leadership over the feudal lords,
but you will not maintain it to the end.”
Having withdrawn, he told others:
“The lord asked the wrong question.
These are matters of Yin and Yang
and not that from which good or bad fortune arises.
Good and bad fortune proceed from men.
It was only because I did not dare to oppose the lord’s expectations.”
B5.16.2 In the summer,
Qí attacked Lì;
they did not prevail
but rescued Xú and returned.
B5.16.3 In the autumn,
the Dí invaded Jìn,
taking Hú,
Chú, and Shòuduó;
they crossed the Fén
and reached Kūndū;
this was due to the defeat of Jìn.
B5.16.4 The King reported the difficulties with the Róng to Qí.
Qí summoned the feudal lords to garrison Zhōu.
B5.16.5 In the winter, the eleventh month, on the day yǐmǎo,
Zhèng killed Zǐhuá.
B5.16.6 In the twelfth month,
there was a meeting at Huái
to plan for Zēng
and also for an eastward expedition.
They walled Zēng.
The laborers were distressed;
one of them climbed a hill at night and cried out:
“There is chaos in Qí!”
They did not finish the walling and returned.
A5.17 The Annals of the Seventeenth Year of Duke Xī
A5.17.1 In the spring of the seventeenth year,
the people of Qí
and the people of Xú attacked Yīngshì.
A5.17.2 In the summer,
Xiàng was destroyed.
A5.17.3 In the autumn,
the Lady Jiāng met the Marquis of Qí at Biàn.
A5.17.4 In the ninth month,
the Duke arrived from the meeting.
A5.17.5 In the winter, the twelfth month, on the day yǐhài,
Xiǎobái, Marquis of Qí, died.
B5.17 Commentary on the Seventeenth Year of Duke Xī
B5.17.1 In the spring of the seventeenth year,
the people of Qí attacked Yīngshì for the sake of Xú,
to retaliate for the campaign of Lóulín.
B5.17.2 In the summer,
Yǔ, the Crown Prince of Jìn, became a hostage in Qín.
Qín returned the region of Hédōng
and gave him a wife.
When Duke Huì was in Liáng,
the Earl of Liáng gave him a wife.
Liáng Yíng became pregnant
but her term was exceeded.
Diviner Zhāofù and his son divined regarding it.
The son said:
“She will give birth to one boy and one girl.”
Zhāofù said:
“It is so.
The boy will be a servant to others,
and the girl will be a concubine to others.”
Therefore, they named the boy Yǔ
and the girl Qiè.
When Prince Yǔ went west as a hostage,
Qiè became a palace waiting-woman there.
B5.17.3 The army destroyed Xiàng.
At the meeting of Huái,
the Duke had business with the feudal lords
and had not yet returned
when they took Xiàng.
The people of Qí considered this a cause for punishment
and detained the Duke.
B5.17.4 In the autumn,
Shēng Jiāng, on account of the Duke,
met the Marquis of Qí at Biàn.
In the ninth month,
the Duke arrived.
The record states
“arrived from the meeting,”
to indicate that there was still business with the feudal lords,
and also to conceal the matter.
The Marquis of Qí had three principal wives:
Wáng Jī,
Xú Yíng,
and Cài Jī,
none of whom had a son.
The Marquis of Qí was fond of his harem
and had many favorites;
there were six favorites within the harem whose status was equal to that of a wife:
Elder Wèi Jī,
who bore Wǔmèng;
Younger Wèi Jī,
who bore Duke Huì;
Zhèng Jī,
who bore Duke Xiào;
Gè Yíng,
who bore Duke Zhāo;
Mì Jī,
who bore Duke Yì;
and Huázǐ of Sòng,
who bore Prince Yōng.
The Duke and Guǎn Zhòng had entrusted Duke Xiào to Duke Xiāng of Sòng
to be the crown prince.
Yōng Wū had favor with Elder Wèi Jī
and, through the eunuch Shìrén Diāo,
presented delicacies to the Duke
and also gained favor.
The Duke promised them to establish Wǔmèng.
When Guǎn Zhòng died,
the five princes all sought to be established.
In the winter, in the tenth month, on the day yǐhài,
Duke Huán of Qí died.
Yì Yá entered
and, with Shìrén Diāo, relied on the harem favorites
to kill the various officials
and establish Prince Wúkuī.
Duke Xiào fled to Sòng.
In the twelfth month, on the day yǐhài,
the announcement of death was made.
On the day xīnsì,
the coffin was placed in the hall at night.
A5.18 The Annals of the Eighteenth Year of Duke Xī
A5.18.1 In the spring of the eighteenth year,
the royal first month,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the people of Wèi,
and the people of Zhū attacked Qí.
A5.18.2 In the summer,
the army rescued Qí.
A5.18.3 In the fifth month, on the day wùyín,
the army of Sòng and the army of Qí fought at Yǎn.
The army of Qí was signally defeated.
A5.18.4 The Dí rescued Qí.
A5.18.5 In the autumn, the eighth month, on the day dīnghài,
buried Duke Huán of Qí.
A5.18.6 In the winter,
the people of Xíng
and the people of Dí attacked Wèi.
B5.18 Commentary on the Eighteenth Year of Duke Xī
B5.18.1 In the spring of the eighteenth year,
Duke Xiāng of Sòng led the feudal lords to attack Qí.
In the third month,
the people of Qí killed Wúkuī.
B5.18.2 The Earl of Zhèng for the first time went to court in Chǔ.
The Viscount of Chǔ bestowed metal upon him;
soon after, he regretted it
and made a covenant with him, saying:
“Do not use it to cast weapons!”
Therefore, he used it to cast three bells.
B5.18.3 The people of Qí intended to establish Duke Xiào
but were not a match for the followers of the four princes;
they subsequently fought with the people of Sòng.
In the summer, in the fifth month,
Sòng defeated the army of Qí at Yǎn,
established Duke Xiào, and returned.
In the autumn, in the eighth month,
they buried Duke Huán of Qí.
B5.18.4 In winter,
the people of Xíng
and the Dí people invaded Wèi,
besieging Tùpǔ.
The Lord of Wèi offered to cede the state to his paternal uncles, elder and younger brothers, and sons.
When he assembled the masses,
he said,
"If anyone can govern it,
I, Huǐ, request to follow him."
The masses would not agree,
and only then did he station the army at Zǐlóu.
The Dí army withdrew.
B5.18.5 The Earl of Liáng expanded his state
but could not populate it.
He named it Xīnlǐ,
and Qín took it.
A5.19 The Annals of the Nineteenth Year of Duke Xī.
A5.19.1 In the spring of the nineteenth year,
in the third month of the King’s calendar,
the people of Sòng seized Viscount Yīng Qí of Téng.
A5.19.2 In summer, in the sixth month,
the Duke of Sòng,
the people of Cáo,
and the people of Zhù made a covenant at Cáonán.
A5.19.3 The Viscount of Zēng met for a covenant at Zhù.
On the day Qǐyǒu,
the people of Zhù seized the Viscount of Zēng
and sacrificed him.
A5.19.4 In autumn,
the people of Sòng besieged Cáo.
A5.19.5 The people of Wèi invaded Xíng.
A5.19.6 In winter,
they met with the people of Chén,
the people of Cài,
the people of Chǔ,
and the people of Zhèng for a covenant at Qí.
A5.19.7 Liáng perished.
B5.19 The Commentary on the Nineteenth Year of Duke Xī.
B5.19.1 In the spring of the nineteenth year,
they finally walled it and resided there.
B5.19.2 The people of Sòng seized Duke Xuān of Téng.
B5.19.3 In summer,
the Duke of Sòng made Duke Wén of Zhù sacrifice the Viscount of Zēng at the altar of Cìsuī,
wishing thereby to make the Dōngyí submit.
Sīmǎ Zǐyú said:
“In antiquity, the six types of domestic animals were not used to sacrifice for one another,
and for small matters, one did not use a large sacrificial animal;
how much more would one dare to use a human?
Sacrifices are performed for the sake of people.
People are the masters of the spirits.
If you use a human,
who would enjoy the offering?
Duke Huán of Qí preserved three states that had perished
to bring the feudal lords into submission,
yet righteous men still said his virtue was thin.
Now, in a single meeting,
you treat the rulers of two states with cruelty
