and further use them to sacrifice to licentious and dark spirits—
if you seek hegemony by this means,
will it not be difficult?
To obtain a natural death would be a stroke of luck.”
B5.19.4 In autumn,
the people of Wèi invaded Xíng
to retaliate for the campaign at Tùpǔ.
At this time, there was a great drought in Wèi.
Divination was made regarding performing rites to the mountains and rivers,
but it was not auspicious.
Nìng Zhuāngzǐ said:
“Formerly when Zhōu suffered famine,
it conquered Yīn and the year became bountiful.
Now Xíng is currently without the Way,
and the feudal lords have no leader.
Perhaps Heaven wishes to have Wèi punish Xíng?”
This advice was followed.
When the army was raised, it rained.
B5.19.5 The people of Sòng besieged Cáo,
to punish it for not submitting.
Zǐyú said to the Duke of Sòng:
“King Wén heard that the state of Chóng was in moral disorder and invaded it.
The army stayed for thirty days but they did not surrender.
He withdrew to cultivate his teachings and then invaded again;
they surrendered before the ramparts.
The Book of Odes says:
‘His example was for his own wife,
reaching to his brothers,
and so he governed his family and state.’
Now, might there not still be some deficiency in your virtue?
Yet you invade others;
what of that?
Why not for a while internally examine your virtue!
Act only after there is no deficiency.”
B5.19.6 Duke Mù of Chén requested to cultivate good relations with the feudal lords,
so as not to forget the virtue of Duke Huán of Qí.
In winter,
they made a covenant at Qí,
to cultivate the good relations of Duke Huán.
B5.19.7 Liáng perished.
Its ruler is not recorded,
for he brought it upon himself.
Initially,
the Earl of Liáng was fond of earthworks;
he frequently built walls but did not occupy them.
The people were exhausted and could not bear it;
then he said,
“Some bandits are about to arrive.”
He then dug ditches around the lord’s palace
and said,
“Qín is about to surprise us.”
The people were terrified and collapsed;
Qín then took Liáng.
A5.20 The Annals of the Twentieth Year of Duke Xī.
A5.20.1 In the spring of the twentieth year,
the South Gate was newly built.
A5.20.2 In summer,
the scion of Gào came for an audience.
A5.20.3 On the day Yǐsì of the fifth month,
the West Palace suffered a fire.
A5.20.4 The people of Zhèng entered Huá.
A5.20.5 In autumn,
the people of Qí
and the Dí people made a covenant at Xíng.
A5.20.6 In winter,
the people of Chǔ invaded Suí.
B5.20 The Commentary on the Twentieth Year of Duke Xī.
B5.20.1 In the spring of the twentieth year,
the South Gate was newly built.
This was recorded
because it was not at the proper time.
Whenever opening
or closing,
one should follow the seasons.
B5.20.2 The people of Huá rebelled against Zhèng
and submitted to Wèi.
In summer,
the Noble Scion Shì of Zhèng
and Xiè Dǔkòu led an army to enter Huá.
B5.20.3 In autumn,
Qí and the Dí made a covenant at Xíng,
to plan against the difficulties Wèi was causing Xíng.
At this time, Wèi was just then harassing Xíng.
B5.20.4 Suí led the feudal lords to the east of the Hàn River to rebel against Chǔ.
In winter,
Dòu Gǔyūtù of Chǔ led an army to invade Suí,
reached a settlement, and returned.
The superior man says:
“Suí’s being invaded
was due to not measuring its own strength.
If one acts after measuring one’s strength,
errors will be few.
Whether success or failure is good, it depends on oneself;
does it depend on others?
The Book of Odes says:
‘Should I not be out early and late?
But I say the dew on the path is too much.’”
B5.20.5 Duke Xiāng of Sòng wished to assemble the feudal lords.
Zāng Wénzhòng heard of this
and said,
“If one follows others with one’s desires,
then it is possible;
if one makes others follow one's desires,
success is rare.”
A5.21 The Annals of the Twenty-first Year of Duke Xī.
A5.21.1 In the spring of the twenty-first year,
the Dí invaded Wèi.
A5.21.2 The people of Sòng,
the people of Qí,
and the people of Chǔ made a covenant at Lùshàng.
A5.21.3 In summer,
there was a great drought.
A5.21.4 In autumn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Viscount of Chǔ,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Cài,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Baron of Xǔ,
and the Earl of Cáo met at Yú.
They seized the Duke of Sòng in order to invade Sòng.
A5.21.5 Winter,
the Duke attacked Zhū.
A5.21.6 The people of Chǔ sent Yí Shēn to present the spoils of victory.
A5.21.7 In the twelfth month, on the day guǐchǒu,
the Duke met the feudal lords to covenant at Bó,
and released the Duke of Sòng.
B5.21 *The Zǔo Commentary: Twenty-first Year of Duke Xī*
B5.21.1 In the spring of the twenty-first year,
the people of Sòng made a covenant at Lùshàng
to seek the leadership of the feudal lords from Chǔ.
The people of Chǔ agreed to it.
Gōngzǐ Mùyí said:
“For a small state to struggle for the leadership of a covenant
is a calamity.
Sòng will likely perish!
It is fortunate if it only meets defeat later.”
B5.21.2 In the summer,
there was a great drought.
The Duke wanted to burn a shamaness
and a cripple.
Zāng Wénzhòng said:
“That is not a preparation for drought.
Repairing the inner and outer city walls,
reducing meals,
being economical in expenditures,
attending to the harvest,
and encouraging sharing—
these are the priorities.
What can the shamaness and the cripple do?
If Heaven wanted to kill them,
it would have been better not to give them life;
if they are able to cause drought,
burning them would only make it worse.”
The Duke followed his advice.
That year,
there was famine but it did not cause great harm.
B5.21.3 In the autumn,
the feudal lords met the Duke of Sòng at Yú.
Zǐyú said:
“The calamity will probably be right here!
The Lord’s desires are excessive;
how can anyone endure it?”
Thereupon, Chǔ seized the Duke of Sòng to attack Sòng.
In the winter,
they met at Bó to release him.
Zǐyú said:
“The calamity is not yet over;
it was not enough to punish the Lord.”
Sù, Xūjù,
and Zhuānyú
were of the Fēng surname;
they actually presided over the sacrifices to Tàihào and the Jì River,
in order to serve the Zhūxià.
The people of Zhū destroyed Xūjù.
The Lord of Xūjù came as a refugee,
because of Chéng Fēng.
Chéng Fēng spoke to the Duke on his behalf,
saying:
“To honor the illustrious sacrifices
and protect the small and weak
is the ritual of Zhōu;
for the Barbarians to harass the Chinese states
is the calamity of Zhōu.
If you restore Xūjù,
this honors Tàihào
and the Jì
and restores the sacrifices,
thereby averting calamity.”
A5.22 *The Annals: Twenty-second Year of Duke Xī*
A5.22.1 In the spring of the twenty-second year,
the Duke attacked Zhū
and took Xūjù.
A5.22.2 In the summer,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Baron of Xǔ,
and the Viscount of Téng attacked Zhèng.
A5.22.3 In the autumn, in the eighth month, on the day dīngwèi,
there was a battle with the people of Zhū at Shēngjīng.
A5.22.4 In the winter, in the eleventh month, on the day jǐsì, the first day of the month,
the Duke of Sòng and the people of Chǔ fought at Hóng;
the army of Sòng was utterly defeated.
B5.22 *The Zǔo Commentary: Twenty-second Year of Duke Xī*
B5.22.1 In the spring of the twenty-second year,
he attacked Zhū
and took Xūjù,
returning its ruler there;
this was in accordance with ritual.
B5.22.2 In the third month,
the Earl of Zhèng went to Chǔ.
B5.22.3 In the summer,
the Duke of Sòng attacked Zhèng.
Zǐyú said:
“What was called calamity is here.”
B5.22.4 Formerly,
when Píng Wáng moved to the east,
Xīn Yǒu went to Yīchuān
and saw someone with unbound hair sacrificing in the wilds.
He said:
“In less than a hundred years,
this will be the land of the Róng!
Their rituals have already perished.”
In the autumn,
Qín
and Jìn moved the Lùhún Róng to Yīchuān.
B5.22.5 Crown Prince Yǔ of Jìn was a hostage in Qín;
when he was about to flee back,
he said to Lady Yíng:
“Will you return with me?”
She replied:
“You,
the Crown Prince of Jìn,
suffered humiliation in Qín.
Your desire to return
is surely appropriate.
My lord sent me, his humble servant, to serve you with towel and comb
in order to steady you.
To follow you and return
would be to abandon my lord’s command.
I do not dare follow you,
nor do I dare speak of it.”
He then fled back.
B5.22.6 Fù Chén spoke to the King, saying:
“I pray you recall Tàishū.
The *Shī* says:
‘Harmonize and associate with neighbors,
and marriage relations will be very close.’
If we brothers are not in harmony,
how can we complain that the feudal lords are not at peace?”
The King was pleased.
Prince Dài returned from Qí to the capital,
as the King had summoned him.
B5.22.7 Because of the Xūjù incident, the people of Zhū
sent out an army.
The Duke held Zhū in contempt,
and resisted them without making preparations.
Zāng Wénzhòng said:
“No state is too small
to be treated lightly.
Without preparation,
even if numerous,
one cannot be relied upon.
The *Shī* says:
‘Apprehensive and careful,
as if on the brink of a deep abyss,
as if treading on thin ice.’
It also says:
‘Be reverent, be reverent!
Heaven is clearly manifest;
its mandate is not easily kept!’
Even with the brilliant virtue of the former kings,
there was nothing they did not find difficult,
nothing they did not fear—
how much more so for our small state!
May your Lordship not say that Zhū is small;
even a wasp or scorpion has poison,
how much more so a state!”
He did not listen.
In the eighth month, on the day dīngwèi,
the Duke and the army of Zhū fought at Shēngjīng,
and our army was utterly defeated.
The people of Zhū captured the Duke’s helmet
and hung it on the Yúmén.
B5.22.8 The people of Chǔ attacked Sòng to save Zhèng.
The Duke of Sòng was about to fight,
and the Grand Minister of War Gù remonstrated, saying:
“Heaven abandoned Shāng long ago;
if your Lordship tries to revive it,
it cannot be forgiven.”
He did not listen.
In the winter, the eleventh month, on the day jǐsì, the first day of the month,
the Duke of Sòng and the people of Chǔ fought at Hóng.
The people of Sòng had already formed their ranks,
while the people of Chǔ had not yet finished crossing the river.
The Minister of War said:
“They are many and we are few;
while they have not finished crossing,
I pray we strike them.”
The Duke said:
“It is not permitted.”
Once they had crossed but not yet formed their ranks,
he spoke to him again.
The Duke said:
“Not yet.”
Only after they were arrayed did he strike them,
and the army of Sòng was utterly defeated.
The Duke was wounded in the thigh.
The palace guards were wiped out.
The people of the state all blamed the Duke.
The Lord said:
“A superior man does not wound again one who is already wounded,
nor does he take prisoner those with graying hair.
In the military practices of the ancients,
they did not rely on narrow passes or obstacles.
Although I am but the remnant of a fallen state,
I will not sound the drums before the enemy has formed their ranks.”
Zǐyú said:
“You do not yet know war.
With a powerful enemy,
if they are in a narrow pass and not yet in formation,
that is Heaven assisting us.
To drum and attack them while they are obstructed,
is that not fitting?
Even then, one should still have apprehension.
Moreover, those who are strong today
are all our enemies.
Even if they are as old as the elderly,
if we capture them, we take them;
what concern is there for graying hair?
To make clear the sense of shame and
to teach warfare
is for the purpose of killing the enemy.
If a wound has not yet caused death,
why not wound again?
If one cherishes the idea of not wounding again,
then it is as if one should not wound at all;
if one cherishes those with graying hair,
then it is as if one should submit to them.
The three armies are used for what is advantageous;
the gongs and drums are for making sound and raising spirit.
To use what is advantageous,
it is acceptable to attack at a narrow pass;
when the sound is full and the will is focused,
it is acceptable to drum against a disorganized enemy.”
B5.22.9 On the morning of bǐngzǐ,
the wives of Zhèng Wén Gōng, the Lady Mǐ and
the Lady Jiāng, welcomed the Viscount of Chǔ at Kēzé.
The Viscount of Chǔ had Shī Jìn show them the captives and the cut-off left ears.
The superior man said:
“This was not in accordance with ritual.
Women should not go outside the gate to see off or welcome guests;
even when seeing brothers, they should not cross the threshold;
military matters should not be brought near women’s utensils.”
On dīngchǒu,
the Viscount of Chǔ entered Zhèng to be feasted.
There were nine offerings of wine,
the gifts in the courtyard were in hundreds,
and six types of additional bamboo and wooden vessels were added.
When the feast ended,
he left at night.
Wén Mǐ escorted him to the army.
He took two ladies of the Jī clan from Zhèng and returned.
Shū Zhān said:
“The King of Chǔ will likely not die a natural death!
In performing rituals, he ended by having no distinctions.
Having no distinctions cannot be called ritual.
How will he die a natural death?”
Because of this, the feudal lords knew he would not ultimately achieve hegemony.
A5.23 Classic of Lord Xī, Twenty-Third Year
A5.23.1 In the spring of the twenty-third year,
the Marquis of Qí attacked Sòng
and besieged Mín.
A5.23.2 In the summer, the fifth month, on gēngyín,
Zīfǔ, the Duke of Sòng, died.
A5.23.3 In the autumn,
the people of Chǔ attacked Chén.
A5.23.4 In the winter, the eleventh month,
the Master of Qǐ died.
B5.23 Commentary of Lord Xī, Twenty-Third Year
B5.23.1 In the spring of the twenty-third year,
the Marquis of Qí attacked Sòng
and besieged Mín
to punish them for not participating in the covenant in Qí.
B5.23.2 In the summer, the fifth month,
Sòng Xiāng Gōng died,
because of the wound he received at Hóng.
B5.23.3 In the autumn,
Chéng Déchén of Chǔ led an army to attack Chén,
to punish them for having divided loyalties toward Sòng.
He then took Jiāo
and Yí,
walled Dùn, and returned.
Zǐwén considered this to be his merit
and made him Lìngyǐn.
Shūbó said:
“What will you do about the state?”
He replied:
“I do this to stabilize the state.
If one has great merit
but does not have a high office,
of such people who can remain tranquil,
how many are there?”
B5.23.4 In the ninth month,
Jìn Huì Gōng died.
Huái Gōng was established.
He ordered that no one should follow those in exile.
He set a time limit;
if they did not arrive within the limit,
there would be no pardon.
Hú Tū’s sons Máo and Yǎn were following Zhòng’ěr in Qín,
and they were not recalled.
In the winter,
Huái Gōng seized Hú Tū
and said:
“If your sons come, you will be spared.”
He replied:
“That a son is able to serve in office
because his father taught him loyalty
is the regulation of old.
To record one’s name on a tablet
and present a ritual gift
means that to have divided loyalty is a crime.
Now my sons’
names have been with Zhòng’ěr
for many years.
If I were to recall them now,
it would be teaching them to have divided loyalty.
If a father teaches his son to have divided loyalty,
how can he serve his lord?
That punishments are not excessive
is the lord’s brilliance
and the subject’s desire.
If excessive punishment is used to satisfy one’s desires,
who then would be without guilt?
I have heard your command.”
Then he was killed.
Bǔ Yǎn claimed illness and did not go out,
saying:
“The ‘Book of Zhōu’ has it:
‘Only when there is great brilliance
will people submit.’
He himself is not brilliant
and kills people to satisfy his desires;
is it not difficult then?
The people see no virtue
and hear only of executions;
what future can he have?”
B5.23.5 In the eleventh month,
Qǐ Chéng Gōng died.
The record says
‘the Master,’
because Qǐ
followed the customs of the Yí.
His personal name was not recorded
because he had not entered into a covenant.
In all cases where feudal lords have a covenant,
when one dies, the announcement of death includes the name;
this is the ritual.
If the name is announced,
then it is also recorded;
otherwise not,
to avoid recording what was not officially reported.
B5.23.6 When Zhòng’ěr, the Young Lord of Jìn, encountered trouble,
the people of Jìn attacked him at Púchéng.
The people of Púchéng wanted to fight,
but Zhòng’ěr would not allow it,
saying:
“I rely on the command of my lord and father
and enjoy the livelihood provided by him,
and it is through this that I have gained the support of the people.
To have people and then use them to resist him,
no crime is greater.
I shall flee.”
So he fled to the Dí.
Those following him were Hú Yǎn,
Zhào Shuāi,
Diān Jié,
Wèi Wǔzǐ, and
Sīkōng Jìzǐ.
The Dí attacked Qiángjiùrú
and captured two daughters,
Shū Kuí and
Jì Kuí,
and presented them to the Young Lord.
The Young Lord took Jì Kuí,
who gave birth to Bó Tiáo and
Shū Liú;
he gave Shū Kuí to Zhào Shuāi as a wife,
who gave birth to Dùn.
When he was about to go to Qí,
he said to Jì Kuí:
“Wait for me twenty-five years;
if I do not return, then you may remarry.”
She replied:
“I am already twenty-five years old;
if I wait another such period to remarry,
I will be going to my coffin.
I beg to wait for you.”
He stayed with the Dí for twelve years and then departed.
Passing through Wèi,
Wèi Wéngōng did not treat him with courtesy.
Departing from Wǔlù,
he begged for food from a rustic;
the rustic gave him a clod of earth.
The Gōngzǐ was angry
and wished to whip him.
Zǐ Fàn said:
"It is a gift from Tiān."
He bowed his head and received it
and carried it in his carriage.
Reaching Qí,
Qí Huángōng gave him a wife
and twenty teams of horses.
The Gōngzǐ was content there.
His followers thought this was not right.
When they were about to depart,
they plotted under a mulberry tree.
A silkworm servant was up in the tree
and told Jiāng Shì.
Jiāng Shì killed her
and said to the Gōngzǐ:
"You have ambitions for the four quarters;
as for the one who heard of them,
I have killed her."
The Gōngzǐ said:
"There is no such thing."
Jiāng said:
"Go!
To indulge in affection and ease
is truly to ruin one's reputation."
The Gōngzǐ would not agree.
Jiāng plotted with Zǐ Fàn
and sent him away after getting him drunk.
When he woke up,
he chased Zǐ Fàn with a halberd.
Reaching Cáo,
Cáo Gònggōng heard that his ribs were all in one piece
and wished to observe him naked.
While he was bathing,
he drew near and watched him.
The wife of Xī Fùjī said:
"I observe that the followers of the Jìn Gōngzǐ
are all sufficient to be Xiàngguó.
If he uses them as ministers,
this gentleman will certainly return to his state.
Returning to his state,
he will surely achieve his will among the Zhūhóu.
Achieving his will among the Zhūhóu
and punishing those who were discourteous,
Cáo will be the first.
Why do you not early on distinguish yourself from the others?"
Thereupon he presented a tray of food
and placed a jade disc in it.
The Gōngzǐ accepted the food and returned the jade disc.
Reaching Sòng,
Sòng Xiānggōng presented him with twenty teams of horses.
Reaching Zhèng,
Zhèng Wéngōng also did not treat him with courtesy.
Shū Zhān remonstrated, saying:
"I have heard that for those whom Tiān has opened the way,
other men cannot reach them.
The Jìn Gōngzǐ has three such signs;
Tiān perhaps intends to establish him;
Your Lordship should treat him with courtesy!
When a man and woman of the same surname marry,
their offspring do not flourish.
The Jìn Gōngzǐ
is born of the Jī clan,
yet has survived until now;
that is the first.
Despite the distress of exile,
Tiān has not given peace to the state of Jìn;
this likely means Tiān is about to open the way for him;
that is the second.
He has three officers
who are sufficient to be superior to other men
and follow him;
that is the third.
Jìn and Zhèng are of equal rank;
when a younger relative passes through,
one should naturally treat him with courtesy,
how much more so for one whom Tiān has opened the way!"
He did not listen.
Reaching Chǔ,
Chǔzǐ gave a banquet for him
and said:
"If the Gōngzǐ returns to the state of Jìn,
then with what will you repay Bùgǔ?"
He replied:
"Beautiful women, jade, and silks
are things Your Lordship already possesses;
feathers, hair,
ivory, and hides
are produced in Your Lordship's lands.
Those which flow to the state of Jìn
are merely Your Lordship's leftovers;
with what could I repay Your Lordship?"
The Viscount said:
"Even so,
with what would you repay me?"
He replied:
"If by Your Lordship's divine influence
I should return to the state of Jìn,
and if Jìn and Chǔ should mobilize their armies
and meet in the Zhōngyuán,
I will withdraw from Your Lordship by three stages of a march.
If then I do not receive your command to desist,
then with my left hand holding the whip and
the unstrung bow,
and with my right hand holding the quiver and
bow-case,
I shall maneuver against Your Lordship."
Zǐyù requested to kill him.
Chǔzǐ said:
"The Jìn Gōngzǐ is broad-minded yet frugal,
cultured yet courteous.
His followers are disciplined yet magnanimous,
loyal and capable.
The Jìnhóu has no kin,
and both those outside and inside the state dislike him.
I have heard that among those of the Jī surname,
the descendants of Táng Shū,
those who would later decline are the others;
will the revival not be through the Jìn Gōngzǐ!
When Tiān is about to raise someone up,
who can cast him down?
To oppose Tiān
must surely bring great disaster."
He then sent him to Qín.
Qínbó presented him five women,
among whom was Huái Yíng.
She held the pitcher to pour water for him to wash;
when he had finished, he waved her away.
She was angry
and said:
"Qín
and Jìn are equals;
why do you treat me as a social inferior?"
The Gōngzǐ was afraid,
stripped off his upper garment and submitted as a prisoner.
On another day,
the Jūn gave a banquet for him.
Zǐ Fàn said:
"I am not as cultured as Zhào Cuī;
I ask that Zhào Cuī be allowed to follow you."
The Gōngzǐ recited "Hé Shuǐ."
The Jūn recited "Liù Yuè."
Zhào Cuī said:
"Chóng'ěr, bow to thank him for his gift!"
The Gōngzǐ descended,
bowed, and touched his head to the ground;
the Jūn descended one step
to decline the honor.
Zhào Cuī said:
"Your Lordship has addressed Chóng'ěr with the mandate for assisting the Tiānzǐ;
how could Chóng'ěr dare not bow?"
A5.24 Xīgōng Èrshísì Nián Jīng
A5.24.1 In the spring of the twenty-fourth year,
in the Royal first month.
A5.24.2 In the summer,
the Dí attacked Zhèng.
A5.24.3 In the autumn,
in the seventh month.
A5.24.4 In the winter,
the Tiānwáng left his capital and resided in Zhèng.
A5.24.5 Jìnhóu Yíwú died.
B5.24 Xīgōng Èrshísì Nián Zhuàn
B5.24.1 In the spring of the twenty-fourth year,
in the Royal first month,
Qínbó escorted him back.
It is not recorded [in the Jīng]
because the entry was not formally announced.
When they reached the Hé,
Zǐ Fàn handed a jade disc to the Gōngzǐ,
saying:
"I have carried your bridle and halter
following my Jūn as you traveled throughout the world;
my offenses have been many.
Even I know this,
how much more so must my Jūn?
I ask to flee from here."
The Gōngzǐ said:
"If I do not remain of one heart with you, my Jiùshì,
may I be as this clear water!"
He threw the jade disc into the Hé.
They crossed the Hé,
besieged Lìnghú,
entered Sāngquán,
and took Jiùshuāi.
In the second month, on the day jiǎwǔ,
the army of Jìn encamped at Lúliǔ.
The Earl of Qín sent Gōngzǐ Zhí to the Jìn army.
The army retreated,
and encamped at Xún.
On the day xīnchǒu,
Hú Yǎn and the great officers of Qín
and Jìn made a covenant at Xún.
On the day rényín,
the Gōngzǐ joined the Jìn army.
On the day bǐngwǔ,
he entered Qǔwò.
On the day dīngwèi,
he entered Jiàng
and held court at the Wǔ Temple.
On the day wùshēn,
he had Huái Gōng killed at Gāoliáng.
This is not recorded,
also because it was not reported.
Lǚ
and Xì feared the pressure upon them,
and were about to burn the ducal palace and assassinate the Marquis of Jìn.
The eunuch Pī requested an audience.
The Duke sent someone to reprimand him,
and declined to see him,
saying:
"In the campaign of Púchéng,
your ruler ordered you to wait one night,
but you arrived immediately.
Later, when I followed the Lord of Dí
to hunt on the banks of the Wèi River,
you came on behalf of Huì Gōng seeking to kill me.
He ordered you to wait three nights,
but you arrived on the second night.
Although you had your ruler's orders,
why were you so quick?
The sleeve you cut off is still here.
Begone!"
He replied:
"I thought that when your Lordship entered the state,
you would have understood.
If you have not yet understood,
you will again encounter trouble.
A ruler's command is single;
that is the rule of old.
To remove what the ruler dislikes,
one only looks to one's strength.
The man of Pú
or the man of Dí,
what were they to me?
Now that your Lordship has ascended the throne,
are there no Pú
or Dí?
Huán Gōng of Qí set aside the matter of the arrow shot at his belt buckle
and made Guǎn Zhòng his chancellor.
If your Lordship acts differently,
why should I wait for an insulting command?
Many people are leaving;
is it only this punished official?"
The Duke saw him,
and he told of the trouble.
In the third month,
the Marquis of Jìn secretly met the Earl of Qín at Wángchéng.
On the day jǐchǒu, the last day of the month,
the ducal palace caught fire.
Xiá Shēng
and Xì Ruì did not capture the Duke,
so they went to the banks of the Hé,
where the Earl of Qín enticed and killed them.
The Marquis of Jìn welcomed back Lady Yíng and returned.
The Earl of Qín sent three thousand men as guards to Jìn,
who were truly servants of order and discipline.
Formerly,
the Marquis of Jìn's attendant Tóuxū,
who was in charge of the treasury,
when the Marquis went into exile,
stole the contents of the treasury and fled,
using it all to seek the Marquis's restoration.
When the Marquis entered,
he sought an audience.
The Duke declined on the grounds that he was washing his hair.
He said to the attendant:
"When washing the hair, the heart is turned upside down;
when the heart is turned upside down, one's plans are reversed.
It is only natural that I am not seen.
Those who stayed were the guardians of the state;
those who left were the servants of the horse's halter.
Both are acceptable.
Why must you blame those who stayed?
If a ruler of a state makes an enemy of a common man,
those who are fearful will be many."
The attendant reported this,
and the Duke immediately saw him.
The people of Dí returned Jì Wěi to Jìn
and requested to keep her two sons.
Wén Gōng gave Zhào Shuāi a wife,
who bore Yuán Tóng,
Bǐng Kuò,
and Lóu Yīng.
Zhào Jī requested to welcome Dùn and his mother,
but Zǐyú declined.
Lady Jī said:
"To obtain favor and forget the old,
how can one command people?
You must welcome them!"
She firmly requested it,
and he consented.
When they came,
she considered Dùn to be talented,
so she firmly requested of the Duke
to make him the legitimate heir,
and made her three sons rank below him.
She made Shū Wěi the primary wife
and placed herself below her.
The Marquis of Jìn rewarded those who followed him into exile;
Jiè Zhītuī did not speak of reward,
and no reward reached him.
Zhītuī said:
"Xiàn Gōng had nine sons;
only our Lord remains.
Huì and Huái had no close ones;
those inside and outside the state abandoned them.
Heaven has not yet cut off Jìn,
so there must be a ruler.
He who presides over the sacrifices of Jìn,
who could it be but our Lord?
Heaven indeed established him,
yet these gentlemen consider it their own effort;
is this not a deceit?
To steal someone's property
is called theft;
how much more so to be greedy for the achievement of Heaven
and consider it one's own power?
The inferiors regard their crimes as righteous,
and the superior rewards their treachery.
Superiors and inferiors deceive each other;
it is difficult to live with them."
His mother said:
"Why not also seek it?
If you die,
whom will you resent?"
He replied:
"To find fault and then imitate it,
the crime is even greater.
Furthermore, I have spoken words of resentment,
and I will not eat his food."
His mother said:
"At least let him know about it;
how about that?"
He replied:
"Speech
is the ornament of the person.
When the person is about to be hidden,
why use ornaments?
That would be seeking to be conspicuous."
His mother said:
"Can you truly be like this?
I will go into hiding with you."
They then went into hiding and died.
The Marquis of Jìn searched for him but did not find him.
He designated Miánshàng as his ritual field,
saying:
"To record my error
and to honor a good man."
B5.24.2 When Zhèng entered Huá
the people of Huá submitted to his command.
The army returned,
and they again turned to Wèi.
Gōngzǐ Shì of Zhèng
and Xièdǔ Yúmí led an army to attack Huá.
The King sent Bófú
and Yóu Sūnbó to Zhèng to request mercy for Huá.
The Earl of Zhèng was resentful that when Huì Wáng was restored,
he did not grant the cup of rank to Lì Gōng,
and was also resentful that Xiāng Wáng favored Wèi and Huá.
Therefore, he did not obey the King's command
and seized the two gentlemen.
The King was angry
and intended to attack Zhèng with the help of the Dí.
Fù Chén remonstrated, saying:
"It cannot be.
Your servant has heard:
In the highest antiquity, people were soothed by virtue;
next, by showing affection to relatives,
so that they reached out to one another.
Formerly, Zhōu Gōng lamented that the two uncles were not in harmony,
so he enfeoffed relatives
to serve as a screen to protect Zhōu.
Guǎn, Cài,
Chéng, Huò,
Lǔ, Wèi,
Máo, Dān,
Gào, Yōng,
Cáo, Téng,
Bì, Yuán,
Fēng, and Xún
were the Zhāo descendants of Wén."
Yú, Jìn,
Yìng, and Hán
are the descendants of King Wǔ.
Fán, Jiǎng,
Xíng, Mào,
Zuò, and Jì
are the descendants of Zhōu Gōng.
Shào Mù Gōng was concerned that the virtue of Zhōu was not consistent,
so he gathered the clan in Chéngzhōu
and composed a poem,
saying:
“The flowers of the cherry tree,
how brilliant are the calyx and bracts.
Of all the people today,
none are like brothers.”
Its fourth stanza says:
“Brothers quarrel within the walls,
but outside they resist insult.”
In this way,
even if brothers have small resentments,
they do not discard their fine kinship.
Now the Son of Heaven cannot endure a small resentment
and so abandons the kinship of Zhèng;
what can be done about it?
Rewarding merit, loving kin, being close to the intimate, and honoring the worthy
are the greatest of virtues.
Approaching the deaf, following the blind, associating with the obstinate, and employing the slanderous
are the greatest of evils.
Abandoning virtue
and exalting evil
are the greatest of calamities.
Zhèng has the merit of Kings
Píng and Huì,
and has the kinship of Kings
Lì and Xuān;
they have discarded favorites
and employed three worthy men;
among the various Jī states, they are close;
thus the four virtues are complete in them.
Ears that do not hear the harmony of the five sounds
are “deaf”;
eyes that do not distinguish the patterns of the five colors
are “blind”;
a heart that does not follow the canons of virtue and righteousness
is “obstinate”;
a mouth that does not speak words of loyalty and trust
is “slanderous.”
The Dí follow all of these;
thus the four evils are complete in them.
When Zhōu possessed admirable virtue,
they still said
“none are like brothers,”
so they established the feudal states.
In cherishing and soothing the world,
they still feared external insults;
of those who ward off insults,
none are like close kin,
so they used kin as a screen for Zhōu.
Shào Mù Gōng also said this.
Now that the virtue of Zhōu has declined,
if it further changes the ways of
Zhōu
and Shào
to follow various evils,
is this not impermissible?
The people have not forgotten the calamity,
yet the King rouses it again;
what will he do about the legacy of Wén
and Wǔ?”
The King did not listen
and sent Tuí Shū
and Táo Zǐ to lead out the Dí army.
In summer,
the Dí attacked Zhèng
and took Lì.
The King was grateful to the Dí people
and intended to make their daughter his Queen.
Fù Chén remonstrated, saying:
“It cannot be.
I have heard it said:
‘The one who repays grows weary,
but the one who bestows is never satisfied.’
The Dí are inherently greedy,
and the King further encourages them.
A woman’s power is limitless,
and a wife’s resentment never ends;
the Dí will surely become a disaster.”
The King again did not listen.
Previously,
Gān Zhāo Gōng was favored by Huì Hòu;
Huì Hòu intended to establish him,
but died before it happened.
Zhāo Gōng fled to Qí;
the King restored him,
but he had an illicit affair with the lady of the Kuí clan.
The King dismissed the lady of the Kuí clan.
Tuí Shū
and Táo Zǐ said:
“We were the ones who sent for the Dí;
the Dí will surely resent us.”
They then supported Dà Shū
to attack the King.
The King’s guards were about to resist them,
but the King said:
“What would my late mother say of me?
I would rather let the feudal lords deal with it.”
The King then went out,
and when he reached Kǎn Kǎn,
the people of the capital received him.
In autumn,
Tuí Shū
and Táo Zǐ supported Dà Shū with the Dí army to attack Zhōu,
heavily defeating the Zhōu army
and capturing Zhōu Gōng Jìfù,
Yuán Bó,
Máo Bó,
and Fù Chén.
The King went to Zhèng
and resided in Fàn.
Dà Shū resided in Wēn with the lady of the Kuí clan.
B5.24.3 Zǐ Zāng, the younger brother of Zhèng Zǐ Huá, fled to Sòng,
as he liked to collect kingfisher-feather caps.
The Earl of Zhèng heard of it and disliked it,
so he sent a bandit to lure him away.
In the eighth month,
the bandit killed him between Chén and Sòng.
The gentleman says:
“If one’s attire is inappropriate,
it brings disaster to oneself.
The Shī says:
‘That person there,
does not match his robes.’
Zǐ Zāng’s end
was due to his mismatch!
The Shī says:
‘Bringing sorrow upon oneself,’
which refers to Zǐ Zāng.
The Xià Shū says:
‘The earth is leveled and the heavens perfected,’
which means things are in proportion.”
B5.24.4 Sòng made peace with Chǔ,
and Duke Chéng of Sòng went to Chǔ.
On his return,
he entered Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng was going to host a feast for him
and asked Huáng Wǔ Zǐ about the rites.
He replied:
“Sòng
is the descendant of the previous dynasty;
to Zhōu, they are guests.
When the Son of Heaven has a sacrifice,
he sends them the sacrificial meat;
when there is a mourning,
he bows to them.
A lavish and generous reception is appropriate.”
The Earl of Zhèng followed this,
and in hosting the Duke of Sòng,
he added extra honors,
which was ritual propriety.
B5.24.5 In winter,
the King sent an envoy to announce the distress,
saying:
“I, the Unworthy One, lack virtue
and have offended the favored Zǐ Dài, my younger brother by the same mother.
I am now in the border area of Zhèng at Fàn;
I dare to inform you, my Uncle.”
Zàng Wén Zhòng replied:
“The Son of Heaven is covered in dust abroad;
how could I not rush to inquire about my official duties?”
The King sent Jiǎn Shī Fù to inform Jìn
and sent Zuǒ Yān Fù to inform Qín.
The Son of Heaven does not “go out,”
but the Record says,
“The Heavenly King went out and resided in Zhèng,”
because he was avoiding the difficulty caused by his younger brother.
The Son of Heaven wearing mourning clothes
and using a humble name
was ritual propriety.
B5.24.6 The Earl of Zhèng, along with Kǒng Jiāngchú,
Shí Jiǎfù,
and Hóu Xuānduō, inspected the officials
and provisions at Fàn,
and only then attended to his private administration;
this was ritual propriety.
B5.24.7 The people of Wèi were going to attack Xíng.
Lǐ Zhì said:
“If one does not gain access to its defenses,
the state cannot be taken.
I request that my brothers take office there.”
They then went
and gained office.
A5.25 Annals of Duke Xī, Twenty-fifth Year
A5.25.1 In the twenty-fifth year, in spring,
in the King’s first month, on the day bǐngwǔ,
the Marquis of Wèi, Huǐ, destroyed Xíng.
A5.25.2 In summer, in the fourth month, on the day guǐyǒu,
the Marquis of Wèi, Huǐ, died.
A5.25.3 Dàng Bó Jī of Sòng came to meet a bride.
A5.25.4 Sòng killed its Grand Master.
A5.25.5 Autumn,
the men of Chǔ besieged Chén
and escorted the Viscount of Dùn back to Dùn.
A5.25.6 Lord Wén of Wèi was buried.
A5.25.7 Winter, the twelfth month, on the day *guǐhài*,
the Lord met with the Master of Wèi and
Jǔ Qìng;
they made a covenant at Táo.
B5.25 The Commentary on the Twenty-fifth Year of Lord Xī
B5.25.1 In the spring of the twenty-fifth year,
the men of Wèi attacked Xíng.
The two Lǐ followed Guó Zǐ
on an inspection of the city walls,
seized him under their arms to throw him outside,
and killed him.
In the first month, on the day *bǐngwǔ*,
the Marquis of Wèi, Huǐ, extinguished Xíng.
They were of the same surname;
therefore, his name was recorded.
Lǐ Zhì made an inscription
which said:
"I seized and killed Guó Zǐ,
and none dared stop me."
B5.25.2 The Earl of Qín stationed his army on the banks of the Hé,
intending to restore the King.
Hú Yǎn said to the Lord of Jìn:
"To seek the leadership of the feudal lords,
nothing is better than serving the King.
The lords will trust it,
and it is also a great righteous cause.
To continue the legacy of King Wén
and spread your trustworthiness among the lords,
now is the time."
He had Bǔ Yǎn perform divination by tortoise shell,
who said:
"It is auspicious.
It is the omen of Huáng Dì's battle at Bǎnquán."
The Lord said:
"I am not equal to that."
The reply was:
"The rituals of Zhōu have not changed;
the King of today
is the Thearch of old."
The Lord said:
"Perform milfoil divination!"
He divined by milfoil
and encountered the hexagram *Dà Yǒu* changing to *Kuí*.
He said:
"It is auspicious.
You have encountered
the hexagram 'The Duke holds a feast for the Son of Heaven'
indeed.
To be victorious in battle and have the King host a feast—
what could be more auspicious?
Moreover, in this hexagram,
Heaven acts as a marsh to face the Sun;
the Son of Heaven humbles his heart to welcome the Lord—
is this not also acceptable?
*Dà Yǒu* goes to *Kuí* and returns;
it is indeed in its proper place."
The Lord of Jìn declined the Qín army
and went downstream.
In the third month, on the day *jiǎchén*,
he halted at Yángfán;
the Right Army besieged Wēn,
while the Left Army welcomed the King.
In the summer, the fourth month, on the day *dīngsì*,
the King entered Wángchéng.
They captured Dàshū at Wēn
and killed him at Xíchéng.
On the day *wùwǔ*,
the Lord of Jìn had an audience with the King.
The King hosted a feast with sweet wine
and commanded that he be rewarded.
He requested a burial tunnel,
but was not granted it.
The King said:
"It is a royal emblem.
Since there is no successor of virtue
and yet there are two Kings,
this is also what you, Uncle, would dislike."
He gave him the fields of Yángfán, Wēn, Yuán, and Cuánmáo.
Jìn then began its opening of Nányáng.
Yángfán did not submit,
so they besieged it.
Cāng Gé shouted:
"Virtue is used to soothe the central states,
and punishment to overawe the four barbarian tribes.
It is right that I dare not submit.
Among these people, who is not a relative of the King?
Should they be made captives?"
Thereupon they let the people depart.
B5.25.3 Autumn,
Qín and Jìn attacked Ruò.
Dòu Kè and Qū Yùkòu of Chǔ, with troops from Shēn and Xī, garrisoned Shāngmì.
The men of Qín passed Xī and entered through the bends,
where they bound the carriage attendants
to besiege Shāngmì,
approaching the walls at dusk.
At night,
they dug a pit, smeared blood, and laid out a document,
pretending to have made a covenant with Zǐyí and Zǐbiān.
The people of Shāngmì were terrified
and said:
"Qín has taken Xī!
The garrison has turned against us!"
Thereupon they surrendered to the Qín army.
The Qín army captured Zǐyí of Shēn and Zǐbiān of Xī and returned.
The Chief Minister of Chǔ, Zǐyù, pursued the Qín army,
but could not catch them.
He then besieged Chén
and escorted the Viscount of Dùn back to Dùn.
B5.25.4 Winter,
the Lord of Jìn besieged Yuán
and ordered three days' worth of rations.
Yuán did not surrender,
so he ordered a withdrawal.
A spy came out
and said:
"Yuán is about to surrender."
The military officers said:
"Please wait for them."
The Lord said:
"Trust
is the treasure of a state,
and that which the people rely on for protection.
If I gain Yuán but lose trust,
how can I protect them?
What would be lost is far more."
He withdrew one stage,
and then Yuán surrendered.
He moved the Earl of Yuán, Guàn, to Jì.
Zhào Shuāi became the Grand Master of Yuán,
and Hú Zhēn became the Grand Master of Wēn.
B5.25.5 The men of Wèi brokered peace between Jǔ and us.
In the twelfth month,
they covenanted at Táo,
renewing the friendly relations of Lord Wén of Wèi
and making peace with Jǔ.
B5.25.6 The Lord of Jìn asked the eunuch Bó Dī about the guard of Yuán.
He replied:
"In the past, Zhào Shuāi followed you with a pot of food;
he was starving on the road but did not eat it."
Therefore, he was sent to reside in Yuán.
A5.26 The Annals of the Twenty-sixth Year of Lord Xī
A5.26.1 In the spring of the twenty-sixth year,
the royal first month,
on the day *jǐwèi*,
the Lord met with the Viscount of Jǔ and
Nìng Sù of Wèi; they made a covenant at Xiàng.
A5.26.2 Men of Qí invaded our western borders.
The Lord pursued the Qí army
as far as Xī,
but could not catch them.
A5.26.3 Summer,
men of Qí attacked our northern borders.
A5.26.4 Men of Wèi attacked Qí.
A5.26.5 Gōngzǐ Suì went to Chǔ to request troops.
A5.26.6 Autumn,
the men of Chǔ extinguished Kuí
and returned with the Viscount of Kuí.
A5.26.7 Winter,
the men of Chǔ attacked Sòng
and besieged Mín.
The Lord, with the Chǔ army, attacked Qí
and took Gǔ.
A5.26.8 The Lord arrived from the attack on Qí.
B5.26 The Commentary on the Twenty-sixth Year of Lord Xī
B5.26.1 In the spring of the twenty-sixth year,
the royal first month,
the Lord met with Duke Zī Pī of Jǔ and
Nìng Zhuāngzǐ,
and they made a covenant at Xiàng,
renewing the covenant of Táo.
B5.26.2 The Qí army invaded our western borders
to punish us for these two covenants.
B5.26.3 In summer,
Qí Xiào Gōng attacked our northern border.
The people of Wèi attacked Qí
because of the covenant at Táo.
The Duke sent Zhǎn Xǐ to reward the army
after having him receive instructions from Zhǎn Qín.
Before the Marquis of Qí entered the border,
Zhǎn Xǐ went to meet him
and said:
"My unworthy ruler heard that your Lordship has personally lifted your jade feet
to visit our humble state,
and has sent me, his humble servant, to reward your attendants."
The Marquis of Qí said:
"Are the people of Lǔ afraid?"
He replied:
"The common people are afraid,
but the superior men are not."
The Marquis of Qí said:
"Your houses are like hanging musical stones,
and there is no green grass in the fields.
On what do you rely that you are not afraid?"
He replied:
"We rely on the mandate of the former kings.
Formerly, Zhōu Gōng
and Tàigōng
were the limbs and heart of the Zhōu house
and assisted King Chéng.
King Chéng rewarded their labors
and granted them a covenant,
saying:
'Let your descendants from generation to generation
do no harm to one another!'
This was recorded in the Covenant Office,
and the Grand Master was in charge of it.
Huán Gōng, for this reason, assembled the feudal lords
to settle their disagreements,
mended their deficiencies,
and rescued them from their disasters,
thus making manifest the old duties.
When your Lordship ascended the throne,
the hope of the feudal lords was:
'May he continue the achievements of Huán!'
Our humble state therefore did not dare to fortify or gather resources,
saying:
'How could he, in the ninth year of his succession,
abandon the mandate and neglect his duties?
What would he do about his late father?
Your Lordship certainly would not do this.'
Relying on this, we are not afraid."
The Marquis of Qí then returned.
B5.26.4 Dōngmén Xiāngzhòng
and Zāng Wénzhòng went to Chǔ to request an army.
Zāngsūn saw Zǐyù
and persuaded him to attack Qí
and Sòng,
because they were not acting as subjects.
B5.26.5 The Viscount of Kuí did not sacrifice to Zhùróng and Yùxióng;
the people of Chǔ rebuked him.
He replied:
"Our former king Xióng Zhì had an illness
from which the spirits would not absolve him,
so he fled to Kuí on his own.
Because of this, we lost our status in Chǔ;
what then is there to sacrifice?"
In autumn,
Chǔ Chéng Déchén
and Dòu Yíshēn led an army and destroyed Kuí,
taking the Viscount of Kuí back with them.
B5.26.6 Because Sòng was on good terms with the Marquis of Jìn,
it rebelled against Chǔ and turned to Jìn.
In winter,
the Chǔ Chancellor Zǐyù
and Marshal Zǐxī
led an army to attack Sòng
and besieged Mǐn.
The Duke used the Chǔ army to attack Qí
and took Gǔ.
Whenever an army
can be directed as one wishes, it is called
"to use" (yǐ).
They placed Huán Gōng's son Yōng in Gǔ;
Yìyá supported him to serve as a support for Lǔ.
Shùhóu, the Chǔ Governor of Shēn, guarded it.
Seven of Huán Gōng's sons
became grandees in Chǔ.
A5.27 《The Annals of the Twenty-seventh Year of Duke Xī》
A5.27.1 In the spring of the twenty-seventh year,
the Viscount of Qǐ came for an audience.
A5.27.2 In summer, in the sixth month, on the day Gēngyín,
Zhāo, the Marquis of Qí, died.
A5.27.3 In autumn, in the eighth month, on the day Yǐwèi,
Qí Xiào Gōng was buried.
A5.27.4 On the day Yǐsì,
the Duke's son Suì led an army and entered Qǐ.
A5.27.5 In winter,
the people of Chǔ,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Cài,
the Earl of Zhèng,
and the Baron of Xǔ besieged Sòng.
A5.27.6 In the twelfth month, on the day Jiǎxū,
the Duke met with the feudal lords
and made a covenant at Sòng.
B5.27 《The Commentary of the Twenty-seventh Year of Duke Xī》
B5.27.1 In the spring of the twenty-seventh year,
Huán Gōng of Qǐ came for an audience.
Because he used the rites of the Yí,
he was called "Viscount."
The Duke looked down on Qǐ
because Qǐ was not respectful.
B5.27.2 In summer,
Qí Xiào Gōng died.
Although there was a grudge against Qí,
the funeral observances were not abandoned,
which was according to ritual.
B5.27.3 In autumn,
the entry into Qǐ
was to punish their lack of ritual.
B5.27.4 The Viscount of Chǔ was about to besiege Sòng.
He sent Zǐwén to train the troops at Kuí.
The training was finished by the end of the morning,
and not a single man was executed.
Zǐyù again trained the troops at Wěi.
It took a whole day to finish;
he whipped seven men
and pierced the ears of three men.
The elders of the state all congratulated Zǐwén.
Zǐwén gave them wine to drink.
Wěi Jiǎ was still young;
he arrived late
and did not offer congratulations.
Zǐwén asked him about it.
He replied:
"I do not know what there is to congratulate.
When you transferred the government to Zǐyù,
you said:
'It is to bring peace to the state.'
If he brings peace within but meets defeat without,
how much will be gained?
Zǐyù's defeat
will be of your making.
If you promoted him and the state is defeated,
what is there to congratulate?
Zǐyù is headstrong and lacks ritual;
he cannot be used to govern the people.
If he has more than three hundred chariots,
he will not be able to return with them.
If he should return and I congratulate you,
what would be the harm in being late?"
In winter,
the Viscount of Chǔ and the feudal lords besieged Sòng.
Gōngsūn Gù of Sòng went to Jìn
to report the emergency.
Xiān Zhěn said:
"Requiting favors,
rescuing from distress,
gaining prestige,
and establishing hegemony—
all depend on this."
Hú Yǎn said:
"Chǔ has just gained Cáo
and has recently formed a marriage alliance with Wèi.
If we attack Cáo
and Wèi,
Chǔ will certainly go to their rescue,
and then Qí
and Sòng will be relieved."
Thereupon a hunt was held at Bèlú,
three armies were formed,
and a commander-in-chief was sought.
Zhào Shuāi said:
"Xì Gǔ will do.
I have often heard his words;
he delights in the Rites
and Music
and is devoted to the Shī and Shū.
The Shī and Shū
are the treasury of righteousness;
the Rites and Music
are the regulations of virtue;
virtue and righteousness
are the root of profit.
The Xià Shū says:
'Reports are received according to words,
tested clearly by achievements,
and chariots and robes are awarded for merit.'
Your Lordship should try him!"
Then he made Xì Hú command the Central Army,
and Xì Zhēn assisted him.
He made Hú Yǎn command the Upper Army,
but Hú Yǎn yielded to Hú Máo
and instead assisted him.
He ordered Zhào Shuāi to be a Qīng,
but Zhào Shuāi yielded to Luán Zhī
and Xiān Zhěn.
He made Luán Zhī command the Lower Army,
and Xiān Zhěn assisted him.
Xún Línfù drove the ruler's chariot,
and Wèi Chōu served as the Attendant on the Right.
When the Marquis of Jìn first entered his state, he taught his people.
After two years,
he wished to employ them in war.
Zǐ Fàn said:
"The people do not yet know righteousness,
and they are not yet settled in their dwellings."
Thereupon
he went out and settled King Xiāng,
and upon entering, he devoted himself to benefiting the people;
the people then cherished their livelihoods.
He was about to employ them.
Zǐ Fàn said:
"The people do not yet know good faith,
and its application has not yet been publicized."
Thereupon he attacked Yuán
to demonstrate good faith to them.
Among the people who exchanged goods,
none sought excess,
and their words were clearly verified.
The Duke said:
"Is it possible now?"
Zǐ Fàn said:
"The people do not yet know ritual propriety,
and their reverence has not yet arisen."
Thereupon he held a Great Hunt
to demonstrate ritual propriety to them,
and established the Zhízhì
to regulate the official posts.
The people’s understanding was no longer confused,
and only after that did he employ them.
They drove out the garrison from Gǔ,
relieved the siege of Sòng,
and in one battle became Hegemon;
this was the result of the teaching of Duke Wén.
A5.28 The Classic of Duke Xī, Year 28
A5.28.1 In the spring of the twenty-eighth year,
the Marquis of Jìn invaded Cáo,
and the Marquis of Jìn attacked Wèi.
A5.28.2 Prince Mǎi of Lǔ was garrisoning Wèi,
but did not complete his service;
he was executed.
A5.28.3 The people of Chǔ came to the rescue of Wèi.
A5.28.4 In the third month, on the day bǐngwǔ,
the Marquis of Jìn entered Cáo
and seized the Earl of Cáo.
He handed him over to the people of Sòng.
A5.28.5 In the summer, in the fourth month, on the day jǐsì,
the Marquis of Jìn,
the army of Qí,
the army of Sòng,
and the army of Qín fought with the people of Chǔ at Chéngpú;
the army of Chǔ was utterly defeated.
A5.28.6 Chǔ killed its high official Déchén.
A5.28.7 The Marquis of Wèi fled to Chǔ.
A5.28.8 In the fifth month, on the day guǐchǒu,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Cài,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Viscount of Wèi,
and the Viscount of Jǔ,
and made a covenant at Jiàntǔ.
A5.28.9 The Marquis of Chén went to the meeting.
A5.28.10 The Duke had an audience at the King's residence.
A5.28.11 In the sixth month,
Zhèng, the Marquis of Wèi, returned to Wèi from Chǔ.
Yuán Xuǎn of Wèi fled to Jìn.
A5.28.12 Kuǎn, the Marquis of Chén, died.
A5.28.13 In the autumn,
Bójī of Qǐ came.
A5.28.14 Prince Suì went to Qí.
A5.28.15 In the winter,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Cài,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Viscount of Chén,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
and the people of Qín at Wēn.
A5.28.16 The Heavenly King hunted at Héyáng.
A5.28.17 On the day rénshēn,
the Duke had an audience at the King's residence.
A5.28.18 The people of Jìn seized the Marquis of Wèi
and sent him to the Capital.
Yuán Xuǎn of Wèi returned to Wèi from Jìn.
A5.28.19 The feudal lords then besieged Xǔ.
A5.28.20 Xiāng, the Earl of Cáo, returned to Cáo
and then joined the feudal lords in the siege of Xǔ.
B5.28 The Commentary of Duke Xī, Year 28
B5.28.1 In the spring of the twenty-eighth year,
the Marquis of Jìn was about to attack Cáo
and requested passage through Wèi.
The people of Wèi did not grant it.
He turned back,
crossed at the Southern River (Nánhé),
invaded Cáo, and attacked Wèi.
In the first month, on the day wùshēn,
he took Wǔlù.
In the second month,
Xì Hú of Jìn died.
Yuán Zhěn commanded the Central Army,
and Xū Chén assisted the Lower Army;
it was to exalt virtue.
The Marquis of Jìn
and the Marquis of Qí made a covenant at Liǎnyú.
The Marquis of Wèi requested a covenant,
but the people of Jìn did not grant it.
The Marquis of Wèi wished to side with Chǔ,
but the people of his state did not wish to;
therefore they expelled their ruler
to please Jìn.
The Marquis of Wèi went out to reside in Xiāngniú.
B5.28.2 Prince Mǎi was garrisoning Wèi;
the people of Chǔ came to the rescue of Wèi,
but were unsuccessful.
The Duke of Lǔ feared Jìn
and killed Zǐ Cóng to please them.
He said to the people of Chǔ:
"He did not complete his garrison duty."
B5.28.3 The Marquis of Jìn besieged Cáo.
He attacked the gates,
and many died.
The people of Cáo displayed the corpses on the city walls,
and the Marquis of Jìn was distressed by it.
He listened to a plan of the Yúrén,
and declared:
"We shall camp among the tombs."
The army moved there.
The people of Cáo were terrified,
and for those whose tombs were taken,
they placed them in coffins and brought them out.
Taking advantage of their panic, he attacked them.
In the third month, on the day bǐngwǔ,
he entered Cáo,
rebuking them for not employing Xī Fùjī
while three hundred men rode in grand carriages,
and moreover
he ordered the presentation of the circumstances of their capture.
He ordered that no one enter the palace of Xī Fùjī
and exempted his clan from punishment,
as a reward for his past kindness.
Wèi Chōu
and Diān Jié were angry,
saying:
"Our labors are not considered,
but for whom is this repayment?"
They set fire to the house of the Xī Fùjī family.
Wèi Chōu was injured in the chest.
The Duke wished to kill them
but valued Wèi Chōu’s talent.
He sent someone to inquire
and observe him.
If he was severely ill, he would be killed.
Wèi Chōu bound his chest to see the messenger
and said:
"By your lordship's spiritual power,
is there not peace?"
He leaped high three hundred times
and hopped with bent knees three hundred times.
Then he pardoned him.
He executed Diān Jié as a warning to the army,
and appointed Zhōu Zhī Qiáo
as the Right Attendant of the Chariot.
The people of Sòng sent Ményǐn Bān to the Jìn army to report the emergency.
The Duke said:
"The people of Sòng report an emergency;
if we abandon them, they will break with us,
and if we ask Chǔ to stop, they will not grant it.
I wish to fight,
but Qí and Qín have not yet agreed.
What should be done?"
Xiān Zhěn said:
"Have Sòng leave us and offer bribes to Qí
and Qín,
and let them appeal to Chǔ.
We shall seize the Ruler of Cáo,
and divide the lands of Cáo
and Wèi
to grant them to the people of Sòng.
Chǔ loves Cáo
and Wèi,
and will surely not grant the request.
Rejoicing in the bribes
and angered by the stubbornness,
how could they not fight?"
The Duke was pleased;
he seized the Count of Cáo
and divided the lands of Cáo
and Wèi
to give to the people of Sòng.
The Viscount of Chǔ entered and stayed in Shēn;
he ordered Shēnshū to leave Gǔ
and ordered Zǐyù to leave Sòng,
saying:
"Do not pursue the Jìn army!
The Marquis of Jìn was abroad
for nineteen years,
and ultimately gained the state of Jìn.
Perils and difficulties,
he has experienced them all;
the sincerity and falsehood of the people,
he knows them fully.
Heaven has granted him years
and removed his harms;
what Heaven has established,
how can it be discarded?
The 'Military Records' say:
'When it is appropriate, then return.'
It also says:
'Recognize difficulty and retreat.'
It also says:
'The virtuous cannot be opposed.'
These three records
refer to Jìn."
Zǐyù sent Bó
Fén to request battle,
saying:
"I do not dare to say success is certain,
but I wish to stop the mouths of the slanderous and evil."
The King was angry
and gave him only a small force;
only the West Guǎng
and the East Gōng, along with the six companies of Ruò'áo, actually followed him.
Zǐyù sent Wǎn Chūn to inform the Jìn army, saying:
"I request the restoration of the Marquis of Wèi
and the enfeoffment of Cáo;
then I shall also lift the siege of Sòng."
Zǐfàn said:
"How insolent is Zǐyù!
Our ruler gets one thing,
but their minister gets two;
this must not be tolerated."
Xiān Zhěn said:
"You should grant it!
Bringing peace to others is called propriety;
Chǔ would bring peace to three states with one word,
while we would destroy them with one word.
We would then be the ones without propriety;
how could we fight?
If we do not grant what Chǔ asks,
that is abandoning Sòng;
to rescue them and then abandon them,
what would we say to the feudal lords?
Chǔ has three acts of generosity,
while we have three causes for resentment;
when resentment and enmity are already great,
how shall we fight?
It is better to secretly promise to restore Cáo
and Wèi
to estrange them,
and seize Wǎn Chūn to anger Chǔ,
and then plan further after the battle."
The Duke was pleased.
He then detained Wǎn Chūn in Wèi
and secretly promised to restore Cáo
and Wèi;
Cáo
and Wèi then announced their break with Chǔ.
Zǐyù was angry
and pursued the Jìn army.
The Jìn army retreated.
The army officers said:
"For a ruler to avoid a minister
is a disgrace;
moreover, the Chǔ army is weary;
why retreat?"
Zǐfàn said:
"An army with a righteous cause is strong,
while one with a crooked cause is weary.
Does it depend on duration?
Without the kindness of Chǔ,
we would not have reached this point.
Retreating three stages to avoid them
is how we repay them.
To turn our backs on kindness and go back on our word
in order to oppose our enemy
would make us crooked and Chǔ righteous.
Their troops are well-fed;
they cannot be called weary.
If we retreat and Chǔ returns,
what more shall we seek?
If they do not return,
our ruler will have retreated
and their minister will have encroached;
the crookedness will be theirs."
They retreated three stages.
The Chǔ troops wanted to stop,
but Zǐyù would not allow it.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Wùchén,
the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
Guó Guīfù and
Cuī Yāo of Qí,
and Xiǎozi Yìn of Qín encamped at Chéngpú.
The Chǔ army encamped with their backs to Xī,
and the Marquis of Jìn was troubled by it.
He heard the common people chanting:
"The fields of Yuán are lush;
abandon the old
and plan for the new."
The Duke was uncertain about this.
Zǐfàn said:
"Fight!
If we fight and win,
we will surely gain the feudal lords.
If we do not win,
with the mountains and rivers as our defenses,
there will surely be no harm."
The Duke said:
"What of the kindness of Chǔ?"
Luán Zhēnzǐ said:
"The various houses of Jī in Hànyáng
have all been eliminated by Chǔ.
To think of small kindness and forget great shame
is not as good as fighting."
The Marquis of Jìn dreamed that he was wrestling with the Viscount of Chǔ;
the Viscount of Chǔ pinned him down
and sucked his brains,
so he was afraid.
Zǐfàn said:
"It is auspicious.
We were looking up at Heaven,
while Chǔ was prostrate in its guilt;
we shall surely subdue them."
Zǐyù sent Dòubó to request battle,
saying:
"I request to play a game with your lordship's soldiers;
your lordship may lean on the carriage rail and watch,
and I, Déchén, will also look on."
The Marquis of Jìn sent Luán Zhī to reply,
saying:
"My ruler has heard your command.
The kindness of the Ruler of Chǔ
he has not dared to forget,
which is why we are here.
For the Great Officer's sake we retreated;
how would we dare oppose the Ruler?
Since we have not received permission to withdraw,
I dare to trouble you, Great Officer,
to tell your colleagues:
'Prepare your chariots,
attend reverently to your ruler's business;
we shall meet tomorrow morning.'"
The Jìn army had seven hundred chariots,
with breast-straps, girths, neck-straps, and leg-straps all prepared.
The Marquis of Jìn ascended the ruins of Yǒushēn
to observe the army,
saying:
"The young and the old observe propriety;
they may be used."
Then they cut down the trees there
to augment their weapons.
On the day Jǐsì,
the Jìn army drew up in battle array north of Shēn;
Xū Chén, as assistant of the Lower Army,
opposed the forces of Chén
and Cài.
Zǐyù with the six battalions of the Ruò'áo clan commanded the Center Army,
and said:
“Today Jìn shall surely exist no more.”
Zǐxī commanded the Left,
and Zǐshàng commanded the Right.
Xū Chén covered his horses with tiger skins
and first attacked Chén
and Cài.
Chén
and Cài fled,
and the Chǔ Right Army collapsed.
Hú Máo set up two banners and retreated.
Luán Zhī made the chariots drag brushwood to feign a flight,
and the Chǔ army pursued them.
Yuán Zhěn
and Xì Zhēn with the ducal clans of the Center Army struck them from the flank.
Hú Máo
and Hú Yǎn with the Upper Army attacked Zǐxī from both sides,
and the Chǔ Left Army collapsed.
The Chǔ army was decisively defeated.
Zǐyù collected his remaining troops and halted;
therefore he was not totally defeated.
The Jìn army spent three days lodged
at Gǔ, eating its grain,
and returned on the day guǐyǒu.
On the day jiǎwǔ,
they reached Héngyōng
and built a royal palace at Jiàntǔ.
In the third month of this campaign,
the Earl of Zhèng went to Chǔ
and offered his military assistance.
Because the Chǔ army had been defeated, he was afraid,
and sent Zǐrén Jiǔ to seek peace with Jìn.
Luán Zhī of Jìn entered to perform a covenant with the Earl of Zhèng.
In the fifth month, on the day bǐngwǔ,
the Marquis of Jìn and the Earl of Zhèng made a covenant at Héngyōng.
On the day dīngwèi,
the Chǔ captives were presented to the King:
one hundred chariots with armored horses
and one thousand foot soldiers.
The Earl of Zhèng escorted the King,
using the rituals of King Píng.
On the day jǐyǒu,
the King held a feast with sweet wine
and commanded the Marquis of Jìn to partake in the drinking.
The King ordered the Yǐn clan head, Prince Hǔ,
and the Palace Secretary Shū Xīngfù to issue the decree appointing the Marquis of Jìn as Hegemon,
granting him the robes for a Great Chariot,
the robes for a War Chariot,
one red bow and one hundred red arrows,
one thousand black bows and arrows,
one jar of black millet wine,
and three hundred Tiger Guard soldiers,
saying:
“The King says to Uncle:
‘Respectfully obey the King's command,
to pacify the states of the four quarters
and to punish those who harbor evil against the King.’”
The Marquis of Jìn declined three times,
then accepted the command,
saying:
“Chóng'ěr dares to bow twice and touch his head to the ground,
to receive and extol the Son of Heaven's great and glorious favor
and mandate.”
He received the decree and went out.
He entered and exited for three audiences.
The Marquis of Wèi heard that the Chǔ army had been defeated
and became afraid;
he fled to Chǔ
and then went to Chén,
sending Yuán Xuàn to support Shū Wǔ
to receive the covenant.
On the day guǐhài,
Prince Hǔ made a covenant with the lords at the King's court,
the words of the oath saying:
“All shall support the Royal House
and not harm one another!
Should anyone violate this covenant,
may the bright spirits strike them dead,
causing their armies to fall,
preventing them from enjoying the blessings of their state,
even to their great-great-grandsons,
leaving neither old nor young.”
Superior men considered this covenant to be trustworthy,
and said that Jìn, in this campaign,
was able to conquer through virtue.
B5.28.4 Previously,
Zǐyù of Chǔ had made for himself a cap of fine jade
and jade pendants for its string,
but had not yet worn them.
Before the battle,
he dreamed the River God said to him:
“Give them to me!
I will grant you the elks of Mèngzhū.”
He did not give them.
Dàxīn and Zǐxī sent Róng Huáng to remonstrate,
but he would not listen.
Róng Jì said:
“If dying would benefit the state,
one would still do it;
how much more so for fine jade?
It is but dung and dirt.
If it can bring success to the army,
what is there to love about it?”
He would not listen.
Going out,
he told the two men,
saying:
“It is not the spirits who are defeating the Chief Minister;
if the Chief Minister is not diligent for the people,
he is truly defeating himself.”
After the defeat,
the King sent word to him, saying:
“If the Grandee returns,
what will you say to the elders of Shēn
and Xī?”
Zǐxī
and Sūnbó said:
“Déchén is about to die.”
The two ministers tried to stop him,
saying:
“The Lord will likely execute you anyway.”
When they reached Liángǔ, he died.
The Marquis of Jìn heard of it,
and his subsequent joy was evident;
he said:
“No one can harm me anymore.
Wěi Lǚchén is now the Chief Minister,
but he only serves himself
and does not care for the people.”
B5.28.5 Someone slandered Yuán Xuàn to the Marquis of Wèi, saying:
“He has established Shū Wǔ.”
Yuán Xuàn's son Jiǎo was following the Marquis,
and the Marquis had him killed.
Xuàn
did not abandon the command
and supported Yí Shū in entering and guarding the state.
In the sixth month,
the people of Jìn restored the Marquis of Wèi.
Nìng Wǔzǐ made a covenant with the people of Wèi at Wǎnpú,
saying:
“Heaven has brought disaster upon the state of Wèi,
and the ruler and ministers were not in harmony,
which led to this distress.
Now Heaven has guided their hearts,
making them all humble their minds to follow one another.
Had there not been those who stayed behind,
who would have guarded the altars of the soil and grain?
Had there not been those who went away,
who would have protected the ruler?
Because of the lack of harmony,
we clearly request a covenant before you great spirits
to seek Heaven's grace.
From this day forward,
after the covenant is made,
let those who went away not boast of their efforts,
and let those who stayed not fear being blamed for their crimes.
Should anyone violate this covenant
and act contrary to it,
may the bright spirits and the former lords
investigate and strike them dead.”
When the people of the state heard of this covenant,
they were no longer of two minds.
The Marquis of Wèi entered before the scheduled time;
Nìngzǐ went ahead,
and Zhǎng Zāng was guarding the gate;
thinking Nìngzǐ was a messenger,
the Marquis entered in the same carriage with him.
Young Master Chuánquǎn
and Huà Zhòng were the vanguard;
Shūsūn was about to bathe,
and hearing that the Lord had arrived,
he was joyful,
and ran out clutching his hair;
the vanguard shot and killed him.
The Marquis knew he was innocent,
and pillowed Shūsūn's head on his thigh and wept for him.
Chuánquǎn fled,
and the Marquis had him killed.
Yuán Xuàn fled to Jìn.
B5.28.6 At the Battle of Chéngpú,
the Jìn Center Army was struck by a windstorm in the marsh
and lost the left streamer of the great banner.
Qí Mán violated orders,
so the Marshal killed him
and displayed his body to the feudal lords,
making Máo Fèi take his place.
The army returned.
On the day rénwǔ,
they crossed the River.
Zhōu zhī Qiáo returned home first,
and Shì Huì took over the command of the Right.
In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day bǐngshēn,
the army was withdrawn
and entered Jìn with the music of triumph.
The captives were presented,
and the severed left ears were handed over;
the sacrificial drinking ceremony upon return was held,
and great rewards were bestowed.
A meeting was summoned,
and those who were double-minded were punished.
Zhōu zhī Qiáo was executed to be made an example to the state,
and the people thereupon became greatly submissive.
The superior man said of Wén Gōng:
"He was indeed able to apply punishments;
with three executions the people were submissive.
The Shī says:
'Be kind to this central state,
so as to soothe the four quarters.'
This refers to not failing in rewards
or punishments."
B5.28.7 In winter,
there was a meeting at Wēn
to punish the unsubmissive.
B5.28.8 The Marquis of Wèi and Yuán Xuǎn had a lawsuit;
Nìng Wǔzǐ acted as an assistant,
Zhēn Zhuāngzǐ
acted as the defendant,
and Shì Róng acted as the advocate.
The Marquis of Wèi did not win.
Shì Róng was killed,
and the feet of Zhēn Zhuāngzǐ were cut off;
Nìng Yú was considered loyal
and was pardoned.
The Marquis of Wèi was seized
and sent back to the capital,
where he was confined in a deep room.
Nìngzǐ made it his duty to bring him bags of thick congee there.
Yuán Xuǎn returned to Wèi
and established Gōngzǐ Xiá.
B5.28.9 At this meeting,
the Marquis of Jìn summoned the King
to meet the feudal lords,
and also caused the King to go hunting.
Zhòngní said:
"For a minister to summon a ruler
cannot be taken as a lesson."
Therefore the Shū says:
"The Heavenly King hunted at Héyáng,"
stating that it was not his proper place,
and also to illustrate the virtue of the Marquis.
B5.28.10 On the day rénshēn,
the Duke had an audience at the King's place.
B5.28.11 On the day dīngchǒu,
the feudal lords besieged Xǔ.
B5.28.12 The Marquis of Jìn fell ill.
Hóu Rú, a servant of the Earl of Cáo, bribed the diviner and the scribe
to make them use Cáo as the explanation, saying:
"Duke Huán of Qí held meetings
and enfeoffed those of different surnames;
now your Lordship holds meetings and destroys those of the same surname.
Cáo Shú Zhènduó
was a son of Wén;
your late lord Táng Shú
was a son of Wǔ.
Moreover, to assemble the feudal lords and destroy one's brothers
is not ritual;
to be given commands together with Wèi
but not to be restored together with them
is not good faith;
to have the same crime but different punishments
is not justice.
Ritual is used to carry out righteousness;
good faith is used to maintain ritual;
punishment is used to correct evil.
If you abandon these three,
what will your Lordship do?"
The Duke was pleased,
restored the Earl of Cáo,
and then met the feudal lords at Xǔ.
B5.28.13 The Marquis of Jìn created three ranks to resist the Dí.
Xún Línfù commanded the central rank,
Tǔ Jī commanded the right rank,
and Xiān Miè commanded the left rank.
A5.29 The Classic of the Twenty-ninth Year of Duke Xī
A5.29.1 In the spring of the twenty-ninth year,
Jiè Gèlú came.
A5.29.2 The Duke arrived from the siege of Xǔ.
A5.29.3 In summer, the sixth month,
meeting the King's man,
a man of Jìn,
a man of Sòng,
a man of Qí,
a man of Chén,
a man of Cài,
and a man of Qín,
they made a covenant at Díquán.
A5.29.4 In autumn,
there was a great hailstorm.
A5.29.5 In winter,
Jiè Gèlú came.
B5.29 The Commentary on the Twenty-ninth Year of Duke Xī
B5.29.1 In the spring of the twenty-ninth year,
Jiè Gèlú came for an audience
and lodged at the top of Chāngyǎn.
The Duke was at the meeting,
but he sent him fodder
and rice,
which was in accordance with ritual.
B5.29.2 In summer,
the Duke met Wángzǐ Hǔ, Hú Yǎn of Jìn, Gōngsūn Gù of Sòng, Guó Guīfù of Qí, Yuán Tāotú of Chén, and the young son Yìn of Qín
and made a covenant at Díquán,
renewing the covenant of Jiàntǔ
and also planning to attack Zhèng.
That the names of the ministers were not recorded
was to show disapproval of them.
According to ritual,
ministers do not meet with Dukes or Marquises;
meeting with Earls, Viscounts, or Barons is acceptable.
B5.29.3 In autumn,
there was a great hailstorm,
which caused a disaster.
B5.29.4 In winter,
Jiè Gèlú came;
because he had not seen the Duke,
he came again for an audience.
He was treated with ritual
and extra banquets and gifts.
Jiè Gèlú heard a cow lowing
and said:
"This cow has given birth to three victims for sacrifice,
and all have been used.
Its sound says so."
When they inquired about it, they found it to be true.
A5.30 The Classic of the Thirtieth Year of Duke Xī
A5.30.1 In the spring of the thirtieth year,
the King's first month.
A5.30.2 In summer,
the Dí invaded Qí.
A5.30.3 In autumn,
Wèi killed its grand officer Yuán Xuǎn and Gōngzǐ Xiá.
Zhèng, the Marquis of Wèi, returned to Wèi.
A5.30.4 A man of Jìn
and a man of Qín besieged Zhèng.
A5.30.5 The men of Jiè invaded Xiāo.
A5.30.6 In winter,
the Heavenly King sent Zǎi Zhōu Gōng on a mission of friendly inquiry.
A5.30.7 Gōngzǐ Suì went to the capital,
and then proceeded to Jìn.
B5.30 The Commentary on the Thirtieth Year of Duke Xī
B5.30.1 In the spring of the thirtieth year,
the men of Jìn invaded Zhèng
to see whether it could be attacked or not.
The Dí took advantage of Jìn's preoccupation with Zhèng;
in summer,
the Dí invaded Qí.
B5.30.2 The Marquis of Jìn sent the physician Yǎn to poison the Marquis of Wèi.
Nìng Yú bribed the physician
to make him weaken the poison,
so that he did not die.
The Duke petitioned on his behalf
and presented jade to the King and the Marquis of Jìn,
ten pairs each,
and the King granted the petition.
In autumn,
they finally released the Marquis of Wèi.
The Marquis of Wèi sent bribes to Zhōu Chuán
and Yě Jǐn, saying:
"If you can bring me back in,
I will make you ministers."
Zhōu and Yě killed Yuán Xuǎn and Zǐshì
and Zǐyí.
The Duke entered
and sacrificed to the former lords;
when Zhōu and Yě had already put on their robes
and were about to receive their appointments,
Zhōu Chuán entered first,
and upon reaching the gate,
he was struck by an illness and died.
Yě Jǐn declined the post of minister.
B5.30.3 In the ninth month, on the day jiǎwǔ,
the Marquis of Jìn and
the Earl of Qín besieged Zhèng,
because it had been disrespectful to Jìn
and had been double-dealing with Chǔ.
The army of Jìn was stationed at Hánlíng;
the army of Qín was stationed at Fànnán.
Yì Zhī Hú said to the Earl of Zhèng:
“The state is in danger.
If you send Zhú Zhī Wǔ to see the Ruler of Qín,
the army will surely withdraw.”
The Duke followed this.
He declined, saying:
“When I was in my prime,
I was already not equal to others;
now I am old,
and there is nothing more I can do.”
The Duke said:
“I was unable to employ you earlier;
now, in this emergency, I seek you.
This is my fault.
However, if Zhèng perishes,
it will also be disadvantageous to you.”
He agreed.
At night, he was lowered down by a rope and went out.
He saw the Earl of Qín and said:
“Qín and
Jìn are besieging Zhèng;
Zhèng already knows it will perish.
If the destruction of Zhèng would benefit you,
I would dare to trouble your attendants.
To cross another state to make a distant land your border—
you know its difficulty.
Why use the destruction of Zhèng to strengthen your neighbor?
The neighbor’s gain
is your loss.
If you spare Zhèng and make it your host on the eastern road,
for the coming and going of messengers,
we can provide for their needs,
and you would suffer no harm.
Furthermore, you once bestowed a favor upon the Ruler of Jìn;
he promised you Jiāo and
Xiá,
but having crossed the river in the morning, by evening he was setting up fortifications.
This you know.
Now, as for Jìn,
what satisfaction could it ever have?
Having made Zhèng its eastern border,
it will then want to expand its western border.
If it does not diminish Qín,
where else can it take from?
Diminishing Qín to benefit Jìn—may you consider this.”
The Earl of Qín was pleased,
and made a covenant with the people of Zhèng.
He sent Qǐ Zǐ, Páng Sūn, and Yáng Sūn to garrison it,
and then returned.
Zǐ Fàn requested to attack him.
The Duke said:
“It is not permissible.
Without that man’s power, I would not have reached this point.
To rely on a person’s power and then harm him
is not benevolent;
to lose one’s ally
is not wise;
to replace order with chaos
is not valorous.
We should return.”
He also left.
Previously,
Gōngzǐ Lán of Zhèng had fled to Jìn.
He followed the Marquis of Jìn in attacking Zhèng,
but requested not to participate in the siege of Zhèng.
The Marquis granted this,
and had him wait for orders in the east.
Shí Jiǎfù and
Hóu Xuānduō of Zhèng welcomed him
to be the Crown Prince
in order to seek peace with Jìn.
The people of Jìn granted it.
B5.30.4 In winter,
the King sent Zhōu Gōng Yuè on a mission of state.
At the banquet there were calamus with minced meat,
white and black grains, and salt in the shape of a tiger.
He declined, saying:
“A ruler of a state
whose civility is sufficient to be illustrious
and whose military power is awesome,
then has a banquet with complete items
to symbolize his virtue.
The five flavors are presented,
the fine grains are served,
and salt is shaped like a tiger
to offer tribute to his achievements.
How can I be worthy of this?”
B5.30.5 Dōngmén Xiāngzhòng was about to go on a mission to Zhōu;
he then first went on a mission to Jìn.
A5.31 Classic of the Thirty-First Year of Duke Xī.
A5.31.1 In the spring of the thirty-first year,
the fields west of the Jì were taken.
A5.31.2 Gōngzǐ Suì went to Jìn.
A5.31.3 In the summer, in the fourth month,
they divined four times regarding the Jiāo sacrifice;
it was not favorable,
so they released the sacrificial animal.
They still performed the three Wàng sacrifices.
A5.31.4 In the autumn, in the seventh month.
A5.31.5 In winter,
Qǐ Bó Jī came to seek a wife for her son.
A5.31.6 The Dí besieged Wèi.
In the twelfth month,
Wèi moved to Dìqiū.
B5.31 Commentary for the Thirty-First Year of Duke Xī.
B5.31.1 In the spring of the thirty-first year,
the fields west of the Jì were taken;
this was the partitioning of the territory of Cáo.
Zāng Wénzhòng was sent there;
he stayed overnight at Zhòngguǎn.
A person of Zhòngguǎn told him:
“Jìn has newly gained the allegiance of the feudal lords;
it will surely be close to those who are first.
If you do not travel quickly,
you will not arrive in time.”
He followed this.
The territory of Cáo was partitioned:
from Táo southwards,
extending east to the Jì River,
comprised all of the territory of Cáo.
B5.31.2 Xiāngzhòng went to Jìn
to give thanks for the fields of Cáo.
B5.31.3 In the summer, in the fourth month,
they divined four times regarding the Jiāo sacrifice;
it was not favorable,
so they released the sacrificial animal.
This was contrary to the rites.
They still performed the three Wàng sacrifices;
this also was contrary to the rites.
According to the rites, one does not divine about regular sacrifices,
but one divines about the sacrificial animal
and the day.
When the day for the ox is divined, it is called the sacrificial victim.
To divine regarding the Jiāo sacrifice only after the victim is ready
shows the superiors are indolent
and disrespectful.
The Wàng sacrifice
is a minor part of the Jiāo sacrifice.
If there is no Jiāo sacrifice,
it is also permissible to have no Wàng sacrifice.
B5.31.4 In autumn,
Jìn held a military review at Qīngyuán,
and formed five armies to resist the Dí.
Zhào Cuī was made a high minister.
B5.31.5 In winter,
the Dí besieged Wèi;
Wèi moved to Dìqiū.
The divination said
three hundred years.
Duke Chéng of Wèi dreamed that Kāng Shū said to him:
“Xiàng is snatching away my offerings.”
The Duke ordered a sacrifice to Xiàng.
Nìng Wǔzǐ would not allow it,
saying:
“Spirits and gods do not
enjoy the offerings of those not of their own kind.
What have Qǐ and Zēng done?
It has been a long time since Xiàng received offerings here;
this is not the fault of Wèi.
One must not interrupt the sacrificial orders of King Chéng
and the Duke of Zhōu.
I request that you reverse the order for the sacrifice.”
B5.31.6 Xiè Jià of Zhèng disliked Gōngzǐ Xiá;
the Earl of Zhèng also disliked him.
Therefore Gōngzǐ Xiá fled to Chǔ.
A5.32 Classic of the Thirty-Second Year of Duke Xī.
A5.32.1 In the spring of the thirty-second year,
in the royal first month.
A5.32.2 In the summer, in the fourth month, on the day jǐchǒu,
Jié, Earl of Zhèng, died.
A5.32.3 The people of Wèi invaded the Dí.
In autumn, the people of Wèi and the Dí made a covenant.
A5.32.4 In winter, in the twelfth month, on the day jǐmǎo,
Zhòng’ěr, Marquis of Jìn, died.
B5.32 Commentary for the Thirty-Second Year of Duke Xī.
B5.32.1 In the spring of the thirty-second year,
Dòu Zhāng of Chǔ requested peace with Jìn.
Yáng Chǔfǔ of Jìn responded to it.
Jìn and Chǔ began to have communication.
B5.32.2 In the summer,
there was disorder among the Dí.
The people of Wèi invaded the Dí,
and the Dí requested peace.
In the autumn,
the people of Wèi and the Dí made a covenant.
B5.32.3 In the winter,
Jìn Wén Gōng died.
On the day of Gēngchén,
he was about to be laid in state at Qūwò.
As the coffin left Jiàng,
there was a sound from the coffin like that of a lowing ox.
Bǔ Yǎn made the grandees bow
and said:
"Our ruler is ordering a great matter:
an army from the west will pass over and bypass us;
if we strike it,
we will certainly achieve a great victory."
Qǐ Zǐ sent word from Zhèng to Qín,
saying:
"The people of Zhèng have put me in charge of the keys to their northern gate.
If a secret army comes,
the capital can be taken."
Mù Gōng consulted Jiǎn Shū about this.
Jiǎn Shū said:
"To weary an army to raid a distant place
