is not something I have heard of.
When the army is weary and its strength exhausted,
and the distant ruler is prepared for it—
would that not be impossible?
As for what the army does,
Zhèng is certain to know it.
To toil without a destination
will surely cause rebellious hearts.
Moreover, when marching a thousand lǐ,
who would not know of it?"
The Duke declined his advice.
He summoned Mèng Míng, Xī Qǐ, and Bái Yǐ,
and sent the army out from the East Gate.
Jiǎn Shū wept for them,
saying:
"Mèng Zǐ!
I see the army going out, but I shall not see its return!"
The Duke sent someone to tell him:
"What do you know?
Had you died at a medium age,
the trees on your grave would already be a span in girth."
Jiǎn Shū's son was with the army;
weeping, he saw him off,
saying:
"The people of Jìn will surely resist the army at Yáo.
There are two mounds at Yáo.
The southern mound
is the tomb of Xià Hòu Gāo;
the northern mound
is where Wén Wáng took shelter from the wind and rain.
You will surely die between them;
I will collect your bones there!"
The Qín army then proceeded east.
A5.33 Classic of the 33rd Year of Duke Xī
A5.33.1 In the spring of the thirty-third year,
in the royal second month,
the people of Qín entered Huá.
A5.33.2 The Marquis of Qí sent Guó Guīfù on a mission of friendly inquiry.
A5.33.3 In the summer, in the fourth month, on the day of Xīnsì,
the people of Jìn and the Jiāng Róng defeated the Qín army at Yáo.
A5.33.4 On the day of Guǐsì,
Jìn Wén Gōng was buried.
A5.33.5 The Dí invaded Qí.
A5.33.6 The Duke attacked Zhū and took Zǐlóu.
A5.33.7 In the autumn,
Gōngzǐ Suì led an army to attack Zhū.
A5.33.8 The people of Jìn defeated the Dí at Jī.
A5.33.9 In the winter, in the tenth month,
the Duke went to Qí.
A5.33.10 In the twelfth month,
the Duke arrived from Qí.
A5.33.11 On the day of Yǐsì,
the Duke passed away in the Small Bedchamber.
A5.33.12 Frost fell but did not kill the grass.
Plums and apricots bore fruit.
A5.33.13 The people of Jìn,
the people of Chén,
and the people of Zhèng attacked Xǔ.
B5.33 Commentary for the 33rd Year of Duke Xī
B5.33.1 In the spring of the thirty-third year,
the Qín army passed the North Gate of Zhōu.
Those on the left and right removed their helmets and dismounted.
Those who leaped back into their chariots numbered three hundred chariots.
Wángsūn Mǎn was still young;
observing this,
he said to the King:
"The Qín army is light and lacks ritual;
they will surely be defeated.
Being light, they have few plans;
lacking ritual, they are careless.
Entering dangerous terrain while being careless,
and moreover being unable to plan,
can they avoid defeat?"
When they reached Huá,
a merchant of Zhèng named Xián Gāo, who was going to trade in Zhōu,
met them.
Using four tanned hides as a preliminary gift,
and twelve oxen to reward the army,
he said:
"My humble ruler heard that you, sirs, were going to march your army through our poor city,
and dares to reward your followers.
Our poor city is not substantial,
but for the sake of your followers' stay,
if they stay, we have provided a day's accumulation of supplies;
if they march, we have prepared a night's protection."
He also sent a messenger to report quickly to Zhèng.
Zhèng Mù Gōng sent someone to look at the guest house;
they were bundling their loads,
sharpening their weapons,
and foddering their horses.
He sent Huáng Wǔzǐ to decline their presence,
saying:
"You, sirs, have stayed long in our poor city;
only our dried meat, grain,
and sacrificial animals are exhausted.
Because you are about to depart,
just as Zhèng has the Yuánpǔ park,
so Qín has its Jùpǔ park;
why don't you take our elks and deer
to leave our poor city in peace,
what do you say?"
Qǐ Zǐ fled to Qí;
Féng Sūn
and Yáng Sūn fled to Sòng.
Mèng Míng said:
"Zhèng is prepared;
we cannot hope for success.
If we attack it, we will not conquer;
if we besiege it, there will be no reinforcements.
We should return."
They destroyed Huá and returned.
B5.33.2 Guó Zhuāngzǐ of Qí came on a mission of friendly inquiry.
From the greeting in the suburbs to the presentation of gifts,
the rituals were completed and enhanced with alacrity.
Zāng Wènzhòng said to the Duke:
"Since Guó Zǐ is in charge of the government,
Qí still possesses ritual.
You, my ruler, should go there for an audience.
I have heard:
To submit to those with ritual
is the protection of the altars of the land and grain.
B5.33.3 Yuán Zhěn of Jìn said:
"Qín disregarded Jiǎn Shū
and wearied its people out of greed;
Heaven is offering them to us.
An offer must not be lost;
an enemy must not be released.
If we release the enemy,
trouble will arise;
to disregard Heaven
is inauspicious.
We must certainly attack the Qín army!"
Luán Zhī said:
"We have not yet repaid the favors of Qín,
and yet we attack their army—
would that not be acting against our deceased ruler?"
Xiān Zhěn said:
"Qín did not mourn our loss
and instead attacked our kinsmen.
Since Qín lacks ritual,
what favor is there to speak of?
I have heard:
'To release the enemy for one day
is a trouble for several generations.'
Planning for our children and grandchildren—
can that be called acting against the deceased ruler?"
He then issued the order
and quickly raised the Jiāng Róng.
The young Duke wore black mourning clothes;
Liáng Hóng was the charioteer,
and Lái Jū was the chariot-right.
In the summer, in the fourth month, on the day of Xīnsì,
they defeated the Qín army at Yáo,
and returned having captured Bǎilǐ Mèngmíng Shì, Xī Qǐ Shù, and Bái Yǐ Bǐng.
Then, wearing black mourning clothes, they buried Wén Gōng;
Jìn began to use black for mourning from this time.
Wén Yíng requested the three commanders,
saying:
"They actually caused conflict between our two rulers.
If our ruler could get them and eat them,
he would not be satisfied.
Why should you trouble yourself to punish them here?
Let them return to face execution in Qín,
to satisfy our ruler's desire.
How would that be?"
The Duke granted it.
Xiān Zhěn attended court
and asked about the prisoners from Qín.
The Duke said:
"The Lady requested it,
and I have released them."
Xiān Zhěn was enraged
and said:
"The warriors exerted their strength to capture them on the plains,
but a woman in a moment has released them in the capital.
You have discarded the fruits of the army's victory and encouraged the enemy.
Destruction is not far off!"
Without looking back, he spat.
The Duke sent Yáng Chùfù to pursue them.
He reached them at the Hé,
but they were already in a boat.
Unhitching his left trace-horse,
he presented it to Mèng Míng as a gift by the Duke's command.
Mèng Míng kowtowed and said:
"Through your ruler's favor,
he did not use his captive servants to smear his drums with blood,
but let us return to face execution in Qín.
If our ruler executes us,
we shall not rot even in death.
If we are spared through your ruler's favor,
in three years we shall return to thank him for this gift."
The Bó of Qín, in mourning dress, went to the outskirts
and wept as he faced the army,
saying:
"I went against Jiǎn Shū's advice
and thus brought shame upon you gentlemen.
It is my fault."
He did not replace Mèng Míng,
saying:
"It was my error.
What fault do you, the Dàfū, have?
Moreover, I will not let one mistake obscure a great virtue."
B5.33.4 The Dí invaded Qí,
taking advantage of the mourning in Jìn.
B5.33.5 The Duke attacked Zhū
and took Zǐlóu
to retaliate for the battle of Shēngjīng.
The people of Zhū had prepared no defenses.
In autumn,
Xiāng Zhòng again attacked Zhū.
B5.33.6 The Dí attacked Jìn
and reached Jī.
In the eighth month, on the day wùzǐ,
the Marquis of Jìn defeated the Dí at Jī.
Xì Quē captured the son of the Bái Dí.
Xiān Zhěn said:
"A commoner vented his will toward the ruler
and was not punished;
how can I dare not punish myself?"
He removed his helmet and charged into the Dí army,
where he died.
The Dí people returned his head;
his face looked as if he were alive.
Previously,
when Jiù Jì was on a mission,
he passed through Jì
and saw Xì Quē weeding.
His wife was bringing him food;
they were respectful
and treated each other like guests.
Jiù Jì returned with him
and spoke to Wén Gōng, saying:
"Respect
is the gathering of virtue.
One who can be respectful must have virtue.
Virtue is used to govern the people;
I request my ruler to employ him!
I have heard:
'Go out of the door as if meeting a guest;
undertake affairs as if performing a sacrifice.'
These are the rules of Rén."
The Duke said:
"His father had committed a crime;
is it acceptable?"
He replied:
"Shùn punished Gǔn for his crimes,
but his promotion raised up Yǔ.
Guǎn Jìngzhòng was an enemy of Huán Gōng,
yet he served as prime minister to achieve success.
The *Kāng Gào* says:
'If a father is not kind,
and the son is not respectful;
if an elder brother is not friendly,
and the younger brother is not compliant;
they do not affect each other.'
The *Shī* says:
'In gathering turnip and radish,
do not reject them because of their lower parts.'
You may take his merits."
Wén Gōng appointed him as Dàfū of the Lower Army.
On the return from Jī,
Xiāng Gōng with a triple command appointed Xiān Qiějū to command the Central Army;
with a double command, he rewarded Xū Chén with the district of Xiān Máo,
saying:
"The promotion of Xì Quē
was your merit."
With a single command, he appointed Xì Quē as a Qīng
and returned Jì to him,
though he was not yet in the military ranks.
B5.33.7 In winter,
the Duke went to Qí.
He attended court
and offered condolences for the Dí invasion.
On his return,
he died in the Xiǎo Qǐn,
passing away in peace.
Chén, and Zhèng attacked Xǔ,
punishing its double-dealing with Chǔ.
B5.33.9 The Chǔ Lìngyǐn Zǐshàng invaded Chén and Cài.
Chén and Cài made peace,
and then he attacked Zhèng,
intending to install Gōngzǐ Xiá.
They attacked the Jiézhì Gate;
Xiá fell into the pool of the Zhōu clan.
The Wàipú Kūntún captured him
and presented him.
Wén Fūrén enshrouded and buried him below the wall of Kuì.
B5.33.10 Yáng Chùfù of Jìn invaded Cài;
Zǐshàng of Chǔ went to its rescue
and camped with the Jìn army across the Zhì Hé.
Yángzǐ was troubled by this
and sent word to Zǐshàng, saying:
"I have heard:
'The cultured do not violate what is right;
the martial do not avoid an enemy.'
If you wish to fight,
I will withdraw one stage;
you can then cross and form your ranks.
Whether sooner or later is at your command.
Otherwise,
you should withdraw for me.
Keeping an army in the field and wasting resources
is of no benefit."
He then readied his chariots to wait.
Zǐshàng wanted to cross,
but Dàsūn Bó
said:
"You must not.
The people of Jìn are untrustworthy.
If they attack us when we are halfway across,
it will be too late to regret the defeat.
It is better to withdraw for them."
So he withdrew one stage.
Yángzǐ declared:
"The Chǔ army has fled!"
and then returned home.
The Chǔ army also returned.
Crown Prince Shāngchén slandered Zǐshàng, saying:
"He accepted a bribe from Jìn and avoided them;
this is the shame of Chǔ.
No crime is greater than this."
The King killed Zǐshàng.
B5.33.11 Xǐ Gōng was buried.
It was late
to make the ancestral tablet,
which was a violation of ritual.
Generally, when a ruler dies,
once the final vessels are set, the spirit is joined to the ancestors;
after joining, the tablet is made.
A special sacrifice is offered to the tablet,
and the Zhēng, Cháng, and Dì sacrifices are performed in the temple.
A6.1 The Classic: First Year of Wén Gōng.
A6.1.1 In the first year, spring,
the Royal first month,
the Duke ascended the throne.
A6.1.2 In the second month, on the day guǐhài,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A6.1.3 The Heavenly King sent Shū Fú to attend the burial.
A6.1.4 In summer, the fourth month, on the day dīngsì,
we buried our ruler, Xǐ Gōng.
A6.1.5 The Heavenly King sent Máo Bó to confer the mandate upon the Duke.
A6.1.6 The Marquis of Jìn attacked Wèi.
A6.1.7 Shūsūn Déchén went to the capital.
A6.1.8 The people of Wèi attacked Jìn.
A6.1.9 In autumn,
Gōngsūn Áo met with the Marquis of Jìn at Qī.
A6.1.10 In winter, the tenth month, on the day dìngwèi,
the Heir Apparent of Chǔ, Shāngchén, assassinated his ruler Yūn.
A6.1.11 Gōngsūn Áo went to Qí.
B6.1 Commentary on the First Year of Duke Wén.
B6.1.1 In the spring of the first year,
the King sent the Interior Scribe Shūfú to participate in the burial.
Gōngsūn Áo heard that he was capable of physiognomy,
and presented his two sons to him.
Shūfú said:
“Gǔ will provide for you,
and Nán will bury you.
Gǔ has a full lower face;
he is certain to have descendants in the state of Lǔ.”
B6.1.2 In this year, there was an intercalary third month;
this was not in accordance with ritual.
When the former kings regulated the seasons,
they fixed the beginning at the solstice,
adjusted the middle by the equinoxes,
and returned the remainder at the end.
By fixing the beginning at the solstice,
the sequence is not in error;
by adjusting the middle,
the people are not confused;
by returning the remainder at the end,
affairs are not contradictory.
B6.1.3 In summer, the fourth month, on the day dìngsì,
Duke Xī was buried.
B6.1.4 The King sent Máobó Wèi to confer the charge upon the Duke.
Shūsūn Déchén went to Zhōu to offer thanks.
B6.1.5 In the final years of Duke Wén of Jìn,
the feudal lords attended the court of Jìn;
Duke Chéng of Wèi did not attend,
and sent Kǒng Dá to invade Zhèng,
attacking Mián, Zī, and Kuāng.
After Duke Xiāng of Jìn completed the xiáng sacrifice,
he informed the feudal lords and attacked Wèi,
reaching Nányáng.
Xiān Qiějū said:
“To follow a bad example
is a calamity.
I request that the Lord attend the King’s court,
while I follow the army.”
The Marquis of Jìn attended the King’s court at Wēn.
Xiān Qiějū and Xū Chén attacked Wèi.
In the fifth month, on the day xīnyǒu, the first day of the month,
the Jìn army besieged Qī.
In the sixth month, on the day wùxū,
they took it,
and captured Sūn Zhāozǐ.
The people of Wèi sent word to Chén.
Duke Gòng of Chén said:
“Attack them again,
and I will make excuses for you.”
Kǒng Dá of Wèi led an army to attack Jìn.
The superior man considered this to be in the ancient manner.
In ancient times,
one would bypass a state to plan.
B6.1.6 In autumn,
the Marquis of Jìn defined the boundaries of the fields of Qī,
so Gōngsūn Áo met with him.
B6.1.7 Previously,
the Viscount of Chǔ intended to make Shāngchén the Heir Apparent
and consulted the Chancellor Zǐshàng.
Zǐshàng said:
“Your Lordship is not yet old,
and you have many favorites;
to dismiss him later will cause disorder.
In the appointments of the state of Chǔ,
the preference is always for the youngest.
Furthermore, this man
has the eyes of a wasp and the voice of a jackal;
he is a cruel man
and cannot be established.”
He did not listen.
Later,
he wanted to establish Prince Zhí
and dismiss the Heir Apparent Shāngchén.
Shāngchén heard of this but was not certain;
he told his tutor Pān Chóng:
“How can I find out for sure?”
Pān Chóng said:
“Provide a feast for Jiāng Miě
but show her no respect.”
He followed this.
Jiāng Miě was angry and said:
“Oh!
You menial!
No wonder the King wishes to depose you and establish Zhí.”
He told Pān Chóng:
“It is true.”
Pān Chóng said:
“Can you serve him?”
He said:
“I cannot.”
“Can you go into exile?”
He said:
“I cannot.”
“Can you carry out a great deed?”
He said:
“I can.”
In the tenth month of winter,
he used the palace guards to surround King Chéng.
The King requested to eat bear’s paws and then die.
He would not permit it.
On the day dìngwèi,
the King hanged himself.
They gave him the posthumous title
“Líng,”
but his eyes would not close;
they called him
“Chéng,”
and then they closed.
King Mù was established;
he gave his residence as Heir Apparent to Pān Chóng,
made him the Grand Tutor,
and put him in charge as the Commander of the Ring-Guards.
B6.1.8 Mùbó went to Qí
to pay an initial visit;
this was in accordance with ritual.
Whenever a ruler ascends the throne,
the high ministers go out on joint missions
to renew old friendships,
secure external aid,
maintain good relations with neighboring states,
and thereby protect the altars of soil and grain.
This is the way of loyalty, trustworthiness, and humble yielding.
Loyalty
is the correctness of virtue;
trustworthiness
is the firmness of virtue;
humble yielding
is the foundation of virtue.
B6.1.9 After the campaign of Xiáo,
when the people of Jìn had returned the Qín commanders,
the Great Officers of Qín and the ruler’s attendants all said to the Earl of Qín:
“This defeat
was the fault of Mèngmíng;
you must kill him.”
The Earl of Qín said:
“It was my fault.
The poem by Ruì Liángfū of Zhōu says:
‘The great wind has its path;
greedy people ruin their kind.
If you listen to their words, they respond;
if you recite words, they are as if drunk.
They do not use the good men,
but conversely make me rebellious.’
This was because of greed,
which refers to me.
I was truly greedy and thus brought disaster upon you, sir;
what fault do you have?”
He again put him in charge of the government.
A6.2 Annals for the Second Year of Duke Wén.
A6.2.1 In the spring of the second year,
in the royal second month, on the day jiǎzǐ,
the Marquis of Jìn and the Qín army fought at Péngyá,
and the Qín army was utterly defeated.
A6.2.2 On the day dīngchǒu,
the ancestral tablet of Duke Xī was made.
A6.2.3 In the third month, on the day yǐsì,
an alliance was made with Jìn Chǔfù.
A6.2.4 In summer, the sixth month,
Gōngsūn Áo met with the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Earl of Zhèng,
and Shì Gǔ of Jìn to form an alliance at Chuílǒng.
A6.2.5 It did not rain from the twelfth month
until the autumn, the seventh month.
A6.2.6 In the eighth month, on the day dīngmǎo,
a great sacrifice was held in the Grand Temple,
and the tablet of Duke Xī was advanced.
A6.2.7 In winter,
the people of Jìn,
the people of Sòng,
the people of Chén,
and the people of Zhèng attacked Qín.
A6.2.8 Gōngzǐ Suì went to Qí to present the marriage betrothal gifts.
B6.2 Commentary on the Second Year of Duke Wén.
B6.2.1 In the spring of the second year,
Mèng Míngshì of Qín led an army to attack Jìn,
to avenge the campaign of Xiáo.
In the second month,
the Marquis of Jìn resisted them.
Xiān Qiějū commanded the Central Army,
and Zhào Shuāi assisted him.
Wángguān Wúdì drove the chariot,
and Hú Jùjū served as the spearman on the right.
On the day jiǎzǐ,
they fought the Qín army at Péngyá,
and the Qín army was utterly defeated.
The people of Jìn called the Qín army
“the army that returns the favor.”
Back during the battle at Xiáo,
Liáng Hóng of Jìn drove the chariot,
and Lái Jū was the spearman on the right.
The day after the battle,
Duke Xiāng of Jìn bound the Qín prisoners
and ordered Lái Jū to decapitate them with a dagger-axe.
The prisoners cried out;
Lái Jū dropped his dagger-axe.
Láng Shàn took the dagger-axe to decapitate the prisoners,
captured them and followed the Duke’s chariot.
Consequently, he was made the spearman on the right.
During the campaign at Jī,
Xiān Zhěn dismissed him
and appointed Xù Jiǎnbó.
Láng Shàn was angry.
His friend said,
“Why not die for this?”
Shàn said,
“I have not yet found the place to die.”
His friend said,
“I will create a difficulty for you.”
Shàn said,
“The *Zhōu Zhì* has this saying:
‘If one is brave but harms his superior,
he shall not enter the Bright Hall.’
To die without righteousness
is not bravery.
Being used for the common good is called bravery.
I sought the position on the right through bravery;
being dismissed for lacking bravery
is also my proper place.
To say my superior does not know me,
when the dismissal was appropriate,
means he actually knows me.
You just wait.”
When they reached Péngyá,
after the ranks were formed,
he charged into the Qín army with his subordinates
and died there.
The Jìn army followed him
and greatly defeated the Qín army.
The superior man said,
“Láng Shàn was a superior man in this matter.
The *Shī* says,
‘If the superior man is angry,
the disorder will soon be quelled.’
It also says,
‘The King blazed with anger,
and thus marshaled his troops.’
To be angry without causing disorder
and to follow the army,
this can be called being a superior man.”
The Earl of Qín still employed Mèng Míng.
Mèng Míng improved the state administration
and repeatedly bestowed favors upon the people.
Zhào Chéngzǐ said to the various grand masters,
“The Qín army will come again,
and we must certainly avoid them.
When one is fearful and increases his virtue,
he cannot be withstood.
The *Shī* says,
‘Do you not think of your ancestors?
Cultivate their virtue.’
Mèng Míng has thought of this.
Thinking of virtue without ceasing,
how can he be matched?”
B6.2.2 On dīngchǒu,
the spirit tablet of Duke Xī was made.
It is recorded
because it was not at the proper time.
Because the Duke did not pay court, the people of Jìn
came to punish him;
the Duke went to Jìn.
In the summer, in the fourth month, on jǐsì,
the people of Jìn made Yáng Chùfù covenant with the Duke
in order to humiliate him.
The record says,
“Covenanted with Chùfù of Jìn,”
using his name to show disdain for him.
That he went to Jìn is not recorded
to conceal it.
Before the Duke arrived,
in the sixth month,
Mùbó met with the feudal lords
and the Minister of Works of Jìn, Shì Gǔ, to covenant at Chuílóng,
because Jìn was punishing Wèi.
The record mentions
“Shì Gǔ,”
because he was capable of the task.
The Marquis of Chén requested peace for Wèi from Jìn
and seized Kǒng Dá to please them.
In the autumn, in the eighth month, on dīngmǎo,
a great sacrifice was held at the Grand Temple,
advancing Duke Xī in rank,
which was an inversion of the proper order of sacrifice.
At that time Xiàfù Fújì was the Master of Ceremonies;
he honored Duke Xī
and clearly stated,
“I see the new ghost is great
and the old ghost is small.
Placing the great first and the small after
is the natural order.
Advancing the sage and worthy
is wisdom.
Wisdom and natural order
constitute ritual.”
The superior man considered this a violation of ritual:
“Ritual is never without natural order.
Sacrifice
is a great matter of the state,
and yet it was inverted;
can this be called ritual?
Although a son may be holy and sage,
he has not taken precedence over his father in eating for a long time.
Thus Yǔ did not take precedence over Gǔn,
Tāng did not take precedence over Xiè,
and Wén and Wǔ did not take precedence over Bùkù.
Sòng takes Dì Yǐ as ancestor,
and Zhèng takes King Lì as ancestor,
still honoring their ancestors.
Therefore the *Lǔ Sòng* says,
‘In spring and autumn, never remiss,
the sacrificial offerings are without error.
To the August Sovereign God,
and the August Ancestor Hòujì.’
The superior man says
‘ritual,’
referring to Hòujì being close
and thus preceding the Sovereign God.
The *Shī* says,
‘I asked my aunts,
and then my elder sisters.’
The superior man says
‘ritual,’
referring to the sister being close
and thus preceding the aunt.”
Zhòngní said,
“Zàng Wénzhòng
had three instances of lack of benevolence
and three of lack of wisdom.
Subordinating Zhǎn Qín,
abolishing the six customs barriers,
and having his concubines weave mats
were the three instances of lack of benevolence.
Making empty ritual vessels,
allowing the inversion of sacrifice,
and sacrificing to the Yuánjū bird
were the three instances of lack of wisdom.”
In the winter,
Xiān Qiějū of Jìn, Prince Chéng of Sòng, Yuán Xuǎn of Chén, and Prince Guīshēng of Zhèng attacked Qín,
took Wāng and Péngyá and returned,
to avenge the campaign of Péngyá.
The names of the ministers are not recorded
for the sake of Duke Mù,
to honor Qín;
this is called exalting virtue.
Xiāngzhòng went to Qí to present the betrothal gifts,
which was in accordance with ritual.
Whenever a ruler takes the throne,
he befriends his maternal uncles and nephews,
cultivates marriage alliances,
and marries a principal wife to offer the sacrificial grain,
which is filial piety.
Filial piety is the beginning of ritual.
A6.3 *The Classic of Duke Wén, Third Year*
A6.3.1 In the spring of the third year,
in the royal first month,
Shūsūn Déchén met with the people of Jìn,
Sòng,
Chén,
Wèi,
and Zhèng to attack Shěn.
Shěn collapsed.
A6.3.2 In the summer, in the fifth month,
Wángzǐ Hǔ died.
A6.3.3 The people of Qín attacked Jìn.
A6.3.4 In the autumn,
the people of Chǔ besieged Jiāng.
A6.3.5 Insects rained down in Sòng.
A6.3.6 In winter,
the Duke went to Jìn.
In the twelfth month, on the day jǐsì,
the Duke and the Marquis of Jìn made a covenant.
A6.3.7 Yáng Chùfù of Jìn led an army to attack Chǔ in order to rescue Jiāng.
B6.3 The Commentary for the Third Year of Duke Wén.
B6.3.1 In the spring of the third year,
Zhuāng Shú met with the armies of the feudal lords to attack Shěn,
because it had submitted to Chǔ.
Shěn collapsed.
Whenever the people flee from their superiors, it is called a "collapse" (kuì);
when those in superior positions flee, it is called "fleeing."
B6.3.2 The Marquis of Wèi went to Chén
to acknowledge the peace settlement with Jìn.
B6.3.3 In summer, in the fourth month, on the day yǐhài,
Wáng Shú Wén Gōng died.
A funeral announcement arrived,
and condolences were offered as to a member of a covenant;
this was according to ritual.
B6.3.4 The Earl of Qín attacked Jìn.
He crossed the River and burned his boats.
He took Wángguān and Jiāo.
The people of Jìn did not come out.
Thereupon he crossed from Màojīn,
buried the corpses at Yáo and returned.
He then became hegemon over the Western Róng,
because he used Mèng Míng.
By this the gentleman knows
that Qín Mù was a true ruler:
in promoting people, he was thorough;
in trusting people, he was single-minded.
As for Mèng Míng as a minister:
he was untiring;
he could be fearful and reflective.
As for Zǐsāng’s loyalty:
he knew people;
he could promote the good.
The Shī says:
"Where do we gather the white mugwort?
In the marshes and on the islets.
Where do we use it?
In the service of dukes and marquises."
Qín Mù possessed this.
"Morning and night, never untiring,
to serve the One Man."
Mèng Míng possessed this.
"Leaving plans for his grandsons,
to comfort and protect his descendants."
Zǐsāng possessed this.
B6.3.5 In autumn,
it rained locusts in Sòng;
they fell and died.
B6.3.6 The Chǔ army besieged Jiāng.
Xiān Pǔ of Jìn attacked Chǔ to rescue Jiāng.
In winter,
because of the situation in Jiāng, Jìn reported to the Zhōu court.
Wáng Shú Huán Gōng and
Yáng Chùfù of Jìn attacked Chǔ to rescue Jiāng.
They attacked the gates of Fāngchéng,
encountered Zhū, the son of the Lord of Xī, and then returned.
B6.3.7 The people of Jìn feared they had been discourteous to the Duke,
so they requested a renewal of the covenant.
The Duke went to Jìn
and made a covenant with the Marquis of Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn hosted the Duke at a banquet
and recited "Jīng Jīng Zhě É."
Zhuāng Shú led the Duke down from the hall
to bow.
He said:
"A small state receives orders from a great state;
how would we dare not be careful with our ceremonies?
Your Lordship favors us with great ritual;
what joy could be equal to this?
Indeed, the joy of a small state
is the kindness of a great state."
The Marquis of Jìn descended
and declined the honor.
They ascended the hall,
and the bows were completed.
The Duke recited "Jiā Lè."
A6.4 The Annals of the Fourth Year of Duke Wén.
A6.4.1 In the spring of the fourth year,
the Duke arrived from Jìn.
A6.4.2 In summer,
the lady Jiāng was escorted from Qí.
A6.4.3 The Dí invaded Qí.
A6.4.4 In autumn,
the people of Chǔ extinguished Jiāng.
A6.4.5 The Marquis of Jìn attacked Qín.
A6.4.6 The Marquis of Wèi sent Nìng Yú on a mission of inquiry.
A6.4.7 In winter, in the eleventh month, on the day rényín,
the lady Fèng Shì died.
B6.4 The Commentary for the Fourth Year of Duke Wén.
B6.4.1 In the spring of the fourth year,
the people of Jìn returned Kǒng Dá to Wèi,
considering him a worthy man of Wèi;
therefore they released him.
B6.4.2 In summer,
the Marquis of Wèi went to Jìn to offer thanks.
B6.4.3 The Earl of Cáo went to Jìn for the New Year audience.
B6.4.4 In escorting the lady Jiāng from Qí,
no high minister went;
this was not in accordance with ritual.
By this the gentleman knows that Chū Jiāng would not find sincerity in Lǔ.
It is said:
"To use a costly betrothal but a lowly escort,
for the ruler to treat her as lowly,
to establish her and then neglect her—
this is to abandon trust
and damage her status as mistress of the house.
In a state, there will surely be disorder;
in a family, there will surely be ruin.
Is it not fitting that she found no sincerity?"
The Shī says:
"Awe-struck by the majesty of Heaven,
thus he preserved it."
This refers to respecting the mistress.
B6.4.5 In autumn,
the Marquis of Jìn attacked Qín,
besieging Yuán
and Xīnchéng
to retaliate for the campaign at Wángguān.
B6.4.6 The people of Chǔ extinguished Jiāng.
The Earl of Qín for this reason wore mourning clothes,
moved his residence to a temporary hut,
did not eat full meals,
and exceeded the usual duration.
The grandees remonstrated.
The Earl said:
"An ally has been extinguished;
though I could not save them,
how could I not feel compassion?
I am fearful for myself."
The gentleman says:
"The Shī says:
'Thinking of those two states,
their governance was not successful;
thinking of these four states,
there they investigated and deliberated.'
This refers to Qín Mù."
B6.4.7 Nìng Wǔzǐ of Wèi came on a mission of inquiry.
The Duke held a banquet with him
and recited "Zhàn Lù" and "Tóng Gōng" for him.
He did not decline,
nor did he recite in response.
The Duke sent an usher to inquire privately of him.
He replied:
"I thought
that you were merely practicing your lessons.
Formerly, when the feudal lords had their New Year audience with the King,
the King would feast and entertain them;
on such occasions, 'Zhàn Lù' was recited,
for when the Son of Heaven faces the sun,
the feudal lords obey his commands.
When the feudal lords shared the King's indignation
and presented their achievements,
the King would then grant them one vermilion bow,
a hundred vermilion arrows,
and a thousand black bows and arrows,
to manifest acknowledgement and reward with a feast.
Now I, a subordinate minister, have come to continue old friendships;
Your Lordship has deigned to favor me,
but how would I dare violate the great rituals and bring guilt upon myself?"
B6.4.8 In winter,
Chéng Fèng died.
A6.5 The Annals of the Fifth Year of Duke Wén.
A6.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
in the royal first month,
the King sent Róng Shú to bring mouth-jade,
and also funeral gifts.
A6.5.2 In the third month, on the day xīnhài,
we buried our Little Lord, Chéng Fèng.
A6.5.3 The King sent the Earl of Zhào to come and attend the burial.
A6.5.4 In summer,
Gōngsūn Áo went to Jìn.
A6.5.5 The people of Qín entered Ruò.
A6.5.6 In autumn,
the people of Chǔ extinguished Lìu.
A6.5.7 In winter, in the tenth month, on the day jiǎshēn,
Yè, the Baron of Xǔ, died.
B6.5 Commentary on the Fifth Year of Duke Wén.
B6.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
the King sent Róng Shú to come and provide jade for the mouth and funeral gifts,
and called upon Zhào Zhāo Gōng to come and attend the burial;
this was in accordance with ritual.
B6.5.2 Previously,
Ruò had rebelled against Chǔ to join Qín,
and furthermore was double-minded toward Chǔ.
In the summer,
the people of Qín entered Ruò.
B6.5.3 Liù rebelled against Chǔ to join the Dōng Yí.
In the autumn,
Chéng Dàxīn and
Zhòng Guī of Chǔ led an army and destroyed Liù.
B6.5.4 In the winter,
the Chǔ prince Gōngzǐ Xiè destroyed Liǎo.
When Zāng Wènzhòng heard that Liù and Liǎo were destroyed,
he said:
"Are Gāo Yáo
and Tíng Jiān to be suddenly denied their sacrifices?
When virtue is not established
and the people have no support,
how lamentable!"
B6.5.5 Yáng Chǔfù of Jìn went on a mission to Wèi.
On his return, he passed through Níng,
and Níng Yíng followed him.
Upon reaching Wēn, Níng Yíng returned.
His wife asked him about it.
Yíng said:
"Because of his rigidity.
The *Shāng Shū* says:
'To the sinking and soaking, apply the control of rigidity;
to the high and bright, apply the control of softness.'
That gentleman is singular in his rigidity;
will he not come to a violent end?
Even when Heaven acts with the virtue of rigidity,
it still does not offend the seasons;
how much more so for a man?
Moreover, he is showy but lacks substance,
a place where resentment gathers.
To be offensive and gather resentment
is not the way to secure one's person.
I feared that I would not gain any benefit but instead meet with his calamity,
and so I left him."
Zhào Chéngzǐ, Luán Zhēnzǐ, Huò Bó, and Jiù Jì of Jìn all died.
A6.6 Annals of the Sixth Year of Duke Wén.
A6.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
Duke Xī of Xǔ was buried.
A6.6.2 In the summer,
Jìsūn Xíngfù went to Chén.
A6.6.3 In the autumn,
Jìsūn Xíngfù went to Jìn.
A6.6.4 In the eighth month, on the day yǐhài,
Huān, Lord of Jìn, died.
A6.6.5 In the winter, the tenth month,
Gōngzǐ Suì went to Jìn.
A6.6.6 Duke Xiāng of Jìn was buried.
A6.6.7 Jìn killed its grand officer Yáng Chǔfù.
A6.6.8 Hú Shègū of Jìn fled to the Dí.
A6.6.9 In the intercalary month, the new moon was not announced,
but the court was still held in the ancestral temple.
B6.6 Commentary on the Sixth Year of Duke Wén.
B6.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
Jìn held a grand review at Yí
and disbanded two armies.
Hú Shègū was appointed to command the Mid-army,
and Zhào Dùn was his assistant.
When Yáng Chǔfù arrived from Wēn,
he had the review changed to Dǒng
and switched the command of the Mid-army.
Yángzǐ
was a follower of Chéng Jì,
so he favored the Zhào clan,
and furthermore he believed Zhào Dùn was capable,
saying:
"Employing the capable
is to the state's advantage."
Therefore, he placed him above.
Thus Xuānzǐ began to conduct the state's administration.
He established the administrative canons,
standardized laws and crimes,
clarified judicial cases and penalties,
oversaw the capture of fugitives,
followed established protocols,
cleaned up old corruptions,
based rituals on established ranks,
continued the regular duties of office,
and promoted those who had been overlooked.
When these were completed,
he handed them over to the Grand Tutor Yángzǐ and the Grand Master Jiǎ Tuó
to implement them throughout the state of Jìn
as constant laws.
B6.6.2 Because Zāng Wènzhòng saw the harmony between Chén and Wèi,
he wished to seek good relations with Chén.
In the summer,
Jì Wénzǐ
went on a mission to Chén
and took a wife there.
B6.6.3 Rèn Hǎo, Earl of Qín, died.
The three sons of the Zǐchē clan—Yǎn Xī, Zhòng Háng, and Zhēn Hǔ—were buried as human sacrifices with him.
They were all the finest men of Qín.
The people of the state grieved for them
and composed for them the poem "Huáng Niǎo."
The superior man said:
"It is right that Qín Mù did not become a hegemon!
At death, he abandoned his people.
When the former kings left the world,
they still bequeathed laws,
so how much more wrong it is to take away their good men?
The *Shī* says:
'When the good men are gone,
the state is exhausted and distressed.'
This refers to the lack of good men.
How could he take them away?
The kings of old knew that life does not last long,
so they established the sagacious and wise together,
set up their reputations,
granted them colored insignia,
recorded their wise words,
created for them laws and measures,
displayed for them the standards of art,
led them with examples,
gave them legal systems,
informed them with instructions and canons,
taught them how to guard against gain,
entrusted them with regular ranks,
and guided them with rituals and principles,
so that they would not lose what was appropriate for their land.
All the common people relied on this,
and only then did the kings meet their end.
The sage kings were alike in this.
Now, even if he left no laws
for his descendants,
to furthermore take his best men to die with him
makes it difficult for him to be regarded as a superior ruler."
By this, the superior man knew
that Qín would not again campaign in the east.
B6.6.4 In the autumn,
Jì Wénzǐ was about to go on a mission to Jìn.
He sent for the rituals appropriate for a mission during a time of mourning
before setting out.
Someone said:
"Why use those?"
Wénzǐ said:
"To prepare for the unexpected
is an excellent teaching of old.
To seek and not find is truly difficult.
What harm is there in seeking in advance?"
B6.6.5 In the eighth month, on the day yǐhài,
Jìn Xiāng Gōng died.
Jìn Líng Gōng was young,
and because of the state's difficulties, the people of Jìn
wished to establish an older ruler.
Zhào Mèng said:
"Let us establish Gōngzǐ Yōng.
He loves goodness and is mature;
the former lord loved him,
and he is close to Qín.
Qín
is an old ally.
Establishing one who is good provides stability;
serving an elder is following the proper order;
establishing the loved one is filial;
connecting with an old ally provides peace.
Because of our difficulties,
we wish to establish an older ruler.
With these four virtues,
our difficulties will surely be resolved."
Jiǎ Jì said:
"It is better to establish Gōngzǐ Lè.
Chén Yíng was favored by two lords.
If we establish her son,
the people will surely be at peace with him."
Zhào Mèng said:
"Chén Yíng was of low status;
her rank was among the nine concubines.
What prestige could her son have?
Furthermore, having been favored by two lords
is licentiousness.
As the son of a former lord,
he could not seek a great state
and went out to a small state;
that is lowly."
"The mother is licentious and the son is deviant,
they lack prestige;
Chén is small and distant,
lacking support—
how can he be secured?
Dù Qí, for the sake of the ruler,
yielded to Bì Jí and placed her above herself;
for the sake of the Dí,
she yielded to Jì Wéi and placed herself after her,
so her rank was fourth.
The late ruler therefore loved her son
and had him serve in Qín,
where he became a Second Minister.
Qín is great and near,
sufficient to provide support;
the mother is righteous and the son is loved,
sufficient to overawe the people.
Establishing him—
would that not be acceptable?"
They sent Xiān Miè and Shì Huì to Qín to welcome Gōng Zǐ Yōng.
Jiǎ Jì also sent someone to summon Gōng Zǐ Lè from Chén,
but Zhào Mèng had him killed at Pí.
Jiǎ Jì resented Yáng Zǐ for changing his rank
and knew he had no support in Jìn;
in the ninth month,
Jiǎ Jì sent Xù Jū Jū to kill Yáng Chù fù.
The Annals record:
"Jìn killed its Grand Master,"
because he encroached upon the duties of office.
In winter, the tenth month,
Xiāng Zhòng went to Jìn to attend the burial of Xiāng Gōng.
In the eleventh month, on the day bǐng yín,
Jìn killed Xù Jiǎn Bó.
Jiǎ Jì fled to the Dí.
Xuān Zǐ sent Yú Pián to escort his family and property.
During the hunt at Yí,
Jiǎ Jì had humiliated Yú Pián,
so Yú Pián's men wanted to kill all of the Jiǎ clan to take revenge.
Yú Pián said:
"That is not possible.
I have heard the records of old say:
'Match favors with favors and resentment with resentment,
but do not let it reach the descendants—
this is the way of loyalty.'
The Master was courteous to Jiǎ Jì;
if I use his favor to avenge a private grudge,
would that not be unacceptable?
Relying on another's favor
is not courage.
Reducing one's own resentment
while increasing enmity for the lord
is not wisdom.
Harming the public interest for private reasons
is not loyalty.
If I abandon these three principles,
how can I serve the Master?"
He fully prepared their family, vessels, and goods,
personally led the escort to protect them,
and sent them to the border.
In the intercalary month, the announcement of the new moon was not made;
this was contrary to ritual.
The intercalary month is used to correct the seasons,
the seasons are used to carry out tasks,
the tasks are used to enrich the people's livelihood;
the way of the people's life lies in this.
To not announce the intercalary new moon
is to abandon the seasonal governance—
how can one govern the people?
Annals of Year 7 of Duke Wén
In the spring of the seventh year,
the Duke attacked Zhū.
In the third month, on the day jiǎ xū,
he took Xū Jù.
Then he walled Wú.
In summer, the fourth month,
the Duke of Sòng, Wáng Chén, died.
The people of Sòng killed their Grand Master.
On the day wù zǐ,
the people of Jìn and the people of Qín fought at Lìng Hú.
Xiān Miè of Jìn fled to Qín.
The Dí invaded our western borders.
In autumn, the eighth month,
the Duke met with the feudal lords,
and the Grand Masters of Jìn to covenant at Hù.
In winter,
Xú attacked Jǔ.
Gōng Sūn Áo went to Jǔ to attend the covenant.
Commentary on Year 7 of Duke Wén
In the spring of the seventh year,
the Duke attacked Zhū,
taking advantage of Jìn's difficulties.
In the third month, on the day jiǎ xū,
he took Xū Jù,
and placed a son of Duke Wén there;
this was contrary to ritual.
In summer, the fourth month,
Duke Chéng of Sòng died.
At that time, Gōng Zǐ Chéng was the Right Marshal,
Gōng Sūn Yǒu was the Left Marshal,
Yuè Yù was the Minister of War,
Lín Guàn was the Minister of Education,
Gōng Zǐ Dàng was the Minister of Works,
Huá Yù Shì was the Minister of Justice.
Duke Zhāo intended to remove the various scions.
Yuè Yù said:
"That is not possible.
The ducal kin
are the branches and leaves of the ducal house;
if you remove them,
the root will have nothing to provide shade or protection.
Creeping vines can still protect their roots,
which is why the gentleman uses them as a metaphor—
how much more so for a ruler of a state?
This is what the proverb means by
'Providing shade
while allowing the swinging of an axe'
It must not be done.
May the ruler consider it!
Treat them with virtue,
and they will all be your arms and legs;
who would dare to be double-minded?
Why remove them?"
He did not listen.
The clans of Mù and Xiāng
led the people of the capital to attack the Duke,
killing Gōng Sūn Gù and Gōng Sūn Zhèng in the ducal palace.
The six ministers reconciled with the ducal house,
and Yuè Yù gave up the office of Minister of War
to yield it to Gōng Zǐ Ăng.
Duke Zhāo ascended the throne and buried the late ruler.
The Annals say: "The people of Sòng killed their Grand Master,"
without mentioning names
because they were many,
and also to state that it was not their fault.
Duke Kāng of Qín escorted Gōng Zǐ Yōng to Jìn,
saying:
"When Duke Wén entered,
he had no guard,
so there was the trouble with Lǚ and Xì."
So he gave him many followers and guards.
Mù Yíng daily held the Crown Prince
and wailed in the court,
saying:
"What was the crime of the late ruler?
What is the crime of his heir?
Abandoning the legitimate heir to not establish him
while seeking a ruler from outside—
where will you place this one?"
Leaving the court,
she then carried him to the house of the Zhào clan
and bowed her head to Xuān Zǐ,
saying:
"The late ruler upheld this child and entrusted him to you,
saying:
'If this child is talented,
I receive your blessing;
if he is not talented,
I will only have you to blame.'
Now though the ruler has passed,
the words are still in our ears,
yet you abandon him—
why?"
Xuān Zǐ and the Grand Masters were all troubled by Mù Yíng
and feared being pressured,
so they went back on Xiān Miè
and established Duke Líng,
in order to resist the Qín army.
Jī Zhèng stayed to defend.
Zhào Dùn led the Middle Army,
Xiān Kè assisting him;
Xún Lín Fù assisted the Upper Army;
Xiān Miè led the Lower Army,
Xiān Dū assisting him.
Bù Zhāo drove the chariot,
and Róng Jīn was the chariot-right.
They reached Jǐn Yīn.
Xuān Zǐ said:
"If we receive Qín,
Qín is a guest;
if we do not,
they are invaders.
Since we have not received them,
if we further delay our army,
Qín will develop designs."
Taking the initiative to seize the spirit of the enemy
is a good strategy for an army.
Pursuing a bandit like chasing a fugitive
is a good tactic for an army."
He trained the soldiers,
sharpened the weapons,
fed the horses,
had the men eat early in their quarters,
and moved the army secretly by night.
On the day Wùzǐ,
they defeated the Qín army at Lìnghú,
pursuing them as far as Kūshǒu.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
Xiān Miè fled to Qín,
and Shì Huì followed him.
When Xiān Miè was about to go on his mission,
Xún Línfǔ tried to stop him,
saying:
"The Lady and the Crown Prince are still here,
yet you seek a ruler from outside;
this will surely not work.
Why do you not decline
on the grounds of illness?
If you do not,
disaster will reach you.
Sending an acting minister in your stead
would be acceptable;
why must it be you?
Those in the same office are colleagues;
as I was once your colleague,
how could I dare not do my best for you?"
He did not listen.
Xún recited the third stanza of the poem "Bǎn" for him,
but he still did not listen.
When he went into exile,
Xún Bó sent all of his family and his vessels, belongings, and wealth to Qín,
saying:
"It is for the sake of having been colleagues."
While Shì Huì was in Qín for three years,
he did not see Shì Bó.
His attendants said:
"You were able to follow a man into exile from his state,
yet you cannot see him here;
what is the use of that?"
Shì Jì said:
"I share the same guilt as he;
it was not a righteous act.
Why should I see him?"
Until they returned,
he never saw him.
B6.7.5 The Dí invaded our western borders;
the Duke sent word to Jìn.
Zhào Xuānzǐ sent Jiǎ Jì to inquire of Fèng Shū,
and also to reprimand him.
Fèng Shū asked Jiǎ Jì:
"Between Zhào Shuāi and Zhào Dùn, who is more worthy?"
He replied:
"Zhào Shuāi
is like the sun of a winter day;
Zhào Dùn
is like the sun of a summer day."

B6.7.6 In the autumn, the eighth month, the Marquis of Qí, the Duke of Sòng, the Marquis of Wèi, the Marquis of Chén, the Earl of Zhèng, the Baron of Xǔ, and the Earl of Cáo met with Zhào Dùn of Jìn and made a covenant at Hù,
because the Marquis of Jìn had been established.
The Duke arrived late,
so the place of the meeting was not recorded.
Whenever meeting with the feudal lords,
if the place of the meeting is not recorded,
it is because of being late.
If one arrives late,
the name of the state is not recorded,
to avoid mentioning his lack of promptness.
B6.7.7 Mù Bó took a wife from Jǔ,
named Dài Jǐ,
who gave birth to Wén Bó;
her younger sister Shēng Jǐ gave birth to Huì Shū.
Dài Jǐ died.
He again sought a marriage in Jǔ;
the people of Jǔ declined because of Shēng Jǐ,
so a marriage was sought for Xiāng Zhòng.
In winter,
Xú attacked Jǔ.
The people of Jǔ came to request a covenant.
Mù Bó went to Jǔ to attend the covenant
and also to escort the bride for Zhòng.
When he reached Yānlíng,
he climbed the wall and saw her;
she was beautiful,
so he married her himself.
Zhòng asked to attack him,
and the Duke was about to grant it,
but Shūzhòng Huì Bó remonstrated,
saying:
"I have heard:
'When arms are raised within, it is called disorder;
when raised without, it is called banditry.'
Banditry only affects others,
but disorder affects oneself.
Now if a subject creates disorder and the ruler does not stop it,
thus opening the way for enemies,
what will happen?"
The Duke stopped him.
Huì Bó mediated the matter,
making Zhòng give her up.
Gōngsūn Áo returned her,
and they became brothers again as before.
He followed this.
B6.7.8 Xì Quē of Jìn spoke to Zhào Xuānzǐ, saying:
"In the past, Wèi was not harmonious,
so we took their land.
Now they are harmonious;
it would be proper to return it.
If they rebel and are not punished,
how can we show majesty?
If they submit and are not treated with kindness,
how can we show care?
Without majesty and without care,
how can we show virtue?
Without virtue,
how can one lead the covenants?
You are the prime minister,
leading the feudal lords,
yet if you do not strive for virtue,
what will you do?
The *Xià Shū* says:
'Warn them with excellence,
direct them with majesty,
encourage them with the "Nine Songs,"
and do not let them go to ruin.'
The virtues of the nine achievements can all be sung;
they are called the 'Nine Songs.'
The six treasuries and the three tasks
are called the nine achievements.
Water, fire, metal, wood, earth, and grain
are called the six treasuries;
rectifying virtue, making use of resources, and enriching life
are called the three tasks.
Acting upon them with righteousness
is called virtue and ritual.
Without ritual, there is no joy,
and that is why they rebel.
As for your virtue,
nothing can be sung;
who then will come to you?
Why not let those who are harmonious sing of you?"
Xuānzǐ was pleased.
A6.8 *The Annals of the Eighth Year of Duke Wén*
A6.8.1 In the spring of the eighth year,
the royal first month.
A6.8.2 In summer, the fourth month.
A6.8.3 In autumn, the eighth month, on the day Wùshēn,
the Heavenly King died.
A6.8.4 In winter, the tenth month, on the day Rénwǔ,
Gōngzǐ Suì met Zhào Dùn of Jìn
and made a covenant at Héngyōng.
A6.8.5 On the day Yǐyǒu,
Gōngzǐ Suì met the Luò Róng
and made a covenant at Bào.
A6.8.6 Gōngsūn Áo went to the capital;
before arriving, he returned.
On the day Bǐngxū,
he fled to Jǔ.
A6.8.7 Locusts.
A6.8.8 The people of Sòng killed their Grand Master Sīmǎ.
The Sīchéng of Sòng came in flight.
B6.8 *The Commentary for the Eighth Year of Duke Wén*
B6.8.1 In the spring of the eighth year,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Xiè Yáng to return the lands of Kuāng
and Qī to Wèi,
and also to restore the fief of Gōngxù Chí,
from Shēn to the border of Hǔláo.
B6.8.2 In summer,
the people of Qín attacked Jìn
and took Wǔchéng,
to retaliate for the battle of Lìnghú.
B6.8.3 In autumn,
King Xiāng died.
B6.8.4 The people of Jìn, on account of the covenant at Hù, came to punish the state.
In winter,
Xiāng Zhòng met Zhào Mèng of Jìn
and made a covenant at Héngyōng,
in response to the covenant at Hù.
He then met with the Róng of the Yī and Luò.
The record says "Gōngzǐ Suì"
to honor him.
B6.8.5 Mù Bó went to Zhōu to offer condolences,
but did not arrive;
taking the ceremonial silks, he fled to Jǔ
to follow the lady of the Jǐ clan.
B6.8.6 The Lady of Sòng Xiāng
was the elder sister of Xiāng Wáng.
Zhāo Gōng did not treat her with ritual propriety.
Relying on the Dài Shì clan, the Lady
killed Kǒng Shū, the grandson of Xiāng Gōng, as well as Gōngsūn Zhōnglí and the Dà Sīmǎ, Gōngzǐ Áng.
All were partisans of Zhāo Gōng.
The Sīmǎ died while clutching his staff of office;
therefore, the record used his official title.
Sīchéng Dàng Yìzhū fled to our state;
he handed over his staff of office to the treasury official before departing.
The Duke welcomed him with his official title
and restored both of them to their positions.
He was also recorded by his official title,
for the Duke held both men in high esteem.
B6.8.7 During the hunt at Yí,
the Marquis of Jìn intended to promote Jì Zhèngfù and Xiān Dū,
and he appointed Shì Hú and Liáng Yì'ěr to command the Central Army.
Xiān Kè said,
"The meritorious service of the Hú and Zhào families
must not be set aside."
The Marquis followed this advice.
Xiān Kè seized the fields of Kuǎi Dé at Jǐnyīn.
Consequently, Jì Zhèngfù, Xiān Dū, Shì Hú, Liáng Yì'ěr, and Kuǎi Dé rose in revolt.
A6.9 The Annals of the Ninth Year of Wén Gōng.
A6.9.1 In the spring of the ninth year,
Máo Bó came to request gold.
A6.9.2 The Lady Jiāng Shì went to Qí.
A6.9.3 In the second month,
Shū sūn Déchén went to the capital.
On the day xīnchǒu,
Xiāng Wáng was buried.
A6.9.4 The people of Jìn killed their Great Officer Xiān Dū.
A6.9.5 In the third month,
the Lady Jiāng Shì arrived from Qí.
A6.9.6 The people of Jìn killed their Great Officers Shì Hú and Jì Zhèngfù.
A6.9.7 The people of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
A6.9.8 Gōngzǐ Suì met with the people of Jìn,
Sòng,
Wèi,
and Xǔ to rescue Zhèng.
A6.9.9 In the summer,
the Dí invaded Qí.
A6.9.10 In the autumn, in the eighth month,
Cáo Bó Xiāng died.
In the ninth month on the day guǐyǒu,
there was an earthquake.
A6.9.12 In the winter,
the Viscount of Chǔ sent Jiāo on a mission of friendly inquiry.
A6.9.13 The people of Qín came to present grave clothes for Xī Gōng
and Chéng Fēng.
A6.9.14 Duke Gòng of Cáo was buried.
B6.9 The Commentary on the Ninth Year of Wén Gōng.
B6.9.1 In the spring of the ninth year,
in the King's first month on the day jǐyǒu,
assassins were sent to kill Xiān Kè.
On the day yǐchǒu,
the people of Jìn killed Xiān Dū and Liáng Yì'ěr.
B6.9.2 Máo Bó Wèi came to request gold,
which was contrary to ritual propriety.
It was not recorded as the "King's command"
because the King had not yet been buried.
B6.9.3 In the second month,
Zhuāng Shū went to Zhōu
for the burial of Xiāng Wáng.
B6.9.4 In the third month on the day jiǎxū,
the people of Jìn killed Jì Zhèngfù,
Shì Hú,
and Kuǎi Dé.
B6.9.5 Fàn Shān said to the Viscount of Chǔ,
"The ruler of Jìn is young,
and he does not lead the feudal lords;
the North can be plotted against."
The Viscount of Chǔ encamped his army at Lángyuān to attack Zhèng.
He took Gōngzǐ Jiān, Gōngzǐ Máng, and Lè Ěr prisoner.
Zhèng made peace with Chǔ.
B6.9.6 Gōngzǐ Suì met with Zhào Dùn of Jìn, Huà Ǒu of Sòng, Kǒng Dá of Wèi, and the Great Officer of Xǔ to rescue Zhèng,
but they did not reach the Chǔ army.
The names of the ministers were not recorded
because of their delay,
so as to punish their lack of diligence.
B6.9.7 In the summer,
Chǔ invaded Chén
and captured Húqiū,
because Chén had submitted to Jìn.
B6.9.8 In the autumn,
the Chǔ Gōngzǐ Zhū led an attack from the Dōngyí against Chén;
the people of Chén defeated them
and captured Gōngzǐ Fá.
Chén was afraid
and thus made peace with Chǔ.
B6.9.9 In the winter,
the Chǔ Gōngzǐ Yuèjiāo came on a mission of friendly inquiry;
while holding the ritual silk, he was arrogant.
Shūzhòng Huìbó said,
"This man will surely cause the destruction of the Ruò'áo clan.
Being arrogant toward his former ruler,
the spirits will not grant him blessings."
B6.9.10 The people of Qín came to present grave clothes for Xī Gōng
and Chéng Fēng,
which was in accordance with ritual propriety.
When the feudal lords send condolences and congratulations to one another,
even if they are not at the exact time of the event,
provided there is ritual propriety,
it is recorded
so as not to forget old friendships.
A6.10 The Annals of the Tenth Year of Wén Gōng.
A6.10.1 In the spring of the tenth year,
in the King's third month on the day xīnmǎo,
Zāng sūn Chén died.
A6.10.2 In the summer,
Qín attacked Jìn.
A6.10.3 Chǔ killed its Great Officer Yí Shēn.
A6.10.4 From the first month there was no rain
until the autumn in the seventh month.
A6.10.5 A covenant was made with Sū Zǐ at Nǚlì.
A6.10.6 In the winter,
the Dí invaded Sòng.
A6.10.7 The Viscount of Chǔ
and the Marquis of Cài halted at Juéhé.
B6.10 The Commentary on the Tenth Year of Wén Gōng.
B6.10.1 In the spring of the tenth year,
the people of Jìn attacked Qín
and took Shǎoliáng.
B6.10.2 In the summer,
the Earl of Qín attacked Jìn
and took Běizhēng.
B6.10.3 Previously,
the Chǔ shaman Fàn Wū Yùsì had said to Chéng Wáng, Zǐyù,
and Zǐxī,
"All three rulers will die a violent death."
During the campaign of Chéngpú,
the King remembered this,
so he sent a messenger to stop Zǐyù, saying,
"Do not die."
The messenger did not arrive in time.
He also tried to stop Zǐxī;
Zǐxī had hanged himself, and the rope broke.
The King's messenger arrived just then
and thus stopped him,
and made him the Duke of Shāng.
Moving along the Hàn and up the Jiāng,
he was about to enter Yǐng.
The King was at the Zhǔgōng;
he went down
and saw him.
Zǐxī was afraid,
and he excused himself, saying,
"I escaped death,
but there were slanderous words
saying I was going to flee;
I have come to surrender for death to the Sībài."
The King made him the Gōngyǐn,
but he then plotted with Zǐjiā to assassinate Mù Wáng.
Mù Wáng heard of it,
and in the fifth month,
he killed Dòu Yíshēn and Zhòng Guī.
B6.10.4 In the autumn, in the seventh month,
a covenant was made with Sū Zǐ at Nǚlì,
which was because Qǐng Wáng had been established.
B6.10.5 The Marquis of Chén and the Earl of Zhèng met with the Viscount of Chǔ at Xī.
In the winter,
they then joined the Marquis of Cài to halt at Juéhé,
intending to attack Sòng.
Huà Yùshì of Sòng said,
"Chǔ wishes to weaken us;
should we not first show ourselves as weak?
Why must we make them lure us out?
It is we who are truly incapable;
what crime have the people committed?"
He then went to meet the Viscount of Chǔ,
comforted the troops and accepted orders.
He then led the way to hunt at Mèngzhū.
The Duke of Sòng acted as the right horn,
and the Earl of Zhèng acted as the left horn.
Fù Suì, the Duke of Qīsī, was the Right Minister of War;
Zǐ Zhū and Wén zhī Wúwèi were the Left Ministers of War.
An order was given to harness the carriages early and carry fire-sticks.
The Duke of Sòng disobeyed the order.
Wúwèi whipped the Duke's groom and paraded him through the ranks.
Someone said to Zǐzhōu:
“The ruler of a state must not be humiliated.”
Zǐzhōu said:
“When acting in accordance with one’s office,
what excess is there?
The *Shī* says:
‘The hard he does not spit out,
the soft he does not swallow,’
and ‘Do not indulge the crafty and following,
so as to be cautious of those without limit.’
This is also to not avoid the powerful.
Would I dare to cherish my life and thereby throw my office into disorder?”
B6.10.6 At the meeting of Juéhé,
the Viscount of Jūn fled and returned home.
A6.11 The Classic of the Eleventh Year of Duke Wén
A6.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
the Viscount of Chǔ attacked Jūn.
A6.11.2 In the summer,
Shū Péngshēng met Xì Quē of Jìn at Chéngkuāng.
A6.11.3 In the autumn,
the Earl of Cáo came for an audience at court.
A6.11.4 Gōngzǐ Suì went to Sòng.
A6.11.5 The Dí invaded Qí.
A6.11.6 In winter, the tenth month, on the day jiǎwǔ,
Shūsūn Déchén defeated the Dí at Xián.
B6.11 The Commentary on the Eleventh Year of Duke Wén
B6.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
the Viscount of Chǔ attacked Jūn.
Chéng Dàxīn
defeated the army of Jūn at Fángzhǔ.
Pān Chóng again attacked Jūn,
reaching Yángxué.
B6.11.2 In the summer,
Shūzhòng Huìbó met Xì Quē of Jìn at Chéngkuāng,
to plan against those feudal lords who followed Chǔ.
B6.11.3 In the autumn,
Duke Wén of Cáo came for an audience at court;
having ascended the throne,
he came for a visit.
B6.11.4 Xiāngzhòng went on a friendly mission to Sòng,
and also spoke on behalf of Sīchéng Dàng Yìzhū that he be restored.
Because of this, he congratulated them that the Chǔ army had not caused harm.
B6.11.5 The Sōumán invaded Qí,
and then attacked us.
The Duke divined about sending Shūsūn Déchén to pursue them,
and it was auspicious.
Hóu Shūxià drove for Zhuāngshū;
Mián Fángshēng was the attendant on the right;
and Fùfù Zhōngshēng was the fourth man in the chariot.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day jiǎwǔ,
they defeated the Dí at Xián,
and captured Qiáorú of the Zhǎngdí.
Fùfù Zhōngshēng struck his throat with a spear
and killed him.
They buried his head at the gate of Zǐjū
and named his son Xuānbó after the event.
Formerly,
in the time of Duke Wǔ of Sòng,
the Sōumán attacked Sòng.
Sītú Huángfǔ led an army to resist them.
Nái Bān drove for Huángfǔ Chōngshí;
Gōngzǐ Gǔshēng was the attendant on the right;
and Sīkòu Niúfù was the fourth man in the chariot.
They defeated the Dí at Chángqiū
and captured Yuánsī of the Zhǎngdí.
Two sons of Huángfǔ died there.
The Duke of Sòng therefore rewarded Nái Bān with a gate,
allowing him to consume its taxes;
it was called the Nái Gate.
When Jìn destroyed Lù,
they captured Fénrú, the younger brother of Qiáorú.
In the second year of Duke Huì of Qí,
the Sōumán attacked Qí.
Wángzǐ Chéngfù of Qí captured his younger brother Róngrú
and buried his head at the north gate of Zhōushǒu.
The people of Wèi captured his youngest brother Jiǎnrú.
Because of this, the Sōumán finally perished.
B6.11.6 Zhūrú, the Crown Prince of Chéng, settled himself at Fúzhōng,
but the people of the state did not follow him.
A6.12 The Classic of the Twelfth Year of Duke Wén
A6.12.1 In the spring of the twelfth year,
the royal first month,
the Earl of Chéng came as a refugee.
A6.12.2 The Earl of Qǐ came for an audience at court.
A6.12.3 In the second month, on the day gēngzǐ,
Zǐ Shūjī died.
A6.12.4 In the summer,
the people of Chǔ besieged Cháo.
A6.12.5 In the autumn,
the Viscount of Téng came for an audience at court.
A6.12.6 The Earl of Qín sent Shù on a friendly mission.
A6.12.7 In winter, the twelfth month, on the day wùwǔ,
the people of Jìn and
the people of Qín fought at Héqǔ.
A6.12.8 Jìsūn Xíngfù led an army to wall Zhū and Yùn.
B6.12 The Commentary on the Twelfth Year of Duke Wén
B6.12.1 In the spring of the twelfth year,
the Earl of Chéng died,
and the people of Chéng established a ruler.
The Crown Prince came as a refugee with Fúzhōng and the Chéng jade tablet.
The Duke received him with the ceremonies for a feudal lord;
this was not in accordance with the rites.
Therefore the record says,
“The Earl of Chéng came as a refugee.”
The location is not recorded
to show respect for his status as a feudal lord.
B6.12.2 Duke Huán of Qǐ came for an audience at court;
it was the first time he had paid court to the Duke.
He also requested to divorce Shūjī
but without ending the marriage alliance.
The Duke granted this.
In the second month,
Shūjī died.
The text does not say “of Qǐ”
because she had been divorced.
It records her as “Shūjī,”
indicating she was no longer a wife.
B6.12.3 Dàsūn Bó, the Chief Minister of Chǔ, died,
and Chéng Jiā became Chief Minister.
The various Shū tribes revolted against Chǔ.
In the summer,
Zǐkǒng seized Shūzǐ Píng and Zōngzǐ,
and then besieged Cháo.
B6.12.4 In the autumn,
Duke Zhāo of Téng came for an audience at court;
this was also the first time he had paid court to the Duke.
B6.12.5 The Earl of Qín sent Xīqǐ Shù on a friendly mission,
and to say they were going to attack Jìn.
Xiāngzhòng declined the ritual jade,
saying:
“Your ruler has not forgotten the friendship of our former rulers,
shining upon the state of Lǔ
and comforting its altars of soil and grain.
Bestowing weight upon us with such great vessels,
my unworthy ruler ventures to decline the jade.”
The reply was:
“These meager, worn vessels
are not worthy of being declined.”
The host declined three times.
The guest answered:
“My unworthy ruler wishes to seek blessings from the Duke of Zhōu and the Duke of Lǔ in order to serve your ruler.
These meager, worn vessels of our former rulers
have been sent by him through me, his lowly servant, to your ministers
to serve as tokens of credentials
and to bind our friendly mandates.
They are the means by which my unworthy ruler's mandate is presented
and the friendship between our two states is tied.
For this reason, I venture to present them.”
Xiāngzhòng said:
“If there were no superior men,
how could the state exist?
The state is not lacking.”
He rewarded him generously.
B6.12.6 On account of the battle of Lìnghú,
in winter,
the Earl of Qín attacked Jìn
and took Jīmǎ.
The people of Jìn resisted them.
Zhào Dùn commanded the Central Army,
and Xún Línfù assisted him.
Xì Quē commanded the Upper Army,
and Yú Pián assisted him.
Luán Dùn commanded the Lower Army,
and Xū Jiǎ assisted him.
Fàn Wúxù drove the war-chariot
to follow the Qín army to Héqǔ.
Yú Pián said:
“The Qín army cannot stay long.
I request that we deepen our ramparts and strengthen our camp
to wait for them.”
This was followed.
The people of Qín desired to battle.
The Qín Bó said to Shì Huì:
“How shall we battle?”
He replied:
“The Zhào clan has recently brought forward a subordinate named Yú Pián,
who must certainly be making these plans,
intending to weary our army.
Among the Zhào family, there is a member of a collateral branch named Chuān,
who is the son-in-law of the Ruler of Jìn;
he is favored but weak,
and has no role in military affairs;
he loves bravery but is impulsive,
and furthermore, he resents Yú Pián's assisting of the Upper Army.
If we send light troops to provoke him,
it may work.”
The Qín Bó used a jade bì disk to pray for battle at the Hé.
In the twelfth month, on the day wùwǔ,
the Qín army made a surprise attack on the Jìn Upper Army.
Zhào Chuān pursued them,
but did not catch them.
Upon returning,
he said in anger:
“Wrapping our rations and putting on our armor,
we were surely seeking the enemy.
Now that the enemy has arrived, we do not strike;
what are we waiting for?”
The military officers said:
“The general has someone he is waiting for.”
Chuān said:
“I do not know of plans;
I shall go out alone.”
Thereupon, he went out with his subordinates.
Xuānzǐ said:
“If Qín captures Chuān,
they will have captured a high minister.
If Qín returns home in victory,
how shall we respond?”
Thus, they all went out to battle,
and the two sides withdrew after an engagement.
A Qín envoy warned the Jìn army by night, saying:
“The soldiers of our two lords are not yet weary;
tomorrow we request to meet again.”
Yú Pián said:
“The envoy’s eyes were moving and his speech was unrestrained;
he is afraid of us
and is about to flee.
If we press them at the Hé,
we will surely defeat them.”
Xū Jiǎ and
Zhào Chuān stood at the camp gate and shouted:
“To abandon the dead and wounded before they are collected
is not kind.
Not waiting for the appointed time
and pressing people into a place of danger
is not courageous.”
Thereupon, they stopped.
The Qín army fled during the night.
They again invaded Jìn,
entering Xiá.
B6.12.7 Walls were built at Zhū and Yùn;
this was recorded
because it was done at the proper time.
A6.13 The Classic: The Thirteenth Year of Duke Wén
A6.13.1 In the thirteenth year, in the spring,
in the King’s first month.
A6.13.2 In the summer, in the fifth month, on the day rénwǔ,
Shù, Marquis of Chén, died.
A6.13.3 Qúchú, Zhū Zǐ, died.
A6.13.4 From the first month it did not rain
until the autumn, the seventh month.
A6.13.5 The roof of the Grand Chamber collapsed.
A6.13.6 In the winter,
the Duke went to Jìn.
The Marquis of Wèi met the Duke at Tà.
A6.13.7 The Dí invaded Wèi.
A6.13.8 In the twelfth month, on the day jǐchǒu,
the Duke and the Marquis of Jìn made a covenant.
A6.13.9 The Duke returned from Jìn,
and the Earl of Zhèng met the Duke at Fěi.
B6.13 The Commentary: The Thirteenth Year of Duke Wén
B6.13.1 In the spring of the thirteenth year,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Zhān Jiā to reside in Xiá
to guard the pass of Táolín.
B6.13.2 The people of Jìn were distressed by Qín's employment of Shì Huì.
In the summer,
the six ministers met at Zhūfú.
Zhào Xuānzǐ said:
“Suí Huì is in Qín,
and Jiǎ Jì is among the Dí;
difficulties will arrive any day;
what shall we do?”
Zhōngháng Huánzǐ said:
“I request that we bring back Jiǎ Jì;
he is capable in foreign affairs,
and moreover, his family has old merits.”
Xì Chéngzǐ said:
“Jiǎ Jì caused disorder
and his crimes are great;
he is not as good as Suí Huì.
He can endure a humble position and has a sense of shame;
he is gentle but cannot be violated;
his wisdom is sufficient to be employed.
Furthermore, he is without crime.”
They then sent Wèi Shòuyú to feign
that he was a rebel from Wèi
in order to lure Shì Huì.
They seized his family in Jìn
but allowed them to escape by night.
Shòuyú requested to submit himself to Qín,
and the Qín Bó granted it.
He stepped on Shì Huì’s foot at the court.
The Qín Bó encamped his army on the west of the Hé;
the people of Wèi were on the east.
Shòuyú said:
“I request that one of the people from the east who is able to speak with those few officials
come ahead with me.”
He sent Shì Huì.
Shì Huì declined,
saying:
“The people of Jìn
are like tigers and wolves;
if they go back on their word,
I will die,
and my wife and children will be executed;
this would be of no benefit to you, my lord,
and it would be too late for regrets.”
The Qín Bó said:
“If they go back on their word
and I do not return your family to you,
may it be as the Hé!”
Thereupon, he went.
Rào Zhāo presented him with a horse-whip,
saying:
“Sir, do not say that Qín has no men;
it is just that my plans happen not to be used.”
Once they had crossed,
the people of Wèi shouted and returned home.
The people of Qín returned his family.
Those of his family who remained there became the Liú clan.
B6.13.3 Zhū Wén Gōng
divined about moving the capital to Yì.
The scribe said:
“It is beneficial for the people but not beneficial for the ruler.”
Zhū Zǐ said:
“If it is beneficial for the people,
it is my benefit.
Heaven produced the people and established for them a ruler
in order to benefit them.
Since the people will be benefited,
I must surely share in it.”
His attendants said:
“One's life may be prolonged;
why, my lord, do you not do so?”
Zhū Zǐ said:
“Life lies in nourishing the people.
Whether death comes early or late
is a matter of time.
If the people are indeed benefited,
as for moving the capital,
nothing could be more auspicious!”
They then moved to Yì.
In the fifth month,
Zhū Wén Gōng died.
The superior man said:
“He knew the Mandate.”
B6.13.4 In the autumn, in the seventh month,
the roof of the Grand Chamber collapsed;
this was recorded
because of a lack of reverence.
B6.13.5 In the winter,
the Duke went to Jìn
for an audience
and to renew the covenant.
The Marquis of Wèi met the Duke at Tà,
requesting to make peace with Jìn.
The Duke returned;
the Earl of Zhèng met the Duke at Fěi,
also requesting to make peace with Jìn.
The Duke brought both to a successful conclusion.
The Earl of Zhèng and the Duke held a banquet at Fěi;
Zǐjiā recited "Hóngyàn."
Jì Wénzǐ said:
“Our humble ruler has not yet escaped from this.”
Wénzǐ recited "Sìyuè";
Zǐjiā recited the fourth stanza of "Zàichí."
Wénzǐ recited the fourth stanza of "Cǎiwēi."
The Earl of Zhèng bowed.
The Duke bowed in return.
A6.14 The Annals of Duke Wén, Year 14
A6.14.1 In the fourteenth year, in spring,
in the King's first month,
the Duke arrived from Jìn.
A6.14.2 The people of Zhū attacked our southern border;
Shū Péngshēng led an army to attack Zhū.
A6.14.3 In summer, in the fifth month, on the day yǐhài,
Pān, Marquis of Qí, died.
A6.14.4 In the sixth month,
the Duke met with the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Baron of Xǔ,
the Earl of Cáo,
and Zhào Dùn of Jìn.
On the day guǐyǒu,
they made a common covenant at Xīnchéng.
A6.14.5 In autumn, in the seventh month,
a comet entered the Northern Dipper.
A6.14.6 The Duke arrived from the meeting.
A6.14.7 The people of Jìn tried to install Jiézī in Zhū,
but they were unable to install him.
A6.14.8 In the ninth month, on the day jiǎshēn,
Gōngsūn Áo died in Qí.
A6.14.9 Prince Shāngrén of Qí assassinated his ruler, Shè.
A6.14.10 Zǐ’āi of Sòng came in flight.
A6.14.11 In winter,
Shànbó went to Qí.
A6.14.12 The people of Qí seized Shànbó.
A6.14.13 The people of Qí seized Zǐ Shūjī.
B6.14 The Commentary of Duke Wén, Year 14
B6.14.1 In spring of the fourteenth year,
King Qǐng died.
Zhōu Gōng Yuè and Wángsūn Sū struggled for political power;
therefore, no funeral announcement was made.
Generally, when a King dies or
a Lord dies,
if no announcement is made,
then it is not recorded.
Disasters or
blessings, if not reported,
are also not recorded.
This is to punish lack of respect.
B6.14.2 At the death of Duke Wén of Zhū,
the Duke sent an envoy to offer condolences,
but without respect.
The people of Zhū came to retaliate
and attacked our southern border;
therefore, Huìbó attacked Zhū.
B6.14.3 Zǐ Shūjī was the consort of Duke Zhāo of Qí
and gave birth to Shè.
Shūjī was not favored,
and Shè had no prestige.
Prince Shāngrén frequently bestowed gifts in the state.
He gathered many followers,
exhausting his household resources,
and borrowed from the public officials to continue it.
In summer, in the fifth month,
Duke Zhāo died,
and Shè succeeded to the throne.
B6.14.4 The principal consort of Duke Wén of Zhū was Qí Jiāng,
who bore Duke Dìng;
his second consort was Jìn Jī,
who bore Jiézī.
When Duke Wén died,
the people of Zhū installed Duke Dìng.
Jiézī fled to Jìn.
B6.14.5 In the sixth month,
they made a common covenant at Xīnchéng;
those who followed Chǔ submitted,
and they also made plans regarding Zhū.
B6.14.6 In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day yǐmǎo,
at night,
Shāngrén of Qí assassinated Shè
and offered the throne to Yuán.
Yuán said:
"You have sought this for a long time.
I can serve you.
You should not allow many resentments to accumulate;
will you then spare me?
You do it!"
B6.14.7 A comet entered the Northern Dipper.
Shūfú, the Inner Scribe of Zhōu, said:
"Within seven years,
the rulers of Sòng, Qí, and Jìn will all die in turmoil."
B6.14.8 Zhào Dùn of Jìn, with an army of eight hundred chariots from the regional lords, tried to install Jiézī in Zhū.
The people of Zhū declined, saying:
"Juéqiě, born of Qí, is the elder."
Xuānzǐ said:
"Their argument is reasonable;
to not follow it
would be inauspicious."
Then he returned.
B6.14.9 Zhōu Gōng was about to litigate against Wángsūn Sū in Jìn.
The King turned against Wángsūn Sū
and sent Yǐnshì and Dān Qǐ to litigate against Zhōu Gōng in Jìn.
Zhào Xuānzǐ pacified the Royal House
and restored them.
B6.14.10 King Zhuāng of Chǔ ascended the throne.
Zǐkǒng and Pān Chóng were about to launch a surprise attack on the Shū tribes;
they ordered Prince Xiè and Zǐyí to guard the capital
while they attacked Shūliǎo.
The two men started a rebellion.
They fortified Yǐng
and sent an assassin to kill Zǐkǒng,
but failing this, they returned.
In the eighth month,
the two men took the King of Chǔ out of the capital.
While they were heading for Shāngmì,
Lú Jílí and Shūjūn lured them
and then killed Dòu Kè and Prince Xiè.
Earlier,
Dòu Kè had been imprisoned in Qín.
After the defeat at Xiáo,
Qín sent him back to seek peace.
Peace was made, but he did not achieve his ambitions.
Prince Xiè sought the post of Chief Minister but did not get it;
therefore, the two men started a rebellion.
B6.14.11 When Mùbó followed the woman of the Jǐ lineage,
the people of Lǔ established Wénbó.
Mùbó fathered two sons in Jǔ
and sought to return.
Wénbó made a request on his behalf.
Xiāngzhòng ordered that he not appear at court
but obey orders.
He returned but did not appear in public.
After three years, he took his entire household and went back to Jǔ again.
Wénbó fell ill
and requested:
"Gǔ's son is weak;
I request that Nán be established."
This was granted.
When Wénbó died,
Huìshū was established.
Mùbó requested to return by offering heavy bribes.
Huìshū made the request,
and it was granted.
He was about to come back,
but in the ninth month,
he died in Qí.
A funeral announcement was made
and burial requested,
but it was not granted.
B6.14.12 Gāo Āi of Sòng was the Border Warden of Xiāo.
He was made a minister,
but because he considered the Duke of Sòng's conduct unrighteous, he left
and then came here in flight.
The record says, "Zǐ’āi of Sòng came in flight,"
showing respect for him.
B6.14.13 The people of Qí established Duke Yì.
They sent word to announce the crisis;
therefore, it was recorded as
"the ninth month."
Prince Yuán of Qí
did not comply with Duke Yì's administration;
to the end he did not call him "Duke,"
but called him "that person."
B6.14.14 Xiāngzhòng sent word to the King,
requesting that through the King's favor, Zhāojī be sought from Qí,
saying:
"Since they killed her son,
why keep the mother?
I request to receive her and punish her."
In winter,
Shànbó went to Qí to request Zǐ Shūjī;
the people of Qí seized him.
They also seized Zǐ Shūjī.
A6.15 The Annals of Duke Wén, Year 15
A6.15.1 In the fifteenth year, in spring,
Jìsūn Xíngfù went to Jìn.
A6.15.2 In the third month,
Huásūn, the Minister of War of Sòng, came to make a covenant.
A6.15.3 In summer,
the Earl of Cáo came to court.
A6.15.4 The people of Qí returned the remains of Gōngsūn Áo.
A6.15.5 In the sixth month, on the day xīndǒu, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
Drums were beaten and animals sacrificed at the altar of the land.
A6.15.6 Shàn Bó arrived from Qí.
A6.15.7 Xì Quē of Jìn led an army to attack Cài.
On the day wùshēn,
they entered Cài.
A6.15.8 Autumn,
the people of Qí invaded our western borders.
A6.15.9 Jìsūn Xíngfǔ went to Jìn.
A6.15.10 Winter, eleventh month,
the feudal lords made a covenant at Hù.
A6.15.11 Twelfth month,
the people of Qí came to return Zǐ Shū Jī.
A6.15.12 The Marquis of Qí invaded our western borders,
then attacked Cáo,
and entered its outer walls.
B6.15 The 15th Year of Wén Gōng, Commentary.
B6.15.1 Spring of the fifteenth year,
Jì Wénzǐ went to Jìn
on account of Shàn Bó and Zǐ Shū Jī.
B6.15.2 Third month,
Huá Ǒu of Sòng came to make a covenant,
and his officials all followed him.
The text records: "Huá Sūn, Minister of War of Sòng,"
to show honor to him.
The Duke held a banquet for him.
He declined, saying:
“My lord’s former servant Dū committed a crime against Duke Shāng of Sòng,
and his name is recorded in the annals of the feudal lords.
I, your servant, continue his sacrifices;
how would I dare to insult my lord?
I request to receive your command among the subordinate officers.”
The people of Lǔ considered him clever.
B6.15.3 Summer,
the Earl of Cáo came to court;
this was in accordance with ritual.
Feudal lords visit each other’s courts twice every five years
to cultivate the King’s commands;
this is the ancient regulation.
B6.15.4 Someone of Qí devised a plan for the Mèng clan,
saying:
“Lǔ
is your kin.
If you decorate the coffin and place it at Tángfù,
Lǔ will surely take it.”
They followed this.
The people of Biàn reported it.
Huìshū, still in mourning emaciation,
made a request,
standing at court to wait for the command.
It was granted.
They took the coffin
and held the funeral rites.
The people of Qí escorted it.
The text records:
“The people of Qí returned the remains of Gōngsūn Áo,”
for the sake of the Mèng clan
and because of the state’s affairs.
The burial was like that of Gòngzhòng.
Shēngjǐ did not go to see it
but wailed behind a curtain in the hall.
Xiāngzhòng wished not to wail.
Huìbó said:
“A funeral
is the end of kinship;
though one could not manage the beginning,
a good ending is acceptable.
Shǐ Yì had a saying:
‘Brothers should reach perfection.
Relieving want, congratulating on good fortune, condoling in disaster,
being reverent at sacrifices, and being sorrowful at funerals—
though the feelings differ,
one must not cut off their love;
this is the way of kin.’
If you do not lose the way,
what resentment can you have toward others?”
Xiāngzhòng was pleased
and led his brothers to wail for him.
In later years,
his two sons came;
Mèng Xiànzǐ loved them,
which became known in the state.
Someone slandered them,
saying:
“They are going to kill you.”
Xiànzǐ told Jì Wénzǐ.
The two sons said:
“The master is known for loving us,
while we are known for being about to kill the master;
is this not far from ritual?
It is better to die than to be far from ritual.”
One attacked the gate at Gōuméng,
and the other attacked the gate at Lìqiū; both died.
B6.15.5 Sixth month, first day of the month xīnchǒu,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
They beat drums and used victims at the altar of the land;
this was contrary to ritual.
When there is a solar eclipse,
the Son of Heaven does not have full meals
and has drums beaten at the altar of the land;
the feudal lords use silk offerings at the altar of the land
and have drums beaten at their court,
this is to manifest the service of the spirits, instruct the people, and serve the ruler,
showing that there are ranks of majesty;
this is the ancient way.
B6.15.6 The people of Qí granted Shàn Bó’s request and pardoned him,
sending him to deliver the message.
The text records: “Shàn Bó arrived from Qí,”
to show honor to him.
B6.15.7 At the covenant of Xīnchéng,
the people of Cài did not participate.
Xì Quē of Jìn with the Upper Army
and Lower Army attacked Cài,
saying:
“Our ruler is young;
we must not be idle.”
On the day wùshēn,
they entered Cài
and returned after making a covenant under the city walls.
Generally, when a state is conquered,
it is said to be “extinguished”;
when a major city is captured,
it is said to be “entered.”
B6.15.8 Autumn,
the people of Qí invaded our western borders,
so Jì Wénzǐ reported it to Jìn.

B6.15.9 Winter, eleventh month, the Marquis of Jìn, the Duke of Sòng, the Marquis of Wèi, the Marquis of Cài, the Marquis of Chén, the Earl of Zhèng, the Baron of Xǔ, and the Earl of Cáo made a covenant at Hù,
