renewing the covenant of Xīnchéng
and planning to attack Qí.
The people of Qí bribed the Marquis of Jìn,
so they returned without success.
At that time, there were difficulties with Qí,
so the Duke did not attend the meeting.
The text records: “The feudal lords made a covenant at Hù,”
because they were unable to achieve anything.
Generally, when the feudal lords meet
and the Duke does not participate,
it is not recorded,
so as to conceal the ruler’s fault.
If he participates but it is not recorded,
it is because he arrived late.
B6.15.10 The people of Qí came to return Zǐ Shū Jī,
because of the King's intervention.
B6.15.11 The Marquis of Qí invaded our western borders,
thinking the feudal lords were incapable of action.
He then attacked Cáo,
entered its outer walls,
punishing them for coming to court.
Jì Wénzǐ said:
“Will the Marquis of Qí not escape calamity?
He himself is without ritual,
yet he punishes those who have ritual,
saying:
‘Why do you practice ritual?’
Ritual is to follow Heaven;
it is the Way of Heaven.
He himself goes against Heaven
and yet punishes others;
it will be hard for him to escape.
The Odes say:
‘Why do you not fear each other?
You do not fear Heaven.’
A superior man’s not maltreating the young and lowly
is due to fearing Heaven.
In the Sacrificial Odes of Zhōu it says:
‘Fear the majesty of Heaven,
and thus preserve it.’
If one does not fear Heaven,
how can one preserve anything?
One who takes a state through disorder
and maintains it by following ritual
still fears he will not last to the end;
one who acts frequently without ritual
will not be able to endure.”
A6.16 The 16th Year of Wén Gōng, Classics.
A6.16.1 Spring of the sixteenth year,
Jìsūn Xíngfǔ met with the Marquis of Qí at Yánggǔ,
but the Marquis of Qí did not reach the point of making a covenant.
A6.16.2 Summer, fifth month,
the Duke failed to observe the ritual of the new moon four times.
A6.16.3 Sixth month, on the day wùchén,
Gōngzǐ Suì and the Marquis of Qí made a covenant at Qīqiū.
A6.16.4 Autumn, eighth month, on the day xīnwèi,
the Lady Jiāng died.
A6.16.5 The Quántái tower was demolished.
A6.16.6 The people of Chǔ,
the people of Qín,
and the people of Bā destroyed Yōng.
A6.16.7 In winter, in the eleventh month,
the people of Sòng assassinated their ruler, Chǔjiù.
B6.16 Commentary on the Sixteenth Year of Duke Wén
B6.16.1 In the spring of the sixteenth year,
in the first month of the King’s calendar,
peace was made with Qí.
The Duke was ill
and sent Jì Wénzǐ to meet with the Marquis of Qí at Yánggǔ.
He requested a covenant,
but the Marquis of Qí was unwilling,
saying:
“I request to wait until the Ruler’s recovery.”
B6.16.2 In summer, in the fifth month,
the Duke for four times did not observe the new moon ritual;
this was due to illness.
The Duke sent Xiāng Zhòng to offer bribes to the Marquis of Qí,
and therefore they made a covenant at Qīqiū.
B6.16.3 Snakes emerged from the Quán Palace
and entered the capital,
their number being the same as the late rulers.
In autumn, in the eighth month, on the day xīnwèi,
Shēng Jiāng died.
The Quán Terrace was demolished.
B6.16.4 Chǔ suffered a great famine.
The Róng attacked its southwest,
reaching Mount Fù,
and encamped at Dàlín.
They also attacked its southeast,
reaching Yángqiū,
to invade Zǐzhī.
The people of Yōng led the various Mán tribes to rebel against Chǔ.
The people of Jūn led the Bǎipú to gather at Xuǎn,
intending to attack Chǔ.
Because of this, the northern gates of Shēn and Xī were not opened.
The people of Chǔ planned to move to Bǎngāo.
Wěi Jiǎ said:
“This is not possible.
If we can go there,
the enemy can also go there.
It is better to attack Yōng.
Now the Jūn and the Bǎipú believe that because of our famine we cannot field an army,
and therefore they attack us.
If we send out an army,
they will surely be afraid and return.
The Bǎipú live scattered;
they will each flee to their own towns.
Who will have leisure to plot against others?”
Then the army was sent out.
Within fifteen days,
the Bǎipú withdrew.
From Lú onwards,
they opened the granaries and shared the food.
They halted at Jùshì.
Lú Jìlí was sent to invade Yōng,
reaching Fāngchéng in Yōng.
The people of Yōng pursued them
and captured Zǐ Yángchuāng.
After three nights he escaped
and said:
“The Yōng army is numerous,
and the various Mán have gathered there.
It would be better to return to the main army,
and also call up the King’s troops,
and only advance after joining together.”
Shīshū said:
“This is not possible.
For the time being, encounter them again to make them arrogant.
When they are arrogant and we are incensed,
only then can we overcome them.
This was how the late ruler Fénmào subdued Xíngxí.”
They encountered them again;
they were defeated in seven encounters,
and only the people of Bì, Tiáo, and Yú actually pursued them.
The people of Yōng said:
“Chǔ is no longer worth fighting.”
Consequently, they made no preparations.
The Viscount of Chǔ traveled by post-horses
to meet the army at Línpǐn.
They divided into two columns:
Zǐ Yuè from Shíxī
and Zǐ Bèi from Rèn to attack Yōng.
The people of Qín and the people of Bā followed the Chǔ army.
The various Mán entered a covenant with the Viscount of Chǔ,
and then they destroyed Yōng.
B6.16.5 Sòng Gōngzǐ Bǎo showed courtesy to the people of the state.
When Sòng suffered a famine,
he exhausted his grain to lend it to them.
For those aged seventy and above,
there were none to whom he did not send gifts,
and from time to time he added delicacies and rare treats.
Not a day passed that he did not frequent the gates of the six high ministers.
For the talented men of the state,
there were none he did not serve;
for those of the lineage of Duke Huán and below,
there were none he did not assist.
Gōngzǐ Bǎo was handsome and attractive.
Xiāng Fūren wished to have an affair with him,
but he would not agree,
so she assisted him in his distribution of charity.
Duke Zhāo was without the Way.
The people of the state supported Gōngzǐ Bǎo
by means of the Lady.
At this time, Huà Yuán served as Right Commander,
Gōngsūn Yǒu as Left Commander,
Huà Ǒu as Minister of the Military,
Lín Guàn as Minister of the People,
Dàng Yìzhū as Minister of the City,
and Gōngzǐ Cháo as Minister of Crime.
Earlier,
when Dàng, the Minister of the City, died,
Gōngsūn Shòu declined the post of Minister of the City
and requested to let Yìzhū take it.
Afterwards, he told others:
“The Ruler is without the Way.
My office is close to him,
and I fear disaster will reach me.
If I abandon the office,
then my clan will have no protection.
My son
is my second self;
let him for now delay my death.
Even if I lose my son,
I still will not lose my clan.”
Later,
the Lady intended to have the Duke hunt at Mèngzhū and kill him there.
The Duke knew of this,
but took all his treasures with him on the journey.
Dàng Yìzhū said:
“Why not go to the other feudal lords?”
The Duke said:
“If I cannot please my own grand officers, nor my grandmother, nor the people of the state,
which of the feudal lords would receive me?
Moreover, having been a ruler of men
and then becoming a subject of men—
it is better to die.”
He gave all his treasures to his attendants
and sent them away.
The Lady sent a message telling the Minister of the City to leave the Duke.
He replied:
“To be his minister and yet flee from his difficulties—
how could I face the future rulers?”
In winter, in the eleventh month, on the day jiǎyín,
Duke Zhāo of Sòng was about to hunt at Mèngzhū.
Before he arrived,
Lady Wáng Jī sent the Commander of the Royal Domain to attack and kill him.
Dàng Yìzhū died for him.
The text records:
“The people of Sòng assassinated their ruler Chǔjiù,”
because the ruler was without the Way.
After Duke Wén ascended the throne,
he made his younger brother of the same mother, Xū, the Minister of the City.
Huà Ǒu died,
and he made Dàng Huī the Minister of the Military.
A6.17 Annals of the Seventeenth Year of Duke Wén
A6.17.1 In the spring of the seventeenth year,
the people of Jìn,
the people of Wèi,
the people of Chén,
and the people of Zhèng attacked Sòng.
A6.17.2 In summer, in the fourth month, on the day guǐhài,
our late Lady Shēng Jiāng was buried.
A6.17.3 The Marquis of Qí attacked our western border.
In the sixth month, on the day guǐwèi,
the Duke and the Marquis of Qí made a covenant at Gǔ.
A6.17.4 The feudal lords met at Hù.
A6.17.5 In autumn,
the Duke arrived from Gǔ.
A6.17.6 In winter,
Gōngzǐ Suì went to Qí.
B6.17 Commentary on the Seventeenth Year of Duke Wén
B6.17.1 In the spring of the seventeenth year,
Xún Línfù of Jìn, Kǒng Dá of Wèi, Gōngsūn Níng of Chén, and Shí Chǔ of Zhèng attacked Sòng,
with the proclamation:
“For what reason was the ruler assassinated?”
Yet they confirmed Duke Wén in his position and returned.
The high ministers are not recorded
because they failed in their duty.
B6.17.2 In summer, in the fourth month, on the day guǐhài,
Shēng Jiāng was buried.
Because there were troubles with Qí,
this was delayed.
B6.17.3 The Marquis of Qí attacked our northern border,
and Xiāng Zhòng requested a covenant.
In the sixth month,
they made a covenant at Gǔ.
Jìn Hóu held a hunt at Huángfù,
and then again assembled the zhūhóu at Hù,
to make peace with Sòng.
Gōng did not attend the meeting,
because of the difficulties with Qí.
The record says "zhūhóu",
because there was no merit achieved.
At this time, Jìn Hóu did not see Zhèng Bó,
because he believed he was double-minded toward Chǔ.
Zhèng Zǐjiā sent a messenger
and gave him a letter
to inform Zhào Xuānzǐ,
which said:
"Since my meager ruler ascended the throne three years ago,
he summoned Cài Hóu
to serve your ruler together.
In the ninth month,
Cài Hóu entered our humble city to depart.
Because of the rebellion of Hóu Xuānduō in our humble city,
my meager ruler was thus unable to accompany Cài Hóu.
In the eleventh month,
after overcoming and executing Hóu Xuānduō,
he followed Cài Hóu
to pay court to your officials.
In the sixth month of the twelfth year,
Guīshēng assisted my meager ruler's eldest son Yí
to request Chén Hóu from Chǔ and pay court to all of you.
In the seventh month of the fourteenth year,
my meager ruler again paid court
to complete the matters regarding Chén.
In the fifth month of the fifteenth year,
Chén Hóu went from our humble city to pay court to your ruler.
In the first month of last year,
Zhú Zhīwǔ went to pay court for Yí.
In the eighth month,
my meager ruler again went to pay court.
Considering that Chén and Cài are so close to Chǔ,
yet they do not dare to be double-minded,
it is because of our humble city.
Though our humble city serves your ruler,
why are we not exempted?
During his reign,
he paid court once to Xiāng
and has met your ruler twice.
Yí and several of my lonely self's ministers have also reached Jiàng.
Even though we are a small state,
nothing could exceed this.
Now the great state says:
'You have not satisfied our desires.'
If our humble city were to perish,
nothing more could be added to our plight.
Ancient people had a saying:
'Fearing the head and fearing the tail,
how much of the body is left?'
And also:
'A dying deer does not choose its sounds.'
When a small state serves a great state,
if there is dé,
then it is treated as a person;
if there is no dé,
then it is treated as a deer.
Running headlong into danger,
in an emergency, how can it choose?
Your commands are without limit,
and we know we are facing ruin;
we will gather all our humble taxes and wait at Tiáo.
We await your officials' command.
In the sixth month of the second year of Wén Gōng, on the day Rénshēn,
we paid court to Qí.
In the second month of the fourth year, on the day Rénxū,
for the sake of Qí we invaded Cài,
and also obtained peace with Chǔ.
Living between great states
and following powerful orders,
how can that be a crime?
If the great state does not consider this,
there is nowhere to escape your commands."
Gǒng Shuò of Jìn went to Zhèng to make peace,
Zhào Chuān and Gōngxù Chí became hostages there.
B6.17.5 In autumn,
Zhōu Gān Chǔ defeated the Róng at Shěnchuí,
taking advantage of them while they were drinking wine.
B6.17.6 In winter, the tenth month,
Zhèng crown prince Yí and
Shí Chǔ became hostages in Jìn.
B6.17.7 Xiāng Zhòng went to Qí
to acknowledge the covenant of Gǔ.
Upon returning, he said:
"I have heard that the people of Qí are going to eat the wheat of Lǔ.
From my observation,
they will not be able to.
The words of the Qí ruler are careless.
Zāng Wènzhòng had a saying:
'If the ruler of the people is careless,
he will surely die.'"
A6.18 《Wén Gōng Eighteenth Year Classic》
A6.18.1 In the spring of the eighteenth year,
in the royal second month, on the day Dīngchǒu,
Gōng died at the Tái Hall.
A6.18.2 Qín Bó Yīng died.
A6.18.3 In summer, the fifth month, on the day Wùxū,
the people of Qí assassinated their ruler Shāngrén.
A6.18.4 In the sixth month, on the day Guǐyǒu,
we buried our ruler Wén Gōng.
A6.18.5 In autumn,
Gōngzǐ Suì and
Shúsūn Déchén went to Qí.
A6.18.6 In winter, the tenth month,
Zǐ died.
A6.18.7 Lady Jiāng shì returned to Qí.
A6.18.8 Jìsūn Hángfù went to Qí.
A6.18.9 Jǔ assassinated its ruler Shùqí.
B6.18 《Wén Gōng Eighteenth Year Commentary》
B6.18.1 In the spring of the eighteenth year,
Qí Hóu set a date for the army's mobilization,
but he fell ill.
The doctor said:
"He will not reach autumn;
he is going to die."
When Gōng heard this,
he performed divination,
and said:
"May he not reach the appointed date!"
Huìbó gave the command to the tortoise shell.
Bǔ Chǔqiū interpreted it
and said:
"Qí Hóu will not reach the date,
but it will not be from illness;
nor will my lord hear of it.
There is a calamity in commanding the tortoise."
In the second month, on the day Dīngchǒu,
Gōng died.
B6.18.2 When Qí Yì Gōng was a Gōngzǐ,
he struggled over a field with the father of Bǐng Chǔ
and did not win.
When he ascended the throne,
he dug up the father's corpse and cut off its feet,
and made Chǔ his groom.
He took the wife of Yán Zhí
and made Zhí his assistant charioteer.
In summer, the fifth month,
Gōng was touring Shēnchí.
The two men were bathing in the pool.
Chǔ struck Zhí with a whip.
Zhí was angry.
Chǔ said:
"Someone took your wife and you are not angry;
I whip you once,
why should that hurt?"
Zhí said:
"How does that compare with someone who cannot even feel the pain of his father's feet being cut off?"
Thereupon they plotted to assassinate Yì Gōng,
and placed him in a bamboo grove.
They returned,
set down their cups, and fled.
The people of Qí established Gōngzǐ Yuán.
B6.18.3 In the sixth month,
Wén Gōng was buried.
B6.18.4 In autumn,
Xiāng Zhòng and Zhuāng Shū went to Qí,
because Huì Gōng had been established
and also to acknowledge the burial.
Wén Gōng had two consorts. Jìng Yíng gave birth to Xuān Gōng.
Jìng Yíng was a favorite
and secretly served Xiāng Zhòng.
Xuān Gōng was the elder,
and she entrusted him to Xiāng Zhòng.
Xiāng Zhòng wished to establish him,
but Shúzhòng would not allow it.
Zhòng had an audience with Qí Hóu
and requested it of him.
Qí Hóu, being newly established,
and wishing to be close to Lǔ,
granted it.
B6.18.5 In winter, the tenth month,
Zhòng killed È and Shì,
and established Xuān Gōng.
The record says
"Zǐ died,"
to conceal the truth.
Zhòng, using the ruler's command, summoned Huìbó,
His steward Gōngrǎn Wùrén stopped him,
saying:
“If you enter, you will certainly die.”
Shūzhòng said:
“To die for the ruler’s command is acceptable.”
Gōngrǎn Wùrén said:
“If it were the ruler’s command,
you could die for it;
but it is not the ruler’s command,
why obey?”
He did not listen,
and entered.
They killed him and buried him in horse manure.
Gōngrǎn Wùrén took his family and fled to Cài;
later the Shūzhòng clan was restored.
B6.18.6 Lady Jiāng Shì returned to Qí;
it was a final return.
When she was about to leave,
she wept as she passed through the market,
saying:
“O Heaven!
Zhòng acted without principle,
killing the legitimate heir and setting up the son of a concubine.”
The people in the market all wept.
The people of Lǔ called her Āi Jiāng.
B6.18.7 Duke Jì of Jǔ had an eldest son, Pú,
and also Jìtuó.
He loved Jìtuó and demoted Pú,
and furthermore committed many discourtesies in the state.
Pú used the people of the state to assassinate Duke Jì,
and fled here with his precious jades,
presenting them to Duke Xuān.
The Duke ordered that he be given a city,
saying:
“It must be granted today!”
Jì Wénzǐ sent the Minister of Justice to expel him from the borders,
saying:
“He must reach the border today!”
The Duke asked for the reason.
Jì Wénzǐ had Grand Historian Kè reply, saying:
“The former Great Officer Zāng Wénzhòng
taught Xíngfù the rituals of serving a ruler,
and Xíngfù has followed them in his dealings,
not daring to lose the thread,
saying:
‘When you see one who is ritualistic toward his ruler,
serve him,
as a filial son supports his parents;
when you see one who is unritualistic toward his ruler,
punish him,
as a hawk or kite pursues a sparrow.’
The former ruler, the Duke of Zhōu, established the *Rites of Zhōu*,
saying:
‘Use standards to observe virtue,
virtue to handle affairs,
affairs to measure merit,
and merit to feed the people.’
The *Oath and Command* was written, saying:
‘Destroying standards is villainy;
covering for a villain is concealment.
Stealing wealth is robbery;
robbing ritual vessels is wickedness.
Taking the name of a master of concealment,
and relying on the use of wickedness,
constitutes great evil virtue;
this is a constant law, without pardon.
It is not forgotten in the Nine Punishments.’
Xíngfù has looked at Pú of Jǔ,
and there is nothing in him to take as a standard.
Filiality, respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness are auspicious virtues;
robbery, villainy, concealment, and wickedness are evil virtues.
Now, as for Pú of Jǔ,
if we look for his filiality and respect,
he has assassinated his ruler and father;
if we look for his loyalty and trustworthiness,
he has stolen precious jades.
As for the man,
he is a robber and a villain;
as for the vessels,
they are omens of wickedness.
To protect him and profit from them
is to be a master of concealment.
Using this as a lesson would be confusing,
and the people would have no standard.
He is not measured by goodness,
but is entirely within evil virtue;
therefore we have removed him.
In the past, the lineage of Gāoyáng
had eight talented sons:
Cāngshū, Tuíái, Táoyǎn, Dàlín,
Mángjiàng, Tíngjiān, Zhòngróng, and Shūdá.
They were orderly, sagely, broad-minded, and profound,
discerning, sincere, earnest, and honest.
The people of the world called them the ‘Eight Harmonious Ones’.
The lineage of Gāoxīn
had eight talented sons:
Bófèn, Zhòngkān, Shūxiàn, Jìzhòng,
Bóhǔ, Zhòngxióng, Shūbào, and Jìlí.
They were loyal, solemn, respectful, and admirable,
illustrious, kind, gracious, and harmonious.
The people of the world called them the ‘Eight Virtuous Ones’.
These sixteen clans
continued their excellence through generations,
not letting their reputations fall.
Until the time of Yáo,
Yáo was not able to raise them up.
Shùn served as Yáo’s minister
and raised up the Eight Harmonious Ones,
making them preside over the Earth
to manage the hundred affairs;
nothing was not in seasonal order,
the earth was level and the heavens were complete.
He raised up the Eight Virtuous Ones,
making them spread the Five Teachings to the four quarters:
father’s righteousness, mother’s kindness, elder brother’s friendliness,
younger brother’s respect, and son’s filiality;
there was peace within and success without.
In the past, the lineage of Dìhóng
had an untalented son,
who covered righteousness and hid villainy,
who loved to practice evil virtue;
he consorted with ugly types and wicked things.
He was obstinate, deceitful, and unfriendly,
and with such people he formed cliques;
the people of the world called him Húndùn.
The lineage of Shǎohào
had an untalented son,
who destroyed trust and abandoned loyalty,
and adorned and glorified wicked words;
he schemed slanders and employed deviousness,
practiced calumny and sought out evil,
to slander those of great virtue;
the people of the world called him Qióngqí.
The lineage of Zhuānxū had an untalented son,
who could not be taught or instructed,
and did not understand good words;
when told something he was obstinate,
when left alone he was deceitful,
he was arrogant and resistant to bright virtue,
disturbing the heavenly constants;
the people of the world called him Táowù.
These three lineages
continued their evil through generations,
increasing their bad reputations,
until the time of Yáo,
Yáo was not able to remove them.
The lineage of Jìnyún
had an untalented son,
who was greedy for food and drink,
and craved wealth and bribes;
his covetousness was excessive and extravagant,
he could not be filled or satisfied;
he amassed and accumulated goods,
knowing no bounds or limits,
not sharing with the orphaned or widowed,
and not pitying the poor or destitute;
the people of the world compared him to the three evil ones
and called him Tāotiè.
Shùn served as Yáo’s minister,
received guests at the four gates,
and banished the four evil lineages:
Húndùn, Qióngqí, Táowù, and Tāotiè,
casting them out to the four borders
to ward off the mountain and forest demons.
Therefore, when Yáo passed away
the world was as one,
with one heart supporting Shùn
as the Son of Heaven,
because he raised the sixteen ministers
and removed the four evil ones.
Thus the *Book of Yú* recounts Shùn’s merits,
saying: ‘He carefully displayed the Five Statutes,
and the Five Statutes were followed.’
This means there was no disobedience to the teaching.
It says:
‘He was installed over the hundred managers,
and the hundred managers were in seasonal order.’
This means no affairs were neglected.
It says:
‘He received guests at the four gates,
and the four gates were solemn and grand.’
This means there were no evil men.
Shùn had twenty great merits
and thus became the Son of Heaven.
Now, though Xíngfù has not yet found one auspicious man,
he has removed one evil one.
Of Shùn’s merits,
it is one-twentieth;
perhaps he may escape blame!”
Members of the Wǔ clan of Sòng led the sons of Duke Zhāo,
intending to support Sīchéng Xū to start a rebellion.
In the twelfth month,
the Duke of Sòng killed his younger brother by the same mother, Xū, and the sons of Duke Zhāo,
and sent the clans of Dài, Zhuāng, and Huán to attack the Wǔ clan at the residence of Sīmǎ Zǐbó,
subsequently expelling the clans of Wǔ and Mù.
He made Gōngsūn Shī the Sīchéng.
Prince Cháo died;
he made Yuè Lǚ the Sīkòu,
in order to quiet the people of the state.
A7.1 The Annals: The First Year of Duke Xuān
A7.1.1 First year, spring,
the royal first month,
the Duke ascended the throne.
A7.1.2 Gōngzǐ Suì went to Qí to meet the bride.
A7.1.3 Third month,
Suì arrived from Qí with the Lady Fù Jiāng.
A7.1.4 Summer,
Jìsūn Xíngfù went to Qí.
A7.1.5 Jìn banished its Grand Master Xū Jiǎfù to Wèi.
A7.1.6 The Duke met with the Marquis of Qí at Píngzhōu.
A7.1.7 Gōngzǐ Suì went to Qí.
A7.1.8 Sixth month,
the people of Qí took the fields west of the Jì River.
A7.1.9 Autumn,
the Viscount of Zhū came for an audience.
A7.1.10 The Viscount of Chǔ and
the people of Zhèng invaded Chén,
then invaded Sòng.
Zhào Dùn of Jìn led an army to rescue Chén.
The Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Wèi,
and the Earl of Cáo met the Jìn army at Fěilín,
and attacked Zhèng.
A7.1.11 Winter,
Zhào Chuān of Jìn led an army to invade Chóng.
A7.1.12 The people of Jìn and
the people of Sòng attacked Zhèng.
B7.1 The Zuo Commentary: The First Year of Duke Xuān
B7.1.1 First year, spring,
the royal first month,
Gōngzǐ Suì went to Qí to meet the bride.
This was to honor the ruler's command.
B7.1.2 Third month,
Suì arrived from Qí with the Lady Fù Jiāng.
This was to honor the Lady.
B7.1.3 Summer,
Jì Wénzǐ went to Qí,
offering bribes to request a meeting.
B7.1.4 The people of Jìn punished those who did not obey orders,
banishing Xū Jiǎfù to Wèi
and establishing Xū Kè.
Xiān Xīn fled to Qí.
B7.1.5 They met at Píngzhōu
to stabilize the Duke's position.
B7.1.6 Dōngmén Xiāngzhòng went to Qí
to acknowledge the peace settlement.
B7.1.7 Sixth month,
the people of Qí took the fields west of the Jì River;
because they had established the Duke,
he used the fields to bribe Qí.
B7.1.8 Regarding the assassination of Duke Zhāo by the people of Sòng,
Xún Línfù of Jìn used the armies of the feudal lords
to attack Sòng;
Sòng and Jìn made peace,
and Sòng Wén Gōng received a covenant from Jìn.
They also met the feudal lords at Hù,
intending to punish Qí on behalf of Lǔ,
but they all took bribes
and returned.
Zhèng Mù Gōng said,
"Jìn is not worth following,"
and consequently received a covenant from Chǔ.
Upon the death of Chén Gòng Gōng,
the people of Chǔ did not treat him with ritual.
Chén Líng Gōng received a covenant from Jìn.
Autumn,
the Viscount of Chǔ invaded Chén,
and then invaded Sòng.
Zhào Dùn of Jìn led an army to rescue Chén and Sòng.
They met at Fěilín
to attack Zhèng.
Wěi Jiǎ of Chǔ rescued Zhèng,
meeting the enemy at Běilín,
and captured Jiě Yáng of Jìn.
The people of Jìn then returned.
B7.1.9 Jìn wished to seek peace with Qín.
Zhào Chuān said,
"If I invade Chóng,
and Qín feels concern for Chóng,
they will surely rescue it.
I will use this to seek peace."
Winter,
Zhào Chuān invaded Chóng.
Qín did not grant peace.
B7.1.10 The people of Jìn attacked Zhèng
to retaliate for the battle of Běilín.
At this time the Marquis of Jìn was extravagant;
Zhào Xuānzǐ was in charge of the government
and repeatedly remonstrated but was not listened to;
therefore they could not compete with Chǔ.
A7.2 The Annals: The Second Year of Duke Xuān
A7.2.1 Second year, spring,
the royal second month, Rénzǐ day,
Huà Yuán of Sòng led an army and Gōngzǐ Guīshēng of Zhèng led an army,
and they fought at Dàjí.
The Sòng army was utterly defeated,
and Huà Yuán of Sòng was captured.
A7.2.2 The Qín army attacked Jìn.
A7.2.3 Summer,
the people of Jìn,
the people of Sòng,
the people of Wèi,
and the people of Chén invaded Zhèng.
A7.2.4 Autumn, ninth month, Yǐchǒu day,
Zhào Dùn of Jìn assassinated his ruler Yígāo.
A7.2.5 Winter, tenth month, Yǐhài day,
the Heavenly King died.
B7.2 The Zuo Commentary: The Second Year of Duke Xuān
B7.2.1 Second year, spring,
Gōngzǐ Guīshēng of Zhèng received orders from Chǔ to attack Sòng;
Huà Yuán and Lè Lǚ of Sòng resisted them.
Second month, Rénzǐ day,
they fought at Dàjí.
The Sòng army was utterly defeated.
They took Huà Yuán prisoner,
and captured Lè Lǚ, along with four hundred and sixty armored chariots, two hundred and fifty captives, and one hundred severed ears.
Kuángjiǎo overthrew a man of Zhèng,
and the man of Zhèng fell into a well.
He turned his halberd upside down to pull him out,
and Kuángjiǎo was captured.
The gentleman said:
"To abandon ritual and violate orders,
it is fitting that he became a captive.
To display military force
and resolute determination
in obedience to the rules is called ritual.
To kill the enemy is 'resolute,'
and to fulfill that resolution is 'determination.'
To change these is to deserve execution."
When they were about to fight, Huà Yuán slaughtered sheep to feed the soldiers,
but his driver Yáng Zhēn was not included.
When the battle came,
he said,
"In the matter of the sheep yesterday,
you were in charge;
in the matter of today,
I am in charge."
He drove into the Zhèng army,
thus they were defeated.
The gentleman said
Yáng Zhēn was "not a human being;
because of his private resentment,
he brought defeat to the state and calamity to the people;
what punishment could be greater than this?
What the Odes mean
by 'the lack of goodness in a man'
surely refers to Yáng Zhēn!
He harmed the people to gratify himself."
The people of Sòng offered one hundred war chariots and one hundred teams of four dappled horses to ransom Huà Yuán from Zhèng.
When half had been delivered,
Huà Yuán escaped and returned.
Standing outside the gate,
he announced himself and entered.
He saw Shū Zāng
and said,
"Was it your horses that did it?"
He replied,
"It was not the horses;
it was the man."
After this he fled to another state.
When Sòng was building its walls,
Huà Yuán acted as the supervisor
and inspected the work.
The wall-builders sang:
"Bulging are his eyes,
white is his belly;
he cast away his armor and returned.
Shaggy-bearded, shaggy-bearded,
he cast away his armor and came back again."
He made his Cān Chéng say to them:
"If there are cattle, then there are hides;
rhinoceroses and wild oxen are still many.
If you abandoned your armor, then what of it?"
The laborer said:
"Granting that there are hides,
what about the red lacquer?"
Huà Yuán said:
"Leave them!
Their mouths are many and we are few."
B7.2.2 The Qín army attacked Jìn
to retaliate for Chóng
and subsequently besieged Jiāo.
In summer,
Zhào Dùn of Jìn saved Jiāo,
and then from Yīn Dì,
together with the armies of the Zhū Hóu, he invaded Zhèng
to retaliate for the campaign of Dà Jí.
Dòu Jiāo of Chǔ saved Zhèng,
saying:
"Can one desire the leadership of the Zhū Hóu
yet dislike the difficulties of it?"
He then stationed at Zhèng
to await the Jìn army.
Zhào Dùn said:
"That Zōng is competing for power in Chǔ;
it will likely perish soon.
Let us just let its disease increase."
He then left them.
B7.2.3 Jìn Líng Gōng did not act as a ruler:
he levied heavy taxes to decorate his walls with carvings;
he shot at people with pellets from atop a terrace
to watch them dodge the pellets;
when the cook undercooked the bear's paws,
he killed him,
placed him in a basket,
and made women carry him across the court.
Zhào Dùn and Shì Jì saw his hand
and asked for the reason,
becoming distressed by it.
When they were about to remonstrate,
Shì Jì said:
"If the remonstrance is not accepted,
then no one can follow up.
Huì asks to go first;
if it is not accepted,
then you follow it up."
He advanced three times
and reached the eaves,
after which the ruler looked at him
and said:
"I know my fault
and shall change it."
Bowing his head to the ground, he replied:
"Who among men is without fault?
If one has a fault and can change it,
no good is greater.
The Shī says:
'None but have a beginning,
but few can have an end.'
Since it is so,
then those who can mend their faults are few.
If you, My Lord, can have an end,
then it will be the security of the altars of the state;
it is not only the Qún Chén who will rely on it."
It also says:
"When the Gǔn robes have a flaw,
only Zhòng Shān Fǔ can mend it,"
meaning he could mend faults.
"If you, My Lord, can mend your faults,
the Gǔn will not be discarded."
Yet he still did not change.
Xuān Zǐ repeatedly remonstrated,
so the Gōng became distressed by it
and sent Chú Ní to assassinate him.
Going in the morning,
the bedroom door was already open;
Zhào Dùn was in full ceremonial dress and about to go to court.
It was still early,
so he sat and dozed.
Chú Ní withdrew
and sighed, saying:
"Not forgetting reverence—
he is a true master of the people.
To assassinate the master of the people
is disloyalty;
to abandon the ruler's command
is untrustworthiness.
To have one of these
is not as good as dying."
He struck his head against a scholar-tree and died.
In the autumn, the ninth month,
the Jìn Hóu gave Zhào Dùn wine to drink,
but he had hidden armored soldiers
and intended to attack him.
His chariot-right Tí Mí Míng knew of it
and hurried up the hall,
saying:
"For a servant to attend a ruler's feast
beyond three cups of wine
is contrary to ritual."
He then supported him down the hall.
The Gōng set a mastiff on them;
Míng fought and killed it.
Zhào Dùn said:
"To abandon men and use dogs,
though it be fierce, what of it!"
They fought while exiting.
Tí Mí Míng died for him.
Initially,
Xuān Zǐ had hunted at Shǒu Shān
and stayed at Yì Sāng,
where he saw Líng Zhé starving
and asked about his distress.
He said:
"I have not eaten for three days."
He fed him,
but he kept half.
When asked about it,
he said:
"I have been in service for three years
and do not know if my mother still lives.
Now I am near her,
so I ask to give this to her."
He made him finish it
and prepared for him a basket of food and meat,
placing them in a sack to give him.
Later, this man became a guard for the Gōng
and reversed his spear to ward off the Gōng's followers,
allowing Zhào Dùn to escape.
When asked for the reason,
he replied:
"I am the starving man of Yì Sāng."
When asked his name and residence,
he withdrew without telling
and subsequently fled into exile.
On the day Yǐchǒu,
Zhào Chuān killed Líng Gōng at Táo Yuán.
Xuān Zǐ had not yet left the mountains and returned.
The Dà Shǐ wrote:
"Zhào Dùn assassinated his ruler,"
and displayed it in the court.
Xuān Zǐ said:
"It was not so."
He replied:
"You are the Zhèng Qīng;
in fleeing you did not cross the border,
and upon returning you did not punish the assassin.
If it was not you, then who was it?"
Xuān Zǐ said:
"Alas!
The Shī says:
'My cherishings
have brought this grief upon myself.'
It must refer to me."
Kǒng Zǐ said:
"Dǒng Hú
was a fine historian of old;
in his method of writing, he did not conceal.
Zhào Xuān Zǐ
was a fine Dà Fū of old;
for the sake of the law, he accepted the evil name.
What a pity!
Had he crossed the border, he would have been exempt."
Xuān Zǐ sent Zhào Chuān to welcome Gōng Zǐ Hēi Tún from Zhōu and established him.
On the day Rénshēn,
he held court at the Wǔ Gōng.
B7.2.4 Initially,
in the rebellion of Lì Jī,
an oath was made not to harbor the Gōng's various sons;
from then on, Jìn had no Ducal Clan.
When Chéng Gōng took the throne,
he then gave office to the legitimate sons of the Qīng
and provided them with land,
making them the Gōng Zú.
He also gave office to the other sons,
who were also called Yú Zǐ;
the sons of their concubines became Gōng Xíng.
Jìn thus had the Gōng Zú, Yú Zǐ, and Gōng Xíng.
Zhào Dùn requested to make Kuò the Gōng Zú,
saying:
"He is the beloved son of Jūn Jī Shì.
Were it not for Jūn Jī Shì,
then your servant would be a man of the Dí."
The Gōng granted it.
In winter,
Zhào Dùn became the head of the Máo Chē lineage
and made Píng Jì, with his original lineage, the Dà Fū of the Gōng Zú.
A7.3 The Classic for the Third Year of Xuān Gōng
A7.3.1 In the spring of the third year,
in the royal first month,
the mouth of the ox for the Jiāo sacrifice was injured;
the divination for the ox was changed.
The ox died,
so the Jiāo sacrifice was not performed.
Yet the Sān Wàng sacrifices were held.
A7.3.2 Kuāng Wáng was buried.
A7.3.3 The Viscount of Chǔ attacked the Róng of Lùhún.
A7.3.4 In summer,
the people of Chǔ invaded Zhèng.
A7.3.5 In autumn,
the Chìdí invaded Qí.
A7.3.6 The army of Sòng besieged Cáo.
A7.3.7 In winter, on the tenth month, on the day bǐngxū,
Lán, the Earl of Zhèng, died.
A7.3.8 Zhèng Mù Gōng was buried.
B7.3 The Commentary on the Third Year of Duke Xuān
B7.3.1 In the spring of the third year,
the jiāo sacrifice was not performed,
yet the wàng sacrifice was;
both were contrary to ritual.
The wàng sacrifice
belongs to the category of the jiāo sacrifice.
Since the jiāo was not performed,
it would also have been acceptable if the wàng was not performed.
B7.3.2 The Marquis of Jìn attacked Zhèng,
reaching Yán.
Zhèng made peace with Jìn,
and Shì Huì entered to make a covenant.
B7.3.3 The Viscount of Chǔ attacked the Róng of Lùhún,
and subsequently reached the Luò River,
reviewing his troops at the border of Zhōu.
King Dìng sent Wángsūn Mǎn to welcome the Viscount of Chǔ.
The Viscount of Chǔ asked about the size
and weight of the tripods.
Mǎn replied:
"The right to rule lies in virtue, not in the tripods.
Formerly, when the Xià dynasty possessed virtue,
the distant regions depicted their creatures
and the nine pastors contributed metal;
they cast the tripods representing those creatures,
and all things were thus provided for,
so that the people might know the spirits and the wicked spirits.
Therefore, when the people entered the rivers, marshes, mountains, and forests,
they did not encounter anything unfavorable.
The chīmèi and wǎngliǎng
could not meet them.
By this means, harmony was established between the upper and lower worlds,
so as to receive the blessings of Heaven.
Jié had a darkened virtue,
so the tripods were transferred to Shāng,
where they remained for six hundred years.
Zhòu of Shāng was cruel and oppressive,
and the tripods were transferred to Zhōu.
When virtue is beautiful and bright,
though the tripods are small,
they are heavy.
When it is wicked, devious, dark, and chaotic,
though they are large,
they are light.
Heaven blesses bright virtue,
and provides it a place to rest.
King Chéng fixed the tripods at Jiárǔ,
divining for thirty generations
and seven hundred years;
this is the command of Heaven.
Although the virtue of Zhōu has declined,
the mandate of Heaven has not yet changed.
The weight of the tripods
is not yet to be questioned."
B7.3.4 In summer,
the people of Chǔ invaded Zhèng
because Zhèng had sided with Jìn.
B7.3.5 Duke Wén of Sòng had been on the throne for three years
when he killed his younger brother of the same mother, Xū, and the sons of Duke Zhāo;
this was the plot of the Wǔ clan.
He ordered the clans of Dài and Huán to attack the Wǔ clan at the residence of Sīmǎ Zǐbó,
and expelled all the clans of Wǔ and Mù.
The clans of Wǔ and Mù attacked Sòng with the army of Cáo.
In autumn,
the army of Sòng besieged Cáo,
to retaliate for the rebellion of the Wǔ clan.
B7.3.6 In winter,
Duke Mù of Zhèng died.
Previously,
Duke Wén of Zhèng had a concubine of low rank named Yàn Jí,
who dreamed that a heavenly messenger gave her an orchid,
and said:
"I am Bó Tiáo.
I
am your ancestor.
Take this as your son.
Because the orchid has the fragrance of the state,
people will wear and cherish him like this."
Later, Duke Wén saw her,
gave her an orchid, and lay with her.
She declined, saying:
"Your handmaid is without talent,
but if I am fortunate enough to have a son,
and it is not believed,
may I dare to use the orchid as evidence?"
The Duke said:
"Yes."
She gave birth to Duke Mù,
and named him Lán.
Duke Wén had an affair with the wife of Zhèngzǐ, Chén Guī,
who gave birth to Zǐhuá and Zǐzāng.
Zǐzāng committed an offense and fled.
The Duke lured Zǐhuá
and killed him in Nánlǐ,
and sent assassins to kill Zǐzāng between Chén and Sòng.
He also married a woman from Jiāng,
who gave birth to Gōngzǐ Shì.
When Shì went to court in Chǔ,
the people of Chǔ poisoned him,
and he died at Yè.
He also married a woman from Sū,
who gave birth to Zǐxiá and Zǐyúmí.
Yúmí died early.
Xiè Jià disliked Xiá,
and Duke Wén also disliked him,
so he was not established as heir.
The Duke expelled all the princes,
and Gōngzǐ Lán fled to Jìn,
following Duke Wén of Jìn in the attack on Zhèng.
Shí Guǐ said:
"I have heard that when the Jī and Jí clans pair together,
their descendants will surely be numerous.
Jí
is a lucky person,
the primary consort of Hòujì.
Now Gōngzǐ Lán
is a nephew of the Jí clan;
Heaven may perhaps open a way for him.
He will surely become the ruler,
and his descendants will surely be numerous.
If we take him in first,
we can secure his favor."
Together with Kǒng Jiāngchú and Hóu Xuānduō, he brought him in;
they made a covenant in the Dà Gōng
and established him,
in order to make peace with Jìn.
When Duke Mù became ill,
he said:
"When the orchid dies,
I shall surely die too!
It is that by which I live."
When the orchid was cut, he died.
A7.4 The Annals of the Fourth Year of Duke Xuān
A7.4.1 In the spring of the fourth year,
in the King's first month,
the Duke and the Marquis of Qí made peace with Jǔ and Tán.
The people of Jǔ would not agree.
The Duke attacked Jǔ,
and took Xiàng.
A7.4.2 Dào, the Earl of Qín, died.
A7.4.3 In summer, the sixth month, on the day yǐyǒu,
Gōngzǐ Guīshēng of Zhèng assassinated his ruler, Yí.
A7.4.4 The Chìdí invaded Qí.
A7.4.5 In autumn,
the Duke went to Qí.
A7.4.6 The Duke arrived from Qí.
A7.4.7 In winter,
the Viscount of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
B7.4 The Commentary on the Fourth Year of Duke Xuān
B7.4.1 In the spring of the fourth year,
the Duke and the Marquis of Qí made peace with Jǔ and Tán;
the people of Jǔ would not agree.
The Duke attacked Jǔ
and took Xiàng,
which was contrary to ritual.
One should bring peace to states through ritual,
not through disorder.
To attack without governing
is disorder.
If one uses disorder to pacify disorder,
what governance is there?
Without governance,
how can ritual be practiced?
B7.4.2 A person of Chǔ presented a soft-shell turtle to Duke Líng of Zhèng.
Gōngzǐ Sòng and Zǐjiā were about to be received.
Zǐgōng's index finger twitched,
and showing it to Zǐjiā,
he said:
"On other days when this happened to me,
I was sure to taste some extraordinary delicacy."
When they entered,
the cook was about to butcher a soft-shelled turtle.
They looked at each other and laughed.
The Duke asked about it,
and Zǐ Jiā told him.
When the Great Officers were served the turtle
soup, the Duke summoned Zǐ Gōng but did not give him any.
Zǐ Gōng was angry;
he dipped his finger into the cauldron,
tasted it, and went out.
The Duke was angry
and wished to kill Zǐ Gōng.
Zǐ Gōng plotted with Zǐ Jiā to strike first.
Zǐ Jiā said:
"When an animal is old,
one still hesitates to kill it,
how much more so your ruler?"
Zǐ Gōng in turn slandered Zǐ Jiā.
Zǐ Jiā was afraid and followed him.
In summer,
they assassinated Lord Líng.
The record says: "Guī Shēng of Zhèng assassinated his ruler Yí,"
because his power was insufficient to stop it.
The gentleman says:
"To be benevolent but not martial
is to be unable to achieve anything."
Whenever a ruler is assassinated,
if the ruler is named,
it means the ruler was without the Way;
if the minister is named,
it is the minister's crime.
The people of Zhèng wished to establish Zǐ Liáng.
He declined, saying:
"If based on worthiness,
then Qù Jí is insufficient;
if based on the order of succession,
then Prince Jiān is older."
Thus, they established Lord Xiāng.
Lord Xiāng wished to remove the Mù clan
but spare Zǐ Liáng.
Zǐ Liáng would not allow it,
saying:
"If the Mù clan should be preserved,
then that is indeed my wish.
If they are to be destroyed,
then let all be destroyed;
what should Qù Jí do alone?"
Thus, the Duke let them stay,
and they all served as Great Officers.
B7.4.3 Previously,
the Sīmǎ of Chǔ, Zǐ Liáng, had a son, Yuè Jiāo.
Zǐ Wén said:
"You must kill him!
This child
has the appearance of a bear or tiger and the voice of a jackal or wolf;
if he is not killed,
he will surely destroy the Ruò'áo clan.
The proverb says:
'A wolf cub has a wild heart.'
This one is a wolf;
can he be raised?"
Zǐ Liáng would not allow it.
Zǐ Wén considered it a matter of great sorrow.
When he was about to die,
he gathered his clan
and said:
"If Yuè Jiāo takes charge of the government,
then leave quickly
so as not to be reached by disaster."
And he wept, saying:
"Ghosts still seek food;
will the ghosts of the Ruò'áo clan not go hungry?"
When Lìngyǐn Zǐ Wén died,
Dòu Bān became Lìngyǐn,
and Zǐ Yuè became Sīmǎ.
Wěi Jiǎ was the Gōngzhèng;
he slandered Zǐ Yáng and killed him.
Zǐ Yuè became Lìngyǐn,
and Wěi Jiǎ himself became Sīmǎ.
Zǐ Yuè also grew to hate him,
so with the Ruò'áo clan,
he imprisoned Bó Yīng at Liáoyáng and killed him.
He then occupied Zhēngyě
and prepared to attack the King.
The King offered the sons of three kings as hostages,
but he would not accept them.
The armies faced off at the banks of the Zhāng.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day wùxū,
the Viscount of Chǔ fought the Ruò'áo clan at Gāohǔ.
Bó Fèn shot at the King;
the arrow passed over the chariot pole,
reached the drum base,
and stuck into the dīngníng bell.
He shot again;
the arrow passed over the chariot pole
and pierced the canopy hub.
The army was afraid
and retreated.
The King sent someone to inspect the army, saying:
"My late ruler King Wén conquered Xī
and obtained three arrows;
Bó Fèn stole two of them,
and they are now exhausted."
They beat the drums and advanced,
finally destroying the Ruò'áo clan.
Previously,
Ruò'áo had married in Yùn
and fathered Dòu Bó Bǐ.
When Ruò'áo died,
Bó Bǐ followed his mother and was raised in Yùn.
He had illicit relations with the daughter of the Master of Yùn,
and Zǐ Wén was born.
The Lady of Yùn had him abandoned in the Mèng marsh.
A tiger suckled him.
The Master of Yùn was hunting
and saw him;
he was afraid and returned.
The Lady told him the truth,
so he sent someone to retrieve the child.
The people of Chǔ call suckling 'gǔ'
and call a tiger 'yūtù';
therefore, they named him Gǔ Yūtù.
The Master of Yùn gave his daughter to Bó Bǐ as a wife.
This child was Lìngyǐn Zǐ Wén.
His grandson, the Zhēnyǐn Kè Huáng, was on a mission to Qí;
on his return, he reached Sòng
and heard of the rebellion.
His followers said:
"You cannot enter."
The Zhēnyǐn said:
"If I abandon the King's command,
who else will receive it?
The ruler
is like Heaven;
can one escape Heaven?"
So he returned,
reported on his mission,
and then surrendered himself to the Minister of Justice.
The King remembered Zǐ Wén's governance of the state of Chǔ
and said:
"If Zǐ Wén has no descendants,
how can we encourage goodness?"
He ordered him to be restored to his position
and changed his name to Shēng.
B7.4.4 In winter,
the Viscount of Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
for Zhèng had not yet submitted.
A7.5 The Classic of the Fifth Year of Lord Xuān
A7.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
the Duke went to Qí.
A7.5.2 In summer,
the Duke arrived from Qí.
A7.5.3 In autumn, the ninth month,
Gāo Gù of Qí came to meet Shū Jī.
A7.5.4 Shūsūn Déchén died.
A7.5.5 In winter,
Gāo Gù of Qí and Lady Shū Jī came.
A7.5.6 The people of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
B7.5 The Commentary of the Fifth Year of Lord Xuān
B7.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
the Duke went to Qí.
Gāo Gù caused the Marquis of Qí to detain the Duke
so that he could request Shū Jī for himself.
B7.5.2 In summer,
the Duke arrived from Qí;
this was recorded
because it was an error.
B7.5.3 In autumn, the ninth month,
Gāo Gù of Qí came to meet the bride,
acting on his own behalf.
Therefore the record says "met Shū Jī,"
for a minister meeting his own bride.
B7.5.4 In winter,
they came;
this was to return the horses.
B7.5.5 The Viscount of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
Chén made peace with Chǔ.
Xún Línfù of Jìn rescued Zhèng
and attacked Chén.
A7.6 The Classic of the Sixth Year of Lord Xuān
A7.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
Zhào Dùn of Jìn
and Sūn Miǎn of Wèi invaded Chén.
A7.6.2 In summer, the fourth month.
A7.6.3 In autumn, the eighth month,
there was an infestation of locusts.
A7.6.4 In winter, the tenth month.
B7.6 (The Commentary on the 6th Year of Duke Xuān)
B7.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
Jìn and Wèi invaded Chén,
because Chén had sided with Chǔ.
B7.6.2 In the summer,
Dìngwáng sent Zǐfú to seek a queen from Qí.
B7.6.3 In the autumn,
the Chìdí attacked Jìn,
besieging Huái and Xíngqiū.
The Marquis of Jìn wished to attack them.
Zhōngháng Huánzǐ said:
"Let them distress their people,
to fill up the measure of their crimes.
Then they can be exterminated.
The *Zhōu Shū* says,
'Exterminate the Róng-Yīn,'
this is what that refers to."
B7.6.4 In the winter,
Shào Huángōng welcomed the King's queen from Qí.
B7.6.5 The people of Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
made peace, and returned.
B7.6.6 Gōngzǐ Mànmǎn of Zhèng spoke with Wángzǐ Bóliào,
desiring to become a high minister.
Bóliào told others:
"Lacking virtue yet being greedy,
his case is that of the hexagram *Fēng* ䷶ changing to *Lí*
䷝ in the *Zhōu Yì*;
he will not last beyond this."
After one year,
the people of Zhèng killed him.
A7.7 (The Classic of the 7th Year of Duke Xuān)
A7.7.1 In the spring of the seventh year,
the Marquis of Wèi sent Sūn Liángfū to come for a covenant.
A7.7.2 In the summer,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Qí to invade Lái.
A7.7.3 In the autumn,
the Duke arrived from invading Lái.
A7.7.4 There was a great drought.
A7.7.5 In the winter,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng, and
the Baron of Cáo at Hēirǎng.
B7.7 (The Commentary on the 7th Year of Duke Xuān)
B7.7.1 In the spring of the seventh year,
Sūn Huánzǐ of Wèi came for a covenant;
this was the beginning of diplomatic relations.
They also planned a meeting with Jìn.
B7.7.2 In the summer,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Qí to invade Lái,
but he was not involved in the planning.
Whenever an army goes out,
if one participated in the planning, it is written as 'and' (*jí*);
if one did not participate in the planning, it is written as 'met with' (*huì*).
B7.7.3 The Chìdí invaded Jìn,
taking the grain of Xiàngyīn.
B7.7.4 Zhèng made peace with Jìn;
this was the plan of Gōngzǐ Sòng.
Therefore, he assisted the Earl of Zhèng in the meeting.
In the winter,
they made a covenant at Hēirǎng.
Wángshū Huángōng presided over it,
to plan for those not in harmony.
When the Marquis of Jìn was established,
the Duke did not pay court,
nor did he send a Great Officer for a friendly mission.
The people of Jìn detained the Duke at the meeting.
There was a covenant at Huángfù,
but the Duke did not participate in the covenant.
He was released through a bribe.
Therefore, the covenant of Hēirǎng was not recorded,
to conceal the matter.
A7.8 (The Classic of the 8th Year of Duke Xuān)
A7.8.1 In the spring of the eighth year,
the Duke arrived from the meeting.
A7.8.2 In the summer, in the sixth month,
Gōngzǐ Suì went to Qí;
upon reaching Huáng, he returned.
On the day *Xīnsì*, there was a sacrifice in the Grand Temple;
Zhòng Suì died at Chuí.
On the day *Rénwǔ*,
the *Yì* sacrifice was still performed.
The *Wàn* dancers entered,
but the flutes were removed.
On the day *Wùzǐ*, the Lady Yíng-shì passed away.
A7.8.5 The Jìn army and
the Báidí invaded Qín.
A7.8.6 The people of Chǔ destroyed Shūliǎo.
A7.8.7 In the autumn, in the seventh month, on the day *Jiǎzǐ*,
the sun was eclipsed;
it was total.
A7.8.8 In the winter, in the tenth month, on the day *Jǐchǒu*,
we buried our Little Lord Jìng Yíng.
It rained, and the burial could not be completed.
On the day *Gēngyín*,
the burial was completed at midday.
A7.8.9 They walled Píngyáng.
A7.8.10 The Chǔ army attacked Chén.
B7.8 (The Commentary on the 8th Year of Duke Xuān)
B7.8.1 In the spring of the eighth year,
the Báidí made peace with Jìn.
In the summer,
they joined Jìn to invade Qín.
The people of Jìn captured a Qín spy
and killed him in the market of Jiàng;
after six days, he revived.
B7.8.2 There was a sacrifice in the Grand Temple;
when Xiāng Zhòng died and the *Yì* sacrifice was performed,
it was against ritual.
B7.8.3 Because the various Shū tribes had rebelled
, they attacked Shūliǎo,
destroying it.
The Viscount of Chǔ marked its boundaries.
Upon reaching Huánruì,
he made a covenant with Wú and Yuè and then returned.
B7.8.4 Xū Kè of Jìn had the *gǔ* disease;
Xì Quē took charge of the government.
In the autumn,
Xū Kè was deposed,
and Zhào Shuò was made assistant to the Lower Army.
B7.8.5 In the winter,
Jìng Yíng was buried.
Due to drought, there was no hemp,
so they first used kudzu for the funeral ropes.
It rained,
and the burial could not be completed;
this was in accordance with ritual.
According to ritual,
when divining the burial date,
one first picks the most distant day
to avoid any lack of cherished memory.
B7.8.6 The walling of Píngyáng
was recorded
because it was done at the proper time.
B7.8.7 Chén made peace with Jìn.
The Chǔ army attacked Chén,
made peace, and returned.
A7.9 (The Classic of the 9th Year of Duke Xuān)
A7.9.1 In the spring of the ninth year,
in the Royal first month,
the Duke went to Qí.
The Duke arrived from Qí.
A7.9.3 In the summer,
Zhòngsūn Miè went to the Capital.
A7.9.4 The Marquis of Qí attacked Lái.
A7.9.5 In the autumn,
Gēnmóu was taken.
A7.9.6 In the eighth month,
the Viscount of Téng died.
A7.9.7 In the ninth month,
the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng, and
the Baron of Cáo met at Hù.
A7.9.8 Xún Línfù of Jìn led an army to attack Chén.
A7.9.9 On the day *Xīnyǒu*, Hēitún, the Marquis of Jìn, died at Hù.
A7.9.10 In the winter, in the tenth month, on the day *Guǐyǒu*,
Zhèng, the Marquis of Wèi, died.
A7.9.11 The people of Sòng besieged Téng.
A7.9.12 The Viscount of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
Xì Quē of Jìn led the army to save Zhèng.
Chén killed its Grand Master Xiè Yě.
The Commentary on Year Nine of Duke Xuān.
Year nine, spring,
the King sent an envoy to request a courtesy visit.
Summer,
Mèng Xiànzǐ made a courtesy visit to Zhōu.
The King considered him well-versed in ritual,
and rewarded him generously.
Autumn,
Gēnmóu was taken;
this expresses the ease of it.
Duke Zhāo of Téng died.
There was a meeting at Hù,
to punish those who were not harmonious.
The Marquis of Chén did not attend the meeting.
Xún Línfù of Jìn led the armies of the feudal lords to attack Chén.
The Marquis of Jìn died at Hù,
and they returned.
Winter,
the people of Sòng besieged Téng,
taking advantage of the mourning for the ruler.
Duke Líng of Chén, together with Kǒng Níng and Yí Hángfù, had illicit relations with Xià Jī;
they each wore her undergarments
to joke in the court.
Xiè Yě remonstrated, saying:
"When the ruler and ministers display lewdness,
the people have nothing to emulate,
and what is heard is not good.
May your Lordship put them away."
The Duke said:
"I can change."
The Duke told the two men.
The two men requested to kill him;
the Duke did not forbid it,
and so they killed Xiè Yě.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The *Odes* say:
'When the people are many in perversity,
do not establish perversity yourself.'
Does this not refer to Xiè Yě?"
Because of the campaign of Lì, the Viscount of Chǔ
attacked Zhèng.
Xì Quē of Jìn saved Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng defeated the Chǔ army at Liǔfén.
The people of the state were all joyful,
but Zǐliáng alone worried, saying:
"This is a disaster for the state;
the day of my death is not far off."
The Annals of Year Ten of Duke Xuān.
Year ten, spring,
the Duke went to Qí.
The Duke arrived from Qí.
The people of Qí returned to us the fields west of the Jì.
Summer, the fourth month, on the day Bǐngchén,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
On the day Jǐsì,
Marquis Yuán of Qí died.
The Cuī clan of Qí fled to Wèi.
The Duke went to Qí.
In the fifth month,
the Duke arrived from Qí.
On the day Guǐsì,
Xià Zhēngshū of Chén assassinated his ruler Píngguó.
In the sixth month,
the Sòng army attacked Téng.
Gōngsūn Guīfù went to Qí.
They buried Duke Huì of Qí.
People of Jìn,
people of Sòng,
people of Wèi,
and people of Cáo attacked Zhèng.
Autumn,
the Heavenly King sent Wáng Jìzǐ to come on a courtesy visit.
Gōngsūn Guīfù led an army to attack Zhū
and took Yì.
There were great floods.
Jìsūn Hángfù went to Qí.
Winter,
Gōngsūn Guīfù went to Qí.
The Marquis of Qí sent Guó Zuǒ to come on a courtesy visit.
There was famine.
The Viscount of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
The Commentary on Year Ten of Duke Xuān.
Year ten, spring,
the Duke went to Qí.
Because we were submissive, the Marquis of Qí
returned the fields west of the Jì.
Summer,
Duke Huì of Qí died.
Cuī Zhù was favored by Duke Huì;
the Gāo and Guó clans feared his encroaching power.
When the Duke died, they drove him out;
he fled to Wèi.
The record says "the Cuī clan,"
as it was not his personal crime;
moreover, he was reported by his clan name,
and not by his personal name.
Whenever a Grand Master of the feudal lords leaves in exile,
the report to the feudal lords says:
"Such-and-such, the guarding servant of the such-and-such clan,
having failed to guard the ancestral temple,
dares to make this report."
If there are envoys with jade and silk, the report is made;
otherwise,
it is not.
The Duke went to Qí to attend the funeral.
Duke Líng of Chén drank wine with Kǒng Níng and Yí Hángfù at the Xià residence.
The Duke said to Hángfù:
"Zhēngshū looks like you."
He replied:
"He also looks like your Lordship."
Zhēngshū was resentful of this.
When the Duke went out,
he shot and killed him from the stable.
The two men fled to Chǔ.
The people of Téng relied on Jìn and did not serve Sòng.
In the sixth month,
the Sòng army attacked Téng.
Zhèng made peace with Chǔ.
The armies of the feudal lords attacked Zhèng;
they reached a settlement and returned.
Autumn,
Duke Kāng of Liú came to return a courtesy visit.
The army attacked Zhū
and took Yì.
Jì Wénzǐ made his first courtesy visit to Qí.
Winter,
Zǐjiā went to Qí
because of the attack on Zhū.
Guó Wǔzǐ came to return a courtesy visit.
The Viscount of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
Shì Huì of Jìn saved Zhèng,
chasing the Chǔ army to the north of the Yǐng.
The armies of the feudal lords garrisoned Zhèng.
Zǐjiā of Zhèng died.
The people of Zhèng, punishing the disorder of Duke Yōu,
chopped the coffin of Zǐjiā
and drove out his clan.
They reburied Duke Yōu
and gave him the posthumous title
"Líng."
The Annals of Year Eleven of Duke Xuān.
Year eleven, spring,
the King’s first month.
Summer,
the Viscount of Chǔ,
the Marquis of Chén,
and the Earl of Zhèng made a covenant at Chénlíng.
Gōngsūn Guīfù met with the people of Qí to attack Jǔ.
Autumn,
the Marquis of Jìn met the Dí at Cuánhán.
Winter, the tenth month,
the people of Chǔ killed Xià Zhēngshū of Chén.
On the day Dīnghài,
the Viscount of Chǔ entered Chén.
He restored Gōngsūn Níng
and Yí Hángfù to Chén.
The Commentary on Year Eleven of Duke Xuān.
B7.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
Chǔzǐ invaded Zhèng and reached Lì.
Zǐliáng said:
“Jìn and Chǔ do not strive for virtue
but contend with weapons;
it is acceptable to follow whoever comes.
Jìn and Chǔ lack good faith;
how can we have good faith?”
Thus they followed Chǔ.
In the summer,
Chǔ made a covenant at Chénlíng,
as Chén and Zhèng submitted.
B7.11.2 The Zuǒyǐn of Chǔ, Zǐzhòng, invaded Sòng;
the Wáng waited at Yán.
B7.11.3 The Lìngyǐn Wěi Àiliè walled Yí;
he had the border-wardens plan the work
and handed it over to the Sītú.
He measured the labor and assigned the days,
distributed the materials,
leveled the planks and poles,
weighed the baskets and shovels,
standardized the earth and supplies,
calculated the distances,
surveyed the foundations,
prepared the dried provisions,
and assessed the officials.
The work was completed in thirty days,
not deviating from the original plan.
B7.11.4 Xì Chéngzǐ of Jìn sought peace with the various Dí.
The various Dí were weary of the service for the Chìdí,
and thus submitted to Jìn.
In the autumn,
they met at Cuánhán,
as the various Dí submitted.
On this expedition,
the various Dàfū wanted to summon the Dí.
Xì Chéngzǐ said:
“I have heard that
without virtue,
nothing is better than diligence;
without diligence,
how can one seek others?
Being able to be diligent,
there will be succession.
One should follow them.”
The *Shī* says:
‘Wén Wáng was diligent indeed.’
Even Wén Wáng was diligent,
how much more so for one of little virtue?”
B7.11.5 In the winter,
because of the turmoil caused by the Xià Shì in Chén,
Chǔzǐ invaded Chén.
He said to the people of Chén:
“Do not move!
I am going to punish the Shǎoxī Shì.”
He then entered Chén,
killed Xià Zhēngshū,
and dismembered him at the Lìmén.
Consequently, he made Chén a Xiàn.
Chénhóu was in Jìn.
Shēn Shūshí was on a mission to Qí;
when he returned,
he reported his mission
and withdrew.
The Wáng sent someone to reprimand him,
saying:
“Xià Zhēngshū acted without principle
and murdered his ruler;
I punished and executed him together with the Zhūhóu;
the Zhūhóu and Xiàngōng all congratulated me,
but you alone did not congratulate me.
Why is that?”
He replied:
“May I still offer an explanation?”
The Wáng said:
“You may!”
He said:
“Xià Zhēngshū murdered his ruler,
his crime was indeed great;
to punish and execute him
was your righteousness, my Lord.
However, people also have a saying:
‘Leading an ox to tread on another’s field,
and then seizing the ox.’
Leading an ox to tread on a field
is indeed a crime;
but seizing the ox,
the punishment is already too heavy.
When the Zhūhóu followed you,
they said it was to punish the guilty.
Now that you have made Chén a Xiàn,
you are greedy for its wealth.
You summoned the Zhūhóu for punishment
but returned with greed;
is this not unacceptable?”
The Wáng said:
“Excellent!
I had not heard this.
If I restore it,
is it possible?”
He replied:
“That is what we small people call
‘taking it from one’s bosom and giving it back’.”
Thus he re-enfeoffed Chén.
From each Xiāng he took one person to return with,
calling them the Xiàzhōu.
Therefore the *Annals* say: “Chǔzǐ entered Chén.
He restored Gōngsūn Níng and Yí Xíngfù to Chén,”
recording it
as being according to ritual.
B7.11.6 In the campaign of Lì,
the Zhèngbó fled back,
and since then Chǔ had not had its way there.
After Zhèng received the covenant at Chénlíng,
it also sought to serve Jìn.
A7.12 *Xuān Gōng Shí-èr Nián Jīng*
A7.12.1 In the spring of the twelfth year,
Chén Líng Gōng was buried.
A7.12.2 Chǔzǐ besieged Zhèng.
A7.12.3 In the summer, in the sixth month, on the *yǐmǎo* day,
Xún Línfù of Jìn led an army and fought with Chǔzǐ at Bì;
the Jìn army was utterly defeated.
A7.12.4 Autumn, seventh month.
A7.12.5 In the winter, in the twelfth month, on the *wùyín* day,
Chǔzǐ destroyed Xiāo.
A7.12.6 The people of Jìn,
Sòng,
Wèi,
and Cáo made a covenant at Qīngqiū.
A7.12.7 The Sòng army invaded Chén.
The people of Wèi rescued Chén.
B7.12 *Xuān Gōng Shí-èr Nián Zhuàn*
B7.12.1 In the spring of the twelfth year,
Chǔzǐ besieged Zhèng
for seventeen days.
The people of Zhèng divined about making peace,
and it was inauspicious;
they divined about lamenting in the Dàgōng
and moving chariots out into the streets,
and it was auspicious.
The people of the capital held a great lamentation;
those guarding the battlements all wept.
Chǔzǐ withdrew his army.
The people of Zhèng repaired the walls.
He advanced and besieged it again;
after three months, he captured it.
He entered through the Huángmén
and reached the Kuílù.
The Zhèngbó, with his torso bared and leading a sheep,
went to meet him,
saying:
“I have been abandoned by Heaven,
unable to serve you,
causing you to harbor anger
and reach our humble city;
this is my crime;
how could I dare not to listen to your commands?
Whether you take us as captives to the south of the River
to fill the seacoast,
it is only your command;
whether you divide us to bestow upon the Zhūhóu
and make us slaves,
it is only your command.
If you kindly look back on our former friendship
and seek blessings from Lì, Xuān, Huán, and Wǔ,
and do not extinguish our altars,
allowing us to change and serve you,
being equal to the nine Xiàn,
that would be your grace
and my wish,
but it is not what I dare hope for.
I dare reveal my innermost heart;
may you, my Lord, consider it.”
Those to his left and right said:
“This must not be granted;
having gained the state, there should be no pardon.”
The Wáng said:
“Their ruler can humble himself before others;
he will surely be able to use his people with trust.
How can we hope to take it?”
He withdrew thirty *lǐ*
and granted them peace.
Pān Wāng entered to conclude the covenant;
Zǐliáng went out as a hostage.
B7.12.2 In the summer, in the sixth month,
the army of Jìn went to rescue Zhèng.
Xún Línfù commanded the Central Army,
and Xiān Hú assisted him;
Shì Huì commanded the Upper Army,
and Xì Kè assisted him;
Zhào Shuò commanded the Lower Army,
and Luán Shū assisted him.
Zhào Kuò and Zhào Yīngqí served as Grand Officers of the Central Army,
Gǒng Shuò and Hán Chuān as Grand Officers of the Upper Army,
and Xún Shǒu and Zhào Tóng as Grand Officers of the Lower Army.
Hán Jué served as the Sīmǎ.
Upon reaching the Hé River,
they heard that Zhèng had already made peace with Chǔ.
Huánzǐ wished to return,
saying:
"If we cannot reach Zhèng in time and yet exhaust the people,
what use is there for this?
If we move only after Chǔ has returned,
it will not be too late."
Suí Wǔzǐ said:
"Excellent.
Huì has heard that in using an army,
one acts after observing a weakness.
If Virtue, Punishment, Governance, Affairs, Statutes, and Ritual are not altered,
they cannot be opposed;
for such, we do not undertake a campaign.
The Ruler of Chǔ punished Zhèng,
angered by its double-dealing
but pitying its humble submission.
When they rebelled, he attacked them;
when they submitted, he released them.
Virtue and Punishment are thus established.
Attacking the rebellious
is Punishment;
being gentle to the submissive
is Virtue;
these two are established.
Last year he entered Chén,
and this year he entered Zhèng,
yet the people are not weary or exhausted,
and the ruler has no grievances or complaints;
Governance has its constant principles.
Setting out with the Jīngshī formation,
the merchants, farmers, artisans, and traders
do not lose their livelihoods,
and the soldiers and charioteers are harmonious and friendly;
Affairs are not neglected.
Wěi Áo serves as the Chancellor,
selecting the fine statutes of the State of Chǔ;
when the army marches,
the right side guards the carriage shafts,
the left side pursues the grass for bedding,
the vanguard carries the signal flags to provide against the unforeseen,
the center holds the authority of command,
and the rear provides the elite strength.
The various officials move according to their emblems,
and the military administration is prepared without needing to be cautioned;
he is able to use the Statutes.
In the appointments of their ruler,
those of the same clan are selected from among relatives,
and those of different clans are selected from old associates.
Promotions do not overlook virtue,
and rewards do not overlook merit.
The elderly receive additional kindness,
and travelers are given lodging.
Between the superior man and the commoner,
there are distinctions in dress and insignia.
The noble have their constant honor,
and the lowly have their graded awe;
Ritual is not violated.
Virtue is established, Punishment is carried out,
Governance is accomplished, Affairs are timely,
Statutes are followed, and Ritual is harmonious.
How can we oppose them?
To advance when seeing the possible,
and to retreat when knowing the difficult,
is the good administration of an army.
Incorporating the weak and attacking the benighted
is the good constant principle of military force.
You should for now put the army in order and manage the military!
There are still those who are weak and benighted,
why must it be Chǔ?
Zhòng Huǐ had a saying:
'Take over the disordered and insult the dying,'
this is incorporating the weak.
The song 'Zhuó' says:
'O, how glorious is the King's army!
Following and nourishing it through this darkness,'
this means overcoming the benighted.
The song 'Wǔ' says:
'None can compete with its brilliance.'
To comfort the weak and overcome the benighted
so as to strive for brilliance,
is acceptable."
Zhìzǐ said:
"It is not acceptable.
The reason why Jìn holds hegemony
is that the army is martial and the ministers put forth effort.
Now to lose the feudal lords
cannot be called effort;
to have an enemy and not follow them
cannot be called martial.
If the hegemony is lost because of me,
it would be better to die.
Furthermore, having set out with a full army,
to retreat upon hearing that the enemy is strong
is not the act of a man.
Being appointed as a commander of the army,
and yet ending up as less than a man,
only you gentlemen can do it,
but I will not."
With the Assistant of the Central Army, he crossed the river.
Zhì Zhuāngzǐ said:
"This army is in peril!
The Zhōu Yì has this,
in the hexagram Shī ䷆ changing to Lín
it says:
'An army sets out according to law;
if not good,
there is misfortune.'
When those in charge are compliant, it results in good;
when they are contrary, it is not good.
A multitude scattering becomes weak;
a river blocked becomes a marsh.
There is law when things are as they should be,
therefore it is called law. If not good,
it means the law is exhausted.
Being full and yet becoming exhausted,
it is cut short and lacks order,
which is why it is misfortune.
Not proceeding is called Lín;
to have a commander but not follow him,
what 'Lín' could be worse than this?
It refers to this situation.
If they truly encounter the enemy,
they will surely be defeated.
Zhìzǐ is responsible for it;
even if he escapes and returns,
there will certainly be great calamity."
Hán Xiànzǐ said to Huánzǐ:
"If Zhìzǐ falls into danger with a partial force,
your guilt will be great.
You are the Commander-in-Chief;
if the army does not follow orders,
whose fault is it?
Losing subordinates and losing the army,
the guilt is already heavy;
it is better to advance.
If the matter is not successful,
the blame will be shared.
Rather than bearing the guilt alone,
if all six of us share it,
is that not better?"
The army then crossed the river.
The Viscount of Chǔ moved his army north and camped at Yán.
Shěn Yǐn commanded the Central Army,
Zǐzhòng commanded the Left,
Zǐfǎn commanded the Right,
intending to water their horses in the Hé River and then return.
Upon hearing that the Jìn army had already crossed,
the King wished to return,
but his favorite, Wǔ Cān, wished to fight.
The Lìngyǐn Sūnshū Áo did not wish to,
saying:
"Last year we entered Chén,
this year we entered Zhèng,
it has not been without incident.
If we fight and are not successful,
will the flesh of Cān be enough to eat?"
Cān said:
"If the matter is successful,
Sūnshū will be seen as lacking in strategy.
If it is not successful,
my flesh will be in the Jìn army,
how could you get to eat it?"
The Lìngyǐn turned the carriage shafts southward
and reversed the banners.
Wǔ Cān said to the King:
"The administrators of Jìn are new
and have not yet been able to carry out orders.
Their assistant Xiān Hú is stubborn and unkind,
and is unwilling to follow orders.
Their three commanders
act on their own and cannot succeed.
They listen to no superior;
whom will the multitude follow?
In this campaign,
the Jìn army will surely be defeated.
Moreover, for a King to flee from subjects,
what of the Altars of Soil and Grain?"
The King was troubled by this
and told the Lìngyǐn to change the direction of the carriage shafts
and head north,
camping at Guǎn to wait for them.
The Jìn army was between Áo and Hào.
Huáng Xù of Zhèng was sent to the Jìn army,
saying:
"The fact that Zhèng followed Chǔ
was for the sake of its altars of soil and grain;
they did not have a double heart.
The Chǔ army has won sudden victories and become arrogant;
their army is weary,
and they have not set up defenses.
If you attack them,
the Zhèng army will support us,
and the Chǔ army will surely be defeated."
Zhì Zǐ said:
"Defeating Chǔ and making Zhèng submit depends on this moment.
We must grant it!"
Luán Wǔ Zǐ said:
"Since Chǔ overcame Yōng,
their ruler hasn't spent a single day without examining the people of the capital and instructing them on the hardships of the people's livelihood,
the unpredictability of when disaster might arrive,
and the fact that vigilance and fear must not be neglected.
While in the army,
there is no day he does not inspect the military supplies
and repeatedly warn them
that victory cannot be guaranteed,
and that although Zhòu won a hundred victories, he ultimately had no successors.
He instructs them using the examples of Ruò Áo
and Fén Mào,
who rode in brushwood carts and wore ragged clothes to open up the mountains and forests.
He admonishes them, saying:
'The livelihood of the people depends on diligence;
with diligence, there will be no lack.'
They cannot be called arrogant.
The former Great Officer Zǐ Fàn had a saying:
'An army with a righteous cause is strong;
one with a crooked cause is weary.'
We are without virtue,
and we have invited resentment from Chǔ.
We are in the wrong while Chǔ is in the right;
they cannot be called weary.
Their ruler's war chariots are divided into two Guǎng units;
each Guǎng has one hundred chariots,
and each chariot has its accompanying foot soldiers and auxiliary wagons.
When the Right Guǎng is first harnessed,
they serve until midday;
then the Left Guǎng takes over,
continuing until dusk.
The palace officials take turns during the night
to prepare for the unexpected.
They cannot be said to be without defense.
Zǐ Liáng
is an excellent man of Zhèng;
Shī Shū
is a person of high standing in Chǔ.
Shī Shū has entered into a covenant,
and Zǐ Liáng is in Chǔ;
Chǔ and Zhèng are close.
They come to urge us to fight;
if we win, they will come to us;
if we do not win, they will follow Chǔ.
They are using us as a divination!
Zhèng cannot be followed."
Zhào Kuò and Zhào Tóng said:
"Since leading the army here,
we have sought only the enemy.
To defeat the enemy and gain dependencies,
what more are we waiting for?
We must follow Zhì Zǐ!"
Zhī Jì said:
"Yuán and Píng are men of disaster."
Zhào Zhuāng Zǐ said:
"How excellent is Luán Bó!
If his words are implemented,
he will surely lead the state of Jìn for a long time."
The Junior Steward of Chǔ went to the Jìn army
and said:
"My ruler encountered misfortune in his youth
and is not skilled in refined speech.
He heard that the two former rulers' movements in this campaign
were intended to instruct and stabilize Zhèng.
How would he dare seek to offend Jìn?
Do not remain here for a long time, gentlemen!"
Suí Jì replied:
"Formerly, King Píng commanded our late ruler Marquis Wén, saying:
'Together with Zhèng, support the House of Zhōu on both sides,
and do not neglect the King's command!'
Now Zhèng does not follow the lead;
my ruler has sent his ministers to question Zhèng.
How would we dare to dishonor your scouts?
I venture to bow in receipt of your ruler's command."
Zhì Zǐ considered this to be fawning
and sent Zhào Kuò to follow and change the message,
saying:
"The envoy misspoke.
My ruler has sent his ministers to retrace the tracks of our great state in Zhèng,
saying:
'Do not avoid the enemy!'
We, your servants, have nowhere to flee from this command."
The Viscount of Chǔ again sent an envoy to seek peace with Jìn,
the people of Jìn agreed,
and a day was set for the covenant.
Xǔ Bó of Chǔ drove the chariot for Yuè Bó,
with Shè Shū as the chariot-right,
to challenge the Jìn army to battle.
Xǔ Bó said:
"I have heard that those who challenge to battle
drive with lowered banners and graze the enemy ramparts
before returning."
Yuè Bó said:
"I have heard that those who challenge to battle
shoot the best arrows from the left,
take the reins for the driver,
while the driver descends
to adjust the horses and the harness before returning."
Shè Shū said:
"I have heard that those who challenge to battle
enter the ramparts from the right,
cut off ears and seize captives before returning."
They each performed what they had heard and turned back.
The people of Jìn pursued them,
closing in from the left and right.
Yuè Bó shot the horses on the left
and the men on the right;
those closing in could not advance.
Only one arrow remained.
An eland rose up in front of them;
he shot the eland, hitting it in the spine.
Bào Guǐ of Jìn was right behind them;
Yuè Bó sent Shè Shū to present the eland to him,
saying:
"Since the season is not right
and the time for offering game has not yet arrived,
I venture to offer this as food for your attendants."
Bào Guǐ stopped the pursuit
and said:
"Their left man is a good archer,
and their right man has eloquent speech;
they are gentlemen."
So they escaped.
Wèi Qí of Jìn sought an appointment in the ducal clan
but did not get it;
he was angry
and wished to cause the defeat of the Jìn army.
He requested to challenge the enemy to battle,
but it was not granted.
He requested to be an envoy,
and it was granted.
He then went,
requested battle,
and returned.
Pān Dǎng of Chǔ pursued him
as far as Yíngzé,
where they saw six elands;
Pān Dǎng shot one eland and turned back to present it,
saying:
"You have military matters to attend to;
might the gamekeepers not be providing enough fresh meat?
I venture to offer this to your attendants."
Shū Dǎng ordered to let him go.
Zhào Zhān sought to be a Minister but did not get it,
and he was angry at missing the Chǔ challengers;
he requested to challenge the enemy,
but it was not granted.
He requested to call for a covenant,
which was granted;
both he and Wèi Qí received the command and went.
Xì Xiàn Zǐ said:
"Two resentful men have gone;
if we are not prepared,
we will surely be defeated."
Zhì Zǐ said:
"The people of Zhèng urged us to fight,
but we did not dare follow them;
the people of Chǔ sought peace,
but we cannot be on good terms with them.
The army has no fixed orders;
why make many preparations?"
Shì Jì said:
"It is good to be prepared.
If those two men anger Chǔ,
and the people of Chǔ take advantage of us,
the loss of our army will be imminent.
It is better to be prepared.
If Chǔ has no ill intent,
and we remove preparations for the covenant,
what harm is there to our friendship?
If they come with ill intent
and we are prepared,
we will not be defeated.
Furthermore, even when feudal lords meet,
the military guards are not removed;
this is for vigilance."
Zhì Zǐ would not agree.
Shì Jì sent Gǒng Shuò and Hán Chuān to lead seven ambushes in front of Mount Áo;
therefore, the Upper Army was not defeated.
Zhào Yīng Qí sent his followers to prepare boats at the River beforehand;
therefore, when defeated, he was the first to cross.
After Pān Dǎng had pursued Wèi Qí,
Zhào Zhān arrived at the Chǔ army at night;
he spread a mat outside the camp gate
and sent his followers inside.
Chǔ Zǐ organized thirty chariots as a personal guard,
divided into Left and Right units.
The Right Guǎng harnessed at cockcrow
and unharnessed at midday;
the Left then took over,
and unharnessed at sunset.
Xǔ Yǎn drove the Right Guǎng,
Yǎng Yóujī served as the spearman on the right;
Péng Míng drove the Left Guǎng,
Qū Dàng served as the spearman on the right.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
the King rode in the Left Guǎng
to pursue Zhào Zhān.
Zhào Zhān abandoned his chariot and fled into the forest;
Qū Dàng grappled with him
and obtained his armored skirt.
The Jìn people feared that the two men would provoke the Chǔ army,
so they sent a heavy chariot to meet them.
Pān Dǎng saw the dust in the distance
and sent a galloper to report, saying:
“The Jìn army has arrived!”
The Chǔ people also feared the King might enter the Jìn army,
so they went out in battle formation.
Sūnshū said:
“Advance!
Better that we press upon others
than others press upon us.
The Shī says:
‘Ten great chariots
led the way to open the path,’
this means getting ahead of others.
The Jūnji Zhì says,
‘To be ahead of others is to snatch their spirit,’
so pressing upon them is appropriate.”
They then rapidly advanced the army;
chariots galloped and footmen ran,
falling upon the Jìn army.
Huán Zǐ did not know what to do
and beat the drum within the army, saying:
“Those who cross first shall have rewards!”
The Central and Lower Armies fought for boats,
and the severed fingers in the boats could be scooped up by the handful.
The Jìn army shifted to the right,
but the Upper Army did not move.
Gōngyǐn Qí led the Right Guard troops
to pursue the Lower Army.
Chǔ Zǐ sent Táng Jiǎo and Cài Jiūjū to tell Táng Huì Hóu:
“I, the Bùgǔ, am without virtue and greedy,
thus encountering a great enemy;
this is my fault.
However, if Chǔ is not victorious,
it will be your shame.
I venture to rely on your spirit
to assist the Chǔ army.”
He sent Pān Dǎng
to lead forty reserve chariots,
following Táng Hóu
to act as the Left Guard,
to follow the Upper Army.
Jū Bó said:
“Shall we wait for them?”
Suí Jì said:
“The Chǔ army is just now in its full strength;
if they concentrate on us,
our army will surely be wiped out.
It is better to gather our troops and leave.
To share the blame and save the people—
is that not also acceptable?”
He brought up the rear with his troops and retreated,
so they were not defeated.
The King saw the Right Guǎng
and was about to mount it.
Qū Dàng blocked the entrance
and said:
“Your Majesty began with that one,
and must also end with it.”
From then on, Chǔ's personal guard gave precedence to the Left.
Some of the Jìn people got their chariots stuck in a rut
and could not advance;
a Chǔ person advised them to remove the crossbar.
After advancing a little,
the horses turned back;
