he again advised them to pull out the flag
and lower the yoke-bar,
and then they got out.
Looking back, they said:
“We are not as skilled at fleeing as your great state!”
Zhào Zhān
used his two fine horses to save his older brother and uncle,
and returned with another horse.
Encountering the enemy and unable to escape,
he abandoned his chariot and fled into the forest.
Féng Dàfū was riding with his two sons
and told them not to look back.
They looked back and said:
“Old man Zhào is behind us.”
He was angry with them
and made them get down,
pointing to a tree and saying:
“I will leave your corpses here.”
He gave the hand-strap to Zhào Zhān,
who thereby escaped.
The next day,
following the markers to identify the corpses,
both were found together under the tree.
Chǔ’s Xióng Fùjī captured Zhì Yìng.
Zhì Zhuāngzǐ
returned with his clan to rescue him;
Chú Wǔzǐ drove the chariot,
and many soldiers of the Lower Army followed him.
Every time he shot,
he drew an arrow,
and if it was a fine one,
he placed it in the quiver of Chúzǐ.
Chúzǐ said angrily:
“Is it not your son you seek,
yet you care for the reeds?
The reeds of Dǒngzé—
can they ever be exhausted?”
Zhì Jì said:
“Without returning the sons of others,
how can I get my own son back?
It is because I cannot shoot recklessly.”
He shot Liányǐn Xiānglǎo
and captured him,
then loaded his corpse;
he shot Gōngzǐ Gǔchén
and captured him.
With these two, he returned.
When evening fell,
the Chǔ army encamped at Bì.
The remaining Jìn army could not encamp
and crossed the river at night,
with sounds of struggle throughout the night.
On the day Bǐngchén,
the Chǔ baggage train arrived at Bì,
and they then halted at Héngyōng.
Pān Dǎng said:
“Why does Your Majesty not build a Wǔjūn
and gather the Jìn corpses to make a Jīngguān?
I have heard
that overcoming an enemy must be shown to descendants
so as not to forget military achievements.”
Chǔ Zǐ said:
“This is not something you understand.
In the written script,
‘stopping the halberd’ constitutes ‘martial.’
When Wǔ Wáng overcame Shāng,
he composed the Sòng which says:
‘Collect the shields and spears,
case the bows and arrows.
I seek admirable virtue
and spread it through this Xià;
truly the King preserves it.’
He also composed the Wǔ,
the final stanza of which says:
‘Strengthen and settle your achievements.’
Its third stanza says:
‘Spreading this long-sustained thought,
I go only seeking peace.’
Its sixth stanza says:
‘Bring peace to the myriad states
and frequent bountiful years.’
Now martial power
forbids violence, stores away weapons, preserves the great mandate,
settles achievements, pacifies the people,
harmonizes the masses, and enriches wealth;
therefore he made his descendants not forget its stanzas.
Now I have caused the bones of two countries to be exposed—
that is violence;
displaying weapons to overawe the feudal lords—
that is not storing away weapons;
being violent and not storing away weapons,
how can I preserve the great mandate?
Jìn still exists;
how can achievements be settled?
There is still much that goes against the people’s desires;
how can the people be pacified?
Without virtue yet forcefully contending with the feudal lords,
how can the masses be harmonized?
Taking advantage of others’ peril
and finding peace in others’ chaos
to take as my own glory—
how can wealth be enriched?
Martial power has seven virtues;
I have not one,
so how can I show it to my descendants?
Let us build a temple to the former kings
to report the completion of the matter and that is all;
martial glory is not my achievement.
In ancient times, the enlightened kings attacked the irreverent
and took the ringleaders to bury them,
making it a great punishment;
thus there were Jīngguān
to punish the wicked.
Now the guilt is not fixed in one place,
and the people have all exhausted their loyalty
to die for their lord’s command;
how then could I make a Jīngguān?”
He offered sacrifices at the Hé,
built a temple for his late ancestors,
and reported the completion of the work before returning.
B7.12.3 In this campaign,
Shí Zhì of Zhèng actually led the Chǔ army into the state,
intending to divide Zhèng
and establish Gōngzǐ Yúchén as ruler.
On the day Xīnwèi,
Zhèng killed Púshū and Zǐfú.
The superior man said,
“When Shǐ Yì spoke of
‘not relying on disorder,’
he meant this kind of situation.
The Shī says,
‘Disorder and separation bring distress;
where shall one go to find refuge?’
It is indeed to those who rely on disorder that refuge goes!”
B7.12.4 The Earl of Zhèng and the Baron of Xǔ went to Chǔ.
B7.12.5 In autumn,
the Jìn army returned.
Huánzǐ requested the death penalty,
and the Marquis of Jìn wished to grant it.
Shì Zhēnzǐ remonstrated, saying,
“This cannot be done.
During the campaign of Chéngpú,
the Jìn army ate the enemy's grain for three days,
yet Duke Wén still had a look of worry.
Those around him said,
‘You have joy yet you worry;
would you then be happy if you had cause for worry?’
The Duke said,
‘Déshén is still there;
my worry has not ceased.
Even a cornered beast still fights;
how much more so the chief minister of a state?’
Not until Chǔ killed Zǐyù
did the Duke show a joy that could be seen.
He said,
‘There is no one left to harm me.’
That was Jìn’s second victory
and Chǔ’s second defeat;
because of it, Chǔ was not competitive for two generations.
Today, Heaven has perhaps given Jìn a great warning,
but if you also kill Línfù
to add to Chǔ’s victory,
might we not be uncompetitive for a long time?
In Línfù’s service to his ruler,
when advancing he thinks of showing total loyalty,
and when retreating he thinks of mending his faults;
he is a protector of the altars of the state.
How can you kill him?
His defeat
is like an eclipse of the sun or moon;
what does it diminish of their brightness?”
The Marquis of Jìn had him restored to his position.
B7.12.6 In winter,
the Viscount of Chǔ attacked Xiāo.
Huà Jiāo of Sòng led the men of Cài to rescue Xiāo.
The people of Xiāo imprisoned Xióngxiàng Yíliáo and Gōngzǐ Bǐng.
The King said,
“Do not kill them;
I will retreat.”
The people of Xiāo killed them anyway.
The King was enraged
and subsequently besieged Xiāo.
Xiāo collapsed.
Shēngōng Wūchén said,
“Many of the soldiers are cold.”
The King inspected the three armies,
comforting and encouraging them;
the soldiers of the three armies all felt as if they were wearing padded silk.
They then pressed the attack on Xiāo.
Huán Wúshè spoke with Sīmǎ Mǎo
and shouted for Shēn Shūzhǎn.
Shūzhǎn said,
“Do you have malted wheat?”
He replied,
“No.”
“Do you have wild lovage?”
He replied,
“No.”
“What about the ‘river-fish belly ailment’?”
He replied,
“Watch the dry wells and rescue me.”
“If you prepare a mourning band of cogon grass
and wail at the well, that will be enough.”
The next day,
Xiāo collapsed.
Shēn Shū inspected the wells
and found the mourning band of cogon grass there;
he called out and pulled him out.
B7.12.7 Yuán Hú of Jìn, Huà Jiāo of Sòng, Kǒng Dá of Wèi, and the men of Cáo made a covenant at Qīngqiū,
saying,
“To relieve the distressed
and punish the double-dealing.”
On this occasion, the names of the high ministers were not recorded
because they did not fulfill their words.
B7.12.8 For the sake of the covenant, Sòng
attacked Chén.
The people of Wèi rescued them.
Kǒng Dá said,
“Our late ruler had an agreement with them.
If the great state punishes us,
I will die for it.”
A7.13 The Annals of the 13th Year of Duke Xuān
A7.13.1 In the spring of the thirteenth year,
the Qí army attacked Jǔ.
A7.13.2 In summer,
the Viscount of Chǔ attacked Sòng.
A7.13.3 In autumn,
there were locusts.
A7.13.4 In winter,
Jìn killed its high official Xiān Hú.
B7.13 The Commentary for the 13th Year of Duke Xuān
B7.13.1 In the spring of the thirteenth year,
the Qí army attacked Jǔ,
because Jǔ relied on Jìn and did not serve Qí.
B7.13.2 In summer,
the Viscount of Chǔ attacked Sòng
because Sòng had rescued Xiāo.
The superior man said,
“Of the covenant of Qīngqiū,
only Sòng can be exempt from blame.”
B7.13.3 In autumn,
the Chìdí attacked Jìn
and reached Qīng;
Xiān Hú had summoned them.
B7.13.4 In winter,
the people of Jìn punished the defeat at Bì and the invasion at Qīng;
they laid the blame on Xiān Hú and killed him,
completely exterminating his clan.
The superior man said,
“‘When evil comes,
one has brought it upon oneself’—
does this not refer to Xiān Hú!”
B7.13.5 Regarding the covenant of Qīngqiū,
because Wèi had rescued Chén, Jìn
punished them.
They sent messengers who would not depart,
saying,
“If the guilt is not assigned,
an army will be turned against you.”
Kǒng Dá said,
“If it benefits the altars of the state,
please let me use my case to appease them,
citing my own actions as the reason for the guilt.
I was in charge of the government
and resisted the punishment of the great state;
who else should be held responsible?
I will die for it.”
A7.14 The Annals of the 14th Year of Duke Xuān
A7.14.1 In the spring of the fourteenth year,
Wèi killed its high official Kǒng Dá.
A7.14.2 In summer, in the fifth month, on the day Rénshēn,
Shòu, Earl of Cáo, died.
A7.14.3 The Marquis of Jìn attacked Zhèng.
A7.14.4 In autumn, in the ninth month,
the Viscount of Chǔ besieged Sòng.
A7.14.5 Duke Wén of Cáo was interred.
A7.14.6 In winter,
Gōngsūn Guīfù met the Marquis of Qí at Gǔ.
B7.14 The Commentary for the 14th Year of Duke Xuān
B7.14.1 In the spring of the fourteenth year,
Kǒng Dá died by hanging himself;
the people of Wèi used this to appease Jìn
and were thus exempted.
They then announced it to the feudal lords, saying,
“Our ruler had an unworthy servant, Dá,
who brought our humble state into conflict with the great state.
He has already submitted to his crime;
we venture to inform you.”
The people of Wèi, regarding his achievement as a great service,
restored his son’s household
and had him return to his father’s position.
B7.14.2 In summer,
the Marquis of Jìn attacked Zhèng
because of the battle of Bì.
He informed the feudal lords,
held a military review there, and returned.
This was the plan of Zhōngháng Huánzǐ,
who said,
“Show them our good order
and make them deliberate before coming to us.”
The people of Zhèng were afraid,
and they sent Zǐ Zhāng to replace Zǐ Liáng in Chǔ.
The Earl of Zhèng went to Chǔ,
for the purpose of plotting against Jìn.
Because Zhèng considered Zǐ Liáng to be observant of ritual,
they recalled him.
B7.14.3 The Viscount of Chǔ sent Shēn Zhōu on a mission of state to Qí,
saying:
"Do not request passage through Sòng."
He also sent Gōngzǐ Féng on a mission to Jìn,
without requesting passage through Zhèng.
Shēn Zhōu, because he had offended Sòng during the service at Mèng Zhū,
said:
"Zhèng is clear-sighted while Sòng is deaf;
the envoy to Jìn will come to no harm,
but I shall certainly die."
The King said:
"If they kill you,
I will attack them."
He presented his son Shēn Xī to the King and then departed.
When he reached Sòng,
the people of Sòng stopped him.
Huà Yuán said:
"To pass through our territory without requesting passage
is to treat us as a mere border hamlet.
To be treated as a border hamlet
is to be destroyed.
If we kill their envoy,
they will certainly attack us.
If they attack us,
we will also be destroyed.
The destruction is the same in either case."
Thereupon they killed him.
When the Viscount of Chǔ heard of this,
he threw down his sleeves and rose up.
His shoes reached him at the Zhìhuáng,
his sword reached him outside the Qǐnmén,
and his carriage reached him at the market of Púxū.
In autumn, in the ninth month,
the Viscount of Chǔ besieged Sòng.
B7.14.4 In winter,
Gōngsūn Guīfù met the Marquis of Qí at Gǔ,
where he saw Yàn Huánzǐ
and spoke with him about Lǔ;
he was full of joy.
Huánzǐ said to Gāo Xuānzǐ:
"Zǐjiā will surely face exile!
He is too fondly attached to Lǔ.
Fond attachment leads to greed,
and greed leads to plotting against others.
If one plots against others,
others will also plot against oneself.
When a whole state plots against him,
how can he not go into exile?"
B7.14.5 Mèng Xiànzǐ spoke to the Duke, saying:
"I have heard that for a small state to escape trouble from a large state,
it must send missions and present goods,
so that there are courtyard displays in hundreds;
it must attend court and present its achievements,
so that there are ceremonial appearances and colored patterns,
auspicious and virtuous with additional gifts,
all to plan against not escaping destruction.
If one waits until punishment is coming to offer bribes,
then it will be too late.
Now that Chǔ is in Sòng,
my lord, you should consider this!"
The Duke was pleased.
A7.15 The Canon of the Fifteenth Year of Duke Xuān
A7.15.1 In the spring of the fifteenth year,
Gōngsūn Guīfù met with the Viscount of Chǔ at Sòng.
A7.15.2 In summer, in the fifth month,
the people of Sòng and the people of Chǔ made peace.
A7.15.3 In the sixth month, on the day guǐmǎo,
the army of Jìn extinguished the Lù clan of the Chìdí
and returned with Lùzǐ Yīng'ér as a captive.
A7.15.4 The people of Qín attacked Jìn.
A7.15.5 Wáng Zházǐ killed Zhào Bó and
Máo Bó.
A7.15.6 In autumn,
there were locusts.
A7.15.7 Zhòngsūn Miè met with Gāo Gù of Qí at Wúlóu.
A7.15.8 For the first time, a tax was levied on the acreage of fields.
A7.15.9 In winter,
locust larvae appeared.
A7.15.10 There was a famine.
B7.15 The Commentary on the Fifteenth Year of Duke Xuān
B7.15.1 In the spring of the fifteenth year,
Gōngsūn Guīfù met with the Viscount of Chǔ at Sòng.
B7.15.2 The people of Sòng sent Yuè Yīngqí to report the emergency to Jìn,
and the Marquis of Jìn wished to rescue them.
Bó Zōng said:
"You must not.
The ancients had a saying:
'Though the whip be long,
it does not reach the horse's belly.'
Heaven is currently granting favor to Chǔ;
one cannot yet contend with them.
Although Jìn is strong,
can it oppose Heaven?
A proverb says:
'High and low depend on the mind.'
Rivers and marshes accept filth,
mountains and thickets hide diseases,
fine jade conceals flaws,
and a ruler of a state must endure disgrace;
this is the Way of Heaven.
My lord, you should wait!"
Thereupon he stopped.
He sent Jiě Yáng to Sòng
to tell them not to surrender to Chǔ,
saying:
"The armies of Jìn have all been raised
and will soon arrive."
The people of Zhèng captured him and presented him to Chǔ.
The Viscount of Chǔ bribed him heavily
to make him reverse his message.
He did not agree.
After three requests, he agreed.
They had him climb a tower-chariot
to shout to the people of Sòng and inform them.
Instead, he delivered the command of his own ruler.
The Viscount of Chǔ was about to kill him
and sent someone to speak to him, saying:
"You already gave your word to me,
yet you went back on it.
For what reason?
It is not that I lack trustworthiness;
it is you who have cast it away.
Quickly, go to your punishment!"
He replied:
"I have heard
that a ruler being able to issue commands constitutes righteousness,
a subject being able to carry out commands constitutes trustworthiness,
and trustworthiness carrying out righteousness constitutes benefit.
To plan without losing benefit
in order to protect the altars of Earth and Grain
is to be a lord of the people.
Righteousness has no double-dealing trust,
and trustworthiness has no double-dealing commands.
Your bribing me
was a failure to understand the nature of commands.
Having received a command and set out,
I would die rather than let it fall;
how then could I be bribed?
My agreeing to you
was to fulfill my command.
To die while fulfilling my command
is my lot.
If my ruler has a trustworthy subject
and I, his humble servant, obtain a proper end
in death,
what more could I seek?"
The Viscount of Chǔ released him to return home.
In summer, in the fifth month,
the army of Chǔ was about to leave Sòng.
Shēn Xī kowtowed before the King's horse
and said:
"Wúwèi knew he would die
but did not dare neglect the King's command,
yet now the King is abandoning his word."
The King could not answer.
Shēn Shūshí was driving the chariot
and said:
"If we build houses
and have the tillers return to the fields,
Sòng will certainly obey your commands."
The King followed this.
The people of Sòng were afraid,
and they sent Huà Yuán to enter the Chǔ army by night.
He climbed onto the bed of Zǐfǎn
and woke him up,
saying:
"My ruler has sent me, Yuán, to report our distress,
saying:
'In my humble city, we are exchanging our children to eat them
and splitting their bones for fuel.
Even so,
as for a covenant made under the city walls,
even if it means the state perishes,
we cannot follow it.
If you withdraw from us by thirty lǐ,
we will listen to your every command.'"
Zǐfǎn was afraid,
and made a covenant with him,
and reported it to the King.
He retreated thirty lǐ,
and Sòng and Chǔ made peace.
Huá Yuán became a hostage.
The covenant said:
"I will not deceive you,
and you shall not suspect me."
B7.15.3 The wife of the Lùzǐ Yīng'ér
was the elder sister of Jìn Jǐng Gōng.
Fèngshū took charge of the government and killed her,
and also injured the Lùzǐ's eye.
The Marquis of Jìn was going to attack him.
All the Grand Masters said:
"It is not possible.
Fèngshū has three outstanding talents;
it is better to wait for his successor."
Bó Zōng said:
"You must attack him.
The Dí have five crimes;
though their outstanding talents are many,
how can they help them?
Not performing sacrifices
is the first.
Being addicted to wine
is the second.
Abandoning Zhòng Zhāng and seizing the land of the Lí clan
is the third.
Cruelty toward our Bó Jī
is the fourth.
Injuring his ruler's eye
is the fifth.
Relying on his outstanding talents
and not using flourishing virtue,
this increases his crimes.
A successor might perhaps reverently uphold virtue and righteousness
to serve spirits and men
and extend and strengthen their mandate;
how can we wait for such a one?
If we do not punish the guilty
and say 'we will wait for a successor,'
and the successor has no grounds for being punished,
would that not be impossible?
Relying on talent and numbers
is the way to ruin.
Shāng Zhòu followed it,
and thus was destroyed.
When Heaven goes against the seasons, it is a disaster;
when Earth goes against nature, it is an omen;
when the people go against virtue, it is a rebellion.
When there is rebellion, then omens and disasters arise.
Therefore, in writing,
the reversal of 'right' (zhèng) is 'lack' (fá).
These are all present in the Dí."
The Marquis of Jìn followed this.
In the sixth month, on the day guǐmǎo,
Xún Línfù of Jìn defeated the Red Dí at Qūliáng.
On the day xīnhài,
they destroyed Lù.
Fèngshū fled to Wèi.
The people of Wèi returned him to Jìn,
and the people of Jìn killed him.
B7.15.4 Wángsūn Sū contended for the government with the Shào clan and
the Máo clan.
He sent Wángzǐ Jié to kill Shào Dài Gōng and Máo Bó Wèi,
and finally established Shào Xiāng.
B7.15.5 In autumn, in the seventh month,
Qín Huán Gōng attacked Jìn
and halted at Fǔshì.
On the day rénwǔ,
the Marquis of Jìn reviewed the troops at Jì
to take the Dí territory;
he established the Marquis of Lí and returned.
When he reached Luò,
Wèi Kē defeated the Qín army at Fǔshì
and captured Dù Huí,
who was the strongman of Qín.
Earlier,
Wèi Wǔzǐ had a favored concubine
who had no son.
When Wǔzǐ became ill,
he ordered Kē, saying:
"You must marry her off."
When he became critically ill,
he said:
"You must make her a human sacrifice!"
When he died,
Kē married her off,
saying:
"When he was critically ill, his mind was confused;
I follow his order when he was sane."
During the battle of Fǔshì,
Kē saw an old man knotting grass
to trip up Dù Huí.
Dù Huí stumbled and fell,
and thus he was captured.
At night, he dreamed of him, who said:
"I am the father of the woman you married off.
Because you followed your late father's sane command,
I have thus repaid you."
B7.15.6 The Marquis of Jìn rewarded Huánzǐ with one thousand households of Dí subjects;
he also rewarded Shì Bó with the district of Guāyǎn,
saying:
"That I have gained the Dí territory
is your merit.
Without you,
I would have lost Bó shì (Xún Línfù)."
Yángshé Zhí spoke in praise of this reward,
saying:
"What the *Zhōu Shū* calls
'employing the meritorious and respecting the reverent'
surely refers to this matter.
Shì Bó employed Zhōngháng Bó,
and the ruler trusted him;
he also employed Shì Bó.
This is what is called illustrious virtue.
The means by which Wén Wáng founded the Zhōu
did not exceed this.
Therefore, the *Shī* says,
'Spreading gifts, he established Zhōu';
he was able to bestow.
Following this path,
what would not succeed?"
B7.15.7 The Marquis of Jìn sent Zhào Tóng to present Dí captives at Zhōu,
but he was disrespectful.
Liú Kāng Gōng said:
"In less than ten years,
Yuán Shū will surely have a great calamity.
Heaven has taken away his spirit."
B7.15.8 For the first time, a tax was levied on the acre;
this was not in accordance with ritual.
Grain output should not exceed the tribute,
in order to make wealth abundant.
B7.15.9 In winter,
locust larvae appeared,
and there was famine.
It was fortunate.
A7.16 The Classic of the Sixteenth Year of Duke Xuān
A7.16.1 In the sixteenth year, in spring,
in the King's first month.
The people of Jìn destroyed the Red Dí Jiǎ clan and the Liúyú.
A7.16.2 In summer,
the Xuān Xiè of Chéngzhōu caught fire.
A7.16.3 In autumn,
Bó Jī of Tán returned.
A7.16.4 In winter,
there was a great harvest.
B7.16 The Commentary of the Sixteenth Year of Duke Xuān
B7.16.1 In the spring of the sixteenth year,
Shì Huì of Jìn led an army to destroy the Red Dí Jiǎ clan, the Liúyú, and the Duóchén.
In the third month,
he presented the Dí captives.
The Marquis of Jìn requested from the King,
and on the day wùshēn,
with sacrificial robes and cap, he appointed Shì Huì to command the Central Army
and to serve as the Grand Tutor.
Because of this, the thieves of the state of Jìn fled to Qín.
Yángshé Zhí said:
"I have heard:
'When Yǔ promoted good men,
the men who were not good kept their distance.'
This is surely what it means.
The *Shī* says:
'Apprehensive and careful,
as if on the brink of a deep abyss,
as if treading on thin ice.'
This describes a good man being in high position.
When a good man is in high position,
then the state has no people who rely on luck.
The proverb says:
'When the people have much luck,
it is the state's misfortune.'
This refers to having no good man in position."
B7.16.2 In summer,
the Xuān Xiè of Chéngzhōu caught fire;
someone set fire to it.
Regarding fires in general:
a fire caused by people is called *huǒ* (fire);
a fire caused by Heaven is called *zāi* (disaster).
B7.16.3 In autumn,
Bó Jī of Tán returned;
she had been sent away.
Because of the troubles of the Máo and
Shào clans,
the Royal House was again in disorder,
and Wángsūn Sū fled to Jìn.
The people of Jìn restored him.
Winter,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Huì to restore peace to the Royal House;
King Dìng entertained him at a banquet.
Duke Xiāng of Yuán assisted in the rites.
The meat was served in jointed, steamed pieces.
Wǔ Jì privately asked the reason for this.
When the King heard of it,
he summoned Wǔ Zǐ and said:
“Jì-shì!
Have you not heard?
At a royal entertainment, there is the presentation of whole carcasses;
at a banquet, there are jointed meats.
A Duke is entitled to an entertainment;
a Minister is entitled to a banquet.
This is the ritual of the Royal House.”
Wǔ Zǐ returned
and studied the ritual codes
to cultivate the laws of the State of Jìn.
A7.17 The Classic of the Seventeenth Year of Duke Xuān
A7.17.1 In the seventeenth year, in spring,
in the royal first month, on the day Gēngzǐ,
Xǐ Wǒ, Baron of Xǔ, died.
A7.17.2 On the day Dīngwèi,
Shēn, Marquis of Cài, died.
A7.17.3 In summer,
Duke Zhāo of Xǔ was buried.
A7.17.4 Duke Wén of Cài was buried.
A7.17.5 In the sixth month, on the day Guǐmǎo,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A7.17.6 On the day Jǐwèi,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Cáo,
and the Viscount of Zhū,
and they made a covenant together at Duàndào.
A7.17.7 In autumn,
the Duke arrived from the meeting.
A7.17.8 In winter, in the eleventh month, on the day Rénwǔ,
Shūxì, the younger brother of the Duke, died.
B7.17 The Commentary on the Seventeenth Year of Duke Xuān
B7.17.1 In the seventeenth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Xì Kè to summon Qí to a meeting.
Duke Qǐng of Qí placed some women behind a curtain
to let them observe him.
When Xì Zǐ ascended the hall,
the women laughed from within the room.
Xiànzǐ was angry;
he went out and swore, saying:
“If I do not avenge this,
may I be unable to cross the River!”
Xiànzǐ returned first
and sent Luán Jīnglú to wait for orders in Qí,
saying:
“If you do not obtain a favorable outcome regarding Qí,
do not return to report your mission.”
When Xì Zǐ arrived,
he requested to attack Qí.
The Marquis of Jìn did not grant it.
He requested to use his own private retainers,
and again the Marquis did not grant it.
The Marquis of Qí sent Gāo Gù, Yàn Ruò,
Cài Zhāo, and Nánguō Yǎn to the meeting.
When they reached Liǎnyú, Gāo Gù fled and returned home.
In summer,
they met at Duàndào,
to punish those who were double-minded.
They covenanted at Juǎnchǔ,
refusing the men of Qí.
The Jìn people seized Yàn Ruò at Yěwáng,
seized Cài Zhāo at Yuán,
and seized Nánguō Yǎn at Wēn.
Miáo Bènhuáng was on a mission
and saw Yàn Huánzǐ.
When he returned,
he spoke to the Marquis of Jìn, saying:
“What crime has Yàn-zǐ committed?
Formerly, when the feudal lords served our late ruler,
they all acted as if they could not do enough;
but if they spoke, all the ministers did not believe them,
and so the feudal lords all developed double-minded intentions.
The ruler of Qí feared he would not receive proper ritual treatment,
therefore he did not come out himself
but sent these four gentlemen to come.
Some of those around him discouraged him,
saying:
‘If the ruler does not go out,
they will surely seize our envoys.’
Therefore Gāo-zǐ fled when he reached Liǎnyú.
But these three gentlemen said:
‘If we break the friendly relations between our rulers,
we would rather return and die for it.’
For this reason, they faced danger and came.
If we had properly welcomed them
to cherish those who come;
but instead we have seized them,
thereby confirming the discouragement of Qí.
Have we not already erred?
To err and not change,
and furthermore to persist in it long,
so that regret is established—
what benefit is there in that?
Giving those who turned back a justification,
and harming those who came,
thereby frightening the feudal lords—
what use will that be?”
The Jìn people relaxed their custody of them,
and they escaped.
In autumn, in the eighth month,
the Jìn army returned.
B7.17.2 Fàn Wǔzǐ was about to retire due to old age;
he summoned Wénzǐ and said:
“Xiè!
I have heard this:
those whose joy and anger follow the proper categories are few;
those who shift them are truly many.
The *Classic of Poetry* says:
‘If the superior man is angry,
the disorder might quickly be checked.
If the superior man is joyful,
the disorder might quickly be ended.’
The joy and anger of the superior man
are used to end disorder.
As for that which does not end,
it must surely increase.
Does Xì-zǐ perhaps wish to end disorder in Qí?
If not,
I fear he will increase it.
I am going to retire;
by letting Xì-zǐ fulfill his ambition,
perhaps there will be some relief.
You must follow the other gentlemen with nothing but reverence.”
He then requested to retire.
Xì Xiànzǐ took charge of the government.
B7.17.3 In winter,
Shūxì, the younger brother of the Duke, died;
he was the Duke's brother by the same mother.
In all cases of a Crown Prince's brother by the same mother,
while the Duke is alive, he is called *Gōngzǐ*;
when he is no longer alive, he is called *Dì*.
In all cases where the term *Dì* is used,
it always means a brother by the same mother.
A7.18 The Classic of the Eighteenth Year of Duke Xuān
A7.18.1 In the eighteenth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn
and Zāng, the Heir Apparent of Wèi, attacked Qí.
A7.18.2 The Duke attacked Qǐ.
A7.18.3 In summer, in the fourth month.
A7.18.4 In autumn, in the seventh month,
the people of Zhū slaughtered the Viscount of Zèng in Zèng.
A7.18.5 On the day Jiǎxū,
Lǚ, Viscount of Chǔ, died.
A7.18.6 Gōngsūn Guīfù went to Jìn.
A7.18.7 In winter, in the tenth month, on the day Rénxū,
the Duke passed away in the main state chamber.
A7.18.8 Guīfù returned from Jìn
and reached Shēng.
He then fled to Qí.
B7.18 The Commentary on the Eighteenth Year of Duke Xuān
B7.18.1 In the eighteenth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn
and Zāng, the Crown Prince of Wèi, attacked Qí,
and reached Yánggǔ.
The Marquis of Qí met with the Marquis of Jìn,
and they covenanted at Zēng,
sending Gōngzǐ Qiáng as a hostage to Jìn.
The Jìn army returned.
Cài Zhāo
and Nánguō Yǎn fled and returned home.
B7.18.2 In summer,
the Duke sent an envoy to Chǔ to request troops,
wishing to use them to attack Qí.
B7.18.3 In autumn,
the people of Zhū slaughtered the Viscount of Zèng in Zèng.
In all cases, when one from within treats their ruler cruelly, it is called *shì*;
when it is from without, it is called *qiāng*.
B7.18.4 King Zhuāng of Chǔ died,
so the troops of Chǔ did not set out.
Subsequently, Jìn troops were used,
and because of this, Chǔ had the campaign at Shǔ.
B7.18.5 Because Xiāng Zhòng had established the Duke, Gōngsūn Guīfù
enjoyed favor;
he wished to remove the Sān Huán
in order to strengthen the ducal house.
He plotted with the Duke
and went on a mission to Jìn,
intending to use the people of Jìn to remove them.
In winter,
the Duke passed away.
Jì Wénzǐ spoke at the court,
saying:
"The one who made me kill the legitimate heir
and establish the son of a concubine, thereby losing great support,
was indeed Zhòng!"
Zàng Xuānshū said angrily:
"At that time you could not manage it;
what is the crime of the descendant?
If you wish to remove him,
I, Xǔ, request to remove him."
They then expelled the Dōngmén clan.
Zǐjiā returned;
when he reached Shēng,
he erected an altar and curtains
and reported back to his subordinates.
Having reported back,
he bared his shoulder, bound his hair,
took his place and wailed,
and after three leaps, he departed.
He then fled to Qí.
The text writes, "Guīfù returned from Jìn,"
as a way of commending him.
A8.1 Annals of the First Year of Duke Chéng
A8.1.1 In the first year, spring,
the King's first month,
the Duke ascended the throne.
A8.1.2 In the second month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
we buried our ruler, Duke Xuān.
A8.1.3 There was no ice.
A8.1.4 In the third month,
the "hill-armor" tax was established.
A8.1.5 In summer,
Zàngsūn Xǔ and the Marquis of Jìn made a covenant at Chìjí.
A8.1.6 In autumn,
the King's army was defeated at Máoróng.
A8.1.7 In winter, the tenth month.
B8.1 Commentary of the First Year of Duke Chéng
B8.1.1 In the first year, spring.
The Marquis of Jìn sent Xiá Jiā to make peace between the Róng and the King;
Duke Xiāng of Shàn went to Jìn to acknowledge the settlement.
Duke Kāng of Liú intercepted the Róng,
intending to then attack them.
Shūfú said:
"To turn one's back on a covenant and deceive a great state
will surely result in defeat.
To turn one's back on a covenant is inauspicious;
to deceive a great state is unrighteous.
When gods and men do not assist,
how can one prevail?"
He did not listen
and then attacked the Máoróng.
In the third month, on the day Guǐwèi,
they were defeated at Xúwúshì.
B8.1.2 Because of the troubles with Qí,
the "hill-armor" tax was established.
B8.1.3 Hearing that Qí was about to lead out the armies of Chǔ,
in summer,
they made a covenant at Chìjí.
In autumn,
the King's men came to report the defeat.
In winter,
Zàng Xuānshū ordered the collection of taxes,
the repair of defenses and the preparation of equipment,
saying:
"Qí and Chǔ have formed an alliance,
and we have newly made a covenant with Jìn.
Jìn and Chǔ are contending for alliances;
the army of Qí will surely arrive.
Although the men of Jìn attack Qí,
Chǔ will surely rescue them;
thus Qí and Chǔ are united against us.
To know the difficulty and have preparations is how one can succeed."
A8.2 Annals of the Second Year of Duke Chéng
A8.2.1 In the second year, spring,
the Marquis of Qí attacked our northern border.
A8.2.2 In summer, the fourth month, on the day Bǐngxū,
Sūn Liángfū of Wèi led an army and fought with the army of Qí at Xīnzhù;
the army of Wèi was defeated.
A8.2.3 In the sixth month, on the day Guǐyǒu,
Jìsūn Xíngfù,
Zàngsūn Xǔ,
Shūsūn Qiáorú,
and Gōngsūn Yīngqí led an army to meet Xì Kè of Jìn,
Sūn Liángfū of Wèi,
and Prince Shǒu of Cáo, and fought with the Marquis of Qí at Ān;
the army of Qí was defeated.
A8.2.4 In autumn, the seventh month,
the Marquis of Qí sent Guó Zuǒ to the army.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
they made a covenant with Guó Zuǒ at Yuánlóu.
A8.2.5 In the eighth month, on the day Rénwǔ,
Duke Bǎo of Sòng died.
On the day Gēngyín,
Marquis Sù of Wèi died.
A8.2.7 The fields of Wènyáng were taken.
A8.2.8 In winter,
the army of Chǔ
and the army of Zhèng invaded Wèi.
A8.2.9 In the eleventh month,
the Duke met Prince Yīngqí of Chǔ at Shǔ.
A8.2.10 On the day Bǐngshēn,
the Duke and the people of Chǔ,
Qín,
Sòng,
Chén,
Wèi,
Zhèng,
Qí,
Cáo,
Zhū,
Xuē,
and Zéng made a covenant at Shǔ.
B8.2 Commentary of the Second Year of Duke Chéng
B8.2.1 In the second year, spring,
the Marquis of Qí attacked our northern border
and besieged Lóng.
Lú Pú Jiùkuí, a favorite of Duke Qǐng, attacked the gate.
The people of Lóng captured him.
The Marquis of Qí said:
"Do not kill him;
I will make a covenant with you
and will not enter your territory to build fortifications."
They did not listen,
but killed him and exposed his body on the city wall.
The Marquis of Qí personally beat the drum,
and his soldiers scaled the wall.
In three days,
they took Lóng.
They then invaded southward
and reached Cháoqiū.
B8.2.2 The Marquis of Wèi sent Sūn Liángfū, Shí Jì, Nìng Xiāng, and Xiàng Qín to lead an invasion of Qí,
and they encountered the army of Qí.
Shí Zǐ wished to return.
Sūn Zǐ said:
"It is not possible.
Having led an army to attack others,
to encounter their army and return—
what will you say to the ruler?
If you knew you were incapable,
then you should not have set out.
Now that we have encountered them,
it is better to fight."
In summer,
it occurred.
Shí Chéngzǐ said:
"The army is defeated;
if you do not wait a little,
the multitude will be completely terrified.
If you lose the troops,
how will you report back?"
No one replied.
He spoke again:
"You
are a high minister of the state.
If you fall,
it will be a disgrace.
You retreat with the multitude;
I will stay here."
He also announced
that many chariots were coming.
The army of Qí then stopped
and halted at Jūjū.
Zhòngshū Yúxī of Xīnzhù
rescued Sūn Huánzǐ,
and Huánzǐ thereby escaped.
Afterwards,
the people of Wèi rewarded him with a city.
He declined,
but requested the use of curved chimes
and decorated horse girths for court audiences.
They granted this.
Zhòngní heard of it and said:
"What a pity!
It would have been better to give him more cities.
Only regalia and titles
cannot be lent to others;
they are what the ruler presides over.
Titles are used to manifest trust,
trust is used to guard regalia,
regalia are used to contain ritual,
ritual is used to practice righteousness,
righteousness is used to produce benefit,
and benefit is used to pacify the people—
these are the great principles of government.
If these are lent to others,
it is giving away the government to them.
Once government is lost,
the state follows it,
and it cannot be stopped."
B8.2.3 Sūn Huánzǐ returned to Xīnzhù,
did not enter,
and then went to Jìn to beg for an army.
Zāng Xuānshū also went to Jìn
to beg for an army.
Both sought support from Xì Xiànzǐ.
The Marquis of Jìn granted them seven hundred chariots.
Xì Zǐ said:
"This was the levy for the Battle of Chéngpú.
With the brilliance of the former ruler and the solemnity of the former ministers,
victory was achieved.
Compared to those former ministers,
I am not even fit to be their servant.
I request eight hundred chariots."
This was granted.
Xì Kè commanded the central army,
Shì Xiè assisted the upper army,
Luán Shū commanded the lower army,
and Hán Jué served as the Marshall
to rescue Lǔ
and Wèi.
Zāng Xuānshū met the Jìn army
and guided them.
Jì Wénzǐ led an army to join them.
Upon reaching the territory of Wèi,
Hán Xiànzǐ was about to execute a man.
Xì Xiànzǐ galloped over
intending to save him.
When he arrived,
the man had already been executed.
Xì Zǐ ordered that the head be quickly displayed to the public,
and told his attendant:
"I am sharing the blame."
The army followed the Qí army to Shēn.
On the day of Rénshēn in the sixth month,
the army arrived at the foot of Mount Míjī.
The Marquis of Qí sent an envoy to request battle,
saying:
"You have troubled the ruler’s army to visit our humble domain.
My humble forces are not many,
but I request an audience tomorrow morning."
The reply was:
"Jìn, Lǔ, and Wèi are brothers.
They came to tell us:
'The Great State
vents its resentment upon our humble territory morning and evening.'
Our ruler could not bear it,
so he sent his ministers to petition the Great State,
requesting that you do not let your armies linger in our territory.
We can advance but cannot retreat;
the ruler need not trouble himself to issue orders."
The Marquis of Qí said:
"The ministers' agreement
is my wish;
if you did not agree,
I would still see you."
Gāo Gù of Qí entered the Jìn army,
lifted a stone and threw it at someone,
captured him, mounted his chariot,
tied a mulberry root to it,
and paraded around the Qí camp,
saying:
"Let those who want courage buy my leftover courage!"
On the day of Guǐyǒu,
the armies arrayed at Ān.
Bǐng Xià drove for the Marquis of Qí,
and Féng Chǒufù was the chariot-right.
Jiě Zhāng of Jìn drove for Xì Kè,
and Zhèng Qiūhuǎn was the chariot-right.
The Marquis of Qí said:
"I will destroy them
before having my morning meal."
Without armoring the horses, they galloped forward.
Xì Kè was wounded by an arrow;
blood flowed down to his shoes,
but he did not stop the beat of the drum.
He said:
"I am suffering!"
Zhāng Hóu said:
"Since the first clash,
arrows have pierced my hand and elbow,
but I broke them off to keep driving.
The left wheel is dark red with blood;
how would I dare speak of suffering?
Sir, you must endure it!"
Zhèng Qiūhuǎn said:
"Since the first clash,
whenever there was a difficult spot,
I always got down to push the chariot.
Did you notice?
Yet indeed, you are suffering!"
Zhāng Hóu said:
"The ears and eyes of the army
are on our flag and drum;
advance and retreat follow them.
As long as there is one person in this chariot,
the task can be accomplished.
Why
let suffering ruin the ruler's great undertaking?
Donning armor and grasping weapons
is fundamentally about facing death.
Suffering is not yet death;
sir, you must exert yourself!"
With his left hand, he gathered the reins,
and with his right, he took up the mallet and drummed.
The horses bolted and could not be stopped;
the army followed them.
The Qí army suffered a crushing defeat.
They pursued them,
circling Mount Huábùzhù three times.
Hán Jué had dreamed that Zǐyú
said to him:
"In the morning, avoid the left and right!"
Therefore, he drove from the center
while pursuing the Marquis of Qí.
Bǐng Xià said:
"Shoot the driver;
he is a gentleman."
The Duke said:
"To call him a gentleman and then shoot him
is against ritual."
He shot the one on the left,
who fell out of the chariot.
He shot the one on the right,
who died inside the chariot.
Qí Wú Zhāng had lost his chariot
and said to Hán Jué:
"Please let me ride along!"
He tried the left and right sides,
but Hán Jué elbowed him away from both
and made him stand in the back.
Hán Jué leaned down
to settle the position of his chariot-right.
Féng Chǒufù exchanged places with the Duke.
Just as they reached Huáquán,
the outer trace-horse got caught on a tree
and stopped.
Féng Chǒufù had been lying in the carriage,
and a snake came out from under him.
He struck it with his arm,
was injured, and hid the wound;
therefore he could not push the chariot
and they were overtaken.
Hán Jué held the horse's halter in front of the chariot,
bowed twice and touched his head to the ground,
and presented a goblet of wine with a jade disk,
saying:
"Our ruler sent his ministers
to petition on behalf of Lǔ and Wèi,
saying:
'Do not let your armies fall into the ruler's territory.'
I, your humble servant, have been unfortunate
to be assigned to the ranks of war,
and have no place to hide or escape.
Furthermore, I feared that fleeing or avoiding
would disgrace both rulers.
I, your servant, have disgraced your warriors;
I dare to report my lack of talent
as I take this post to fill a vacancy."
Féng Chǒufù ordered the Duke to step down
and go to Huáquán to get a drink.
Zhèng Zhōu Fù
was driving an auxiliary chariot,
with Wǎn Fá as the chariot-right;
they picked up the Marquis of Qí and escaped.
Hán Jué presented Féng Chǒufù.
Xì Xiànzǐ was about to execute him,
and he called out:
"From this day forth, there will be no one to take upon himself the hardships of his ruler in his stead.
Here is one who did so,
and is he to be executed?"
Xìzǐ said:
"If a man does not find it difficult to die to spare his ruler,
and I execute him,
it would be inauspicious.
Pardon him
to encourage those who serve their rulers."
So he released him.
The Marquis of Qí escaped
and searched for Chǒufù,
entering and exiting the fray three times.
Each time he came out,
the Qí army retreated with their commander.
He entered the ranks of the Dí,
and the Dí soldiers all drew their halberds
and covered him with their shields.
Thus he entered the Wèi army,
and the Wèi army let him pass.
He then entered through Xúguān.
The Marquis of Qí saw a guard
and said:
"Strive on!
The Qí army has been defeated!"
He encountered a woman.
The woman said:
"Has the ruler escaped?"
He said:
"He has escaped."
She said:
"Has the Ruì Sītú escaped?"
He said:
"He has escaped."
She said:
"If the ruler and my father have escaped,
what more can I ask?"
Then she fled.
The Marquis of Qí considered her to have propriety.
Later he inquired about her;
she was the wife of the Bì Sītú.
He gave her Shíjiào.
The Jìn army followed the Qí army,
entering from Qiūyú.
They attacked Mǎjīng.
The Marquis of Qí sent Bīn Mèirén to offer bribes
of the Jì Yǎn tripod,
jade chimes, and land.
"If this is not acceptable," he said,
"then let them do as they wish."
Bīn Mèirén presented the bribes.
The people of Jìn did not accept,
saying:
"You must take Xiāotóng Shūzǐ as a hostage,
and make all the furrows within the borders of Qí
run east."
He replied:
"Xiāotóng Shūzǐ is no other than
the mother of our humble ruler.
If regarded as an equal,
then she is also the mother of the Jìn ruler.
You, sir, are proclaiming the great commands to the feudal lords,
yet you say one must take his mother as a hostage
to establish trust;
what would the King’s command say to that?
Moreover, this is to issue a command based on unfiliality.
The Shī says:
'The filial son’s devotion is never exhausted,
it is forever bestowed upon your kind.'
If you issue commands to the feudal lords based on unfiliality,
would that not be a departure from virtuous conduct?
The former kings established the boundaries of the world,
according to the suitability of the soil,
and distributed its benefits.
Thus the Shī says:
'I marked the boundaries, I regulated the lands;
south and east run the furrows.'
Now you, sir, are marking the boundaries of the feudal lords,
but you say 'simply make all the furrows run east.'
This is only for the benefit of your war chariots,
without regard for the suitability of the soil;
would that not be a violation of the commands of the former kings?
To go against the former kings is unrighteous;
how then can you be the leader of the alliance?
In this, Jìn truly has a deficiency.
When the Four Kings ruled as kings,
they established virtue and fulfilled common desires;
when the Five Hegemons ruled as hegemons,
they toiled to soothe the people,
to serve the King’s command.
Now you, sir, seek to assemble the feudal lords
to satisfy boundless desires.
The Shī says:
'He spreads his governance with ease and abundance;
all blessings gather there.'
If you are not easy and abundant,
and you cast away all blessings,
how will the feudal lords be harmed?
If it is not so,
my ruler’s command to me, his servant,
provides an answer.
He said:
'You have brought the ruler’s army to trouble our humble state.
Our humble provisions are insufficient
to feast your followers.
Fearing the ruler’s awe,
our troops were defeated.
If you, sir, would graciously seek the welfare of the state of Qí
and not destroy its altars of soil and grain,
but allow it to continue the old friendship,
then as for these worn vessels of the former rulers
and our lands, we would not dare to be begrudging.
If you still do not permit this,
we request to gather our remaining forces
and fight one last battle with our backs to the city.
If our humble state is lucky,
it will follow your command;
how much more so if it is unlucky,
would we dare but to listen only to your command?'"
Lǔ and Wèi remonstrated, saying:
"Qí hates us.
Those who have died
were all close and dear ones.
If you, sir, do not permit this,
their enmity against us will surely be extreme.
As for you,
what more do you seek?
You have obtained the treasures of their state,
and we have also obtained land,
and the difficulties are eased;
the glory is great.
Whether Qí or Jìn prevails is granted only by Heaven;
must it necessarily be Jìn?"
The people of Jìn granted it.
He replied:
"Your ministers led the levies and chariots
to petition for Lǔ and Wèi.
If there is a pretext
to report back to our ruler,
it is your grace.
How could we dare but to listen only to your command?"
Qín Zhèng came from the army
to meet the Duke.
In autumn, in the seventh month,
the Jìn army and Guó Zuǒ of Qí made a covenant at Yuánlóu.
They made the people of Qí return
our lands of Wènyáng.
The Duke met the Jìn army at Shàngmíng.
He bestowed upon the three commanders first-class chariots
and robes of the third rank.
The Sīmǎ, Sīkōng, Yúshuài,
Hòuzhèng, and Yàlǚ
all received robes of the first rank.
B8.2.4 In the eighth month,
Sòng Wén Gōng died.
For the first time, there was a lavish burial:
using clam shells and charcoal,
increasing the number of chariots and horses,
and for the first time using human sacrifices;
the heavy vessels were prepared.
The outer coffin had four slopes,
and the inner coffin had sideboards
of juniper.
Gentlemen said of Huá Yuán and Yuè Jǔ
that in this matter they were not true ministers.
A minister
is one who manages troubles and removes delusions,
and for this reason, he faces death to remonstrate.
Now these two men,
while the ruler was alive, indulged his delusions,
and when he died, they increased his extravagance;
this is abandoning the ruler to evil.
What kind of ministers are they?"
B8.2.5 In the ninth month,
Wèi Mù Gōng died.
The three gentlemen of Jìn came from the military campaign
to offer condolences,
and they wailed outside the Great Gate.
The people of Wèi went to meet them,
and the women wailed inside the gate.
The seeing-off was also like this.
Subsequently, this was always done for burials.
B8.2.6 When Chǔ punished the Xià Shì of Chén,
Zhuāng Wáng wished to take Xià Jī.
Shēngōng Wùchén said:
"This must not be.
You, my ruler, summoned the feudal lords
to punish a crime.
Now if you take Xià Jī,
it is because you covet her beauty.
To covet beauty is licentiousness.
Licentiousness is a great offense."
The *Zhōu Shū* says,
“Illustrate virtue and be cautious with punishments,”
which was how Wén Wáng established the Zhōu.
“Illustrating virtue”
means striving to exalt it;
“being cautious with punishments”
means striving to avoid them.
“If you rouse the feudal lords
and thereby incur great punishment,
that is not being cautious.
May Your Majesty consider this!”
The King then desisted.
Zǐfǎn wanted to take her,
but Wūchén said:
“This is an unlucky person.
She caused the early death of Zǐmán,
killed Yùshū,
led to the assassination of Líng Hóu,
the execution of Xià Nán,
drove out Kǒng and Yí,
and brought ruin to the state of Chén.
Why would anyone want someone so unlucky?
Life is indeed difficult;
would one not find death anyway?
There are many beautiful women in the world;
why must it be this one?”
Zǐfǎn then desisted.
The King gave her to the Liányǐn Xiānglǎo.
Xiānglǎo died at Bì,
and his body was not recovered.
His son Hēiyāo committed incest with her.
Wūchén sent a message to her,
saying:
“Return home,
and I will formally wed you.”
He also had someone from Zhèng summon her,
saying:
“The body can be recovered;
you must come to receive it.”
Xià Jī told the King.
The King asked Qū Wū.
He replied:
“The message is trustworthy.
Zhì Yīng’s father
was a favorite of Chéng Gōng
and is the younger brother of Zhōngháng Bó;
he has newly become the assistant of the Central Army
and is on good terms with Huáng Xù of Zhèng;
he loves this son dearly.
He will surely use Zhèng to return the Prince
and the body of Xiānglǎo in order to seek him.
The people of Zhèng are fearful because of the Battle of Bì
and wish to curry favor with Jìn;
they will surely grant it.”
The King sent Xià Jī back.
As she was about to leave,
she said to those seeing her off:
“If I do not get the body,
I shall not return.”
Wūchén sent betrothal gifts to Zhèng,
and the Earl of Zhèng agreed.
When Gòng Wáng ascended the throne,
he was about to undertake the campaign of Yángqiáo
and sent Qū Wū on a mission to Qí
to announce the date of the military operations.
Wūchén took his entire household and departed.
Shēnshū Guì followed his father
and was going to Yǐng
when he encountered him,
saying:
“How strange!
This gentleman has the look of one fearing the three armies,
yet also has the joy of ‘Sāngzhōng.’
He is surely about to steal a wife and flee.”
When he arrived in Zhèng,
he sent his assistant back with the diplomatic gifts
and departed with Xià Jī.
He intended to flee to Qí.
The army of Qí had just been defeated,
so he said:
“I will not dwell in a defeated state.”
He then fled to Jìn
and, through the introduction of Xì Zhì,
became a minister in Jìn.
The people of Jìn made him the Grand Master of Xíng.
Zǐfǎn requested
that he be bribed into detention with heavy gifts.
The King said:
“Stop!
Though he erred in his personal schemes,
he was loyal in his counsel to our late ruler.
Loyalty
is the strength of the state;
it covers many faults.
Moreover, if he can benefit their state,
even with heavy gifts,
would Jìn agree?
If he is of no benefit to Jìn,
Jìn will discard him;
why go to the trouble of bribing them to detain him?”
B8.2.7 The Jìn army returned;
Fàn Wénzǐ entered last.
Wǔzǐ said:
“Did you not make me look out for you?”
He replied:
“The army has been successful,
and the people of the state joyfully come to meet it.
If I entered first,
their eyes and ears would be fixed on me;
this would be taking the credit from the commander.
Therefore, I did not dare.”
Wǔzǐ said:
“I know now that you will escape calamity.”
Xì Bó had an audience.
The Duke said:
“It was by your strength!”
He replied:
“It was your instruction, My Lord,
and the strength of the various gentlemen.
What strength did I have in it?”
Fàn Shū had an audience,
and the Duke commended him as he had Xì Bó.
He replied:
“It was what Gēng ordered
and what Kè regulated.
What strength did I, Xiè, have in it?”
Luán Bó had an audience,
and the Duke did the same.
He replied:
“It was the counsel of Xiè
and the soldiers following orders.
What strength did I, Shū, have in it?”
B8.2.8 Xuān Gōng had sent to seek friendly relations with Chǔ,
but Zhuāng Wáng died,
and Xuān Gōng passed away,
so they were unable to establish the friendship.
The Duke ascended the throne,
accepted a covenant from Jìn,
and joined Jìn in attacking Qí.
The people of Wèi did not send an envoy to Chǔ
but also accepted a covenant from Jìn
and followed in the attack on Qí.
Therefore, the Lìngyǐn of Chǔ, Zǐzhòng,
undertook the campaign of Yángqiáo to rescue Qí.
As he was about to raise the army,
Zǐzhòng said:
“The King is young,
and the various ministers are not equal to those of the late Grand Masters.
Only with a large army will it be possible.
The *Shī* says:
‘Ample and many were the officers,
through whom Wén Wáng enjoyed repose.’
If Wén Wáng still used a multitude,
how much more so for the likes of us?
Moreover, our late ruler, Zhuāng Wáng, charged us saying:
‘If one lacks virtue to reach far-off places,
there is nothing better than being kind and compassionate to one’s people
and using them well.’”
Then they conducted a grand census,
cancelled debts,
reached out to widowers,
relieved the needy,
and pardoned crimes.
The entire army was mobilized,
and all the King’s elite troops marched.
Péng Míng drove the war chariot,
Jǐng Gōng of Cài was on the left,
and Líng Gōng of Xǔ was on the right.
The two rulers were young,
so they were both forcibly capped.
In winter,
the Chǔ army invaded Wèi,
then proceeded to invade us, encamping at Shǔ.
They sent Zāngsūn to go to them.
He declined, saying:
“Chǔ is far away and has been long in the field;
they will surely retreat soon.
To receive credit without having achieved anything,
I do not dare.”
The Chǔ invasion reached Yángqiáo.
Mèngsūn requested to go and bribe them
with carpenters,
needleworkers, and weavers,
a hundred of each,
and with Gōnghéng as a hostage,
to request a covenant.
The people of Chǔ agreed to a peace.
In the eleventh month,

the Duke, along with Prince Yīngqí of Chǔ, the Marquis of Cài, the Baron of Xǔ, the Grand Master of the Right Yuè of Qín, Huá Yuán of Sòng, Gōngsūn Níng of Chén, Sūn Liángfū of Wèi, Prince Qùjí of Zhèng, and a Grand Master of the state of Qí, made a covenant at Shǔ.
The names of the ministers were not recorded
because it was a deficient covenant.
Because they feared Jìn and secretly made a covenant with Chǔ,
it is therefore called
a “deficient covenant.”
The Marquis of Cài and the Baron of Xǔ were not recorded
because they rode in Chǔ chariots,
which is called “losing one’s position.”
The noble man said:
"Is one’s position not something about which one must be careful!
The lords of Cài and Xǔ,
once they lost their positions,
were no longer ranked among the feudal lords;
how much more so for those below them!
The *Shī* says:
'Unremitting in his position,
the people find their rest.'
This is what it refers to."
When the Chǔ army reached Sòng,
Gōnghéng fled and returned.
Zāng Xuānshū said:
"Héngfù could not endure a few years without leisure,
and thereby abandoned the state of Lǔ;
what will become of the state?
Who will remain?
Those who follow will surely have to take up this man’s burden!
The state is abandoned."
On this expedition,
Jìn avoided Chǔ,
fearing their numbers.
The noble man said:
"Numbers are something that cannot be disregarded.
When Great Officers conduct the government,
they still overcome through numbers;
how much more so for an enlightened ruler who is good at using his multitude?
What the *Tàishì* calls 'The millions of Shāng were divided,
while the ten men of Zhōu were united,'
is about the multitude."
B8.2.9 The Marquis of Jìn sent Gǒng Shuò
to present the spoils of the victory over Qí to Zhōu.
The King did not grant an audience,
and sent Shàn Xiānggōng to decline,
saying:
"When the Mányí, Róng, and Dí
do not follow the King's commands,
but are excessive and dissolute and destroy the constant rules,
and the King commands they be attacked,
then spoils are presented.
The King personally receives them and rewards them,
in order to punish the disrespectful and encourage those with merit.
When brothers
or maternal relatives
encroach upon and damage the King's territory,
and the King commands they be attacked,
it is merely reported as a matter of business;
no success is presented as spoils,
in order to respect those close and dear
and forbid excessive evil.
Now my Uncle has been successful
and has achieved merit against Qí,
but he did not send a high minister
to settle and soothe the Royal House;
the one he sent to soothe me was indeed the Earl of Gǒng,
and as the Earl of Gǒng came,
he has no official duty in the Royal House,
and moreover, violates the rituals of the former kings.
Although I might wish to favor the Earl of Gǒng,
how could I dare abandon the old statutes and thereby disgrace my Uncle?
Now Qí
is a state of maternal relatives
and the descendants of the Grand Tutor.
Would I not also be excessive and follow their desires
so as to anger my Uncle?
Or could it be that he cannot be remonstrated with and instructed?"
Shì Zhuāngbó was unable to answer.
The King ordered the gifts to be handed over to the three officers,
and treated him with the ritual for when a Marquis or Earl defeats an enemy and sends a Great Officer
to announce the celebration,
one grade lower than the ritual for a high minister.
The King held a banquet with the Earl of Gǒng
and gave him private gifts.
He sent an assistant to tell him:
"It was not according to ritual,
so do not record it!"
A8.3 The Classic for the Third Year of Duke Chéng
A8.3.1 In the third year, in spring,
in the King’s first month,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
and the Earl of Cáo to attack Zhèng.
A8.3.2 On the day Xīnhài,
Duke Mù of Wèi was buried.
A8.3.3 In the second month,
the Duke arrived from the attack on Zhèng.
A8.3.4 On the day Jiǎzǐ,
the New Palace was damaged by fire.
For three days there was wailing.
A8.3.5 On the day Yǐhài,
Duke Wén of Sòng was buried.
A8.3.6 In summer,
the Duke went to Jìn.
A8.3.7 Prince Qùjí of Zhèng led an army to attack Xǔ.
A8.3.8 The Duke arrived from Jìn.
A8.3.9 In autumn,
Shúsūn Qiáorú led an army to besiege Jí.
A8.3.10 The Great Rain Sacrifice was performed.
A8.3.11 Xì Kè of Jìn
and Sūn Liángfū of Wèi attacked the Qiángjiùrú.
A8.3.12 In winter, the eleventh month,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Xún Gēng on a mission of friendly inquiry.
A8.3.13 The Marquis of Wèi sent Sūn Liángfū on a mission of friendly inquiry.
A8.3.14 On the day Bǐngwǔ,
the Duke made a covenant with Xún Gēng.
A8.3.15 On the day Dīngwèi,
the Duke made a covenant with Sūn Liángfū.
A8.3.16 Zhèng attacked Xǔ.
B8.3 The Commentary for the Third Year of Duke Chéng
B8.3.1 In the spring of the third year,
the feudal lords attacked Zhèng
and halted at Bóniú,
to punish it for the battle of Bì.
Then they invaded the eastern parts of Zhèng.
Prince Yǎn of Zhèng led an army to resist them,
causing the eastern borderers to lie in ambush at Màn,
and defeated them at Qiūyú.
Huáng Xù went to Chǔ to present the spoils of victory.
B8.3.2 In summer,
the Duke went to Jìn
to give thanks for the lands of Wènyáng.
B8.3.3 Xǔ relied on Chǔ and did not serve Zhèng;
Zǐliáng of Zhèng attacked Xǔ.
B8.3.4 The people of Jìn returned Prince Gǔchén of Chǔ and the corpse of the Liányǐn Xiānglǎo to Chǔ,
in order to seek the release of Zhì Yīng.
At this time Xún Shǒu was assisting the Middle Army,
so the people of Chǔ agreed to it.
The King saw Zhì Yīng off
and said:
"Do you perhaps resent me?"
He replied:
"The two states took up arms.
I, your servant, lacked talent
and was not equal to my post,
thus becoming a captive.
Your officers did not
use my blood to smear the drums,
but allowed me to return to face execution;
this is Your Majesty's kindness.
I, your servant, am truly untalented;
whom would I dare to resent?"
The King said:
"In that case, do you feel grateful to me?"
He replied:
"The two states looked after their altars of soil and grain
and sought to relieve their people,
each punishing its own anger
to pardon one another.
Both sides released their bound prisoners
to complete their friendship.
Since the two states have friendship,
I was not personally involved in it;
whom would I dare to feel grateful to?"
The King said:
"When you return,
how will you repay me?"
He replied:
"I, your servant, am not worthy of harboring resentment,
and Your Majesty is not worthy of receiving gratitude.
With neither resentment nor gratitude,
I do not know how I would repay."
The King said:
"Even so,
you must tell me."
He replied:
"By Your Majesty's spiritual power,
I, your bound servant, am able to return my bones to Jìn.
If my ruler sees fit to execute me,
in death I shall not be forgotten.
If he follows Your Majesty's kindness and spares me,
giving me to Your Majesty's external servant, Xún Shǒu,
Shǒu will then request from my ruler
that I be executed at the ancestral temple;
there too, in death, I shall not be forgotten."
If I do not receive your command,
and you allow me to succeed to my ancestral office,
and next attend to the affairs of state,
leading a secondary army
to repair the borders.
Even if I encounter your ministers,
I would not dare to evade them;
I will exhaust my strength to the point of death,
without any double-heartedness,
to fulfill the rituals of a subject—
this is how I shall repay you."
The King said:
"Jìn cannot yet be contended with."
He treated him with great ritual and sent him back.
B8.3.5 In autumn,
Shūsūn Qiáorú besieged Jí
and took the fields of Wènyáng.
Jí did not submit,
therefore he besieged it.
B8.3.6 Xì Kè of Jìn
and Sūn Liángfū of Wèi attacked Qiángjiùrú,
punishing the remnants of the Chì Dí there.
Qiángjiùrú collapsed,
because the ruler had lost the support of the people.
B8.3.7 In winter, the eleventh month,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Xún Gēng to come on a mission of state,
and to seek a renewal of the alliance.
The Marquis of Wèi sent Sūn Liángfū to come on a mission of state,
and to seek a renewal of the alliance.
The Duke asked Zāng Xuānshū, saying:
"As for Zhòngháng Bó in Jìn,
his position is third;
as for Sūn Zǐ in Wèi,
his position is High Minister;
who shall be prioritized?"
He replied:
"The High Minister of a secondary state
corresponds to the Middle Minister of a great state;
the Middle Minister [of a secondary state] corresponds to the Lower Minister [of a great state];
the Lower Minister [of a secondary state] corresponds to a High Grand Master [of a great state].
The High Minister of a small state
corresponds to the Lower Minister of a great state;
the Middle Minister [of a small state] corresponds to a High Grand Master [of a great state];
the Lower Minister [of a small state] corresponds to a Lower Grand Master [of a great state].
High and low being thus
is the regulation of antiquity.
Wèi, in relation to Jìn,
cannot be considered a secondary state.
Jìn is the leader of the alliance;
one should prioritize it."
On the day bǐngwǔ,
they allied with Jìn;
on the day dīngwèi,
they allied with Wèi,
which was in accordance with ritual.
B8.3.8 In the twelfth month, on the day jiǎxū,
Jìn established six armies.
Hán Jué, Zhào Kuò, Gǒng Shuò, Hán Chuān,
Xún Zhuī, and Zhào Zhān all became Ministers,
to reward their merit at Ān.
B8.3.9 The Marquis of Qí held an audience in Jìn
and was about to present the jade ritual object.
Xì Kè hurried forward and said:
"On this expedition,
you, My Lord, were made a laughingstock for women
—it was a disgrace—
my meager lord does not dare to accept this [gesture of submission]."
The Marquis of Jìn held a banquet for the Marquis of Qí.
The Marquis of Qí looked at Hán Jué.
Hán Jué said:
"Does My Lord know Jué?"
The Marquis of Qí said:
"Your clothing has changed."
Hán Jué ascended the hall,
raised his goblet and said:
"That I, your servant, did not dare to cherish my life
was so that both lords could be here in this hall today."
B8.3.10 When Xún Yíng was in Chǔ,
a merchant of Zhèng intended to place him in a storage bag to get him out.
After they had planned it,
but before they set out,
the people of Chǔ returned him.
The merchant went to Jìn,
and Xún Yíng treated him well,
as if he had actually rescued him.
The merchant said:
"I do not have that merit,
how could I dare to have the reward for it?
I am a small man,
and cannot grossly deceive a gentleman."
He then went to Qí.
A8.4 The Annals of Duke Chéng, Fourth Year.
A8.4.1 In the fourth year, in spring,
the Duke of Sòng sent Huà Yuán to come on a mission of state.
A8.4.2 In the third month, on the day rénshēn,
Jiān, Earl of Zhèng, died.
A8.4.3 The Earl of Qǐ came for an audience.
A8.4.4 In summer, the fourth month, on the day jiǎyín,
Zāngsūn Xǔ died.
A8.4.5 The Duke went to Jìn.
A8.4.6 Duke Xiāng of Zhèng was buried.
A8.4.7 In autumn,
the Duke arrived from Jìn.
A8.4.8 In winter,
the walls of Yùn were built.
A8.4.9 The Earl of Zhèng attacked Xǔ.
B8.4 Commentary on Duke Chéng, Fourth Year.
B8.4.1 In the fourth year, in spring,
Huà Yuán of Sòng came on a mission of state
to establish relations for the succeeding ruler.
B8.4.2 The Earl of Qǐ came for an audience
because Shū Jī had returned.
B8.4.3 In summer,
the Duke went to Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn saw the Duke
but was disrespectful.
Jì Wénzǐ said:
"The Marquis of Jìn will certainly not escape calamity.
The Odes say:
'Be reverent, be reverent!
Heaven is clearly manifest,
its mandate is not easily kept!'
Now, the mandate of the Marquis of Jìn depends on the feudal lords;
can he afford not to be reverent?"
B8.4.4 In autumn,
the Duke arrived from Jìn
and wished to seek peace with Chǔ
and rebel against Jìn.
Jì Wénzǐ said:
"This cannot be.
Although Jìn is without the Way,
it cannot yet be rebelled against.
The state is large and its ministers are harmonious;
moreover, it is near to us.
The feudal lords listen to it;
we cannot yet show duplicity toward it.
The records of Scribe Yì contain this:
'If they are not of our kin,
their hearts must be different.'
Although Chǔ is large,
it is not of our kin;
would it be willing to cherish us?"
The Duke then stopped.
B8.4.5 In winter, the eleventh month,
Gōngsūn Shēn of Zhèng led an army
to define the borders of the Xǔ fields.
The people of Xǔ defeated them at Zhǎnbēi.
The Earl of Zhèng attacked Xǔ,
taking the fields of Chù, Rèn, and Língdùn.
Luán Shū of Jìn commanded the Central Army,
with Xún Shǒu assisting him,
and Shì Xiè assisting the Upper Army,
to save Xǔ and attack Zhèng,
taking Fàn and Jì.
Zǐfǎn of Chǔ came to save Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng and the Baron of Xǔ pleaded their cases before him;
Huáng Xù managed the arguments for the Earl of Zhèng.
Zǐfǎn could not decide the matter
and said:
"If you lords would deign to visit my meager ruler,
my meager ruler and his several ministers will together hear what you two lords desire;
then the settlement might be known.
Otherwise,
I, Cè, am not sufficient
to know the settlement of the two states."
B8.4.6 Zhào Yīng of Jìn
had an illicit affair with Zhào Zhuāng Jī.
A8.5 The Annals of Duke Chéng, Fifth Year.
A8.5.1 In the fifth year, in spring,
the royal first month,
Shū Jī of Qǐ came back.
A8.5.2 Zhòngsūn Miè went to Sòng.
A8.5.3 In summer,
Shūsūn Qiáorú met Xún Shǒu of Jìn at Gǔ.
Mount Liáng collapsed.
A8.5.5 In autumn,
there were great floods.
A8.5.6 In winter, the eleventh month, on the day jǐyǒu,
the Heavenly King died.
A8.5.7 In the twelfth month, on the day jǐchǒu,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Zhū,
and the Earl of Qǐ to swear a covenant together at Chóngláo.
B8.5 Commentary on the Fifth Year of Duke Chéng
B8.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
Yuán and Píng were exiled to Qí.
Yīng said:
"As long as I am here,
the Luán clan will not act.
If I am gone,
my two elder brothers will surely have cause for worry.
Moreover, everyone has things they are capable of
and things they are not;
if you let me be,
what harm is there?"
They did not listen.
Yīng dreamed that a messenger of Heaven said to him:
"Sacrifice to me,
and I will bless you."
He sent someone to ask Shì Zhēnbó about it.
Zhēnbó said:
"I do not know."
Shortly after, he told his
people, saying:
"The spirits bless the benevolent and bring calamity to the licentious.
If one is licentious and receives no punishment,
that is already a blessing.
If he sacrifices,
will he avoid death?"
Yīng sacrificed to him,
and on the day after the sacrifice, he died.
B8.5.2 Mèng Xiànzǐ went to Sòng
to reciprocate the visit of Huá Yuán.
B8.5.3 In the summer,
Xún Shǒu of Jìn went to Qí to meet the bride;
therefore Xuānbó provided provisions at Gǔ.
B8.5.4 Liángshān collapsed,
and the Marquis of Jìn sent a messenger to summon Bó Zōng.
Bó Zōng made way for a heavy carriage
and said:
"Clear the way for the messenger's carriage!"
The man with the heavy carriage said:
"Waiting for me
is not as fast as taking a shortcut."
Bó Zōng asked where he was from.
He said:
"I am a man of Jiàng."
Bó Zōng asked him about the affairs of Jiàng.
He said:
"Liángshān collapsed,
and they are about to summon Bó Zōng to deliberate on it."
Bó Zōng asked what should be done.
He said:
"When a mountain has decayed soil, it collapses;
what can be done about it?
The ruler of a state presides over its mountains and rivers;
therefore, when a mountain collapses or a river runs dry,
the ruler for this reason does not have full meals,
wears plain clothes, rides an unadorned carriage,
suspends music, leaves his palace for a temporary residence,
offers sacrifices with prayers,
and the scribes deliver the ritual speeches
according to the rites.
It is simply like this.
Even if it is Bó Zōng,
what can he do about it?"
Bó Zōng requested to see him.
He would not agree.
Thereupon Bó Zōng reported this
and followed the advice.
B8.5.5 Duke Líng of Xǔ complained about the Earl of Zhèng to Chǔ.
In the sixth month,
Duke Dào of Zhèng went to Chǔ to litigate;
he did not win,
and the people of Chǔ seized Huáng Xù and Zǐ Guó.
Therefore, when the Earl of Zhèng returned,
he sent Gōngzǐ Yǎn to request peace with Jìn.
In the autumn, the eighth month,
the Earl of Zhèng and Zhào Tóng of Jìn swore a covenant at Chuíjí.
B8.5.6 Gōngzǐ Wéiguī of Sòng
had been a hostage in Chǔ and returned;
Huá Yuán held a feast for him.
Wéiguī requested to shout and beat drums while going out,
and to shout and beat drums while returning,
saying:
"We are practicing an attack on the Huá clan."
The Duke of Sòng killed him.
B8.5.7 In the winter,
they swore a covenant at Chóngláo,
because Zhèng had submitted.
The feudal lords planned to meet again,
but the Duke of Sòng sent Xiàng Wèirén to decline
on account of the troubles involving Zǐ Líng.
B8.5.8 In the eleventh month, on the day jǐyǒu,
King Dìng passed away.
A8.6 Annals of the Sixth Year of Duke Chéng
A8.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
in the royal first month,
the Duke arrived from the meeting.
A8.6.2 In the second month, on the day xīnsì,
the Wǔ Temple was established.
A8.6.3 We took Zhuān.
A8.6.4 Sūn Liángfū of Wèi led an army to invade Sòng.
A8.6.5 In the summer, the sixth month,
the Viscount of Zhū came for an audience.
A8.6.6 Gōngsūn Yīngqí went to Jìn.
A8.6.7 On the day rénshēn,
the Earl of Zhèng, Fèi, died.
A8.6.8 In the autumn,
Zhòngsūn Miè
and Shúsūn Qiáorú led armies to invade Sòng.
A8.6.9 Gōngzǐ Yīngqí of Chǔ led an army to attack Zhèng.
A8.6.10 In the winter,
Jìsūn Xíngfù went to Jìn.
A8.6.11 Luán Shū of Jìn led an army to rescue Zhèng.
B8.6 Commentary on the Sixth Year of Duke Chéng
B8.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
the Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn
to offer thanks for the peace;
Zǐ Yóu assisted him.
He presented the jade at the east of the eastern pillar.
Shì Zhēnbó said:
"The Earl of Zhèng will surely die!
He has abandoned himself.
His gaze flows and his pace is fast;
he is not at ease in his position;
he will likely not last long."
B8.6.2 In the second month,
Jì Wénzǐ established the Wǔ Temple on account of the achievement at Ān,
which was not in accordance with the rites.
Relying on others to rescue one from difficulty
cannot be a reason to establish a 'Martial' temple.
Establishing 'Martial' merit should come from oneself,
not from others.
B8.6.3 As for 'Taking Zhuān,'
this describes how easy it was.
B8.6.4 In the third month,
Bó Zōng and Xiàyáng Yuè of Jìn, Sūn Liángfū,
Nìng Xiāng of Wèi, the people of Zhèng,
the Róng of the Yī and Luò rivers,
the Lùhún,
and the Mán clan invaded Sòng
because Sòng had declined to attend the meeting.
They stationed their army at Zhēn.
The people of Wèi did not maintain their defenses.
Yuè wanted to launch a surprise attack on Wèi,
saying:
"Even if we cannot enter the city,
if we return with many captives,
any offense will not be punished by death."
Bó Zōng said:
"You must not.
Wèi only trusts Jìn,
which is why their army is in its outskirts
and they have made no preparations.
If we launch a surprise attack on them, this is abandoning trust.
Even if there are many captives from Wèi,
if Jìn has no trust,
how can we seek the leadership of the feudal lords?"
Thereupon they stopped.
When the army returned, the people of Wèi mounted their parapets.
B8.6.5 The people of Jìn planned to leave Old Jiàng.
The various grandees all said:
"We must reside in the lands of the Xún and Xiá clans;
it is fertile and rich, and near the salt marshes;
it is profitable for the state and pleasant for the ruler;
it must not be lost."
Hán Xiànzǐ was in command of the New Central Army
and also served as the Grandee of the Charioteers.
The Duke bowed and entered.
Xiànzǐ followed.
The Duke stood in the court of the sleeping chambers
and said to Xiànzǐ:
"What do you think?"
"It is not possible.
In the lands of the Xún and Xiá clans, the soil is thin and the water is shallow;
impurities easily come to the surface.
When impurities easily surface, the people are distressed.
When the people are distressed, they live in damp and cramped conditions,
and thus they suffer from diseases like edema and swollen legs.
It is not as good as Xīntián.
There the soil is thick and the water is deep.
Living there, one does not fall ill.
There are the Fén and Kuài rivers to flush away its impurities.
Moreover, the people follow instruction;
it is a benefit for ten generations.
Now, mountains, marshes, forests, and salt-flats
are the treasures of a state.
When a state is rich,
then the people become proud and idle.
By being close to such treasures,
the ducal house then becomes poor.
It cannot be called a place of joy."
The Duke was pleased
and followed his advice.
In the summer, in the fourth month, on the day Dīngchǒu,
Jìn moved its capital to Xīntián.
B8.6.6 In the sixth month,
Zhèng Dào Gōng died.
B8.6.7 Zǐshū Shēngbó went to Jìn,
to receive the command to attack Sòng.
B8.6.8 In the autumn,
Mèng Xiànzǐ and Shúsūn Xuānbó invaded Sòng;
this was by the command of Jìn.
B8.6.9 Zǐzhòng of Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
because Zhèng followed Jìn.
B8.6.10 In the winter,
Jì Wénzǐ went to Jìn,
to offer congratulations on the moving of the capital.
B8.6.11 Luán Shū of Jìn went to the rescue of Zhèng,
and encountered the Chǔ army at Ràojiǎo.
The Chǔ army withdrew.
The Jìn army then invaded Cài.
The Chǔ princes Gōngzǐ Shēn and Gōngzǐ Chéng used the troops of Shēn and Xī to rescue Cài,
resisting them at Sāngsuì.
Zhào Tóng and Zhào Kuò wanted to fight
and requested permission from Wǔzǐ.
Wǔzǐ was about to grant it.
Zhì Zhuāngzǐ, Fàn Wénzǐ, and
Hán Xiànzǐ remonstrated, saying:
"It is not possible.
We came to rescue Zhèng.
The Chǔ army has left us,
and for us to have come as far as here
is merely a shifting of the slaughter.
To kill without end
and further anger the Chǔ army,
we will surely not win the battle.
Even if we do win,
it would not be good.
To lead out a full army
and merely defeat two counties of Chǔ,
what glory is there in that?
If we cannot defeat them,
the disgrace would be extreme.
It is better to return."
Thereupon they returned.
At that time, many of the army commanders wanted to fight.
Someone said to Luán Wǔzǐ:
"A sage shares the same desires as the masses,
and thus he accomplishes things.
Why do you not follow the majority?
You are in charge of the great administration,
and should consider the people.
Of your eleven assistants,
those who do not wish to fight
are only three.
Those who wish to fight can be called a majority.
The *Shāngshū* says:
'When three people perform divination,
follow the two.'
This is because they are the majority."
Wǔzǐ said:
"When excellence is equal, one follows the majority.
Now, excellence
is the master of the masses.
These three ministers are masters [of excellence];
they can be considered a majority.
To follow them,
is that not also acceptable?"
A8.7 The Annals of the Seventh Year of Chéng Gōng
A8.7.1 In the spring of the seventh year,
in the royal first month,
mice gnawed the horns of the bull for the suburban sacrifice;
another bull was selected by divination.
Mice again gnawed its horns,
so the bull was released.
A8.7.2 Wú attacked Tán.
A8.7.3 In the summer, in the fifth month,
the Earl of Cáo came for an audience.
A8.7.4 The suburban sacrifice was not performed,
but the Three Gazes sacrifice was still held.
A8.7.5 In the autumn,
Gōngzǐ Yīngqí of Chǔ led an army to attack Zhèng.
The Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
and the Earl of Qǐ to rescue Zhèng.
In the eighth month, on the day Wùchén,
they formed a covenant at Mǎlíng.
A8.7.7 The Duke arrived from the meeting.
A8.7.8 Wú entered Zhōulái.
A8.7.9 In the winter,
the Great Rain Sacrifice was performed.
A8.7.10 Sūn Línfù of Wèi fled to Jìn.
B8.7 The Commentary for the Seventh Year of Chéng Gōng
B8.7.1 In the spring of the seventh year,
Wú attacked Tán,
and Tán came to terms.
Jì Wénzǐ said:
"The Central States do not organize their armies,
so the barbarians come to attack,
and yet no one cares.
Truly there is no one who is compassionate!
The *Shī* says:
'Unpitying is Great Heaven;
disorder knows no end.'
Is this not what it means?
If those above are not compassionate,
who will not suffer disorder?
Our downfall will come any day."
The superior man says:
"Knowing fear such as this,
one will not perish."
B8.7.2 Zǐliáng of Zhèng assisted Chéng Gōng in going to Jìn,
to have an audience
and to express gratitude for the dispatch of the army.
B8.7.3 In the summer,
Cáo Xuān Gōng came for an audience.
B8.7.4 In the autumn,
Zǐzhòng of Chǔ attacked Zhèng
and stationed his army at Fàn.
The regional lords rescued Zhèng.
Gòngzhòng and Hóuyǔ of Zhèng confronted the Chǔ army,
captured Zhōng Yí, the Duke of Yún,
and presented him to Jìn.
In the eighth month,
they formed a covenant at Mǎlíng,
renewing the covenant of Chóngláo,
and because Jǔ had submitted.
The men of Jìn returned with Zhōng Yí
and imprisoned him in the military storehouse.
B8.7.5 In the campaign where Chǔ besieged Sòng,
when the army returned,
Zǐzhòng requested to take land from Shēn
and Lǚ for his reward lands.
The King granted it.
Wūchén, the Duke of Shēn, said:
"It is not possible.
This is why Shēn and Lǚ were established as districts;
they are used for levies
to defend against the north.
If you take them,
it is as though Shēn
and Lǚ no longer exist,
and Jìn and Zhèng will surely reach as far as the Hàn River."
The King then stopped.
Because of this, Zǐzhòng harbored a grudge against Wūchén.
Zǐfǎn wanted to take Xià Jī,
but Wūchén stopped him,
then eventually took her himself
and fled;
Zǐfǎn also harbored a grudge against him.
When Gòng Wáng ascended the throne,
Zǐzhòng and Zǐfǎn killed the members of Wūchén’s clan—Zǐyán and Zǐdàng—as well as the Qīngyǐn Fújì and Hēiyào, the son of Xiānglǎo,
and divided their households.
Zǐzhòng took Zǐyán's household;
he had the Shěnyǐn and Wángzǐ Bà divide Zǐdàng's household;
and Zǐfǎn took the households of Hēiyào and the Qīngyǐn.
Wūchén sent a letter from Jìn to the two men,
saying:
"Because you served your lord with slander, evil, and greed,
and killed many innocent people,
I will certainly make you exhausted from rushing about on missions
until you die."
Wūchén requested to be sent as an envoy to Wú,
and the Marquis of Jìn granted it.
Shòumèng, the Viscount of Wú, was pleased with him.
He then established communications between Wú and Jìn,
going to Wú with a single squad of soldiers.
He left behind half of his chariots there.
Along with his archers and charioteers,
