he taught the people of Wú how to ride in chariots,
taught them battle formations,
and taught them to rebel against Chǔ.
He placed his son Húyōng there,
making him an envoy in Wú.
Wú then began to attack Chǔ, Cháo, and Xú,
and Zǐzhòng rushed about on missions.
During the meeting at Mǎlíng,
Wú entered Zhōulái,
and Zǐzhòng rushed from Zhèng on a mission.
Thus, within a single year, Zǐzhòng and Zǐfǎn rushed about on missions seven times.
Those among the Mányí barbarians who belonged to Chǔ,
Wú took them all.
Because of this, Wú began to grow great
and opened communications with the upper states.
B8.7.6 Duke Dìng of Wèi detested Sūn Línfù.
In winter,
Sūn Línfù fled to Jìn.
The Marquis of Wèi went to Jìn,
and Jìn supported Sūn Línfù in Qī.
A8.8 The Annals of the Eighth Year of Duke Chéng
A8.8.1 In the spring of the eighth year,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Hán Chuān to come and speak about the fields of Wènyáng,
returning them to Qí.
A8.8.2 Luán Shū of Jìn led an army to invade Cài.
A8.8.3 Gōngsūn Yīngqí went to Jǔ.
A8.8.4 The Duke of Sòng sent Huá Yuán to come on a mission of state.
A8.8.5 In summer,
the Duke of Sòng sent Gōngsūn Shòu to come and present the betrothal gifts.
A8.8.6 Jìn executed its grand masters Zhào Tóng and
Zhào Guò.
A8.8.7 In the seventh month of autumn,
the Son of Heaven sent the Earl of Shào to come and confer a command upon the Duke.
A8.8.8 In the tenth month of winter, on the day guǐmǎo,
Shū Jī of Qǐ died.
A8.8.9 The Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Xiè to come on a mission of state.
A8.8.10 Shūsūn Qiáorú met Shì Xiè of Jìn,
the people of Qí,
and the people of Zhū to attack Tán.
A8.8.11 The people of Wèi came to escort a bride.
B8.8 The Commentary of the Eighth Year of Duke Chéng
B8.8.1 In the spring of the eighth year,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Hán Chuān to come and speak about the fields of Wènyáng,
returning them to Qí.
Jì Wénzǐ gave him a farewell banquet
and spoke privately to him,
saying:
"A great state establishes righteousness
to act as the leader of the covenant;
for this reason, the feudal lords
cherish its virtue and fear its punishment,
and thus have no divided heart.
Regarding the fields of Wènyáng,
they were the former possessions of our humble state,
but you used your army against Qí
and caused them to be returned to our humble state.
Now there is a second command,
saying
'Return them to Qí.'
When trustworthiness is used to practice righteousness,
and righteousness is used to fulfill commands,
that is what a small state looks for and cherishes.
If trustworthiness cannot be known
and righteousness has nowhere to stand,
then among the feudal lords of the four quarters,
who will not become detached?
The Book of Odes says:
'The woman has done nothing wrong,
but the man has doubled his conduct.
The man's behavior has no limit;
he is inconsistent in his virtue.'
Within seven years,
giving once and taking back once—
what could be more inconsistent than this?
If a man is inconsistent,
he even loses his mate;
how much more so for a leader of the covenant?
A leader of the covenant should use virtue as his basis,
but if he is inconsistent,
how can he long hold the feudal lords?
The Book of Odes says:
'His plans were not far-reaching,
and for this he is greatly censured.'
I, Hángfù, fear that Jìn's plans are not far-reaching
and will lose the feudal lords,
therefore I dare to speak privately of this."
B8.8.2 Luán Shū of Jìn invaded Cài,
and subsequently invaded Chǔ,
capturing Shēn Lí.
When the Chǔ army was returning,
Jìn invaded Shěn
and captured Yī, the son of the ruler of Shěn. Previously,
he had followed Zhī, Fàn, and Hán.
The superior man says:
"To follow what is good like a flowing stream—
how appropriate!
The Book of Odes says:
'The joyful and easy-going gentleman,
does he not cultivate men?'
This is seeking goodness!
If one cultivates men,
then there will be achievements."
During this expedition,
the Earl of Zhèng was about to meet the Jìn army
and attacked the eastern gate of Xǔ,
achieving a great victory.
B8.8.3 Shēngbó went to Jǔ
to meet a bride.
B8.8.4 Huá Yuán of Sòng came on a mission of state
to present gifts for Gòng Jī.
B8.8.5 In summer,
the Duke of Sòng sent Gōngsūn Shòu to come and present the betrothal gifts,
which was in accordance with ritual.
B8.8.6 Zhào Zhuāng Jī of Jìn,
because of the exile of Zhào Yīng,
slandered them to the Marquis of Jìn,
saying:
"Yuán and Píng are about to start a rebellion."
Luán and Xì acted as witnesses.
In the sixth month,
Jìn executed Zhào Tóng and Zhào Guò.
Wǔ followed the Jī lady and was raised
in the Duke's palace.
Their fields were given to Qí Xī.
Hán Jué said to the Marquis of Jìn:
"The merit of Chéng Jì
and the loyalty of Xuān Mèng
are now without an heir.
Those who do good will be afraid.
The virtuous kings of the three dynasties
all preserved the favor of Heaven for several hundred years.
Could it be that there were no wicked kings among them?
They relied on their wise predecessors
to avoid disaster.
The Book of Zhōu says:
'One does not dare to insult the widower or the widow.'
This is to illustrate virtue."
Thereupon, he established Wǔ
and returned the fields to him.
B8.8.7 In autumn,
Duke Huán of Shào came to confer a command upon the Duke.
B8.8.8 The Marquis of Jìn sent Shēn Gōng Wūchén to Wú,
and he requested passage through Jǔ.
He stood with the Lord of Qúqiū by a pond,
and said:
"The city walls are already in poor condition."
The Viscount of Jǔ said:
"In this remote and crude place among the barbarians,
who would consider me a threat?"
He replied:
"As for those who craftily desire to expand their borders
to benefit their altars of soil and grain,
what state lacks them?
It is only so,
and for this reason, there are many great states.
It is just that some are thinking of it and some are given rein to do so.
Even a brave man double-bolts his door;
how much more so for a state?"
B8.8.9 In winter,
Shū Jī of Qǐ died.
She had returned from Qǐ,
and therefore it was recorded.
B8.8.10 Shì Xiè of Jìn came on a mission of state
to speak about attacking Tán,
because it was serving Wú.
The Duke bribed him
to request a delay of the military campaign.
Wénzǐ would not agree,
saying:
"A ruler’s command should not be inconsistent;
without trust, one cannot stand.
In ritual, there are no additional gifts;
in affairs, there are no double successes.
If your lord comes after the other feudal lords,
then my unworthy lord will not be able to serve your lord.
I, Xiè, shall report this back."
Jì Sūn was afraid
and sent Xuān Bó to lead the army to join in the attack on Tán.
B8.8.11 The people of Wèi came to provide bridesmaid-consorts for Gòng Jī;
this was in accordance with ritual.
Whenever a feudal lord marries off a daughter,
those of the same surname provide bridesmaid-consorts,
while those of different surnames do not.
A8.9 The Classic of the Ninth Year of Duke Chéng
A8.9.1 In the spring of the ninth year,
in the royal first month,
the Earl of Qǐ came to meet the remains of Shū Jī to take them back.
A8.9.2 The Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
and the Earl of Qǐ,
and they made a covenant together at Pú.
A8.9.3 The Duke arrived from the meeting.
A8.9.4 In the second month,
Bó Jī went to Sòng to be married.
A8.9.5 In the summer,
Jì Sūn Háng fù went to Sòng to deliver the bride.
A8.9.6 The people of Jìn came to provide bridesmaid-consorts.
A8.9.7 In the autumn, in the seventh month, on the day bǐngzǐ,
the Marquis of Qí, Wú yě, died.
A8.9.8 The people of Jìn seized the Earl of Zhèng.
A8.9.9 Luán Shū of Jìn led an army to attack Zhèng.
A8.9.10 In the winter, in the eleventh month,
Duke Qǐng of Qí was buried.
A8.9.11 Prince Yīng qí of Chǔ led an army to attack Jǔ.
On the day gēngshēn,
Jǔ collapsed.
The people of Chǔ entered Yùn.
A8.9.12 The people of Qín and
the Bái Dí attacked Jìn.
A8.9.13 The people of Zhèng besieged Xǔ.
A8.9.14 They fortified the inner wall.
B8.9 The Commentary of the Ninth Year of Duke Chéng
B8.9.1 In the spring of the ninth year,
Duke Huán of Qǐ came to meet the remains of Shū Jī,
because he had requested it.
When Shū Jī of Qǐ died,
it was recorded for the sake of Qǐ.
The meeting of Shū Jī
was recorded for the sake of our state.
B8.9.2 Because the lands of Wènyáng had been returned,
the feudal lords were disloyal to Jìn.
The people of Jìn were afraid,
and they met at Pú
to renew the covenant of Mǎlíng.
Jì Wén zǐ said to Fàn Wén zǐ:
"If virtue is not strong,
what is the point of renewing the covenant?"
Fàn Wén zǐ said:
"To soothe them with diligence,
to treat them with leniency,
to control them with strength,
and to bind them with the bright spirits—
winning over the submissive and attacking the disloyal,
this is the next best thing to virtue."
On this journey,
they intended to meet Wú for the first time,
but the people of Wú did not arrive.
B8.9.3 In the second month,
Bó Jī went to Sòng to be married.
B8.9.4 The people of Chǔ sought Zhèng with heavy bribes,
and the Earl of Zhèng met with the Prince of Chǔ,
Chéng, at Dèng.
B8.9.5 In the summer,
Jì Wén zǐ went to Sòng to deliver the bride.
When he returned to report his mission,
the Duke gave a banquet for him.
He recited the fifth stanza of the "Hán yì."
Mù Jiāng came out from her room,
bowed twice,
and said:
"The Grand Master has undergone diligent toil,
not forgetting the late ruler,
extending it to the succeeding ruler,
and bestowing it upon this widow;
the late ruler still has hope.
I venture to bow in thanks for the Grand Master's great diligence."
She then recited the final stanza of the "Lǜ yī" and went back inside.
B8.9.6 The people of Jìn came to provide bridesmaid-consorts;
this was in accordance with ritual.
B8.9.7 In the autumn,
the Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn.
The people of Jìn punished him for his disloyalty
to them by siding with Chǔ,
and they seized him at Tóng dī.
B8.9.8 Luán Shū attacked Zhèng.
The people of Zhèng sent Bó Juān to negotiate peace,
but the people of Jìn killed him.
This was not in accordance with ritual.
When armies are engaged,
it is permissible for envoys to be among them.
Zǐ Zhòng of Chǔ invaded Chén to rescue Zhèng.
B8.9.9 The Marquis of Jìn was inspecting the military storehouse
when he saw Zhōng Yí.
He asked about him, saying:
"The one wearing a southern cap and bound,
who is he?"
The official replied:
"He is a prisoner from Chǔ presented by the people of Zhèng."
The Duke ordered him to be released.
He summoned him and consoled him.
Zhōng Yí bowed twice with his head to the ground.
The Duke asked about his family's lineage.
He replied: "I am a musician."
The Duke said:
"Can you play music?" He replied:
"It was my late father's official duty;
how could I dare have any other concern?"
The Duke had a zither given to him, and he played a southern air.
The Duke said:
"What is your King like?"
He replied:
"It is not something a lowly person such as I can know."
The Duke insisted on asking.
He replied:
"When he was the Crown Prince,
the Grand Tutor and Junior Tutor supported him;
he would attend on Yīng qí in the morning
and on Cè in the evening.
I know nothing else."
The Duke told Fàn Wén zǐ about this.
Wén zǐ said:
"The prisoner from Chǔ
is a gentleman.
In his speech, he cites his ancestors' profession,
showing he does not turn his back on his roots.
In music, he plays the tunes of his native land,
showing he does not forget the old.
In mentioning the Crown Prince,
he is restrained and without personal bias.
In naming the two ministers,
he shows respect for his ruler.
Not turning back on roots
is benevolence.
Not forgetting the old
is trustworthiness.
Being without personal bias
is loyalty.
Respecting the ruler
is intelligence.
Benevolence is used to approach affairs,
trustworthiness to maintain them,
loyalty to complete them,
and intelligence to carry them out.
Even if an affair is great,
it will surely succeed.
Why not return him
and have him bring about peace
between Jìn and Chǔ?"
The Duke followed this advice,
treated him with great ritual courtesy,
and sent him back to seek peace.
B8.9.10 In the winter, in the eleventh month,
Zǐ Zhòng of Chǔ came from Chén to attack Jǔ
and besieged Qú qiū.
The walls of Qú qiū were in poor condition;
the masses collapsed
and fled to Jǔ.
On the day wùshēn,
Chǔ entered Qú qiū.
The people of Jǔ imprisoned Prince Píng of Chǔ.
The people of Chǔ said:
"Do not kill him;
I will take him as a captive upon my return."
The people of Jǔ killed him, and the Chǔ army besieged Jǔ.
The walls of the city of Jǔ were also in poor condition.
On the day Gēngshēn,
Jǔ collapsed.
Chǔ then entered Yùn;
this was because Jǔ had no preparations.
The noble man said:
"To rely on being remote and not make preparations
is the greatest of crimes;
to prepare in advance for the unexpected
is the greatest of virtues.
Jǔ relied on its remoteness
and did not repair its inner and outer walls;
within the space of twelve days,
Chǔ conquered its three capitals.
Was it not due to a lack of preparation!
The *Shī* says:
'Though you have silk and hemp,
do not discard the broom-sedge and rush-grass;
though you have ladies from the Jī and Jiāng clans,
do not discard those who are worn and haggard;
among all the noble men,
none should fail to provide for when things are lacking.'
This means that preparation must never cease."
B8.9.11 The people of Qín and
the Bái Dí attacked Jìn,
because the feudal lords were of divided mind.
B8.9.12 The people of Zhèng besieged Xǔ
to show Jìn that they were not anxious about their ruler.
This was a plan by Gōngsūn Shēn,
who said:
"If we send out our army to besiege Xǔ
as if we are about to establish another ruler,
and thereby delay the envoys from Jìn,
Jìn will surely return our ruler."
B8.9.13 Wall-building was done in Zhōngchéng;
this was recorded
because it was done at the proper time.
B8.9.14 In the twelfth month,
the Viscount of Chǔ sent Gōngzǐ Chén to Jìn
to reciprocate the mission of Zhōng Yí
and to request the cultivation of good relations and the formation of a treaty.
A8.10 *The Classic of Duke Chéng, Tenth Year*
A8.10.1 In the spring of the tenth year,
Hēibèi, the younger brother of the Marquis of Wèi, led an army to invade Zhèng.
A8.10.2 In the summer, the fourth month,
five divinations were made for the border sacrifice;
they were not favorable,
so the border sacrifice was not performed.
A8.10.3 In the fifth month,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
and the Earl of Cáo to attack Zhèng.
A8.10.4 The people of Qí came to provide bridesmaid-concubines.
A8.10.5 On the day Bǐngwǔ,
Nuò, the Marquis of Jìn, died.
A8.10.6 In the autumn, the seventh month,
the Duke went to Jìn.
A8.10.7 In the winter, the tenth month.
B8.10 *The Commentary of Duke Chéng, Tenth Year*
B8.10.1 In the spring of the tenth year,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Dí Fá to Chǔ
to reciprocate the mission of the Grand Steward Zǐshāng.
B8.10.2 Zǐshū Hēibèi of Wèi invaded Zhèng;
this was by the command of Jìn.
B8.10.3 Gōngzǐ Bān of Zhèng heard of the plot of Shūshēn.
In the third month,
Zǐrú established Gōngzǐ Xū.
In the summer, the fourth month,
the people of Zhèng killed Xū
and established Kūnwán;
Zǐrú fled to Xǔ.
Luán Wǔzǐ said:
"The people of Zhèng are establishing a ruler.
If we hold one of them prisoner,
what benefit is there?
It is better to attack Zhèng and return their ruler to them,
so as to seek a settlement."
The Marquis of Jìn was ill.
In the fifth month,
Jìn established the Crown Prince Zhōupú as the ruler
and met the feudal lords to attack Zhèng.
Zǐhǎn of Zhèng offered the bells of Duke Xiāng as a bribe;
Zǐrán swore a covenant at Xiūzé,
and Zǐsì became a hostage.
On the day Xīnsì,
the Earl of Zhèng returned.
B8.10.4 The Marquis of Jìn dreamed of a great demon
with hair reaching the ground,
beating its chest and leaping,
saying:
"You killed my grandsons;
that was unrighteous.
I have received permission from the Supreme Deity!"
It smashed the main gate and the chamber gate and entered.
The Duke was afraid
and entered his private room.
It smashed that door as well.
The Duke awoke
and summoned the shaman of Sāngtián.
The shaman's words matched the dream.
The Duke said:
"What will happen?"
He said:
"You will not eat of the new harvest."
The Duke became critically ill
and sought a physician from Qín.
The Earl of Qín sent Physician Huǎn to treat him.
Before he arrived,
the Duke dreamed that his illness turned into two young boys
who said:
"That man
is a fine physician;
we fear he will harm us.
Where can we flee from him?"
One of them said:
"If we stay above the diaphragm
and below the heart,
what can he do to us?"
The physician arrived
and said:
"The illness cannot be treated.
It is above the diaphragm
and below the heart.
It cannot be attacked with moxibustion,
it cannot be reached with acupuncture,
and medicines will not reach there.
It cannot be treated."
The Duke said:
"He is a fine physician indeed."
He presented him with generous gifts and sent him back.
On the day Bǐngwǔ in the sixth month,
the Marquis of Jìn wanted to eat wheat;
he ordered the official in charge of the fields to present the wheat,
and the official in charge of food prepared it.
He summoned the shaman of Sāngtián,
showed him the food, and then had him killed.
As he was about to eat,
his stomach became bloated;
he went to the toilet,
fell in, and died.
A minor official had dreamed that morning of carrying the Duke
on his back to ascend to heaven;
when mid-day came,
he carried the Marquis of Jìn out of the toilet,
and subsequently he was buried with him as a human sacrifice.
B8.10.5 The Earl of Zhèng punished those who had established the ruler;
on the day Wùshēn,
he killed Shūshēn and Shūqín.
The noble man said:
"Loyalty is an excellent virtue,
yet even if the person is not the right sort, it is still not acceptable;
how much more so if the deed is not excellent?"
B8.10.6 In the autumn,
the Duke went to Jìn.
The people of Jìn detained the Duke
and made him wait for the funeral.
At this time, Dí Fá had not yet returned.
B8.10.7 In the winter,
Duke Jǐng of Jìn was buried.
The Duke attended the funeral procession,
but none of the other feudal lords were present.
The people of Lǔ felt this was a humiliation,
so it was not recorded,
to conceal the matter.
A8.11 *The Classic of Duke Chéng, Eleventh Year*
A8.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
in the royal third month,
the Duke arrived from Jìn.
A8.11.2 The Marquis of Jìn sent Xì Chōu on a mission of friendly inquiry;
on the day Jǐchǒu,
he swore a covenant with Xì Chōu.
A8.11.3 In the summer,
Jìsūn Xíngfù went to Jìn.
A8.11.4 In the autumn,
Shúsūn Qiáorú went to Qí.
A8.11.5 In the winter, the tenth month.
B8.11 *The Commentary of Duke Chéng, Eleventh Year*
B8.11.1 In the eleventh year, in spring,
in the royal third month,
the Duke arrived from Jìn.
The people of Jìn
believed that the Duke was double-minded toward Chǔ,
and therefore they detained the Duke.
The Duke requested to accept a covenant,
and only after that was he sent back.
B8.11.2 Xì Chōu came on a mission of state,
and to oversee a covenant.
B8.11.3 Shēng Bó's mother
was not formally betrothed.
Mù Jiāng said:
“I do not treat a concubine as a sister-in-law.”
She gave birth to Shēng Bó and then was sent away;
she married Guǎn Yúxī in Qí,
bore two sons, became a widow,
and returned to Shēng Bó.
Shēng Bó made his maternal younger brothers Great Officers
and married his maternal younger sister to Shī Xiàoshū.
Xì Chōu came on a mission of state
and sought a wife from Shēng Bó.
Shēng Bó took the wife of the Shī clan to give to him.
The woman said:
“Even birds and beasts do not lose their mates;
what will you do?”
He said:
“I cannot face death and ruin.”
The woman then departed.
She bore two sons for the Xì clan.
When the Xì clan fell,
the people of Jìn returned her to the Shī clan.
The Shī clan met her at the Hé River
and drowned her two sons.
The woman said angrily:
“If one cannot protect his own spouse
and loses her,
and then cannot nurture another's orphans
but kills them,
how will he reach his end?”
She then swore an oath against the Shī clan.
B8.11.4 In summer,
Jì Wénzǐ went to Jìn
to return the mission
and to oversee the covenant.
B8.11.5 Zhōu Gōng Chǔ disliked
the pressure from Huì
and Xiāng;
moreover, he contended for the administration with Bó Yǔ.
Not being successful,
he left in anger.
When he reached Yángfán,
the King sent Liú Zǐ to bring him back.
They made a covenant at Juàn and he entered.
Three days later he left again
and fled to Jìn.
B8.11.6 In autumn,
Xuān Bó went on a mission to Qí
to renew former good relations.
B8.11.7 Xì Zhì of Jìn
disputed with Zhōu over the fields of Hòu.
The King ordered Liú Kāng Gōng
and Shàn Xiāng Gōng to litigate the matter in Jìn.
Xì Zhì said:
“Wēn
is my former fief,
therefore I do not dare to lose it.”
Liú Zǐ
and Shàn Zǐ said:
“Formerly, when Zhōu conquered Shāng,
it had the feudal lords settle their boundaries.
Sū Fènshēng held Wēn as the Minister of Justice,
and along with Tán Bó Dá, was enfeoffed at the Hé River.
The Sū clan went to the Dí;
moreover, they could not get along with the Dí and fled to Wèi.
King Xiāng rewarded the service of Wén Gōng
and bestowed Wēn upon him.
The Hú clan
and the Yáng clan occupied it first,
and only later did it come to you.
If we investigate its history,
it is a city of the King’s officials;
how could you obtain it?”
The Marquis of Jìn ordered Xì Zhì
not to dare to dispute it.
B8.11.8 Huá Yuán of Sòng was on good terms with the Lìngyǐn Zǐzhòng,
and also on good terms with Luán Wǔzǐ.
Hearing that the people of Chǔ had already permitted Jìn's Dí Fá to conclude peace
and had sent him back to report his mission,
in winter,
Huá Yuán went to Chǔ
and then went to Jìn
to consolidate the peace between Jìn
and Chǔ.
B8.11.9 Qín
and Jìn made peace,
and were to meet at Lìnghú.
The Marquis of Jìn arrived there first.
The Earl of Qín was unwilling to cross the Hé River
and halted at Wángchéng.
He sent Shǐ Kē to covenant with the Marquis of Jìn
on the east side of the Hé.
Xì Chōu of Jìn covenanted with the Earl of Qín
on the west side of the Hé.
Fàn Wénzǐ said:
“What benefit is there in this covenant?
Covenants
are used to guarantee trust.
The meeting place
is the beginning of trust.
If one does not follow through at the start,
what guarantee can there be?”
The Earl of Qín returned and turned his back on the peace with Jìn.
A8.12 The Classic of the Twelfth Year of Duke Chéng
A8.12.1 In the twelfth year, in spring,
the Duke of Zhōu fled to Jìn.
A8.12.2 In summer,
the Duke met the Marquis of Jìn
and the Marquis of Wèi at Suǒzé.
A8.12.3 In autumn,
the people of Jìn defeated the Dí at Jiāogāng.
A8.12.4 In winter, the tenth month.
B8.12 The Commentary for the Twelfth Year of Duke Chéng
B8.12.1 In the twelfth year, in spring,
the King sent an envoy to announce the trouble involving the Duke of Zhōu.
The text says:
“The Duke of Zhōu fled to Jìn.”
Generally, for those from Zhōu, the term “fled out” is not used;
it is used here because the Duke of Zhōu left of his own accord.
B8.12.2 Huá Yuán of Sòng succeeded in consolidating the peace between Jìn
and Chǔ.
In the fifth month, in summer,
Shì Xiè of Jìn met the Prince of Chǔ, Bā,
and Xǔ Yǎn.
On the day guǐhài,
they covenanted outside the west gate of Sòng,
saying:
“Between Jìn and Chǔ, let there be no mutual resort to arms.
Let our likes and dislikes be the same.
Let us share concern for disasters and dangers
and provide relief for calamities and distress.
If anyone harms Chǔ,
then Jìn shall strike them;
if it is to Jìn,
Chǔ shall do likewise.
Gifts of state shall be exchanged
and the roads shall not be obstructed.
We will counsel those who are not in harmony
and punish those who do not attend the court.
If anyone violates this covenant,
may the bright spirits strike them down,
causing their armies to be defeated,
and preventing them from enjoying the blessings of their state.”
The Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn to accept the peace
and met at Suǒzé,
because the peace was concluded.
B8.12.3 The Dí took advantage of the Sòng covenant
to invade Jìn,
believing it was unprepared.
In autumn,
the people of Jìn defeated the Dí at Jiāogāng.
B8.12.4 Xì Zhì of Jìn went to Chǔ on a mission of state
and to oversee the covenant.
The Viscount of Chǔ held a feast for him.
Zǐfǎn acted as the assistant
and had an underground chamber made
where bells were suspended.
As Xì Zhì was about to ascend,
the metal music struck up from below.
Startled, he hurried out.
Zǐfǎn said:
“The sun is setting.
Our humble ruler is waiting.
Sir, please enter!”
The guest said:
“The ruler has not forgotten the friendship with former rulers,
extending it even to me, a lowly servant;
he bestows great ritual upon me
and doubles it with complete music.
If heaven grants its blessing
and the two rulers meet,
what could replace this?
Your servant does not dare to enter.”
Zǐfǎn said:
“If heaven grants its blessing
and the two rulers meet,
will they not simply present each other with a single arrow?
What use would music be?
Our humble ruler is waiting.
Sir, please enter!”
Bīn said:
“If I yield to him with a single arrow,
among the greatest of calamities,
what blessing would that bring?
In an age of order,
when the feudal lords have leisure from the Son of Heaven’s affairs,
they pay visits to each other’s courts,
and thus there are the rituals of offerings and banquets.
Offerings serve to teach reverence and frugality,
while banquets serve to show kindness and benevolence.
Through reverence and frugality, ritual is practiced,
and through kindness and benevolence, government is distributed.
When government is completed through ritual,
the people find rest because of it.
The various officials carry out their duties,
attending court in the morning and leaving only in the evening;
this is how the Gōng and Hóu protect and shield their people.
Therefore, the Shī says:
‘Valiant is the military man,
a shield and wall to the Gōng and Hóu.’
When it comes to an age of disorder,
the feudal lords are greedy and rash,
their invasive desires know no restraint,
they struggle over mere spans of land to the point of exhausting their people,
and they make light of their military men,
treating them as their own core, limbs, and claws and teeth.
Therefore, the Shī says:
‘Valiant is the military man,
the core of the Gōng and Hóu.’
When the Way prevails in the world,
the Gōng and Hóu can serve as shield and wall for the people,
and control their core.
In disorder, it is the reverse.
Now your words
are the way of disorder;
they cannot be taken as a model.
However, you, my master,
are my lord;
how could I dare not follow you?”
He then entered,
completed the task,
and upon returning told this to Fàn Wénzǐ.
Wénzǐ said:
“Lacking ritual,
he will surely break his word.
The day of my death is not far off!”
In winter,
the Chǔ prince Bà went to Jìn to pay a courtesy visit
and to preside over a covenant.
In the twelfth month,
the Marquis of Jìn and the Chǔ prince Bà made a covenant at Chìjí.
A8.13 The Classic of the Thirteenth Year of Duke Chéng
A8.13.1 In the spring of the thirteenth year,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Xì Qǐ to come and request troops.
A8.13.2 In the third month,
the Duke went to the capital.
A8.13.3 In the summer, in the fifth month,
the Duke came from the capital
and subsequently met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the people of Zhū,
and the people of Téng to attack Qín.
A8.13.4 Lú, the Earl of Cáo, died with the army.
A8.13.5 In the autumn, in the seventh month,
the Duke arrived from the attack on Qín.
A8.13.6 In winter,
Duke Xuān of Cáo was buried.
B8.13 The Commentary of the Thirteenth Year of Duke Chéng
B8.13.1 In the spring of the thirteenth year,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Xì Qǐ to come and request troops,
but his management of the matter was disrespectful.
Mèng Xiànzǐ said:
“The Xì clan will surely perish!
Ritual
is the trunk of the self;
respect
is the foundation of the self.
Xìzǐ lacks a foundation.
Moreover, as the secondary minister of the former ruler,
he received a command to seek troops
to protect the altars of the land and grain,
yet he was indolent;
this is discarding the ruler’s command.
If he does not perish, what else would happen?”
B8.13.2 In the third month,
the Duke went to the capital.
Xuānbó desired a gift,
so he requested to be sent first.
The King treated him with the rituals of an envoy.
Mèng Xiànzǐ followed.
The King made him the second envoy
and rewarded him heavily.
The Duke and the feudal lords had an audience with the King,
and then followed Duke Kāng of Liú and Duke Sù of Chéng
to meet with the Marquis of Jìn to attack Qín.
Chéngzǐ received the sacrificial meat at the Altar of the Earth,
but was disrespectful.
Liúzǐ said:
“I have heard this:
People receive the middle ground of Heaven and Earth to be born;
this is what is called their mandate.
Therefore, there are rules for movement, ritual, righteousness, and dignity,
in order to settle this mandate.
Those who are capable nourish it to find blessing,
while those who are not capable ruin it and bring on calamity.
For this reason, the gentleman is diligent in ritual,
and the petty man exerts his strength.
In being diligent in ritual, nothing is better than attaining respect;
in exerting strength, nothing is better than being earnest and sincere.
Respect lies in nourishing the spirits;
sincerity lies in maintaining one’s occupation.
The great affairs of the state
lie in sacrifice and warfare.
In sacrifice, there is the holding of the cooked meat;
in warfare, there is the receiving of the raw meat;
these are the great nodes of the spirits.
Now Chéngzǐ is indolent,
he has discarded his mandate.
Will he not fail to return?”
B8.13.3 In the summer, on the day wùwǔ of the fourth month,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Lǚ Xiāng to break off relations with Qín,
saying:
“In the past, reaching back to our Duke Xiàn and your Duke Mù, they were on good terms,
pooling their efforts and sharing their hearts,
renewing this through covenants and oaths,
and reinforcing it through marriages.
Heaven brought calamity upon the state of Jìn;
Duke Wén went to Qí,
and Duke Huì went to Qín.
Lacking good fortune,
Duke Xiàn passed away.
Duke Mù did not forget the old virtue
and enabled our Duke Huì to uphold the sacrifices in Jìn.
Yet he could not achieve great merit,
and thus occurred the battle at Hán.
Regret also arose in Duke Mù’s heart,
and so he gathered our Duke Wén;
this was the achievement of Duke Mù.
Duke Wén personally donned helmet and armor,
traversed mountains and rivers,
crossed over dangers and obstacles,
and campaigned against the feudal lords of the east.
The descendants of Yú, Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu
were brought to pay court to Qín,
and so he had already repaid the old virtue.
The people of Zhèng encroached upon your borders;
our Duke Wén led the feudal lords and Qín to besiege Zhèng.
The grand masters of Qín did not consult with our late ruler,
but took it upon themselves to make a covenant with Zhèng.
The feudal lords resented this
and were about to direct their force against Qín.
Duke Wén was fearful
and pacified the feudal lords,
so that the Qín army was able to return without harm;
this was a great favor we did for the West.
Lacking good fortune,
Duke Wén passed away.
Duke Mù was not kind;
he held our ruler in contempt after his death,
took light of our Duke Xiāng,
invaded our land of Yáo,
wickedly cut off our friendship,
attacked our fortified cities,
wiped out our Bì and Huá,
scattered our brothers,
disturbed our alliance,
and overturned our state.
Our Duke Xiāng did not forget your ruler’s former merit,
yet he feared the downfall of the altars of land and grain,
and for this reason there was the battle of Yáo.
Still, he wished to seek pardon from Duke Mù.
Duke Mù would not listen
and approached Chǔ to plot against us.
Heaven moved his heart,
King Chéng lost his life,
and Duke Mù was therefore unable to carry out his will against us.
When Mù and Xiāng passed away,
Kāng and Líng ascended to their positions.
Duke Kāng
was born of our house,
yet he wished to cut away and diminish our ducal house,
overturn our altars of land and grain,
and lead our destructive enemies
to come and shake our borders;
for this reason there was the campaign of Lìnghú.
Kāng still did not repent,
entering our Héqǔ,
attacking our Sùchuān,
capturing our Wángguān,
and destroying our Jīmǎ;
this is why there was the Battle of Héqǔ.
That the eastern road is not open
is because Kānggōng has severed our friendship.
"When it came to your succession,
our ruler Jǐnggōng craned his neck, looked westward and said:
'Perhaps he will comfort me!'
You also did not graciously uphold the alliance,
taking advantage of our trouble with the Dí,
entered our Héxiàn,
burned our Jī and Gào,
mowed down our agricultural crops,
and slaughtered our borderlands;
this is why there was the gathering at Fǔshì.
You also regretted the extension of misfortune
and wished to seek blessings from the former rulers Xiàngōng and Mùgōng;
you sent Bóchē to come and command our Jǐnggōng, saying:
'I and you shall share friendship and discard ill-will,
restoring former virtues
to commemorate previous achievements.'
Before the oath was concluded,
Jǐnggōng passed away;
our humble ruler therefore had the meeting at Lìnghú.
You were again unpropitious,
betraying and abandoning the alliance and oath.
The Báidí and you share the same province;
they are your enemies,
but they are our relations by marriage.
You came to bestow a command, saying:
'I and you shall attack the Dí.'
Our humble ruler did not dare to look back at the marriage ties,
fearing your majesty,
and received the command from the officials.
You were double-minded toward the Dí,
saying:
'Jìn is about to attack you.'
The Dí responded and yet were resentful,
and therefore they informed us.
The people of Chǔ detested your vacillating virtue,
and also came to inform us, saying:
'Qín has turned its back on the alliance of Lìnghú
and has come to seek an alliance with us:
"Clearly proclaim to Hàotiān Shàngdì,
the three Gōng of Qín,
and the three Wáng of Chǔ, saying:
'Though I go in and out with Jìn,
I look only to profit.'
Bùgǔ detested his lack of established virtue,
and therefore I make it known,
to punish his lack of single-mindedness." '
When the feudal lords fully heard these words,
they were heartbroken and had splitting headaches,
and they drew close to Guǎrén.
Guǎrén leads them to listen to your commands,
seeking only friendship.
If you graciously care for the feudal lords,
show pity to Guǎrén,
and grant them an alliance,
then it is the wish of Guǎrén
to bring peace to the feudal lords
and withdraw;
how would I dare seek disorder?
If you do not bestow great kindness,
Guǎrén is not talented,
and will be unable to lead the feudal lords to withdraw.
I dare to fully disclose this to the Zhíshì,
so that the Zhíshì may truly plan for what is profitable.' "
Qín Huángōng
having already made the alliance of Lìnghú with Jìn Lìgōng,
then also summoned the Dí and Chǔ,
wishing to lead them to attack Jìn;
for this reason, the feudal lords were in harmony with Jìn.
Luán Shū of Jìn commanded the Central Army,
and Xún Gēng assisted him;
Shì Xiè commanded the Upper Army,
and Xì Qí assisted him;
Hán Jué commanded the Lower Army,
and Xún Yīng assisted him;
Zhào Zhān commanded the New Army,
and Xì Zhì assisted him.
Xì Yì drove the war chariot,
and Luán Zhēn was the attendant on the right.
Mèng Xiànzǐ said:
"The commanders of Jìn are in harmony;
the army must achieve great merit."
On the day Dīnghài of the fifth month,
the army of Jìn, along with the armies of the feudal lords,
fought the army of Qín at Másuì.
The army of Qín was utterly defeated;
they captured Chéng Chā of Qín and the bùgēng Nǚfù.
Cáo Xuāngōng died in the army.
The army then crossed the Jīng River,
reached Hóulì and returned.
They met Jìnhóu at Xīnchǔ.
Chéng Sùgōng died at Xiá.
B8.13.4 On the night of day Dīngmǎo in the sixth month,
Zhèng Gōngzǐ Bān from Zī
sought to enter the Grand Palace
but could not;
he killed Zǐyìn
and Zǐyǔ
and returned the troops to the marketplace.
On the day Jǐsì,
Zǐsì
led the people of the state to take an oath at the Grand Palace,
then followed and completely burned them out,
killing Zǐrú, Zǐmáng,
Sūnshū, and Sūnzhī.
B8.13.5 The people of Cáo sent Gōngzǐ Fùchú to keep guard
and sent Gōngzǐ Xīnshí to meet the funeral of Cáobó.
In autumn,
Fùchú killed the heir apparent
and established himself.
The feudal lords then requested to punish him.
The people of Jìn, because of the toil of the campaign,
requested to wait for another year.
In winter,
they buried Cáo Xuāngōng.
After the burial, Zǐzāng was about to flee,
and all the people of the state were about to follow him.
Chénggōng was then afraid,
confessed his guilt,
and made entreaty to him.
Then he returned
and surrendered his city.
A8.14 The Chénggōng Shísìnián Jīng
A8.14.1 In the spring of the fourteenth year,
in the Wáng Zhēngyuè,
Jǔzǐ Zhū died.
A8.14.2 In summer,
Sūn Línfù of Wèi returned to Wèi from Jìn.
A8.14.3 In autumn,
Shúsūn Qiáorú went to Qí to meet a bride.
A8.14.4 Zhèng Gōngzǐ Xǐ led an army to attack Xǔ.
A8.14.5 In the ninth month,
Qiáorú arrived from Qí with the Fūrén Fù Jiāngshì.
A8.14.6 In winter, in the tenth month on the day Gēngyín,
Wèihóu Zāng died.
A8.14.7 Qínbó died.
B8.14 The Chénggōng Shísìnián Zhuàn
B8.14.1 In the spring of the fourteenth year,
Wèihóu went to Jìn,
and Jìnhóu insisted that he see Sūn Línfù there.
Dìnggōng would not agree.
In summer,
after Wèihóu had returned,
Jìnhóu sent Xì Chōu to escort Sūn Línfù
and present him.
Wèihóu wished to decline.
Dìng Jiāng said:
"You must not.
He is the successor of a ministerial clan of the former rulers,
and a great state has made this request.
If you do not grant it,
we will perish.
Although you detest him,
is it not better than perishing?
My Lord, please endure it!
To pacify the people and forgive a ministerial clan—
is that not also acceptable?"
Wèihóu saw him and restored him.
Wèihóu feasted Kǔchéng Shū,
and Nìng Huìzǐ assisted.
Kǔchéng Shū was arrogant.
Nìngzǐ said:
"The house of Kǔchéng Shū will surely perish!
In ancient times, the purpose of feasts and banquets
was to observe deportment
and examine fortune and misfortune;
therefore the Shī says:
'The rhino-horn cups are curved,
the fine wine is mellow.
Their interaction is not arrogant,
ten thousand blessings come seeking them.'
Now the Master is arrogant;
this is the way to bring about disaster."
B8.14.2 In autumn,
Xuānbó went to Qí to meet a bride.
Calling by the clan name
is to honor the ruler's command.
B8.14.3 In the eighth month,
Zhèng Zǐhǎn invaded Xǔ,
but was defeated there.
On the day wùxū,
the Earl of Zhèng again invaded Xǔ.
On the day gēngzǐ, he entered its outer wall.
The people of Xǔ made peace
by means of the fief of Shū Shēn.
B8.14.4 In the ninth month,
Qiáorú escorted the lady Fù Jiāng Shì as she arrived from Qí.
Her clan name was omitted
to show honor to the lady.
Therefore, the superior man said:
"The terminology of the *Chūnqiū*
is subtle yet manifest,
recorded yet obscure,
graceful yet complete in its composition,
exhaustive yet not offensive,
punishing evil and encouraging good.
If not a sage,
who could have composed it?"
B8.14.5 The Marquis of Wèi was ill.
He ordered Kǒng Chéngzǐ and
Nìng Huìzǐ
to establish Jìng Sì's son Kàn as the Heir Apparent.
In the winter, the tenth month,
Duke Dìng of Wèi passed away.
The lady Jiāng Shì, after finishing her wailing and resting,
saw that the Heir Apparent showed no grief.
He did not restrict his drinking within the inner chambers.
She sighed and said:
"This man,
will not only be the ruin of the state of Wèi,
but it must surely begin with this widow.
Alas!
Heaven brings calamity upon the state of Wèi!
I was unable to have Zhuān
preside over the altars of the soil and grain."
When the high officials heard this,
none were not shaken with fear.
From then on, Sūn Wénzǐ did not dare
to keep his precious vessels in Wèi.
He placed them all in Qī
and treated the high officials of Jìn with great kindness.
A8.15 The Annals of the Fifteenth Year of Duke Chéng.
A8.15.1 In the spring of the fifteenth year,
in the royal second month,
Duke Dìng of Wèi was buried.
A8.15.2 In the third month, on the day yǐsì,
Zhòng Yīngqí passed away.
A8.15.3 On the day guǐchǒu,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Heir Apparent Chéng of Sòng,
Guó Zuǒ of Qí,
and the people of Zhū for a covenant at Qī.
The Marquis of Jìn seized the Earl of Cáo and returned with him to the Capital.
A8.15.4 The Duke arrived from the meeting.
A8.15.5 In the summer, the sixth month,
Duke Gù of Sòng passed away.
A8.15.6 The Viscount of Chǔ invaded Zhèng.
A8.15.7 In the autumn, the eighth month, on the day gēngchén,
Duke Gòng of Sòng was buried.
A8.15.8 Huà Yuán of Sòng fled to Jìn.
A8.15.9 Huà Yuán of Sòng returned from Jìn to Sòng.
A8.15.10 Sòng killed its high official Shān.
A8.15.11 Yú Shí of Sòng fled to Chǔ.
A8.15.12 In the winter, the eleventh month,
Shūsūn Qiáorú met with Shì Xiè of Jìn,
Gāo Wújiù of Qí,
Huà Yuán of Sòng,
Sūn Línfù of Wèi,
Young Lord Qiú of Zhèng,
and the people of Zhū to meet with the state of Wú at Zhōnglí.
A8.15.13 Xǔ moved to Yè.
B8.15 The Commentary on the Fifteenth Year of Duke Chéng.
B8.15.1 In the spring of the fifteenth year,
the meeting at Qī
was to punish Duke Chéng of Cáo.
He was seized and returned to the Capital.
The record says
"The Marquis of Jìn seized the Earl of Cáo,"
because it did not involve his people.
Whenever a ruler does not follow the proper way toward his people,
and the feudal lords punish and seize him,
then it says,
"Such-and-such person seized such-and-such a Marquis";
otherwise, it is not so recorded.
The feudal lords were going to present Zǐzāng to the King
to establish him as ruler.
Zǐzāng declined, saying:
"The ancient records have a saying:
'The sage fulfills the standard of integrity;
the next best maintains integrity;
the lowest loses integrity.'
To serve as a ruler is not my integrity.
Although I cannot be a sage,
would I dare to lose the maintenance of integrity?"
He then fled to Sòng.
B8.15.2 In the summer, the sixth month,
Duke Gòng of Sòng passed away.
B8.15.3 When Chǔ was about to send its army northward,
Zǐnáng said:
"We have just made a covenant with Jìn and now turn our backs on it;
might that not be unacceptable?"
Zǐfǎn said:
"If the enemy presents an advantage, we advance.
What covenant is there to speak of?"
Shēn Shūshí was old
and was in Shēn;
hearing of this,
he said:
"Zǐfǎn will surely not escape disaster.
Trustworthiness is used to maintain ritual propriety;
ritual propriety is used to protect one's person.
If trustworthiness and ritual propriety are lost,
and one wishes to escape,
can it be done?"
The Viscount of Chǔ invaded Zhèng
and reached Bàosuì.
He then invaded Wèi
and reached Shǒuzhǐ.
Zǐhǎn of Zhèng invaded Chǔ
and took Xīnshí.
Luán Wǔzǐ wanted to retaliate against Chǔ.
Hán Xiànzǐ said:
"There is no need.
Let them increase their crimes,
and the people will rebel against them.
Without the people,
with whom will they fight?"
B8.15.4 In the autumn, the eighth month,
Duke Gòng of Sòng was buried.
At this time, Huà Yuán was the Minister of the Right,
Yú Shí was the Minister of the Left,
Dàng Zé was the Minister of War,
Huà Xǐ was the Minister of Instruction,
Gōngsūn Shī was the Minister of Works,
Xiàng Wèirén was the Grand Minister of Justice,
Lín Zhū was the Lesser Minister of Justice,
Xiàng Chù was the Grand Steward,
and Yú Fǔ was the Lesser Steward.
Dàng Zé weakened the ducal house
and killed Young Lord Féi.
Huà Yuán said:
"I serve as the Minister of the Right.
The instruction of ruler and subject
is what the Minister oversees.
Now the ducal house is debased
and I cannot rectify it.
My crime is great.
Since I cannot manage my office,
how dare I rely on favor?"
He then fled to Jìn.
The two Huàs
were of the Dài clan;
the Minister of Works
was of the Zhuāng clan;
the six other officials were all of the Huán clan.
Yú Shí was going to stop Huà Yuán.
Yú Fǔ said:
"If the Minister of the Right returns,
he will surely punish us,
and that will be the end of the Huán lineage."
Yú Shí said:
"If the Minister of the Right happens to return,
even if he is permitted to punish us,
he surely will not dare.
Moreover, he has many great achievements
and the people of the state are with him.
If he does not return,
I fear the Huán lineage will have no one to maintain the sacrifices
in Sòng.
If the Minister of the Right carries out punishments,
there is still Xù remaining.
Though the Huán lineage may decline,
it will only be partial."
Yú Shí personally stopped Huá Yuán at the Hé.
He requested permission to punish the Dàng clan,
which was granted,
and then he returned.
He sent Huá Xǐ and Gōngsūn Shī to lead the people of the capital
to attack the Dàng clan,
and they killed Zǐ Shān.
The *Annals* state: "Sòng killed its Dàfū Shān,"
meaning he had turned against his own clan.
Yú Shí, Xiàng Wèirén, Lín Zhū, Xiàng Dài,
and Yú Fǔ went out to stay on the Suī.
Huá Yuán sent someone to stop them,
but it was not possible.
In the tenth month of winter,
Huá Yuán personally went to stop them,
but it was not possible,
and then he returned.
Yú Fǔ said:
"If we do not follow him now,
we will not be able to enter.
The Yòushī's eyes move quickly and his speech is rapid;
he has unusual intentions.
If he were not going to admit us,
he would now be galloping."
They climbed a hill to watch him,
and he was indeed galloping.
They raced after him,
but he had breached the banks of the Suī,
closed the gates, and climbed the battlements.
The Zuǒshī,
the two Sīkòu,
and the two Zǎi then fled to Chǔ.
Huá Yuán appointed Xiàng Xù as Zuǒshī,
Lǎo Zuǒ as Sīmǎ,
and Yuè Yì as Sīkòu,
to pacify the people of the capital.
B8.15.5 The three Xiè of Jìn hated Bó Zōng;
they slandered and killed him,
as well as Luán Fújì.
Bó Zhōulí fled to Chǔ.
Hán Xiànzǐ said:
"Will the Xiè clan not escape ruin?
Good men
are the bond of Heaven and Earth,
yet they have suddenly cut them off.
If they do not perish,
what are they waiting for?"
At first,
whenever Bó Zōng went to court,
his wife would always warn him, saying:
"'The thief hates the master of the house,
and the people dislike their superiors.'
You love to speak directly;
you will surely meet with disaster."
B8.15.6 In the eleventh month,
they met with Wú at Zhōnglí;
this was the beginning of communication with Wú.
B8.15.7 Xǔ Líng Gōng feared pressure from Zhèng
and requested to move to Chǔ.
On the day xīnychǒu,
Chǔ Gōngzǐ Shēn moved Xǔ to Yè.
A8.16 *The Canon of the Sixteenth Year of Chéng Gōng*
A8.16.1 In the spring of the sixteenth year,
in the royal first month,
it rained, and there was ice on the trees.
A8.16.2 In the fourth month of summer, on the day xīnwèi,
Téng Zǐ died.
A8.16.3 Zhèng Gōngzǐ Xǐ led an army to invade Sòng.
A8.16.4 In the sixth month, on the day bǐngyín, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A8.16.5 Jìn Hóu sent Luán Yǎn to come and request an army.
A8.16.6 On the last day of the month, the day jiǎwǔ,
Jìn Hóu, Chǔ Zǐ,
and Zhèng Bó fought at Yānlíng.
Chǔ Zǐ
and the Zhèng army were utterly defeated.
A8.16.7 Chǔ killed its Dàfū Gōngzǐ Cè.
A8.16.8 In autumn,
the Gōng met Jìn Hóu,
Qí Hóu,
Wèi Hóu,
Huá Yuán of Sòng,
and the people of Zhū at Shāsuí;
they did not see the Gōng.
A8.16.9 The Gōng arrived from the meeting.
A8.16.10 The Gōng met Yǐnzǐ,
Jìn Hóu,
Qí Guó Zuǒ,
and the people of Zhū to attack Zhèng.
A8.16.11 Cáo Bó returned from the capital.
A8.16.12 In the ninth month,
the people of Jìn seized Jìsūn Xíngfù
and detained him at Tiáoqiū.
A8.16.13 In the tenth month of winter, on the day yǐhài,
Shúsūn Qiáorú fled to Qí.
A8.16.14 In the twelfth month, on the day yǐchǒu,
Jìsūn Xíngfù and Xiè Chōu of Jìn made a covenant at Hù.
A8.16.15 The Gōng arrived from the meeting.
A8.16.16 On the day yǐyǒu,
Gōngzǐ Yǎn was assassinated.
B8.16 *The Commentary of the Sixteenth Year of Chéng Gōng*
B8.16.1 In the spring of the sixteenth year,
Chǔ Zǐ, from Wǔchéng, sent Gōngzǐ Chéng
to seek peace with Zhèng by offering the lands of Rǔyīn.
Zhèng rebelled against Jìn,
and Zǐsì followed Chǔ Zǐ to make a covenant at Wǔchéng.
B8.16.2 In the fourth month of summer,
Téng Wén Gōng died.
B8.16.3 Zhèng Zǐhǎn attacked Sòng;
the Sòng generals Jiāng Chú
and Yuè Jù were defeated at Shuòpēi.
They retreated
and stayed at Fūqú,
but were not on guard.
The people of Zhèng ambushed them,
defeated them at Shuòlíng,
and captured Jiāng Chú
and Yuè Jù.
Sòng had relied on its victory.
B8.16.4 Wèi Hóu attacked Zhèng,
reaching Míngyàn,
on account of Jìn.
B8.16.5 Jìn Hóu was about to attack Zhèng.
Fàn Wénzǐ said:
"If our desires were fulfilled
and all the lords rebelled,
Jìn could then be successful.
If only Zhèng rebels,
the worries of the state of Jìn
can be expected immediately."
Luán Wǔzǐ said:
"We cannot lose the feudal lords during our time;
we must attack Zhèng."
They then raised an army.
Luán Shū commanded the central army,
and Shì Xiè assisted him;
Xiè Qí commanded the upper army,
and Xún Yǎn assisted him;
Hán Jué commanded the lower army;
Xiè Zhì assisted the new army.
Xún Yíng remained behind to defend.
Xiè Chōu went to Wèi
and then to Qí;
at both, he requested armies.
Luán Yǎn came to request an army.
Mèng Xiànzǐ said:
"There will be victory."
On the day wùyín,
the Jìn army set out.
The people of Zhèng heard that there was a Jìn army,
and sent word to Chǔ;
Yáo Gòu’ěr went with them.
Chǔ Zǐ went to rescue Zhèng.
The Sīmǎ commanded the central army,
the Lìngyǐn commanded the left,
and the Yòuyǐn Zǐxīn commanded the right.
Passing through Shēn,
Zǐfǎn went in to see Shēn Shūshí
and said:
"How will the army fare?"
He replied:
"Virtue, punishment, ritual, righteousness,
rites, and good faith
are the instruments of war.
Virtue is for bestowing favor,
punishment for correcting evil,
ritual for serving the spirits,
righteousness for establishing profit,
rites for following the seasons,
and good faith for preserving things.
When the people's livelihood
is abundant and virtue is correct,
when things are used profitably and affairs are regulated,
when the seasons are favorable and things are completed,
when those above and below are in harmony,
when actions are not contrary to order,
when everything requested is provided,
and each knows their proper limit.
Therefore the *Shī* says:
'He established our numerous people;
Therefore, the spirits bestow blessings upon them,
and there are no disasters in the seasons.
The people’s livelihood is abundant and prosperous,
and they are harmonious and obedient.
None fail to exert their full strength
to follow the orders of their superiors
and risk death to make up for any deficiencies.
This is the reason why victory is achieved in battle.
Now Chǔ abandons its people internally
and cuts off its friendly ties externally.
It profanes solemn covenants
and goes back on its spoken promises.
It acts in violation of the proper times
and exhausts the people to satisfy its whims.
The people do not know what to trust;
they are blamed whether they advance or retreat.
When people worry about where they will end up,
who would risk death for them?
You should exert yourself!
I shall not see you again."
Yáo Gù'ěr returned first,
and Zisì questioned him.
He replied:
"Their march is fast,
and they cross dangerous terrain without being in order.
Speed leads to a loss of focus;
lack of order
means losing the ranks.
When focus is lost
and ranks are broken,
how can they fight?
Chǔ is in a state of alarm and cannot be effectively used."
In the fifth month,
the Jìn army crossed the Hé.
Hearing that the Chǔ army was about to arrive,
Fàn Wénzǐ wished to return,
saying:
"If we pretend to flee from Chǔ,
we can ease our worries.
Now, convening the Zhūhóu
is not something I am capable of;
let us leave it to those who are capable.
If we, as fellow ministers, are harmonious
in serving our ruler,
that is enough."
Wǔzǐ said:
"That is not possible."
In the sixth month,
Jìn and Chǔ met at Yānlíng.
Fàn Wénzǐ did not wish to fight.
Xì Zhì said:
"In the Battle of Hán,
Huì Gōng could not reorganize his army;
in the campaign of Jī,
Xiān Zhěn did not return to report;
in the army of Bì,
Xún Bó did not return on his chariot.
These were all shames for Jìn.
You have also seen the deeds of our late rulers.
Now if we avoid Chǔ,
it will further increase our shame."
Wénzǐ said:
"When our former rulers fought frequently,
there were reasons for it.
Qín, Dí,
Qí, and Chǔ were all strong.
If we did not exert our full strength,
our descendants would have been weakened.
Now three of the strong ones have submitted,
and only Chǔ remains as a rival.
Only a Shèngrén can be without trouble from both without and within.
If one is not a Shèngrén,
peace without will surely bring trouble within;
why not leave Chǔ alone
to serve as an external fear?"
On the last day of the month, Jiǎwǔ,
Chǔ pressed against the Jìn army at dawn and deployed for battle.
The military officers were troubled by this.
Fàn Gài hurried forward
and said:
"Fill the wells and level the stoves;
deploy within the camp,
and leave space between the ranks.
Whether Jìn or Chǔ is granted victory is for Tiān to decide;
why be troubled by it?"
Wénzǐ took up a halberd and chased him away,
saying:
"The survival or downfall of the state
rests with Tiān;
what does a child like you know?"
Luán Shū said:
"The Chǔ army is light and flighty;
if we strengthen our fortifications and wait for them,
they will surely retreat in three days.
If we attack them as they retreat,
we will surely gain victory."
Xì Zhì said:
"Chǔ has six vulnerabilities
that we must not miss.
Their two Qīng hate each other;
the Wáng's personal troops are based on old ties;
the Zhèng troops are in formation but not orderly;
the Mán troops are an army but not in formation;
they deployed without avoiding the Huì day;
their ranks are noisy;
when they come together, the noise increases.
Each looks back over his shoulder,
and none have the heart for battle.
Being old does not mean they are good;
since they have violated Tiān’s taboos,
we are certain to overcome them."
Chǔ Zǐ climbed a lookout cart
to observe the Jìn army.
Zǐzhòng had the Dàzǎi Bó Zhōulí attend behind the Wáng.
The Wáng said:
"They are galloping to the left and right;
why?"
He replied:
"They are summoning the military officers."
"They have all gathered in the central army."
He replied:
"They are planning together."
"They are setting up a tent."
He replied:
"They are reverently divining before their late rulers."
"They have taken down the tent."
He replied:
"They are about to issue orders."
"There is much noise,
and the dust is rising."
He replied:
"They are about to fill the wells and level the stoves
to form their ranks."
"They have all mounted their chariots,
and the attendants on the left and right have taken their weapons and descended."
He replied:
"They are listening to the oath."
"Will they fight?"
He replied:
"That cannot be known yet."
"They have mounted, and the attendants on the left and right have all descended again."
He replied:
"They are praying for the battle."
Bó Zhōulí reported on the Gōng's personal troops to the Wáng.
Miáo Bènhuáng was at the side of the Jìn Hóu
and also reported on the Wáng's personal troops.
Both said:
"The finest men of the state are there,
and they are many;
they cannot be withstood."
Miáo Bènhuáng said to the Jìn Hóu:
"The best of Chǔ
are only in the royal clan of the central army.
Please divide our elite troops
to attack their left and right flanks,
and then converge our four armies on the Wáng's personal troops;
we will certainly defeat them soundly."
The Gōng divined it with stalks.
The Shǐ said:
"It is auspicious.
The Guà encountered is Fù,
which says:
'The southern state is distressed;
shoot their great Wáng,
hitting his eye.'
With the state distressed and the Wáng wounded,
what else is there to wait for but their defeat?"
The Gōng followed this.
There was a marsh in front of them,
so they all diverged to the left and right to avoid it.
Bù Yì drove for Jìn Lì Gōng,
and Luán Zhēn was the Yòu.
Péng Míng drove for Chǔ Gòng Wáng,
and Pān Dǎng was the Yòu.
Shí Shǒu drove for Zhèng Chéng Gōng,
and Táng Gǒu was the Yòu.
The Luán and Fàn clans flanked the Gōng's chariot as they advanced.
They became stuck in the marsh.
Luán Shū was about to carry the Jìn Hóu.
Zhēn said:
"Shū, move back!
The state has its great responsibilities;
how can you take them all upon yourself?
To usurp another’s office
is an encroachment;
to lose one's own office
is negligence;
to leave one's post
is a violation.
These are three crimes
that must not be committed."
He then heaved the Gōng's chariot out of the marsh.
On the day of *Guǐsì*,
a partisan of *Pān Wāng* and *Yǎng Yóujī*
set a piece of armor on its side and shot at it,
piercing through seven layers.
They showed it to the King,
saying:
“With two such ministers as these,
why worry about the battle?”
The King said angrily:
“This is a great disgrace to the state!
Tomorrow morning when you shoot,
you shall die by your skill.”
*Lǚ Qǐ* dreamed of shooting the moon
and hitting it,
then retreating into the mud.
He had it divined,
and the diviner said:
“The surname *Jī*
is the sun;
a different surname
is the moon.
This must be the King of *Chǔ*.
Shooting and hitting him,
then retreating into the mud—
you too must surely die.”
When it came to the battle,
he shot King *Gòng*, hitting his eye.
The King summoned *Yǎng Yóujī*,
gave him two arrows,
and ordered him to shoot *Lǚ Qǐ*.
He hit his neck,
and *Lǚ Qǐ* fell over his quiver.
*Yǎng Yóujī* reported back with one arrow left.
*Xì Zhì* encountered the troops of the Viscount of *Chǔ* three times.
Whenever he saw the Viscount of *Chǔ*,
he would certainly dismount,
remove his helmet, and hurry forward like the wind.
The Viscount of *Chǔ* sent the Master of Works *Xiāng* to inquire after him with a bow,
saying:
“While the affairs of battle are at their peak,
there is a gentleman wearing leggings of light-colored leather,
a true gentleman.
Recognizing and seeing Unworthy Me, he hurried along;
might he not have been injured?”
*Xì Zhì* received the guest,
removed his helmet to receive the message,
and said:
“Your Majesty’s outside servant has come
to follow my humble ruler’s military service.
By Your Majesty’s spiritual power,
I am occasionally clad in armor and helmet,
so I do not dare to bow in receipt of your command.
I venture to report my restlessness
for the honor of Your Majesty’s command.
Because of the current affairs,
I venture to salute the messenger.”
He saluted the messenger three times and withdrew.
*Hán Jué* of *Jìn* pursued the Earl of *Zhèng*.
His charioteer *Dù Hùnluó* said:
“Shall we follow him quickly?
His charioteer looks back repeatedly,
his eyes are not on the horses;
he can be overtaken.”
*Hán Jué* said:
“One cannot disgrace the ruler of a state a second time.”
So he stopped.
*Xì Zhì* pursued the Earl of *Zhèng*.
His spearman on the right, *Fú Hànhú*, said:
“The spies have intercepted him.
I will leap onto his chariot
and take him prisoner down.”
*Xì Zhì* said:
“To harm the ruler of a state is a punishable crime.”
He also stopped.
*Shí Shǒu* said:
“Duke *Yì* of *Wèi* only failed because he did not lower his flags;
that is why he was defeated at *Yíng*.”
So he put the pennons inside his quiver.
*Táng Gǒu* said to *Shí Shǒu*:
“You are at the ruler’s side;
the defeat is a great one.
I am not as good as you;
you use your skill to help the ruler escape,
and I ask to stay behind.”
Then he died.
The *Chǔ* army was pressed against a dangerous place.
*Shūshān Rǎn* said to *Yǎng Yóujī*:
“Although the King gave an order,
for the sake of the state,
you must shoot.”
So he shot;
discharging twice,
all the targets were killed.
*Shūshān Rǎn* seized a man and threw him,
hitting a chariot
and breaking its crossbar.
The *Jìn* army then stopped.
They captured Prince *Fèi* of *Chǔ*.
*Luán Zhēn* saw the flag of *Zǐzhòng*
and requested, saying:
“The *Chǔ* people say that flag
is the signal-flag of *Zǐzhòng*;
that must be *Zǐzhòng* over there.
Formerly, when I served as an envoy to *Chǔ*,
*Zǐzhòng* asked about the courage of the state of *Jìn*.
I replied,
‘We like to be orderly with a multitude.’
He said,
‘And what else?’
I replied,
‘We like to be at ease.’
Now the two states are engaged in war,
and messengers are not being sent;
this cannot be called orderly.
Facing the matter
and breaking my word
cannot be called being at ease.
I request to offer him a drink.”
The Duke permitted it.
He sent a messenger carrying a wine vessel to present a drink,
reaching *Zǐzhòng*,
and saying:
“My humble ruler lacks messengers;
he has ordered *Zhēn* to drive and hold a spear,
so he cannot personally reward your followers.
He has sent me to offer this drink.”
*Zǐzhòng* said:
“That gentleman once spoke with me in *Chǔ*;
it must be for that reason.
Is he not mindful?”
He accepted it and drank,
then released the messenger and beat the drums again.
They fought until morning,
and the stars were seen before they finished.
*Zǐfǎn* ordered the military officers to inspect the wounded,
supplement the soldiers and chariots,
repair the armor and weapons,
inspect the chariots and horses,
and eat at cockcrow,
listening only for orders.
The people of *Jìn* were worried about this.
*Miáo Bènhuáng* went around and proclaimed:
“Inspect the chariots and supplement the soldiers,
feed the horses and sharpen the weapons,
arrange the ranks and solidify the lines,
eat on your mats and repeat the prayers—
we shall fight again tomorrow!”
Then they released a *Chǔ* prisoner.
The King heard of this
and summoned *Zǐfǎn* to plan.
*Gǔyáng Shù* offered wine to *Zǐfǎn*;
*Zǐfǎn* got drunk and could not see the King.
The King said:
“Heaven is defeating *Chǔ* indeed!
I cannot wait.”
Then he fled by night.
*Jìn* entered the *Chǔ* camp
and ate their grain for three days.
*Fàn Wénzǐ* stood before the war horses
and said:
“The ruler is young,
and the ministers are not talented;
how did we reach this point?
The ruler must be cautious!
The *Zhōu Shū* says:
‘The Mandate is not constant.’
This refers to having virtue.”
The *Chǔ* army returned,
and reaching *Xiá*,
the King sent a message to *Zǐfǎn*, saying:
“Among the former Great Officers who lost their armies,
the ruler was not present.
You should not consider this your fault;
it is the fault of Unworthy Me.”
*Zǐfǎn* bowed twice, touching his head to the ground, and said:
“If my ruler grants me death,
I shall die and yet be immortal.
My soldiers indeed fled;
it is my crime.”
*Zǐzhòng* again spoke to *Zǐfǎn*, saying:
“Those who previously lost their armies,
you have heard of them as well.
Why not consider the outcome?”
He replied:
“Even if the former Great Officers had not done so,
the Great Officer has commanded *Cè*,
and how would *Cè* dare to be unrighteous?
*Cè* lost the ruler’s army;
how could I dare to forget my death?”
The King sent someone to stop him,
but he died before they reached him.
On the day of the battle,
*Guó Zuǒ* and *Gāo Wújiù* reached the army;
the Marquis of *Wèi* departed from *Wèi*;
the Duke departed from *Huàituí*.
*Xuānbó* had an illicit affair with *Mù Jiāng*;
he wanted to remove the *Jì* and *Mèng* families
and take over their households.
When he was about to depart,
Mù Jiāng escorted the Duke,
and ordered him to expel the two gentlemen.
The Duke informed her of the difficulties with Jìn,
saying:
“I request to return and then listen to your command.”
Jiāng was angry;
Gōng Zǐ Yǎn and Gōng Zǐ Chú hurried past,
and she pointed at them, saying:
“If you will not,
these are both rulers.”
The Duke waited at Huài Tuí,
reinforced the palace,
alerted the guards and established a defense,
and only then departed;
because of this, he was late.
He sent Mèng Xiàn Zǐ to guard the Duke’s palace.
B8.16.6 In autumn,
there was a meeting at Shā Suí
to plan an attack on Zhèng.
Xuān Bó sent word to inform Xì Chōu, saying:
“The Marquis of Lǔ waited at Huài Tuí
in order to wait for the winner.”
Xì Chōu commanded the New Army
and also served as a Gōng Zú Dà Fū,
managing the eastern feudal lords.
He took bribes from Xuān Bó
and complained about the Duke to the Marquis of Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn did not see the Duke.
B8.16.7 The people of Cáo petitioned Jìn, saying:
“Since our late ruler Xuān Gōng ascended the throne,
the people of the state said:
‘What shall we do?
Our worries have not yet ceased.’
And then you punished our late ruler,
by causing the loss of the stabilizer of the altars of the state of Cáo,
the prince;
this is to utterly destroy Cáo. Did our late ruler perhaps have a crime?
If there were a crime,
then you, my lord, would have listed him in the assembly.
If you, my lord, do not neglect virtue and punishment
in acting as hegemon to the feudal lords,
how could you alone neglect our humble city?
We venture to privately state this.”
B8.16.8 In the seventh month,
the Duke met with Yǐn Wǔ Gōng and the feudal lords to attack Zhèng.
When he was about to depart,
Jiāng again commanded the Duke as before.
The Duke again reinforced the defense and then departed.
The armies of the feudal lords halted at the west of Zhèng;
our army halted at Dū Yáng,
not daring to pass through Zhèng.
Zǐ Shū Shēng Bó sent Shū Sūn Bào
to request to meet the Jìn army
and provided a meal in the outskirts of Zhèng.
The army was met and arrived.
Shēng Bó did not eat for four days while waiting for them;
only after feeding the messengers did he himself eat.
B8.16.9 The feudal lords moved to Zhì Tián.
Zhì Wǔ Zǐ assisted the Lower Army
and led the armies of the feudal lords to invade Chén,
reaching Míng Lù.
They then invaded Cài.
Before they returned,
the feudal lords moved to Yǐng Shàng.
On the day wùwǔ,
Zǐ Hǎn of Zhèng attacked their camp at night;
Sòng, Qí, and Wèi all lost their camps.
B8.16.10 The people of Cáo again petitioned Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn said to Zǐ Zāng:
“Return,
and I will return your ruler.”
Zǐ Zāng returned,
and the Earl of Cáo returned.
Zǐ Zāng surrendered all his estates and his rank as minister
and did not go out.
B8.16.11 Xuān Bó sent word to inform Xì Chōu, saying:
“That Lǔ has Jì and Mèng
is like Jìn having Luán and Fàn;
government orders are finalized there.
Now their plan says:
‘The government of Jìn has many factions
and cannot be followed.
We would rather serve Qí or Chǔ;
whether we survive or perish,
we will not follow Jìn.’
If you wish to have your way in Lǔ,
please detain Háng Fù and kill him;
I will kill Miè,
and when we serve Jìn,
there will be no duplicity.
If Lǔ is not duplicitous,
the small states will certainly be harmonious.
Otherwise,
upon their return, they will certainly rebel.”
In the ninth month,
the people of Jìn seized Jì Wén Zǐ at Tiáo Qiū.
The Duke returned
and waited at Yùn,
sending Zǐ Shū Shēng Bó to request Jì Sūn from Jìn.
Xì Chōu said:
“If you remove Zhòng Sūn Miè
and detain Jì Sūn Háng Fù,
I will give the state to you,
and you will be closer to the ducal house.”
He replied:
“As for Qiáo Rú’s true feelings,
you must have heard of them.
If you remove Miè and Háng Fù,
that would be to utterly abandon the state of Lǔ
and to criminalize my ruler.
If you do not yet abandon us
and kindly seek the blessing of Zhōu Gōng
to allow my ruler to serve the ruler of Jìn,
then those two men
are the ministers of the altars of the state of Lǔ.
If they perish in the morning,
Lǔ will certainly perish by evening.
Given that Lǔ is so close to its enemies,
if it perishes and becomes an enemy,
how could you have time to manage it?”
Xì Chōu said:
“I will request estates for you.”
He replied:
“I, Yīng Qí,
am a common servant of Lǔ;
how would I dare rely on a great state to seek riches?
I have come with my ruler’s command to make this request;
if I obtain what I request,
your gift to me, my lord, will already be great;
what else should I seek?”
Fàn Wén Zǐ said to Luán Wǔ Zǐ:
“Jì Sūn in Lǔ
has served as minister to two rulers.
His concubines do not wear silk,
and his horses do not eat grain;
can he not be called loyal?
To believe in slander and evil and abandon the loyal and good,
what will the feudal lords think?
Zǐ Shū Yīng Qí follows his ruler’s command
without selfishness,
plans for his state without duplicity,
and in looking after himself does not forget his ruler.
If you ignore his request,
that would be to abandon a good man.
You should consider it!”
Thereupon they agreed to peace with Lǔ
and pardoned Jì Sūn.
In winter, in the tenth month,
they expelled Shū Sūn Qiáo Rú
and held a covenant against him.
Qiáo Rú fled to Qí.
In the twelfth month,
Jì Sūn and Xì Chōu made a covenant at Hù;
when he returned,
he executed Gōng Zǐ Yǎn.
He summoned Shū Sūn Bào from Qí
and established him.
Shēng Mèng Zǐ of Qí
had an affair with Qiáo Rú
and had him placed between the houses of Gāo and Guó.
Qiáo Rú said:
“I cannot commit a crime a second time.”
He then fled to Wèi,
where he was also placed among the ministers.
B8.16.12 The Marquis of Jìn sent Xì Zhì to present the spoils of the victory over Chǔ to Zhōu;
he spoke with Shàn Xiāng Gōng
and repeatedly boasted of his own merits.
Shàn Zǐ said to the grandees:
“Wēn Jì
will likely perish!
He is ranked below seven men,
yet he seeks to eclipse those above him.
The accumulation of resentment
is the root of disorder.
Having much resentment and providing a ladder for disorder,
how can he remain in his position?
The *Book of Xià* says:
‘Does resentment lie only in what is manifest?
Plan for what is not seen.’
One must be careful with small things.
Now he makes it manifest;
how can he survive?”
A8.17 The Classic of the Seventeenth Year of Duke Chéng
A8.17.1 In the spring of the seventeenth year,
Běi Gōng Kuò of Wèi led an army to invade Zhèng.
A8.17.2 In summer,
the Duke met with Yǐn Zǐ,
Shàn Zǐ,
the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Cáo,
and the people of Zhū to attack Zhèng.
A8.17.3 In the sixth month, on the *yǐyǒu* day,
a covenant was made at Kēlíng.
A8.17.4 In autumn,
the Duke arrived from the meeting.
A8.17.5 Gāo Wújiù of Qí fled to Jǔ.
A8.17.6 In the ninth month, on the *xīnchǒu* day,
the *jiāo* sacrifice was performed.
A8.17.7 The Marquis of Jìn sent Xún Yíng to come and request troops.
A8.17.8 In winter,
the Duke met the Master of Shàn,
the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Cáo,
men of Qí,
and men of Zhū to attack Zhèng.
A8.17.9 In the eleventh month,
the Duke arrived from the attack on Zhèng.
A8.17.10 On the *rénshēn* day,
Gōngsūn Yīngqí died at Líshèn.
A8.17.11 In the twelfth month, on the *dīngsì* day, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A8.17.12 Juéqiě, Viscount of Zhū, died.
A8.17.13 Jìn killed its high officials Xì Qí,
Xì Chōu,
and Xì Zhì.
A8.17.14 The people of Chǔ extinguished Shūyōng.
B8.17 *The Zuǒ Commentary on the Seventeenth Year of Duke Chéng*
B8.17.1 In the spring of the seventeenth year, in the royal first month,
Zǐsì of Zhèng invaded Xū and
Huá of Jìn.
Běigōng Kuò of Wèi rescued Jìn,
invaded Zhèng,
and reached Gāoshì. In the summer, in the fifth month,
Crown Prince Kūnwán and
Hóu Nòu of Zhèng became hostages in Chǔ;
Gōngzǐ Chéng and
Gōngzǐ Yín
garrisoned Zhèng.
B8.17.2 The Duke met Duke Wǔ of Yǐn, Duke Xiāng of Shàn, and the other lords to attack Zhèng,
from Xìtóng to Qǔwěi.
B8.17.3 Fàn Wénzǐ of Jìn returned from Yānlíng
and instructed his ritual officers to pray for his death,
saying:
"The ruler is arrogant and extravagant, yet he has overcome the enemy.
This is Heaven increasing his malady.
Difficulties are about to arise.
If you love me, just pray
for my speedy death.
That I might not reach the time of trouble is the blessing of the Fàn clan."
In the sixth month, on the *wùchén* day,
Shì Xiè died.
B8.17.4 On the *yǐyǒu* day,
they entered into a covenant at Kēlíng,
renewing the covenant of Qī.
B8.17.5 Zǐzhòng of Chǔ rescued Zhèng
and stationed his army at Shǒuzhǐ.
The lords returned.
B8.17.6 Qìng Kè of Qí had an illicit affair with Shèng Mèngzǐ.
Wearing women's clothes and riding in a hand-drawn carriage,
he entered the gate.
Bào Qiān saw this
and told Guó Wǔzǐ.
Wǔzǐ summoned Qìng Kè and rebuked him.
Qìng Kè did not go out for a long time
and told the Lady:
"Guózi has criticized me."
The Lady was angry.
Guózi assisted Duke Líng at the meeting,
while Gāo and Bào remained to guard.
When they were returning
and were about to arrive,
they closed the gates
and searched for intruders.
Mèngzǐ slandered them, saying:
"Gāo
and Bào are going to refuse the ruler’s entry
and set up Gōngzǐ Jiǎo;
Guózi knows about it."
In the autumn, in the seventh month, on the *rényín* day,
they cut off Bào Qiān's feet
and banished Gāo Wújiù.
Wújiù fled to Jǔ.
Gāo Ruò rebelled at Lú.
The people of Qí came to summon Bào Guó
and established him.
Previously,
Bào Guó had left the Bào clan and come
to be a servant to Shī Xiàoshū.
The Shī clan divined for a steward,
and Kuāng Jùxū was auspicious.
The Shī clan's steward had a town of one hundred households.
When the town was given to Kuāng Jùxū
and he was made steward,
he yielded it to Bào Guó and presented the town to him.
Shī Xiàoshū said:
"You were the one for whom it was auspicious."
He replied:
"If I can give it to one who is loyal and good,
what greater auspiciousness could there be?"
Bào Guó served the Shī clan with loyalty;
therefore, the people of Qí took him
and made him the successor of the Bào clan.
Zhòngní said:
"The wisdom of Bào Zhuāngzǐ
was not equal to that of a mallow;
even a mallow can protect its own roots."
B8.17.7 In the winter,
the lords attacked Zhèng.
In the tenth month, on the *gēngwǔ* day,
they besieged Zhèng.
Gōngzǐ Shēn of Chǔ rescued Zhèng
and stationed his army on the Rǔ River.
In the eleventh month,
the lords returned.
B8.17.8 Previously,
Shēngbó dreamed of crossing the Huán River.
Someone gave him fine gems, and he ate them.
He wept and his tears became fine gems,
filling his bosom.
Then he sang a song:
"Crossing the waters of the Huán,
I am gifted with fine gems.
Returning, returning!
Fine gems fill my bosom!"
Fearful, he did not dare to interpret the dream.
Returning from Zhèng,
on the *rénshēn* day,
when he reached Líshèn, he interpreted it,
saying:
"I was afraid of dying,
so I did not dare interpret it.
Now my followers are numerous
and have followed me for three years;
there is no harm."
Having spoken of this
in the evening, he died.
B8.17.9 The Marquis of Qí made Cuī Zhù
a high official
and made Qìng Kè his assistant,
leading the army to besiege Lú.
Guó Zuǒ was following the lords in the siege of Zhèng;
because of the trouble, he requested
to return.
He then went to the army at Lú,
killed Qìng Kè,
and rebelled with Gǔ.
The Marquis of Qí made a covenant with him at Xúguān
and restored him.
In the twelfth month,
Lú surrendered.
He sent Guó Shèng to report the trouble to Jìn
and to await orders at Qīng.
B8.17.10 Duke Lì of Jìn was extravagant
and had many favorites from outside the court.
On returning from Yānlíng,
he wished to remove all the various high officials
and establish his personal attendants.
Because of the dismissal of Xū Kè, Xū Tóng
bore a grudge against the Xì clan
and became a favorite of Duke Lì.
Xì Qí took away the lands of Yíyáng Wǔ,
and Wǔ was also a favorite of Duke Lì.
Xì Chōu and Zhǎngyú Jiǎo disputed over land;
Xì Chōu seized him and put him in stocks,
binding him to the same carriage shaft as his parents, wife, and children.
Afterward, Jiǎo also became a favorite of Duke Lì.
Luán Shū bore a grudge against Xì Zhì
because he did not follow his advice
and yet defeated the Chǔ army;
he wished to depose him.
He sent Gōngzǐ Fá of Chǔ
to tell the Duke:
"In this battle,
Xì Zhì actually summoned my ruler.
Because the eastern army had not yet arrived
and the commanders of the army were not all present,
he said:
'This army will certainly be defeated,
and I will then support Sūn Zhōu
to serve your ruler.'"
The Duke announced this to Luán Shū.
Shū said:
"It is likely so.
If not,
how could he not worry about death,
and instead receive an envoy from the enemy?
Why does the ruler not try sending him to Zhōu
and observe him?"
Xì Zhì went on a mission to Zhōu,
and Luán Shū sent Sūn Zhōu to meet him.
The Duke sent someone to spy on them,
and it was confirmed.
Consequently, he resented Xì Zhì.
Duke Lì went hunting;
he first hunted with women and drank wine,
and later ordered the high officials to hunt.
Xì Zhì presented a boar,
but the eunuch Mèng Zhāng snatched it away,
so Xì Zhì shot and killed him.
The Duke said:
"Jì Zǐ deceives me!"
Duke Lì was about to cause trouble.
Xū Tóng said:
"You must first eliminate the three Xìs.
Their clan is large
and has many enemies.
Eliminating a large clan
ensures you are not pressured;
eliminating those with many enemies
will be of use."
The Duke said:
"Indeed."
The Xì clan heard of this.
Xì Qí wanted to attack the Duke,
saying:
"Even if I die,
the ruler will surely be endangered."
Xì Zhì said:
"That by which a person stands
is trustworthiness, wisdom, and courage.
Trustworthiness is not rebelling against the ruler;
wisdom is not harming the people;
courage is not creating disorder.
If these three are lost,
who would side with me?
To die with many resentments against one,
how could that be of any use?
If the ruler has a subject and kills him,
what will be said of the ruler?
If I have guilt,
my death is already late.
If he kills the innocent,
he will lose his people;
if he desires peace,
can he obtain it?
I shall only await his command.
Having received the ruler's salary,
one gathers followers.
To have followers and contest the ruler's command,
what crime could be greater than that?"
On the day Rénwǔ,
Xū Tóng
and Yí Yáng Wǔ led eight hundred armored men
to attack the Xì clan.
Cháng Yú Jiǎo requested not to use the multitude,
and the Duke sent Qīng Fèi Tuí to assist him.
Drawing their halberds and tucking in their robes,
they feigned to be litigants.
As the three Xìs were about to confer in the pavilion,
Jiǎo used a halberd to kill Jū Bó
and Kǔ Chéng Shū at their seats.
Wēn Jì said:
"It is to escape the ruler's majesty."
He then hurried away.
Jiǎo caught up to him at his carriage
and killed him with a halberd.
All their corpses were displayed in the court.
Xū Tóng used armored men to seize Luán Shū
and Zhōngháng Yǎn in the court.
Jiǎo said:
"If you do not kill these two,
trouble will surely reach the ruler."
The Duke said:
"In one morning, three high ministers have been turned into corpses;
I cannot bear to add to them."
He replied:
"Others will be able to bear harming the ruler.
I have heard that disorder from the outside is villainy,
and from the inside is lawlessness.
Manage villainy with virtue;
manage lawlessness with punishment.
To kill without bestowing virtue
cannot be called virtue;
to have subjects pressuring the ruler and not punish them
cannot be called punishment.
If virtue and punishment are not established,
villainy and lawlessness will both arrive.
I request to leave."
He then fled to the Dí.
The Duke sent a message to the two men, saying:
"I have carried out punishment against the Xì clan.
The Xì clan has already suffered for their crimes.
May you high officials not be humiliated;
resume your positions!"
They both bowed twice with their heads to the ground and said:
"The ruler punishes the guilty
and spares us from death;
it is the ruler's favor.
Even if we two subjects should die,
how could we dare forget the ruler's virtue?"
Then they both returned.
The Duke made Xū Tóng a high minister.
The Duke was traveling in Jiànglì,
and Luán Shū and Zhōngháng Yǎn then seized the Duke there.
They summoned Shì Gài,
but Shì Gài declined.
They summoned Hán Jué,
and Hán Jué declined,
saying:
"In the past, I was cared for by the Zhào clan.
Despite the slanders of Mèng Jī,
I was able to avoid using weapons.
The ancients had a saying:
'Even if an old ox is killed, no one dares to take charge of the carcass.'
