How much more so for the ruler?
If you gentlemen cannot serve the ruler,
what use have you for Jué?"
B8.17.11 Because of the defeat of the Chǔ army,
the people of Shūyōng led the people of Wú to besiege Cháo,
attack Jià,
and besiege Lí and Huǐ.
They then relied on Wú and made no defenses.
The Chǔ prince Tuóshī launched a surprise attack on Shūyōng
and destroyed it.
B8.17.12 On the last day of the intercalary month, Yǐmǎo,
Luán Shū and Zhōngháng Yǎn killed Xū Tóng.
The people did not side with the Xì clan,
but Xū Tóng had led the ruler to create disorder;
therefore, the records all state:
"Jìn killed its high official."
A8.18 The Annals of the Eighteenth Year of Duke Chéng
A8.18.1 In the spring of the eighteenth year,
in the royal first month,
Jìn killed its high official Xū Tóng.
A8.18.2 On the day Gēngshēn,
Jìn assassinated its ruler Zhōupú.
A8.18.3 Qí killed its high official Guó Zuǒ.
A8.18.4 The Duke went to Jìn.
A8.18.5 In the summer,
the Viscount of Chǔ
and the Earl of Zhèng attacked Sòng.
Yú Shí of Sòng re-entered Péngchéng.
A8.18.6 The Duke arrived from Jìn.
A8.18.7 The Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Gài to come with friendly inquiries.
A8.18.8 In the autumn,
the Earl of Qǐ came to court.
A8.18.9 In the eighth month,
the Viscount of Zhū came to court.
A8.18.10 A deer park was built.
A8.18.11 On the day Jǐchǒu,
the Duke passed away in the main hall.
A8.18.12 In the winter,
the people of Chǔ
and the people of Zhèng invaded Sòng.
A8.18.13 The Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Fáng to come and request troops.
A8.18.14 In the twelfth month,
Zhòngsūn Miè met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Viscount of Zhū,
and Cuī Zhù of Qí, to join a covenant at Xūtǐng.
A8.18.15 On the day Dīngwèi,
our ruler, Duke Chéng, was buried.
B8.18 The Commentary on the Eighteenth Year of Duke Chéng
B8.18.1 In the spring of the eighteenth year,
in the royal first month, on the day Gēngshēn,
Luán Shū and Zhōngháng Yǎn of Jìn sent Chéng Huá
to assassinate Jìn Lì Gōng.
They buried him outside the east gate of Yì
with a single carriage.
They sent Xún Yíng and Tǔ Fáng to welcome Zhōuzǐ from the Capital
and establish him;
he was fourteen years old.
The high officials welcomed him at Qīngyuán.
Zhōuzǐ said,
"I originally had no wish for this;
though it has come to this,
is it not indeed Heaven's will!
Now, when people seek a ruler,
it is to have him issue commands.
If you establish one but do not follow him,
what use is a ruler?
If you gentlemen are to employ me, let it be today;
if not, let that also be today.
To be reverent and follow the ruler
is what the spirits will bless."
They replied,
"It is the wish of all the ministers;
how could we dare not listen only to your commands?"
On the day Gēngwǔ,
they made a covenant and he entered,
lodging at the residence of the Bózǐ Tóng clan.
On the day Xīnsì, he held audience at the Wǔgōng.
He expelled seven people who did not act as ministers.
Zhōuzǐ had an elder brother who was not intelligent,
unable to distinguish beans from wheat,
and therefore could not be established.
B8.18.2 Because of the trouble of the Qìng clan in Qí,
on the last day of the month, Jiǎshēn,
the Marquis of Qí sent Shì Huámiǎn
to kill Guó Zuǒ with a halberd
at the court of the inner palace.
Shī fled to the consort's palace.
The text says,
"Qí killed its high official Guó Zuǒ,"
because he abandoned commands,
killed without authorization,
and rebelled using Gǔ.
He sent the people of Qīng to kill Guó Shèng.
Guó Ruò fled to Lǔ.
Wáng Qiū fled to Lái.
Qìng Fēng became a high official,
and Qìng Zuǒ became the Minister of Justice.
Later,
the Marquis of Qí brought back Guó Ruò
and made him succeed the Guó clan;
this was in accordance with ritual.
B8.18.3 In the second month, on the day Yǐyǒu, the first day of the month,
Jìn Hóu Dào Gōng ascended the throne at court.
He began to appoint the various officials,
distributed grants, canceled debts,
reached out to widowers and widows,
assisted those abandoned or stagnant,
rectified the destitute,
relieved those in disaster and suffering,
prohibited excess and wickedness,
lightened taxes and levies,
pardoned crimes and offenses,
economized on utensils, and employed the people at the proper seasons,
desiring not to violate the agricultural times.
He appointed Wèi Xiāng, Shì Fáng, Wèi Jié,
and Zhào Wǔ as ministers;
Xún Jiā, Xún Huì, Luán Yǎn, and Hán Wújì
as high officials of the ducal clan,
to instruct the sons and brothers of the ministers
in reverence, frugality, filiality, and fraternal respect.
He made Shì Wòzhuó the Great Tutor
to cultivate the laws of Fàn Wǔzǐ;
Yòuháng Xīn was made Minister of Works
to cultivate the laws of Shì Wěi.
Biàn Jiǔ was the chariot driver,
and the Master of the Stables was subordinate to him,
to instruct all the drivers to know righteousness.
Xún Bīn was the attendant on the right,
and the Officer of Gentlemen was subordinate to him,
to instruct the brave and strong soldiers to be employed at the right times.
The ministers had no shared drivers,
and he established army commanders to manage them.
Qí Xī was the Commander of the Central Army,
with Yángshé Zhí assisting him;
Wèi Jiàng was the Minister of War,
and Zhāng Lǎo was the chief of scouts.
Duó Èkòu was the Commander of the Upper Army,
with Jí Yǎn as his Minister of War,
to instruct the infantry and chariots
to be unified in obeying orders.
Chéng Zhèng was the driver of the ruler's horses,
and the six grooms were subordinate to him,
to instruct the various grooms to know ritual.
All the heads of the six offices
were praised by the people.
Promotions did not miss merit,
offices did not change their principles,
ranks did not exceed virtue,
the army did not insult the authorities,
the brigades did not press upon the army,
and the people had no slanderous words;
this was how he restored the hegemony.
B8.18.4 The Duke went to Jìn
to attend the audience of the succeeding ruler.
B8.18.5 In the summer, the sixth month,
Zhèng Bó invaded Sòng,
reaching outside the Cáo Gate.
Then he met with Chǔ Zǐ to attack Sòng,
taking Zhāojiá.
Zǐxīn of Chǔ and Huáng Chén of Zhèng
invaded Chénggào
and took Yōuqiū.
Together they attacked Péngchéng
and installed Yú Shí, Xiàng Wèirén,
Lín Zhū, Xiàng Dài,
and Yú Fǔ of Sòng there,
leaving three hundred chariots to garrison it before returning.
The text says, "Re-entered."
Whenever one leaves his state,
and the state welcomes and establishes him,
it is called
"Entered";
if he recovers his position,
it is called
"Returned Home";
if feudal lords install him,
it is called
"Returned";
if it involves evil, it says "Re-entered."
The people of Sòng were troubled by this.
Xījū Wú said,
"Why?
If the people of Chǔ shared our hatred
and showed us favor,
we would certainly serve them
and not dare to be double-minded.
But a great state is never satisfied;
even if it treats us as a border town, it still feels resentment.
Otherwise,
they gather those I hate,
make them assist in their government,
to take advantage of my rifts—
that would also be my trouble.
Now they are going to exalt the wicked among the feudal lords
and divide their land
to block the Great Road.
To gratify the wicked and alienate the submissive,
to poison the feudal lords
and frighten Wú
and Jìn—
our gains will be many,
so it is not my worry.
Furthermore, why serve Jìn?
Jìn will certainly worry about this."
B8.18.6 The Duke arrived from Jìn.
Fàn Xuānzǐ of Jìn came on a mission of courtesy
and to return the visit.
The gentleman said that Jìn was ritual in this.
B8.18.7 In the autumn,
Qǐ Huán Gōng came for an audience,
to console the Duke
and to ask about the affairs of Jìn.
The Duke told him about the ruler of Jìn.
Thereupon the Earl of Qǐ went frequently for audience in Jìn
and requested a marriage alliance.
B8.18.8 In the seventh month,
Lǎo Zuǒ and
Huá Xǐ of Sòng besieged Péngchéng;
Lǎo Zuǒ died there.
B8.18.9 In the eighth month,
Zhū Xuān Gōng came for an audience,
coming to appear upon his accession.
B8.18.10 They built the deer park;
it is recorded
because it was not the right time.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
the Duke died in the Lùqǐn;
this means it was in the proper way.
B8.18.12 In the winter, the eleventh month,
Zǐzhòng of Chǔ went to save Péngchéng
and attacked Sòng.
Huá Yuán of Sòng went to Jìn to report the emergency.
Hán Xiànzǐ was in charge of government
and said,
"If you wish to win over people,
you must first work hard for them.
Achieving hegemony and securing the borders
starts with Sòng."
The Marquis of Jìn stationed his army at Táigǔ
to save Sòng.
They encountered the Chǔ army at the valley of Míjiǎo, and the Chǔ army retreated.
B8.18.13 Shì Fáng of Jìn came to request an army.
Jì Wénzǐ asked Zāng Wǔzhòng about the number of troops,
who replied:
“In the campaign against Zhèng,
Zhì Bó indeed came;
he was the assistant of the Lower Army.
Now Zhì Jì also assists the Lower Army;
to act as in the campaign against Zhèng is acceptable.
In serving a great state,
not to lose the order of rank and to add respect
is ritual.”
They followed this.
B8.18.14 In the twelfth month,
Mèng Xiànzǐ met at Xū Tīng,
to plan the rescue of Sòng.
The people of Sòng declined the feudal lords
and requested an army to besiege Péngchéng.
Mèng Xiànzǐ requested leave from the feudal lords
and returned earlier to attend a burial.
B8.18.15 On dīngwèi,
our ruler Lord Chéng was buried. This was recorded because it was in proper order.
A9.1 The Annals of the First Year of Lord Xiāng
A9.1.1 In the first year, spring,
Royal first month,
the Lord ascended the throne.
A9.1.2 Zhòngsūn Miè met with Luán Yǎn of Jìn,
Huà Yuán of Sòng,
Nìng Zhí of Wèi,
the people of Cáo,
the people of Jǔ,
the people of Zhū,
the people of Téng,
and the people of Xuē to besiege Péngchéng in Sòng.
A9.1.3 In summer,
Hán Jué of Jìn led an army to attack Zhèng;
Zhòngsūn Miè met with Cuī Zhù of Qí,
the people of Cáo,
the people of Zhū,
and the people of Qǐ and halted at Zèng.
A9.1.4 In autumn,
Prince Rénfū of Chǔ led an army to invade Sòng.
A9.1.5 In the ninth month, on xīnyǒu,
the Heavenly King died.
A9.1.6 The Viscount of Zhū came for an audience.
A9.1.7 In winter,
the Marquis of Wèi sent Gōngsūn Piáo on a mission of inquiry.
The Marquis of Jìn sent Xún Yíng on a mission of inquiry.
B9.1 The Commentary on the First Year of Lord Xiāng
B9.1.1 In the first year, spring, on jǐhài,
they besieged Péngchéng in Sòng.
It was not Sòng territory;
it was recorded retrospectively.
At this time, they punished Lǔ Shí for the sake of Sòng,
therefore it is called Sòng territory;
moreover, as it did not give place to the rebels,
it is called Sòng’s intent.
Péngchéng surrendered to Jìn.
The people of Jìn took the five high officials of Sòng
who were in Péngchéng and returned,
placing them in Hùqiū.
The people of Qí did not join at Péngchéng,
and the people of Jìn took this as a reason for punishment.
In the second month,
Crown Prince Guāng of Qí became a hostage in Jìn.
B9.1.2 In summer, the fifth month,
Hán Jué and Xún Yǎn of Jìn led the armies of the feudal lords to attack Zhèng,
entered its outer wall,
and defeated its infantry on the Wěi River.
Then the armies of the eastern lords halted at Zèng
to wait for the Jìn army.
The Jìn army, from Zhèng, used the army at Zèng to invade Jiāo, Yí, and Chén in Chǔ.
The Marquis of Jìn and the Marquis of Wèi halted at Qī
to act as support.
B9.1.3 In autumn,
Zǐxīn of Chǔ rescued Zhèng
and invaded Lǚ and Liú in Sòng.
Zǐrán of Zhèng invaded Sòng
and took Quǎnqiū.
B9.1.4 In the ninth month,
the Viscount of Zhū came for an audience,
which was ritual.
B9.1.5 In winter,
Zǐshū of Wèi and Zhì Wǔzǐ of Jìn came on missions of inquiry,
which was ritual.
Whenever a feudal lord ascends the throne,
small states pay court to him,
and great states send missions of inquiry to him,
to continue friendship, establish trust,
plan affairs, and supplement deficiencies;
these are the greatest parts of ritual.
A9.2 The Annals of the Second Year of Lord Xiāng
A9.2.1 In the second year, spring,
Royal first month,
they buried King Jiǎn.
A9.2.2 The army of Zhèng attacked Sòng.
A9.2.3 In summer, the fifth month, on gēngyín,
the Lady Jiāng died.
A9.2.4 In the sixth month, on gēngchén,
Count Gùn of Zhèng died.
A9.2.5 The army of Jìn,
the army of Sòng,
and Nìng Zhí of Wèi invaded Zhèng.
A9.2.6 In autumn, the seventh month,
Zhòngsūn Miè met with Xún Yíng of Jìn,
Huà Yuán of Sòng,
Sūn Línfù of Wèi,
and the people of Cáo
and Zhū at Qī.
A9.2.7 On jǐchǒu,
our Little Lady Qí Jiāng was buried.
A9.2.8 Shūsūn Bǎo went to Sòng.
A9.2.9 In winter,
Zhòngsūn Miè met with Xún Yíng of Jìn,
Cuī Zhù of Qí,
Huà Yuán of Sòng,
Sūn Línfù of Wèi,
the people of Cáo,
the people of Zhū,
the people of Téng,
the people of Xuē,
and the people of Xiǎo Zhū at Qī,
and subsequently walled Hǔláo.
A9.2.10 Chǔ killed its high official Prince Shēn.
B9.2 The Commentary on the Second Year of Lord Xiāng
B9.2.1 In the second year, spring,
the army of Zhèng invaded Sòng,
which was an order from Chǔ.
B9.2.2 The Marquis of Qí attacked Lái.
The people of Lái sent Zhèng Yúzǐ to bribe Sùshā Wèi with horses and cattle,
a hundred head of each,
and the Qí army then returned.
Superior men thereby knew why Lord Líng of Qí was called
“Líng.”
B9.2.3 In summer,
Qí Jiāng died.
Previously,
Mù Jiāng had ordered the selection of beautiful catalpa wood
to make a coffin and a large zither for herself.
Jì Wénzǐ took these for the burial.
The superior man said:
“This was not ritual.
Ritual involves no reversal.
A wife
is one who cares for the mother-in-law.
To diminish the mother-in-law to provide for the wife
—no reversal is greater than this.
The Odes say:
‘Only the wise man,
when told wise words,
follows the path of virtue.’
Jìsūn was thus not wise.
Furthermore, Lady Jiāng
was the grandmother of the ruler.
The Odes say:
‘Make wine and sweet spirits,
offer them to the ancestors and grandmothers,
to fulfill all rituals
and bring down many blessings.’”
B9.2.4 The Marquis of Qí sent the various ladies of the Jiāng clan
and the women of the ancestral house to attend the burial,
and summoned the Viscount of Lái.
The Viscount of Lái did not come,
so Yàn Ruò walled Dōngyáng to press him.
B9.2.5 Lord Chéng of Zhèng was ill.
Zǐsì requested to rest the shoulders with Jìn.
The Lord said:
“The ruler of Chǔ, because of Zhèng,
personally received an arrow in his eye.
This was for no one else
but for me.
If I turn my back on him,
that would be discarding both effort and word.
Who then would be close to me?
As for sparing me,
that is up to you gentlemen.”
In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day Gēngchén,
Earl Gǔn of Zhèng died.
Thereupon Zǐhǎn took charge of the state,
Zǐsì conducted the government,
and Zǐguó served as the Sīmǎ.
The army of Jìn invaded Zhèng.
The various grandees wished to follow Jìn.
Zǐsì said,
"The mandate of the office has not yet changed."
They met at Qī,
to deliberate on the matter of Zhèng.
Mèng Xiànzǐ said,
"I request that we fortify Hǔláo to pressure Zhèng."
Zhī Wǔzǐ said,
"Excellent.
At the meeting of Zēng,
you heard the words of Cuīzǐ;
now he has not come.
That Téng, Xuē, and Xiǎozhū did not arrive
is all because of Qí.
My ruler's concern is not only Zhèng.
I, Yīng, shall report back to my ruler
and request it from Qí.
If the request is granted and I inform you,
it will be your achievement.
If the request is not granted,
the matter will then lie with Qí.
Your request
is a blessing for the feudal lords.
How could it be only my ruler who relies on it?"
B9.2.6 Mùshū went on a mission to Sòng,
to communicate with the successor ruler.
B9.2.7 In winter,
they met again at Qī;
Cuī Wǔzǐ of Qí and the grandees of Téng, Xuē, and Xiǎozhū all attended the meeting,
because of the words of Zhī Wǔzǐ.
Consequently, they fortified Hǔláo.
The people of Zhèng then made peace.
B9.2.8 Gōngzǐ Shēn of Chǔ served as the Right Sīmǎ;
he received many bribes from small states
to pressure Zǐzhòng and Zǐxīn.
The people of Chǔ killed him;
therefore the Record says,
"Chǔ killed its grandee, Gōngzǐ Shēn."
A9.3 The Classics of the Third Year of Lord Xiāng
A9.3.1 In the spring of the third year,
Gōngzǐ Yīngqí of Chǔ led an army to attack Wú.
A9.3.2 The Duke went to Jìn.
A9.3.3 In summer, the fourth month, on the day Rénxū,
the Duke and the Marquis of Jìn made a covenant at Chángshū.
A9.3.4 The Duke arrived from Jìn.
A9.3.5 In the sixth month,
the Duke met with Shànzǐ,
the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
and the Heir Apparent Guāng of Qí.
On the day Jǐwèi,
they made a joint covenant at Jīzé.
A9.3.6 The Marquis of Chén sent Yuán Qiáo to the meeting.
A9.3.7 On the day Wùyín,
Shūsūn Bào and the grandees of the feudal lords made a covenant with Yuán Qiáo of Chén.
A9.3.8 In autumn,
the Duke arrived from the meeting.
A9.3.9 In winter,
Xún Yīng of Jìn led an army to attack Xǔ.
B9.3 The Commentary for the Third Year of Lord Xiāng
B9.3.1 In the spring of the third year,
Zǐzhòng of Chǔ attacked Wú,
forming a select army.
They conquered Jiūzī
and reached Héngshān.
He sent Dèng Liào to lead three hundred soldiers in braided armor
and three thousand in silk-lined armor
to invade Wú.
The people of Wú intercepted and attacked them,
capturing Dèng Liào.
Those who were able to escape
were only eighty in braided armor and three hundred in silk-lined armor.
Zǐzhòng returned;
when he had celebrated the return with drinking for three days,
the people of Wú attacked Chǔ
and took Jià.
Jià
was a fine city,
and Dèng Liào
was also a fine officer of Chǔ.
The noble man said,
"In this campaign of Zǐzhòng,
what was gained was not equal to what was lost."
The people of Chǔ blamed Zǐzhòng for this.
Zǐzhòng was distressed by it,
and consequently suffered a heart ailment and died.
B9.3.2 The Duke went to Jìn,
which was his first audience.
In summer,
they made a covenant at Chángshū.
Mèng Xiànzǐ assisted.
The Duke performed the full kowtow.
Zhī Wǔzǐ said,
"The Son of Heaven is present,
and yet your Lordship deigns to perform the full kowtow;
my ruler is fearful."
Mèng Xiànzǐ said,
"Since my humble state is situated on the eastern frontier
and is in close proximity to enemies,
my ruler looks to your Lordship for support;
how could he dare not perform the full kowtow?"
B9.3.3 Because Zhèng had submitted,
and wishing also to cultivate friendly relations with Wú,
Jìn prepared to assemble the feudal lords.
They sent Shì Gài to announce to Qí, saying,
"My ruler has sent Gài to say
that because the year has not been easy and unexpected events have not been guarded against,
my ruler wishes to meet with one or two of his brothers
to consult about the lack of harmony.
He requests your Lordship to grace the meeting
and has sent Gài to beg for a covenant."
The Marquis of Qí wished not to grant this,
but found it difficult to be the cause of disharmony,
so he made a covenant outside the Éi.
B9.3.4 Qí Xī requested retirement;
the Marquis of Jìn asked him about a successor.
He recommended Xiè Hú,
who was his enemy;
they were about to appoint him, but he died.
He asked again.
He replied,
"Wǔ will do."
At that time Yángshé Zhí had died,
and the Marquis of Jìn said,
"Who can succeed him?"
He replied,
"Chì will do."
Thereupon, they made Qí Wǔ the Commandant of the Central Army,
and Yángshé Chì assisted him.
The noble man said of Qí Xī,
"In this, he was able to promote the good.
Recommending his enemy
was not for the sake of flattery;
establishing his son
was not out of favoritism;
promoting his subordinate
was not for factionalism.
The *Shāng Shū* says,
'Without partiality, without factionalism,
the King’s Way is broad and grand';
it must be speaking of Qí Xī.
Xiè Hú was promoted,
Qí Wǔ attained his position,
and Bóhuá obtained his office.
In establishing one office, three achievements were accomplished,
because he was able to promote the good.
It is only the good
who can promote their own kind.
The *Shī* says,
'Only because he possesses it,
does he resemble it';
Qí Xī possessed it."
B9.3.5 In the sixth month,
the Duke met with Duke Qǐng of Shàn and the feudal lords.
On the day Jǐwèi,
they made a joint covenant at Jīzé.
The Marquis of Jìn sent Xún Huì to meet the Viscount of Wú at the Huái River,
but the Viscount of Wú did not arrive.
B9.3.6 Zǐxīn of Chǔ served as the Lìngyǐn;
he was greedy and covetous toward small states,
so Duke Chéng of Chén sent Yuán Qiáo to the meeting to seek peace.
The Marquis of Jìn sent Hé Zǔfù to inform the feudal lords.
In autumn,
Shūsūn Bào and the grandees of the feudal lords made a covenant with Yuán Qiáo of Chén;
Chén requested to submit.
B9.3.7 The Marquis of Jìn's brother, Yánggān,
disrupted the ranks at Qǔliáng;
Wèi Jiàng executed his driver.
The Marquis of Jìn was angry
and said to Yángshé Chì,
"I assembled the feudal lords
to gain honor.
Now Yánggān has been disgraced;
what humiliation could be greater than this?
You must kill Wèi Jiàng;
do not fail!"
He replied:
"Jiàng has no divided heart.
In serving the ruler, he does not avoid difficulties;
having committed a crime, he does not flee from punishment.
Since he was about to come to offer his resignation,
why was it necessary to disgrace him with a command?"
When he finished speaking,
Wèi Jiàng arrived,
handed his letter to a servant,
and was about to fall on his sword.
Shì Fáng and Zhāng Lǎo stopped him.
The Duke read his letter,
which said:
"In former days, you, my ruler, were short of servants,
so you made this servant your Sīmǎ.
I have heard that
'leading the masses with compliance is what constitutes being martial,
and in military matters, to face death
without violating orders is what constitutes respect.'
You, my ruler, assembled the feudal lords;
how could I, your servant, dare not to be respectful?
If the ruler's army is not martial
and the officials are not respectful,
no crime could be greater.
I feared that this 'death'
would reach Yáng Gān,
and there would be no way for me to escape the crime.
Being unable to provide instruction,
even to the point of using the axe,
my crime is heavy;
how could I dare not to comply and further anger my ruler's heart?
I request to return and face death before the Sīkòu."
The Duke went out barefoot and said:
"My words
were out of personal affection;
your punishment, my master,
was according to military ritual.
I have a brother
whom I could not teach or instruct,
causing Gān to violate your great command;
this is my own fault.
Sir, do not double my fault;
I venture to make this my request."
The Lord of Jìn considered that Wèi Jiàng was able
to use punishments to assist the people.
Upon the return from the campaign,
he gave him a ritual feast
and made him an assistant in the New Army.
Zhāng Lǎo became the Sīmǎ of the Central Army,
and Shì Fù became the Hòuyǎn.
B9.3.8 Chǔ’s Sīmǎ, Gōngzǐ Héjì, invaded Chén,
because Chén had rebelled.
B9.3.9 Duke Líng of Xǔ served Chǔ
and did not attend the meeting at Jīzé.
In winter,
Zhī Wǔzǐ of Jìn led an army to attack Xǔ.
A9.4 The Classic of the Fourth Year of Duke Xiāng
A9.4.1 In the spring of the fourth year,
in the King's third month, on the day jǐyǒu,
Wǔ, the Lord of Chén, died.
A9.4.2 In summer,
Shūsūn Bǎo went to Jìn.
A9.4.3 In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day wùzǐ,
the Lady of the Sì clan died.
A9.4.4 Chén Chéng Gōng was buried.
A9.4.5 In the eighth month, on the day xīnhài,
our Little Lord Dìng Sì was buried.
A9.4.6 In winter,
the Duke went to Jìn.
A9.4.7 The people of Chén besieged Dùn.
B9.4 The Commentary on the Fourth Year of Duke Xiāng
B9.4.1 In the spring of the fourth year,
because of Chén’s rebellion, the Chǔ army
was still at Fányáng.
Hán Xiànzǐ was concerned about this
and said at court:
"King Wén led the rebellious states of Yīn to serve Zhòu,
only because he knew the proper time.
Now we are changing this;
how difficult it will be!"
B9.4.2 In the third month,
Chén Chéng Gōng died.
The people of Chǔ were about to attack Chén,
but upon hearing of the mourning, they stopped.
The people of Chén did not obey orders.
Zāng Wǔzhòng heard of this
and said:
"Since Chén does not submit to Chǔ,
it will certainly perish.
A great state followed ritual toward them,
yet they did not submit;
even for a large state, there would be calamity,
let alone a small one?"
In summer,
Péng Míng of Chǔ invaded Chén,
because of Chén’s lack of ritual propriety.
B9.4.3 Mùshū went to Jìn
to return the visit of Zhī Wǔzǐ.
The Lord of Jìn entertained him with a feast.
When the bells played the three pieces of "Sìxià,"
he did not bow.
When the musicians sang the three pieces of "Wénwáng,"
he again did not bow.
When they sang the three pieces of "Lùmíng,"
he bowed three times.
Hán Xiànzǐ sent the messenger Zǐyuán to ask him,
saying:
"You have honored our humble city with the command of your ruler.
According to the rituals of our former lords,
we relied on music
to honor you.
You, sir, passed over the great pieces
and bowed repeatedly for the lesser ones.
I venture to ask what ritual this is?"
He replied:
"The 'Sānxià'
is what the Son of Heaven uses to entertain the great lords;
I, your servant, dare not even hear it.
'Wénwáng'
is the music for when two rulers meet;
I, your servant, dare not be part of it.
'Lùmíng'
is how a ruler praises my humble ruler;
how could I dare not bow for such praise?
'Sìmǔ'
is how a ruler rewards the labors of an envoy;
how could I dare not bow repeatedly?
In 'Huánghuángzhěhuá,'
the ruler instructs the envoy, saying:
'You must consult extensively.'
I have heard that:
'To seek advice from the virtuous is called zī;
to consult with relatives is called xún;
to consult on ritual is called dù;
to consult on affairs is called zhōu;
and to consult on difficulties is called móu.'
Since I have obtained these five virtues,
how could I dare not bow repeatedly?"
B9.4.4 In autumn,
Dìng Sì died.
She was not laid in state in the temple,
there was no inner coffin,
and no sacrifice to appease the soul.
Jiàng Qìng said to Jì Wénzǐ:
"You are the chief minister,
yet the funeral of the Little Lord is incomplete;
this is failing to serve the ruler to the end.
When the ruler grows up,
who will receive the blame?"
Previously,
Jìsūn had planted six catalpa trees for himself
outside the east gate of Pǔpǔ.
Jiàng Qìng requested the wood,
and Jìsūn said:
"Go ahead."
Jiàng Qìng used the catalpa trees of Pǔpǔ,
and Jìsūn did not stop him.
The noble man said:
"What the 'Records' mean by
'To commit many acts of ritual impropriety
will surely bring trouble upon oneself'
must refer to this!"
B9.4.5 In winter,
the Duke went to Jìn to attend to administrative matters.
The Lord of Jìn entertained the Duke with a feast.
The Duke requested that Zèng be attached to Lǔ.
The Lord of Jìn did not grant it.
Mèng Xiànzǐ said:
"Because our humble ruler is so close to his enemies,
he wishes to serve you steadfastly
without failing in his official duties.
Zèng provides no military levies to the Sīmǎ;
as for the morning and evening commands given by your officials to our humble state,
our humble state is small and cramped,
and any deficiency would become a crime;
therefore our humble ruler wishes to gain assistance from Zèng."
The Lord of Jìn granted it.
B9.4.6 The people of Chǔ used Dùn to spy on Chén
and invaded it,
so the people of Chén besieged Dùn.
B9.4.7 Jiāfù, the Master of Wúzhōng, sent Mèng Lè to Jìn,
using Wèi Zhuāngzǐ as an intermediary
to present skins of tigers and leopards
in order to request peace with various Róng tribes.
The Lord of Jìn said:
"The Róng and Dí are without kinship and are greedy;
it is better to attack them."
Wèi Jiàng said:
"The feudal lords have newly submitted,
and Chén has newly come to seek peace;
they will be watching us.
If we show virtue,
they will be harmonious;
if not,
they will become estranged.
To fatigue the army against the Róng
while Chǔ attacks Chén,
we will surely be unable to save it;
this is to abandon Chén.
All the Huá states will surely revolt.
The Róng are like birds and beasts.
To gain the Róng and lose the Huá,
would that not be unacceptable?
The 'Exhortations of Xià' has a saying:
'There was Hòu Yì of Yǒu Qióng.'"
The Duke said:
"What was Hòu Yì like?"
He replied:
"In the past, when the house of Xià was declining,
Hòu Yì moved from Chú to Qióng Shí,
and using the people of Xià, he replaced the Xià administration.
Relying on his archery,
he did not cultivate the affairs of the people,
but indulged in hunting wild animals on the plains.
He discarded Wǔ Luó, Bó Yīn, Xióng Kūn, and Máng Yǔ,
and employed Hán Zhuó.
Hán Zhuó
was a slanderous youth of the Bó Míng clan.
Hán, the lord of Bó Míng, discarded him,
but Yí Yì took him in,
trusted him and employed him,
making him his prime minister.
Zhuó practiced fawning within the court
and bestowed bribes without,
fooling the people
and encouraging Yì to indulge in hunting.
He cultivated deceit and wickedness
to take over Yì's state and family;
inside and out, all submitted to him.
Yì still did not repent.
As he was returning from the hunt,
his household attendants killed and boiled him,
to feed him to his sons.
His sons could not bear to eat him
and died at the gate of Qióng.
Mǐ fled to the Yǒu Gé clan.
Zhuó took Yì's wife
and sired Jiāo and Xì;
relying on his slander, wickedness, and deceit,
and showing no virtue to the people.
He sent Jiāo to lead the army
and destroy the Zhēn Guàn and Zhēn Xún clans.
He settled Jiāo in Guò
and Xì in Gē.
Mǐ, coming from the Yǒu Gé clan,
gathered the remnants of the two states
to destroy Zhuó and establish Shào Kāng.
Shào Kāng destroyed Jiāo in Guò,
and Hòu Zhù destroyed Xì in Gē.
Yǒu Qióng was thus extinguished,
because they had lost the people.
In the past, in Zhōu,
when Xīn Jiǎ was Grand Scribe,
he commanded the hundred officials
to admonish the King regarding his faults.
In the 'Admonition of the Forester,' it says:
'Vast are the traces of Yǔ;
he mapped out the Nine Provinces
and opened up the nine roads.
People have their chambers and temples,
beasts have their lush grass;
each has its proper place,
and through virtue, they are not disturbed.
But the sovereign Yí Yì
was obsessed with wild animals;
he forgot the concerns of the state
and thought only of the does and stags.
Military force should not be used repeatedly,
but his use of it did not expand the house of Xià.
As the servant of the beasts in charge of the plains,
I venture to tell the charioteer.'
The 'Admonition of the Forester' being thus,
how can we not take warning?"
At that time, the Marquis of Jìn was fond of hunting,
so Wèi Jiàng spoke of this.
The Duke said:
"In that case, is there nothing better than making peace with the Róng?"
He replied:
"Making peace with the Róng has five benefits:
The Róng and Dí move their dwellings frequently for pasture,
they value goods and lightly regard land;
land can be purchased from them—
this is the first.
The borders will not be alarmed,
the people can be at ease in their fields,
and the farmers can complete their work—
this is the second.
When the Róng and Dí serve Jìn,
our four neighbors will be shaken and awed,
and the feudal lords will be awed and cherished—
this is the third.
Pacifying the Róng with virtue,
the troops will not be fatigued,
and the armor and weapons will not be worn out—
this is the fourth.
Taking Hòu Yì as a mirror
and using virtue as a measure,
those far away will come and those nearby will be at peace—
this is the fifth.
May my lord consider it!"
The Duke was pleased
and sent Wèi Jiàng to make a covenant with the various Róng.
He cultivated the affairs of the people
and hunted only at the proper times.
B9.4.8 In the winter, in the tenth month,
the people of Zhū and Jǔ attacked Zéng.
Zāng Hé went to rescue Zéng,
invaded Zhū,
and was defeated at Hú Dài.
The people of the capital who met the funeral procession
all bound their hair with hemp;
Lǔ began the practice of hemp-binding for mourning at this time.
The people of the capital sang a rhyme:
"Zāng's fox-fur robe
defeated us at Hú Dài.
Our lord is but a youth,
yet he employs a dwarf.
A dwarf, a dwarf,
who caused our defeat by Zhū."
A9.5 The Classic of the Fifth Year of Duke Xiāng
A9.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
the Duke arrived from Jìn.
A9.5.2 In the summer,
the Earl of Zhèng sent Gōngzǐ Fā on a mission of courtesy.
A9.5.3 Shūsūn Bǎo
and the heir apparent of Zéng, Wū, went to Jìn.
A9.5.4 Zhòngsūn Miè
and Sūn Línfù of Wèi met with the people of Wú at Shàndào.
A9.5.5 In the autumn,
the great sacrifice for rain was held.
A9.5.6 Chǔ killed its high official Gōngzǐ Rénfū.
The Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
the Viscount of Téng,
the Earl of Xuē,
the Heir Apparent of Qí, Guāng,
the people of Wú,
and the people of Zéng at Qī.
A9.5.8 The Duke arrived from the meeting.
A9.5.9 In the winter,
Chén was garrisoned.
A9.5.10 Gōngzǐ Zhēn of Chǔ led an army to attack Chén.
The Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
and the Heir Apparent of Qí, Guāng, to rescue Chén.
A9.5.12 In the twelfth month,
the Duke arrived from the rescue of Chén.
A9.5.13 On the day xīnwèi,
Jìsūn Xíngfù died.
B9.5 The Commentary of the Fifth Year of Duke Xiāng
B9.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
the Duke arrived from Jìn.
B9.5.2 The King sent Wángshū Chénshēng to complain about the Róng to Jìn;
the people of Jìn seized him.
Shì Fáng went to the capital
to report Wángshū’s duplicity in siding with the Róng.
B9.5.3 In the summer,
Zǐguó of Zhèng came on a mission of courtesy
to announce the succession of the new ruler.
B9.5.4 Mù Shū presented the Heir Apparent of Céng to Jìn,
to finalize the attachment of Céng.
The Record states,
"Shū Sūn Bào and the Céng Heir Apparent Wū went to Jìn,"
indicating he was ranked alongside the Grand Officers of Lǔ.
B9.5.5 The Master of Wú sent Shòu Yuè to Jìn,
to apologize for not attending the meeting at Jī Zé,
and to request to join the friendship of the feudal lords.
The people of Jìn were going to convene the feudal lords for him,
so they sent Lǔ and Wèi to meet Wú first
and to announce the date of the meeting.
Therefore, Mèng Xiàn Zǐ and Sūn Wén Zǐ
met with Wú at Shàn Dào.
B9.5.6 Autumn,
the Great Rain Sacrifice was performed
because of the drought.
B9.5.7 The people of Chǔ punished Chén for its rebellion,
saying,
"It was because the Lìng Yǐn Zǐ Xīn was truly greedy and grasping."
They then killed him.
The Record states,
"Chǔ killed its Grand Officer Gōng Zǐ Rén Fū,"
because of his greed.
The Noble Man said,
"King Gòng of Chǔ was not appropriate in his punishments.
The *Shī* says,
'The way of Zhōu is level and straight,
My heart is bright and clear.
If the discussion of affairs is not good,
The people gather to stabilize it.'
He himself lacked good faith
and killed a man to satisfy his own desire;
is that not difficult?
The *Xià Shū* says,
'Accomplishing sincerity brings success.'"
B9.5.8 In the ninth month on the day bǐngwǔ,
they covenanted at Qī,
to meet with Wú,
and to order the garrisoning of Chén.
Mù Shū considered the attachment of Céng to be disadvantageous,
so he sent a Grand Officer of Céng to receive orders at the meeting.
B9.5.9 Zǐ Náng of Chǔ became Lìng Yǐn.
Fàn Xuān Zǐ said,
"We have lost Chén.
The people of Chǔ punished the double-dealer
and established Zǐ Náng;
he will surely change their conduct
and swiftly punish Chén.
Chén is close to Chǔ,
and the people are in distress morning and night;
how can they not go to them?
To possess Chén
is not our concern;
it is only acceptable to be without it."
Winter,
the feudal lords garrisoned Chén.
Zǐ Náng attacked Chén.
In the eleventh month on the day jiǎwǔ,
they met at Chéng Dì to rescue it.
B9.5.10 Jì Wén Zǐ died.
When the Grand Officers entered for the enshrouding,
the Duke was in his place.
The Steward prepared the household utensils
as provision for the burial.
There were no concubines wearing silk,
no horses eating grain,
no hoarded gold or jade,
and no duplicate sets of precious vessels.
By this, the Noble Man knew
Jì Wén Zǐ's loyalty to the Ducal House:
"He served as minister to three rulers
and had no private accumulation;
can he not be called loyal?"
A9.6 The Annals of Duke Xiāng, Sixth Year
A9.6.1 In the sixth year, spring,
the King's third month, on the day rénwǔ,
Bó of Qǐ, Gū Róng, died.
A9.6.2 Summer,
Huá Ruò of Sòng came in flight.
A9.6.3 Autumn,
the burial of Duke Huán of Qǐ.
A9.6.4 The Viscount of Téng came to court.
A9.6.5 The people of Jǔ extinguished Céng.
A9.6.6 Winter,
Shū Sūn Bào went to Zhū.
A9.6.7 Jì Sūn Sù went to Jìn.
A9.6.8 In the twelfth month,
the Marquis of Qí extinguished Lái.
B9.6 The Commentary of Duke Xiāng, Sixth Year
B9.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
Duke Huán of Qǐ died.
For the first time, the death was announced with his name,
because of the covenant of alliance.
B9.6.2 Huá Ruò and Lè Pèi of Sòng were familiar with each other from youth;
when they grew up, they teased each other
and also slandered each other.
Zǐ Dàng became angry
and used a bow to pin Huá Ruò's neck in the court.
Duke Píng saw this
and said,
"Being the Minister of War yet pinned in the court,
it will be difficult for him to be victorious."
He then expelled him.
Summer,
Huá Ruò of Sòng came in flight.
Sī Chéng Zǐ Hǎn said,
"To have the same crime but different punishments
is not proper law.
To carry out a private execution in the court—
what crime could be greater?"
He also expelled Zǐ Dàng.
Zǐ Dàng shot an arrow at Zǐ Hǎn's gate
and said,
"How many days will pass before you follow me!"
Zǐ Hǎn treated him as kindly as before.
B9.6.3 Autumn,
Duke Chéng of Téng came to court;
it was his first audience with the Duke.
B9.6.4 The people of Jǔ extinguished Céng;
Céng had relied on its bribes.
B9.6.5 Winter,
Mù Shū went to Zhū
on a mission of state
and to cultivate peace.
B9.6.6 The people of Jìn, because of the Céng matter, came to
punish Lǔ,
saying,
"Why was Céng allowed to perish?"
Jì Wǔ Zǐ went to Jìn for an audience
and to receive their commands.
B9.6.7 In the eleventh month,
the Marquis of Qí extinguished Lái;
Lái had relied on its stratagems.
At the time of Zhèng Zǐ Guó's mission of state,
in the fourth month,
Yàn Ruò fortified Dōng Yáng
and then besieged Lái.
On the day jiǎyín,
they filled the moat around the city
and reached the battlements.
In the month when Duke Huán of Qǐ died,
on the day yǐwèi,
Wáng Qiū led an army along with Zhèng Yú Zǐ and the people of Táng to attack the Qí army;
the Qí army greatly defeated them.
On the day dīngwèi,
they entered Lái.
Duke Gòng of Lái, Fú Róu, fled to Táng.
Zhèng Yú Zǐ and Wáng Qiū fled to Jǔ,
and the people of Jǔ killed them.
In the fourth month,
Chén Wú Yǔ presented the ancestral vessels of Lái in the Temple of Duke Xiāng.
Yàn Ruò besieged Táng,
and in the eleventh month on the day bǐngchén, he extinguished it.
He moved the people of Lái to Ní.
Gāo Hòu and Cuī Zhù settled their fields.
A9.7 The Annals of Duke Xiāng, Seventh Year
A9.7.1 In the seventh year, spring,
the Viscount of Tán came to court.
A9.7.2 Summer, the fourth month,
there were three divinations for the Suburban Sacrifice,
but none were followed,
so the sacrificial victim was released.
A9.7.3 The Viscount of Little Zhū came to court.
A9.7.4 The walls of Bì were built.
A9.7.5 Autumn,
Jì Sūn Sù went to Wèi.
A9.7.6 In the eighth month,
there was an infestation of locusts.
A9.7.7 Winter, the tenth month,
the Marquis of Wèi sent Sūn Lín Fù on a mission of state.
On the day rénxū,
they covenanted with Sūn Lín Fù.
A9.7.8 Gōng Zǐ Zhēn of Chǔ led an army to besiege Chén.
A9.7.9 In the twelfth month,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
and the Viscount of Zhū at Wéi.
Kūnwán, the Earl of Zhèng, was going to the meeting,
but before he saw the feudal lords,
on the day bǐngxū,
he died at Cào.
A9.7.10 The Marquis of Chén fled and returned home.
B9.7 Commentary on the Seventh Year of Duke Xiāng
B9.7.1 In the spring of the seventh year,
the Viscount of Tán came to court;
it was his first audience with the Duke.
B9.7.2 In summer, in the fourth month,
they divined by turtle shell three times regarding the Jiao sacrifice,
but the response was unfavorable;
they then released the sacrificial animal.
Mèng Xiànzǐ said:
"From this time forward
I know the value of turtle-shell and milfoil divination.
Now, the Jiao sacrifice to Hòujì
is to pray for agricultural affairs.
Therefore, the Jiao is performed when the insects start to stir,
and one plows after the Jiao.
Now, having already plowed, we divine for the Jiao;
it is only fitting that the response was unfavorable."
B9.7.3 Nán Yí was the Governor of Bì.
Shúzhòng Zhāobó was the Superintendent of Waterways;
he wished to curry favor with the Jì lineage
and sought to ingratiate himself with Nán Yí.
He said to Yí:
"Please build a wall for Bì;
I will provide you with many laborers."
Therefore, the Jì lineage walled Bì.
B9.7.4 Duke Mù of Lesser Zhū came to court;
it was also his first audience with the Duke.
B9.7.5 In autumn,
Jì Wǔzǐ went to Wèi
to return the visit of Zǐshū
and to apologize for the delay in returning the visit,
showing there was no disloyalty.
B9.7.6 In winter, in the tenth month,
Hán Xiànzǐ of Jìn announced his retirement due to old age.
Mùzǐ of the Ducal Clan
had a debilitating chronic illness,
yet they were going to establish him as the head of the lineage.
He declined, saying:
"The *Shī* says:
'Is it not early and late?
But they say the road is heavy with dew.'
It also says:
'If you do not attend to it in person,
the common people will not trust you.'
I, Wújì, have no talent.
If I decline,
would that not be acceptable?
I ask that you establish Qǐ.
He associates with Tián Sū,
and is said to 'love benevolence.'
The *Shī* says:
'Peacefully attend to your position,
and love what is upright and straight.
The spirits will hear this,
and grant you great blessings.'
Caring for the people is virtue;
uprightness and straightness are correctness;
correcting the crooked is straightness;
and harmonizing these is benevolence.
In this way,
the spirits will listen
and great blessings will descend.
If we establish him,
would it not be acceptable?"
On the day gēngxū,
Hán Xiànzǐ sent Xuānzǐ to court
and then retired.
The Marquis of Jìn considered Hán Wújì to be benevolent
and put him in charge of the Grand Masters of the Ducal Clan.
B9.7.7 Sūn Wénzǐ of Wèi came on a mission of state,
to thank the Duke for Wǔzǐ's words,
and to renew the alliance made by Sūn Huánzǐ.
When the Duke ascended the platform, he also ascended.
Shúsūn Mùzǐ acted as the master of ceremonies;
he hurried forward
and said:
"At the meetings of the feudal lords,
our humble ruler has never followed after the ruler of Wèi.
Now you, sir, do not follow after our humble ruler;
our humble ruler does not know what he has done wrong.
Sir, please be a bit more patient!"
Sūn Wénzǐ had no reply,
nor did his expression show any change.
Mùshū said:
"The Sūn lineage will surely perish.
To be a minister yet act like a ruler,
and to err without changing,
is the root of destruction.
The *Shī* says:
'Returning from the palace to eat,
walking with a self-possessed gait.'
This refers to the followers.
If one acts as an equal yet walks with such a gait,
he will surely break."
B9.7.8 Zǐnáng of Chǔ besieged Chén;
the lords met at Wéi to rescue it.
B9.7.9 When Duke Xī of Zhèng was the Crown Prince,
in the sixteenth year of Duke Chéng,
he went to Jìn with Zǐhǎn,
and was not treated with ritual courtesy there.
He also went to Chǔ with Zǐfēng,
and there too he was not treated with ritual courtesy.
In his first year as ruler, when he went to court in Jìn,
Zǐfēng wanted to complain to Jìn and have him deposed,
but Zǐhǎn stopped him.
When they were about to meet at Wéi,
Zǐsì was acting as his assistant,
and the Duke again showed him no ritual courtesy.
His attendants remonstrated with him,
but he would not listen;
they remonstrated again,
and he killed them.
Upon reaching Cào,
Zǐsì sent an assassin to murder Duke Xī at night,
and reported to the feudal lords that he had died of malaria.
Duke Jiǎn was five years old;
they supported him and established him as ruler.
B9.7.10 The people of Chén were distressed by Chǔ.
Qìng Hǔ and Qìng Yín said to the people of Chǔ:
"We will send Lordship Huáng to you,
and then you may seize him."
The people of Chǔ followed this.
The two Qìngs sent word to the Marquis of Chén at the meeting,
saying:
"The people of Chǔ have seized Lordship Huáng.
If you do not return,
your ministers cannot bear the threat to the altars and ancestral temple,
and we fear there may be other plans."
The Marquis of Chén fled and returned home.
A9.8 Annals of the Eighth Year of Duke Xiāng
A9.8.1 In the spring of the eighth year,
in the royal first month,
the Duke went to Jìn.
A9.8.2 In summer,
Duke Xī of Zhèng was buried.
A9.8.3 The people of Zhèng invaded Cài
and captured Lordship Xiè of Cài.
A9.8.4 Jìsūn Sù met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the people of Qí,
the people of Sòng,
the people of Wèi,
and the people of Zhū at Xíngqiū.
A9.8.5 The Duke arrived from Jìn.
A9.8.6 The people of Jǔ attacked our eastern border.
A9.8.7 In autumn, in the ninth month,
the great rain-making sacrifice was performed.
A9.8.8 In winter,
Lordship Zhēn of Chǔ led an army to attack Zhèng.
A9.8.9 The Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Gài on a mission of state.
B9.8 Commentary on the Eighth Year of Duke Xiāng
B9.8.1 In the spring of the eighth year,
the Duke went to Jìn
for an audience,
and also to hear the regulations for court audiences and missions.
B9.8.2 The various lordships of Zhèng,
because of the death of Duke Xī,
conspired against Zǐsì.
Zǐsì struck first.
In summer, in the fourth month, on the day gēngchén,
he executed Zǐhú, Zǐxī, Zǐhóu, and Zǐdīng.
Sūn Jī and Sūn È fled to Wèi.
B9.8.3 On the day gēngyín,
Zǐguó and Zǐ'ěr of Zhèng invaded Cài
and captured the Minister of War of Cài, Lordship Xiè.
The people of Zhèng were all pleased,
except Zǐchǎn who did not agree,
saying:
"When a small state lacks civil virtue
but gains military merit,
no disaster is greater.
When the people of Chǔ come to punish us,
can we afford not to follow them?"
"If we follow them,
the army of Jìn will surely arrive.
With Jìn and Chǔ both attacking Zhèng,
from now on the state of Zhèng will not find peace for four or five years."
Zǐguó was angry with him and said:
"What do you know!
The state has its great commands,
and there are presiding ministers.
For a youth to speak on such matters,
you will surely be executed!"
B9.8.4 In the fifth month, on the day jiǎchén,
they met at Xíngqiū
to mandate the frequency of court visits and missions,
making the grand masters of the feudal lords listen to the commands.
Jìsūn Sù, Gāo Hòu of Qí, Xiàng Xù of Sòng, Nìng Zhí of Wèi, and a grand master of Zhū attended the meeting.
The Earl of Zhèng presented the spoils of victory at the meeting;
therefore, he personally listened to the commands.
The grand masters were not recorded
in order to show respect for the Marquis of Jìn.
B9.8.5 The people of Jǔ attacked our eastern borders
to demarcate the fields of Zēng.
B9.8.6 In the autumn, in the ninth month,
a great rain-seeking sacrifice was performed
because of a drought.
B9.8.7 In winter,
Zǐnáng of Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
punishing them for their invasion of Cài.
Zǐsì, Zǐguó, and Zǐ’ěr wished to follow Chǔ,
while Zǐkǒng, Zǐjiǎo, and Zǐzhǎn wished to wait for Jìn.
Zǐsì said:
"The *Odes of Zhōu* have it, saying:
'To wait for the Yellow River to clear,
how long is a man's life?
When divinations are many and consultations numerous,
they only serve to create a net of complications.'
Deliberating with many clans,
when the people have many disagreements,
will result in nothing being achieved.
The people are in urgent distress;
let us follow Chǔ for now
to provide relief for our people.
If the Jìn army arrives,
we shall then follow them as well.
Respectfully providing offerings of silk
to wait upon whoever comes
is the way of a small state.
Sacrificial animals, jade, and silk
should be ready at both borders
to wait upon the strong
and thereby protect the people.
If the invaders do not cause harm
and the people are not exhausted or ill,
is that not acceptable?"
Zǐzhǎn said:
"The means by which the small serve the great
is good faith.
If a small state lacks good faith,
military disorder will arrive daily,
and its ruin will be imminent.
The good faith of the five meetings,
if we now turn our backs on it,
even if Chǔ rescues us,
of what use will that be?
Chǔ's befriending us is without sincerity;
to treat us as a border territory is their real desire;
they cannot be followed.
It is better to wait for Jìn.
The ruler of Jìn is currently enlightened;
his four armies have no deficiencies;
his eight ministers are in harmony;
he will certainly not abandon Zhèng.
The Chǔ army has come from afar;
their provisions are about to run out;
they will certainly return quickly.
What is there to worry about?
I, Shè, have heard it said:
'There is no staff like good faith.'
To maintain a complete defense to weary Chǔ
and to rely on good faith while waiting for Jìn,
is that not acceptable?"
Zǐsì said:
"The *Odes* say:
'The counselors are very many,
and therefore nothing is settled.
Their speeches fill the court;
who dares to take the blame?
It is like planning a journey with those who will not walk;
therefore, one does not get on the road.'
I request that we follow Chǔ;
I, Fēi, will accept the blame."
Thus they made peace with Chǔ
and sent Wángzǐ Bópián to inform Jìn,
saying:
"Your Lordship commanded our humble city:
'Repair your chariot taxes,
alert your foot soldiers,
to punish those who are rebellious and predatory.'
The people of Cài did not comply;
the people of our humble city did not dare to rest in peace,
but called up all our humble levies
to carry out the punishment in Cài,
capturing the Minister of War Xiè,
and presenting him at Xíngqiū.
Now Chǔ has come to punish us, saying:
'For what reason did you take up arms against Cài?'
They burned our suburbs and fortifications
and overran our inner and outer walls.
The multitudes of our humble city,
husbands and wives, men and women,
have had no leisure to rest
while trying to save one another.
Being utterly overwhelmed and overthrown,
we had nowhere to make our appeal.
Among the people who died or fled,
if they were not someone's fathers or elder brothers,
then they were their sons or younger brothers.
Everyone is in sorrow and pain,
not knowing where to find protection.
The people, knowing they were at their wits' end,
accepted a covenant with Chǔ.
I, the lonely one, and my few ministers could not prevent it,
and we do not dare not to inform you."
Zhì Wǔzǐ sent the messenger Zǐyuán to respond to him, saying:
"Your Lordship received commands from Chǔ,
yet you did not even send a single messenger
to inform my unworthy ruler,
but immediately sought peace with Chǔ.
Since it is what your Lordship desires,
who dares to oppose your Lordship?
My unworthy ruler will lead the feudal lords to meet you beneath your city walls.
May your Lordship consider this."
B9.8.8 Fàn Xuānzǐ of Jìn came on a mission of state,
and thanked our Duke for the honor of his previous visit,
and announced that they would use the army against Zhèng.
Our Duke entertained him at a banquet.
Xuānzǐ recited the ode "Biào yǒu méi".
Jì Wǔzǐ said:
"Who would dare not to?
To use an analogy of plants and trees,
our unworthy ruler's relationship to your Lordship
is like being of the same scent and flavor.
We joyfully accept your command;
how could there be any question of the time?"
Wǔzǐ recited the ode "Jiǎogōng".
As the guest was about to leave,
Wǔzǐ recited the ode "Tónggōng".
Xuānzǐ said:
"At the battle of Chéngpú,
my late ruler Duke Wén
presented his achievements at Héngyōng
and received the red bow from King Xiāng,
to be kept as a treasure for his descendants.
I, Gài,
am a descendant who maintains the office of my late ruler;
how could I dare not to accept your command?"
Noble men considered this to show knowledge of ritual.
A9.9 The Annals of the Ninth Year of Lord Xiāng.
A9.9.1 In the ninth year, in spring,
there was a fire in Sòng.
A9.9.2 In summer,
Jìsūn Sù went to Jìn.
A9.9.3 In the fifth month, on the day xīnyǒu,
the Lady Jiāng died.
A9.9.4 In the autumn, in the eighth month, on the day guǐwèi,
our minor ruler Mùjiāng was buried.
A9.9.5 In winter,
the Duke met the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Count of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
the Viscount of Téng,
the Count of Xuē,
the Count of Qǐ,
the Viscount of Xiǎozhū,
and Guāng, the Heir Apparent of Qí, to attack Zhèng.
In the twelfth month, on the day jǐhài,
they made a covenant together at Xì.
A9.9.6 The Viscount of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
B9.9 The Commentary of the Ninth Year of Lord Xiāng.
B9.9.1 In the ninth year, in spring,
there was a fire in Sòng.
Yuè Xǐ was the Minister of Works
and was in charge of the administration.
He appointed the head of the Bó clan to be the Minister of Neighborhoods.
Where the fire had not yet reached,
they tore down small houses
and plastered the large houses,
He displayed the baskets and poles;
prepared the ropes and buckets,
and readied the water vessels;
weighed the light and heavy,
stored up the floodwaters,
and accumulated earth and plaster;
patrolled the length of the walls,
repaired the defenses,
and marked the fire lanes.
He made Huá Chén provide the regular laborers,
ordered the Suìzhèng to bring in the suburban guards,
and rush to the site of the fire.
He made Huá Yuè regulate the officers of the Right, and each officer attended to his department.
Xiàng Xù regulated the Left,
and it was the same.
He made Lè Chuán prepare the instruments of punishment,
and it was the same.
He made Huáng Yún order the Xiàozhèng to bring out the horses,
the Gōngzhèng to bring out the chariots,
prepare the armor and weapons,
and organize the military guard.
He made Xīsū Wú organize the treasury guard,
and ordered the Sīgōng and the Xiàngbó to alert the palace.
The Two Masters ordered the four Xiāngzhèng
to reverently offer sacrifices;
the Invoker and the Clan Head used horses at the four walls,
and sacrificed to Pán Gēng outside the West Gate.
The Marquis of Jìn asked Shì Ruò:
"I have heard
that from the disaster in Sòng one may know the Way of Heaven.
Why is that?"
He replied:
"The Fire Masters of antiquity
sometimes received offerings at the Xīn star,
and sometimes at the Zhù star,
in order to regulate the appearance and disappearance of fire.
Therefore, Zhù is the Chúnhuǒ,
and Xīn is the Dàhuǒ.
The Fire Master of the Tāotáng clan, È Bó,
lived in Shāngqiū
and sacrificed to the Dàhuǒ,
using fire to record the seasons.
Xiāng Tǔ followed this practice;
thus the Shāng people take the Dàhuǒ as their principal star.
When the Shāng people observe the signs of their calamities and failures,
they must begin with fire.
For this reason, it is known daily that there is a Way of Heaven."
The Duke said: "Can this be certain?"
He replied:
"It lies in the Way.
When a state is in chaos and lacks signs,
it cannot be known."
B9.9.2 In summer,
Jì Wǔzǐ went to Jìn
to return the visit of Xuānzǐ.
B9.9.3 Mù Jiāng died in the East Palace.
When she first went there and divined by stalks,
she encountered the eighth of Gèn
The scribe said:
"This is called Gèn changing to Suí
Suí
means going out.
You, my lady, must quickly go out!"
Jiāng said:
"No!
Of this, the Zhōu Yì says:
'Suí
means Great, Penetrating, Beneficial, and Firm;
no blame.'
Greatness
is the chief of the body.
Penetration
is the assembly of excellence.
Benefit
is the harmony of righteousness.
Firmness
is the trunk of affairs.
Embodying benevolence is sufficient to lead people;
excellence of virtue is sufficient to accord with ritual;
benefiting things is sufficient to harmonize righteousness;
firmness and stability are sufficient to manage affairs.
Since this is so,
it cannot be falsified;
therefore, although it is Suí, there is no blame.
Now I am a woman,
yet I participated in disorder.
I was originally in a low position
yet was not benevolent;
I cannot be called 'Great.'
I did not bring peace to the state;
I cannot be called 'Penetrating.'
I acted and harmed myself;
I cannot be called 'Beneficial.'
I abandoned my position and pursued beauty;
I cannot be called 'Firm.'
One who possesses these four virtues
follows Suí and is without blame.
I have none of them;
how can I be 'following'?
Since I have chosen evil,
how can I be without blame?
I must die here
and shall not be able to get out."
B9.9.4 Marquis Jǐng of Qín sent Shì Yá to request an army from Chǔ
to attack Jìn;
the Viscount of Chǔ granted it.
Zǐ Náng said:
"It is not possible;
at present, we cannot contend with Jìn.
The ruler of Jìn categorizes the capable and employs them;
in his promotions, he does not fail in his choices;
in his appointments, he does not change their methods.
His ministers yield to the virtuous;
his grandees do not fail in their duties;
his officers compete in being instructed;
his common people apply their strength to farming.
Merchants, artisans, and servants do not think of changing their trades.
Hán Jué is old,
and Zhì Yíng receives orders from him to conduct the government.
Fàn Gài is younger than Zhōngháng Yǎn, yet Zhōngháng Yǎn places him above himself
and makes him assistant of the Middle Army.
Hán Qǐ is younger than Luán Yǎn,
yet Luán Yǎn places him above himself
and makes him assistant of the Upper Army.
Wèi Jiàng has many merits,
yet he considers Zhào Wǔ to be worthy
and acts as his assistant.
The ruler is enlightened, and the ministers are loyal;
those above yield, and those below compete.
At such a time,
Jìn cannot be rivaled.
Only by serving them can we succeed.
May my lord consider it!"
The King said:
"I have already granted it.
Even if we are not equal to Jìn,
I must send out the army."
In autumn,
the Viscount of Chǔ encamped his army at Wǔchéng
to act as support for Qín.
The people of Qín invaded Jìn.
Jìn suffered from famine
and could not retaliate.
B9.9.5 In winter, the tenth month,
the feudal lords attacked Zhèng.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
Jì Wǔzǐ, Cuì Zhù of Qí, and Huáng Yún of Sòng followed Xún Yíng and Shì Gài in attacking the Zhuān Gate.
Běigōng Kuò of Wèi, the men of Cáo, and the men of Zhū followed Xún Yǎn and Hán Qǐ in attacking Shīzhīliáng.
The men of Téng and the men of Xuē followed Luán Yǎn and Shì Fáng in attacking the North Gate.
The men of Qǐ and the men of Ní followed Zhào Wǔ and Wèi Jiàng to cut down the roadside chestnut trees.
On the day Jiǎxū,
the army was at Fàn.
An order was issued to the feudal lords:
"Repair the equipment,
fill the provisions,
send back the old and young,
house the sick at Hǔláo,
grant a general amnesty, and
besiege Zhèng."
The people of Zhèng were afraid
and sought peace.
Zhōngháng Xiànzǐ said:
"Let us proceed to besiege them
to wait for the Chǔ people to come to their rescue,
and then fight them.
Otherwise,
there will be no success."
Zhì Wǔzǐ said:
"Grant them a covenant and withdraw the army
to exhaust the Chǔ people.
We shall divide our four armies into three divisions,
and with the elite of the feudal lords,
meet those who come.
While we are not yet weary,
Chǔ will be unable to act.
This is better than fighting.
To satisfy oneself by exposing bones on the battlefield
is not the way to contend.
Great toil has not yet ceased.
Superior men labor with their minds,
and lesser men labor with their strength;
this was the institution of the former kings."
The feudal lords all did not wish to fight,
so they granted Zhèng peace.
In the eleventh month, on the day Jǐhài,
they made a covenant at Xì;
Zhèng submitted.
When they were about to make the covenant,
the six ministers of Zhèng—Gōngzǐ Fēi, Gōngzǐ Fā, Gōngzǐ Jiā, Gōngsūn Zhé, Gōngsūn Chài, and Gōngsūn Shèzhī—together with their grandees and heirs of noble houses, all followed the Earl of Zhèng.
Shì Zhuāngzǐ of Jìn drew up the text of the covenant,
which said:
"From this day after the covenant is made,
if the state of Zhèng does not solely obey the commands of Jìn,
or if it harbors divergent intentions,
let it be as this covenant specifies!"
Gōngzǐ Fēi stepped forward and said:
“Heaven has brought calamity upon the state of Zhèng,
causing it to reside between two great powers.
The great power does not bestow virtuous words
but uses disorder to coerce us,
preventing our ghosts and spirits from receiving their pure sacrifices,
and preventing our people from enjoying the benefits of their land.
Husbands and wives suffer in bitterness and cramped distress,
with nowhere to voice their grievances.
From today, after the covenant is sworn,
if the state of Zhèng does not follow only those who possess ritual and strength and can protect the people,
and if we dare to have other intentions,
may it be the same as this!”
Xún Yǎn said:
“Change the text of the covenant!”
Gōngsūn Shèzhī said:
“We have called upon the great spirits to witness these words.
If they can be changed,
then the great power can also be betrayed.”
Zhì Wǔzǐ said to Xiànzǐ:
“I am indeed lacking in virtue,
yet I coerce people with a covenant;
how can this be ritual?
Without ritual,
how can one lead a covenant?
Let us conclude the covenant for now and withdraw,
cultivate our virtue, rest our army, and then come back;
in the end, we will certainly obtain Zhèng.
Why must it be today?
If I lack virtue,
the people will abandon me;
why would it only be Zhèng?
If we can rest and harmonize,
people from far away will come;
why rely on Zhèng?”
Thereupon they swore the covenant and returned.
B9.9.6 The people of Jìn did not achieve their aim in Zhèng,
so they led the lords to attack it again.
In the twelfth month, on the day guǐhài,
they attacked three of its gates.
In the intercalary month, on the day wùyín,
they crossed the Yīnbǎn,
and invaded Zhèng.
They halted at Yīnkǒu and then returned.
Zǐkǒng said:
“The Jìn army can be struck;
the army is old and weary,
and they have the intent to return home;
we will certainly defeat them greatly.”
Zǐzhǎn said:
“It is not possible.”
B9.9.7 The Duke escorted the Marquis of Jìn,
and the Marquis of Jìn held a banquet for the Duke on the Banks of the Hé,
asking the Duke’s age.
Jì Wǔzǐ replied:
“In the year of the meeting at Shāsuí,
our ruler was born.”
The Marquis of Jìn said: “It has been twelve years;
this is called one cycle,
one cycle of a star.
A ruler of a state has a son at fifteen;
to have a son upon being capped is the ritual.
You, Ruler, can now be capped.
Grand Master, why not prepare the capping equipment?”
Wǔzǐ replied:
“When the Ruler is capped,
it must be performed with the rituals of libation and sacrifice,
regulated by the music of metal and stone,
and held in the ancestral temple of the former rulers.
Now our ruler is on a journey;
it cannot be fully prepared.
We request to go to a brother state
and borrow what is needed there.”
The Marquis of Jìn said:
“Agreed.”
The Duke returned,
reached Wèi,
and was capped in the temple of Chéng Gōng,
borrowing the bells and chimes there;
this was in accordance with ritual.
B9.9.8 The Master of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
Zǐsì was about to make peace with Chǔ.
Zǐkǒng and Zǐjiǎo said:
“We swore a covenant with the great power;
before the blood on our mouths is dry, we would turn our backs on it—
is that permissible?”
Zǐsì and Zǐzhǎn said:
“Our covenant certainly said,
‘Follow only the strong.’
Now the Chǔ army has arrived,
and Jìn does not save us,
thus Chǔ is the strong one.
As for the words of the covenant oath,
how would we dare to turn our backs on them?
Moreover, a coerced covenant lacks substance,
and the spirits do not preside over it.
What they preside over is only good faith;
good faith is
the token of words,
and the master of goodness;
therefore they preside over it.
The bright spirits do not sanctify a coerced covenant;
turning one’s back on it
is permissible.”
Thereupon they made peace with Chǔ.
Gōngzǐ Bàróng entered to swear the covenant,
and they swore a covenant together at Zhōngfēn.
The wife of Chǔ Zhuāng died,
and the King returned before he could settle Zhèng.
B9.9.9 The Marquis of Jìn returned
and planned how to give rest to the people.
Wèi Jiàng requested to grant remissions
and to distribute stored grain to lend.
From the Duke downwards,
if any had stores,
they brought them all out.
In the state there were no stagnant stores,
and there were also no destitute people;
the Duke did not monopolize profits,
and there were also no greedy people.
For prayers they used silk instead of victims,
for guests they used a single victim,
utensils were not newly made,
and carriages and robes were supplied from what was ready.
After this was practiced for a full year,
the state then had moderation.
Through three campaigns,
Chǔ was unable to contend with them.
A9.10 The Annals of Duke Xiāng, Year Ten
A9.10.1 In the spring of the tenth year,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
the Viscount of Téng,
the Earl of Xuē,
the Earl of Qǐ,
the Viscount of Xiǎo Zhū,
and the Heir Apparent Guāng of Qí, to meet with Wú at Zhā.
A9.10.2 In summer, in the fifth month on the day jiǎwǔ,
they then destroyed Bìyáng.
A9.10.3 The Duke arrived from the meeting.
A9.10.4 Gōngzǐ Zhēn of Chǔ
and Gōngsūn Zhé of Zhèng led armies to attack Sòng.
A9.10.5 The Jìn army attacked Qín.
A9.10.6 In autumn,
the people of Jǔ attacked our eastern border.
A9.10.7 The Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
the Heir Apparent Guāng of Qí,
the Viscount of Téng,
the Earl of Xuē,
the Earl of Qǐ,
and the Viscount of Xiǎo Zhū to attack Zhèng.
A9.10.8 In winter,
thieves killed Gōngzǐ Fēi of Zhèng,
Gōngzǐ Fā,
and Gōngsūn Zhé.
A9.10.9 They garrisoned Hǔláo in Zhèng.
A9.10.10 Gōngzǐ Zhēn of Chǔ led an army to rescue Zhèng.
A9.10.11 The Duke arrived from the attack on Zhèng.
B9.10 The Zuo Commentary on Duke Xiāng, Year Ten
B9.10.1 In the spring of the tenth year,
they met at Zhā;
this was to meet with Shòumèng, the Viscount of Wú.
In the third month on the day guǐchǒu,
Gāo Hòu of Qí assisted the Heir Apparent Guāng,
and because of the previous meeting with the feudal lords at Zhōnglí,
he was disrespectful.
Shì Zhuāngzǐ said:
“Master Gāo assists the Heir Apparent in meeting the feudal lords,
intending to protect the altars of grain and soil,
yet in all things he is disrespectful;
this is to abandon the altars of grain and soil.
Will he not fail to escape calamity?”
In summer, in the fourth month on the day wùwǔ,
they met at Zhā.
Xún Yǎn and Shì Gǎi of Jìn requested to attack Bìyáng,
so as to enfeoff Xiàng Xū of Sòng there.
Xún Yīng said:
"The city is small but strong;
to conquer it is no feat of valor,
while failing to conquer it would be a laughingstock."
They requested it insistently.
On the day bǐngyín,
they besieged it,
but could not take it.
A retainer of the Mèng clan named Qín Jǐnfù
pulled a heavy supply cart to the labor service.
The people of Bìyáng opened the gate,
and the soldiers of the various lords rushed the gate.
When the portcullis was dropped,
Hé of Zōu held it up with his hands
to allow those who had entered the gate to escape.
Dí Sīmí lifted a wheel of a great chariot,
covered it with armor,
and used it as a shield.
Holding it in his left hand,
and pulling out a halberd with his right,
he broke through to form a passage for his squad.
Mèng Xiànzǐ said:
"This is what the *Shī* means by
'possessing strength like a tiger'."
The defenders let down a cloth,
and Qín Jǐnfù climbed it;
when he reached the battlements, he cut it.
He fell,
but they let it down again.
He recovered
and went up again three times.
The defenders offered him their excuses,
and so he withdrew.
He took the severed cloth
and displayed it throughout the army for three days.
The army of the lords stayed long at Bìyáng.
Xún Yǎn and
Shì Gǎi requested of Xún Yīng, saying:
"The floods will soon fall,
and we fear we will not be able to return.
We request to withdraw the army."
Zhì Bó was angry
and threw a small stool at them,
which passed between them,
saying:
"The two of you devised this affair,
and only afterward do you tell me this.
I fear chaotic commands,
so I did not oppose you.
You have troubled the ruler
and raised the various lords,
dragging an old man all the way here.
Now you have no military achievement to show,
and yet you wish to shift the blame to me
by saying:
'It was he who truly withdrew the army;
otherwise,
we would have conquered it.'
I am a weak old man;
can I bear such a heavy burden?
If in seven days you do not conquer it,
I shall surely take my retribution from you!"
In the fifth month, on the day gēngyín,
Xún Yǎn and Shì Gǎi led the troops to attack Bìyáng,
personally braving arrows and stones.
On the day jiǎwǔ,
they destroyed it.
The *Chūn Qiū* records "then destroyed Bìyáng",
to say that the action followed from the assembly of lords.
They gave it to Xiàng Xū.
Xiàng Xū declined, saying:
"If the ruler still deigns to pacify and comfort the state of Sòng,
and uses Bìyáng to enlighten my ruler,
then the ministers will be at ease.
What gift could be better than that?
If you grant it solely to me,
it would mean I raised the lords for my own enfeoffment.
What crime could be greater than that?
I dare to request this even at the cost of death."
They then gave it to the Gōng of Sòng.
The Gōng of Sòng entertained the Hóu of Jìn at Chǔqiū,
requesting to use the *Sānglín* music.
Xún Yīng declined.
Xún Yǎn and Shì Gǎi said:
"Among the lords, Sòng and Lǔ
are the states where ritual is observed.
Lǔ has the Dì music,
which is used for guests and sacrifices.
If Sòng uses *Sānglín* to entertain the ruler,
is it not also acceptable?"
When the dance began, the master of music signaled with the jīngxià banner.
The Hóu of Jìn was frightened and retreated into his chamber.
They removed the banner,
and after the feast was concluded, they returned.
When they reached Zhùyōng,
he fell ill.
Upon divination,
the *Sānglín* appeared.
Xún Yǎn and Shì Gǎi wanted to go back and offer prayers,
but Xún Yīng would not allow it,
saying:
"I declined the ritual;
they insisted on it.
If there are indeed ghosts and gods,
the blame will fall upon them."
The Hóu of Jìn recovered somewhat,
and he returned with the Zǐ of Bìyáng,
whom he presented at the Wǔgōng temple,
calling him a 'barbarian captive'.
Bìyáng
belonged to those of the Yún surname.
He had the Royal Historian of Zhōu select a successor of that clan,
and settled them in Huòrén,
which was according to ritual.
When the army returned,
Mèng Xiànzǐ appointed Qín Jǐnfù as his chariot-right.
Qín Jǐnfù fathered Qín Pīzī,
who served Zhòngní.
In the sixth month,
Zǐnáng of Chǔ and Zǐ’ěr of Zhèng attacked Sòng,
camping at Zǐwú.
On the day gēngwǔ,
they besieged Sòng,
and attacked the Tóngmén gate.
Xún Yīng of Jìn attacked Qín
in retaliation for its invasion.
The Hóu of Wèi went to the rescue of Sòng,
camping at Xiāngniú.
Zǐzhǎn of Zhèng said:
"We must attack Wèi.
Otherwise,
it will appear that we are not with Chǔ.
Having offended Jìn,
if we also offend Chǔ,
what will become of our state?"
Zǐsì said:
"The state is weary."
Zǐzhǎn said:
"Offending two great powers
will certainly lead to destruction.
Is weariness
not better than destruction?"
All the Great Officers agreed.
Therefore, Huáng’ěr of Zhèng led an army to invade Wèi,
by the command of Chǔ.
Sūn Wénzǐ divined about pursuing them
and presented the crack to Dìng Jiāng.
Lady Jiāng asked the interpretation.
It said:
"The crack is like a mountain.
A husband goes on campaign,
and loses his hero."
Lady Jiāng said:
"The campaigner losing his hero
is an advantage for those repelling invaders.
Let the Great Officers plan for it!"
The people of Wèi pursued them,
and Sūn Kuài captured Huáng’ěr of Zhèng at Quǎnqiū.
In the autumn, in the seventh month,
Zǐnáng of Chǔ and Zǐ’ěr of Zhèng invaded our western border.
On their return,
they besieged Xiāo.
On the day bǐngyín of the eighth month,
they conquered it.
In the ninth month,
Zǐ’ěr invaded Sòng's northern border.
Mèng Xiànzǐ said:
"Zhèng will surely have a disaster!
Its military activity is far too excessive.
Even Zhōu could not withstand such excess,
how much less Zhèng!
If there is a disaster,
it will surely fall upon its three men in power!"
Jǔ took advantage of the lords being occupied,
and thus invaded our eastern border.
The lords attacked Zhèng.
Cuī Zhù of Qí sent Crown Prince Guāng ahead to the army,
and thus he took precedence over the ruler of Téng.
On the day jǐyǒu,
they camped at Niúshǒu.
Previously,
Zǐsì and Wèi Zhǐ had a dispute.
When about to resist the army of the lords,
Zǐsì reduced the number of Wèi Zhǐ's chariots.
When Wèi Zhǐ distinguished himself in battle,
he again disputed with him.
Zǐsì suppressed Wèi Zhǐ, saying:
"Your chariots are not according to ritual."
Then he would not let him present his captives.
Previously,
when Zǐsì was making irrigation channels for the fields,
the Sī clan, Dǔ clan, Hóu clan, and Zǐshī clan all lost land.
Therefore, these five clans gathered a crowd of dissatisfied people
and used the followers of the Gōngzǐ
to start a rebellion.
Thereupon, Zǐsì took charge of the state,
Zǐguó became the Sīmǎ,
Zǐ'ěr became the Sīkōng,
and Zǐkǒng became the Sītú.
In the winter, the tenth month, on the day Wùchén,
Wèi Zhǐ, Sī Chén, Hóu Jìn, Dǔ Nǚfù, and Zǐ Shīpú led rebels to enter the capital.
At dawn, they attacked the presiding ministers at the court of the West Palace (Xīgōng),
killing Zǐsì, Zǐguó, and Zǐ'ěr,
and kidnapping the Earl of Zhèng to take him to the North Palace (Běigōng).
Zǐkǒng knew of the plot,
and thus he was not killed.
The Annals records them as "robbers,"
meaning that no high officials were among them.
Zǐxī heard of the robbers,
and without taking precautions, he went out,
setting out his father's corpse in state and then pursuing the robbers.
The robbers entered the North Palace.
He then returned,
distributed armor,
but many of his servants and concubines fled,
and many of his utensils and goods were lost.
Zǐchǎn heard of the robbers;
he set guards at the gates,
gathered the various officers,
closed the treasuries and storehouses,
carefully secured the stores,
and after completing defensive preparations and forming his ranks, he went out
with seventeen war chariots.
Having set out his father's corpse, he attacked the robbers at the North Palace.
Zǐjiǎo led the people of the capital to assist him,
and they killed Wèi Zhǐ and Zǐ Shīpú;
the rest of the robbers were all killed.
Hóu Jìn fled to Jìn,
while Dǔ Nǚfù, Sī Chén, Wèi Piān, and Sī Qí fled to Sòng.
Zǐkǒng took charge of the state
and prepared a written covenant
to define the order of ranks and the authority of governance.
The high officials, the various officers, and the sons of noble families would not comply.
He was about to execute them,
but Zǐchǎn stopped him,
asking to burn the document for them.
Zǐkǒng would not agree,
saying:
"I made the document to stabilize the state;
if I burn it because the masses are angry,
then it is the masses who govern.
Would the state not then be in difficulty?"
Zǐchǎn said:
"The anger of the masses is hard to oppose,
and personal desires are hard to fulfill.
To combine these two difficulties to stabilize the state
is the path to peril.
It is better to burn the document to appease the masses;
you will get what you desire,
and the masses will also find peace.
Is that not acceptable?
Personal desires lead to no success,
and opposing the masses invites disaster.
You must follow this!"
He then burned the document outside the Cāng Gate,
and only then were the people settled.
B9.10.10 The armies of the feudal lords walled Hǔláo
and garrisoned it.
The Jìn army walled Wú and Zhì,
and Shì Fáng and Wèi Jiàng garrisoned them.
The Annals records "Garrisoning Hǔláo of Zhèng,"
though it was not Zhèng's territory,
to indicate that it would eventually be returned to Zhèng.
Zhèng then made peace with Jìn.
B9.10.11 Zǐnáng of Chǔ came to the rescue of Zhèng.
In the eleventh month,
the armies of the feudal lords circled around Zhèng and headed south,
reaching Yánglíng.
The Chǔ army did not retreat.
Zhī Wǔzǐ wanted to retreat,
saying:
"If we now flee from Chǔ,
Chǔ will certainly become arrogant;
once they are arrogant, they can be fought."
Luán Yǎn said:
"Fleeing from Chǔ
is a shame for Jìn.
To assemble the feudal lords only to increase our shame
is worse than death.
I will advance alone."
The army then advanced.
On the day Jǐhài,
they encamped with the Chǔ army with the Yǐng River between them.
Zǐjiǎo said:
"Since the feudal lords have already formed an agreement,
they will certainly not fight.
If we follow Chǔ, Jìn will retreat;
if we do not follow them, they will still retreat.
When they retreat,
Chǔ will certainly besiege us.
Since Jìn will retreat anyway,
it is better to follow Chǔ
to make the Jìn coalition retreat."
At night they crossed the Yǐng
and made a covenant with the people of Chǔ.
Luán Yǎn wanted to attack the Zhèng army,
but Xún Yīng would not allow it,
saying:
"We truly cannot resist Chǔ,
nor can we protect Zhèng;
what crime has Zhèng committed?
It is better to leave them with the grievance and return.
If we attack their army now,
Chǔ will certainly rescue them.
If we fight and do not win,
we will be mocked by the feudal lords.
Since victory cannot be guaranteed,
it is better to return."
On the day Dīngwèi,
the armies of the feudal lords returned,
invading the northern borders of Zhèng as they went home.
The people of Chǔ also returned.
B9.10.12 Wángshū Chénshēng and Bóyú struggled for administrative power.
The King favored Bóyú.
Wángshū Chénshēng fled in anger.
When he reached the Yellow River,
the King called him back
and killed Shǐ Jiǎo to appease him.
He did not enter the capital,
but settled there.
The Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Gài to pacify the Royal House.
Wángshū and Bóyú pleaded their cases.
Wángshū's steward and Bóyú's grand officer Xiá Qín sat for the trial in the Royal Court.
Shì Gài heard the case.
Wángshū's steward said:
"Even people from wattle-gate and hole-in-the-wall dwellings all insult their superiors;
it is indeed hard to be a superior!"
Xiá Qín said:
"In the past, when King Píng moved to the east,
our seven clans followed the King.
The sacrificial animals were fully prepared,
and the King relied on them,
granting us the covenant of the Red-haired Bull,
which said:
'From generation to generation, you shall not lose your offices.'
If we were people of wattle-gates and holes-in-the-walls,
could we have reached the east?
And what would the King have relied upon?
Now, ever since Wángshū became minister,
government is conducted through bribes,
and punishments are waived for favorites.
The officers and their troops
cannot bear the weight of his wealth.
How could we not end up in wattle-gates and holes-in-the-walls?
Let the great state consider this!
If those below have no justice,
then what can be called 'rectification'?"
Fàn Xuānzǐ said:
"Whomever the Son of Heaven favors,
my ruler also favors;
whomever he opposes,
my ruler also opposes."
He ordered the Wángshū clan and Bóyú to present their documents for comparison.
The Wángshū clan could not produce their tally.
Wángshū fled to Jìn.
It was not recorded in the Annals
because it was not announced.
Duke Jìng of Shàn became a high minister
to assist the Royal House.
A9.11 The Classic for the Eleventh Year of Duke Xiāng
A9.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
in the royal first month,
the three armies were established.
A9.11.2 In the summer, the fourth month,
divination for the Jiāo sacrifice was performed four times,
but the results were not favorable,
and so the Jiāo sacrifice was not performed.
A9.11.3 Gōngsūn Shèzhī of Zhèng led an army to invade Sòng.
A9.11.4 The Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Cáo,
Heir Apparent Guāng of Qí,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
