the Viscount of Téng,
the Earl of Xuē,
the Earl of Qǐ,
and the Viscount of Little Zhū to attack Zhèng.
A9.11.5 In the autumn, the seventh month, on the day Jǐwèi,
they made a covenant together north of Bóchēng.
A9.11.6 The Duke arrived back from the attack on Zhèng.
A9.11.7 The Viscount of Chǔ
and the Earl of Zhèng attacked Sòng.
A9.11.8 The Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Cáo,
Heir Apparent Guāng of Qí,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
the Viscount of Téng,
the Earl of Xuē,
the Earl of Qǐ,
and the Viscount of Xiǎo Zhū to attack Zhèng,
meeting at Xiāoyú.
A9.11.9 The Duke arrived from the meeting.
A9.11.10 The people of Chǔ seized the Zhèng envoy Liáng Xiāo.
A9.11.11 In winter,
the people of Qín attacked Jìn.
B9.11 *Zhuàn* of the Eleventh Year of Duke Xiāng.
B9.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
Jì Wǔzǐ was about to establish three armies
and told Shūsūn Mùzǐ:
"I request to establish three armies,
each to levy for its own army."
Mùzǐ said:
"The administration will soon fall to you,
and you will certainly be unable to handle it."
Wǔzǐ firmly requested it.
Mùzǐ said:
"In that case, shall we make a covenant?"
So they covenanted at Xīhóng
and swore an oath at Wǔfùzhīqú.
In the first month,
they established the three armies,
dividing the Ducal House into three parts
and each taking one part.
Each of the three masters dismantled their own chariots.
The Jì clan made those among their chariot personnel
who entered with their corvée-service cities
exempt from levies,
while those who did not enter were levied double.
The Mèng clan made half of them servants,
like sons or younger brothers.
The Shūsūn clan made all of them servants;
otherwise, they would not be released.
B9.11.2 The people of Zhèng were distressed by the troubles caused by Jìn and Chǔ.
The various grand masters said:
"If we do not follow Jìn,
the state will nearly perish.
Chǔ is weaker than Jìn,
yet Jìn does not press us hard.
If Jìn does press us,
Chǔ will avoid it.
What can be done
to make the Jìn army exert themselves to the death for us,
so that Chǔ does not dare to oppose them?
Only then can we firmly side with Jìn."
Zǐzhǎn said:
"If we act poorly toward Sòng,
the feudal lords will surely arrive,
and we will then follow them and covenant.
When the Chǔ army arrives,
we shall follow them again,
and then the Jìn anger will be extreme.
Jìn can come frequently,
while Chǔ will be unable to;
we can then firmly side with Jìn."
The grand masters were pleased with this
and caused the border officials to provoke Sòng.
Xiàng Xù of Sòng invaded Zhèng
and made great captures.
Zǐzhǎn said:
"It is now acceptable to raise an army and attack Sòng.
If we attack Sòng,
the feudal lords' attack on us will surely be rapid;
we will then obey their commands
and also report to Chǔ.
When the Chǔ army arrives,
we will then covenant with them
while giving heavy bribes to the Jìn army;
then we will be spared."
In summer,
Zǐzhǎn of Zhèng invaded Sòng.
B9.11.3 In the fourth month,
the feudal lords attacked Zhèng.
On the day *jǐhài*,
Heir Apparent Guāng of Qí
and Xiàng Xù of Sòng
arrived first at Zhèng
and attacked the East Gate.
That evening,
Xún Yíng of Jìn arrived at the western suburbs
and invaded the old territory of Xǔ to the east.
Sūn Línfù of Wèi invaded its northern borders.
In the sixth month,
the feudal lords met at Běilín
and stationed their army at Xiàng.
Turning to the right,
they halted at Suǒ.
They besieged Zhèng,
displayed their forces at the South Gate,
and crossed westward at Jìsuì.
The people of Zhèng were afraid
and then sued for peace.
In autumn, in the seventh month,
they made a joint covenant at Bó.
Fàn Xuānzǐ said:
"If we are not careful,
we will surely lose the feudal lords.
If the feudal lords are worn out on the road
and achieve nothing,
can they be without double-mindedness?"
Then they covenanted.
The text of the covenant stated:
"All of us in this joint covenant:
do not hoard grain,
do not block profits,
do not harbor villains,
do not keep evildoers.
Rescue one another from disasters and calamities,
show sympathy in times of misfortune and rebellion.
Share the same likes and dislikes,
and support the Royal House.
If anyone violates this command,
may the Overseer of Caution, the Overseer of Covenants,
the famous mountains, the famous rivers,
the various spirits and sacrifices,
the former kings and former lords,
and the ancestors of the seven surnames and twelve states—
may the bright spirits execute them,
cause them to lose their people,
cast down their mandate and destroy their lineage,
and overthrow their state and house."
B9.11.4 Zǐnáng of Chǔ requested troops from Qín.
Zhān, the Grand Master of the Right of Qín, led an army to follow the Viscount of Chǔ
to attack Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng went to meet them.
On the day *bǐngzǐ*,
they attacked Sòng.
B9.11.5 In the ninth month,
the feudal lords brought out all their forces to again attack Zhèng.
The people of Zhèng sent Liáng Xiāo
and the Grand Steward Shí Chuò to Chǔ
to announce they were about to submit to Jìn,
saying:
"I, the lonely one, for the sake of the state altars,
cannot cherish the Ruler.
If the Ruler can pacify Jìn with jade and silk,
or else use military might to overawe them,
that would be my wish."
The people of Chǔ seized them.
The *Annals* records him as 'Envoy'
to indicate he was sent on a mission.
The armies of the feudal lords displayed their forces at the East Gate of Zhèng.
The people of Zhèng sent Prince Bópián to sue for peace.
On the day *jiǎxū*,
Zhào Wǔ of Jìn entered to covenant with the Earl of Zhèng.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the day *dīnghài*,
Zǐzhǎn of Zhèng went out to covenant with the Marquis of Jìn.
In the twelfth month, on the day *wùyín*,
they met at Xiāoyú.
On the day *gēngchén*,
they pardoned the Zhèng prisoners,
treated them all with ritual and returned them;
they withdrew the scouts
and prohibited looting.
The Marquis of Jìn sent Shū Xì
to announce this to the feudal lords.
The Duke sent Zāngsūn Hé to reply:
"Among all of us in this covenant,
when a small state has a fault
and a large state carries out punishment,
if there is a gift to offer,
it is rare that they are not pardoned.
My ruler has heard your command."
The people of Zhèng bribed the Marquis of Jìn
with Master Kuí, Master Chù, and Master Juān; fifteen pairs each of wide chariots and covered chariots,
fully equipped with armor and weapons,
totaling one hundred war chariots;
two sets of musical bells
along with their large bells and stone chimes;
and sixteen female musicians.
The Marquis of Jìn gave half of the music to Wèi Jiàng,
saying:
"You taught me to harmonize with the various Róng and Dí
so as to rectify the various Huá states.
Within eight years,
we have nine times assembled the feudal lords,
like the harmony of music,
with nothing that is not in accord.
I ask to enjoy this music with you."
He declined, saying:
"That the Róng and Dí are at peace
is a blessing to the state.
Within eight years,
you have convened the feudal lords nine times.
That the lords harbor no ill will
is due to your spiritual influence, my Lord,
and the toil of these various gentlemen.
What effort did I contribute?
Moreover, I wish for my Lord to be content in his pleasure
while considering its end.
The *Shī* says:
'Joyful is the gentleman,
the protector of the Son of Heaven’s state.
Joyful is the gentleman,
in whom blessings and rewards reside.
He bestows favors on those to his left and right,
and they follow his lead.'
Now, music is for making virtue secure,
righteousness is for dwelling in it,
ritual is for practicing it,
trustworthiness is for guarding it,
benevolence is for encouraging it,
and only then can one protect the states,
share in blessings and rewards, and attract those from afar.
This is what is meant by 'pleasure.'
The *Shū* says:
'In safety, think of danger.'
Thinking leads to preparation,
and preparation prevents misfortune.
I venture to offer this as a regulation."
The Duke said:
"As for your teaching,
how could I dare not to accept your command!
Yet, were it not for you,
I would have had no way to deal with the Róng,
nor could I have crossed the River.
Now, rewards
are the statutes of the state;
they are stored in the Archives of Covenants
and cannot be discarded.
You must accept them!"
It was from this point that Wèi Jiàng first had the music of metal and stone;
this was in accordance with ritual.
B9.11.6 Shùzhǎng Bǎo and Shùzhǎng Wǔ of Qín led an army to attack Jìn in order to rescue Zhèng.
Bǎo entered Jìn territory first.
Shì Fáng resisted him,
but he belittled the Qín army and failed to make preparations.
On the day rénwǔ,
Wǔ crossed the river from Fǔshì
and joined with Bǎo to strike the Jìn army.
On the day jǐchǒu,
Qín and Jìn fought at Lì,
and the Jìn army was utterly defeated
because they had made light of Qín.
A9.12 The Annals of the Twelfth Year of Duke Xiāng
A9.12.1 In the spring of the twelfth year,
in the King's third month,
the people of Jǔ attacked our eastern border
and besieged Tái.
A9.12.2 Jìsūn Sù led an army to rescue Tái,
and subsequently entered Yùn.
A9.12.3 In the summer,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Fáng to come on a mission of friendly inquiries.
A9.12.4 In the autumn, in the ninth month,
Chéng, the Master of Wú, died.
A9.12.5 In the winter,
Gōngzǐ Zhēn of Chǔ led an army to invade Sòng.
A9.12.6 The Duke went to Jìn.
B9.12 The Commentary on the Twelfth Year of Duke Xiāng
B9.12.1 In the spring of the twelfth year,
the people of Jǔ attacked our eastern border
and besieged Tái.
Jì Wǔzǐ rescued Tái
and subsequently entered Yùn,
taking its bell to make a ritual vessel for the Duke.
B9.12.2 In the summer,
Shì Fáng of Jìn came on a mission of friendly inquiries
and also to return thanks for the military assistance.
B9.12.3 In the autumn,
Shòumèng, the Master of Wú, died.
Mourning was held in the Zhōu Temple;
this was in accordance with ritual.
Whenever there is a funeral for a feudal lord,
those of a different surname
mourn outside the city;
those of the same surname
mourn in the ancestral temple of the clan;
those of the same lineage
mourn in the temple of the founding ancestor;
those of the same branch
mourn in the temple of the deceased father.
For this reason, since Lǔ belongs to the various Jī states,
mourning was held in the Zhōu Temple;
for the states of Xíng, Fán, Jiǎng, Máo, Zuò, and Jì,
mourning is held in the Temple of the Duke of Zhōu.
B9.12.4 In the winter,
Zǐnáng of Chǔ and Shùzhǎng Wúdì of Qín attacked Sòng,
stationing their army at Yángliáng
in order to retaliate for Jìn taking Zhèng.
B9.12.5 King Líng sought a queen from Qí,
and the Marquis of Qí asked Àn Huánzǐ for a response.
Àn Huánzǐ replied:
"The ritual phrases of the former kings include this:
When the Son of Heaven seeks a queen from the feudal lords,
the feudal lord responds:
'The daughters born of the primary wife are such-and-such number;
the children of the concubines are such-and-such number.'
If there are no daughters but there are elder or younger sisters and paternal aunts,
then he says:
'The remaining daughters of my predecessor, the late Lord So-and-so, whom I now guard, are such-and-such number.'"
The Marquis of Qí agreed to the marriage.
The King sent Yīn Lǐ to conclude the agreement.
B9.12.6 The Duke went to the court of Jìn
and also to thank Shì Fáng for the honor of his visit;
this was in accordance with ritual.
B9.12.7 Qín Yíng went to Chǔ.
Zǐgēng, the Minister of War of Chǔ, went on a mission of friendly inquiries to Qín
to provide comfort to the lady;
this was in accordance with ritual.
A9.13 The Annals of the Thirteenth Year of Duke Xiāng
A9.13.1 In the spring of the thirteenth year,
the Duke arrived from Jìn.
A9.13.2 In the summer,
Shī was taken.
A9.13.3 In the autumn, in the ninth month, on the day gēngchén,
Shěn, the Master of Chǔ, died.
A9.13.4 In the winter,
Fáng was fortified.
B9.13 The Commentary on the Thirteenth Year of Duke Xiāng
B9.13.1 In the spring of the thirteenth year,
the Duke arrived from Jìn,
and Mèng Xiànzǐ recorded the hardships in the temple;
this was in accordance with ritual.
B9.13.2 In the summer,
there was chaos in Shī,
and it split into three.
Our army went to rescue Shī
and subsequently took it.
Whenever the text records 'took,'
it indicates it was easy;
when a great army is used, it says 'extinguished';
when no territory is gained, it says 'entered.'
B9.13.3 Xún Yíng and Shì Fáng died,
and the Marquis of Jìn held a hunt at Miánshàng
to organize his troops.
He appointed Shì Gǎi to lead the Central Army.
He declined, saying:
"Bóyóu is my senior.
In the past, I studied under Zhībó,
and for that reason I assisted him;
it was not because I was more worthy.
I request to follow Bóyóu."
He then appointed Xún Yǎn to lead the Central Army,
with Shì Gǎi assisting him.
He appointed Hán Qǐ to lead the Upper Army,
but he declined in favor of Zhào Wǔ.
He then turned to Luán Yǎn,
who declined, saying:
"I am not as capable as Hán Qǐ.
Hán Qǐ wishes to place Zhào Wǔ above himself;
you should listen to him, my Lord."
He appointed Zhào Wǔ to lead the Upper Army,
with Hán Qǐ assisting him;
Luán Yǎn led the Lower Army,
with Wèi Jiàng assisting him.
The New Army had no commander.
The Marquis of Jìn found it difficult to find the right person,
so he made the petty officers
lead their soldiers and official subordinates
to follow the Lower Army;
this was in accordance with ritual.
Because of this, the people of the state of Jìn were in great harmony,
and the feudal lords subsequently became concordant.
The gentleman says:
"Yielding
is the master of ritual.
Fàn Xuānzǐ yielded,
and those below him all yielded.
Though Luán Yǎn was arrogant,
he did not dare to act against the consensus.
Because Jìn was thus brought to peace,
several generations relied upon it.
How fine it is to find a model in goodness!"
If one person models goodness,
the myriad people will live in joy and harmony;
can one not strive for this!
The *Shū* says:
"When the One Man has cause for celebration,
the myriad people rely on him,
and their peace will be everlasting."
Is this not what that means!
At the rise of *Zhōu*,
its *Shī* said:
"Taking *Wén Wáng* as a model,
the ten thousand states were inspired to trust."
This refers to modeling goodness.
When it declined,
its *Shī* said:
"The grandees are not impartial;
I alone am worthy in my service,"
which refers to not yielding.
In a well-ordered age,
the gentlemen value ability
and yield to those below them;
the commoners exert themselves in farming
to serve those above them.
Thus, those above and below possess ritual propriety,
and slander and evil are expelled and kept distant,
because there is no contention;
this is called "Excellent Virtue."
When it is in disorder,
the gentlemen boast of their achievements
to impose upon the commoners,
and the commoners brag of their skills
to insult the gentlemen.
Thus, those above and below lack ritual propriety,
and disorder and cruelty arise together,
because of contending for superiority;
this is called "Dark Virtue."
The ruin of a state
always inevitably stems from this.
B9.13.4 The Viscount of *Chǔ* fell ill
and informed the grandees, saying:
"I, the unworthy one, lack virtue,
having taken charge of the altars of soil and grain at a young age.
I was ten years old when I lost the former ruler,
and before I could learn the instructions of the tutors and guardians,
I received many blessings.
Because of this lack of virtue,
I lost my army at *Yān*,
thereby shaming the altars of soil and grain
and causing grief to you grandees;
this has been quite extensive.
If, by the spiritual power of you grandees,
I am able to keep my head and die a natural death,
so that for the seasonal sacrifices and the burial,
and in following the former ruler in the ancestral temple,
I request my posthumous title to be
either '*Líng*' or '*Lì*.'
You grandees choose between them."
No one replied.
Only after five requests
did they agree.
In autumn,
King *Gòng* of *Chǔ* died.
*Zǐnáng* deliberated on the posthumous title.
The grandees said:
"The ruler has already given his command."
*Zǐnáng* said:
"The ruler's command was reverent (*gòng*);
how could we ruin it?
The illustrious state of *Chǔ*,
the ruler presided over it,
soothing and possessing the *Mán* and *Yí* tribes,
broadly conquering the Southern Sea
and making them subject to the *Zhūxià*;
yet he knew his own faults.
Can he not be called reverent (*Gòng*)?
I request that he be given the posthumous title '*Gòng*.'"
The grandees followed his advice.
B9.13.5 *Wú* invaded *Chǔ*.
*Yǎng Yóujī* rushed to the scene,
and *Zǐgēng* followed him with an army.
*Yǎngshū* said:
"*Wú* is taking advantage of our mourning;
they think we are unable to field an army.
They will surely underestimate us and be off-guard.
You should set three ambushes to wait for me;
I will go and lure them."
*Zǐgēng* followed this.
They fought at *Yōngpǔ*,
and greatly defeated the *Wú* army,
capturing Prince *Dǎng*.
The gentleman considered *Wú* to be unkind.
The *Shī* says:
"Unkind is Great Heaven;
disorder has no end."
B9.13.6 In winter,
the walls of *Fáng* were built.
Recording this event
shows it was at the proper time.
At that time, they were going to build the walls early,
but *Zāng Wǔzhòng* requested to wait until the agricultural work was finished;
this was in accordance with ritual.
B9.13.7 *Liáng Xiāo* and Grand Ritual Master *Shí Chuò* of *Zhèng* were still in *Chǔ*.
*Shí Chuò* said to *Zǐnáng*:
"The former kings would divine for an expedition for five years,
and every year practiced its auspicious omens.
When the omens were repeated, they would set out.
If they were not repeated,
they would further cultivate virtue and divine again.
Now *Chǔ* is truly not strong;
what is the crime of the envoys?
To detain one high minister of *Zhèng*
in order to remove their pressure,
will only make them harmonious with each other and hate *Chǔ*,
and thus strengthen their ties to *Jìn*.
What use is this?
It is better to let them return and have their mission canceled,
so they will resent their ruler
and hate their grandees,
and thus pull against each other.
Would that not be better?"
The people of *Chǔ* sent them back.
A9.14 The Annals of the Fourteenth Year of Duke *Xiāng*
In the spring of the fourteenth year,
in the King's first month,
*Jìsūn Sù*
and *Shū Lǎo* met with *Shì Gài* of *Jìn*,
men of *Qí*,
men of *Sòng*,
men of *Wèi*,
*Gōngsūn Chài* of *Zhèng*,
men of *Cáo*,
men of *Jǔ*,
men of *Zhū*,
men of *Téng*,
men of *Xuē*,
men of *Qǐ*,
and the men of *Xiǎo Zhū* met with *Wú* at *Xiàng*.
In the second month, on the day *yǐwèi*, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
In the fourth month of summer, *Shúsūn Bào* met with *Xún Yǎn* of *Jìn*,
men of *Qí*,
men of *Sòng*,
*Běigōng Kuò* of *Wèi*,
*Gōngsūn Chài* of *Zhèng*,
men of *Cáo*,
men of *Jǔ*,
men of *Zhū*,
men of *Téng*,
men of *Xuē*,
men of *Qǐ*,
and the men of *Xiǎo Zhū* to attack *Qín*.
On the day *jǐwèi*, the Marquis of *Wèi* fled to *Qí*.
The people of *Jǔ* invaded our eastern border.
In autumn, Prince *Zhēn* of *Chǔ* led an army to attack *Wú*.
In winter, *Jìsūn Sù* met with *Shì Gài* of *Jìn*,
*Huà Yuè* of *Sòng*,
*Sūn Línfù* of *Wèi*,
*Gōngsūn Chài* of *Zhèng*,
men of *Jǔ*,
and men of *Zhū* at *Qī*.
B9.14 The Commentary on the Fourteenth Year of Duke *Xiāng*
In the spring of the fourteenth year,
*Wú* reported its defeat to *Jìn*.
The meeting at *Xiàng*
was for the purpose of planning against *Chǔ* on behalf of *Wú*.
*Fàn Xuānzǐ* enumerated the lack of virtue in *Wú*
in order to dismiss the people of *Wú*.
They seized Prince *Wùlóu* of *Jǔ*
because he had communicated with an envoy from *Chǔ*.
They were about to seize the *Róng* prince *Jūzhī*.
*Fàn Xuānzǐ* personally reprimanded him in the court,
saying:
"Come!
You of the *Jiāng Róng* clan!
Formerly, the people of *Qín* forced and drove your ancestor *Wúlí* from *Guāzhōu*.
Your ancestor *Wúlí*, wearing a rush-mat cloak
and braving thorns and brambles,
came to submit to our former ruler.
Our former ruler, Duke *Huì*, had a meager amount of land
which he split with you to live off.
Now, the feudal lords' service to our ruler is not as it was before;
likely because words have been leaked,
it is due to your responsibility.
For the meeting tomorrow morning,
you shall not participate.
If you do,
He replied:
"In the past, the people of Qín relied on their numbers,
were greedy for land,
and drove us, the various Róng, away.
Duke Huì displayed his great virtue
and said to us, the various Róng:
'These are the descendants of the Sì Yuè;
let us not cut them off or abandon them.'
He granted us the fields of the southern border,
where foxes and wildcats dwelt
and jackals and wolves howled.
We, the various Róng, cleared away the thorns and brambles,
drove away the foxes, wildcats, jackals, and wolves,
and became the non-encroaching, non-rebelling subjects of the former lords,
even until now without double-heartedness.
In the past, Duke Wén and Qín attacked Zhèng.
The people of Qín secretly made a covenant with Zhèng
and left a garrison there,
and thus occurred the battle of Yáo.
Jìn resisted them from above,
and the Róng blocked them from below.
The Qín army did not return;
we, the various Róng, truly [assisted Jìn].
It was
just like hunting a deer:
the Jìn people held its horns,
the various Róng pulled its hind legs,
and together with Jìn brought it down.
Why should the Róng not be spared blame?
From that time on,
in the many military services of Jìn,
we, the various Róng, have followed in succession through the seasons
to follow the ministers in charge,
just as in the spirit of Yáo.
How would we dare keep our distance?
Now, perhaps the official's armies truly have some deficiency
that alienates the feudal lords,
and yet you blame us, the various Róng!
We, the various Róng, in food, drink, and clothing
are not the same as the Huá.
Our ritual gifts do not circulate with yours,
and our languages are not mutually understood.
What evil could we do?
Not participating in the meeting
causes us no regret."
He recited the poem "Qīng Yíng" and withdrew.
Xuān Zǐ apologized
and had him attend to the affairs of the meeting,
achieving a state of harmony.
Then Zǐ Shū Qí Zǐ
acted as the assistant to Jì Wǔ Zǐ for the meeting.
From then on, the people of Jìn lightened the tribute from Lǔ
and increased their respect for its envoys.
B9.14.2 Zhū Fán, the ruler of Wú, having finished the period of mourning,
was about to establish Jì Zhá as ruler.
Jì Zhá declined, saying:
"At the death of Duke Xuān of Cáo,
the feudal lords and the people of Cáo did not consider the [rightful] ruler of Cáo righteous
and were going to establish Zǐ Zāng.
Zǐ Zāng left them
and ultimately would not become ruler,
so as to establish the ruler of Cáo.
The Superior Man says
'He was able to maintain his integrity.'
You, my lord,
are the rightful successor;
who would dare to interfere with you?
Possessing the state
is not my integrity.
Although I, Zhá, am untalented,
I wish to follow the example of Zǐ Zāng
so as not to lose my integrity."
When they insisted on establishing him,
he abandoned his household and went to farm,
so they let the matter rest.
B9.14.3 In summer,
the grand masters of the feudal lords followed the Marquis of Jìn to attack Qín,
to retaliate for the campaign of Yuè.
The Marquis of Jìn stayed at the border
and sent the six ministers to lead the armies of the feudal lords to advance.
Reaching the Jīng River,
they did not cross.
Shū Xiàng saw Shū Sūn Mù Zǐ;
Mù Zǐ recited the poem "Páo Yǒu Kǔ Yè."
Shū Xiàng withdrew and prepared boats.
The people of Lǔ and Jǔ were the first to cross.
Zǐ Jiǎo of Zhèng saw Běi Gōng Yì Zǐ of Wèi and said:
"If one joins with others but is not firm,
no hatred is greater than that.
What about the altars of the land and grain?"
Yì Zǐ was pleased.
The two men saw the armies of the feudal lords
and encouraged them to cross.
They crossed the Jīng and camped.
The people of Qín poisoned the upper reaches of the Jīng,
and many of the soldiers died.
Zǐ Jiǎo, the Minister of War of Zhèng, led the Zhèng army to advance,
and all the armies followed him
until they reached Yù Lín,
but they did not obtain a peace agreement.
Xún Yǎn gave the order:
"At cockcrow, harness the horses,
fill in the wells and level the hearths.
Look only to my horse's head."
Luán Yǎn said:
"In the orders of the state of Jìn,
there has never been such a thing.
My horse's head wishes to go east."
Then he returned.
The Lower Army followed him.
The Scribe of the Left said to Wèi Zhuāng Zǐ:
"Will you not wait for Zhōng Háng Bó?"
Zhuāng Zǐ said:
"The master's order was to follow the commander.
Luán Bó
is my commander;
I will follow him.
Following my commander
is how I wait for the master."
Bó Yóu said:
"My order was truly a mistake,
but what use is regret now?
I have abandoned many to be captured by Qín."
Then he ordered a general retreat.
The people of Jìn called it
"The Campaign of Delay."
Luán Zhēn said:
"This campaign
was to retaliate for the defeat at Yuè.
Since the campaign again has no merit,
it is the shame of Jìn.
I hold two positions on the war chariot;
how dare I not be ashamed?"
With Shì Yǎng, he charged into the Qín army
and died there.
Shì Yǎng returned.
Luán Yǎn said to Shì Gǎi:
"My younger brother did not wish to go,
but you called him.
My younger brother is dead
while you have come back;
this means you killed my younger brother.
If you do not leave,
I will kill you too."
Shì Yǎng fled to Qín.
At that time, Cuī Zhù of Qí, Huá Yuè of Sòng, and Zhòng Jiāng met to attack Qín.
They were not recorded
because they were remiss.
The previous meeting at Xiàng was the same.
Běi Gōng Kuò of Wèi was not recorded at Xiàng,
but was recorded for the attack on Qín
because he was acting as a substitute.
The Earl of Qín asked Shì Yǎng:
"Among the grand masters of Jìn, who will be the first to perish?"
He replied:
"It will likely be the Luán clan!"
The Earl of Qín said:
"Because of their arrogance?"
He replied: "Yes.
Luán Yǎn's arrogance and cruelty are already extreme,
but he may still escape ruin.
It will fall upon Yíng!"
The Earl of Qín said:
"Why is that?"
He replied:
"Wǔ Zǐ's virtue was among the people,
just as the people of Zhōu remember Shào Gōng,
loving even his sweet pear tree;
how much more so his son?
When Luán Yǎn dies,
Yíng's goodness will not yet have reached the people,
and what Wǔ Zǐ bestowed will have faded away,
while the resentment against Yǎn will truly be manifest.
It will surely rest upon him."
The Earl of Qín considered these wise words,
and on his behalf requested from Jìn that he be restored.
B9.14.4 Duke Xiàn of Wèi invited Sūn Wén Zǐ and Nìng Huì Zǐ to a meal.
They both put on their court robes and went to court.
The day grew late and they were not summoned,
for he was shooting wild geese in the park.
The two men followed him there,
and without taking off his leather cap, he spoke with them.
The two men were angry.
Sūn Wén Zǐ went to Qī,
and Sūn Kuài entered the capital as an envoy.
The Duke gave him wine to drink
and ordered the Music Master to sing the final stanza of the poem "Qiǎo Yán."
The Music Master declined.
Shī Cáo asked to do it.
Previously,
the Duke had a favored concubine
and sent Shī Cáo to teach her the qín;
Shī Cáo whipped her.
The Duke was angry
and whipped Shī Cáo three hundred times.
Therefore, Shī Cáo wished to sing it
to anger Sūn Zǐ
and thereby get revenge on the Duke.
The Lord had someone sing it,
and then recite it.
Kuǎi was afraid
and told Wén Zǐ.
Wén Zǐ said:
"The ruler is jealous of me;
if we do not act first,
we will surely die."
He gathered his family in Qī and entered the capital,
where he saw Qú Bóyù
and said:
"The ruler's tyranny
is known to you.
I greatly fear the state will be overturned;
what should be done about it?"
He replied:
"The ruler governs his state;
how could a minister dare to interfere?
Even if I did interfere,
how do I know it would be for the better?"
Then he left,
departing through the near gate.
The Lord sent Zǐ Jiǎo, Zǐ Bó,
and Zǐ Pí to make a covenant with Sūn Zǐ at Qiū Gōng, but Sūn Zǐ killed all of them.
In the fourth month on the day jǐwèi,
Zǐ Zhǎn fled to Qí,
and the Lord went to Juàn.
He sent Zǐ Háng to petition Sūn Zǐ,
but Sūn Zǐ killed him as well.
The Lord fled to Qí;
the Sūn clan pursued him,
defeated the Lord's followers at Ā Zé,
and the people of Juàn captured him.
Previously,
Yǐn Gōngtuó learned archery from Yǔ Gōngchā,
and Yǔ Gōngchā learned archery from Gōngsūn Dīng.
The two of them pursued the Lord,
while Gōngsūn Dīng drove the chariot for the Lord.
Zǐ Yú said:
"To shoot would be to turn against my teacher;
not to shoot would lead to my execution;
is it ritual to shoot?"
He shot at the two yoke-ends
and returned.
Yǐn Gōngtuó said:
"You were his teacher,
but I am distant from him."
He then turned back to pursue them.
Gōngsūn Dīng handed the reins to the Lord and shot at him,
piercing his arm.
Zǐ Xiān followed the Lord.
Upon reaching the border, the Lord sent the Zhù Zōng to report his flight
and to declare his innocence.
Dìng Jiāng said:
"If there are no gods,
why report?
If there are,
they cannot be deceived.
Since he has guilt,
how can he report that he has none?
To abandon the high ministers and plot with petty officials
is one crime.
The late Lord had high ministers to serve as teachers and guardians, yet he treated them with tyrannical contempt;
this is the second crime.
I served the late Lord with towel and comb,
yet he treated me like a common concubine;
this is the third crime.
Report the flight only;
do not report that he is without guilt!"
The Lord sent Hòu Chéngshū to offer condolences to Wèi,
saying:
"My unworthy ruler has sent me, Jí,
having heard that your Lord does not comfort the state
and has crossed into another border;
how could he not offer condolences?
Because of our covenant,
Jí was allowed to speak privately to the officials in charge,
saying:
'There was a ruler who was not kind,
and ministers who were not clever;
the ruler did not forgive,
and the ministers did not fulfill their duties;
excess and venting increased;
what should be done?'"
The people of Wèi sent Tàshū Yí to reply,
saying:
"We ministers, being untalented,
offended our unworthy ruler.
Our unworthy ruler did not apply the law to us
but sadly abandoned us,
causing your Lord concern.
Your Lord has not forgotten the friendship with our late Lord,
condescending to console us ministers
and showing deep sympathy.
We dare to bow for the command
and bow again for your great gift."
Hòu Sūn returned,
reported his mission,
and told Zāng Wǔzhòng:
"The Lord of Wèi will surely return!
He has Tàshū Yí to keep watch within
and his brother Zhuàn to go out with him.
One comforts the internal,
the other manages the external;
how could he not return?"
The people of Qí lodged the Lord of Wèi in Lái.
When he returned,
he brought back the provisions of Lái.
The Right Minister Gǔ followed him
but then fled back;
the people of Wèi were going to kill him.
He defended himself, saying:
"I did not like the start.
I was a fox-fur coat with lambskin sleeves."
So they pardoned him.
The people of Wèi established Gōngsūn Piāo,
with Sūn Línfù and Nìng Zhí as his assistants,
to follow the commands of the feudal lords.
While the Lord of Wèi was in Lái,
Zāng Hé went to Qí to console the Lord of Wèi.
The Lord of Wèi spoke with him
arrogantly.
He withdrew and told his men:
"The Lord of Wèi will not get back in.
His words are like dung.
In exile and yet not changing,
how can he recover his state?"
Zǐ Zhǎn and Zǐ Xiān heard of this,
saw Zāng Hé,
and spoke with him;
they spoke with reason.
Zāng Sūn was pleased
and told his men:
"The Lord of Wèi will surely enter.
As for those two,
one pulls him
and the other pushes him;
even if he did not want to enter,
could he help it?"
B9.14.5 The army returned from attacking Qín.
The Lord of Jìn abolished the New Army;
this was ritual.
An established state does not exceed half the army of the Son of Heaven.
Zhōu has six armies;
for the greatest of the feudal lords,
three armies are appropriate.
At this time, Zhī Shuò
fathered Yíng and died;
six years after Yíng was born, Wǔ Zǐ died.
Zhì Qiú was also young;
none could yet be established.
The New Army had no commander,
so it was abolished.
B9.14.6 Shī Kuàng was in attendance on the Lord of Jìn.
The Lord of Jìn said:
"The people of Wèi expelled their ruler;
is that not excessive?"
He replied:
"Perhaps it was their ruler who was truly excessive.
A good ruler rewards the good and punishes the excessive,
nourishes the people like his children,
covers them like Heaven,
and contains them like Earth.
The people serve their ruler,
love him like parents,
look up to him like the sun and moon,
respect him like the gods,
and fear him like thunder;
how could he be expelled?
A ruler
is the host of the spirits and the hope of the people.
If he distresses the people,
leaves the spirits in want and lacks sacrifices,
causes the people to lose hope,
and leaves the state altars without a host,
then what use is he?
If he is not removed, what should be done?
Heaven gave birth to the people and established for them a ruler,
to have him manage and shepherd them,
so they do not lose their nature.
For the ruler, there are assistants,
to have them teach and protect him,
so he does not exceed proper measure.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven has Dukes,
the feudal lords have Ministers,
Ministers establish side-chambers,
Great Officers have secondary lineages,
Officers have friends,
and the commoners, artisans, merchants, grooms, lackeys, shepherds, and stable-hands all have intimates
to assist and help one another.
If there is good, they reward it;
if there is error, they correct it;
if there is distress, they rescue them;
if there is failure, they reform it.
From the King down,
each has fathers, elder brothers, sons, and younger brothers
to supplement and supervise his governance."
The scribes record in books,
the blind musicians compose poems,
the masters of ceremonies recite admonitions,
the grandees offer counsel and instruction,
the officers transmit words,
the commoners voice criticisms,
the merchants and travelers speak in the marketplace,
and all the artisans offer their skills.
Therefore, the *Xià Shū* says:
"The heralds with wooden-clapper bells make their rounds on the roads,
the officials and teachers correct one another,
and the artisans apply their professional skills to provide remonstrance."
In the first month of spring,
this is done
to correct any lapses in regular conduct.
Heaven’s love for the people is great indeed!
How could it allow one man to behave willfully over the people,
to follow his own excesses,
and to discard the nature of Heaven and Earth?
It surely cannot be so."
B9.14.7 In autumn,
because of the campaign of Yōngpǔ,
Zǐnáng led his army to Táng
to attack Wú.
Wú did not come out to fight, so he returned.
Zǐnáng was in the rear-guard;
thinking that Wú was incapable, he was not on his guard.
The people of Wú, from the narrow pass of Gāozhōu,
intercepted and attacked them.
The people of Chǔ were unable to rescue one another,
and the people of Wú defeated them,
capturing the Chǔ prince Gōngzǐ Yígǔ.
B9.14.8 The King sent Liú Dìnggōng
to confer a command upon the Marquis of Qí,
saying:
"In the past, the Elder Uncle Tàigōng
assisted our former kings,
served as the limbs of the Zhōu house,
and acted as the teacher and protector of the myriad people.
His descendants were granted the title of Grand Master for generations,
to serve as a beacon by the eastern sea.
That the royal house has not collapsed
is truly dependent on the Elder Uncle.
Now I command you, Huán,
to follow the statutes of your uncle’s line,
to continue the work of your ancestors,
and not to disgrace your predecessors.
Be reverent!
Do not neglect my command!"
B9.14.9 The Marquis of Jìn asked Zhōngháng Xiànzǐ about the affairs of Wèi.
He replied,
"It is better to take this opportunity to settle it.
Wèi now has a ruler;
if we attack it,
we may not achieve our aims
and will only fatigue the lords.
Shǐ Yì had a saying:
'Take advantage of stability and soothe them.'
Zhònghuǐ had a saying:
'Despise those who are perishing;
take those who are in disorder.
To push over the perishing and strengthen the surviving
is the way of the state.'
May my lord settle the affairs of Wèi
and wait for the right time!"
In winter,
there was a meeting at Qī
to plan the stabilization of Wèi.
B9.14.10 Fàn Xuānzǐ borrowed feathered banners from Qí
and did not return them;
the people of Qí began to be disloyal.
B9.14.11 Chǔ's Zǐnáng returned from the campaign against Wú
and died.
When he was about to die,
his last words to Zǐgēng were:
"You must build walls for Yǐng!"
The superior man said:
"Zǐnáng was loyal.
When the ruler died,
he did not forget to enhance his fame;
when he himself was about to die,
he did not forget to protect the altars of the state.
Can he not be called loyal?
Loyalty
is the hope of the people.
The *Shī* says:
'The conduct returned to Zhōu,
what the myriad people hoped for';
this is loyalty."
A9.15 Annals of the Fifteenth Year of Lord Xiāng
A9.15.1 In the spring of the fifteenth year,
the Duke of Sòng sent Xiàng Xù on a friendly mission.
In the second month, on the day jǐhài,
an alliance was made with Xiàng Xù at Liú.
A9.15.2 Liú Xià went to meet the Queen at Qí.
A9.15.3 In summer,
the Marquis of Qí attacked our northern borders
and besieged Chéng.
The Duke went to rescue Chéng
and reached Yù.
A9.15.4 Jìsūn Sù
and Shúsūn Bào led the army to build the outer walls of Chéng.
A9.15.5 In autumn, in the eighth month on the day dīngsì,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A9.15.6 The people of Zhū attacked our southern borders.
A9.15.7 In winter, in the eleventh month on the day guǐhài,
the Marquis of Jìn, Zhōu, died.
B9.15 Commentary of the Fifteenth Year of Lord Xiāng
B9.15.1 In the spring of the fifteenth year,
Xiàng Xù of Sòng came on a friendly mission
and also to renew the alliance.
He met Mèng Xiànzǐ
and criticized his house,
saying:
"You have a fine reputation, but you beautify your house;
this is not what was expected."
He replied,
"While I was in Jìn,
my brother built it.
To destroy it would be a heavy labor,
and besides, I did not dare to interfere."
B9.15.2 The officials followed Shàn Jìnggōng to meet the Queen at Qí.
No high ministers went;
this was not in accordance with ritual.
B9.15.3 Gōngzǐ Wǔ became the Chancellor,
Gōngzǐ Bàróng became the Right Chancellor,
Wěizǐ Féng became the Grand Marshal,
Gōngzǐ Tuóshī became the Right Marshal,
Gōngzǐ Chéng became the Left Marshal,
Qū Dào became the Mò'áo,
Gōngzǐ Zhuīshū became the Zhēnyǐn,
Qū Dàng became the Liányǐn,
and Yǎng Yóujī became the Gōngjiùyǐn,
in order to pacify the people of the state.
The superior man said:
"In this, Chǔ showed it could appoint the right men to office.
Appointing men to office
is the urgent task of a state.
If one can appoint the right men,
then the people will have no covetous hearts.
The *Shī* says,
'Ah, I think of the person,
placed in that Zhōu rank';
this refers to appointing the right men.
The King and the Dukes, Marquises, Earls, Viscounts, and Barons, the Diàn, Cǎi, and Wèi officials, and the Grandees, each occupying their respective rank,
is what is called the 'Zhōu ranks'."
B9.15.4 During the rebellion of the Wèi and Sī clans in Zhèng,
the remaining rebels were in Sòng.
On account of Zǐxī, Bóyǒu, and Zǐchǎn, the people of Zhèng
offered bribes to Sòng,
including forty teams of horses, along with Shī Fá and Shī Huì.
In the third month,
Gōngsūn Hēi was sent there as a hostage.
The Sīchéng Zǐhǎn
handed over Dǔ Nǚfù, Wèi Piān, and Sī Qí to them,
but he spared the good Sī Chén and allowed him to escape,
entrusting him to Jì Wǔzǐ,
who placed him in Biàn.
The people of Zhèng minced those three men into pickles.
Shī Huì passed by the Sòng court
and was about to relieve himself.
His attendant said:
"This is the court."
Huì said:
"There are no men here."
The attendant said:
"It is the court;
why do you say there are no men?"
Huì said:
"There must be no men.
If there were still men,
how could they exchange ministers of a thousand-chariot state for a blind musician of lewd music?
It must be because there are no men."
Zǐhǎn heard this
and insistently requested and returned them.
B9.15.5 In summer,
the Marquis of Qí besieged Chéng
because of his disloyalty toward Jìn.
At this time, the outer walls of Chéng were built.
B9.15.6 In autumn,
the people of Zhū attacked our southern borders,
and an envoy was sent to report it to Jìn.
Jìn was about to hold a meeting to punish Zhū and Jǔ,
but the Marquis of Jìn fell ill,
and so it was stopped.
In winter,
Lord Dào of Jìn died,
and so they were unable to hold the meeting.
B9.15.7 Gōngsūn Xià of Zhèng went to Jìn for the funeral,
and Zǐjiǎo attended the burial.
B9.15.8 A certain person of Sòng obtained a piece of jade
and presented it to Zǐhǎn.
Zǐhǎn would not accept it.
The person who presented the jade said:
“I showed it to a jade carver,
and the jade carver considered it a treasure,
therefore I dared to present it.”
Zǐhǎn said:
“I consider not being greedy to be my treasure;
you consider the jade to be your treasure.
If you give it to me,
we both lose our treasures.
It is not as good as each person keeping his own treasure.”
The man kowtowed and reported, saying:
“A common man harboring a jade disk
cannot cross the countryside safely.
I offer this to request to be spared from death.”
Zǐhǎn placed him in his own neighborhood,
had a jade carver work it for him,
and after the man became wealthy, he sent him back to his place.
B9.15.9 In the twelfth month,
a man of Zhèng seized the wife of Dǔ Gǒu
and gave her to the Fàn family.
A9.16 The Classic of the Sixteenth Year of Duke Xiāng
A9.16.1 In the sixteenth year, spring,
the King's first month,
Duke Dào of Jìn was buried.
A9.16.2 In the third month,
the Duke met the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Count of Zhèng,
the Count of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
the Earl of Xuē,
the Earl of Qǐ,
and the Viscount of Lesser Zhū at Jùliáng.
On wùyín,
the grandees made a covenant.
A9.16.3 The men of Jìn seized the Viscount of Jǔ and
the Viscount of Zhū and returned with them.
A9.16.4 The Marquis of Qí invaded our northern border.
A9.16.5 In summer,
the Duke arrived from the meeting.
A9.16.6 In the fifth month, on jiǎzǐ,
there was an earthquake.
A9.16.7 Shū Lǎo met the Count of Zhèng,
Xún Yǎn of Jìn,
Nìng Zhí of Wèi,
and the men of Sòng to invade Xǔ.
A9.16.8 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí invaded our northern border
and besieged Chéng.
A9.16.9 The Great Sacrifice for Rain was performed.
A9.16.10 In winter,
Shūsūn Bǎo went to Jìn.
B9.16 The Commentary on the Sixteenth Year of Duke Xiāng
B9.16.1 In the spring of the sixteenth year,
Duke Dào of Jìn was buried.
Duke Píng ascended the throne;
Yángshé Xì became his tutor,
Zhāng Jūnchén became the Sīmǎ of the Central Army,
Qǐ Xī, Hán Xiāng, Luán Yíng, and Shì Yǎng became grandees of the Ducal Clan,
and Yúqiū Shū became the driver of the chariot horses.
They changed their ritual robes, reorganized the offices,
and performed the zhēng sacrifice at Qùwò.
Having alerted the guards and moved south,
they met at Jùliáng.
They ordered the return of encroached fields.
Because of us,
they seized Duke Xuān of Zhū and Duke Líbí of Jǔ,
and said:
“You have been communicating with envoys from Qí and Chǔ.”
The Marquis of Jìn held a banquet with the lords at Wēn,
and had the various grandees dance,
saying:
“The poems you sing must be appropriate to the occasion.”
The poem of Gāo Hòu of Qí was not appropriate.
Xún Yǎn was angry
and said:
“The lords have divergent intentions!”
He had the various grandees make a covenant with Gāo Hòu,
but Gāo Hòu fled and returned home.
Thereupon Shūsūn Bǎo, Xún Yǎn of Jìn, Xiàng Xù of Sòng, Nìng Zhí of Wèi, Gōngsūn Chài of Zhèng, and the grandee of Lesser Zhū made a covenant,
saying:
“Together we shall punish those who do not attend court.”
B9.16.2 The Baron of Xǔ requested to move to Jìn.
The lords then moved Xǔ,
but the grandees of Xǔ would not agree;
the men of Jìn sent the lords back.
Zǐjiǎo of Zhèng heard that they were about to invade Xǔ,
so he assisted the Count of Zhèng
to follow the army of the lords.
Mùshū followed the Duke.
Qǐzǐ led an army to meet Xún Yǎn of Jìn.
The Classic says “met the Count of Zhèng”
because of his rank as an Earl.
In summer, the sixth month,
they halted at Yùlín.
On gēngyín,
they invaded Xǔ
and halted at Hánshì.
B9.16.3 Xún Yǎn and Luán Yàn of Jìn led an army to invade Chǔ
in order to retaliate for the campaign of Yángliáng in Sòng.
Prince Gé of Chǔ led an army
and fought the Jìn army at Zhànbǎn.
The Chǔ army was utterly defeated.
The Jìn army then invaded the region outside Fāngchéng,
and once again invaded Xǔ before returning.
B9.16.4 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí besieged Chéng;
Mèng Rǔzǐ Sù intercepted him.
The Marquis of Qí said:
“This man loves bravery;
let us leave him to make a name for him.”
Sù then blocked the Hǎijìng pass and returned.
B9.16.5 In winter,
Mùshū went to Jìn on a mission of state
and also spoke of the trouble with Qí.
The men of Jìn said:
“Because our ruler has not yet performed the dì sacrifice and the people have not yet rested,
otherwise,
we would not dare forget your trouble.”
Mùshū said:
“Because the people of Qí, morning and night, vent their resentment upon the lands of our humble state,
for this reason we make this great request.
The emergency of our humble state
is such that the morning cannot wait for the evening;
we stretch our necks to look west and say:
‘Might they come soon!’
By the time the officers of Jìn find leisure,
I fear it will be too late.”
He saw Zhōngháng Xiànzǐ
and recited the poem “Qífù.”
Xiànzǐ said:
“I, Yǎn, acknowledge my fault.
How could I dare not follow you
to join in worrying for the altars of the state,
so as to let Lǔ come to this!”
He saw Fàn Xuānzǐ
and recited the final stanza of the poem “Hóngyàn.”
Xuānzǐ said:
“I, Gài, am here.
How could I dare let Lǔ be without a place of gathering?”
A9.17 The Classic of the Seventeenth Year of Duke Xiāng
A9.17.1 In the seventeenth year, spring,
the King's second month, on gēngwǔ,
Kèng, Viscount of Zhū, died.
A9.17.2 The men of Sòng invaded Chén.
A9.17.3 In summer,
Shí Mǎi of Wèi led an army to invade Cáo.
A9.17.4 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí invaded our northern border
and besieged Táo.
Gāo Hòu led an army to invade our northern border
and besieged Fáng.
A9.17.5 In the ninth month,
the Great Sacrifice for Rain was performed.
A9.17.6 Huá Chén of Sòng fled to Chén.
A9.17.7 In winter,
the men of Zhū invaded our southern border.
B9.17 The Commentary on the Seventeenth Year of Duke Xiāng
B9.17.1 In the spring of the seventeenth year,
Zhuāng Cháo of Sòng invaded Chén
and captured Sītú Áng,
because Chén had treated Sòng with contempt.
B9.17.2 Sūn Kuài of Wèi was hunting in Cáo Suì,
and watered his horses at Zhòngqiū,
where his men broke a water pitcher.
The people of Zhòngqiū closed the gates and reviled him,
saying:
“You personally expelled your ruler,
and your father has become an evil ghost.
Not worrying about this,
why are you hunting?”
In summer,
Shí Mǎi and Sūn Kuǎi of Wèi attacked Cáo,
and took Zhòngqiū.
The people of Cáo complained to Jìn.
B9.17.3 Because the people of Qí had not achieved their aims against us,
in autumn,
the Qí Hóu attacked our northern border
and besieged Táo.
Gāo Hòu besieged Zāng Hé at Fáng.
The army from Yángguān went to meet Zāngsūn,
and reached Lǚsōng.
Zōu Shū Hé, Zāng Chóu, and Zāng Jiǎ led three hundred armored men
to attack the Qí army by night,
and having escorted him, they returned.
The Qí army departed from there.
The people of Qí captured Zāng Jiān.
The Qí Hóu sent Sùshā Wèi to console him
and say, "Do not die."
Jiān bowed his head and said:
"I bow in thanks for the honor of your command.
But if your ruler's grace is not complete,
you further let your punished official act with courtesy toward a Qīng."
He used a peg to gouge his wound and died.
B9.17.4 In winter,
the people of Zhū attacked our southern border,
for the sake of Qí.
B9.17.5 Huà Yuè of Sòng died.
Huà Chén weakened the house of Gāobǐ,
and sent a brigand to kill its steward, Huà Wú.
Six brigands used double-edged blades to kill him at the Lú Mén,
behind the house of the Zuǒ Shī.
The Zuǒ Shī was afraid
and said:
"This old man is without guilt."
The brigands said:
"Gāobǐ has a private grievance against Wú."
They then imprisoned his wife
and said:
"Give me your large jade disk."
The Sòng Gōng heard of this
and said:
"As for Chén, he is not only acting violently toward his own clan,
but is greatly throwing the government of the state of Sòng into disorder;
he must be expelled."
The Zuǒ Shī said:
"Chén
is also a Qīng.
When a high official is uncompliant,
it is a disgrace to the state.
It is better to cover it up."
So they let him be.
The Zuǒ Shī made a short whip for himself;
whenever he passed the gate of Huà Chén,
he would surely gallop.
In the eleventh month, on the day jiǎwǔ,
the people of the capital were chasing a rabid dog.
The rabid dog entered the house of Huà Chén,
and the people of the capital followed it.
Huà Chén was afraid
and subsequently fled to Chén.
B9.17.6 Huáng Guófù of Sòng was the Dà Zǎi,
and built a terrace for Píng Gōng,
which interfered with the harvest.
Zǐhǎn requested to wait until the agricultural work was completed,
but the Gōng would not permit it.
The builders sang:
"The pale one of Zémén
is indeed the one who started our labor.
The dark one in the city
is indeed the one who comforts our hearts."
Zǐhǎn heard this,
personally took a switch
to drive the builders,
and whipped those who were not diligent,
saying:
"Commoners like us
all have houses
to avoid dryness, dampness, cold, and heat.
Now the ruler is building a terrace,
and if it is not completed quickly,
how can we fulfill our labor?"
The singers then stopped.
Someone asked the reason.
Zǐhǎn said:
"The state of Sòng is small,
and to have both curses and blessings
is the root of calamity."
B9.17.7 Yàn Huánzǐ of Qí died.
Yàn Yīng wore the unhemmed sackcloth of coarse hemp,
with a headband of hemp, a sash, and a staff.
He wore shoes of sedge,
ate congee,
lived in a lean-to hut,
and slept on straw with a grass pillow.
His steward said:
"This is not the ritual for a Dàfū."
He said:
"Only a Qīng is a Dàfū."
A9.18 《Xiāng Gōng Shí Bā Nián Jīng》
A9.18.1 In the spring of the eighteenth year,
the Bái Dí came.
A9.18.2 In summer,
the people of Jìn seized the Wèi Xíngrén Shí Mǎi.
A9.18.3 In autumn,
the Qí army attacked our northern border.
A9.18.4 In winter, the tenth month,
the Gōng met with the Jìn Hóu,
Sòng Gōng,
Wèi Hóu,
Zhèng Bó,
Cáo Bó,
Jǔ Zǐ,
Zhū Zǐ,
Téng Zǐ,
Xuē Bó,
Qǐ Bó,
and Xiǎo Zhū Zǐ to together besiege Qí.
A9.18.5 Cáo Bó Fùchú died in the army.
A9.18.6 Chǔ Gōngzǐ Wǔ led an army to attack Zhèng.
B9.18 《Xiāng Gōng Shí Bā Nián Zhuàn》
B9.18.1 In the spring of the eighteenth year,
the Bái Dí came for the first time.
B9.18.2 In summer,
the people of Jìn seized the Wèi Xíngrén Shí Mǎi at Zhǎngzǐ
and seized Sūn Kuǎi at Chúnliú
because of Cáo.
B9.18.3 In autumn,
the Qí Hóu attacked our northern border.
Zhōngháng Xiànzǐ was about to attack Qí
and dreamed that he was in a lawsuit with Lì Gōng,
in which he did not win.
The Gōng struck him with a halberd,
and his head fell in front of him.
He knelt and put it back on,
and carrying it, he ran
and saw the Wū Gāo of Gěngyáng.
On another day,
he saw him on the road;
he spoke with him,
and it was the same as the dream.
The Wū said:
"This year, my lord will surely die.
If you have an undertaking in the east,
then you can succeed."
Xiànzǐ agreed.
The Jìn Hóu attacked Qí.
When about to cross the Hé,
Xiànzǐ tied two pairs of jade with red silk
and prayed, saying:
"Qí Huán relies on his natural defenses
and trusts in his many people.
He has abandoned friendship and turned his back on alliances,
and he oppresses the divine masters.
Your great-grandson-subject Biāo is about to lead the Zhūhóu to punish him,
and your official-subject Yǎn will indeed lead the way.
If we are victorious and successful,
and do not bring shame to the spirits,
your official-subject Yǎn will not dare to cross back.
Only you, O spirits, may judge this."
He sank the jade and crossed.
In winter, the tenth month,
they met at Lǔ Jì,
renewed the agreement of Jùliáng,
and together attacked Qí.
The Qí Hóu resisted them at Píngyīn,
dug a moat at Fángmén and defended it,
stretching for a lǐ.
Sùshā Wèi said:
"If we cannot fight,
it is better to defend the narrows."
The Hóu did not listen.
The soldiers of the Zhūhóu attacked the gate,
and many people of Qí died.
Fàn Xuānzǐ told Xī Wénzǐ,
saying:
"I know you;
would I dare hide the truth?
The people of Lǔ and Jǔ have both requested to enter from their own directions with a thousand chariots each,
and we have already granted it.
If they enter,
your ruler will surely lose his state.
Why do you not consider this?"
Zǐjiā informed the Gōng.
The Gōng was afraid.
Yàn Yīng heard of this
and said:
"The ruler was already lacking in courage,
and now having heard this,
The Marquis of Qí ascended Mount Wū to look at the Jìn army.
The people of Jìn sent the Sīmǎ to reconnoiter the hazards of the mountains and marshes.
Even in places he did not reach,
he necessarily set up flags and arrayed them sparsely.
He made those riding in the chariots
place a real person on the left and a dummy on the right.
With flags in front,
the chariots dragged brushwood and followed them.
The Marquis of Qí saw this
and, fearing their great numbers,
he then abandoned his position and returned.
On the day Bǐngyín, the last day of the month,
the Qí army fled by night.
Shī Kuàng told the Marquis of Jìn:
“The sounds of the birds and crows are joyful;
the Qí army must have fled.”
Xíng Bó told Zhōngháng Bó:
“There is the sound of horses whinnying for their companions;
the Qí army must have fled.”
Shū Xiàng told the Marquis of Jìn:
“There are crows on the city walls;
the Qí army must have fled.”
In the eleventh month, on the day Dīngmǎo, the first day of the month,
they entered Píngyīn
and then pursued the Qí army.
Sùshā Wèi linked large carts together
to block the narrow passes and acted as the rear guard.
Zhí Chuò and
Guō Zuì said:
“For you to act as the rear guard for the state’s army
is a disgrace to Qí.
You should go ahead first!”
They then took his place as the rear guard.
Wèi killed horses in the narrow pass
to block the road.
Zhōu Chuò of Jìn caught up with them
and shot an arrow at Zhí Chuò,
hitting him in the shoulder.
Two arrows flanked his neck.
He said:
“Stop,
and you will be a captive of the Three Armies;
if you do not stop,
I will shoot you through the center.”
Looking back, he said:
“Grant me a private oath.”
Zhōu Chuò said: “May it be like the sun!”
He then relaxed his bow and bound him from behind.
His right-hand attendant, Jù Bǐng, also laid down his weapon
and bound Guō Zuì.
Both were bound with their armor fastened at the neck
and seated beneath the drums of the central army.
The people of Jìn wanted to pursue those who had returned,
but Lǔ and Wèi requested to attack the hazardous places.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
Xún Yǎn and Shì Gài led the central army to conquer Jīngzī.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
Wèi Jiàng and Luán Yíng led the lower army to conquer Shī;
Zhào Wǔ and
Hán Qǐ led the upper army to besiege Lú,
but did not conquer it.
In the twelfth month, on the day Wùxū,
they reached Qínzhōu
and cut down the catalpas of Yōngmén.
Fàn Yāng attacked the gate at Yōngmén,
and his driver, Zhuī Xǐ, killed a dog inside the gate with a dagger-axe.
Mèng Zhuāngzǐ cut down its wood
to make a qín for the Duke.
On the day Jǐhài,
they burned Yōngmén and the western and southern outer suburbs.
Liú Nán and
Shì Ruò led the armies of the feudal lords to burn the bamboo and trees of Shēnchí.
On the day Rényín,
they burned the eastern and northern outer suburbs.
Fàn Yāng attacked the gate at Yángmén.
Zhōu Chuò attacked the gate at Dōnglǘ;
his left trace-horse being pressed,
he turned around within the gate
and used his whip-butt to count the gate leaves.
The Marquis of Qí harnessed his chariot,
intending to flee to Yóutáng.
The Crown Prince and Guō Róng held back the horses,
saying:
“The enemy army is fast and swift;
it is a raid.
They will soon retreat;
why should my lord be afraid?
Furthermore, the master of the altars of soil and grain cannot act lightly;
acting lightly, he will lose the people.
My lord must wait for them!”
He was about to drive over them.
The Crown Prince drew his sword and cut the traces,
and then he stopped.
On the day Jiǎchén,
they invaded eastward as far as the Wéi River
and southward as far as the Yí River.
B9.18.4 Zǐkǒng of Zhèng wanted to remove the various high officials;
he intended to rebel against Jìn and raise the Chǔ army
to remove them.
He sent a message to Zǐgēng,
but Zǐgēng did not agree.
The Viscount of Chǔ heard of this
and sent the Yántúnyǐn Yí to tell Zǐgēng:
“The people of the state say that I, the Bùgǔ, preside over the altars of soil and grain
yet do not send out the army,
so that in death I would not be following the rituals.
Since I, the Bùgǔ, ascended the throne,
it has now been five years,
yet the troops have not gone out.
People will think that I, the Bùgǔ, am seeking my own ease
and have forgotten the legacy of my predecessors.
High officials, consider this;
what shall be done?”
Zǐgēng sighed and said:
“Does the King think that I, Wǔ, cherish ease?
It is because I wish to benefit the state.”
He saw the messenger,
bowed his head to the ground, and replied:
“The feudal lords are currently at peace with Jìn;
I request to test them.
If it is possible,
you, my lord, can follow up.
If not,
we can withdraw the army and retreat,
which can be done without harm,
and you, my lord, will also not be disgraced.”
Zǐgēng led the army and reviewed the troops at Fén.
At this time, Zǐjiǎo, Bóyǒu, and Zǐzhāng followed the Earl of Zhèng to attack Qí,
while Zǐkǒng, Zǐzhǎn, and Zǐxī stayed to guard.
The latter two knew of Zǐkǒng’s plot
and completed their defenses and entered the stronghold.
Zǐkǒng did not dare to meet the Chǔ army.
The Chǔ army attacked Zhèng
and halted at Yúlíng.
The Right Army fortified Shàngjí
and then crossed the Yǐng River.
They halted at Zhānrán.
Wěi Zǐféng and Gōngzǐ Gé led an elite force
to invade Fèihuá, Xūmí, Xiànyú, and Yōngliáng;
they circled back to the right of Méishān,
invaded the northeast of Zhèng,
and returned upon reaching Chóngláo.
Zǐgēng attacked the gate at Chúnmén,
stayed for two nights under the city walls, and then returned,
crossing below Yúchǐ.
Heavy rain caught them.
Many in the Chǔ army froze,
and the laborers almost all perished.
The people of Jìn heard there was a Chǔ army.
Shī Kuàng said:
“It will do no harm.
I have repeatedly sung the north wind,
and then sung the south wind.
The south wind is not strong
and has many sounds of death.
Chǔ will surely have no success.”
Dǒng Shū said:
“The Way of Heaven is mostly in the northwest.
The southern army is acting out of season;
it will surely have no success.”
Shū Xiàng said:
“It depends on the virtue of their ruler.”
A9.19 The Classic of Duke Xiāng, Nineteenth Year
A9.19.1 In the spring of the nineteenth year,
in the royal first month,
the feudal lords made a covenant at Zhùkē.
The people of Jìn seized the Master of Zhū.
A9.19.2 The Duke arrived from attacking Qí.
A9.19.3 Lands of Zhū were taken,
starting from the Huò River.
A9.19.4 Jìsūn Sù went to Jìn.
A9.19.5 The burial of Duke Chéng of Cáo.
A9.19.6 In the summer,
Sūn Línfù of Wèi led an army to attack Qí.
A9.19.7 In the autumn, in the seventh month, on the day Xīnmǎo,
Huán, the Marquis of Qí, died.
A9.19.8 Shì Gài of Jìn led an army to invade Qí,
reaching Gǔ.
Hearing that the Marquis of Qí had died,
he then returned.
A9.19.9 In the eighth month, on the day Bǐngchén,
Zhòngsūn Miè died.
A9.19.10 Qí killed its high official Gāo Hòu.
A9.19.11 Zhèng killed its high official Gōngzǐ Jiā.
A9.19.12 In the winter,
the burial of Duke Líng of Qí.
The western outer wall was fortified.
Shūsūn Bào met Shì Gài of Jìn at Kē.
Wǔchéng was fortified.
*The Commentary on the Nineteenth Year of Duke Xiāng*
In the spring of the nineteenth year,
the feudal lords returned from the banks of the Yí River
and made a covenant at Dūyáng,
saying:
"The great shall not encroach upon the small."
They detained Duke Dào of Zhū
because he had attacked us.
Then they halted on the banks of the Sì River
and delimited our fields.
They took fields from Zhū
and returned them to us from the Huò River.
The Marquis of Jìn returned first.
The Duke entertained the six ministers of Jìn at Pǔpǔ
and bestowed upon them the robes of the third rank;
the military commanders, the Sīmǎ, the Sīkōng, the chariot commanders, and the scouts all received robes of the first rank;
he presented Xún Yǎn with bundles of silk, added jade bi-disks, and teams of four horses,
and gave precedence to the tripod of Shòumèng of Wú.
Xún Yǎn had an ulcerous tumor
that broke out on his head.
He crossed the Yellow River,
reached Zhùyōng,
and fell ill,
with his eyes protruding.
The grandees who had returned earlier all came back.
Shì Gài asked to see him,
but was not admitted.
He asked about a successor,
and Xún Yǎn said:
"The nephew of Zhèng will do."
In the second month, on the day jiǎyín,
he died,
but his eyes remained open,
and he could not receive the jade in his mouth.
Xuānzǐ washed his hands and stroked him,
saying:
"In serving Wú, how could I dare not to be like serving my master!"
He still watched.
Luán Huáizǐ said:
"Is it perhaps because he did not finish the business in Qí?"
Then he stroked him again and said:
"Master, if you must end here,
if I do not continue the business in Qí,
may the River be my witness!"
Then he closed his eyes
and received the jade.
Xuānzǐ went out
and said:
"I have been shallow in being a man."
Luán Fáng of Jìn led an army to follow Sūn Wénzǐ of Wèi to attack Qí.
Jì Wǔzǐ went to Jìn to thank them for the army,
and the Marquis of Jìn entertained him.
Fàn Xuānzǐ was in charge of government
and recited the poem "Shǔ Miáo."
Jì Wǔzǐ rose,
bowed twice with his head to the ground,
and said:
"The small states' looking up to the great state
is like the hundred grains looking up to the nourishing rain.
If you constantly nourish them,
the world will be harmonious,
and how could it only be our humble town?"
He recited the poem "Liù Yuè."
Jì Wǔzǐ used the weapons obtained from Qí to cast the Línzhōng bell
and inscribed the achievements of Lǔ upon it.
Zāng Wǔzhòng said to Jìsūn:
"This is not in accordance with ritual.
As for inscriptions:
the Son of Heaven records virtuous character;
the feudal lords record the times and calculate achievements;
the grandees speak of military expeditions.
Now to speak of military expeditions
is to take a lower rank;
to calculate achievements
is to borrow from others;
to speak of the times
is to have greatly obstructed the people;
how can this be used for an inscription?
Moreover, when a large state attacks a small one,
it takes its spoils
to make ritual vessels,
inscribing its achievements
to show to descendants,
to illustrate bright virtue
and to punish the lack of ritual.
Now you are borrowing the strength of others to save yourselves from death;
how can you inscribe that?
Small states are favored by large ones,
but to display what was captured so as to anger them
is the way to ruin."
The Marquis of Qí married from Lǔ
a lady named Yán Yì Jī,
who had no children.
Her niece, Zōng Shēng Jī,
gave birth to Guāng,
who was made the heir apparent.
Among the other sons were those of Zhòng Jǐ and Róng Jǐ;
Róng Jǐ was favored.
Zhòng Jǐ gave birth to Yá
and entrusted him to Róng Jǐ.
Róng Jǐ asked for him to be made the heir apparent,
and the Marquis granted it.
Zhòng Jǐ said:
"You must not.
To discard the regular order
is inauspicious;
to come between the feudal lords
is difficult.
As for Guāng's standing,
he is already ranked among the feudal lords.
Now to discard him without cause
is to unilaterally dismiss a peer of the feudal lords,
and thus to court difficulty and commit an inauspicious act.
You will surely regret it."
The Duke said:
"It is within my power alone."
He then sent Heir Apparent Guāng to the east.
He made Gāo Hòu tutor to Yá,
whom he made heir apparent,
and Sùshā Wèi was made the junior tutor.
When the Marquis of Qí fell ill,
Cuī Zhù secretly brought back Guāng,
and as the illness became critical, he was established.
Guāng killed Róng Jǐ
and exposed her corpse in the court,
which was not in accordance with ritual.
Women are not subject to such punishments.
Even if there were such punishment,
it should not be in the court or marketplace.
In summer, in the fifth month, on the last day of the month, rénchén,
Duke Líng of Qí died.
Duke Zhuāng ascended the throne.
He seized Young Lord Yá at the hill of Jùdú.
Because Sùshā Wèi had replaced him,
Wèi fled to Gāotáng to revolt.
Shì Gài of Jìn invaded Qí,
reached Gǔ,
and upon hearing of the mourning, he returned,
which was in accordance with ritual.
In the fourth month, on the day dīngwèi,
Gōngsūn Chài of Zhèng died,
and the news was sent to the grandees of Jìn.
Fàn Xuānzǐ spoke to the Marquis of Jìn,
because of his skill in the campaign against Qín.
In the sixth month,
the Marquis of Jìn requested from the King,
and the King posthumously bestowed upon him a Great Chariot
to be used in the funeral procession,
which was in accordance with ritual.
In autumn, in the eighth month,
Cuī Zhù of Qí killed Gāo Hòu at Shǎilán
and confiscated his household.
The text records, "Qí killed its grandee,"
because he followed the ruler in his delusion.
When Zǐkǒng of Zhèng was in charge of government, he was autocratic.
The people of the state were distressed by him,
so they punished those involved in the trouble at the Western Palace and the army of the Pure Gate.
Zǐkǒng bore the guilt
and defended himself with his own armor and the armor of the families of Zǐgé and Zǐliáng.
On the day jiǎchén,
Zǐzhǎn
and Zǐxī led the people of the state to attack him,
killed Zǐkǒng,
and divided his household.
The text records
"Zhèng killed its grandee,"
because of his autocracy.
Zǐrán and Zǐkǒng
were sons of Sòng Jǐ;
Shì Zǐkǒng
was the son of Guī Guī.
Guī Guī's rank was next to Sòng Jǐ,
and they were close to each other;
the two Zǐkǒngs were also close to each other.
In the fourth year of Duke Xī,
Zǐrán died;
in the first year of Duke Jiǎn,
Shì Zǐkǒng died.
Sītú Kǒng actually managed the households of Zǐgé and Zǐliáng;
the three households were as one,
and therefore they were involved in the disaster.
Zǐgé
and Zǐliáng fled to Chǔ.
Zǐgé became the Right Yin.
The people of Zhèng made Zǐzhǎn manage the state,
Zǐxī oversaw the government,
and they established Zǐchǎn as a minister.
B9.19.10 Qìng Fēng of Qí besieged Gāotáng,
but did not overcome it.
In winter, the eleventh month,
the Lord of Qí besieged it.
He saw Wèi on top of the city wall
and called to him,
whereupon he came down.
When he asked about the defenses there,
he reported that there were no preparations.
The Lord bowed to him,
and then he ascended again.
Hearing that the army was about to attack,
the people of Gāotáng were fed.
Zhí Chuò and Gōng Lúhuì lowered ropes at night to admit the army,
and they pickled Wèi in the army camp.
B9.19.11 The western outer wall of the city was fortified,
for fear of Qí.
B9.19.12 Qí made peace with Jìn,
and they covenanted at Dàsuì.
Therefore, Mùshū met Fàn Xuānzǐ at Kē.
Mùshū saw Shūxiàng
and recited the fourth stanza of "Zài Chí."
Shūxiàng said:
"How would I, Xì, dare not accept your command!"
Mùshū returned and said:
"Qí is still not settled;
one cannot but be afraid."
He then fortified Wǔchéng.
B9.19.13 Shí Gòngzǐ of Wèi died,
and Dàozǐ did not mourn.
Kǒng Chéngzǐ said:
"This is called tripping up one's own roots;
he surely will not possess his ancestral line."
A9.20 *The Annals of Duke Xiāng, Twentieth Year*
A9.20.1 In the twentieth year, spring,
the King's first month, on the day xīnhài,
Zhòngsūn Sù met with the people of Jǔ and covenanted at Xiàng.
A9.20.2 In summer,
the sixth month, on the day gēngshēn,
the Duke met the Lord of Jìn,
the Lord of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Lord of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
the Viscount of Téng,
the Earl of Xuē,
the Earl of Qǐ,
and the Viscount of Xiǎozhū, and they covenanted at Chányuān.
A9.20.3 In autumn,
the Duke arrived from the meeting.
A9.20.4 Zhòngsūn Sù led an army to attack Zhū.
A9.20.5 Cài killed its Great Officer Gōngzǐ Xiè.
Gōngzǐ Lǚ of Cài fled to Chǔ.
A9.20.6 Huáng, the younger brother of the Lord of Chén, fled to Chǔ.
A9.20.7 Shū Lǎo went to Qí.
A9.20.8 In winter, the tenth month, on the day bǐngchén, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A9.20.9 Jìsūn Sù went to Sòng.
B9.20 *The Zuo Commentary on the Twentieth Year of Duke Xiāng*
B9.20.1 In the twentieth year, spring,
peace was made with Jǔ.
Mèng Zhuāngzǐ met with the people of Jǔ and covenanted at Xiàng,
because of the covenant at Dūyáng.
B9.20.2 In summer,
they covenanted at Chányuān,
because the peace with Qí had been concluded.
B9.20.3 The people of Zhū arrived repeatedly;
because of the affairs of the feudal lords, [Lǔ] was unable to retaliate.
In autumn,
Mèng Zhuāngzǐ attacked Zhū to retaliate against them.
B9.20.4 Gōngzǐ Xiè of Cài wished to bring Cài over to Jìn;
the people of Cài killed him.
Gōngzǐ Lǚ was his younger brother by the same mother,
so he fled to Chǔ.
Qìng Hǔ and Qìng Yín of Chén feared being pressed by Gōngzǐ Huáng
and complained to Chǔ, saying:
"He is plotting with the Sīmǎ of Cài."
The people of Chǔ took this as a cause for punishment,
and Gōngzǐ Huáng fled to Chǔ.
Previously,
Marquis Wén of Cài wished to serve Jìn,
saying:
"The former lord participated in the covenant of Jiàntǔ;
Jìn cannot be abandoned,
and furthermore, we are brothers."
Fearing Chǔ,
he was unable to act on it and died.
The people of Chǔ treated Cài inconsistently;
Gōngzǐ Xiè sought to follow the former lord
to benefit Cài,
but could not and died.
The text states,
"Cài killed its Great Officer Gōngzǐ Xiè,"
indicating that he did not share the same desires as the people.
"Huáng, the younger brother of the Lord of Chén,
fled to Chǔ,"
indicating it was not his crime.
When Gōngzǐ Huáng was about to flee,
he cried out to the capital:
"The Qìng clan is unprincipled;
they seek to monopolize the state of Chén,
they treat their ruler with violence and contempt,
and they drive away his kin.
If they are not destroyed within five years,
then there is no Heaven."
B9.20.5 Qǐzǐ went on his first diplomatic mission to Qí;
this was in accordance with ritual.
B9.20.6 In winter,
Jì Wǔzǐ went to Sòng
to return the mission of Xiàng Xū.
Chǔshī Duàn met him to receive the offering;
he finished by reciting the seventh stanza of "Cháng Dì."
The people of Sòng gave him generous gifts.
When he returned
and reported on his mission,
the Duke hosted a banquet for him
and recited the final stanza of "Yú Lì."
The Duke recited "Nán Shān Yǒu Tái."
Wǔzǐ left his seat
and said:
"Your servant is not worthy."
B9.20.7 Nìng Huìzǐ of Wèi was ill
and summoned Dàozǐ, saying:
"I have committed an offense against the ruler,
and my regret is now of no use.
My name is recorded in the records of the feudal lords,
stating
'Sūn Línfù and Nìng Zhí expelled their ruler.'
If the ruler enters,
then cover it up.
If you can cover it up,
then you are my son.
If you cannot,
though there are ghosts and spirits,
I shall only be hungry
and will not come to receive offerings."
Dàozǐ promised to do so,
and then Huìzǐ died.
A9.21 *The Annals of Duke Xiāng, Twenty-First Year*
A9.21.1 In the twenty-first year, spring,
the King's first month,
the Duke went to Jìn.
A9.21.2 Shùqí of Zhū came as a fugitive
with Qī and Lǘqiū.
A9.21.3 In summer,
the Duke arrived from Jìn.
A9.21.4 In autumn,
Luán Yíng of Jìn fled to Chǔ.
A9.21.5 In the ninth month, on the day gēngxū, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A9.21.6 In winter, the tenth month, on the day gēngchén, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A9.21.7 The Earl of Cáo came to court.
A9.21.8 The Duke met the Lord of Jìn,
the Lord of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Lord of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
and the Viscount of Zhū at Shāngrèn.
B9.21 *The Zuo Commentary on the Twenty-First Year of Duke Xiāng*
B9.21.1 In the twenty-first year, spring,
the Duke went to Jìn
to thank for the army and for taking the fields of Zhū.
B9.21.2 Shùqí of Zhū came as a fugitive with Qī and Lǘqiū;
Jì Wǔzǐ gave him the Duke's paternal aunt in marriage
and gave gifts to all of his followers.
Consequently, there were many thieves in Lǔ.
Jìsūn said to Zāng Wǔzhòng:
"Why do you not investigate the thieves?"
Wǔ Zhòng said:
"It cannot be investigated.
I, Hé, am also unable to do so."
Jì Sūn said:
"I possess the four borders,
yet when I investigate its thieves,
why should it be impossible?
You are the Sīkòu;
your duty should be the removal of thieves.
How can you be unable?"
Wǔ Zhòng said:
"You summon an outside thief
and treat him with great ritual;
how can you stop our own thieves?
You are the Zhèngqīng,
yet you bring in an outside thief;
if you make Hé remove them,
how could I be able?
Shùqí stole a city from Zhū to come here;
you gave him a woman of the Jī clan as a wife,
gave him a city,
and even his followers all received gifts.
If a great thief is treated with ritual, given the ruler’s aunts or sisters and a large city,
and those of the next rank are given grooms, herdsmen, carriages, and horses,
and the lesser ones given clothing, swords, and belts—
this is rewarding thieves.
To reward them and then try to remove them,
some might find that difficult.
I, Hé, have heard
that those in high positions should cleanse their hearts
and be single-minded in their dealings with others;
they should be trusted in their rules and measures,
which must be clearly manifest,
and only then can they govern people.
What the superior does
is what the people turn to.
If the superior does not do something,
yet the people do it,
then punishments are applied,
and none dare not be deterred.
If what the superior does
is also what the people do,
then they are in their proper place;
how then can it be forbidden?
The Xià Shū says:
'Think of this, and it is here;
release this, and it is here;
let renowned words be here;
let truth come from here;
only the Emperor considers merit.'
This refers to being single-minded from within oneself.
Only when trust is single-minded from within oneself
can merit be considered."
Shùqí was not a Qīng,
but because he came with land,
although he was of low rank,
it must be recorded,
for land is held in high regard.
B9.21.3 The Marquis of Qí sent Qìng Zuǒ to be a Dàfū,
again to punish the faction of Gōngzǐ Yá;
he seized Gōngzǐ Mǎi at the mound of Jùdú.
Gōngzǐ Chú came in flight.
Shúsūn Huán fled to Yān.
B9.21.4 In summer,
the Chǔ Zǐgēng died.
The Viscount of Chǔ sent Wěi Zǐféng to be Lìngyǐn,
who consulted Shēnshū Yù.
Shùyù said:
"The state has many favorites and the King is weak;
the state cannot be governed."
Thereupon he declined on account of illness.
It being the height of summer,
he dug into the ground,
placed ice below and a bed upon it.
Wearing double socks
and fur robes,
he ate very little and lay down.
The Viscount of Chǔ sent a physician to see him.
He reported back:
"He is extremely emaciated,
but his vital energy is not yet disturbed."
So the King made Zǐnán the Lìngyǐn.
B9.21.5 Luán Huánzǐ married a daughter of Fàn Xuānzǐ
and they had Huáizǐ.
Because of his exile, Fàn Yāng
resented the Luán clan;
therefore, although he and Luán Yíng were both Gōngzú Dàfū,
they did not get along.
When Huánzǐ died,
Luán Qí had an affair with her steward Zhōu Bīn,
almost ruining the household.
Huáizǐ was distressed by this.
Qí feared his punishment
and slandered him to Xuānzǐ, saying:
"Yíng is going to start a rebellion;
he thinks the Fàn clan caused the death of Huán Zhǔ
and is monopolizing the government.
He says:
'My father drove out Yāng,
yet Xuānzǐ did not show anger but repaid it with favor;
moreover, he made Yāng hold the same office as me and let him monopolize it.
My father died and they became even wealthier.
They caused my father's death and monopolize the state;
there is only death for me,
I will never follow him.'
His plots are like this;
fearing harm to you, my lord,
I dared not keep silent."
Fàn Yāng provided evidence for her.
Huáizǐ was fond of giving,
and many knights turned to him.
Xuānzǐ feared his many followers
and believed the slander.
Huáizǐ was a lower Qīng;
Xuānzǐ sent him to wall Zhù
and then drove him out.
In autumn,
Luán Yíng fled to Chǔ.
Xuānzǐ killed Jī Yí, Huáng Yuān, Jiā Fù, Sīkōng Jìng, Bǐng Yù, Dǒng Shū, Bǐng Shī, Shēn Shū, Yángshé Hǔ, and Shú Pí,
and imprisoned Bóhuá, Shúxiàng, and Jí Yǎn.
Someone said to Shúxiàng:
"You have been implicated in a crime;
is that not a lack of wisdom?"
Shúxiàng said:
"How is it compared to death?
The Shī says:
'At ease, at leisure,
to finish the year.'
This is wisdom."
Lè Wángfù saw Shúxiàng
and said:
"I will plead for you."
Shúxiàng did not respond.
When he went out,
Shúxiàng did not bow to him.
His followers all blamed Shúxiàng.
Shúxiàng said:
"It must be Dàfū Qí."
The household steward heard this
and said:
"When Lè Wángfù speaks to the ruler,
nothing is ever rejected;
he sought to have you pardoned,
yet you did not acknowledge him.
Dàfū Qí is incapable of this,
yet you say it must be him;
why is that?"
Shúxiàng said:
"Lè Wángfù
is a mere follower of the ruler;
how can he effect anything?
When Dàfū Qí recommended people outside his family,
he did not exclude his enemies;
when he recommended people within his family,
he did not skip over his relatives.
Would he leave me out alone?
The Shī says:
'Having great virtue and conduct,
the four states follow him.'
That gentleman is such a man."
The Marquis of Jìn asked Lè Wángfù about Shúxiàng’s crime.
He replied:
"Not abandoning his relatives,
he surely had a part in it."
By this time Qí Xī was old.
Hearing of this,
he took an express carriage to see Xuānzǐ
and said:
"The Shī says:
'Bestow on me boundlessness,
that sons and grandsons may preserve it.'
The Shū says:
'The sage has plans and merits,
with clear evidence and firm preservation.'
One who plans with few errors
and is tireless in kind instruction—
Shúxiàng is such a man.
He is a pillar of the state;
even after ten generations one should still pardon his descendants,
in order to encourage the capable.
Now, for one instance he is not spared,
and thus the pillar of the state is discarded;
is this not delusion?
Gǔn was executed but Yǔ rose;
Yī Yǐn exiled Tàijiǎ but later served him as minister
and in the end showed no resentment;
Guǎn and Cài were put to death,
but Zhōu Gōng assisted the King.
How can you because of Hǔ
discard a pillar of the state?
If you do good,
who would dare not exert themselves?
What is the use of much killing?"
Xuānzǐ was pleased,
shared his carriage with him,
and spoke to the Marquis to have Shúxiàng pardoned.
Qí Xī returned without seeing Shúxiàng,
and Shúxiàng also did not express thanks for the pardon
but simply went to court.
Earlier,
the mother of Shū Xiàng
envied the beauty of the mother of Shū Hǔ
and would not allow her to serve,
so her sons all remonstrated with their mother.
Their mother said:
"Deep mountains and great marshes
truly produce dragons and snakes.
That beautiful one,
I fear she will produce a dragon or snake
to bring disaster to you.
You are of a humble clan.
The state has many great favorites;
if one who is not benevolent interferes among them,
will it not be difficult?
Why should I be stingy with her?"
She sent her to attend the bedchamber,
and she gave birth to Shū Hǔ,
who was handsome and possessed courageous strength.
Luán Huáizǐ favored him,
and therefore the Yángshé clan
