was caught in the disaster.
Luán Yíng passed through Zhōu,
and the western border of Zhōu plundered him.
He spoke to the Messenger, saying:
"The Son of Heaven's petty minister Yíng
has committed an offense against the King's guarding ministers
and is about to flee his punishment.
The crime is heavier than the suburbs and outskirts,
and having nowhere to hide,
I venture to declare my death:
Formerly the petty minister Shū
was able to contribute his strength to the Royal House,
and the King bestowed favor upon him.
His son Yǎn could not maintain his father's labor.
If the Great Lord does not discard the strength of Shū,
this fugitive minister might still have a place to flee.
If you discard the strength of Shū
and think only of the crime of Yǎn,
I
am but a remnant of execution,
and will return to die at Wèishì.
I dare not turn back.
I venture to lay out my body
and await only the Great Lord's command."
The King said:
"To find fault with something and then imitate it
is even worse."
He ordered the Minister of Instruction to forbid those plundering the Luán clan,
and to return what was taken,
and had the officer escort them out through Huànyuán.
B9.21.6 In winter,
Duke Wǔ of Cáo came for an audience;
it was his first appearance.
B9.21.7 There was a meeting at Shāngrèn
to restrict the Luán clan.
The Marquis of Qí and the Marquis of Wèi were disrespectful.
Shū Xiàng said:
"The two lords will surely not escape disaster.
Meetings and audiences
are the constants of ritual;
ritual
is the carriage of government,
and government
is the defense of the person.
To neglect ritual
is to lose government;
to lose government
is to be unable to stand,
and thus there is chaos."
B9.21.8 Zhì Qǐ, Zhōngháng Xǐ, Zhōu Chuò, and Xíng Kuǎi
fled to Qí;
they were all partisans of the Luán clan.
Yuè Wángfù said to Fàn Xuānzǐ:
"Why not bring back Zhōu Chuò and Xíng Kuǎi?
They are brave men."
Xuānzǐ said: "That is the bravery of the Luán clan;
what would I gain from it?"
Wángfù said:
"If you were that Luán clan,
then it would also be your bravery."
Duke Zhuāng of Qí held court
and pointed at Zhí Chuò and Guō Zuì, saying:
"These are my heroes."
Zhōu Chuò said:
"Since the Lord considers them heroes,
who dares not consider them heroes?
However, I am not clever;
at the battle of Píngyīn,
I made the first cry before these two."
Duke Zhuāng instituted a rank for bravery.
Zhí Chuò and Guō Zuì wished to participate in it.
Zhōu Chuò said:
"At the battle of Dōnglǘ,
my left trace-horse was pressed,
I turned back within the gate
and noted the number of gate-leaves;
could such a person participate in this?"
The Duke said:
"You were acting for the Lord of Jìn."
He replied:
"I have recently become a servant,
yet as for those two,
compared to birds and beasts,
I have eaten their meat and I sleep upon their skins."
A9.22 The Annals of Duke Xiāng, Twenty-second Year.
A9.22.1 In the spring of the twenty-second year,
in the King's first month,
the Duke arrived from the meeting.
A9.22.2 Summer, fourth month.
A9.22.3 Autumn, seventh month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
Shū Lǎo died.
A9.22.4 In winter,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
the Earl of Xuē,
the Earl of Qǐ,
and the Viscount of Small Zhū at Shāsuí.
A9.22.5 The Duke arrived from the meeting.
A9.22.6 Chǔ killed its Grand Master Gōngzǐ Zhuīshū.
B9.22 The Commentary of Duke Xiāng, Twenty-second Year.
B9.22.1 In the spring of the twenty-second year,
Zāng Wǔzhòng went to Jìn.
It rained,
and he passed by Yùshū.
Yùshū was in his city,
and being about to drink wine,
he said:
"What use is a sage?
I am about to drink wine,
and that is all;
he travels in the rain,
what is sagely about that?"
Mùshū heard of this
and said:
"He cannot be employed,
and yet he is arrogant toward those who are employed;
he is a maggot of the state."
He ordered his taxes to be doubled.
B9.22.2 In the summer,
the people of Jìn summoned an audience from Zhèng.
The people of Zhèng sent the Shǎozhèng Gōngsūn Qiáo to reply,
saying:
"In the ninth year of Jìn's late ruler, Duke Dào,
our humble ruler then ascended the throne.
Eight months after he ascended,
our late Grand Master Zǐsì
followed our humble ruler to have an audience with the officers-in-charge;
the officers-in-charge were not courteous to our humble ruler,
and our humble ruler was afraid.
Because of this mission,
we had an audience in Chǔ in the sixth month of our second year,
and Jìn therefore had the campaign of Xì.
The people of Chǔ were still competitive
and extended courtesy to our humble state.
Our humble state wished to follow the officers-in-charge,
but feared it would be a great fault,
saying:
'Jìn would probably say that we are not reverent and ritualistic,'
and therefore we did not dare to be disloyal to Chǔ.
In the third month of our fourth year,
the late Grand Master Zǐjiǎo again followed our humble ruler
to observe the openings in Chǔ,
and Jìn then had the campaign of Xiāoyú.
They said of our humble state
that being near to the state of Jìn,
we are like the plants and trees
that share your fragrance and flavor,
so how could we dare to be inconsistent?
Chǔ also was no longer competitive,
so our humble ruler exhausted the produce of his land
and added to it ancestral vessels
to receive the covenant of equality.
Then he led his ministers to follow the officers-in-charge
to meet at the end of the year.
Those who were disloyal to Chǔ,
Zǐhóu and Shí Yú,
were punished upon their return.
The year after Jùliáng,
Zǐjiǎo was old,
so Gōngsūn Xià followed our humble ruler to have an audience with the Lord,
appearing at the Cháng and Zhòu sacrifices,
and participating in holding the sacrificial meat."
In the second year since then,
hearing that you, my lord, were about to pacify the eastern lands,
in the fourth month,
I again attended court to receive instructions.
During the intervals when I did not attend court as scheduled,
not a year passed without sending an envoy,
and not a service was left unperformed.
Because the decrees of your great state are inconsistent,
our state is weary and ill;
unforeseen calamities arrive repeatedly,
and not a day passes without apprehension.
How could we dare to forget our duties?
"If your great state would provide stability and peace,
then we would be in your court morning and evening;
how could we be troubled by your commands?
But if you do not sympathize with our distress,
and instead use it as a pretext for blame,
would we not then be unable to endure your commands,
and be cut off to become enemies?
This is what our humble state fears;
how could we dare forget our lord's commands?
We leave this to your ministers;
may the ministers carefully reconsider it."
B9.22.3 In autumn,
Luán Yíng went from Chǔ to Qí.
Yàn Píngzhòng said to the Marquis of Qí:
"At the meeting in Shāngrèn,
we received commands from Jìn.
Now that we are taking in the Luán family,
what purpose will it serve?
That by which the small serve the great
is good faith.
If good faith is lost,
a state cannot stand.
May my lord consider this."
He did not listen.
He withdrew and told Chén Wénzǐ:
"A ruler maintains good faith,
and a minister maintains reverence.
Loyalty, good faith, sincerity, and respect—
shared by superiors and inferiors alike—
is the Way of Heaven.
Our lord has abandoned these on his own;
he cannot last long."
B9.22.4 In the ninth month,
Gōngsūn Hēigōng of Zhèng was ill.
He returned his fiefs to the Duke,
summoned his household elder
and the head of the clan
to establish Duàn as his heir,
and ordered that official posts be eliminated and sacrifices be reduced.
He used a single ram for regular sacrifices,
and a pig and a sheep for seasonal sacrifices;
they were sufficient for the offerings, and he returned all his other fiefs,
saying:
"I have heard that
living in a chaotic age,
if one who is noble can endure poverty
so that the people have no demands on him,
he may be the last to perish.
Serve the ruler and the other gentlemen with respect and reverence.
Survival lies in respect and caution,
not in wealth."
On the day jǐsì,
Bó Zhāng died.
The noble man says:
"How excellent was his caution!
The Shī says:
'Be careful of your princely measures,
to prepare for the unforeseen.'
Zhèng Zǐzhāng surely possessed this."
B9.22.5 In winter,
a meeting was held at Shāsuí
to again proscribe the Luán family.
Luán Yíng was still in Qí.
Yànzǐ said:
"Calamity is about to break out.
Qí will attack Jìn;
we cannot but be fearful."
B9.22.6 Guān Qǐ of Chǔ was favored by the Lìngyǐn Zǐnán.
Although his stipend had not been increased,
he possessed dozens of horse-teams.
The people of Chǔ were troubled by this,
and the King was going to punish him.
Zǐnán's son, Qìjí, was the King's attendant.
Whenever the King saw him,
he would weep.
Qìjí said:
"My lord has wept for me three times;
may I ask whose fault it is?"
The King said:
"The Lìngyǐn's lack of merit
is something you know.
The state is about to punish him;
will you remain here?"
He replied: "If my father is executed and I remain,
what use would my lord have for me?
If I reveal your command and incur heavy punishment,
I also will not do that."
The King then killed Zǐnán in the court
and dismembered Guān Qǐ by chariots
at the four borders.
Zǐnán's followers said to Qìjí:
"Please move your father's corpse from the court."
He said: "There are rituals for ruler and minister;
this is up to you gentlemen."
After three days,
Qìjí requested the corpse.
The King granted it.
After the burial,
his followers said:
"Shall we flee?"
He said: "I participated in the killing of my father;
if I flee, where would I go?"
They said:
"Then will you serve the King?"
He said:
"To abandon my father to serve his enemy
is something I cannot bear."
Then he hanged himself and died.
The King again appointed Wěi Zǐféng as Lìngyǐn,
Gōngzǐ Yǐ as Sīmǎ,
and Qū Jiàn as Mò'áo.
There were eight men favored by Wěi Zǐféng,
all of whom had no stipends but many horses.
One day at court,
he spoke with Shēnshū Yù,
who did not respond and withdrew.
Wěi Zǐféng followed him,
and he went into the crowd.
He followed him again,
and he then returned home.
After withdrawing from court,
Wěi Zǐféng visited him
and said:
"You have snubbed me three times in the court.
I was afraid
and did not dare not to see you.
If I have faults,
please tell me;
why do you loathe me?"
He replied: "I am afraid of not escaping disaster myself,
how could I dare to advise you?"
He said: "For what reason?"
He replied:
"In the past, Guān Qǐ was favored by Zǐnán;
Zǐnán incurred guilt,
and Guān Qǐ was dismembered by chariots.
Why should I not be afraid?"
Wěi Zǐféng drove his own carriage home,
unable to stay in the middle of the road.
When he arrived,
he said to the eight men:
"I have seen Shēnshū;
he is what is called one who brings the dead back to life
and adds flesh to bones.
It is fine if one who knows me is like him;
otherwise,
please stop."
He dismissed the eight men,
and only then did the King feel at ease with him.
B9.22.7 In the twelfth month,
Yóu Pàn of Zhèng was going to Jìn.
Before he had left the borders,
he encountered a man welcoming a bride,
seized her,
and lodged her in a town.
On the day dīngsì,
the husband attacked Zǐmíng,
killed him,
and went off with his wife.
Zǐzhǎn set aside Liáng and established Tàishū,
saying:
"A minister of the state
is the ruler's second
and the master of the people;
one cannot be careless in this position.
Let us discard those of Zǐmíng's kind."
He sought out the man who had lost his wife
and had him return to his place.
He told the Yóu clan not to harbor resentment,
saying:
"Do not make your evil deeds manifest."
A9.23 Annals of Duke Xiāng, Twenty-third Year.
A9.23.1 In the spring of the twenty-third year,
on the first day of the second month, guǐyǒu,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A9.23.2 In the third month, on the day jǐsì,
Bó Gài of Qǐ died.
A9.23.3 In summer,
Bìwǒ of Zhū came as a fugitive.
A9.23.4 Duke Xiào of Qǐ was buried.
A9.23.5 Chén killed its high officials Qìng Hǔ and Qìng Yín.
A9.23.6 Huáng, the younger brother of the Marquis of Chén, returned from Chǔ to Chén.
A9.23.7 Luán Yíng of Jìn returned to Jìn
and entered Qǔwò.
A9.23.8 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí attacked Wèi
and subsequently attacked Jìn.
A9.23.9 In the eighth month,
Shūsūn Bào led an army to rescue Jìn
and camped at Yōngyú.
A9.23.10 On the day of jǐmǎo,
Zhòngsūn Sù died.
A9.23.11 In winter, in the tenth month on the day of yǐhài,
Zāngsūn Hé fled to Zhū.
A9.23.12 The people of Jìn killed Luán Yíng.
A9.23.13 The Marquis of Qí launched a surprise attack on Jǔ.
B9.23 The Commentary on Duke Xiāng’s Twenty-third Year.
B9.23.1 In the spring of the twenty-third year,
Duke Xiào of Qǐ died,
and Lady Dào of Jìn went into mourning for him.
Duke Píng did not suspend the performance of music,
which was a violation of ritual.
Ritual
requires that ceremonies be suspended for a neighboring state.
B9.23.2 The Marquis of Chén went to Chǔ,
and Prince Huáng complained about the two Qìngs to Chǔ;
the people of Chǔ summoned them.
They sent Qìng Lè to go,
and they killed him.
The Qìng clan used Chén to rebel.
In summer,
Qū Jiàn
followed the Marquis of Chén to besiege Chén.
The people of Chén were building a wall;
a construction board fell and killed someone.
The laborers gave orders to each other
for each to kill their overseer,
and they then killed Qìng Hǔ and Qìng Yín.
The people of Chǔ restored Prince Huáng.
The gentleman said of the Qìng clan:
"One who is unrighteous
cannot be given free rein.
Thus the Shū says:
'The Mandate is not constant.'"
B9.23.3 Jìn was about to marry a daughter to Wú.
The Marquis of Qí sent Xī Guīfù to escort her;
he used a covered cart to carry Luán Yíng and his men-at-arms
and brought them into Qǔwò.
Luán Yíng saw Xū Wǔ at night
and told him of his return.
Xū Wǔ replied: "You must not.
When Heaven has discarded one,
who can raise him up?
You will surely not escape.
It is not that I love my life,
but I know that success will not be achieved."
Yíng said:
"Even so,
if I die because of you,
I shall have no regrets.
I am truly not favored by Heaven;
you are not to blame."
Xū Wǔ consented.
He hid them and gave wine to the people of Qǔwò.
When the music began,
Wǔ said:
"If we could get Luán Rǔzǐ now, what would you think?"
They replied:
"If we found our master and died for him,
it would be as if we did not die."
All sighed,
and some wept.
When the wine cups were being passed,
he spoke again.
They all said:
"If we found our master,
what double-heartedness could there be!"
Yíng came out
and bowed to all of them.
In the fourth month,
Luán Yíng led the armored men of Qǔwò,
and relying on Wèi Xiànzǐ,
entered Jiàng in broad daylight.
Previously,
Luán Yíng had assisted Wèi Zhuāngzǐ in the Lower Army,
and Xiànzǐ was personally close to him,
which is why he relied on him.
The Zhào clan resented the Luán clan because of the troubles of Yuán and Píng.
The Hán and Zhào clans were then on friendly terms.
The Zhōngháng clan resented the Luán clan because of the campaign against Qín,
and was firmly allied with the Fàn clan by marriage.
Zhì Dàozǐ was young
and followed the lead of the Zhōngháng clan.
Chéng Zhèng was a favorite of the Duke.
Only the Wèi clan and the Seven Chariot Great Officers were with him.
Yuè Wángfù was attending Fàn Xuānzǐ.
Someone reported:
"The Luán clan has arrived."
Xuānzǐ was afraid.
Huánzǐ said:
"Escort the ruler to take refuge in the Gù Palace;
then there will surely be no harm.
Moreover, the Luán clan has many enemies.
You are in charge of the government.
The Luán clan is coming from the outside,
while you are in your position;
your advantages are many.
Since you have the power of advantage
and hold the handle over the people,
what should you fear?
As for those the Luán clan has gained,
it is only the Wèi clan,
and they can be taken by force.
Overcoming chaos depends on power;
you must not be lax!"
The Duke had a death in his marital family.
Yuè Wángfù made Xuānzǐ wear black mourning hemp,
a cap, and a headband.
Two women pulled a cart
to go to the Duke,
and they escorted the Duke to the Gù Palace.
Fàn Yāng went to meet Wèi Shū;
Wèi Shū’s ranks were already formed and he was mounted,
about to meet the Luán clan.
Yāng hurried forward
and said:
"The Luán clan is leading rebels to enter.
Yāng’s father and several gentlemen are with the ruler,
and they sent Yāng to meet you.
Yāng requests to be your chariot attendant."
He held the safety strap,
and then leaped onto the chariot.
With his right hand he grasped his sword,
with his left he held the strap,
and ordered the driver to drive out.
The driver asked where to go,
and Yāng said: "To the Duke."
Xuānzǐ met them at the steps,
took his hand,
and bribed him with the district of Qǔwò.
Previously,
Fěi Bào
was a slave whose name was written on the red register.
The Luán clan had a strongman named Dū Róng,
whom the people of the state feared.
Fěi Bào said to Xuānzǐ:
"If you burn the red register,
I will kill Dū Róng."
Xuānzǐ was pleased
and said:
"If you kill him,
if I do not request the ruler to burn the red register,
may the sun be my witness!"
He then sent Bào out and closed the gate.
Dū Róng followed him.
Bào leaped over a low wall and waited for him.
As Dū Róng leaped over,
Bào struck him from behind and killed him.
The followers of the Fàn clan were behind the terrace.
The Luán clan attacked the palace gate.
Xuānzǐ said to Yāng: "Arrows are reaching the ruler's roof;
die for it!"
Yāng used his sword to lead the troops.
The Luán clan retreated;
he took a chariot to follow them.
He encountered Luán Lè
and said:
"Lè, avoid this.
If you die,
I will sue you before Heaven."
Lè shot at him
but missed.
He aimed again,
but the chariot hit the root of a pagoda tree and overturned.
Someone hooked him with a halberd,
severed his arm, and he died.
Luán Fáng was wounded.
Luán Yíng fled to Qǔwò.
The people of Jìn besieged it.
B9.23.4 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí attacked Wèi.
In the vanguard,
Gǔ Róng drove for Wángsūn Huī,
and Shào Yáng was the chariot right.
In the secondary vanguard,
Chéng Zhì drove for Jǔ Héng,
and Zhì, the tutor of Shēn Xiānyú, was the chariot right.
Cáo Kāi drove the ruler's chariot,
and Yànfù Róng was the chariot right.
The second division of chariots:
Shàngzhī Dēng drove for Xíng Gōng,
and Lú Pú Guǐ was the spearman on the right.
The vanguard:
Láo Chéng drove for Xiāng Bàshī,
and Láng Qú Shū was the spearman on the right.
The left wing:
Shāng Zǐchē drove for Hóu Zhāo,
and Huán Tiào was the spearman on the right.
The rear guard:
Shāng Zǐyóu drove for Xiàzhī Yùkòu,
and Cuī Rú was the spearman on the right.
Zhú Yōng Zhī Yuè was the fourth man on the chariot.
From Wèi, they were about to proceed to invade Jìn.
Yàn Píngzhòng said:
"The Lord relies on bravery and strength
to attack the leader of the covenant.
If he does not succeed,
it will be a blessing for the state.
To achieve success without virtue
will surely bring disaster upon the Lord."
Cuī Zhù remonstrated, saying:
"It is not permissible.
I have heard:
'If a small state takes advantage of a great state's setbacks
and brings destruction upon it,
it will certainly suffer the consequences.'
May the Lord consider this."
The Lord would not listen.
Chén Wénzǐ saw Cuī Wǔzǐ
and said:
"What shall be done with the Lord?"
Wǔzǐ said:
"I spoke to the Lord,
but the Lord would not listen.
He considers him the leader of the covenant,
yet seeks to profit from his difficulties.
If the ministers are pressed by urgency,
what will become of the Lord?
You should just stop him."
Wénzǐ withdrew
and told his people:
"Will Cuī Zǐ die?
He criticizes the Lord severely and then goes beyond that;
he will not die a natural death.
To correct the Lord with righteousness
is still a form of restraint on oneself,
how much more so when using ill-will?"
The Marquis of Qí then invaded Jìn
and took Zhāogē.
He divided the army into two columns,
entered Mèngmén,
and climbed Tàiháng.
Zhāng Wǔ stationed the army at Yíngtíng,
garrisoned Píshào,
and built a mound at Shǎoshuǐ
to avenge the battle of Píngyīn,
then returned.
Zhào Shèng led the troops of Dōngyáng to pursue them
and captured Yàn Máo.
In the eighth month,
Shūsūn Bào led an army to rescue Jìn
and halted at Yōngyú,
which was in accordance with ritual.
Jì Wǔzǐ had no son by his primary wife.
Gōngmí was the eldest,
but Jì Wǔzǐ loved Dàozǐ
and wished to establish him as heir.
He consulted Shēn Fēng, saying:
"Mí and Hé, I love them both,
and I wish to select the talented one to establish him."
Shēn Fēng hurried to withdraw,
returned home,
and prepared his whole household to depart.
Another day,
Jì Wǔzǐ consulted him again.
He replied:
"If that is the case,
I shall prepare my worn-out carriage and depart."
Jì Wǔzǐ then stopped.
He consulted Zāng Hé.
Zāng Hé said:
"Give me wine to drink,
and I will establish him for you."
The head of the Jì clan gave a feast for the grand masters,
with Zāng Hé as the chief guest.
After the toast was offered,
Zāngsūn ordered double mats to be placed facing north,
and a new wine jar to be cleansed.
He summoned Dàozǐ,
descended,
and greeted him.
The grand masters all rose.
When the general drinking began,
he summoned Gōngchú
and made him sit according to seniority with Dàozǐ.
Jìsūn lost color.
The Jì clan appointed Gōngchú as the Master of the Horse;
he was resentful and did not go out.
Mǐn Zǐmǎ saw him
and said:
"Do not be like this.
Fortune and misfortune have no gate;
they are only summoned by people themselves.
For one who is a son,
the worry is not being filial,
not having no position.
Respectfully obey your father's commands;
what is there that is constant?
If you can be filial and respectful,
it is possible to be twice as wealthy as the Jì clan.
If you are treacherous and lawless,
it is possible for your misfortune to be twice that of the common people."
Gōngchú agreed with this,
was respectful and attentive morning and night,
and conscientiously fulfilled his official duties.
Jìsūn was pleased,
made him drink his wine,
and when Gōngchú went with the ritual vessels,
Jìsūn bestowed them all upon him.
Therefore the Gōngchú family became wealthy,
and he also went out to serve as the Duke's Left Minister.
Mèngsūn disliked Zāngsūn,
but Jìsūn loved him.
Fēng Diǎn, a groom of the Mèng clan, favored Jié and
said:
"If you follow my words,
you will certainly become the head of the Mèng clan."
He said this repeatedly,
and Jié followed him.
Mèng Zhuāngzǐ became ill;
Fēng Diǎn said to Gōngchú:
"If Jié is established,
please treat the Zāng clan as enemies."
Gōngchú said to Jìsūn:
"The young child Zhì is in his proper place.
But if Jié is established,
then the Jì clan will truly have influence over the Mèng clan."
Jìsūn did not respond.
On the day jǐmǎo,
Mèngsūn died.
Gōngchú supported Jié
and stood him by the side of the door.
Jìsūn arrived,
entered,
wailed,
and as he came out,
said:
"Where is Zhì?"
Gōngchú said:
"Jié is here."
Jìsūn said: "The young child is the elder."
Gōngchú said: "What does being the elder matter?
It is only talent that counts.
Moreover, it was the late Master's command."
They then established Jié.
Zhì fled to Zhū.
Zāngsūn entered to wail;
he was very grieved
and shed many tears.
He came out,
and his driver said:
"Mèngsūn disliked you,
yet you grieve like this.
If Jìsūn were to die,
what would you do?"
Zāngsūn said:
"Jìsūn's love for me
is like a pleasant illness;
Mèngsūn's dislike of me
is like medicine and the acupuncture stone.
A pleasant illness is not as good as a harsh medicine stone.
The stone may keep me alive,
but the pleasantness of the illness
increases its poison.
Now that Mèngsūn is dead,
my own downfall is imminent."
The Mèng clan closed their gates
and told Jìsūn:
"The Zāng clan is about to start a rebellion
and will not let us bury our dead."
Jìsūn did not believe it.
Zāngsūn heard of this
and took precautions.
In the winter, the tenth month,
the Mèng clan was about to clear the way for the funeral
and requested the clearing of the road from the Zāng clan.
Zāngsūn sent the head of the laborers to assist them
in clearing the way at the East Gate,
while he himself followed in armor to watch.
The Mèng clan again told Jìsūn.
Jìsūn was enraged
and ordered an attack on the Zāng clan.
On the day yǐhài,
Zāng Hé cut through the bar of the Lùmén gate
to go out and fled to Zhū.
Initially,
Zāng Xuān Shū married in Zhù,
and sired Jiǎ and Wéi before he died.
He took a second wife, the niece of the first,
who was the sister of Mù Jiāng,
and she sired Hè,
who was raised in the Duke's palace.
Lady Jiāng loved him,
and therefore established him as the heir.
Zāng Jiǎ and Zāng Wéi left to reside in Zhù.
Zāng Wǔ Zhòng sent word from Zhū to inform Zāng Jiǎ
and delivered the Dà Cài tortoise to him,
saying:
"Hè was not clever
and failed to protect the ancestral temple;
I dare inform you of this misfortune.
Hè’s crime
should not lead to the cessation of the ancestral sacrifices.
If you use the Dà Cài tortoise to submit a request,
it might be granted."
Jiǎ said:
"This is a disaster for our house,
not your fault.
Jiǎ has heard your command."
He bowed twice and received the tortoise,
and sent Wéi to submit the request,
but Wéi then requested the position for himself.
Zāngsūn went to Fáng
and sent someone to announce:
"Hè does not seek to cause harm;
his wisdom was merely insufficient.
I do not dare make a private request.
If the former sacrifices are maintained
and the two meritorious services are not abandoned,
how could I dare not yield the city!"
Thereupon they established Zāng Wéi.
Zāng Hè handed over Fáng and fled to Qí.
His people said:
"Will they make us swear an oath?"
Zāngsūn said:
"There is no need for a prepared speech."
When they were about to swear the oath for the Zāng clan,
Jì Sūn summoned the Exterior Scribe
who was in charge of the records of wicked officials
and asked him for the preamble of the oath.
He replied:
"When the oath was made against the Dōngmén clan,
it said:
'Let none be like Dōngmén Suì,
who did not obey the Duke’s command,
killing the legitimate heir and establishing the son of a concubine.'
When the oath was made against the Shūsūn clan,
it said:
'Let none be like Shūsūn Qiáorú,
who wished to abolish the state’s constants
and overthrow the ducal house.'"
Jì Sūn said:
"Zāngsūn’s crime does not reach either of these."
Mèng Jiāo said:
"Why not use his forcing of the gate
and hacking of the bar?"
Jì Sūn used this,
and then swore the oath for the Zāng clan,
saying:
"Let none be like Zāngsūn Hè,
who interfered with the state’s discipline,
forcing the gate and hacking the bar!"
When Zāngsūn heard of this,
he said:
"There is indeed a man of talent in the state;
who could it be?
It must be Mèng Jiāo!"
B9.23.6 The people of Jìn overcame Luán Yíng at Qǔwò
and killed all of the kinsmen and partisans of the Luán clan.
Luán Fáng fled to Sòng.
The Annals write:
"The people of Jìn killed Luán Yíng,"
without mentioning his title of Great Officer,
to indicate that he came from the outside.
B9.23.7 The Marquis of Qí returned from Jìn,
but did not enter his capital,
and instead attacked Jǔ.
He attacked the gate at Qiěyú,
but was wounded in the thigh and withdrew.
On the following day,
being about to fight again,
he set a time for the meeting at Shòushū.
Qǐ Zhí
and Huá Huán put on armor and entered the tunnel of Qiěyú by night,
and stayed overnight in the outskirts of Jǔ.
The next day,
they first encountered the Viscount of Jǔ at Púhóushì.
The Viscount of Jǔ offered them heavy bribes
to spare them from death,
saying:
"I request that we have an oath."
Huá Zhōu replied:
"To be greedy for goods and abandon one's command
is also what my lord hates.
Having received our command at dusk,
and abandoning it before the sun has reached its zenith,
how could we serve our lord?"
The Viscount of Jǔ personally beat the drum
and followed to attack them,
capturing Qǐ Liáng.
The people of Jǔ sued for peace.
The Marquis of Qí returned,
and encountering Qǐ Liáng’s wife in the outskirts,
he sent word to offer his condolences.
She declined, saying:
"If Zhí committed a crime,
why should your command be disgraced?
If he was free from crime,
there is still the humble dwelling of his ancestors;
your humble servant cannot accept condolences in the outskirts."
Thereupon the Marquis of Qí offered his condolences at her house.
B9.23.8 The Marquis of Qí was going to grant land to Zāng Hè.
Zāngsūn heard of this,
went to see the Marquis of Qí,
and spoke with him about attacking Jìn.
He replied:
"Indeed, your soldiers are many,
but you, my lord, are like a mouse.
A mouse
hides by day and moves by night;
it does not nest in the bedchambers or ancestral temples
because it fears people.
Now you, my lord, heard of the disorder in Jìn
and only then acted;
yet you wish to serve them—
if you are not a mouse, what are you?"
Thereupon he did not grant him the land.
Zhòngní said:
"Wisdom is difficult.
Even with the wisdom of Zāng Wǔ Zhòng,
he was not tolerated in the state of Lǔ;
but there was a reason:
his actions were not compliant
and his deeds were not empathetic.
The Xiàshū says:
'Thinking of this and being in this,'
which means compliance in service
and empathy in deeds."
A9.24 The Annals of the 24th Year of Duke Xiāng
A9.24.1 In the spring of the twenty-fourth year,
Shūsūn Bào went to Jìn.
A9.24.2 Zhòngsūn Jié led an army to invade Qí.
A9.24.3 In the summer,
the Viscount of Chǔ attacked Wú.
A9.24.4 In the autumn, in the seventh month, on the day jiǎzǐ, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun,
which was total.
A9.24.5 Cuì Zhù of Qí led an army to attack Jǔ.
A9.24.6 There were great floods.
A9.24.7 In the eighth month, on the day guǐsì, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A9.24.8 The Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
the Viscount of Téng,
the Earl of Xuē,
the Earl of Qǐ,
and the Viscount of Small Zhū at Yíyí.
A9.24.9 In the winter,
the Viscount of Chǔ,
the Marquis of Cài,
the Marquis of Chén,
and the Baron of Xǔ attacked Zhèng.
A9.24.10 The Duke arrived from the meeting.
A9.24.11 Zhēn Yíjiù of Chén fled to Chǔ.
A9.24.12 Shūsūn Bào went to the capital.
A9.24.13 There was a great famine.
B9.24 The Commentary on the 24th Year of Duke Xiāng
B9.24.1 In the spring of the twenty-fourth year,
Mù Shū went to Jìn.
Fàn Xuānzǐ met him
and asked him,
saying:
"The ancients had a saying:
'To die but not decay.'
What does this mean?"
Mù Shū did not yet reply.
Xuānzǐ said:
"In the past, my, Gài's, ancestors
from the time of Yú and before were the Táotáng clan;
under the Xià, they were the Yùlóng clan;
under the Shāng, they were the Shǐwéi clan;
under the Zhōu, they were the Tángdù clan;
now that Jìn leads the alliances of the Xià, we are the Fàn clan.
Is this perhaps what is meant?"
Mù Shū said:
"According to what I, Bào, have heard,
this is called 'hereditary emolument,'
not 'not decaying.'
In Lǔ, there was a former high official named Zāng Wénzhòng.
After his death,
his words remained established.
Is this perhaps what is meant?
I, Bào, have heard:
'Supreme is the establishment of virtue;
next is the establishment of merit;
next is the establishment of words.'
Though a long time passes, these are not discarded.
This is what is called 'not decaying.'
As for preserving the lineage and receiving a clan name
to maintain the ancestral temple
so that the sacrifices are not cut off for generations,
there is no state that does not have this.
Even with the greatest emoluments,
it cannot be called 'not decaying'."
B9.24.2 Fàn Xuānzǐ was governing,
and the tributes of the feudal lords were heavy.
The people of Zhèng were distressed by this.
In the second month,
the Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn.
Zǐchǎn entrusted a letter to Zǐxī
to inform Xuānzǐ,
saying:
"You manage the state of Jìn,
yet the neighboring lords do not hear of your fine virtue,
but hear only of the heavy tributes.
I, Qiáo, am bewildered by this.
I, Qiáo, have heard that a gentleman who leads a state or family
does not fear the lack of wealth,
but fears the difficulty of not having a fine reputation.
If the wealth of the lords accumulates in the public house,
then the lords will become divided.
If you rely on this,
then the state of Jìn will become divided.
If the lords are divided,
then the state of Jìn will be ruined.
If the state of Jìn is divided,
then your own house will be ruined.
Why be so deluded?
Where then will you use the wealth?
"A fine reputation
is the carriage of virtue.
Virtue
is the foundation of the state and family.
If there is a foundation without ruin,
is that not what should be the priority?
Having virtue, one has joy;
with joy, one can endure.
The Classic of Poetry says:
'Joyful is the gentleman,
the foundation of the state and family.'
This is because of fine virtue!
'The Lord on High draws near to you;
do not have a divided heart.'
This is because of a fine reputation!
By practicing empathy and reflection to clarify virtue,
then a fine reputation will carry it and proceed.
Thus those far away arrive and those near are at peace.
Would you not rather have people say of you,
'You truly gave me life,'
than have them say,
'You drained me to live'
The elephant has tusks and thus its body is burned;
this is because of its wealth."
Xuānzǐ was pleased
and lightened the tributes.
On this mission,
the Earl of Zhèng paid court to Jìn.
Because of the heavy tributes previously required,
he also requested to attack Chén.
The Earl of Zhèng kowtowed.
Xuānzǐ declined the gesture.
Zǐxī assisted him,
saying:
"Because the state of Chén relies on its distance and depends on a great state
to oppress and mistreat our humble city,
our humble ruler therefore requests to punish its crimes.
How could he dare not kowtow?"
B9.24.3 Mèng Xiàobó invaded Qí,
for the sake of Jìn.
B9.24.4 In the summer,
the Viscount of Chǔ prepared a naval force to attack Wú,
but he did not maintain military discipline,
and returned without success.
B9.24.5 The Marquis of Qí, having attacked Jìn, grew afraid
and wished to meet the Viscount of Chǔ.
The Viscount of Chǔ sent Wěi Qǐqiáng to Qí to pay a visit
and to request a date for the meeting.
During the Qí sacrifice to the god of the soil,
they inspected the military strength
and allowed the guest to observe it.
Chén Wénzǐ said:
"Qí will soon have enemies.
I have heard
that if military forces are not restrained,
they will surely bring disaster to the clan."
B9.24.6 In the autumn,
the Marquis of Qí heard that a Jìn army was coming
and sent Chén Wúyǔ to follow Wěi Qǐqiáng to Chǔ
to decline the meeting
and to beg for an army.
Cuì Zhù led an army to escort him,
and subsequently attacked Jǔ,
invading Jiègēn.
B9.24.7 A meeting was held at Yíyí
to prepare for an attack on Qí.
Because of floods,
they were not successful.
B9.24.8 In the winter,
the Viscount of Chǔ attacked Zhèng to rescue Qí.
He attacked the East Gate
and stationed his army at Jízé.
The feudal lords returned to rescue Zhèng.
The Marquis of Jìn sent Zhāng Gé and Fǔ Luò to challenge the Chǔ army,
and they requested a driver from Zhèng.
The people of Zhèng divined regarding
Yuǎn Shèquǎn,
and it was auspicious.
Zǐ Dàshū warned him, saying:
"The people of a great state are not to be contended with."
He replied:
"Whether they are many or few,
their being our superiors is the same."
Dàshū said:
"Small mounds do not have pines or cypresses."
The two men were in the tent
and made Shèquǎn sit outside;
after they had eaten,
only then did they let him eat.
They ordered him to drive a war chariot and set out,
while they both rode in a passenger carriage.
When they were about to reach the Chǔ army,
they then followed him into the chariot,
and both sat cross-legged on the rear rail and played the zither.
When they were close,
they charged without telling him.
They both took helmets from their bags and put them on,
entered the camp,
both got down,
wrestled with men and threw them,
and captured and seized prisoners.
They did not wait for him before coming out.
They both leaped into the chariot,
and drew their bows and shot.
Once they had escaped,
they again sat cross-legged on the rear rail and played the zither,
saying: "Gōngsūn!
Those riding in the same chariot
are as brothers.
Why did you again fail to consult with us?"
He replied:
"Previously my mind was set only on entering;
now I am afraid."
They both laughed
and said:
"How quick Gōngsūn is!"
The Viscount of Chǔ returned from Jízé
and sent Wěi Qǐqiáng to lead an army
to escort Chén Wúyǔ.
B9.24.9 Because of Chǔ's naval expedition,
the people of Wú
summoned the people of Shūjiǔ.
The people of Shūjiǔ rebelled against Chǔ. The Viscount of Chǔ stationed his army at Huángpǔ,
and sent Shěn Yǐnshòu and Shī Qílǐ to rebuke them.
The Viscount of Shūjiǔ respectfully met the two men,
and informed them that there was no rebellion,
and requested to receive a covenant.
The two men reported back.
The King wanted to attack them.
Wěi Zǐ said:
"It is not possible.
They have announced they will not rebel,
and they have requested to receive a covenant;
to attack them again
is to attack the guiltless.
For now, return and let the people rest,
and wait for the outcome.
If it concludes without double-dealing,
what more should I seek?
If they still rebel against me, we shall have no lack of excuses,
and we will have merit."
Thereupon they returned.
In B9.24.10, the people of Chén again punished the faction of the Qìng Shì,
and Zhēn Yíjiù fled to Chǔ.
In B9.24.11, the people of Qí built a wall at Jiá.
Mù Shǔ went to Zhōu on a mission of state,
and to offer congratulations on the walling.
The King appreciated his ritual propriety
and bestowed upon him a grand carriage.
In B9.24.12, the Marquis of Jìn (Jìn Hóu) favored Chéng Zhèng
and made him an assistant in the Lower Army.
The Zhèng envoy Gōngsūn Huī went to Jìn on a mission of state.
Chéng Zhèng questioned him,
saying:
"I venture to ask, by what means does one descend the steps?"
Zǐ Yǔ could not answer.
Upon returning, he told Rán Míng about it.
Rán Míng said:
"This man is about to die.
If not,
he will be ruined.
To be noble and yet know fear,
and in fear to think of descending,
that is how one finds the steps.
He is but an inferior person;
why else would he ask?
Furthermore, one who has already ascended and seeks the steps to descend
is a wise person;
it is not Chéng Zhèng.
Is it not that there is a crack leading to ruin!
If not,
he has a delusive illness
and is anxious because he is about to die."
A9.25 The Classic of Duke Xiāng, Twenty-fifth Year
A9.25.1 In the twenty-fifth year, in spring,
Cuī Zhù of Qí led an army to attack our northern border.
A9.25.2 In summer, the fifth month, on the day yǐhài,
Cuī Zhù of Qí assassinated his ruler, Guāng.
A9.25.3 The Duke met with Jìn Hóu,
Sòng Gōng,
Wèi Hóu,
Zhèng Bó,
Cáo Bó,
Jǔ Zǐ,
Zhū Zǐ,
Téng Zǐ,
Xuē Bó,
Qǐ Bó,
and Xiǎo Zhū Zǐ at Yíyí.
A9.25.4 In the sixth month, on the day rénzǐ,
Gōngsūn Shèzhī of Zhèng led an army and entered Chén.
A9.25.5 In autumn, the eighth month, on the day jǐsì,
the lords made a common covenant at Zhòngqiū.
A9.25.6 The Duke arrived from the meeting.
A9.25.7 Wèi Hóu entered Yíyí.
A9.25.8 Qū Jiàn of Chǔ led an army and destroyed Shūjiū.
A9.25.9 In winter,
Gōngsūn Xià of Zhèng led an army to attack Chén.
A9.25.10 In the twelfth month,
È, the Viscount of Wú (Wú Zǐ È), attacked Chǔ,
assaulted the gates at Cháo,
and died.
B9.25 The Commentary of Duke Xiāng, Twenty-fifth Year
B9.25.1 In the twenty-fifth year, in spring,
Cuī Zhù of Qí led an army to attack our northern border
in order to retaliate for the campaign of Xiàobó.
The Duke was distressed by this
and sent word to Jìn.
Mèng Gōngchuò said:
"Cuī Zǐ will have great ambitions,
which do not lie in distressing us;
he will certainly return quickly,
so why worry?
His coming is not as a raider,
and his control over the people is not strict,
which is different from other days."
The Qí army returned without achieving anything.
B9.25.2 The wife of Táng Gōng of Qí
was the elder sister of Dōngguō Yǎn.
Dōngguō Yǎn was a minister to Cuī Wǔzǐ.
When Táng Gōng died,
Yǎn drove the carriage for Wǔzǐ to offer condolences there.
He saw Táng Jiāng
and found her beautiful,
so he had Yǎn take her for him.
Yǎn said:
"Men and women must distinguish their surnames.
Now you, my lord, come from the Dīng line,
and I come from the Huán line;
it is not possible."
Wǔzǐ performed a divination by stalks for it
and encountered the hexagram Kùn changing into Dàguò
The scribes all said, "Auspicious."
He showed it to Chén Wénzǐ,
and Wénzǐ said:
"The husband follows the wind,
and the wind knocks down the wife;
she must not be married.
Moreover, its oracle says:
'Oppressed by rocks,
leaning on thorny brambles;
entering his palace,
he does not see his wife—
ominous.'
'Oppressed by rocks' means
going forward will not succeed;
'leaning on thorny brambles' means
that which one relies on will cause injury;
'entering his palace,
he does not see his wife,
ominous' means
there is nowhere to return."
Cuī Zǐ said:
"She is a widow;
what harm can there be?
The former husband has already borne it."
Thereupon he took her.
Duke Zhuāng had an illicit affair with her
and went to the house of the Cuī family frequently;
he gave Cuī Zǐ's cap to others as a gift.
His attendants said:
"This is not possible."
The Duke said:
"If not for Cuī Zǐ's,
would there be no other caps?"
Cuī Zǐ, because of this,
and also because he used the opportunity of the Duke's attack on Jìn,
said:
"Jìn will certainly retaliate."
He wished to assassinate the Duke to please Jìn,
but did not find an opportunity.
The Duke whipped the attendant Jiǎ Jǔ,
yet kept him near him;
thus Jiǎ Jǔ found an opportunity for Cuī Zǐ against the Duke.
In summer, the fifth month,
because of the campaign of Qiěyú,
Jǔ Zǐ came to pay court to Qí.
On the day jiǎxū,
he was feasted in the northern suburb.
Cuī Zǐ claimed illness
and did not attend to business.
On the day yǐhài,
the Duke inquired after Cuī Zǐ
and then followed after Jiāng Shì.
Jiāng entered into a room
and went out through a side door with Cuī Zǐ.
The Duke tapped on a pillar and sang.
The attendant Jiǎ Jǔ stopped the group of followers
and entered,
closing the gate.
Armed men arose.
The Duke climbed a tower and made a request,
which was not granted;
he requested a covenant,
which was not granted;
he requested to commit suicide in the ancestral temple,
which was not granted.
They all said:
"Your subject Zhù is seriously ill
and cannot listen to your commands.
This is near the Duke's palace,
and your secondary subjects are patrolling to catch those who are licentious;
we know of no other orders."
The Duke climbed over a wall,
but they shot at him,
hitting him in the thigh;
he fell back,
and then they assassinated him.
Jiǎ Jǔ, Zhōu Chuò, Bǐng Shī, Gōngsūn Áo, Fēng Jù, Duó Fù, Xiāng Yī, and Lóu Yīn all died.
Zhù Tuófù was sacrificing at Gāotáng;
when he arrived to report back,
he did not remove his ritual cap and died at the house of the Cuī family.
Shēn Kuài (申蒯),
who attended to the fisherman,
withdrew
and said to his steward:
"You take the family and escape;
I am going to die."
His steward said:
"For me to escape
would be a betrayal of your righteousness."
He died along with him.
The Cuī (崔) clan killed Zōng Miè (鬷蔑) at Píngyīn (平陰).
Yànzǐ (晏子) stood outside the gate of the Cuī (崔) clan.
His followers said:
"Will you die for him?"
He said: "Is he solely my ruler,
that I should die for him?"
They said:
"Will you flee?"
He said:
"Is it my crime,
that I should flee?"
They said:
"Will you return home?"
He said:
"When the ruler is dead,
where is there to return?
Those who rule the people,
is it for the purpose of lording over the people?
They should preside over the Shèjì (Altars of Earth and Grain).
Those who serve as ministers to a ruler,
is it for the sake of their sustenance?
They should sustain the Shèjì.
Therefore, if the ruler dies for the Shèjì,
one dies for it;
if he flees for the Shèjì,
one flees for it.
But if he dies for his own sake
or flees for his own sake,
unless one is his private favorite,
who would dare to take that responsibility?
Moreover, if men have a ruler and assassinate him,
how could I die for him?
And how could I flee with him?
Where else would I return?"
The gate opened and he entered,
pillowing the corpse's thighs on his lap and wailing.
He rose,
leaped three times in mourning, and went out.
People said to Cuī Zǐ (崔子):
"You must kill him!"
Cuī Zǐ (崔子) said:
"He is the hope of the people;
by sparing him,
I shall gain the people."
Lúpú Guǐ (盧蒲癸) fled to Jìn (晉);
Wáng Hé (王何) fled to Jǔ (莒).
When Shūsūn Xuānbó (叔孫宣伯) was in Qí (齊),
Shūsūn Huán (叔孫還) presented his daughter to Líng Gōng (靈公).
She became a favorite
and gave birth to Jǐng Gōng (景公).
On the day dīngchǒu (丁丑),
Cuī Zhù (崔杼) installed him as ruler and acted as Prime Minister,
with Qìng Fēng (慶封) as the Left Prime Minister.
They held a covenant for the people of the state at the Dàgōng (大宮),
saying:
"Anyone who is not aligned with Cuī (崔) and Qìng (慶)..."
Yànzǐ (晏子) looked up to heaven and sighed, saying:
"If I, Yīng (嬰), am not aligned with those who are solely loyal to the ruler and beneficial to the Shèjì,
may the Shàngdì (Supreme Deity) deal with me!"
Then he smeared the blood of the covenant.
On the day xīnsì (辛巳),
the Duke held a covenant with the dàfū (high officials) and the Ruler of Jǔ (Jǔ Zǐ).
The Dàshǐ (Grand Historiographer) wrote:
"Cuī Zhù (崔杼) assassinated his ruler."
Cuī Zǐ (崔子) killed him.
His younger brother succeeded him and wrote the same,
and two more people died.
Another younger brother wrote it again,
and then he let him go.
The Nánshǐ Shì (南史氏) heard that all the Dàshǐ had died,
and set out carrying his bamboo slips.
Hearing that it had already been recorded,
he then returned.
Lǘqiū Yīng (閭丘嬰) wrapped his wife in a curtain and carried her on a carriage,
riding out with Shēn Xiānyú (申鮮虞).
Xiānyú (鮮虞) pushed her down
and said:
"When the ruler was muddled, you could not correct him;
when he was in danger, you could not save him;
when he died, you could not die with him;
yet you know how to hide your favorite.
Who would take you in?"
They traveled until they reached Yǎnzhōng (弇中),
where they were about to lodge.
Yīng (嬰) said:
"Cuī (崔) and Qìng (慶) might pursue us."
Xiānyú (鮮虞) said:
"One against one,
who can make me afraid?"
They then lodged there,
he slept with his head on the reins,
ate after feeding the horses,
and then harnessed them and departed.
After leaving Yǎnzhōng (弇中),
he said to Yīng (嬰):
"Drive fast!
The masses of Cuī (崔) and Qìng (慶)
cannot be withstood."
Then they came to flee.
The Cuī (崔) clan laid Zhuāng Gōng (莊公) in a coffin at the Běiguò (北郭).
On the day dīnghài (丁亥),
they buried him in Shìsūn (士孫) village.
There were four Shà (funeral fans),
no Bì (clearing of the way),
only seven accompanying carriages,
and no weapons or armor.
B9.25.3 The Marquis of Jìn (Jìn Hóu) crossed the river from Pàn (泮),
held a meeting at Yíyí (夷儀),
and attacked Qí (齊),
to retaliate for the campaign at Cháogē (朝歌).
The people of Qí (齊) used the pretext of Zhuāng Gōng's (莊公) death
and sent Xí Chú (隰鉏) to request peace.
Qìng Fēng (慶封) went to the army.
Men and women were arranged by rank.
They bribed the Marquis of Jìn (Jìn Hóu) with ancestral vessels and musical instruments.

From the liùzhèng (six ministers), wǔlì (five officials), sānshí shuài (thirty commanders), the dàfū (high officials) of the sānjūn (three armies), the zhèngzhǎng (heads) of the bǎiguān (hundred offices), the military ranks, and those who remained at their posts, all received bribes.
The Marquis of Jìn (Jìn Hóu) granted it.
He sent Shūxiàng (叔向) to inform the feudal lords.
The Duke sent Zǐfú Huìbó (子服惠伯) to reply, saying:
"Your Lordship pardons the guilty
to pacify a small state;
this is Your Lordship's kindness.
My unworthy ruler has received the command."
B9.25.4 The Marquis of Jìn (Jìn Hóu) sent Wèi Shū (魏舒) and Wǎn Mò (宛沒) to escort the Marquis of Wèi (Wèi Hóu),
intending to have Wèi (衛) grant him Yíyí (夷儀).
Cuī Zǐ (崔子) detained his family
to demand Wǔlù (五鹿).
B9.25.5 Previously,
the Marquis of Chén (Chén Hóu) met with the Viscount of Chǔ (Chǔ Zǐ)
to attack Zhèng (鄭).
For those along the paths of Chén (陳),
wells were filled and trees were felled.
The people of Zhèng (鄭) resented it.
In the sixth month,
Zhèng (鄭) Zǐzhǎn (子展) and Zǐchǎn (子產) led seven hundred chariots to attack Chén (陳),
made a night assault on the city of Chén (陳)
and subsequently entered it.
The Marquis of Chén (Chén Hóu), assisting his Heir Apparent Yǎnshī (偃師), fled to the ancestral tombs.
They met the Sīmǎ (Minister of War) Huánzǐ,
who said:
"Carry me!"
He said:
"I am going to patrol the city."
They met Jiǎ Huò (賈獲),
who was carrying his mother and wife;
he made them get down
and gave his carriage to the Duke.
The Duke said:
"Do not abandon your mother."
He declined, saying:
"It would be inauspicious."
Together with his wife, he assisted his mother in fleeing to the ancestral tombs,
and they also escaped.
Zǐzhǎn (子展) ordered the army not to enter the Duke's palace,
and together with Zǐchǎn (子產), he personally guarded the gates.
The Marquis of Chén (Chén Hóu) sent Sīmǎ Huánzǐ (司馬桓子) to offer bribes of ancestral vessels.
The Marquis of Chén (Chén Hóu) bared his shoulder in submission,
embraced the Shè (Altar of Earth),
and had his subjects, men and women separated, bound as prisoners
to wait in the court.
Zǐzhǎn (子展), holding a tether, appeared before him;
he bowed twice and prostrated, and receiving the ritual drink,
he then presented the offering.
Zǐměi (子美) entered,
counted the captives, and went out.
The Zhù (Invoker) purified the Shè,
the Sītú (Minister of Instruction) presented the people,
the Sīmǎ (Minister of War) presented the tallies,
the Sīkōng (Minister of Works) presented the land,
and then they returned.
B9.25.6 In autumn, in the seventh month on the day jǐsì (己巳),
they held a joint covenant at Zhòngqiū (重丘), because of the peace with Qí (齊).
B9.25.7 Zhào Wénzǐ (趙文子) was in charge of the government;
he ordered that the gifts from the feudal lords be lightened
while their protocol be made more solemn.
Mùshū (穆叔) saw him.
He said to Mùshū (穆叔):
"From now on,
warfare will probably be somewhat reduced.
Cuī (崔) and Qìng (慶) of Qí (齊) have newly gained power
and will seek to be on good terms with the feudal lords.
I, Wǔ (武), know the Lìngyǐn (Prime Minister) of Chǔ (楚).
If we respectfully practice these protocols
and guide them with refined rhetoric
to pacify the feudal lords,
warfare can be ended."
B9.25.8 Wěi Zǐféng (薳子馮) of Chǔ (楚) died.
Qū Jiàn (屈建) became the Lìngyǐn,
and Qū Dàng (屈蕩) became the Mò’áo.
The people of Shūjiū (舒鳩) finally rebelled against Chǔ (楚),
and Lìngyǐn Zǐmù (令尹子木) went to attack them.
When he reached the city of Lí (離),
the people of Wú (吳) came to their rescue.
Zǐmù (子木) hurriedly took the Right Army
to lead the advance,
while Zǐqiáng (子彊), Xī Huán (息桓), Zǐjié (子捷), Zǐpián (子駢), and Zǐyú (子盂) led the Left Army to retreat.
The Wú (吳) army remained between them for seven days.
Zǐqiáng (子彊) said:
"If we wait long, we will be bogged down and cornered.
Being cornered means being captured.
It is better to fight quickly.
I request to use my private troops to lure them.
Select the main army
and form ranks to wait for us.
If we win, then advance;
if we flee, watch us
so that we can escape.
Otherwise,
we will surely be captured by Wú (吳)."
They followed this plan.
The five men led their private troops to attack the Wú (吳) army first.
The Wú (吳) army fled.
They climbed a hill to look out
and saw that the Chǔ (楚) army was not following up;
so they pursued them again
and reached their main force.
The selected troops met them.
The Wú (吳) army was soundly defeated.
They then besieged Shūjiū (舒鳩),
and Shūjiū (舒鳩) collapsed.
In the eighth month,
Chǔ (楚) destroyed Shūjiū (舒鳩).
B9.25.9 Wèi Xiàngōng (衛獻公) entered Yíyí (夷儀).
B9.25.10 Zhèng Zǐchǎn (鄭子產) presented the spoils of victory over Chén (陳) to Jìn (晉),
wearing military uniform to conduct the affair.
The people of Jìn (晉) asked about the crimes of Chén (陳).
He replied:
"In the past, Yú Èfù (虞閼父) was the Director of Potteries for Zhōu (周)
and served our former kings.
Our former kings relied on the utility of his tools
and that he was a descendant of the spirits.
Thus, they gave the eldest daughter, Dà Jī (大姬), in marriage to Húgōng (胡公)
and enfeoffed him in Chén (陳),
to serve as one of the Three Guests.
Thus, Chén (陳) is descended from our Zhōu (周),
and we have relied on them until now.
During the rebellion of Huángōng (桓公),
the people of Cài (蔡) wanted to install their own descendant.
Our former lord Zhuānggōng (莊公) supported Wǔfù (五父) and installed him.
The people of Cài (蔡) killed him,
and we again joined the people of Cài (蔡) in supporting and installing Lìgōng (厲公).
As for Zhuānggōng (莊公) and Xuāngōng (宣公),
both were installed by us.
During the rebellion of the Xià (夏) clan,
Chénggōng (成公) was displaced and wandering;
it was also we who brought him back,
as you, my Lord, know.
Now Chén (陳) has forgotten the great virtue of Zhōu (周),
slighted our great kindness,
abandoned our kinship,
and relied on the masses of Chǔ (楚)
to oppress our humble state.
Their greed was beyond measure,
which is why we made our announcement last year.
Having not yet received a decree of settlement,
there was our campaign at the East Gate.
Among those who blocked the paths of Chén (陳),
wells were filled and trees were cut down.
Our humble state was greatly afraid of failing in strength
and of bringing shame upon Dà Jī (大姬).
Heaven moved their hearts
and opened the mind of our humble state.
Chén (陳) knew its guilt
and surrendered to us.
Therefore, we dare to present these achievements."
The people of Jìn (晉) said:
"Why did you invade a small state?"
He replied:
"According to the commands of the former kings,
wherever the guilt lies,
each should receive their punishment.
Furthermore, in the past, the Son of Heaven’s domain was one qī (圻),
and the states of the lords were one tóng (一同).
From then on, it has diminished.
Now the great states have several qī (圻).
If they did not invade small states,
how could they have reached this size?"
The people of Jìn (晉) said:
"Why are you in military uniform?"
He replied:
"Our former lords Wǔgōng (武公) and Zhuānggōng (莊公) were ministers to King Píng (平王) and King Huán (桓王).
In the campaign of Chéngpú (城濮),
Wéngōng (文公) issued a command,
saying:
'Each shall resume his former office.'
He ordered our Wéngōng (文公) to wear military uniform to assist the King
and to present the spoils of Chǔ (楚).
This is because we do not dare to discard the King's command."
Shì Zhuāngbó (士莊伯) could not refute him
and reported back to Zhào Wénzǐ (趙文子).
Wénzǐ (文子) said:
"His words are reasonable.
To violate what is reasonable
is inauspicious."
So he accepted it.
In winter, the tenth month,
Zǐzhǎn (子展) assisted the Earl of Zhèng (鄭伯) in going to Jìn (晉)
to express thanks for the achievements in Chén (陳).
Zǐxī (子西) again attacked Chén (陳),
and Chén (陳) made peace with Zhèng (鄭).
Zhòngní (仲尼) said:
"The Records (Zhì 志) have it:
'Words are to fulfill the intent,
and literary elegance (wén 文) is to fulfill the words.'
Without words, who would know one’s intent?
If words lack elegance,
they will not travel far.
Jìn (晉) held the hegemony
and Zhèng (鄭) entered Chén (陳);
without refined rhetoric, success would not have been achieved.
One must be careful with rhetoric!"
B9.25.11 Chǔ (楚) Wěi Yǎn (蒍掩) became Sīmǎ (司馬).
Zǐmù (子木) ordered him to organize the levies
and count the armor and weapons.
On the day jiǎwǔ (甲午),
Wěi Yǎn (蒍掩) registered the lands and fields:
he measured the mountains and forests,
cataloged the marshes and wetlands,
distinguished the hills and mounds,
marked the salty barrens,
counted the floodplains,
mapped the reservoirs,
surveyed the plains and embankments,
designated pastures on the lowlands and riverbanks,
and divided the fertile lands into well-fields.
He calculated income to fix the levies,
levying chariots and registering horses,
and determining the number of chariot soldiers, infantry, and those with armor and shields.
Once completed,
he presented it to Zǐmù (子木);
it was in accordance with ritual.
B9.25.12 In the twelfth month,
the King of Wú (吳子), Zhūfán (諸樊), attacked Chǔ (楚)
to retaliate for the naval battle.
He attacked the gate of Cháo (巢).
Niúchén (牛臣) of Cháo (巢) said:
"The King of Wú (吳) is brave but reckless.
If we open the gate for him,
he will personally approach it.
I will get a chance to shoot him,
and he will surely be killed.
If this ruler dies,
our borders will have some peace."
His advice was followed.
The King of Wú (吳子) approached the gate;
Niúchén (牛臣) hid behind a low wall to shoot him,
and he died.
B9.25.13 The Viscount of Chǔ (楚子) rewarded Zǐmù (子木) for destroying Shūjiū (舒鳩).
He declined, saying:
"This was the achievement of the late Grandee Wěizǐ (蒍子)."
He gave the reward to Wěi Yǎn (蒍掩).
B9.25.14 Jìn (晉) Chéng Zhèng (程鄭) died.
Zǐchǎn (子產) first came to know Ránmíng (然明)
and asked him about governing.
He replied:
"Treat the people as your children.
When you see the malevolent,
punish them
as a hawk or falcon chases birds and sparrows."
Zǐchǎn (子產) was pleased
and told this to Zǐ Dàshū (子大叔),
adding:
"In the past,
I only saw Miè's (蔑) face,
but now I see his heart."
Zǐ Dàshū (子大叔) asked Zǐchǎn (子產) about governing.
Zǐchǎn (子產) said:
"Governing is like farming;
think of it day and night.
Think of its beginning
to achieve its end,
and practice it from morning till evening.
In action, do not exceed your thoughts,
just as a farm has its boundaries;
then errors will be few."
B9.25.15 Wèi Xiàngōng (衛獻公) sent word from Yíyí (夷儀) to speak with Nìng Xǐ (甯喜),
and Nìng Xǐ (甯喜) agreed to it.
Dàshū Wénzǐ (大叔文子) heard of this
and said:
"Alas!
It is as the Shī (詩) says:
'My own person is not liked,
how can I worry about my posterity?'"
Nìng Zǐ can be said to have no concern for what comes after him.
Will this be acceptable?
It is almost certainly not.
In the conduct of a superior man,
he considers the end
and considers the return.
The *Shū* says:
“Be careful at the beginning and respectful at the end,
and in the end you will not be in distress.”
The *Shī* says:
“Day and night without remissness,
so as to serve the One Man.”
Now Nìng Zǐ regards his ruler
as less than a game of go;
how can he escape?
A go player who raises a piece without a fixed purpose
will not defeat his opponent;
how much more so when one sets up a ruler
and does not have him fixed?
He will certainly not escape.
A ministerial clan of nine generations,
destroyed in a single move—
how lamentable indeed!”
B9.25.16 In the year of the meeting at Yíyí,
the people of Qí walled Jiá.
In the fifth month,
Qín and Jìn made peace.
Hán Qǐ of Jìn went to Qín to preside over the covenant,
and Chē, the Earl of Qín, went to Jìn to preside over the covenant.
Peace was made but not solidified.
A9.26 The Classic of the Twenty-Sixth Year of Duke Xiāng
A9.26.1 In the spring of the twenty-sixth year,
in the King’s second month, on the day xīnmǎo,
Nìng Xǐ of Wèi assassinated his ruler Piào.
A9.26.2 Sūn Línfù of Wèi entered Qī to rebel.
A9.26.3 On the day jiǎwǔ,
Kàn, Marquis of Wèi, returned to Wèi.
A9.26.4 In the summer,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Xún Wú on a mission of state.
A9.26.5 The Duke met with people of Jìn,
Liáng Xiāo of Zhèng,
people of Sòng,
and people of Cáo at Chányuān.
A9.26.6 In the autumn,
the Duke of Sòng killed his heir apparent Cuó.
A9.26.7 The people of Jìn seized Nìng Xǐ of Wèi.
A9.26.8 In the eighth month, on the day rénwǔ,
Nìng, Baron of Xǔ, died in Chǔ.
A9.26.9 In the winter,
the Viscount of Chǔ,
the Marquis of Cài,
and the Marquis of Chén attacked Zhèng.
A9.26.10 Duke Líng of Xǔ was buried.
B9.26 The Commentary of the Twenty-Sixth Year of Duke Xiāng
B9.26.1 In the spring of the twenty-sixth year,
Zhēn, the younger brother of the Earl of Qín, went to Jìn to renew the peace.
Shū Xiàng ordered the summoning of the messenger Zǐyuán.
The messenger Zǐzhū said,
“I, Zhū, am the one on duty.”
He said this three times,
but Shū Xiàng did not respond.
Zǐzhū became angry
and said,
“Our rank and title are the same;
why dismiss Zhū in the court?”
He grasped his sword and went after him.
Shū Xiàng said,
“Qín and Jìn have not been at peace for a long time.
In the business of today,
if fortunately we succeed,
the state of Jìn will rely on it.
If we do not succeed,
the bones of the three armies will be exposed.
Zǐyuán conveys the words of the two states
without partiality,
while you often alter them.
One who uses craftiness to serve the ruler
is someone I can keep away.”
He brushed his robes and followed him.
People saved him.
Duke Píng said,
“Jìn is perhaps near success!
What my ministers struggle over are great matters.”
Shī Kuàng said,
“The ducal house is to be feared for its lowliness.
When ministers do not compete in heart
but struggle with force,
when they do not strive for virtue but struggle for superiority,
and their private desires are already excessive,
how can it not become lowly?”
B9.26.2 Duke Xiàn of Wèi sent Zǐxiān to negotiate his restoration,
but he declined.
Jìng Sì forcefully commanded him.
He replied,
“The ruler lacks good faith;
I fear I will not escape.”
Jìng Sì said,
“Even so,
do it for my sake.”
He consented.
Previously,
Duke Xiàn had sent someone to speak with Nìng Xǐ,
and Nìng Xǐ said,
“Zǐxiān must be present.
Otherwise,
it will certainly fail.”
Therefore, the Duke sent Zǐxiān.
Zǐxiān, having not obtained his request from Jìng Sì,
spoke with Nìng Xǐ using the Duke’s command,
saying:
“If you return him,
the government will be directed by the Nìng clan,
and the sacrifices alone shall be mine.”
Nìng Xǐ told Qú Bóyù.
Bóyù said,
“I, Yuàn, did not hear of the ruler’s departure;
how would I dare hear of his entry?”
Thereupon he left,
exiting through a nearby pass.
Nìng Xǐ told the Right Minister Gǔ.
Right Minister Gǔ said,
“This is not acceptable.
If one has offended two rulers,
who in the world would support him?”
Dào Zǐ said,
“I received my charge from my ancestors,
and I cannot change it.”
Gǔ said,
“I request to be sent there to observe him.”
Thereupon he saw the Duke at Yíyí.
He returned
and said,
“The ruler has been stranded in distress abroad for twelve years,
yet he shows no look of sorrow,
nor does he speak words of leniency;
he is still the same man.
If you do not stop,
your death will be within days.”
Dào Zǐ said,
“Zǐxiān is there.”
Right Minister Gǔ said,
“Even if Zǐxiān is there,
what benefit is it?
Many people can bring about ruin;
what is he to us?”
Dào Zǐ said,
“Even so,
it cannot be stopped.”
Sūn Wénzǐ was in Qī,
Sūn Jiā was on a mission to Qí,
and Sūn Xiāng remained to keep watch.
In the second month, on the day gēngyín,
Nìng Xǐ and Right Minister Gǔ
attacked the Sūn clan,
but they did not succeed, and Bóguó was wounded.
Nìng Zǐ went out
and stayed in the outskirts.
Bóguó died,
and the Sūn clan wailed at night.
The people of the capital summoned Nìng Zǐ,
and Nìng Zǐ again attacked the Sūn clan,
and overcame them.
On the day xīnmǎo,
they killed Zǐshū and the Crown Prince Jiǎo.
The text says,
“Nìng Xǐ assassinated his ruler Piào,”
meaning that the guilt lay with the Nìng clan.
Sūn Línfù went to Jìn with Qī.
The text says, “entered Qī to rebel,”
placing the guilt on the Sūn clan.
A minister’s emoluments
are in fact possessed by the ruler.
If it is righteous, he advances;
if not, he withdraws himself and retires.
To monopolize emoluments to carry out one’s schemes
is a crime deserving of death.
On the day jiǎwǔ,
the Marquis of Wèi entered.
The text says, “returned,”
because the state admitted him.
To those grandees who met him at the border,
he took their hands and spoke with them;
to those who met him on the road,
he bowed to them from his carriage;
to those who met him at the gate,
he only nodded to them.
The Duke arrived,
and sent someone to reprimand Tàishū Wénzǐ, saying:
“I have been in distress in exile abroad.
All of you have enabled me to hear day and night
the news from the state of Wèi,
yet you alone have not been with me.
An ancient saying goes:
‘That which should not be resented,
do not resent.’
I do resent it.”
He replied:
“I know my crime.
I am not talented;
I could not carry the reins and halters
to follow you among the grooms and herdsmen—
this is my first crime.
There are those who went out
and those who stayed behind.
I was unable to serve both sides,
communicating the words of the outside and inside to serve the ruler—
this is my second crime.
Having these two crimes,
how would I dare to forget the death I deserve?”
He then departed
and left through the nearby pass.
The Duke sent someone to stop him.
B9.26.3 The people of Wèi invaded the eastern border of Qī.
Sūn Shì complained to Jìn.
Jìn garrisoned Máo Shì.
Zhí Chuò attacked Máo Shì
and killed three hundred Jìn guards.
Sūn Kuài pursued him,
but did not dare to strike.
Wénzǐ said:
“He is not even equal to a whetstone.”
He then followed the Wèi army
and defeated them at Yǔ.
Yōng Chú captured Zhí Chuò.
They again complained to Jìn.
B9.26.4 The Earl of Zhèng rewarded the merit of entering Chén.
In the third month, on the day jiǎyín, the first day of the month,
he feasted Zǐzhǎn
and granted him the First Chariot and the robes of Three Appointments,
with eight cities first.
He granted Zǐchǎn the Second Chariot
and the robes of Two Appointments,
with six cities first.
Zǐchǎn declined the cities,
saying:
“From the top down,
the reduction by two
is the ritual.
My position is fourth,
and furthermore, the merit belongs to Zǐzhǎn.
I do not dare to reach the level of the rewarded ritual;
I beg to decline the cities.”
The Earl insisted on giving them to him,
so he accepted three cities.
Gōngsūn Huī said:
“Zǐchǎn will likely soon understand the government.
His yielding does not deviate from the rites.”
B9.26.5 Because of Sūn Shì, the people of Jìn
summoned the feudal lords,
intending to punish Wèi.
In the summer,
Zhòngháng Mùzǐ came on a mission
to summon the Duke.
B9.26.6 The Viscount of Chǔ and the people of Qín invaded Wú
and reached Yúlóu.
They heard that Wú was prepared and returned.
They then invaded Zhèng.
In the fifth month,
they arrived at Chéngjūn.
Huáng Jié of Zhèng was garrisoning it.
He came out
to battle the Chǔ army
and was defeated.
Chuānfēng Xū captured Huáng Jié.
Gōngzǐ Wéi contested this with him,
and they sought a decision from Bó Zhōulí.
Bó Zhōulí said:
“Let us ask the prisoner.”
He then made the prisoner stand.
Bó Zhōulí said:
“Those who are contending
are noble gentlemen;
how could you not know them?”
He raised his hand
and said:
“This gentleman is Wángzǐ Wéi,
the noble younger brother of our ruler.”
He lowered his hand
and said:
“This person is Chuānfēng Xū,
the district magistrate of the area outside Fāngchéng.
Who captured you?”
The prisoner said:
“Jié met the Prince
and was overcome by him.”
Xū was angry
and drew a halberd to chase Wángzǐ Wéi,
but could not reach him.
The people of Chǔ took Huáng Jié back with them.
Yìn Jǐnfù had garrisoned Chéngjūn with Huáng Jié; the people of Chǔ captured him
and presented him to Qín.
The people of Zhèng took goods from the Yìn family
to request his release.
Zǐ Tàishū was the Lìngzhèng
and made the request.
Zǐchǎn said:
“He will not be obtained.
To receive the merit of Chǔ
and then take goods from Zhèng
cannot be called acting as a state;
Qín will not do that.
If you say:
‘We bow in gratitude for your labor on behalf of the state of Zhèng.
Were it not for your favor,
the Chǔ army would still be at the walls of our humble city,’
then it might be possible.”
They did not follow this
and went.
The people of Qín did not give him up.
They changed the gifts
and followed Zǐchǎn’s words,
and only then did they obtain him.
B9.26.7 In the sixth month,
the Duke met Zhào Wǔ of Jìn, Xiàng Xù of Sòng, Liáng Xiāo of Zhèng, and the people of Cáo at Chányuān,
to punish Wèi
and to define the boundaries of the Qī fields.
They took sixty families of the Yì clan from the western border of Wèi
and gave them to Sūn Shì.
Zhào Wǔ is not recorded
out of respect for the Duke.
Xiàng Xù is not recorded
because he arrived late.
Zhèng was listed before Sòng
because it did not lose its place.
Thereupon the Marquis of Wèi joined the meeting.
The people of Jìn seized Nìng Xǐ and Běigōng Yí,
and sent Nǚ Qí to return with them first.
The Marquis of Wèi went to Jìn,
and the people of Jìn seized and imprisoned him at the residence of Shì Ruò.
In the autumn, in the seventh month, the Marquis of Qí
and the Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn for the sake of the Marquis of Wèi.
The Marquis of Jìn hosted a feast for both of them.
The Marquis of Jìn recited “Jiā Lè.”
Guó Jǐngzǐ assisted the Marquis of Qí
and recited “Liào Xiāo.”
Zǐzhǎn assisted the Earl of Zhèng
and recited “Zī Yī.”
Shūxiàng commanded the Marquis of Jìn to bow to the two rulers,
saying:
“My ruler dares to bow to the ruler of Qí for securing the ancestral temple of my former ruler,
and dares to bow to the ruler of Zhèng for his loyalty.”
Guózǐ sent Yàn Píngzhòng to speak privately with Shūxiàng,
saying:
“The ruler of Jìn proclaims his brilliant virtue to the feudal lords,
pities their misfortunes and compensates for their deficiencies,
corrects their transgressions and manages their troubles;
this is how he is the leader of the covenant.
Now he seizes a ruler for the sake of a subject;
what of this?”
Shūxiàng told Zhào Wénzǐ,
and Wénzǐ told the Marquis of Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn spoke of the crimes of the Marquis of Wèi
and sent Shūxiàng to inform the two rulers.
Guózǐ recited “Pèi Zhī Róu Yǐ,”
and Zǐzhǎn recited “Jiāng Zhòngzǐ Xī,”
and the Marquis of Jìn then permitted the Marquis of Wèi to return.
Shūxiàng said:
“Among the Seven Mù of Zhèng,
the Hǎn Shì will be the last to perish;
Zǐzhǎn is frugal and single-minded.”
B9.26.8 Previously,
Sītu Ruì of Sòng had a daughter
who was red and hairy.
He abandoned her at the foot of an embankment.
A concubine of Gòngjī took her in
and named her Qì.
When she grew up, she was beautiful.
Duke Píng entered in the evening,
and Gòngjī ate with him.
The Duke saw Qì
and looked at her;
she was extraordinary.
Gòngjī introduced her into the palace service.
She became a favorite
and gave birth to Zuǒ,
who was ugly but gentle.
The Crown Prince Cuò was handsome but obstinate.
Hé the Zuǒshī feared and hated him.
The eunuch Huìqiáng Yīlì was the Crown Prince’s inner tutor
but was not favored.
In autumn,
an envoy from Chǔ paid a visit to Jìn,
and passed through Sòng.
The Heir Apparent knew of this
and requested to entertain him in the countryside;
the Duke sent him to go.
Yī Lì requested to follow him.
The Duke said, "Does he not hate you?"
He replied,
"A petty man’s service to a superior man is such that,
though the superior hates him, he does not dare stay far away,
and though the superior likes him, he does not dare stay too close;
he respectfully awaits orders—
how would he dare have a divided heart?
Even if there are those who attend to his external needs,
there is no one to attend to his internal needs;
I request to go."
The Duke sent him.
When he arrived,
he dug a pit,
used a sacrificial animal,
placed a written covenant upon it,
and summoned the spirits to witness;
then he galloped back to inform the Duke,
saying,
"The Heir Apparent is about to start a rebellion;
he has already made a covenant with the envoy from Chǔ."
The Duke said,
"He is my son;
what else could he seek?"
He replied, "He wants to succeed you quickly."
The Duke sent someone to observe it,
and indeed there was evidence of it.
When the Duke asked the Lady and the Zuǒshī,
they both said,
"We have indeed heard of it."
The Duke imprisoned the Heir Apparent.
The Heir Apparent said,
"Can only Zuǒ save me?"
He summoned him and sent him to plead,
saying,
"If he does not come by midday,
I know I shall die."
The Zuǒshī heard this
and spoke to him boisterously to delay him.
The time passed,
and the Heir Apparent then hanged himself and died.
Zuǒ became the Heir Apparent.
When the Duke gradually heard that he had been innocent,
he then boiled Yī Lì.
The Zuǒshī saw the person who was exercising the horses of the Lady
and questioned him.
He replied,
"They belong to the family of the Ruler's Lady."
The Zuǒshī said,
"Who is the Ruler's Lady?
Why do I not know of her?"
The stableman returned
and told the Lady.
The Lady sent him a gift of brocade and horses,
preceding them with jade,
saying,
"The Ruler's discarded concubine sends so-and-so to offer these."
The Zuǒshī changed the address to "Ruler's Lady"
and then bowed twice with his head to the ground and accepted them.
B9.26.9 The Earl of Zhèng returned from Jìn
and sent Zǐxī to Jìn on a mission,
saying by way of speech,
"My ruler came and troubled your officers;
fearing that he could not escape blame,
he has sent Xià to apologize for his lack of cleverness."
The superior man says,
"He is good at serving a great state."
B9.26.10 In the beginning,
Wǔ Cān of Chǔ was friends with the Grand Master Zǐzhāo of Cài,
and his son Wǔ Jǔ was on good terms with Shēngzǐ.
Wǔ Jǔ married a daughter of Wángzǐ Móu.
Wángzǐ Móu served as the Shēngōng and fled;
the people of Chǔ said,
"Wǔ Jǔ actually escorted him away."
Wǔ Jǔ fled to Zhèng
and was then about to flee to Jìn.
Shēngzǐ was about to go to Jìn
and met him in the suburbs of Zhèng;
they spread thorns and ate together,
and talked of how to restore him to his former position.
Shēngzǐ said,
"You go;
I will surely have you restored."
When Xiàng Xù of Sòng was about to make peace between Jìn and Chǔ,
Shēngzǐ went on a mission to Jìn
and returned by way of Chǔ.
The Lìngyǐn Zǐmù spoke with him
and asked about the affairs of Jìn,
and furthermore said,
"Between the grandees of Jìn and those of Chǔ, who are more worthy?"
He replied,
"The high ministers of Jìn are not as good as those of Chǔ,
but their grandees are worthy;
they all have the talent of high ministers.
Like the wood of the Qǐ and Zǐ trees, or leather and hides,
they come from Chǔ.
Though Chǔ has talent,
Jìn actually employs it."
Zǐmù said,
"Do they alone not have kinsmen or relatives by marriage?"
He replied,
"Although they have them,
those who employ the talent of Chǔ are truly many.
Guīshēng has heard this:
One who is good at governing a state
grants rewards without error and applies punishments without excess.
If rewards are erroneous,
one fears they will reach immoral people;
if punishments are excessive,
one fears they will reach good people.
If by misfortune one makes an error,
better it be erroneous rewards
than excessive punishments.
Rather than lose a good person,
it is better to benefit an immoral one.
If there are no good people,
then the state will follow them into ruin.
The Shī says,
'The people are gone,
and the state is exhausted and diseased';
this refers to the lack of good people.
Therefore the Xiàshū says,
'Rather than kill the innocent,
it is better to fail in the application of normal laws.'
This is for fear of losing the good.
The Shāngsòng has it saying,
'Neither erroneous nor excessive,
he did not dare to be idle or careless.
He gave orders to the lower states,
establishing their blessings';
this is how Tāng obtained the blessings of Heaven.
Those who governed the people in antiquity
encouraged rewards and were cautious of punishments,
and sympathized with the people without tiring.
They rewarded in spring and summer
and punished in autumn and winter.
Therefore, when about to reward,
one added to the meals;
adding to the meals meant feasting and gifts;
by this we know they encouraged rewards.
When about to punish,
one did not serve the full meat course;
not serving it meant removing the music;
by this we know they were cautious of punishments.
Rising early and sleeping late,
tending to the government morning and evening;
by this we know they sympathized with the people.
These three
are the great principles of ritual.
Where there is ritual, there is no failure.
Now Chǔ has many excessive punishments,
and its grandees flee for their lives to the four directions,
acting as chief strategists for others
to harm the state of Chǔ;
it cannot be cured;
this is what is called being incapable.
In the rebellion of Zǐyí,
Xīgōng fled to Jìn;
the people of Jìn placed him at the rear of the war chariots
to act as their chief strategist.
In the battle of Rǎojiǎo,
Jìn was about to retreat,
but Xīgōng said,
'The Chǔ army is frivolous and unsteady,
and it is easy to shake them.
If we beat many drums with a uniform sound
and attack them at night,
the Chǔ army will surely flee.'
The people of Jìn followed this,
and the Chǔ army collapsed in the night.
Jìn then invaded Cài,
attacked Shěn,
captured its ruler,
and defeated the armies of Shēn and Xī at Sāngsuì,
capturing Shēn Lì and returned.
Zhèng thereafter did not dare face south.
That Chǔ lost the Huáxià was the doing of Xīgōng.
The father and elder brother of Yōngzǐ slandered Yōngzǐ,
and the ruler and grandees did not clarify the matter;
Yōngzǐ fled to Jìn,
and the people of Jìn gave him Xù,
making him their chief strategist.
In the battle of Péngchéng,
Jìn and Chǔ met in the valley of Míjiǎo.
Jìn was about to retreat,
but Yōngzǐ issued an order to the army, saying,
'Send home the old and the young,
return the orphaned and the sick;
where two people from a family serve,
send home one of them.'
Selecting the soldiers and inspecting the chariots,
feeding the horses and taking an early meal,
arraying the army and burning the camps,
tomorrow we shall fight.'
The envoy who returned
released the prisoners of Chǔ.
The Chǔ army collapsed at night,
Jìn forced Péngchéng to surrender and returned it to Sòng,
and returned with Yú Shí.
Chǔ lost the Dōngyí,
Zǐxīn died because of it,
which was the doing of Yōngzǐ.
Zǐfǎn and Zǐlíng competed for Xià Jī,
and Yōng obstructed the matter;
Zǐlíng fled to Jìn.
The people of Jìn gave him Xíng,
made him a chief strategist,
to defend against the Běidí,
and opened communication between Wú and Jìn.
He taught Wú to rebel against Chǔ,
taught them chariot-driving, archery, driving, and raiding,
and made his son Hú Yōng
the envoy of Wú there.
Wú then attacked Cháo, took Jià,
conquered Jí, and entered Zhōulái.
Chǔ was exhausted by constant mobilization,
and it remains a source of trouble to this day;
this was the doing of Zǐlíng.
During the Ruò'áo rebellion,
Bóbèn's son Bènhuáng fled to Jìn.
The people of Jìn gave him Miáo,
and made him a chief strategist.
In the campaign of Yānlíng,
Chǔ pressed upon the Jìn army at dawn and set its ranks.
Jìn was about to flee,
but Miáo Bènhuáng said:
'The excellence of the Chǔ army lies in its center
army, the royal clansmen alone;
if we fill the wells and level the hearths,
complete our formation to face them,
and have Luán and Fàn change their positions to lure them,
Zhōngháng and the two Xì will surely defeat the two Mù lineages,
and then we can strike their royal clansmen from four directions,
surely defeating them heavily.'
The people of Jìn followed this,
the Chǔ army was heavily defeated,
the King was wounded and the army was extinguished,
and Zǐfǎn died because of it.
Zhèng rebelled and Wú rose;
Chǔ lost the feudal lords,
which was the doing of Miáo Bènhuáng."
Zǐmù said:
"That is indeed how it was."
Shēngzǐ said:
"Now there is something even more serious than this.
Jiāo Jǔ married the daughter of Shēn Gōngzǐ Móu;
Zǐmóu committed a crime and fled,
and the ruler and high officers said to Jiāo Jǔ:
'You actually sent him away.'
In fear, he fled to Zhèng,
stretching his neck to look southward,
saying:
'Perhaps they will pardon me.'
But no one planned for it.
Now he is in Jìn.
The people of Jìn are about to give him a district,
to rank him with Shúxiàng.
If he plots to harm the state of Chǔ,
will it not be a source of trouble?"
Zǐmù was afraid,
and reported it to the King,
who increased his salary and rank and restored him.
Shēngzǐ sent Jiāo Míng to meet him.
B9.26.11 Duke Líng of Xǔ went to Chǔ,
