to request an attack on Zhèng,
saying:
"If the army is not raised,
I shall not return."
In the eighth month,
he died in Chǔ.
The Viscount of Chǔ said:
"If we do not attack Zhèng,
how shall we seek the feudal lords?"
In the winter, the tenth month,
the Viscount of Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
and the people of Zhèng were about to resist him.
Zǐchǎn said:
"Jìn and Chǔ are about to make peace,
and the feudal lords are about to be in harmony;
the King of Chǔ has therefore blindly come this one time.
It is better to let him have his way and return,
then peace will be easy to achieve.
For the nature of petty men,
who take pleasure in bravery,
and are reckless in the face of calamity,
seeking to satisfy their own nature
and to gain fame thereby,
is not to the advantage of the state;
why follow them?"
Zǐzhǎn was pleased
and did not resist the invaders.
In the twelfth month, on the day yǐyǒu,
they entered Nánlǐ,
demolished its walls,
forded the river at the Yuè clan's place,
and attacked the gate at Shīzhīliáng.
The portcullis was dropped,
and nine people were captured.
They forded the Fàn and returned.
Afterward, Duke Líng of Xǔ was buried.
B9.26.12 The people of Wèi returned the Lady of Wèi to Jìn,
and then the Marquis of Wèi was released.
By this the superior man knows that Duke Píng's governance was failing.
B9.26.13 Hán Xuānzǐ of Jìn went on a mission to Zhōu,
and the King sent someone to request his business.
He replied:
"The Jìn official Shì Qǐ will submit the seasonal tribute to the royal officers;
there is no other business."
When the King heard this,
he said:
"Will the Hán clan not flourish and prosper in Jìn!
Their words do not deviate from the old traditions."
B9.26.14 In the year when the people of Qí walled Jiá,
in that summer,
Wū Yú of Qí fled to Jìn with Lǐnqiū,
attacked Yángjiǎo of Wèi,
and took it;
then he attacked our Gāoyú.
There was heavy rain,
and they entered through the drainage vents,
put on armor in the armory,
and climbed the walls,
conquering and taking it.
He also took a town in Sòng.
Then Fàn Xuānzǐ died,
and the feudal lords could not manage the matter.
When Zhào Wénzǐ took charge of the government,
he finally settled it.
Wénzǐ spoke to the Marquis of Jìn, saying:
"Jìn is the leader of the alliance;
if the feudal lords invade one another,
we punish them and make them return the land.
Now the towns held by Wū Yú
are all of the kind for which punishment is due,
yet we are greedy for them;
this is no way to be the leader of an alliance.
I request that we return them."
The Duke said:
"Yes.
Who can be sent?"
He replied:
"Xū Liángdài can do it without using the army."
The Marquis of Jìn sent him.
A9.27 *The Annals of Duke Xiāng, Twenty-seventh Year*
A9.27.1 In the spring of the twenty-seventh year,
the Marquis of Qí sent Qìng Fēng on a mission of state.
A9.27.2 In summer,
Shúsūn Bào met with Zhào Wǔ of Jìn,
Qū Jiàn of Chǔ,
Gōngsūn Guīshēng of Cài,
Shí È of Wèi,
Kǒng Huàn of Chén,
Liáng Xiāo of Zhèng,
the people of Xǔ,
and the people of Cáo at Sòng.
A9.27.3 Wèi killed its high officer Nìng Xǐ.
A9.27.4 Zhuān, the younger brother of the Marquis of Wèi, fled to Jìn.
A9.27.5 In autumn,
the seventh month, on the day xīnsì,
Bào and the high officers of the feudal lords made a covenant at Sòng.
A9.27.6 In winter, the twelfth month, on the day yǐhài, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
B9.27 *The Commentary of Duke Xiāng, Twenty-seventh Year*
B9.27.1 In the spring of the twenty-seventh year,
Xū Liángdài made all those who had lost their towns
prepare their chariots and foot soldiers to receive the land;
it had to be complete.
He made Wū Yú prepare his chariots and foot soldiers
to receive his enfeoffment.
Wū Yú went out with his multitude;
he had the feudal lords pretend to hand over the enfeoffments for Wū Yú
to those entitled,
and then they seized him,
and captured all of them.
They took all the towns,
and returned them to the feudal lords.
Because of this, the feudal lords were at peace with Jìn.
Qìng Fēng of Qí came on a mission of state,
his chariot was beautiful.
Mèngsūn said to Shúsūn:
"Qìngjì's chariot,
is it not beautiful!"
Shū Sūn said:
"Bào has heard it said:
'If one's attire is beautiful but does not match one's status,
one will surely meet an evil end.'
What is the use of a beautiful carriage?"
Shū Sūn ate with Qìng Fēng
and was disrespectful.
He recited the poem "Xiàng Shǔ" for him,
but [Qìng Fēng] also did not understand it.
B9.27.3 Nìng Xǐ of Wèi was autocratic,
and the Duke was troubled by it.
Gōngsūn Miǎnyú requested to kill him.
The Duke said:
"Without Master Nìng,
I would not have reached this point.
I have already spoken with him.
The outcome of the matter cannot yet be known,
and it would only result in an evil reputation;
stop."
He replied:
"If your servant kills him,
your Lordship should not be involved in the knowledge of it."
He then plotted with Gōngsūn Wúdì and Gōngsūn Chén,
and sent them to attack the Nìng clan,
but they did not succeed
and both died.
The Duke said:
"The servants were guiltless,
yet father and son died for me!"
In summer,
Miǎnyú again attacked the Nìng clan,
killing Nìng Xǐ and the Yòuzǎi Gǔ,
and exposed their corpses in the court.
Shí È was about to join the covenant in Sòng;
having received his orders and gone out,
he clothed the corpse [of Nìng Xǐ],
pillowed it on his thigh and wept for him.
He wanted to shroud it and flee,
but feared he would not escape,
and moreover said:
"I have received my orders."
So he went on.
Zǐ Xiān said:
"Those who drove me out have left,
and those who brought me back are dead.
Rewards and punishments are without clear rules;
how can people be discouraged or encouraged?
The ruler has lost his trustworthiness,
and the state is without laws;
is this not difficult?
Furthermore, Zhuān actually caused this."
He then fled to Jìn.
The Duke sent someone to stop him,
but it was not possible.
When he reached the Hé,
the Duke again sent someone to stop him;
he stopped the messenger and made a covenant by the Hé.
He resided at Mùmén,
and would not sit facing the state of Wèi.
The Dàfū of Mùmén encouraged him to take office,
but he would not,
saying:
"To take office and then neglect one's duties
is a crime;
to follow [the orders of Wèi]
would make clear the reason why I left.
To whom could I complain?
I can no longer stand in the court of another."
He never took office for the rest of his life.
The Duke mourned him as if wearing the shuì mourning garments for life.
The Duke gave Miǎnyú sixty cities.
He declined, saying:
"Only a Qīng is provided with a hundred cities,
and your servant already has sixty.
For those below to have the salary of those above
is disorder.
I dare not hear of it.
Moreover, it was only because Master Nìng had many cities
that he died;
I fear death will quickly reach me too."
The Duke insisted on giving them to him,
and he accepted half.
He was made Shǎoshī.
The Duke sent for him to be a Qīng,
but he declined, saying:
"Tàishū Yí is single-minded,
and can assist in great matters;
may your Lordship command him."
So he made Wénzǐ a Qīng.
B9.27.4 Xiàng Xù of Sòng was on good terms with Zhào Wénzǐ,
and also on good terms with the Lìngyǐn Zǐmù;
he wished to cease the hostilities of the feudal lords to make a name for himself.
He went to Jìn,
and told Zhào Mèng.
Zhào Mèng consulted with the various Dàfū.
Hán Xuānzǐ said:
"War
is the ruin of the people,
the pest of wealth and resources,
and the great calamity of small states.
If someone will cease it,
even though it might be said to be impossible,
we must surely grant it.
If we do not grant it,
Chǔ will grant it,
to summon the feudal lords,
and then we will lose our position as the leader of the covenant."
The people of Jìn granted it.
He went to Chǔ,
and Chǔ also granted it.
He went to Qí,
and the people of Qí found it difficult.
Chén Wénzǐ said:
"Jìn
and Chǔ have granted it;
how can we stop?
Moreover, when people say
'cease hostilities,'
and we do not grant it,
then we will certainly alienate our people;
what use will we have for them?"
The people of Qí granted it.
It was announced to Qín,
and Qín also granted it.
They all announced it to the small states,
and held a meeting in Sòng.
In the fifth month, on the day jiǎchén,
Zhào Wǔ of Jìn arrived in Sòng.
On bǐngwǔ,
Liáng Xiāo of Zhèng arrived.
On the first day of the sixth month, dìngwèi,
the people of Sòng hosted Zhào Wénzǐ,
with Shū Xiàng as the assistant.
The Sīmǎ set out the jointed meat platters;
this was the ritual.
Zhòngní allowed this ritual to be cited,
considering it to be rich in refined expressions.
On wùshēn,
Shū Sūn Bào, Qìng Fēng of Qí, Chén Xūwú, and Shí È of Wèi arrived.
On jiǎyín,
Xún Yíng of Jìn followed Zhào Wǔ and arrived.
On bǐngchén,
Zhū Dào Gōng arrived.
On rénxū,
Gōngzǐ Hēigōng of Chǔ arrived first,
to complete the agreement with Jìn.
On dìngmǎo,
Xiàng Xù of Sòng went to Chén,
following Zǐmù to complete the agreement with Chǔ.
On wùchén,
Téng Chéng Gōng arrived.
Zǐmù said to Xiàng Xù,
requesting that the followers of Jìn and Chǔ meet each other crosswise.
On gēngwǔ,
Xiàng Xù reported back to Zhào Mèng.
Zhào Mèng said:
"Jìn, Chǔ, Qí, and Qín
are equals;
Jìn's inability to command Qí
is like Chǔ's inability to command Qín.
If the ruler of Chǔ can cause the ruler of Qín to humble himself in our humble state,
how would my ruler dare not insistently request the same of Qí?"
On rénshēn,
the Zuǒshī reported back to Zǐmù.
Zǐmù sent a swift messenger to inform the King.
The King said:
"Leaving aside Qí and Qín,
have the other states meet each other."
In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day wùyín,
the Zuǒshī arrived.
That night,
Zhào Mèng and Zǐxī made a covenant,
using the words of Qí.
On gēngchén,
Zǐmù arrived from Chén.
Kǒng Huàn of Chén and Gōngsūn Guīshēng of Cài arrived.
The Dàfū of Cáo and Xǔ all arrived.
They used fences for their camps.
Jìn and Chǔ each occupied one side.
Bó Sù said to Zhào Mèng:
"The atmosphere of Chǔ is very sinister;
I fear trouble."
Zhào Mèng said:
"If we turn back to the left and enter Sòng,
what can they do to us?"
On xīnsì,
they were about to covenant outside the west gate of Sòng.
The people of Chǔ wore armor under their garments.
Bó Zhōulí said:
"To assemble the armies of the feudal lords
and show bad faith,
is that not unacceptable?
The feudal lords look for good faith from Chǔ,
and that is why they come to submit.
If there is no good faith,
that is to abandon the means by which Chǔ gains the submission of the feudal lords."
He persistently requested that the armor be removed.
Zǐmù said:
“Jìn and Chǔ have lacked good faith for a long time;
things are done only for benefit.
If one can satisfy one's ambitions,
what use is there for good faith?”
The Dàzǎi withdrew
and told others:
“The Lìngyǐn will soon die;
it will not take three years.
To seek to satisfy one's ambitions while abandoning good faith—
will those ambitions be satisfied?
Ambition is used to generate words;
words are used to manifest good faith;
good faith is used to establish ambition.
These three together define it.
If good faith is lost,
how can he reach three years?”
Zhào Mèng was concerned about Chǔ wearing armor underneath their robes,
and he told Shūxiàng.
Shūxiàng said:
“What harm is there?
If an ordinary man acts without good faith even once,
it is still unacceptable,
and he will simply end up dead alone.
If one convenes the ministers of the feudal lords
and acts without good faith,
he will certainly not succeed.
The one who eats his words is not a source of distress to you;
it is not your concern.
Now, to summon people with good faith
but to carry it out with deception,
no one will certainly stand with him;
how then can he harm us?
Moreover, we rely on Sòng because they are weary and distressed,
so they can fight to the death.
If we join Sòng in fighting to the death,
even if Chǔ were twice as strong, it would be fine;
why should you fear them?
Furthermore, it will not come to this.
They claim to stop the fighting to summon the feudal lords,
but if they take up arms to harm us,
our cause will be greatly strengthened;
it is not something to worry about.”
Jì Wǔzǐ sent a message to Shūsūn in the name of the Duke, saying:
“Look to Zhū and Téng.”
Afterward, the people of Qí requested Zhū,
and the people of Sòng requested Téng,
but neither was allowed to join the covenant.
Shūsūn said:
“Zhū and Téng
are the private subjects of others;
we
are a sovereign state.
For what reason should we look to them?
Sòng and Wèi
are our equals.”
Then they swore the covenant.
Therefore, the classic does not record his clan name,
to indicate that he disobeyed the command.
Jìn and Chǔ struggled over who should go first.
The people of Jìn said:
“Jìn has long been the leader of the feudal lords’ covenants;
there has never been one who went before Jìn.”
The people of Chǔ said:
“You say that Jìn and Chǔ are equals;
if Jìn always goes first,
then Chǔ is the weaker one.
Moreover, Jìn and Chǔ have alternately presided over the covenants of the feudal lords for a long time;
how could it be solely Jìn?”
Shūxiàng said to Zhào Mèng:
“The feudal lords submit to the virtue of Jìn,
not to its presiding over the covenant.
You should focus on virtue
and not struggle to go first.
Furthermore, when the feudal lords covenant,
small states must surely have someone presiding over the covenant;
if Chǔ acts as Jìn’s junior,
is that not also acceptable?”
Thus they let the people of Chǔ go first.
The classic records Jìn first,
because Jìn possessed good faith.
On the day Rénwǔ,
the Duke of Sòng hosted a banquet for the grandees of Jìn and Chǔ.
Zhào Mèng was the guest of honor;
Zǐmù spoke with him,
but he could not answer;
he had Shūxiàng attend and speak for him,
and then Zǐmù could not answer either.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
the Duke of Sòng and the grandees of the feudal lords swore the covenant outside Méngmén.
Zǐmù asked Zhào Mèng:
“What was the virtue of Fàn Wǔzǐ like?”
He replied:
“The master’s household affairs were well-ordered;
in his speech to the state of Jìn, he held nothing back;
his invocators and scribes presented the truth to the ghosts and spirits
without words of shame.”
Zǐmù returned and told the King.
The King said:
“How lofty indeed!
He could satisfy both spirits and men;
it is fitting that he gloriously assisted five rulers
to become leaders of the covenant.”
Zǐmù also told the King:
“It is fitting that Jìn is the hegemon;
they have Shūxiàng to assist their ministers,
while Chǔ has no one to match him;
we cannot compete with them.”
Xún Yíng of Jìn then went to Chǔ to preside over the covenant.
B9.27.5 The Earl of Zhèng hosted a banquet for Zhào Mèng
at Chuílǒng;
Zǐzhǎn, Bóyǒu, Zǐxī, Zǐchǎn, Zǐtàishū, and the two Zǐshí followed him.
Zhào Mèng said:
“Seven gentlemen follow their ruler
to honor me, Wǔ.
I request that you all recite poems
to complete the ruler’s gift;
I, Wǔ, shall also observe the ambitions of the seven gentlemen.”
Zǐzhǎn recited “Cǎochóng.”
Zhào Mèng said:
“Excellent!
A lord of the people!
However, I, Wǔ,
am not worthy of it.”
Bóyǒu recited “Chún Zhī Bìbì.”
Zhào Mèng said:
“Words of the bed and mat should not cross the threshold;
how much less so in the open field?
This is not what an envoy should hear.”
Zǐxī recited the fourth stanza of “Shǔmiáo.”
Zhào Mèng said:
“My ruler is present;
what can I, Wǔ, do?”
Zǐchǎn recited “Xísāng.”
Zhào Mèng said:
“I, Wǔ, request to accept its final stanza.”
Zǐtàishū recited “Yě Yǒu Màncǎo.”
Zhào Mèng said:
“It is the kindness of you, sir.”;
Yìn Duàn recited “Xīshuài.”
Zhào Mèng said:
“Excellent!
A lord who preserves his house!
I have expectations for you.”
Gōngsūn Duàn recited “Sānghù.”
Zhào Mèng said:
“‘Neither partial nor arrogant’;
where else would blessings go?
If you maintain these words,
even if you wished to decline blessings and emoluments,
could you do so?”
When the banquet ended,
Wénzǐ said to Shūxiàng:
“Bóyǒu will soon be punished.
Poetry is used to express ambition;
his ambition slanders his superiors
and he publicly expresses resentment,
yet he uses it to honor a guest.
How can he last long?
He will be lucky if he is the last to perish.”
Shūxiàng said:
“Indeed.
He is already extravagant;
the saying ‘not reaching five harvests’
refers to that gentleman.”
Wénzǐ said:
“The others are all lords of several generations.
Zǐzhǎn will be the one who perishes last;
being in a high position, he does not forget to be humble.
The Yìn clan is next;
he is joyful but not dissipated.
Joy is used to pacify the people,
and he does not use them excessively.
To be the last to perish—
is that not appropriate!”
B9.27.6 The Zuǒshī of Sòng requested a reward,
saying:
“I request cities to escape death.”
The Duke gave him sixty cities
and showed this to Zǐhǎn.
Zǐhǎn said:
“For all the small states among the feudal lords,
the reason Jìn and Chǔ use military force to overawe them
is so that after they are in fear, superiors and inferiors are kind and harmonious;
after they are kind and harmonious, they can stabilize their state
to serve the great states;
this is how they are preserved.
Without being awed, they become arrogant;
with arrogance, disorder arises;
with disorder, they will surely be destroyed;
this is how they perish.
Heaven produced the five materials,
and the people use them all;
none can be discarded.
Who can eliminate weapons?
The establishment of weapons has existed for a long time;
It is that by which the unruly are overawed
and civil virtue is manifested.
By it the *Shèngrén* rise;
by it the rebellious are cast down.
The arts of rising and falling, of survival and ruin,
of darkness and light,
all have their origin in military force.
And yet you seek to abolish it;
is this not a delusion?
To deceive the *Zhūhóu* with a delusive doctrine—
no crime is greater than this.
Even if there were no great punishment,
to furthermore seek a reward
is the height of insatiability."
He whittled down the document and threw it away.
The *Zuǒshī* declined the cities.
The *Xiàng* clan wanted to attack the *Sīchéng*.
The *Zuǒshī* said:
"I was about to perish,
and the *Fūzǐ* preserved me;
no kindness is greater than this.
Can he then be attacked?"
The *Jūnzǐ* said:
"'That man there
is the *Sīzhí* of the state.'
This refers to *Lè Xǐ*!
'By what means can he comfort me?
I shall receive it.'
This refers to *Xiàng Xù*!"
B9.27.7 In *Qí*, *Cuī Zhù* had *Chéng* and *Qiáng* by his first wife, who then died.
He married *Dōngguō Jiāng*,
and she bore *Míng*.
*Dōngguō Jiāng* entered the family with an orphan,
named *Táng Wújiù*,
who along with *Dōngguō Yǎn* assisted the *Cuī* clan.
*Cuī Chéng* was ill,
so he was set aside,
and *Míng* was established.
*Chéng* requested to retire in *Cuī*,
and *Cuī Zǐ* granted it.
*Yǎn* and *Wújiù* would not give it to him,
saying:
"*Cuī*
is the ancestral city;
it must remain with the *Zōngzhǔ*."
*Chéng* and *Qiáng* were angry
and intended to kill them.
They informed *Qìng Fēng*, saying:
"The *Fūzǐ*’s person
is also known to you.
He follows only *Wújiù* and *Yǎn*,
and his senior kinsmen are unable to gain access.
We greatly fear they will harm the *Fūzǐ*,
so we venture to inform you."
*Qìng Fēng* said:
"You may withdraw for now.
I will consider it."
He told *Lúpú Piè*.
*Lúpú Piè* said:
"That man
is the ruler's enemy.
Perhaps Heaven is about to abandon him.
If his family is in disorder,
why should you be distressed?
The weakening of the *Cuī*
is the strengthening of the *Qìng*."
Another day they informed him again.
*Qìng Fēng* said:
"If it benefits the *Fūzǐ*,
they must be removed.
If there is difficulty,
I will help you."
In the ninth month, on the day *gēngchén*,
*Cuī Chéng* and *Cuī Qiáng* killed *Dōngguō Yǎn* and *Táng Wújiù* in the court of the *Cuī* clan.
*Cuī Zǐ* was angry and came out,
but his followers all fled.
He sought someone to prepare his carriage
but could find no one.
He had a *Yǔrén* prepare the carriage
and a *Sìrén* drive it as he went out,
saying:
"The *Cuī* clan has been blessed;
if it stops with me, it is still acceptable."
He then went to see *Qìng Fēng*.
*Qìng Fēng* said:
"*Cuī* and *Qìng* are as one.
How could they dare do this?
Please let me punish them for you."
He sent *Lúpú Piè* to lead armored soldiers
to attack the *Cuī* clan.
The *Cuī* clan fortified their palace and defended it.
They could not overcome them,
so they made the people of the capital help them.
They then wiped out the *Cuī* clan,
killing *Chéng* and *Qiáng*,
and took all the family members captive.
His wife hanged herself.
*Piè* reported back to *Cuī Zǐ*
and drove him back home.
When he arrived,
he had no home to return to.
Thereupon he hanged himself.
*Cuī Míng* escaped by night to the *Dàmù*.
On the day *xīnsì*,
*Cuī Míng* fled here.
*Qìng Fēng* took charge of the state.
B9.27.8 *Wěi Bà* of *Chǔ* went to *Jìn* to attend the swearing of the covenant.
The *Jìn Hóu* entertained him.
As he was about to leave, he recited the poem *Jì Zuì*.
*Shū Xiàng* said:
"That the *Wěi* clan should have successors in the state of *Chǔ*
is only right!
In carrying out the ruler's commands,
he does not forget diligence.
*Zǐdàng* will soon be in charge of the government.
Using diligence to serve the ruler,
he will surely be able to nourish the people;
where else would the government go?"
B9.27.9 During the disorder of the *Cuī* clan,
*Shēn Xiānyú* fled here,
working as a hired laborer in the fields
while mourning for *Zhuāng Gōng*.
In winter,
the people of *Chǔ* summoned him;
he then went to *Chǔ*
and became the *Yòuyǐn*.
B9.27.10 On the first day of the eleventh month, *yǐhài*,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
The *chén* was in *Shēn*;
the *Sīlì* was in error;
he has twice missed the intercalary month.
A9.28 *Xiāng Gōng* Twenty-eighth Year Classic
A9.28.1 In the spring of the twenty-eighth year,
there was no ice.
A9.28.2 In summer,
*Shí È* of *Wèi* fled to *Jìn*.
A9.28.3 The *Zhū Zǐ* came to court.
A9.28.4 In autumn, in the eighth month,
the *Dàyú* was performed.
A9.28.5 *Zhòngsūn Jié* went to *Jìn*.
A9.28.6 In winter,
*Qìng Fēng* of *Qí* fled here.
A9.28.7 In the eleventh month,
the *Gōng* went to *Chǔ*.
A9.28.8 In the twelfth month, on the day *jiǎyín*,
the *Tiānwáng* died.
A9.28.9 On the day *yǐwèi*,
*Zhāo*, the *Chǔ Zǐ*, died.
B9.28 *Xiāng Gōng* Twenty-eighth Year Commentary
B9.28.1 In the spring of the twenty-eighth year,
there was no ice.
*Zǐ Shèn* said:
"This year *Sòng* and *Zhèng* will likely suffer from famine!
Jupiter is in *Xīngjì*,
but it is moving excessively into *Xuánxiāo*.
Because of this, there is a seasonal disaster;
*Yīn* cannot withstand *Yáng*.
*Shé* rides *Lóng*;
*Lóng* is the star of *Sòng*
and *Zhèng*.
*Sòng* and *Zhèng* will surely have a famine.
*Xuánxiāo*
is the middle of *Xū*.
*Xiāo* is a name for depletion.
When the earth is empty and the people are depleted,
how could there not be famine?"
B9.28.2 In summer,
the *Qí Hóu*, *Chén Hóu*, *Cài Hóu*, *Běiyàn Bó*, *Qǐ Bó*, *Hú Zǐ*, *Shěn Zǐ*, and the *Báidí* came to court in *Jìn*,
because of the Covenant of *Sòng*.
As the *Qí Hóu* was about to depart,
*Qìng Fēng* said:
"We did not participate in the covenant;
why go to *Jìn*?"
*Chén Wénzǐ* said:
"To put service first and gifts later
is ritual propriety.
When the small serve the great,
and they have not yet had the chance to serve,
to follow them according to their wishes
is ritual propriety.
Even though we did not participate in the covenant,
would we dare rebel against *Jìn*?
The Covenant of *Zhòngqiū*
must not be forgotten.
You should encourage him to go!"
B9.28.3 The people of Wèi punished the faction of the Nìng family,
so Shí È fled to Jìn.
The people of Wèi established his nephew Pǔ
to maintain the sacrifices of the Shí family;
this was in accordance with ritual.
B9.28.4 Duke Dào of Zhū came for an audience;
this was a seasonal attendance.
B9.28.5 In the autumn, the eighth month,
the great rain sacrifice was performed
because of drought.
B9.28.6 The Marquis of Cài returned from Jìn
and entered Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng hosted a banquet for him,
but he was disrespectful.
Zǐchǎn said:
“The Marquis of Cài will likely not escape!
The other day when he passed through here,
the Lord sent Zǐzhǎn to go and greet him outside the East Gate,
and he was arrogant.
I said he might still change.
Now returning, he receives the banquet but is indolent;
this is indeed his nature.
He rules a small state,
serves a large state,
and makes indolence and arrogance his character;
how will he die a natural death?
If he does not escape,
it must be caused by his son.
As a ruler,
he is licentious and does not act as a father.
I, Qiáo, have heard
that for those like this,
there is always calamity through the son.”
B9.28.7 Mèng Xiàobó went to Jìn
to report that because of the Covenant of Sòng
he would go to Chǔ.
B9.28.8 When the Marquis of Cài went to Jìn,
the Earl of Zhèng sent Yóu Jí to Chǔ.
Upon reaching the Hàn River,
the people of Chǔ turned him back,
saying:
“At the Covenant of Sòng,
your lord personally graced us.
Now that you have come,
our lonely lord says that you should return for the time being.
I will send a post-horse to ask Jìn and then inform you.”
Zǐ Dàshū said:
“At the Covenant of Sòng,
your lord’s command was to benefit small states
and also to let them stabilize their altars of soil and grain,
pacify their people,
and receive Heaven’s blessing through ritual.
This was your lord’s decree
and the hope of the small states.
Therefore, our lonely lord sent Jí to offer these furs and silks,
because the years are difficult,
to pay respects to your subordinates.
Now the ministers have a command saying:
‘What do you have to do with government orders?’
You must make your ruler abandon his defensive borders,
traverse mountains and rivers,
brave frost and dew,
to satisfy your lord’s heart.
The small states look to your lord;
how could we dare not obey the command?
But is this not perhaps contrary to the words of the covenant,
thereby causing a lack in your lord’s virtue,
and being disadvantageous to the ministers?
The small states fear this.
Otherwise,
what toil would we dare to dread?”
Zǐ Dàshū returned
and reported his mission.
He told Zǐzhǎn:
“The Viscount of Chǔ is about to die.
He does not cultivate the virtue of his government
but is greedy and ignorant regarding the feudal lords,
using them to satisfy his desires.
Wanting to last long,
is that possible?
The *Zhōu Yì* has it
in the change from *Fù* ䷗ to *Yí*
it says,
‘Confused return,
misfortune,’
does this not refer to the Viscount of Chǔ?
Wanting to return to his desires
while abandoning his foundation,
with no place to return to;
this is called ‘confused return.’
Can there be anything but misfortune?
Our lord should go;
after attending the funeral and returning,
it will satisfy the heart of Chǔ.
For nearly ten years Chǔ
will be unable to care about the feudal lords;
then I can rest our people.”
Bì Zào said:
“This year the King of Zhōu and the Viscount of Chǔ will both die.
The Year Star has left its station
and lodges in next year’s station,
harming the tail of the Bird;
Zhōu and Chǔ will suffer for it.”
In the ninth month,
Yóu Jí of Zhèng went to Jìn
to report that they would attend the court of Chǔ
to follow the Covenant of Sòng.
Zǐchǎn assisted the Earl of Zhèng to go to Chǔ.
At their lodgings, they did not build an altar.
An external servant said:
“In the past, when the former high officers assisted the former lords to visit the four states,
they never failed to build an altar.
From then until now, this has been followed.
Now you lodge in the grass;
is this not perhaps unacceptable?”
Zǐchǎn said:
“When a great state visits a small one,
then an altar is made;
when a small state visits a great one,
if they just lodge, that is enough;
why use an altar?
I, Qiáo, have heard:
A great state visiting a small one has five beauties:
forgiving its crimes and offenses,
pardoning its errors and slips,
rescuing it from disasters and calamities,
rewarding its virtue and regulating its punishments,
and teaching it where it falls short.
The small state is not distressed,
it cherishes and submits as if returning home;
therefore an altar is built
to manifest its merit,
announcing to later generations
not to be negligent in virtue.
A small state visiting a great one has five evils:
pleading regarding its crimes and offenses,
requesting pardon for its inadequacies,
carrying out its administrative duties,
providing its official tributes,
and obeying its seasonal commands.
Otherwise,
it doubles its silks and coins
to congratulate its blessings
and condole its misfortunes.
These are all calamities for a small state;
why use an altar to manifest its calamities?
This is how to tell one's descendants:
it is better not to manifest calamities.”
B9.28.9 Qìng Fēng of Qí loved hunting and was fond of wine.
He gave the government to Qìng Shè,
then he moved his household wealth to the house of Lúpú Miè,
exchanged wives, and drank wine.
After several days,
the court of the capital was moved there.
He allowed those among the exiles who could find the assassins
to report it and return;
therefore Lúpú Guǐ returned.
Guǐ became a servant to Zǐzhī;
he gained favor,
and Zǐzhī gave him a daughter in marriage.
Qìng Shè’s retainers said to Lúpú Guǐ:
“Men and women should distinguish surnames.
You did not avoid your own clan surname;
why?”
He said:
“Since the clan does not avoid me,
why should I alone avoid them?
In reciting poems and taking passages out of context,
I take what I seek;
how would I recognize the clan?”
Guǐ spoke for Wáng Hé and brought him back.
Both men were favorites;
they were made to hold the spears in the bedchamber and precede or follow him.
For the Duke’s meal, there were two chickens daily;
the cook secretly replaced them with ducks.
The charioteer knew of this;
he removed the meat
and served only the broth.
Zǐyǎ and Zǐwěi were angry.
Qìng Fēng told Lúpú Miè.
Lúpú Miè said:
“Compare them to birds and beasts;
I am living and sleeping with them.”
He sent Xī Guīfù to tell Yàn Píngzhòng.
Píngzhòng said:
“My followers are not enough to be of use,
and my knowledge is not enough to plan.
I dare not speak my words;
if there is a covenant, it will be acceptable.”
Zǐjiā said:
“Since your words are thus,
why use a covenant?”
He told Běiguō Zǐchē.
Zǐchē said:
“Each person has their way of serving the ruler;
it is not something I can assist with.”
Chén Wénzǐ said to Huánzǐ:
“Disaster is about to break out;
what shall we gain?”
He replied:
"I obtained a hundred carts of the Qìng family's timber at Zhuāng."
Wénzǐ said:
"You can carefully guard it now."
Lúpú Guǐ and
Wáng Hé divined about attacking the Qìng family;
they showed the omen to Zǐzhī,
saying:
"Someone divined about attacking an enemy,
and ventures to present the omen."
Zǐzhī said:
"Victory,
seeing blood."
In the winter, the tenth month,
Qìng Fèng hunted in Lái,
and Chén Wúyǔ followed him.
On the day bǐngchén,
Wénzǐ sent someone to summon him,
and he requested, saying:
"Wúyǔ's mother is critically ill;
he requests to return."
Qìng Jì divined regarding this,
showed him the omen,
and said:
"Death."
He held the tortoise shell and wept,
then allowed him to return.
Qìng Sì heard of it
and said:
"Disaster is about to break out."
He said to Zǐjiā:
"Return quickly;
the disaster will certainly break out at the cháng sacrifice.
If you return now, you may still make it."
Zǐjiā did not listen,
nor did he have any intention of changing.
Zǐxī said:
"We are lost!
We will be fortunate if we can find refuge in Wú or Yuè."
Chén Wúyǔ crossed the river,
and he destroyed the boats and broke the bridges.
Lúpú Jiāng said to Guǐ:
"If you have a matter and do not tell me,
it will certainly not be successful."
Guǐ told her.
Jiāng said:
"The master is headstrong;
if no one stops him,
he will not fail to go out.
I request to stop him."
Guǐ said:
"Very well."
In the eleventh month, on the day yǐhài,
the cháng sacrifice was held at the temple of Tàigōng,
and Qìng Shè presided over the matters.
Lúpú Jiāng told him,
and furthermore tried to stop him,
but he did not listen,
saying:
"Who would dare?"
He then went to the Lord.
Má Yīng acted as the personator;
Qìng Xiè made the first offering.
Lúpú Guǐ and Wáng Hé held the chamber halberds;
the Qìng family surrounded the Lord's palace with their armored men.
The grooms of the Chén and Bǎo families acted as performers.
The Qìng family's horses were easily startled;
the soldiers all removed their armor,
tethered their horses,
and drank wine,
while watching the performers,
reaching as far as Yúlǐ.
The followers of Luán, Gāo, Chén, and Bǎo
donned the armor of the Qìng family.
Zǐwěi pulled out a rafter,
and struck the door three times.
Lúpú Guǐ stabbed Zǐzhī from behind,
and Wáng Hé struck him with a halberd,
severing his left shoulder.
He still grasped a temple rafter,
shaking the roof ridge.
He threw sacrificial stands and jars,
killing people before he died.
They then killed Qìng Shéng and Má Yīng.
The Lord was afraid.
Bǎo Guó said:
"Your ministers are doing this for the sake of the Lord."
Chén Xūwú escorted the Lord back;
he removed his formal robes and entered the inner palace.
Qìng Fèng returned
and met those reporting the rebellion.
On the day dīnghài,
he attacked the West Gate,
but did not succeed.
He turned to attack the North Gate,
and succeeded.
He entered
and attacked the inner palace,
but did not succeed.
He turned back,
drew up his forces at Yuè,
and requested battle,
but it was not granted,
so he then fled here.
He presented a carriage to Jì Wǔzǐ;
its beautiful polish was like a mirror.
Zhǎn Zhuāngshū saw it
and said:
"The carriage is so polished,
but the people must be exhausted;
it is fitting that he should be ruined."
Shūsūn Mùzǐ provided a meal for Qìng Fèng;
Qìng Fèng performed the sacrificial sprinkling too broadly.
Mùzǐ was not pleased
and ordered a musician to recite for him the poem "Máo Chī,"
but he still did not understand.
Soon after, people from Qí came to rebuke him,
and he fled to Wú.
Gùyú of Wú gave him Zhūfāng,
where he gathered his clan and resided.
He became wealthier than he had been before.
Zǐfú Huìbó said to Shūsūn:
"Heaven is perhaps enriching this licentious man;
Qìng Fèng is wealthy once again."
Mùzǐ said:
"When a good man becomes wealthy, it is called a reward;
when a licentious man becomes wealthy, it is called a calamity.
Heaven is likely bringing calamity upon him;
it will gather them together only to annihilate them."
B9.28.10 On the day guǐsì,
the King of Heaven passed away.
Since no one had yet come to announce the death,
it was not yet recorded,
which was in accordance with ritual.
B9.28.11 During the turmoil of the Cuì family,
many of the young princes were lost.
Therefore, Gùchú was in Lǔ,
Shūsūn Huán was in Yān,
and Jiǎ was at the hill of Gòudú.
When the Qìng family fell,
they were all summoned back;
their ritual vessels and implements were prepared,
and their cities were returned to them.
Yànzǐ was given Bèidiàn
and its sixty border districts,
but he would not accept it.
Zǐwěi said:
"Wealth
is what people desire.
Why do you alone not desire it?"
He replied:
"The Qìng family's cities were enough to satisfy desire,
and for that reason, they perished.
My cities are not enough to satisfy desire;
if you add Bèidiàn to them,
they would then be enough to satisfy desire.
Once desire is satisfied,
ruin will come any day.
While I was abroad,
I could not even govern my own single city.
My not accepting Bèidiàn
is not because I hate wealth,
but because I fear losing wealth.
Furthermore, wealth
is like the set width of cloth or silk.
One makes regulations for it
to ensure it does not shift.
As for the people,
when their livelihood is generous and their usage is beneficial,
one then uses rectified virtue
to set a limit for it,
so as to prevent degradation and arrogance;
this is called 'setting the width of benefit.'
When benefit is excessive, it leads to failure.
I do not dare to be greedy for more;
this is what I mean by 'setting the width'."
Běiguō Zuǒ was given sixty cities,
and he accepted them.
Zǐyǎ was given cities;
he declined many and accepted few.
Zǐwěi was given cities;
he accepted them but gradually returned them.
The Lord considered him loyal,
and so he was favored.
Lúpú Miè was released at the northern border.
They searched for Cuì Zhù's body,
intending to mutilate it,
but could not find it.
Shūsūn Mùzǐ said:
"We must find it.
King Wǔ had ten able ministers;
did Cuì Zhù not have them too?
Without ten people,
it would not have been enough to bury him."
Afterwards,
a servant of the Cuì family said:
"Give me a large jade ring,
and I will present his coffin."
Thereupon they found it.
In the twelfth month, on the *yǐhài* new moon,
the people of Qí moved [the remains of] Zhuāng Gōng
and held the lying-in-state in the Great Hall.
They exposed the coffin and corpse of Cuì Zhù in the marketplace.
The people of the capital still recognized him;
they all said,
"It is Cuì Zǐ!"
B9.28.12 Because of the covenant of Sòng,
the Duke, along with the Duke of Sòng, the Marquis of Chén, the Earl of Zhèng, and the Baron of Xǔ, went to Chǔ.
The Duke passed through Zhèng;
the Earl of Zhèng was not there.
Bó Yǒu went to greet and comfort him at Huángyá,
but was disrespectful.
Mù Shū said:
"If Bó Yǒu does not meet with misfortune in Zhèng,
Zhèng will surely have a great calamity.
Reverence
is the master of the people;
yet he abandons it,
how can he maintain his position?
If the people of Zhèng do not punish him,
they will surely suffer for his crime.
From the banks of the marsh,
the water-shield and pondweed of the runoff,
placed in the ancestral temple,
and presided over by the maiden Jì Lán—
this is reverence.
Can reverence be abandoned?"
When they reached the Hàn,
Kāng Wáng of Chǔ died.
The Duke wished to return.
Shūzhòng Zhāobó said:
"Our journey is for the sake of the state of Chǔ;
how could it be for one person?
Let us proceed!"
Zǐfú Huìbó said:
"A gentleman has long-term plans,
while a petty man follows what is near.
If hunger and cold are not attended to,
who has leisure for what comes after?
It is better to return for the time being."
Shūsūn Mùzǐ said:
"Shūzhòng Zǐ is dedicated to the cause;
Zǐfú Zǐ
is but a beginner."
Róng Chéngbó said:
"He who plans for the distant
is loyal."
The Duke then proceeded.
Xiàng Xū of Sòng said:
"Our journey is for the sake of one person,
not for the sake of Chǔ.
If hunger and cold are not attended to,
who can care for Chǔ?
Let us return for a while to rest the people,
wait for them to establish a ruler,
and then make preparations for it."
The Duke of Sòng then returned.
B9.28.13 Qū Jiàn of Chǔ died;
Zhào Wénzǐ mourned him
as if he were a member of the same alliance,
which was according to ritual.
B9.28.14 The King's messenger came to announce the mourning [for King Líng];
when asked for the day of the collapse,
he announced it as *jiǎyín*.
Therefore it was recorded,
to demonstrate the error.
A9.29 *The Classic of Duke Xiāng, Twenty-Ninth Year*
A9.29.1 In the twenty-ninth year, in spring,
the King's first month,
the Duke was in Chǔ.
A9.29.2 In summer, the fifth month,
the Duke arrived from Chǔ.
A9.29.3 On *gēngwǔ*,
Kàn, the Marquis of Wèi, died.
A9.29.4 A gatekeeper assassinated Yújì, the Viscount of Wú.
A9.29.5 Zhòngsūn Jié met with Xún Yíng of Jìn,
Gāo Zhǐ of Qí,
Huà Dìng of Sòng,
Shìshū Yí of Wèi,
Gōngsūn Duàn of Zhèng,
the people of Cáo,
the people of Jǔ,
the people of Téng,
the people of Xuē,
and the people of Xiǎozhū to wall Qǐ.
A9.29.6 The Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Yāng to come on a mission of state.
The Viscount of Qǐ came to make a covenant.
A9.29.8 Zhá, the Viscount of Wú's envoy, came on a mission of state.
A9.29.9 In autumn, the ninth month,
they buried Wèi Xiàn Gōng.
A9.29.10 Gāo Zhǐ of Qí fled to Běiyàn.
A9.29.11 In winter,
Zhòngsūn Jié went to Jìn.
B9.29 *The Commentary of Duke Xiāng, Twenty-Ninth Year*
B9.29.1 In the twenty-ninth year, in spring, the King's first month,
the Duke was in Chǔ,
which explains why he did not perform the New Year audience at the ancestral temple.
The people of Chǔ made the Duke personally place the shroud;
the Duke was distressed by this.
Mù Shū said:
"If the coffin is exorcised before placing the shroud,
then it is merely presenting silk."
Thereupon, he had a shaman use peach branches and reed brooms to first exorcise the coffin.
The people of Chǔ did not forbid it,
but afterwards they regretted it.
B9.29.2 In the second month, on *guǐmǎo*,
the people of Qí buried Zhuāng Gōng in Běiguō.
B9.29.3 In summer, the fourth month,
they buried Kāng Wáng of Chǔ;
the Duke, along with the Marquis of Chén, the Earl of Zhèng, and the Baron of Xǔ, escorted the burial
as far as outside the western gate,
while the Great Officers of the feudal lords all went as far as the tomb.
Jiǎ Áo of Chǔ ascended the throne,
and Wángzǐ Wéi became the Lìngyǐn.
Zǐyǔ, the Messenger of Zhèng, said:
"This is what is called inappropriate;
he who succeeds him will surely flourish.
Beneath pines and cypresses,
the grass does not grow."
B9.29.4 The Duke returned,
and reached Fāngchéng.
Jì Wǔzǐ took Biàn;
he sent Gōngyě to ask after the Duke,
and sent a sealed letter after him to give to him,
saying:
"I heard that the defenders of Biàn were going to rebel;
I led followers to punish them,
and have already captured it.
I venture to report this."
Gōngyě delivered the message and withdrew;
reaching his lodging,
only then did he hear of the taking of Biàn.
The Duke said:
"He wanted it yet said they were rebelling;
he only shows himself to be distant."
The Duke said to Gōngyě:
"May I enter?"
He replied:
"Your Lordship truly possesses the state;
who would dare oppose Your Lordship?"
The Duke gave Gōngyě the cap and robes.
He firmly declined,
and only accepted after being forced.
The Duke wished not to enter.
Róng Chéngbó recited "Shì Wēi,"
and then they returned.
In the fifth month,
the Duke arrived from Chǔ.
Gōngyě returned his fief to the Jì Shì
and never entered there again.
He said:
"To deceive his lord,
why did he have to use me?"
When Jìsūn saw him,
he spoke of the Jì Shì as in former days;
when he did not see him, he never spoke of the Jì Shì.
When he became ill,
he gathered his retainers
and said:
"When I die,
you must not use the cap and robes for my burial shroud,
as it was not a reward for virtue.
Moreover, do not let the Jì Shì bury me."
B9.29.5 At the burial of Líng Wáng,
the high ministers of Zhèng had duties.
Zǐzhǎn sent Yìn Duàn to go.
Bó Yǒu said:
"He is weak,
he cannot do it."
Zǐzhǎn said:
"Compared to no one going,
although he is weak,
is it not still better?
The *Shī* says:
'The King's business never ends,
No leisure to sit or rest.'
North, south, east, and west,
who dares to rest in peace?
We steadfastly serve Jìn and Chǔ
to protect the Royal House.
When the King's business is not neglected,
what constant rule is there for who goes?"
He then sent Yìn Duàn to Zhōu.
B9.29.6 The people of Wú attacked Chǔ,
and captured prisoners there.
They made one a gatekeeper
and had him guard a boat.
Yú Jì, the Viscount of Wú, went to view the boat,
and the gatekeeper assassinated him with a knife.
B9.29.7 Zǐ Zhǎn of Zhèng died,
and Zǐ Pí succeeded to his position.
At that time, there was a famine in Zhèng,
and it was not yet time for the wheat harvest,
so the people were suffering.
Zǐ Pí, acting on the command of Zǐ Zhǎn, gave grain to the people of the capital;
one zhōng per household.
Because of this, he won the people of the state of Zhèng;
therefore, the Hǎn clan always managed the state's government
and served as the High Minister.
Sīchéng Zǐhǎn of Sòng heard of this
and said:
"Being neighborly to goodness
is what the people hope for."
Sòng also had a famine.
He requested of Duke Píng
to distribute the Duke's grain as loans;
he made all the Grand Officers provide loans as well.
The Sīchéng clan provided loans without recording them
and provided loans for those Grand Officers who had no grain.
There were no starving people in Sòng.
Shú Xiàng heard of this
and said:
"The Hǎn of Zhèng
and the Yuè of Sòng
will be the last to perish;
will both of them not gain control of their states!
The people flock to them.
Bestowing favors without feeling virtuous—
the Yuè clan added to this;
will they not rise and fall with Sòng?"
B9.29.8 Duke Píng of Jìn
was born of a lady from Qǐ,
so he attended to Qǐ.
In the sixth month,
Zhì Dàozǐ assembled the Grand Officers of the feudal lords
to build walls for Qǐ.
Mèng Xiàobó met with them,
and Zǐ Dàshū and Bó Shí of Zhèng went there.
Zǐ Dàshū saw Dàshū Wénzǐ
and spoke with him.
Wénzǐ said:
"How excessive is this building of walls for Qǐ!"
Zǐ Dàshū said:
"What can be done?
The state of Jìn does not care for the deficiencies of the Zhōu royal clan,
but instead protects the remnants of Xià;
its abandonment of the Jī clans
can already be known.
If the Jī clans are abandoned,
who will turn to them?
I, Jí, have heard
that abandoning those who are the same and approaching those who are different
is called 'divergent virtue.'
The Classic of Poetry says:
'Be harmonious and close with your neighbors;
marriages are very many.'
If Jìn is not neighborly,
who will speak with it?"
B9.29.9 Gāo Zǐróng and the Sītu of Sòng saw Zhì Bó;
Nǚ Qí assisted with the ritual.
When the guests left,
Sīmǎ Hóu spoke to Zhì Bó, saying:
"Both of these men will not escape calamity.
Zǐróng is arbitrary,
and the Sītu is extravagant;
both are lords who will lose their houses."
Zhì Bó said:
"How so?"
He replied:
"Being arbitrary leads to a quick end.
Being extravagant will lead to ruin by one's own power.
If one is arbitrary, others will indeed destroy him;
it is about to happen."
B9.29.10 Fàn Xiànzǐ came on a mission of courtesy,
to thank for the walling of Qǐ.
The Duke entertained him at a banquet,
and Zhǎn Zhuāngshū held the offerings.
There were three pairs of archers.
The Duke's officers were not enough,
so they were taken from the house officers.
Of the house officers,
Zhǎn Xiá and Zhǎn Wángfù formed one pair;
of the Duke's officers,
Gōngwū Zhàobó and
Zhòngyán Zhuāngshū formed one pair,
and Céng Gǔfù and Dǎngshū formed one pair.
B9.29.11 The Marquis of Jìn sent Sīmǎ Nǚ Shúhóu to come
and settle the fields of Qǐ,
but he did not return all of them.
Lady Dào of Jìn said indignantly:
"Qí took bribes.
If the late lord had knowledge,
he would not still favor taking them."
The Duke told Shúhóu.
Shúhóu said:
"Yú, Guó, Jiāo, Huá,
Huò, Yáng, Hán, and Wèi
were all of the Jī surname,
and Jìn became great because of them.
If not by encroaching on small states,
where would it take land?
From the reigns of Wǔ and Xiàn downwards,
many states have been annexed;
who can set them right?
Qǐ
is a remnant of Xià,
yet it follows the Dōng Yí.
Lǔ
is the descendant of the Duke of Zhōu,
and is harmonious with Jìn.
Even enfeoffing Lǔ with Qǐ would be acceptable;
why complain about it?
As for Lǔ in relation to Jìn,
tributary duties are not lacking,
curiosities and luxuries arrive on time,
high ministers and grand officers follow one another in our court,
the scribes never stop recording,
and the treasury has no empty months.
If it is like this, it is enough.
Why must we emaciate Lǔ to fatten Qǐ?
Moreover, if the late lord has knowledge,
he would rather favor the Lady,
and why would he use an old servant like me?"
B9.29.12 Duke Wén of Qǐ came
to make a covenant.
The record says
"Viscount,"
to treat him as lowly.
B9.29.13 Noble Son Zhá of Wú came on a mission of courtesy.
He saw Shú sūn Mù zǐ
and was pleased with him.
He said to Mù zǐ:
"Will you not be able to die a natural death?
You love goodness but cannot choose the right people.
I have heard that a gentleman's task lies in choosing people.
You are a principal minister of Lǔ
and are entrusted with its great government;
if you are not careful in your appointments,
how will you be able to bear it?
Disaster will surely reach you!"
He requested to observe the music of Zhōu.
He had the artisans sing for him the Zhōu nán and Shào nán.
He said:
"How beautiful!
The foundation was begun here,
yet it was not yet complete;
however, they were industrious without resentment."
They sang for him the songs of Bèi, Yóng, and Wèi.
He said:
"How beautiful and deep!
They are sorrowful but not distressed.
I have heard that the virtues of Kāng Shú and
Duke Wǔ of Wèi were like this;
these are surely the Airs of Wèi!"
They sang for him the songs of Wáng.
He said:
"How beautiful!
Longing without fear;
is this perhaps the eastward move of Zhōu?"
They sang for him the songs of Zhèng.
He said:
"How beautiful!
But their triviality is already extreme;
the people cannot endure it.
Will this state not be the first to perish?"
They sang for him the songs of Qí.
He said:
"How beautiful!
How expansive!
A great wind indeed!
The one who stands as a model for the Eastern Sea,
is it not Tài Gōng?
The state's future is immeasurable."
They sang for him the songs of Bīn.
He said:
"How beautiful!
How vast!
Joyful without licentiousness;
is this perhaps the Duke of Zhōu's eastward move?"
They sang for him the songs of Qín and he said: "This is what is called the 'Xià' sound.
To be able to be 'Xià' is to be great;
it is the height of greatness.
Is it perhaps the old territory of Zhōu?"
They sang for him the songs of Wèi.
He said:
"How beautiful!
How swirling and breezy!
Grand yet graceful;
dangerous yet easy to traverse.
If one supplements this with virtue,
then one is an enlightened ruler."
They sang for him the songs of Táng,
and he said,
“How deep are the thoughts!
Do they not have the legacy of the Táotáng clan?
If not,
how could the sorrow be so far-reaching?
If they were not the descendants of eminent virtue,
who could be like this?”
They sang for him the songs of Chén,
and he said,
“The state has no master;
can it long endure?”
From the songs of Kuài downwards, he offered no comments.
They sang for him the Xiǎoyǎ,
and he said,
“How beautiful!
Thoughtful without being double-minded,
resentful without speaking out—
is this perhaps the decline of the virtue of Zhōu?
There are still the remaining people of the former kings.”
They sang for him the Dàyǎ,
and he said,
“How vast!
How harmonious and joyous!
Winding but with a straightforward substance—
this must be the virtue of Wénwáng!”
They sang for him the Sòng,
and he said,
“This is the ultimate!
Straightforward but not arrogant,
winding but not submissive,
close but not pressing,
distant but not estranged,
changing but not excessive,
repeating but not wearisome,
mournful but not distressed,
joyful but not dissipated,
used but not exhausted,
broad but not ostentatious,
bestowing but not wasteful,
taking but not greedy,
abiding but not stagnating,
acting but not drifting.
The five notes are in harmony;
the eight winds are balanced.
The rhythm has measure;
the preservation has order;
this is what all great virtues share.”
On seeing the dances Xiàngshuò
and Nányuè,
he said,
“Beautiful,
yet there is still something to be regretted.”
On seeing the dance Dàwǔ,
he said,
“How beautiful!
The greatness of Zhōu,
was it truly like this?”
On seeing the dance Sháohù,
he said,
“The magnanimity of a sage,
and yet there is still a sense of shame in his virtue;
how difficult it is to be a sage!”
On seeing the dance Dàxià,
he said,
“How beautiful!
Diligent without claiming virtue for himself—
if it were not for Yǔ,
who else could have achieved this?”
On seeing the dance Sháoshuò,
he said,
“Virtue has reached its peak!
How great!
Like heaven covering nothing it does not cover,
like earth supporting nothing it does not support.
Even if there were more abundant virtue,
nothing could be added to this;
observation stops here.
If there is other music,
I dare not ask for more.”
When he went on his mission,
it was to announce the succession of the new ruler.
Therefore, he then went on a mission to Qí
and was pleased with Yàn Píngzhòng,
telling him,
“You should quickly hand over your fief and your government post.
Without a fief and without a post,
you will escape disaster.
The government of the state of Qí will soon find a new master;
until it finds that master,
the troubles will not cease.”
Therefore Yànzǐ, through Chén Huánzǐ,
handed over his government post and fief,
and because of this escaped from the disasters of Luán
and Gāo.
He went on a mission to Zhèng
and met Zǐchǎn,
like old friends.
He gave him a belt of plain white silk,
and Zǐchǎn presented him with a garment of fine hemp.
He told Zǐchǎn,
“Those in power in Zhèng are extravagant;
trouble is about to arrive,
and the government will surely fall to you.
When you are in power,
manage it carefully with ritual propriety.
Otherwise,
the state of Zhèng will be ruined.”
He went to Wèi
and was pleased with Qú Yuàn, Shǐ Gǒu, Shǐ Qiū,
Gōngzǐ Jīng, Gōngshū Fā, and Gōngzǐ Zhāo,
saying,
“Wèi has many gentlemen;
there will be no disaster there.”
From Wèi he went to Jìn.
He was about to stay the night in Qī
when he heard the sound of bells
and said,
“How strange!
I have heard
that eloquence without virtue
will surely lead to execution.
That gentleman has offended his ruler and is here;
fear should not even be enough,
so why is there music?
That gentleman being here
is like a swallow nesting on a tent curtain.
Moreover, the ruler is in his coffin;
is it possible to have music?”
So he left.
Wénzǐ heard of this
and for the rest of his life did not listen to the qín or sè zithers.
He went to Jìn
and was pleased with Zhào Wénzǐ, Hán Xuānzǐ,
and Wèi Xiànzǐ,
saying,
“The state of Jìn will likely gather
in the three clans!”
He was pleased with Shū Xiàng.
When he was about to depart,
he said to Shū Xiàng,
“My master, exert yourself!
The ruler is extravagant
and there are many good men,
the grandees are all wealthy;
government will soon be in private hands.
My master, you love uprightness;
you must think of how to escape disaster yourself.”
B9.29.14 In the autumn, the ninth month,
Gōngsūn Chài and Gōngsūn Zào of Qí
banished their grandee Gāo Zhǐ to Běiyàn.
On the day Yǐwèi,
he left.
The Annals record “fled into exile,”
to charge Gāo Zhǐ with the crime.
Gāo Zhǐ loved to take credit for affairs for himself
and was also autocratic;
therefore disaster reached him.
B9.29.15 In winter,
Mèng Xiàobó went to Jìn to return the visit of Fàn Shú.
B9.29.16 Because of the trouble of the Gāo clan,
Gāo Shù rebelled at Lú.
In the tenth month, on the day Gēngyín,
Lǘqiū Yīng led the army to besiege Lú.
Gāo Shù said,
“If only the Gāo clan is allowed to have a successor,
I request to hand over the city.”
The people of Qí established Yàn, the great-grandson of Jìngzhòng,
because they thought well of Jìngzhòng.
In the eleventh month, on the day Yǐmǎo,
Gāo Shù handed over Lú and fled to Jìn.
The people of Jìn built a city at Mián and placed him there.
B9.29.17 Bóyǒu of Zhèng sent Gōngsūn Hēi to Chǔ.
He declined, saying,
“Chǔ and Zhèng are currently on bad terms,
and you send me there;
this is killing me.”
Bóyǒu said,
“It is the work of your family for generations.”
Zǐxī said,
“If it were possible I would go;
if difficult then I stop;
what does ‘generations’ have to do with it?”
Bóyǒu was about to force him to go.
Zǐxī was angry
and was about to attack the Bóyǒu clan.
The grandees mediated between them.
In the twelfth month, on the day Jǐsì,
the grandees of Zhèng made a covenant at the Bóyǒu clan’s house.
Bì Chén said,
“This covenant—
how long will it last?
The Shī says:
‘Gentlemen repeatedly make covenants,
and chaos is thereby prolonged.’
Now this is the way to prolong chaos;
the disaster has not ceased;
it will surely be three years before there can be relief.”
Rán Míng said:
“Where will the government go?”
Bì Chén said:
“That the good replaces the not-good
is the mandate of Heaven;
how could it avoid Zǐchǎn?
His promotions do not skip ranks,
so official positions are orderly.
He chooses the good for promotion,
so the generations flourish.
Heaven has moreover cleared the way for him
by taking away Bó Yǒu’s soul,
and since Zǐxī has passed away,
how can he be avoided?
Heaven has brought calamity to Zhèng for a long time;
it must make Zǐchǎn give it rest,
and then it may yet reach stability.
Otherwise,
it will perish.”
A9.30 The Classic of Duke Xiāng, Thirtieth Year
A9.30.1 In the spring of the thirtieth year,
in the royal first month,
the Viscount of Chǔ sent Wěi Bà to pay a courtesy visit.
A9.30.2 In the summer, in the fourth month,
Bān, the Heir Apparent of Cài, assassinated his ruler, Gù.
A9.30.3 In the fifth month, on the day jiǎwǔ,
Sòng suffered a fire,
and Bó Jī of Sòng died.
A9.30.4 The Heavenly King killed his younger brother Nìngfū.
A9.30.5 Prince Xiá fled to Jìn.
A9.30.6 In the autumn, in the seventh month,
Shū Gōng went to Sòng
to bury Gòng Jī of Sòng.
A9.30.7 Liáng Xiāo of Zhèng fled to Xǔ;
from Xǔ he entered Zhèng,
and the people of Zhèng killed Liáng Xiāo.
A9.30.8 In the winter, in the tenth month,
Duke Jǐng of Cài was buried.
A9.30.9 Men of Jìn,
men of Qí,
men of Sòng,
men of Wèi,
men of Zhèng,
men of Cáo,
men of Jǔ,
men of Zhū,
men of Téng,
men of Xuē,
men of Qǐ,
and men of Xiǎo Zhū met at Chányuān
on account of the fire in Sòng.
B9.30 The Commentary of Duke Xiāng, Thirtieth Year
B9.30.1 In the spring of the thirtieth year,
in the royal first month,
the Viscount of Chǔ sent Wěi Bà to pay a courtesy visit,
to establish relations for the succeeding ruler.
Mùshū asked
how Prince Wéi was managing the government.
He replied:
“Small people like us eat
and listen to affairs;
we still fear not being equal to our orders
and not escaping punishment;
how could we know about the government?”
He persisted in asking,
but he did not tell.
Mùshū told the grandees:
“The Lìngyǐn of Chǔ is about to have a great matter,
and Zǐdàng will assist him in it;
he is hiding its true nature.”
B9.30.2 Zǐchǎn accompanied the Earl of Zhèng to go to Jìn,
and Shū Xiàng asked
about the government of the state of Zhèng.
He replied:
“Whether I shall be able to see you again or not
depends on this year.
Sì and
Liáng are currently contending,
and it is not yet known how it will be settled.
If it is settled,
and I am able to see you,
then it can be known.”
Shū Xiàng said:
“Have they not already been reconciled?”
He replied:
“Bó Yǒu is extravagant and obstinate;
Zǐxī likes being above others;
neither can submit to the other.
Even if they are reconciled,
they are still accumulating hatred for each other;
the day when hatred reaches its peak is not far off.”
B9.30.3 In the second month, on the day guǐwèi,
the wife of Duke Dào of Jìn gave food to the laborers who were building the walls of Qǐ;
a man of Jiàng County happened to be of great age;
having no son, he went
to participate in the meal.
Someone doubted his age
and made him state it.
He said:
“I
am a small man
and do not know how to record years.
In the year I was born,
on the first day of the first month, jiǎzǐ,
there have been four hundred and forty-five jiǎzǐ cycles;
the last cycle up to today is one-third complete.”
The officials ran to ask at the court.
Shī Kuàng said:
“That was the year when Shūzhòng Huìbó of Lǔ met Xì Chéngzǐ at Chéngkuāng.
In that year,
the Dí attacked Lǔ;
Shūsūn Zhuāngshū then defeated the Dí at Xián,
capturing the tall Dí Qiáorú as well as Huǐ and Bào,
and naming his sons after them.
It has been seventy-three years.”
Shǐ Zhào said:
“The character hài has two as its head and six as its body;
the two below are like the body;
this represents the number of his days.”
Shì Wénbó said:
“In that case, it is twenty-six thousand, six hundred and six decades.”
Zhào Mèng asked the magistrate of the county,
and he was one of his subordinates.
He summoned him
and apologized for his error,
saying: “I, Wǔ, am untalented;
holding the great affairs of the ruler,
with the state of Jìn having many troubles,
I have been unable to follow you, my elder,
and have caused you to be disgraced in the mud and mire for a long time;
this is Wǔ’s crime.
I venture to apologize for my lack of talent.”
He then gave him an office,
making him assist in the government.
He declined on account of old age.
He gave him land
and made him the ruler’s Fùtáo official,
and appointed him as the Master of Jiàng County,
while abolishing his post as Superintendent of Chariots.
At this time, the envoy from Lǔ was in Jìn;
on his return, he told the grandees about it.
Jì Wǔzǐ said:
“Jìn must not be taken lightly.
They have Zhào Mèng as a grandee,
they have Bó Xiá as an assistant,
they have Shǐ Zhào and Shī Kuàng
to consult and deliberate with,
and they have Shū Xiàng and Nǚ Qí
to act as teachers and protectors for their ruler.
Their court has many superior men;
how could they be taken lightly!
Only by making an effort to serve them can we succeed.”
B9.30.4 In the summer, in the fourth month, on the day jǐhài,
the Earl of Zhèng and his grandees made a covenant.
The superior man by this knows that the troubles of Zhèng will not cease.
B9.30.5 Marquis Jǐng of Cài had married a wife from Chǔ for the Heir Apparent Bān,
and then had illicit relations with her.
The Heir Apparent assassinated Marquis Jǐng.
B9.30.6 Earlier,
Wáng Dānjì died,
and his son Kuò was about to have an audience with the King
and sighed.
Qiānqī, a son of the House of Shàn, was an attendant for King Líng;
he met him in the court,
heard his sigh,
and said:
“Alas!
It must come to this!”
He went in to report to the King,
and said:
“You must kill him!
He does not look sorrowful but his ambitions are great;
his eyes are restless and his gait is high;
his heart is elsewhere.
If you do not kill him,
he will certainly cause harm.”
The King said:
“What does a young boy know!”
When King Líng passed away,
Dān Kuò wanted to establish Prince Nìngfū.
Nìngfū did not know of it.
On the day wùzǐ,
Dān Kuò surrounded Wěi
and drove out Chéng Qiān.
Qiānqī fled to Píngzhǐ.
In the fifth month, on the day guǐsì,
Yǐn Yánduō, Liú Yì, Shàn Miè,
Gān Guò, and Gǒng Chéng killed Nìngfū.
Kuò, Xiá, and Liào fled to Jìn.
The *Shū* says, "The Heavenly King killed his younger brother Nìngfū,"
because the guilt lay with the King.
B9.30.7 Someone cried out in the Grand Temple of Sòng,
saying:
"Hī-hī,
Out-out!"
A bird sang at the Bóshè,
as if saying
"Hī-hī."
On the day jiǎwǔ,
Sòng suffered a great fire.
Sòng Bó Jī died,
because she waited for her governess.
Superior men said of Sòng Gòng Jī:
"She was a maiden but not a wife.
A maiden waits for others;
a wife acts according to righteousness."
B9.30.8 In the sixth month, Zǐchǎn of Zhèng went to Chén to preside over a covenant;
returning,
he reported his mission.
He told the grandees:
"Chén
is a doomed state;
one cannot associate with it.
They store up grain and millet,
repair the inner and outer city walls,
relying on these two,
but do not soothe their people.
Its ruler is weakly planted,
the young lords are extravagant,
the heir apparent is humble,
the grandees are arrogant,
the government has many factions,
while being situated between great states.
Can it avoid being destroyed?
It will not exceed ten years."
B9.30.9 In autumn, the seventh month, Shū Gōng went to Sòng
to bury Gòng Jī.
B9.30.10 Bó Yǒu of Zhèng was fond of wine.
He made an underground room,
and drank wine at night, striking bells there.
When morning came,
he had not finished.
Those who came to court said:
"Where is the Lord?"
His people said:
"Our Lord is in the Hègǔ."
They all left the court, spreading out on the road and dispersing.
Later, when the court met,
he was again about to send Zǐxī
to Chǔ;
returning, he drank wine.
On gēngzǐ,
Zǐxī, using the armored men of the Sì clan,
attacked and burned his house.
Bó Yǒu fled to Yōngliáng;
he only knew of it after waking up.
Then he fled to Xǔ.
The grandees gathered to deliberate.
Zǐpí said:
"The *Zhònghuǐ zhī Zhì* says:
'Take those in chaos,
insult those who are perishing.
Overthrow the perishing and strengthen the surviving;
this is the profit of the state.'
Hǎn, Sì, and Fēng were born of the same lineage;
Bó Yǒu was arrogant and extravagant,
so he could not escape."
People said Zǐchǎn was siding with the upright and helping the strong.
Zǐchǎn said:
"Is it for my followers?
In the calamities and difficulties of the state,
who knows what will be ruined?
If some lead with strength and uprightness,
then difficulties will not arise.
For now, I will fulfill my place."
On xīnjiǔ,
Zǐchǎn collected the dead of Bó Yǒu's clan
and placed them in coffins,
and before he could consult with others,
he then departed.
Yìn Duàn followed him.
Zǐpí stopped the pursuit.
The crowd said:
"The man does not follow us,
why stop us?"
Zǐpí said:
"The master is ritual towards the dead;
how much more so towards the living?"
So he himself stopped them.
On rényín,
Zǐchǎn entered.
On guǐmǎo,
Zǐshí entered.
They all received the covenant at the house of the Zǐxī clan.
On yǐsì,
the Earl of Zhèng and his grandees made a covenant at the Grand Palace,
and made a covenant with the people of the state outside the Shīzhīliáng.
Bó Yǒu heard that the people of Zhèng had made a covenant against him,
and was angry;
hearing that the armored men of Zǐpí
did not participate in attacking him,
he was happy
and said:
"Zǐpí is with me!"
On guǐchǒu,
at dawn,
he entered from the ditch of the Mùmén,
and through the Master of Horse Jié,
put on armor in the Xiāngkù,
to attack the Old North Gate.
Sì Dài led the people of the state to attack him.
All summoned Zǐchǎn.
Zǐchǎn said:
"When brothers come to this,
I follow what Heaven gives."
Bó Yǒu died in the Yángshì.
Zǐchǎn provided the burial shroud,
pillowed the head on his thigh and wept for him,
and having put him in a coffin, he placed him with Bó Yǒu's ministers
who were at the side of the market,
and later buried him in Dǒuchéng.
The Zǐsì clan wanted to attack Zǐchǎn.
Zǐpí was angry with them,
saying:
"Ritual
is the trunk of the state.
To kill one who has ritual,
no calamity is greater than this."
So they stopped.
Then Yóu Jí went to Jìn;
returning,
he heard of the trouble
and did not enter.
He reported his mission at the border.
In the eighth month, on jiǎzǐ,
he fled to Jìn.
Sì Dài pursued him,
reaching Suānzǎo.
With Zǐshàng
they used two jade tablets as a pledge to the River.
He sent Gōngsūn Xì to enter and covenant with the grandees.
On jǐsì,
he returned again.
The *Shū* says "The people of Zhèng killed Liáng Xiāo,"
not calling him a grandee,
to say he entered from outside.
At the death of Zǐjiǎo,
when they were about to bury him,
Gōngsūn Huī and Bì Zào met at dawn for the matter.
Passing the Bó Yǒu clan's house,
weeds were growing on top of its gate.
Zǐyǔ said:
"Are those weeds still there?"
At that time, the Year-star was in Jiànglóu,
and Jiànglóu was in the center at dawn.
Bì Zào pointed at it
and said:
"He can still last to the end of the year,
but the year will not reach this station again."
When he perished,
the Year-star was at the mouth of Jūzī,
and the next year it reached Jiànglóu.
Pú Zhǎn followed Bó Yǒu,
and died with him.
Yǔ Jié fled to Jìn
and became a grandee of Rèn.
At the meeting of Jīzé,
Lè Chéng of Zhèng fled to Chǔ,
and then went to Jìn.
Yǔ Jié followed him,
and associated with him to serve Zhào Wénzǐ,
speaking of the plan to attack Zhèng.
Because of the covenant of Sòng,
it was not possible.
Zǐpí made Gōngsūn Chú the Master of Horse.
B9.30.11 Wángzǐ Wéi of Chǔ killed the Grand Minister of War Wěi Yǎn
and took his household.
Shēn Wúyǔ said:
"The Prince surely will not escape.
Good men
are the masters of the state.
The Prince assists the state of Chǔ,
and should properly foster these,
but instead he treats them cruelly;
this is to bring calamity to the state.
Furthermore, the Minister of War
is the assistant of the Lìngyǐn,
and the four limbs of the King.
To cut off the master of the people,
to remove one's own assistant,
and to lop off the King's limbs,
thereby bringing calamity to his state—
no inauspiciousness is greater than this.
How can he escape?"
Because of the disaster in Sòng,
the Great Officers of the feudal lords met
to plan for the return of wealth to Sòng.
In the tenth month of winter,
Shūsūn Bào met with Zhào Wǔ of Jìn, Gōngsūn Chài of Qí,
Xiàng Xù of Sòng, Běigōng Tuó of Wèi,
Hǎn Hǔ of Zhèng, and the Great Officer of Xiǎo Zhū at Chányuān.
Since in the end nothing was returned to Sòng,
therefore the names of the individuals were not recorded.
The superior man said:
"Must one not be cautious regarding good faith!
At the meeting of Chányuān,
the High Ministers were not recorded
because of their lack of good faith.
For the High Ministers of the feudal lords,
to meet and yet lack good faith
means that both favor and reputation are discarded;
such is the impossibility of lacking good faith.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'Wén Wáng ascends and descends,
at the left and right of the Lord on High,'
which refers to good faith.
It also says:
'Be good and cautious in your movements,
do not harbor deceit,'
which refers to the lack of good faith."
The record says:
"So-and-so and so-and-so met at Chányuān
because of the disaster in Sòng,"
as a way to blame them.
Not recording the Great Officer of Lǔ
was to conceal it out of shame.
Zǐpí of Zhèng handed over the government to Zǐchǎn.
Zǐchǎn declined, saying:
"The state is small and pressed,
while the clans are large and many are favored;
it cannot be governed."
Zǐpí said:
"I, Hǔ, will lead the way in obeying you,
so who would dare offend you?
You should skillfully assist the state.
No state is too small;
if a small state can serve a large one,
then the state will find ease."
When Zǐchǎn took charge of the government,
there was an affair involving Bó Shí,
and Zǐchǎn bribed him with a city.
Zǐdàshū said:
"The whole state belongs to the state;
why bribe him alone?"
Zǐchǎn said:
"It is truly difficult to be without desires.
If they all attain their desires
so as to follow their duties
and seek success,
if I do not achieve success,
will it not rest with others?
Why be stingy with a city?
Where can the city go?"
Zǐdàshū said:
"What about the surrounding states?"
Zǐchǎn said:
"If we do not conflict with each other
but follow each other,
what will the surrounding states find to blame?
The *Book of Zhèng* says:
'To stabilize the state and house,
one must prioritize the great.'
Let us first stabilize the great
and wait to see where things settle."
Later, Bó Shí became afraid
and returned the city,
but in the end, it was given back to him.
After Bó Yǒu died,
the Grand Historian was sent to command Bó Shí
to become a High Minister;
he declined.
The Grand Historian withdrew,
and then Bó Shí requested the command.
It was commanded again,
and he declined again.
After this happened three times,
he finally received the tablets of office and entered to bow.
Because of this, Zǐchǎn detested his character
and made him rank below himself.
Zǐchǎn caused the capital and the countryside
to have distinct regulations,
and the high and low to have distinct dress;
the fields had boundaries and ditches,
and the cottages and wells were organized into groups of five.
Those among the great men who were loyal and frugal,
he followed and supported them;
those who were arrogant and extravagant,
he brought them to ruin.
Fēng Juǎn was about to perform a sacrifice
and requested to hunt for it.
Zǐchǎn did not permit it,
saying:
"Only the ruler uses fresh meat;
the common people simply provide what they have."
Zǐzhāng grew angry,
withdrew, and mobilized his followers.
Zǐchǎn was about to flee to Jìn,
but Zǐpí stopped him
and drove out Fēng Juǎn.
Fēng Juǎn fled to Jìn.
Zǐchǎn requested to take over his lands and neighborhood,
but restored them after three years;
he returned the lands, the neighborhood, and the income thereof.
After one year of governing,
the people of the carriages sang of him,
saying:
"He takes our clothes and hats and stores them away;
he takes our fields and divides them into fives.
Whoever kills Zǐchǎn,
I will join them."
When three years had passed,
they sang of him again,
saying:
"We have sons and younger brothers,
and Zǐchǎn teaches them;
we have fields,
and Zǐchǎn makes them flourish.
If Zǐchǎn should die,
who could succeed him?"
A9.31 *The Annals of the Thirty-First Year of Duke Xiāng*
A9.31.1 In the thirty-first year, spring,
the royal first month.
A9.31.2 In summer, the sixth month, on the day *xīnsì*,
the Duke died in the Chǔ Palace.
A9.31.3 Autumn,
ninth month, on the day *guǐsì*,
Zǐyě died.
A9.31.4 On the day *jǐhài*,
Zhòngsūn Jié died.
A9.31.5 In winter, the tenth month,
the Viscount of Téng came to the funeral.
A9.31.6 On the day *guǐyǒu*,
our ruler Duke Xiāng was buried.
A9.31.7 In the eleventh month,
the people of Jǔ murdered their ruler Mìzhōu.
B9.31 *The Commentary on the Thirty-First Year of Duke Xiāng*
B9.31.1 In the thirty-first year, spring,
the royal first month,
Mùshú arrived from the meeting.
He saw Mèng Xiàobó
and spoke to him, saying:
"Zhào Mèng is about to die.
His words are careless,
unlike those of a leader of the people.
Moreover, his years have not reached fifty,
yet he mumbles like one of eighty or ninety;
he cannot last long.
If Zhào Mèng dies,
the one who governs will likely be Hánzǐ!
You should speak with Jìsūn
so that you may establish good relations with him;
he is a superior man.
The ruler of Jìn is about to lose control of the government;
if you do not establish relations there
to make Lǔ prepared early,
then once the government is in the hands of the Great Officers,
Hánzǐ will be weak
and the Great Officers will be greedy,
seeking their desires without satisfaction.
Qí and Chǔ are not yet to be allied with;
Lǔ will surely have cause for fear!"
Xiàobó said:
"How long is a human life?
Who can avoid being careless?
Since the morning does not reach the evening,
what use is there in establishing relations?"
Mùshú went out
and told others:
"Mèngsūn is about to die.
I told him of Zhào Mèng’s carelessness,
and he is even worse."
He also spoke with Jìsūn about the situation in Jìn,
but Jìsūn did not follow his advice.
When Zhào Wénzǐ died,
the ducal house of Jìn became lowly,
and the government fell to the extravagant families.
Hán Xuānzǐ governed,
but could not plan for the feudal lords.
Lǔ could not endure the demands of Jìn,
and slanderous evils were many;
thus there was the meeting of Píngqiū.
B9.31.2 Qí Zǐwěi hated Lǘqiū Yīng,
desiring to kill him,
so he sent him to lead an army to attack Yángzhōu.
Our side asked the reason for the army.
In summer, the fifth month,
Zǐwěi killed Lǘqiū Yīng,
and used this to explain the matter to our army.
Gōnglǘ Sǎ, Shěng Zào, Kǒng Huǐ,
and Jiǎ Yín fled to Jǔ.
The various princes were expelled.
B9.31.3 The Duke built a Chǔ style palace.
Mùshū said:
“The *Dàshì* says:
‘What the people desire,
Heaven must follow.’
Our lord desires Chǔ,
therefore he built this palace.
If he does not go to Chǔ again,
he will surely die in this palace.”
In the sixth month, on the day xīnsì,
the Duke passed away in the Chǔ palace.
Shūzhòng Dài
stole his large ritual jade disk
to give to an attendant;
he had it placed in his bosom
and then took it back from him;
because of this, he was found guilty.
They established the son of the Hú woman Jìngguī,
Zǐyě,
who stayed at the Jì clan’s residence.
In autumn, the ninth month, on the day guǐsì,
he died
due to excessive grief.
B9.31.4 On the day jǐhài,
Mèng Xiàobó died.
They established Gōngzǐ Chóu, the son of Jìngguī’s younger sister Qíguī.
Mùshū did not want this,
saying:
“When the heir dies,
if there is a younger brother by the same mother,
then establish him; if not, establish the eldest.
If their ages are equal, choose the virtuous;
if their righteousness is equal,
then use divination;
this is the way of the ancients.
If he is not the legitimate heir,
why must it be the sister’s son?
Furthermore, this man,
while in mourning, shows no sorrow,
and while in grief, has a joyful appearance;
this is called lacking measure.
A man without measure
rarely fails to cause trouble.
If you indeed establish him,
he will surely be a worry for the Jì clan.”
Wǔzǐ did not listen
and finally established him.
By the time of the funeral,
he had changed his mourning garments three times,
yet the hems of the mourning garments were as the previous ones.
At this time, Zhāo Gōng was nineteen years old,
yet he still had the heart of a child;
from this, the gentleman knew
that he would not come to a good end.
B9.31.5 In winter, the tenth month,
Téng Chéng Gōng came to join the funeral;
he was negligent and shed many tears.
Zǐfú Huìbó said:
“The ruler of Téng is about to die.
He is negligent in his position
and his mourning is excessive;
the signs are present at the place of death,
how can he not follow?”
B9.31.6 On the day guǐyǒu,
Xiāng Gōng was buried.
In the month the Duke passed away,
Zǐchǎn accompanied the Earl of Zhèng to Jìn;
because of our mourning, the Marquis of Jìn
did not grant them an audience.
Zǐchǎn ordered
that the walls of their lodging be completely demolished
so as to bring in their carriages and horses.
Shì Wénbó reprimanded him,
saying:
“Because our humble state’s administration and punishments are not regulated,
bandits and robbers are widespread;
there is nothing we can do to protect the dependents of the feudal lords who grace our humble ruler with their presence.
Therefore, we ordered the officials to repair the guest lodgings,
raising their gates high
and making their walls thick,
so that the guest envoys would have no worries.
Now you have destroyed them;
although your followers can be cautious,
what about other guests?
Since our humble state is the leader of the alliance,
we repair and thatch the walls
to wait for the guests.
If everyone destroys them,
how can we provide for the requirements?
Our humble ruler has sent Gài to ask for your instructions.”
He replied:
“Because our humble state is narrow and small,
situated between great powers,
and demands for tribute are made at all times,
therefore we do not dare to live in peace,
but search out all our humble resources
to come and attend to the seasonal duties.
We happened upon a time when you, the ministers, were not free,
and have not yet been granted an audience;
nor have we been permitted to hear your instructions,
and we do not know when the audience will be.
We do not dare to present the gifts,
nor do we dare to leave them exposed.
If we were to present them,
they would be the property of the Lord’s treasury;
unless they are ceremoniously displayed,
we do not dare to hand them over.
If we leave them exposed,
we fear that dryness or dampness out of season
will cause them to rot or be eaten by insects,
thereby increasing the guilt of our humble state.
I, Qiáo, have heard that when Wén Gōng was the leader of the alliance,
his own palaces were low and small,
without observation towers or terraces,
but he elevated and enlarged the lodgings of the feudal lords;
the lodgings were like the Lord’s own chambers.
The storehouses and stables were repaired and maintained;
the Minister of Works would seasonally
level and smooth the roads;
the plasterers would seasonally plaster the lodgings and palaces.
When the guests of the feudal lords arrived,
the foresters set out courtyard torches,
and the attendants patrolled the palace.
The carriages and horses had their place;
the guests’ followers had their relays;
the keepers of the carriages greased the axles;
the menials, herdsmen, and grooms
each looked after their duties.
The various officials
each displayed their goods.
The Duke did not detain the guests,
and yet no affairs were neglected.
He shared their worries and joys,
and if there was business, he personally inspected it.
He taught those who did not know
and relieved those who were insufficient.
When guests arrived, it was like returning home;
they had no disasters or troubles;
they did not fear bandits or robbers,
nor did they suffer from dryness or dampness.
Now the palaces of Tóngdī extend for several lǐ,
while the feudal lords are lodged in the quarters of menials;
the gates do not accommodate carriages,
yet one cannot jump over the walls.
Thieves and robbers walk openly,
and natural plagues are not guarded against.
There is no set time for guest audiences,
and the Lord’s commands cannot be known.
If we do not demolish the walls,
