then there will be nowhere to store the gifts,
and our guilt would be doubled.
I venture to ask you, the minister:
What are your commands?
Although your Lord has the mourning of Lǔ,
it is also a cause of sorrow for our humble state.
If we are permitted to present our gifts,
we will repair the walls before we leave;
this would be your Lord’s kindness,
and we would not dare to shrink from the toil!”
Wénbó reported back.
Zhào Wénzǐ said:
“True.
I am indeed lacking in virtue;
to use the walls of menials to receive the feudal lords
is my fault.”
He sent Shì Wénbó to apologize for his lack of cleverness.
The Marquis of Jìn granted an audience to the Earl of Zhèng,
with increased courtesy,
enriched the feast and gifts, and then saw him off.
Thereupon, he built lodgings for the feudal lords.
Shǔxiàng said:
“Is it not true that rhetoric cannot be dispensed with!
Zǐchǎn has rhetoric,
and the feudal lords rely on it;
why should one abandon rhetoric?
The *Shī* says:
‘When words are harmonious,
the people are in accord;
when words are well-ordered,
the people are at rest.’
He indeed understands this.”
B9.31.7 Zhèng Zǐpí sent Yìn Duàn to Chǔ
to report the mission to Jìn;
this was in accordance with ritual.
B9.31.8 Lí Bǐ Gōng of Jǔ had the sons Qù Jí and Zhǎn Yú.
Having established Zhǎn Yú,
he then deposed him.
Lí Bǐ Gōng was cruel,
and the people of the state were distressed by him.
In the eleventh month,
Zhǎn Yú relied on the people of the state to attack the Viscount of Jǔ,
assassinated him,
and then was established.
Qù Jí fled to Qí;
he was born of a lady from Qí.
Zhǎn Yú
was born of a lady from Wú.
The record says,
"The people of Jǔ assassinated their ruler Mǎi Zhū Chú,"
indicating where the guilt lay.
B9.31.9 The Viscount of Wú sent Qū Hú Yōng
on a mission to Jìn,
to open communication.
Zhào Wén Zǐ questioned him,
saying:
"Will Jì Zǐ of Yán Zhōu Lái eventually be established?
At Cháo, Zhū Fán fell;
a gatekeeper killed Dài Wú.
Heaven seems to be opening the way for him;
how is it?"
He replied:
"He will not be established.
These were the commands of the two kings,
not Heaven opening the way for Jì Zǐ.
If Heaven is opening the way,
it is likely for the current successor!
He has great virtue and acts with measure.
Through virtue, he does not lose the people;
through measure, he does not lose control of affairs.
When the people are close and affairs are in order,
that is Heaven opening the way.
Those who possess the state of Wú—
it must be this ruler's descendants who will ultimately conclude it.
Jì Zǐ
is one who guards his integrity.
Although he might have the state,
he will not be established."
B9.31.10 In the twelfth month,
Běi Gōng Wén Zǐ accompanied Duke Xiāng of Wèi
to go to Chǔ,
because of the Covenant of Sòng.
Passing through Zhèng,
Yìn Duàn went to greet them at Fěi Lín,
following the ritual for a mission
while using words of welcome.
Wén Zǐ entered for the formal visit.
Zǐ Yǔ served as the Messenger;
Féng Jiǎn Zǐ and Zǐ Dà Shū received the guest.
When the business was finished and he came out,
he spoke to the Lord of Wèi, saying:
"Zhèng possesses ritual;
it will be a blessing for several generations.
It will surely not suffer the punishment of the great states!
The Shī says:
'Who can hold what is hot,
without washing with water?'
Ritual to government
is like water to heat.
Water is used to save from heat;
what distress would there be?"
In Zǐ Chǎn's management of the government,
he chose the capable and employed them:
Féng Jiǎn Zǐ was able to decide on great matters;
Zǐ Dà Shū was elegant, refined, and cultured;
Gōng Sūn Huī was able to know the activities of the four neighboring states,
and could distinguish the clans and surnames of their high officers,
their ranks,
their status,
and their abilities,
and he was also good at composing diplomatic speeches;
Bì Chén was able to plan;
if he planned in the countryside, he succeeded,
but if he planned in the city, he did not.
When the state of Zhèng was to have dealings with the feudal lords,
Zǐ Chǎn would then ask
Zǐ Yǔ about the activities of the four states,
and had him compose many diplomatic speeches;
he would ride with Bì Chén to the countryside
to have him plan what was possible;
and then he told Féng Jiǎn Zǐ to decide on it.
When the matter was settled,
he then gave it to Zǐ Dà Shū to execute it
to respond to the guests.
Therefore, they rarely had failures in their affairs.
This is what Běi Gōng Wén Zǐ called
having ritual.
B9.31.11 The people of Zhèng spent time at the village schools
to discuss the government.
Rán Míng said to Zǐ Chǎn:
"What if we destroy the village schools?"
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"Why?
People retire there morning and evening
to discuss whether the government is good or bad.
What they favor,
I implement;
what they dislike,
I change.
They are my teachers.
How could I destroy them?
I have heard of using loyalty and goodness to reduce resentment;
I have not heard of exercising authority to prevent resentment.
Can it not be stopped quickly?
But it is like damming a river.
When a great breach is made,
the people hurt will surely be many;
I will not be able to save them.
It is better to make small breaches to guide the flow;
it is better that I hear it and use it as medicine."
Rán Míng said:
"I, Miè, from now on know that you, sir, are truly worthy of service.
I am truly incompetent.
If you indeed carry this out,
the state of Zhèng will truly rely on it,
and not just we few ministers."
Zhòng Ní heard these words
and said:
"Viewing it from this,
when people say Zǐ Chǎn is not humane,
I do not believe it."
B9.31.12 Zǐ Pí wanted to make Yǐn Hé the governor of a city.
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"He is young;
it is not known if it is possible."
Zǐ Pí said:
"He is honest;
I love him,
and he will not betray me.
Let him go there and learn;
he will then know even better how to govern."
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"It cannot be.
When one loves another,
one seeks to benefit them.
Now you, sir, love this person
but entrust him with government;
this is like having one who cannot yet handle a knife
do the carving;
the injury would truly be great.
Your love for the person
would only result in hurting him;
who then would dare to seek love from you?
You, to the state of Zhèng,
are a main pillar.
If the pillar breaks and the rafters collapse,
I, Qiáo, will be crushed.
How could I not speak fully?
If you have beautiful silk,
you would not let someone learn how to tailor with it.
A high office or a large city
is what protects one's person,
yet you let a learner tailor with them;
is their value not much greater than beautiful silk?
I have heard of learning and afterwards entering government;
I have never heard of using government to learn.
If you indeed carry this out,
there will surely be harm.
It is like hunting:
if one is practiced in archery and driving,
then one can catch game.
If one has never mounted a chariot or practiced archery and driving,
then one only fears failure and being crushed;
what leisure would there be to think of the catch?"
Zǐ Pí said:
"Excellent!
I, Hǔ, am not clever.
I have heard that the gentleman strives to know what is great
and far-reaching,
while the small man strives to know what is small and near.
I
am a small man.
Clothing is attached to my person;
I know it and am careful with it.
High offices and large cities are what protect the person,
but I was distant and negligent toward them.
Without your words,
I would not have known.
Some time ago I said,
'You manage the state of Zhèng,
and I will manage my own house
to find protection there'—
that might have been acceptable.
But now I know it is not enough.
From now on, I request that,
even in my own house,
I will listen to you and act."
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"Men's hearts are as different as their faces;
how would I dare say your face is like mine?
However, what my heart considers dangerous,
I must also report to you."
Zǐ Pí considered him loyal,
and therefore entrusted the government to him;
because of this, Zǐ Chǎn was able to govern the state of Zhèng.
B9.31.13 The Marquis of Wèi was in Chǔ.
Běigōng Wénzǐ
observed the deportment of Lìngyǐn Wéi
and said to the Marquis of Wèi:
“The Lìngyǐn resembles a ruler;
he will have other ambitions.
Even if he achieves his aims,
he will not be able to come to a good end.
The *Shī* says:
‘None do not have a beginning,
but few are able to have an end.’
To have a good end is indeed difficult;
the Lìngyǐn will likely not escape calamity.”
The Duke said:
“How do you know this?”
He replied:
“The *Shī* says:
‘Be reverent and cautious in your dignified deportment,
for it is the model for the people.’
The Lìngyǐn lacks dignified deportment,
so the people have no model.
One whom the people do not model themselves after,
yet who sits above the people,
cannot finish his life peacefully.”
The Duke said: “Excellent!
What is meant by dignified deportment?”
He replied:
“To have majesty such that one is feared is called *wēi*;
to have decorum such that one can be emulated is called *yí*.
A ruler has a ruler’s dignified deportment,
so his ministers fear and love him,
and take him as a pattern and emulate him;
thus he can possess his state and family,
and his good reputation lasts for generations.
A minister has a minister’s dignified deportment,
so those below him fear and love him;
thus he can maintain his office,
preserve his clan, and bring order to his family.
If all levels below follow this pattern,
then those above and below
can strengthen each other.
The *Wèi Shī* says:
‘Dignified deportment is grand and elegant,
it cannot be measured,’
meaning that ruler and minister, superior and inferior, father and son,
brothers, internal and external, great and small,
all have dignified deportment.
The *Zhōu Shī* says:
‘Friends support each other,
supporting with dignified deportment,’
meaning that the way of friends is that they must instruct each other
in dignified deportment.
The *Zhōu Shū* recounts the virtue of Wén Wáng,
saying:
‘Great states feared his power,
small states cherished his virtue,’
meaning they feared and loved him.
The *Shī* says:
‘Without conscious thought or knowledge,
he followed the patterns of the Lord on High,’
meaning he took him as a pattern and emulated him.
Zhòu imprisoned Wén Wáng for seven years,
and the feudal lords all followed him in prison;
Zhòu then became afraid and returned him,
which can be called loving him.
Wén Wáng attacked Chóng;
after two campaigns
they surrendered and became his subjects,
and the Mányí followed and submitted,
which can be called fearing him.
The achievements of Wén Wáng
were recited, sung, and danced by the whole world,
which can be called taking him as a pattern.
The conduct of Wén Wáng
remains a law to this day,
which can be called emulating him.
This is having dignified deportment.
Therefore, a superior man in his position is to be feared;
in his giving and granting, he is to be loved;
in his advancing and retreating, he is to be measured;
in his movements, he is to be patterned;
in his appearance and bearing, he is to be admired;
in his handling of affairs, he is to be a model;
in his virtuous conduct, he is to be emulated;
in his voice and spirit, he is to be pleasing.
His movements have pattern,
his words have order;
as he oversees those below him,
this is called having dignified deportment.”
A10.1 *The Classic of the First Year of Duke Zhāo*
A10.1.1 In the spring of the first year,
in the Royal first month,
the Duke ascended the throne.
A10.1.2 Shūsūn Bǎo met with Zhào Wǔ of Jìn,
Gōngzǐ Wéi of Chǔ,
Guó Ruò of Qí,
Xiàng Xù of Sòng,
Qí È of Wèi,
Gōngzǐ Zhāo of Chén,
Gōngsūn Guīshēng of Cài,
Hàn Hǔ of Zhèng,
the people of Xǔ,
and the people of Cáo at Guó.
A10.1.3 In the third month,
Yùn was taken.
A10.1.4 In the summer,
Zhēn, the younger brother of the Earl of Qín, fled to Jìn.
A10.1.5 On the day Dīngsì of the sixth month,
Huá, the Viscount of Zhū, died.
A10.1.6 Xún Wú of Jìn led the army and defeated the Dí at Dàlǔ.
A10.1.7 In the autumn,
Jǔ Qùjí entered Jǔ from Qí.
Jǔ Zhǎnyú fled to Wú.
A10.1.8 Shū Gōng led the army to mark the boundaries of the fields of Yùn.
A10.1.9 Duke Dào of Zhū was buried.
A10.1.10 In the winter, in the eleventh month on the day Jǐyǒu,
Mǐ, the Viscount of Chǔ, died.
A10.1.11 Gōngzǐ Bǐ of Chǔ fled to Jìn.
B10.1 *The Commentary on the First Year of Duke Zhāo*
B10.1.1 In the spring of the first year,
Gōngzǐ Wéi of Chǔ went on a mission of state to Zhèng,
and also to take a wife from the Gōngsūn Duàn clan.
Wǔ Jǔ served as the deputy.
When they were about to enter the guest house,
the people of Zhèng disliked it.
They sent the messenger Zǐyǔ to speak with him,
and so he stayed at a guest house outside.
After the diplomatic visit was completed,
he was going to use his troops to escort the bride.
Zǐchǎn was concerned about this
and sent Zǐyǔ to decline,
saying:
“Because our humble city is small and cramped,
it is not enough to accommodate your followers.
We request that you receive our instructions at an altar.”
The Lìngyǐn ordered the Grand Magistrate Bó Zhōulí to reply,
saying:
“Your ruler has deigned to bestow a favor upon our humble Great Officer Wéi,
saying that Wéi shall cause the Fēng clan to care for and possess your house.
Wéi has spread out the mats
and announced it in the temples of Zhuāng Gōng and Gòng Gōng before coming.
If you grant it in the wild,
it is to cast your ruler’s gift into the overgrown weeds,
and it means our humble Great Officer cannot be ranked among the various ministers.
Not only that,
but you also cause Wéi to deceive his former lords;
he would not be able to serve as an elder to our humble ruler,
and he would have no face to return.
We only ask that you, Great Officer, consider it.”
Zǐyǔ said:
“A small state having no crime
is itself a crime if it relies on others.
We were going to rely on your great state to bring peace to ourselves,
but might you not be harboring treacherous intentions to plot against us?
If a small state loses its reliance
and is punished by the feudal lords,
causing all to be resentful,
then it is the fear of disobeying your ruler’s command
or having some obstruction to its implementation that concerns us.
Otherwise,
our humble city
and all its guest-house attendants,
how would they dare to begrudge the ancestral temple of the Fēng clan?”
Wǔ Jǔ knew they were prepared
and requested to enter with their arrows reversed in their quivers.
This was granted.
In the first month on the day Yǐwèi,
they entered,
took the bride, and departed.
Then they met at Guó,
seeking to renew the alliance of Sòng.
Qí Wǔ said to Zhào Wénzǐ:
“At the alliance of Sòng,
the people of Chǔ got their way over Jìn.
Now the Lìngyǐn’s lack of good faith
is something known to the feudal lords.
If you are not on your guard,
I fear it will be just as it was in Sòng.
Zǐmù’s trustworthiness was praised among the feudal lords,
and yet he still deceived Jìn and took precedence over it;
how much more so for one who is exceptionally untrustworthy?”
That Chǔ has again attained its will over Jìn
is a disgrace to Jìn.
You have assisted the state of Jìn
as the leader of the covenant
for seven years now.
Twice you have assembled the Zhū Hóu,
and thrice you have assembled the Dà Fū.
You have subdued Qí and the Dí,
brought peace to Dōng Xià,
quelled the disorders of Qín,
and walled Chún Yú.
The troops have not been exhausted,
the state has not been fatigued,
the people have no slanders or complaints,
the Zhū Hóu have no resentment,
and Heaven has sent no great disasters.
This is all due to your strength.
You have achieved a fine reputation,
yet if you end it in disgrace,
I, Wǔ, am fearful of this;
you, my master, must not fail to be on guard."
Wén Zǐ said:
"I, Wǔ, have received your favor.
However, at the Covenant of Sòng,
Zǐ Mù had the heart of one who brings calamity to others,
while I, Wǔ, had the heart of a benevolent man.
This is why Chǔ rode over Jìn.
Now I, Wǔ, still have this same heart;
even if Chǔ again practices usurpation,
it is not something that will harm me.
I, Wǔ, will take good faith as the foundation
and follow it in my actions.
It is like a farmer
weeding and hilling his crops.
Though there may be famine,
there will surely be years of plenty.
Moreover, I have heard
that one who can be faithful will not be subordinate to others;
I have not yet been able to achieve this.
The Shī says:
'Without usurpation, without harming,
few fail to be a model,'
which refers to good faith.
One who can be a model for others
will not be subordinate to others.
I do not find this difficult,
and so Chǔ is not a source of worry."
The Chǔ Lìng Yǐn Wéi requested to use sacrificial animals and read the old texts, simply placing them upon the animal;
the people of Jìn permitted it.
In the third month, on the day Jiǎ Chén,
they swore the covenant.
Chǔ Gōng Zǐ Wéi displayed his ceremonial robes and detached his guards.
Shū Sūn Mù Zǐ said:
"The Gōng Zǐ of Chǔ is magnificent!
He is like a ruler!"
Zhèng Zǐ Pí said:
"Two spear-bearers have come forward."
Cài Zǐ Jiā said:
"With the cattail-enclosure having people in front,
is it not also acceptable?"
Chǔ Bó Zhōu Lí said:
"For this journey,
he requested and borrowed these from my lowly ruler."
The Zhèng Xíng Rén Huī said:
"What is borrowed will not be returned."
Bó Zhōu Lí said:
"You should rather worry about Zǐ Xī's desire to be rebellious and deceitful."
Zǐ Yǔ said:
"The one who fits the jade disk is still there;
if what is borrowed is not returned,
will you not have cause for worry?"
Guó Zǐ of Qí said:
"I feel pity on behalf of these two gentlemen."
Chén Gōng Zǐ Zhāo said:
"Without worry, what can be accomplished?
These two gentlemen are joyful."
Wèi Qí Zǐ said:
"If one understands this,
even if there is worry, what harm is there?"
Sòng Zuǒ Shī Hé said:
"The great states give orders,
and the small states comply;
I know only how to comply."
Jìn Lè Wáng Fù said:
"The final stanza of Xiǎo Mín is excellent;
I shall follow it."
After retiring from the meeting,
Zǐ Yǔ said to Zǐ Pí:
"Shū Sūn's words were sharp yet tactful;
the Sòng Zuǒ Shī was concise yet ritualistic;
Lè Wáng Fù was polite and respectful.
You and Zǐ Jiā held your ground;
all are lords who can preserve their generations.
As for the Dà Fū of Qí, Wèi, and Chén, they will likely not escape calamity!
Guó Zǐ feels pity on behalf of others;
Zǐ Zhāo finds joy in worry;
Qí Zǐ, though worried, thinks it is no harm.
Now, to feel pity for what one cannot reach,
to find joy in what is worrisome,
and to worry but think it is no harm,
are all ways to invite sorrow;
sorrow will surely reach them.
The Dà Shì says:
'What the people desire,
Heaven will surely follow.'
These three Dà Fū have shown signs of worry;
how can worry fail to arrive?
To know things through words—
this is what is meant by that."
B10.1.2 Jì Wǔ Zǐ attacked Jǔ
and took Yùn.
The people of Jǔ reported this at the meeting.
Chǔ informed Jìn, saying:
"The renewed covenant has not yet concluded,
yet Lǔ has attacked Jǔ,
desecrating the solemn covenant.
We request to execute their envoy."
Lè Huán Zǐ assisted Zhào Wén Zǐ;
he wished to seek goods from Shū Sūn
and intercede for him.
He sent someone to request a belt from him,
but Shū Sūn would not give it.
Liáng Qí Jìng said:
"Goods are used to shield one's person;
why do you begrudge it?"
Shū Sūn said:
"The assembly of Zhū Hóu
is to protect the Shè Jì.
If I escape through a bribe,
Lǔ will certainly be attacked by an army;
this would be bringing calamity upon it.
What kind of protection would that be?
When people have a wall,
it is to block out evil.
If the wall develops cracks and crumbles,
whose fault is it?
To protect it and then do evil to it—
I would be even worse.
Although I resent Jì Sūn,
what crime has the state of Lǔ committed?
The Shū goes out while the Jì stays behind;
this has its origin from of old.
Whom then should I resent?
However, Fù is greedy for bribes;
if I do not give it to him,
he will not stop."
He called the messenger,
tore the silk from his robes and gave it to him,
saying:
"The belt is too narrow for this."
Zhào Mèng heard of this
and said:
"Not to forget one's state when facing calamity
is loyalty;
to think of difficulty without overstepping one's office
is trustworthiness;
to plan for the state and forget death
is integrity;
to manage these three for one's lord
is righteousness.
Having these four virtues,
can he yet be executed?"
He then requested of Chǔ, saying:
"Although Lǔ is guilty,
its official did not avoid the difficulty,
and he feared your majesty's awe while respecting your commands.
If you spare him
to encourage your own attendants,
it would be well.
If your own subordinates
do not avoid filth when at home
and do not flee from difficulty when abroad,
what worry would you have?
What worry arises from
is filth that is not managed
and difficulty that is not defended against;
this is where it originates.
If one can manage these two,
what else is there to worry about?
If one does not keep those of ability at peace,
who will follow him?
Shū Sūn Bào of Lǔ can be called able;
I request that you spare him
to keep those of ability at peace.
If you hold an assembly and pardon the guilty,
and furthermore reward the worthy,
which of the Zhū Hóu would not joyfully look toward Chǔ and turn to it,
regarding the distant as if they were near?
Border towns
belong now to one, now to another;
what constancy is there?
The commands of a true Wáng or Bà
delineate the borders
and establish officials there,
raising banners
and making known the regulations and commands,"
If there are transgressions, there are punishments,
yet they still cannot be made uniform.
Thus Yú had the Sānmiáo,
Xià had Guàn and Hù,
Shāng had Shǐ and
Pī,
and Zhōu had Xú and Yǎn.
Since there have been no good kings,
the feudal lords have vied for advancement,
disrespectfully presiding over joint alliances;
how could they again be made uniform?
Caring for the great and setting aside the small
is sufficient to be the leader of an alliance;
why use more than that?
As for the trimming of borders,
what state is without it?
Among those who lead joint alliances,
who can settle such disputes?
When Wú and Pú have a conflict,
would the officials of Chǔ concern themselves with an alliance?
Regarding the border matters of Jǔ,
if Chǔ does not concern itself with them,
and the feudal lords are not troubled,
is that not also acceptable?
Jǔ and Lǔ have contested Yùn
for a long time.
If there is no great harm to their altars of soil and grain,
there is no need to oppose it.
Eliminating trouble and pardoning the good,
none will not strive to encourage this.
You should consider it."
They firmly requested this of Chǔ,
and the people of Chǔ granted it,
thus releasing Shūsūn.
B10.1.3 The Lìngyǐn feasted Zhào Mèng,
and recited the first stanza of the "Dà Míng."
Zhào Mèng recited the second stanza of the "Xiǎo Wǎn."
When the business was finished,
Zhào Mèng said to Shūxiàng:
"The Lìngyǐn considers himself a king;
what do you think of it?"
He replied:
"The King is weak,
and the Lìngyǐn is strong;
it may be possible!
Although it is possible,
it will not last to the end."
Zhào Mèng said:
"For what reason?"
He replied:
"Using strength to overcome the weak and being content with it
is strength that is unrighteous.
To be strong while being unrighteous,
one’s downfall must be swift.
The Shī says,
'Illustrious was the royal house of Zhōu,
yet Bāo Sì destroyed it,'
which means strength that is unrighteous.
If the Lìngyǐn becomes King,
he must seek the support of the feudal lords.
Jìn is somewhat weak,
and the feudal lords will go to him.
If he gains the feudal lords,
his cruelty will increase greatly,
and the people will not be able to bear it;
how will it end well?
Now, taking by force
and overcoming through unrighteousness,
he will surely take this as his way.
If one's way is through excess and cruelty,
it cannot last long."
B10.1.4 In the summer, in the fourth month,
Zhào Mèng, Shūsūn Bào, and the Grand Master of Cáo entered Zhèng,
and the Earl of Zhèng feasted them together.
Zǐpí invited Zhào Mèng,
and when the rites were finished,
Zhào Mèng recited the "Hù Yè."
Zǐpí then invited Mùshū
and informed him.
Mùshū said:
"Zhào Mèng desires a single-offering ceremony;
you should follow his wish."
Zǐpí said:
"Would I dare?"
Mùshū said:
"It is what the man desires,
so why would you not dare?"
When it came to the feast,
the sacrificial vessels for the five-offering ceremony were prepared under the tent.
Zhào Mèng declined them
and privately said to Zǐchǎn:
"I, Wǔ, have requested this of the Prime Minister."
Thereupon the single-offering ceremony was used.
Zhào Mèng was the chief guest.
After the rites were finished, they held a banquet.
Mùshū recited the "Què Cháo,"
and Zhào Mèng said:
"I, Wǔ, am not worthy of it."
He then recited the "Cǎi Fán,"
saying:
"The small states are the white mugwort,
and the large states gather and use it;
what fruit is there that is not by command?"
Zǐpí recited the final stanza of "Yě Yǒu Sǐ Jūn,"
Zhào Mèng recited the "Cháng Dì,"
and said:
"We brothers are close and thus at peace;
even the shaggy dogs can be kept from barking."
Mùshū, Zǐpí, and the Grand Master of Cáo rose,
bowed,
raised the rhinoceros-horn cups,
and said:
"The small states rely on you,
and know we shall be spared from calamity."
They drank wine and were happy;
Zhào Mèng went out and said:
"I shall not return to this place again."
B10.1.5 The Son of Heaven sent Liú Dìnggōng to greet Zhào Mèng at Yǐng,
and he was lodged at Luòruì.
Liú Zǐ said: "How magnificent is the achievement of Yǔ!
His illustrious virtue is far-reaching.
Had it not been for Yǔ,
we might have become fish!
That you and I wear our caps and robes,
governing the people and presiding over the feudal lords,
is due to the power of Yǔ.
Why do you not also extend the achievements of Yǔ and give great protection to the people?"
He replied:
"As an old man, I fear only guilt and calamity;
how can I care for things far away?
My sort just barely manages to eat;
in the morning we do not plan for the evening;
how could we last for long?"
Liú Zǐ returned
and told the King, saying:
"The proverb says, 'When an old man is about to gain wisdom, senility reaches him';
does this not refer to Zhào Mèng?
He is the Prime Minister of Jìn
and leads the feudal lords,
yet he ranks himself with bondservants,
saying that in the morning he does not plan for the evening;
he has abandoned both spirits and men.
When the spirits are angry and the people rebel,
how can he last long?
Zhào Mèng will not see another year.
When the spirits are angry,
they do not enjoy his sacrifices;
when the people rebel,
they do not attend to his business.
When sacrifices and business are not followed,
how can he last the year?"
B10.1.6 Shūsūn returned,
and Zēng Yāo drove for Jìsūn to greet him.
From dawn until midday, he did not come out.
Zēng Yāo said to Zēng Fù,
saying:
"From dawn until midday—
I know my fault.
Lǔ maintains the state through mutual forbearance.
If one forbears on the outside
but does not forbear on the inside,
what use is that?"
Zēng Fù said:
"Having been away for several months,
to spend one morning like this—
what harm is there in it?
If one trades and wants to profit,
can one dislike the noise?"
Zēng Fù said to Shūsūn:
"You may come out now."
Shūsūn pointed to a pillar
and said:
"Though I dislike it,
can it be removed?"
Then he went out to see him.
B10.1.7 The sister of Xúwú Fàn of Zhèng was beautiful;
Gōngsūn Chǔ had already become engaged to her,
but Gōngsūn Hēi also sent someone to forcefully present the betrothal gifts.
Fàn was afraid
and informed Zǐchǎn.
Zǐchǎn said:
"This is because the state lacks governance;
it is not your concern.
Simply give her to whomever she desires."
Fàn requested of the two men
that the girl be allowed to choose.
They both agreed to it.
Zǐxī entered in full ceremonial dress,
laid out his gifts, and went out.
Zǐnán entered in military attire,
shot arrows to the left and right,
and leaped into his chariot and went out.
The woman observed them from her room
and said,
"Zǐxī is truly handsome,
but Zǐnán
is the manly one.
For a husband to be a husband and a wife to be a wife
is what is called harmony."
She married into the family of Zǐnán.
Zǐxī was angry,
and soon after, he concealed armor in a case to go see Zǐnán,
intending to kill him and take his wife.
Zǐnán learned of this,
seized a halberd and pursued him;
reaching the crossroads,
he struck him with the halberd.
Zǐxī returned wounded
and told the Grand Officers, saying,
"I went to see him with good intentions,
not knowing he had different aims,
and thus I was wounded."
The Grand Officers all deliberated on the matter.
Zǐchǎn said,
"Their righteousness being equal,
the younger and lower-ranking one is at fault;
the guilt lies with Chǔ."
Thereupon they seized Zǐnán
and enumerated his crimes,
saying,
"There are five great principles of the state,
and you have violated them all.
To fear the awe-inspiring power of the ruler,
to obey his administration,
to respect those of high rank,
to serve one's elders,
and to care for one's kin—
these five are what sustain a state.
Now while the ruler is in the state,
you used weapons,
which is not fearing his awe-inspiring power;
you violated the regulations of the state,
which is not obeying the administration;
Zǐxī
is a Grand Officer of the first rank,
while you
are a favored Grand Officer of lower rank,
yet you did not defer to him,
which is not respecting high rank;
being younger and showing no restraint,
you did not serve your elder;
using weapons against your cousin,
you did not care for your kin.
The ruler says,
'I cannot bear to kill you,
so I pardon you by sending you far away.'
Exert yourself
and go quickly,
lest you increase your guilt!"
On the day Gēngchén in the fifth month,
Zhèng banished Yóu Chǔ to Wú.
When about to send Zǐnán away,
Zǐchǎn consulted Dàshū.
Dàshū said,
"I, Jí, cannot even protect my own person;
how could I protect my clan?
That
is a matter of state administration,
not a private grievance.
You are planning for the state of Zhèng;
if it is beneficial, then carry it out—
what further doubt is there?
When Zhōu Gōng killed Guǎn Shū and exiled Cài Shū,
was it because he did not love them?
It was for the sake of the royal house.
If I, Jí, were to commit a crime,
you would likewise carry out the law on me;
why should the various members of the Yóu clan be any different?"
B10.1.8 Hòuzǐ of Qín was a favorite of Duke Huán,
and they were like two rulers during the reign of Duke Jǐng.
His mother said,
"If you do not leave,
I fear you will be selected for punishment."
On the day Guǐmǎo,
Zhēn went to Jìn
with a thousand chariots.
The record says,
"Zhēn, the brother of the Earl of Qín, fled to Jìn,"
which is to place the blame on the Earl of Qín.
Hòuzǐ feasted the Marquis of Jìn,
having built a bridge of boats on the Hé River;
every ten lǐ he changed his chariots,
all the way from Yōng to Jiàng.
He returned to fetch gifts and silk for the exchange of toasts,
completing the business with eight trips back and forth.
Sīmǎ Hóu questioned him,
saying,
"Are these all your chariots?"
He replied,
"This is what is called many.
If I could have had fewer than this,
how would I have been able to see you?"
Nǚ Shūqí reported this to the Duke
and said,
"The Prince of Qín will surely return.
I have heard that if a gentleman can recognize his faults,
he will certainly have good plans.
Good plans
are what Heaven assists."
Hòuzǐ saw Zhào Mèng.
Zhào Mèng said,
"When will you return?"
He replied,
"I, Zhēn, feared being selected for punishment by my ruler,
and for this reason I am here;
I shall wait for the succeeding ruler."
Zhào Mèng said,
"What is the ruler of Qín like?"
He replied,
"He is without the Way."
Zhào Mèng said,
"Will he perish?"
He replied,
"Why should he?
If a single generation is without the Way,
the state will not yet come to an end.
A state's existence between heaven and earth
is supported by various factors.
Unless there is excess for several generations,
it cannot be destroyed."
Zhào Mèng said,
"Will he die young?"
He replied,
"There are signs of it."
Zhào Mèng said,
"How long will it be?"
He replied,
"I, Zhēn, have heard that
if a state is without the Way but the grain of the year is harmonious and ripe,
it is Heaven assisting it.
Such cases rarely exceed five harvests."
Zhào Mèng looked at the shadow
and said,
"Morning and evening do not reach each other;
who can wait for five?"
Hòuzǐ went out
and told people, saying,
"Zhào Mèng is about to die.
Governing the people,
he trifles with the years and is weary of the days;
how much longer can he last?"
B10.1.9 Because of the disorder caused by Yóu Chǔ in Zhèng,
on the day Dīngsì in the sixth month,
the Earl of Zhèng and his Grand Officers held a covenant at the house of Gōngsūn Duàn.
Hǎn Hǔ, Gōngsūn Qiáo, Gōngsūn Duàn,
Yìn Duàn, Yóu Jí,
and Sì Dài held a private covenant outside the Guīmén gate;
this was actually at Xūnsuì.
Gōngsūn Hēi forced himself into the covenant
and made the Grand Historian record his name,
also saying
"the Seven Gentlemen."
Zǐchǎn did not punish him.
B10.1.10 Mùzǐ of Zhōngháng in Jìn defeated the Wúzhōng and various Dí tribes at Tàiyuán;
this was because he prioritized the infantry.
When about to fight,
Wèi Shū said,
"They are on foot and we are in chariots;
the place we have met is also narrow.
If we combine ten men to a chariot,
we will surely win.
If we hem them in the narrows,
we will win again.
I request that we all act as infantry,
starting with me."
Thereupon they dismantled the chariots to form ranks,
with every five chariots making three squads.
A favorite of Xún Wú refused to become an infantryman;
he was beheaded and his head displayed to the troops.
Five formations were made separate from one another:
the "pairs" in front,
the "fives" behind,
the "concentrated" forming the right wing,
the "triple" forming the left wing,
and the "side" acting as the front defense
to lure them.
The Dí laughed at them.
Before the Dí had formed their own ranks, the Jìn troops pressed upon them
and soundly defeated them.
B10.1.11 Zhǎnyú of Jǔ was established as ruler
and took away the stipends of the various princes.
Prince Qìjí was summoned from Qí.
In autumn,
Prince Chú of Qí escorted Qìjí back,
and Zhǎnyú fled to Wú.
Shūgōng led an army to mark the boundaries of the fields of Yùn,
taking advantage of the disorder in Jǔ.
At this time, Wùlóu and
Màohú of Jǔ, as well as Prince Mièmíng, fled to Qí with Dàpáng and Chángyímǐ.
The Jūnzǐ said:
"That Jǔ Zhǎn was not established [as ruler]
was indeed because he discarded men!
Can men be discarded?
The *Shī* says:
'That there is no competition is because of the men,'
how excellent!"
B10.1.12 The Jìn Hóu was ill.
The Zhèng Bó sent Gōngsūn Qiáo to Jìn to pay respects
and also to inquire about the illness.
Shū Xiàng asked him,
saying:
"Our ruler’s illness is severe.
The diviners say:
'Shí Shěn
and Tái Dài are the malevolent spirits,'
but the scribes do not know who they are.
I venture to ask, what gods are these?"
Zǐchǎn said:
"Formerly, Gāoxīn Shì had two sons;
the elder was called È Bó,
and the younger was called Shí Shěn.
They lived in the vast forests
and could not get along,
daily seeking shields and spears
to attack each other.
Hòudì did not approve of this
and moved È Bó to Shāngqiū
to preside over the Chén star.
The Shāng people followed this,
so Chén is the Shāng star.
He moved Shí Shěn to Dàxià
to preside over the Shēn star.
The Táng people followed this
in serving the Xià and Shāng dynasties.
The descendant of their final generation was called Táng Shù Yú.
When Wǔ Wáng's consort Yì Jiāng was first pregnant with Dàshù,
she dreamed that the Emperor said to her:
'I have named your son Yú;
I shall give him Táng
and entrust him to Shēn,
so that he may cause his descendants to flourish.'
When he was born,
there were markings on his hand saying 'Yú,'
so he was named accordingly.
When Chéng Wáng destroyed Táng,
he enfeoffed Dàshù there;
thus Shēn is the Jìn star.
From this perspective,
then Shí Shěn
is the god of Shēn.
Formerly, Jīntiān Shì had a descendant called Mèi,
who served as the Xuánmíng Master.
He fathered Yǔngé and Tái Dài.
Tái Dài was able to carry on his office;
he cleared the Fén and Táo rivers
and dammed the great marshes
to dwell in Dàyuán.
The Emperor praised him for this
and enfeoffed him at Fénchuān;
Shěn, Sì, Rù, and Huáng truly maintain his sacrifices.
Now Jìn presides over the Fén and has destroyed them.
From this perspective,
then Tái Dài
is the god of the Fén.
However, these two
do not affect the ruler’s person.
As for the spirits of mountains and rivers,
one offers sacrifices to them for disasters of floods, droughts, pestilence, and disease;
as for the spirits of the sun, moon, stars, and planets,
when snow, frost, wind, and rain come at improper times,
one offers sacrifices to them.
As for your ruler’s person,
it is a matter of movement and rest, eating and drinking, sorrow and joy.
What have the spirits of mountains, rivers, stars, and planets to do with it?
I have heard
that a Jūnzǐ has four times:
the morning to attend to governance,
the day to inquire and consult,
the evening to refine orders,
and the night to rest the person.
Thus he regulates and vents his *qì*,
not letting it be blocked, obstructed, or stagnant so as to distress the body.
In this way, the mind is not troubled,
and the hundred measures are not confused.
Now, could it be that by making these things one-sided,
illness has been produced?
I have also heard
that the inner chambers should not include those of the same surname,
for their offspring will not flourish.
When beauty is first exhausted,
then illness is produced in each other.
The Jūnzǐ therefore detests it.
Thus the *Zhì* says:
'When buying a concubine and not knowing her surname,
divine about it.'
Violating these two things
is what the ancients were cautious about.
Men and women being distinguished by surname
is the great regulation of ritual.
Now your ruler has four women of the Jī surname in his inner chambers;
could it not be this?
If it arises from these two things,
nothing can be done.
If the four Jī women are reduced, there may be hope;
otherwise, illness will surely be produced."
Shū Xiàng said:
"Excellent!
I, Xì, had not heard this before;
this is all truly so."
Shū Xiàng went out,
and the messenger Huī escorted him.
Shū Xiàng asked about the situation in Zhèng
and also about Zǐ Xī.
Huī replied:
"How much longer will he last!
He lacks ritual and likes to insult people;
he relies on wealth and belittles his superiors.
He cannot last long."
The Jìn Hóu heard Zǐchǎn’s words
and said:
"He is a learned Jūnzǐ."
He rewarded him generously.
The Jìn Hóu sought a doctor from Qín.
The Qín Bó sent Doctor Hé to examine him.
He said:
"The illness cannot be treated.
This is what is called being too close to women;
the illness produced is like *gǔ*.
It is not caused by spirits or food;
it is delusion that has led to the loss of will.
The good minister is about to die;
the mandate of Heaven will not protect him."
The Duke said:
"Should women not be approached?"
Hé replied:
"Regulate it.
The music of the former kings
was that by which the hundred matters were regulated.
Thus there are the five regulations;
slow and fast, fundamental and incidental, follow each other,
and the sound descends from the middle note.
After the five descents,
no further playing is permitted.
After that, there are confused hands and excessive sounds,
which indulge and clog the mind and ears,
so that one forgets peace and harmony;
the Jūnzǐ does not listen to them.
It is the same with all things.
When it reaches confusion,
one should stop;
then illness is not produced.
When a Jūnzǐ approaches the qín and sè,
it is to maintain decorum and regulation,
not to indulge the heart.
Heaven has six *qì*,
which descend to produce the five flavors,
manifest as the five colors,
and are verified as the five sounds.
Excess produces the six diseases.
The six *qì* are called Yīn, Yáng, Wind, Rain, Darkness, and Light.
They divide into the four seasons
and are ordered by the five regulations.
Excess results in calamity:
excess of Yīn causes cold diseases,
excess of Yáng causes heat diseases,
excess of Wind causes diseases of the extremities,
excess of Rain causes abdominal diseases,
excess of Darkness causes diseases of delusion,
excess of Light causes diseases of the heart.
Women
are Yáng objects but belong to the time of Darkness;
excess produces diseases of internal heat, delusion, and *gǔ*.
Now your ruler is without regulation and without timing;
how can he avoid reaching this state?"
He went out
and told this to Zhào Mèng.
Zhào Mèng said:
"Who is the 'good minister'?"
Hé replied:
"It refers to you, my lord.
You have assisted the state of Jìn
for eight years now.
Jìn is without disorder,
and the feudal lords have no grievances;
this can be called good.
I have heard
that a great minister of a state
finds glory in his favors and emoluments
and takes responsibility for the great regulations.
If calamity and misfortune arise
and he does nothing to change them,
he will surely receive the blame.
Now the ruler has reached excess to the point of producing illness
and will soon be unable to care for the altars of soil and grain;
what misfortune could be greater?
You, my lord, cannot restrain him;
that is why I said it."
Zhào Mèng said:
"What is meant by 'gǔ'?"
The reply was:
"It is that which is produced by excessive indulgence and deluded confusion.
In the script,
the characters for 'vessel' and 'insects' make up 'gǔ'.
Flying grain is also called 'gǔ'.
In the *Zhōu Yì*,
women deluding men,
and the wind blowing down the mountain are called 'Gǔ'.
All of these belong to the same category."
Zhào Mèng said:
"He is a fine physician."
He bestowed generous gifts upon him and sent him back.
Prince Wéi of Chǔ sent Prince Hēigōng
and Bó Zhōulǐ to wall Chóu, Yuè, and Jiá.
The people of Zhèng were afraid.
Zǐchǎn said:
"There is no harm.
The Lìngyǐn is about to carry out a great undertaking,
and first he is removing these two men.
The disaster will not reach Zhèng,
so why worry about it?"
In winter,
Prince Wéi of Chǔ was about to go on a diplomatic mission to Zhèng,
with Wǔ Jǔ as his assistant.
Before they had left the borders,
they heard that the King was ill and returned.
Wǔ Jǔ proceeded with the mission.
In the eleventh month, on the day jǐyǒu,
Prince Wéi arrived.
He entered to inquire about the King's illness,
strangled and assassinated him,
and then killed the King's two sons, Mù and Píngxià.
Yòuyǐn Zǐgàn fled to Jìn,
Gōngjiùyǐn Zǐxī fled to Zhèng,
and they killed the Grand Architect Bó Zhōulǐ at Jiá.
They buried the King at Jiá,
and he was called Jiá'áo.
An envoy was sent to Zhèng,
and Wǔ Jǔ asked how the announcement of the successor should be phrased.
The reply was:
"The humble Great Officer Wéi."
Wǔ Jǔ changed it, saying:
"Wéi, the eldest son of King Gòng."
Zǐgàn fled to Jìn
with five chariots in his train.
Shūxiàng had him eat together with the Prince of Qín,
each receiving rations for a hundred men.
Zhào Wénzǐ said:
"The Prince of Qín is wealthy."
Shūxiàng said:
"One obtains salary through virtue,
ranks virtue by age,
and for those of the same age, by honor.
A prince's rank is based on his state;
I have never heard of it being based on wealth.
Furthermore, for one to leave his state with a thousand chariots,
his resistance against authority must have been extreme.
The *Shī* says:
'He does not insult the widower or the widow,
nor does he fear the strong and resistant.'
Qín and Chǔ
are equals."
When Hòuzǐ was made to sit in order of precedence with Zǐgàn,
he declined, saying:
"Zhēn feared being selected,
and the Prince of Chǔ did not succeed,
which is why we both came here;
we are at your command.
However, for me to be ranked with a guest,
is that not improper?
Shǐ Yì had a saying:
'If one is not a guest,
what is there to fear?'"
King Líng of Chǔ ascended the throne.
Wěi Bà became Lìngyǐn,
and Wěi Qǐqiáng became Grand Architect.
Yóu Jí of Zhèng went to Chǔ
for the burial of Jiá'áo
and to pay respects on the establishment of the new ruler.
Upon his return,
he said to Zǐchǎn:
"Prepare the traveling equipment.
The King of Chǔ is arrogant and extravagant
and takes pleasure in his own deeds.
He will certainly convene the feudal lords;
the day of my departure is not far off."
Zǐchǎn said:
"He will not be able to do so for several years."
In the twelfth month,
after Jìn had performed the winter sacrifice,
Zhào Mèng went to Nányáng
to meet with Mèngzǐ Yú.
On the first day of the month, jiǎchén,
the winter sacrifice was performed at Wēn;
on the day gēngxū,
he died.
The Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn to offer condolences,
but returned upon reaching Yōng.
The Classics for the Second Year of Duke Zhāo.
In the spring of the second year,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Hán Qǐ on a diplomatic mission.
In summer,
Shū Gōng went to Jìn.
In autumn,
Zhèng killed its Great Officer Gōngsūn Hēi.
In winter,
the Duke went to Jìn
but returned upon reaching the Yellow River.
Jìsūn Sù went to Jìn.
The Commentary for the Second Year of Duke Zhāo.
In the spring of the second year,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Hán Xuánzǐ on a diplomatic mission
and to announce that he was in charge of the government;
for him to come and visit
was in accordance with ritual.
He observed books with the Grand Historian,
seeing the *Yì*, the *Xiàng*, and the *Lǔ Chūnqiū*.
He said:
"The rituals of Zhōu are all in Lǔ.
Only now do I know the virtue of the Duke of Zhōu and why the Zhōu ruled as kings."
The Duke entertained him.
Jì Wǔzǐ recited the final stanza of "Mián".
Hánzǐ recited "Jiǎogōng".
Jì Wǔzǐ bowed
and said:
"I dare to bow for your mending the deficiencies of our humble state;
our ruler has something to hope for."
Wǔzǐ recited the final stanza of "Jié".
After the entertainment,
they banqueted at the Jì residence.
There was a fine tree there,
and Xuánzǐ praised it.
Wǔzǐ said:
"How could I, Sù, dare not to tend and cultivate this tree,
so as not to forget 'Jiǎogōng'?"
Then he recited "Gāntáng".
Xuánzǐ said:
"I, Qǐ, am not worthy of this;
I cannot be compared to the Duke of Shào."
Xuánzǐ then went to Qí to deliver the engagement gifts.
He met Zǐyǎ.
Zǐyǎ summoned Zǐqí
and had him see Xuánzǐ.
Xuánzǐ said:
"He is not one who can preserve a family;
he will not act as a proper subject."
He met Zǐwěi.
Zǐwěi presented Qiáng.
Xuánzǐ spoke of him as he had of Zǐqí.
Many of the Great Officers laughed at this,
but only Yànzǐ believed him,
saying:
"That man
is a gentleman.
A gentleman is trustworthy;
he must have some way of knowing it."
From Qí, he went on a mission to Wèi.
The Marquis of Wèi entertained him.
Běigōng Wénzǐ recited "Qí Ào",
and Xuánzǐ recited "Mùguā".
In the fourth month of summer,
Hán Xū went to Qí to escort the bride.
Chén Wúyǔ of Qí escorted the lady,
delivering Shǎojiāng.
Shǎojiāng was favored by the Marquis of Jìn,
and the Marquis of Jìn called her "Shǎo Qí".
Claiming that Chén Wúyǔ was not a high official,
they seized him at Zhōngdū.
Shǎojiāng pleaded for him,
saying:
"The escort followed the rank of those who went to receive her.
Fearing a great state,
they still had to make changes,
and this is how the confusion arose."
Shū Gōng went on a mission to Jìn,
returning the visit of Xuánzǐ.
The Marquis of Jìn sent someone to welcome him in the suburbs,
but he declined, saying:
"Our ruler sent me, Gōng, to continue our old friendship,
expressly saying,
'Do not dare to act as a guest,'
'simply convey the message to the officers in charge.'
If our humble state is magnanimously treated,
how could I dare to trouble a suburban envoy?
I beg to decline."
At the presentation of the guesthouse,
he declined, saying:
"My ruler commanded me, his humble subject, to come and continue our old friendship.
To have this friendship joined and completed
is my good fortune.
How could I dare to trouble you for this grand guesthouse!"
Shūxiàng said:
"Zishūzi knows the rituals!
I have heard it said:
'Loyalty and trustworthiness
are the vessels of ritual;
humility and yielding
are the essence of ritual.'
In declining, he did not forget his state—
that is loyalty and trustworthiness.
Putting his state first and himself last—
that is humility and yielding.
The Shī says:
'Be reverent and cautious in your dignified demeanor,
so as to be near to those of virtue.'
This gentleman is near to virtue."
B10.2.4 In autumn,
Gōngsūn Hēi of Zhèng was about to start a rebellion.
He wished to remove the Yóu lineage and take their position,
but his wound flared up and he did not succeed.
The Sì lineage and various grand masters wished to kill him.
Zǐchǎn was in the countryside;
hearing of this,
he feared he would not arrive in time
and reached the city by post-carriage.
He sent an official to enumerate his crimes,
saying:
"During the rebellion of Bóyǒu,
because of the affairs of the great states,
you were not punished.
You have a rebellious heart that is never satisfied,
and the state cannot endure you.
Arbitrarily attacking Bóyǒu
is your first crime.
Fighting with your brothers over the household
is your second crime.
At the covenant of Xūnsuì,
you falsified the ruler's position—
that is your third crime.
You have three capital crimes;
how can you endure them?
If you do not die quickly,
the great execution will arrive."
He bowed twice with his head to the ground
and pleaded, saying:
"My death is imminent;
do not help Heaven commit cruelty."
Zǐchǎn said:
"Who among men does not die?
That a wicked person does not come to a natural end
is fate.
To commit wicked deeds
is to be a wicked person.
If I do not help Heaven,
should I help a wicked person?"
He requested that Yìn be made the Chǔshī.
Zǐchǎn said:
"If Yìn is talented,
the ruler will employ him;
if he is not talented,
he will follow you day and night.
You do not care about your own crimes,
so what else do you request?
If you do not die quickly,
the Sìkòu will arrive."
On the day Rényín of the seventh month,
he hanged himself.
His body was exposed at the crossroads of the Zhōu lineage,
and a piece of wood was placed over it.
B10.2.5 Shàojiāng of Jìn died.
The Duke went to Jìn,
and when he reached the River,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Wénbó to decline his visit,
saying:
"She was not a principal wife;
please, my lord, do not trouble yourself."
The Duke returned.
Jìsūn Sù then presented the mourning garments.
Shūxiàng spoke of Chén Wúyǔ to the Marquis of Jìn, saying:
"What crime has he committed?
You sent a member of the ducal clan to welcome her,
and Qí sent a high grand master to escort her.
Yet you say they were not respectful;
you are making demands out of greed.
If the state was disrespectful,
why seize its envoy?
Your punishments are already biased;
how can you be the leader of the covenant?
Moreover, Shàojiāng left words."
In the tenth month, in winter,
Chén Wúyǔ returned.
In the eleventh month,
Yìn Duàn of Zhèng went to Jìn to offer condolences.
A10.3 The Classic of the Third Year of Duke Zhāo.
A10.3.1 In the spring of the third year,
in the royal first month, on the day Dīngwèi,
Yuán, the Viscount of Téng, died.
A10.3.2 In summer,
Shū Gōng went to Téng.
A10.3.3 In the fifth month,
Duke Chéng of Téng was buried.
A10.3.4 In autumn,
the Viscount of Xiǎozhū came for an audience.
A10.3.5 In the eighth month,
the great rain sacrifice was performed.
A10.3.6 In winter,
there was a great storm of hail.
A10.3.7 Kuǎn, the Earl of Běiyàn, fled to Qí.
B10.3 The Commentary of the Third Year of Duke Zhāo.
B10.3.1 In the spring of the third year,
in the royal first month,
Yóu Jí of Zhèng went to Jìn
to attend the funeral of Shàojiāng.
Liáng Bǐng and Zhāng Tì met him.
Liáng Bǐng said:
"How extreme it is,
that you have come for this!"
Zǐdàshū said:
"Could I have avoided it?
Formerly, when Duke Wén and Duke Xiāng were hegemons,
they made it their business not to trouble the feudal lords.
They ordered the feudal lords to send missions every three years
and to have an audience every five years.
If there was business, they met;
if there was disagreement, they held a covenant.
When a ruler died,
a grand master offered condolences
and a minister assisted with the funeral.
For a ruler's wife,
a serviceman offered condolences
and a grand master attended the funeral.
These were sufficient to manifest ritual, assign tasks, and plan for deficiencies—nothing more.
No additional orders were given.
Now for the funeral of a favored concubine,
we do not dare choose our own status
and are counted among those mourning a primary wife.
We only fear incurring a penalty;
how could we dare to dread the trouble?
Since Shǎoqí was favored and died,
Qí will surely provide a successor.
This year I will have to come again to congratulate them;
this trip is not the only one."
Zhāng Tì said:
"Excellent!
I have been able to hear these rules!
However, from now on you will likely have no more such tasks.
It is like fire:
when the fire star is at its culmination,
the cold or heat then recedes.
This is the peak;
can it not but recede?
Jìn is about to lose the feudal lords,
and the lords will seek to be troubled but will not be able to."
The two grand masters withdrew.
Zǐdàshū told someone:
"Zhāng Tì has wisdom;
is he not like one following in the footsteps of a superior man?"
B10.3.2 On the day Dīngwèi,
Yuán, the Viscount of Téng, died. Since he was a member of the covenant,
his personal name was recorded.
B10.3.3 The Marquis of Qí sent Yàn Yīng to request a successor wife from Jìn,
saying:
"My ruler sent me, Yīng, to say:
'I wish to serve you morning and night without tire,
and was about to offer hostages and gifts so as not to miss the proper time,
but my state was beset with many difficulties,
and thus I did not succeed.
My late ruler's daughter of humble worth was sent to fill your inner palace
and to bring glory to my hopes,
but she was unfortunate
and died an early death,
causing me to lose hope.
If you, my lord, do not forget the friendship of our former rulers,
and show kindness to the state of Qí,
deigning to accept me,
seeking blessings from Tàigōng and Dīnggōng,
shining upon my humble city
and stabilizing its altars of soil and grain,
then there are still daughters of the former ruler and remaining paternal aunts and sisters, so many people.'"
If your Lordship does not abandon my humble city,
and condescends to send Dǒng Zhèn to choose one
to fill the ranks of the concubines,
it is my hope."
Hán Xuānzǐ sent Shū Xiàng to respond, saying:
"It is my lord’s wish as well.
My lord cannot alone shoulder the affairs of the altars of soil and grain,
and does not yet have a formal mate.
As he is in mourning garments,
he has not yet dared to request it.
Since your Lordship has condescended to command,
no favor could be greater.
If you graciously favor our humble city,
cherish the state of Jìn,
and grant it a mistress for the inner palace,
it is not only my lord
but all the ministers who will truly receive your bounty;
from Táng Shū downward, the ancestors will truly be honored and celebrate it."
Once the marriage was concluded,
Yàn Zǐ received the ritual gifts,
and Shū Xiàng accompanied him to a banquet
where they spoke together.
Shū Xiàng said:
"How is Qí doing?"
Yàn Zǐ said:
"This is a degenerate age;
I do not know if Qí will not eventually belong to the Chén family.
The Duke has abandoned his people,
and they are turning to the Chén family.
Qí formerly had four measures:
the dòu, the qū, the fǔ, and the zhōng.
Four shēng make a dòu;
each is multiplied by four in turn
to reach the fǔ.
Ten fǔ make a zhōng.
The Chén family’s first three measures were each increased by one unit,
so their zhōng is larger.
They lend using their private measures,
but collect using the public measures.
Timber from the mountains is as plentiful as at market,
but no profit is added to the mountains;
fish, salt, clams, and oysters
add no profit to the sea.
The people divide their labor into three parts:
two parts go to the Duke,
and they clothe and feed themselves with only one part.
The Duke’s granaries are full of rotting and worm-eaten grain,
while the three classes of elders suffer from cold and hunger.
In the markets of the capital,
ordinary shoes are cheap, but prosthetic shoes for the maimed are expensive.
The people are in pain and distress,
and someone comforts them.
They love them like parents,
and flow to them like running water.
Even if they did not wish to win over the people,
how could they avoid it?
Jī Bó, Zhí Bǐng, Yú Suì, and Bó Xì,
who assist Hú Gōng and Dà Jī, are already in Qí."
Shū Xiàng said:
"True.
Even our own ruling house
is now in a degenerate age.
War horses are not harnessed,
the ministers do not lead the army,
the Duke’s chariots have no riders,
and the ranks of soldiers have no leaders.
The common people are exhausted and worn out,
while the palaces and houses grow more extravagant.
The bodies of those starved to death in the roads are in sight of one another,
while the wealth of the women is excessively abundant.
When the people hear the Duke’s commands,
they flee as if from bandits or enemies.
The Luán, Xì, Xū, Yuán, Hú,
Xù, Qìng, and Bó families have been reduced to the status of servants.
Government is in the hands of private houses,
and the people have nowhere to turn.
The ruler does not reform himself daily,
but uses pleasure to drown his worries.
Regarding the degradation of the ruling house,
what day of hope remains?
The inscription on the Chán Dǐng says:
'At dawn, be greatly illustrious;
later generations will still be idle.' How much more so when one does not reform daily;
can it last long?"
Yàn Zǐ said:
"What will you do, sir?"
Shū Xiàng said:
"The ducal clan of Jìn is finished.
I, Xì, have heard that
when a ruling house is about to fall,
its clansmen—its branches and leaves—fall first,
and then the Duke follows them.
Of my, Xì’s, own lineage of eleven clans,
only the Yángshé clan remains.
Furthermore, I, Xì, have no son.
The ruling house lacks proper measure;
if I am lucky enough to die naturally, how could I expect to receive ancestral sacrifices?"
Earlier,
Jǐng Gōng wished to change Yàn Zǐ’s residence,
saying:
"Your house is near the market;
it is low-lying, cramped, noisy, and dusty;
it is not fit to live in.
Please let me change it for one that is bright and high."
He declined, saying:
"Your Lordship’s former servant was accommodated there;
I am not worthy to succeed him,
so it is already too extravagant for me.
Furthermore, a lowly person like me being near the market
can get what I need morning and evening;
this is an advantage for a lowly person.
How could I dare to trouble the neighborhood officials?"
The Duke laughed and said:
"Since you live near the market,
do you know what is expensive and what is cheap?"
He replied:
"Since I benefit from it,
how could I dare not to know?"
The Duke said:
"What is expensive?
What is cheap?"
At that time, Jǐng Gōng was excessive in his punishments,
and there were those selling prosthetic shoes for the maimed;
so he replied:
"Prosthetic shoes are expensive;
ordinary shoes are cheap."
After he had told this to the ruler,
he mentioned it while speaking with Shū Xiàng.
Because of this, Jǐng Gōng reduced the punishments.
The noble man says:
"The words of a benevolent man,
how broad is their benefit!
With one word from Yàn Zǐ,
the Marquis of Qí reduced punishments.
The Shī says:
'If the noble man is blessed,
disorder will soon come to an end.'
Does this not refer to this!"
When Yàn Zǐ went to Jìn,
the Duke changed his residence.
When he returned,
it was completed.
After expressing his thanks,
he then tore it down
and made it into neighborhood houses,
all just as they were before.
Then he made the former residents return,
saying:
"A proverb says:
'It is not the house that one divines for,
but the neighbors that one divines for.'
You gentlemen had already divined for your neighbors.
To go against the divination is inauspicious.
A noble man does not violate what is ritual,
and a common man does not violate what is inauspicious;
this is the system of old.
How could I dare to violate it?"
In the end, he restored his old residence,
but the Duke would not permit it.
He petitioned through Chén Huánzǐ,
and only then did the Duke permit it.
B10.3.4 In the summer, in the fourth month,
the Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn,
with Gōngsūn Duàn as his assistant.
He was very respectful and humble,
violating nothing in the rituals.
The Marquis of Jìn commended him,
gave him a tablet of command,
saying:
"Zǐ Fēng performed service for the state of Jìn;
I have heard of it and not forgotten.
I grant you the fields of Zhōu
to reward your former meritorious services."
Bó Shí bowed twice with his head to the ground,
received the tablet, and went out.
The noble man says:
"Ritual—
is it not the most urgent thing for a man!
Though Bó Shí was arrogant,
by performing the rituals for Jìn just once,
he still received its emoluments;
how much more so if one follows ritual from beginning to end!
The Shī says:
'If a man has no ritual,
why does he not die quickly?'
Does this not refer to this!"
Earlier,
the district of Zhōu
had been the fief of Luán Bào.
When the Luán family was destroyed,
Fàn Xuānzǐ, Zhào Wénzǐ, and Hán Xuānzǐ all desired it.
Wénzǐ said:
"Wēn
is my district."
Èr Xuānzǐ said:
"Since the separation from Xì Chēng,
it has been three generations.
Of the separate districts of Jìn, it is not only Zhōu;
who shall be granted to govern it?"
Wénzǐ was troubled by this
and so he left it alone.
Èr Xuānzǐ said:
"I cannot use a righteous argument and then benefit myself."
Both left it alone.
When Wénzǐ was in charge of government,
Zhào Huò said:
"You may now take Zhōu."
Wénzǐ said:
"Withdraw!
The words of those two gentlemen
were righteous.
To violate righteousness
is a calamity.
I cannot even govern my own district,
so what use have I for Zhōu,
that I should use it to court calamity?
A gentleman says:
'It is indeed difficult not to know.
To know and yet not follow,
no calamity is greater than this.'
Whoever mentions Zhōu shall surely die!"
The Fēng clan formerly served the Hán clan.
When Bó Shí obtained Zhōu,
Hán Xuānzǐ requested it for him
for the sake of having him take it back again.
B10.3.5 In the fifth month,
Shū Gōng went to Téng
to bury Téng Chéng Gōng,
with Zǐfú Jiāo as his assistant.
When they reached the outskirts,
they encountered the anniversary of the death of Yì Bó.
Jìngzǐ would not enter.
Huì Bó said:
"Public affairs have public benefits
and no private taboos.
Jiāo requests to enter first."
He then first received the lodging.
Jìngzǐ followed him.
B10.3.6 Hán Qǐ of Jìn went to Qí to meet a bride.
Because Shǎo Jiāng was favored, Gōngsūn Chài
substituted the Duke's daughter with his own child
and married her to the young lord.
People said to Xuānzǐ:
"Zǐwěi has deceived Jìn;
why does Jìn accept it?"
Xuānzǐ said:
"I wish to gain Qí
rather than keep her who is favored at a distance;
will the favor then come?"
B10.3.7 In the autumn, the seventh month,
Hǎn Hǔ of Zhèng went to Jìn
to congratulate the lady
and also to report, saying:
"The people of Chǔ daily summon our humble state because we did not attend court for the enthroned king.
If our humble state goes there,
then we fear the ministers will say our meager ruler has a change of heart;
if we do not go,
then there is the Sòng zhī Méng.
Advancing or retreating, it is a crime.
Our meager ruler sent Hǔ to explain this."
Xuānzǐ had Shū Xiàng reply, saying:
"If your ruler deigns to have our meager ruler in mind,
what harm is there in being in Chǔ?
It is to observe the Sòng zhī Méng.
If your ruler but thinks of the covenant,
our meager ruler will know he is exempt from blame.
If your ruler does not have our meager ruler in mind,
though he morning and evening deigns to be in our humble state,
our meager ruler would be suspicious.
If your ruler truly has the heart,
why deign to send this command?
Your ruler should go!
If he has our meager ruler in mind,
being in Chǔ is like being in Jìn."
Zhāng Tì sent someone to say to Dàshū:
"Since your return,
this small person has been cleaning the humble hut of my ancestors,
saying:
'The master is about to come.'
Now it is actually Zǐpí who has come;
this small person is disappointed."
Dàshū said:
"Jí is of low rank
and did not get to come.
Fearing the great state
and honoring the lady,
and Mèng said
'You shall have no duties,'
Jí hopes for that."
B10.3.8 Xiǎo Zhū Mù Gōng came to court, and Jì Wǔzǐ wanted to treat him as a subordinate.
Mù Shū said:
"That will not do;
Cáo, Téng, and the two Zhū indeed do not forget our friendship.
We should receive them with respect,
and even then we fear their double-mindedness.
If we now humble one who is friendly,
how can we welcome the group of friends?
One should follow the old custom and add respect to it.
The Zhì says:
'One who can be respectful will have no disaster.'
It also says:
'To respectfully welcome those who come
is what Heaven blesses.'"
Jìsūn followed this.
B10.3.9 In the eighth month,
there was a great sacrifice for rain
because of a drought.
B10.3.10 Qí Hóu hunted in Jǔ.
Lúpú Miè saw him,
wept,
and requested, saying:
"My hair is all like this;
what can I do?"
The Duke said:
"Very well.
I will tell the two gentlemen."
He returned and told them.
Zǐwěi wanted to restore him,
but Zǐyǎ would not allow it,
saying:
"His hair is short but his heart is very long;
he might even come to reside in our place."
In the ninth month,
Zǐyǎ exiled Lúpú Miè to Běiyàn.
B10.3.11 Yān Jiǎn Gōng had many favorites,
and wanted to remove the various grand officers and establish his favorites.
In winter,
the grand officers of Yān acted together to kill the Duke's external favorites.
The Duke was afraid
and fled to Qí.
The record says:
"Běiyàn Bó Kuǎn fled to Qí,"
which was to blame him.
B10.3.12 In the tenth month,
Zhèng Bó went to Chǔ,
with Zǐchǎn as his assistant.
Chǔ Zǐ entertained him
and recited the poem Jí Rì.
After the entertainment,
Zǐchǎn then prepared the hunting equipment,
and the king went hunting in the Jiāngnán zhī Mèng.
B10.3.13 Gōngsūn Zào of Qí died.
Sīmǎ Zào saw Yànzǐ
and said:
"We have lost Zǐyǎ as well."
Yànzǐ said:
"A pity!
Zǐqí will not escape;
how perilous!
The Jiāng clan is weakening,
and the Guī clan is about to start flourishing.
If the Èr Huì were both brilliant, it might still be fine;
but now that one more of them is weakened,
the Jiāng clan is indeed in danger!"
A10.4 The Annals of the Fourth Year of Zhāo Gōng.
A10.4.1 In the spring of the fourth year,
in the royal first month,
it rained heavily with hail.
A10.4.2 In the summer,
Chǔ Zǐ,
Cài Hóu,
Chén Hóu,
Zhèng Bó,
Xǔ Nán,
Xú Zǐ,
Téng Zǐ,
Dùn Zǐ,
Hú Zǐ,
Shěn Zǐ,
Xiǎo Zhū Zǐ,
Sòng Shìzǐ Zuǒ,
and the Huái Yí met at Shēn.
A10.4.3 The people of Chǔ seized Xú Zǐ.
A10.4.4 In the autumn, the seventh month,
Chǔ Zǐ,
Cài Hóu,
Chén Hóu,
Xǔ Nán,
Dùn Zǐ,
Hú Zǐ,
Shěn Zǐ,
and the Huái Yí invaded Wú,
seized Qìng Fēng of Qí
and killed him.
Then they destroyed Lài.
A10.4.5 In the ninth month,
they took Zéng.
A10.4.6 In winter, in the twelfth month, on the day yǐmǎo,
Shūsūn Bào died.
B10.4 The Commentary for the Zhāo Gōng Fourth Year
B10.4.1 In the spring of the fourth year,
in the Wáng’s first month,
Xǔ Nán went to Chǔ,
and Chǔ Zǐ detained him;
then he detained Zhèng Bó,
and returned to hunt in the fields of Jiāngnán,
and Xǔ Nán was present there.
He sent Jiāo Jǔ to Jìn to request the Zhūhóu;
the two Jūn waited for him.
Jiāo Jǔ delivered the mission, saying:
“My Wáng sent me, Jǔ, to say:
‘Recently, the Jūn showed favor
by granting a covenant at Sòng,
saying:
“The followers of Jìn and Chǔ shall see each other interchangeably.”
Because the years have not been easy,
I wish to establish friendship with you, my Jūn,
and have sent Jǔ to ask for an audience.
If the Jūn has no concerns from the four directions,
then I wish to borrow your prestige to make a request to the Zhūhóu.’”
Jìn Hóu wished to refuse.
Sīmǎ Hóu said:
“You must not.
Chǔ Wáng is currently extravagant.
Perhaps Tiān wishes to gratify his heart,
to increase his poison,
and then send down punishment upon him;
it cannot yet be known.
Whether he can bring things to an end
is also not yet known.
Jìn and Chǔ are only as Tiān assists them;
one cannot contend with him.
The Jūn should grant it to him
and cultivate virtue to await his return.
If he returns to virtue,
we should still serve him,
how much more so the Zhūhóu?
If he goes toward excess and cruelty,
Chǔ will abandon him,
then with whom would we need to contend?”
The Gōng said:
“Jìn has three reasons for not being in danger;
what enemy could it have?
Our state is naturally strong and has many horses;
Qí and Chǔ have many difficulties.
Having these three things,
in what direction would we not succeed?”
He replied:
“Relying on defenses and horses,
and taking pleasure in the difficulties of neighboring states—
these are three reasons for danger.
Sìyuè, Sāntú, Yángchéng,
Dàshì, Jīngshān, and Zhōngnán
are the natural defenses of the Jiǔzhōu;
they are not held by a single surname.
The northern lands of Jì,
where horses are bred,
have no rising states there.
Relying on defenses and horses
cannot be considered security;
it has been so since ancient times.
Therefore, the former Wáng made it their business to cultivate virtuous reputation to make offerings to the spirits and people;
I have not heard of them making a business of defenses and horses.
The difficulties of neighboring states
are not something to take pleasure in.
Some have many difficulties and thereby strengthen their state
and open up their territory;
some have no difficulties and thereby lose their state
and lose their guarded borders;
how can one take pleasure in difficulties?
Qí had the difficulty of Zhòngsūn
and obtained Huán Gōng,
relying on him to this day.
Jìn had the difficulties of Lǐ and Pī,
and obtained Wén Gōng,
whereby it became the leader of the covenants.
Wèi
and Xíng had no difficulties,
yet the enemy still caused them to lose their states.
Therefore, the difficulties of others
are not something to take pleasure in.
If one relies on these three things
and does not cultivate governance and virtue,
one will not even have time to avoid ruin;
how then could one succeed?
The Jūn should grant it!
Zhòu practiced excess and cruelty,
while Wén Wáng was kind and harmonious;
Yīn thereby fell,
and Zhōu thereby rose;
did they contend for the Zhūhóu?”
He then granted the request of the Chǔ envoy.
He sent Shú Xiàng to reply:
“My Jūn has the affairs of the altars of soil and grain,
and therefore cannot meet with you during the spring and autumn seasons.
The Zhūhóu—
the Jūn truly possesses them;
why must you deign to send a command?”
Jiāo Jǔ then requested a marriage alliance,
and Jìn Hóu granted it.
Chǔ Zǐ asked Zǐchǎn:
“Will Jìn grant me the Zhūhóu?”
He replied: “They will grant them to you, my Jūn.
Jìn Jūn is at ease with little,
and his mind is not on the Zhūhóu.
His Dàfū seek many things for themselves,
and none of them correct their Jūn.
Furthermore, the covenant at Sòng said they should be as one.
If they do not grant them to the Jūn,
what use would that covenant be?”
The Wáng said:
“Will the Zhūhóu come?”
He replied:
“They will certainly come.
Following the covenant of Sòng,
and receiving the Jūn’s favor,
not fearing the great state,
for what reason would they not come?
Those who do not come—will they not be Lǔ, Wèi, Cáo, and Zhū?
Cáo fears Sòng,
Zhū fears Lǔ,
and Lǔ and Wèi are pressured by Qí and close to Jìn;
only these will not come.
As for the rest,
they are within the Jūn’s reach;
who would dare not arrive?”
The Wáng said:
“In that case, is there nothing I seek that cannot be attained?”
He replied:
“If you seek to gratify your own desires at the expense of others,
it is not possible;
if you share the same desires with others,
all will succeed.”
B10.4.2 There was a great storm of hail.
Jì Wǔzǐ asked Shēn Fēng:
“Can hail be warded off?”
He replied:
“When a Shèngrén is on the throne,
there is no hail.
Even if there is,
it does not cause a disaster.
In ancient times, when the sun was in Běilù, they stored the ice;
when it was seen in the morning in Xīlù, they brought it out.
When they stored the ice,
in deep mountains and remote valleys,
where the shade is solid and the cold is intense—it was from there they took it.
When they brought it out,
for the emoluments and ranks of the court,
for guests, meals, funerals, and sacrifices—
it was then that it was used.
When they stored it,
they used a black bull and black millet to offer to Sīhán.
When they brought it out,
they used peach-wood bows and thorn arrows
to eliminate its calamities.
Its extraction and introduction were timely.
Of those with the emolument of eating meat,
all participated in receiving the ice.
For the Dàfū and Mìngfù, ice was used for bathing the deceased.
They sacrificed to Sīhán and then stored it;
they offered a lamb and then opened the icehouse;
the Gōng was the first to use it;
when the Huǒ star appeared, they completed its distribution;
from Mìngfū and Mìngfù down to the old and the sick,
none did not receive ice.
Shānrén collected it,
Xiànrén transported it,
Yúrén delivered it,
and Lìrén stored it.
Now, ice is strengthened by the wind,
and it is brought out by the wind.
If its storage is thorough,
and its use is universal,
then in winter there is no excessive Yáng,
in summer no hidden Yīn,
in spring no biting winds,
in autumn no bitter rains;
when thunder comes forth, it does not shock;
there are no calamities of frost or hail,
pestilence does not descend,
and the people do not die young or in epidemics.
Nowadays, the ice from rivers and ponds is discarded and not used;
the wind does not pass through but kills,
and thunder does not break forth but shocks.
As for hail becoming a disaster,
who can ward it off?
The final stanza of the Qīyuè
is the way of storing ice.”
B10.4.3 In the summer,
the Zhūhóu went to Chǔ,
but Lǔ, Wèi, Cáo, and Zhū did not attend the meeting.
Cáo and Zhū excused themselves on account of difficulties,
Lǔ Gōng excused himself on account of the seasonal sacrifices,
and Wèi Hóu excused himself on account of illness.
Zhèng Bó first waited at Shēn.
In the sixth month, on the day bǐngwǔ,
Chǔ Zǐ assembled the Zhūhóu at Shēn.
Jiāo Jǔ spoke to Chǔ Zǐ, saying:
“I have heard that when the Zhūhóu have no one to turn to,
they turn to ritual.
Now that my Lord has first gained the adherence of the Zhūhóu,
you should be cautious regarding ritual.
Whether the hegemony succeeds or fails
depends on this meeting.
Xià Qǐ had the feast at Jūntái,
Shāng Tāng had the mandate at Jǐngbó,
Zhōu Wǔ had the oath at Mèngjīn,
Chéng had the hunt at Qíyáng,
Kāng had the court assembly at Fènggōng,
Mù had the meeting at Túshān,
Qí Huán had the army at Zhàolíng,
and Jìn Wén had the covenant at Jiàntǔ.
Which of these will my Lord use?
Sòng Xiàng Xū and Zhèng Gōngsūn Qiáo are present;
they are the finest among the Zhūhóu.
My Lord should choose from between them.”
Wáng said:
“I will use the model of Qí Huán.”
Wáng sent someone to ask about ritual from the Zuǒshī and Zǐchǎn.
The Zuǒshī said:
“Small states practice them,
large states use them;
how would I dare not present what I have heard?”
He presented six rituals for a Gōng to assemble the Zhūhóu.
Zǐchǎn said:
“Small states fulfill their duties;
how would I dare not present what I keep?”
He presented six rituals for a Bó, Zǐ, or Nán to meet a Gōng.
The Jūnzǐ said that the Zuǒshī was good at preserving the ways of former generations,
and Zǐchǎn was good at acting as a minister for a small state.
Wáng made Jiāo Jǔ attend behind him to correct any errors,
but through the completion of the matter, he did not offer any corrections.
Wáng asked for the reason,
and he replied:
“Regarding ritual,
there were six things I had never seen before;
how then could I offer corrections?”
Sòng Dàzǐ Zuǒ arrived late.
Wáng was hunting at Wǔchéng
and for a long time did not grant him an audience.
Jiāo Jǔ requested to deliver an apology.
Wáng sent him to go,
and he said:
“It so happened that there were matters concerning the ancestral temple at Wǔchéng.
My humble ruler was about to offer silk in sacrifice,
so he ventures to apologize for the delay in the audience.”
Xú Zǐ,
who was born of a woman from Wú,
was believed to be double-minded,
and therefore was seized at Shēn.
Chǔ Zǐ showed off extravagance to the Zhūhóu.
Jiāo Jǔ said:
“The matters of the Liù Wáng and Èr Gōng
were all to show ritual to the Zhūhóu,
which is why the Zhūhóu followed their commands.
Xià Jié held the meeting at Réng,
and the Yǒumín rebelled against him.
Shāng Zhòu held the hunt at Lí,
and the Dōng Yí rebelled against him.
Zhōu Yōu held the covenant at Dàshì,
and the Róng and Dí rebelled against him.
These were all to show arrogance to the Zhūhóu,
which is why the Zhūhóu abandoned their commands.
Now if my Lord acts with arrogance,
will you not perhaps fail to succeed?”
Wáng did not listen.
Zǐchǎn saw the Zuǒshī and said:
“I no longer worry about Chǔ.
He is arrogant and rejects admonition;
it will not be more than ten years.”
The Zuǒshī said:
“True.
If he is extravagant for less than ten years,
the evil will not spread far.
Only after evil has spread far will he be abandoned.
Goodness is the same;
only after virtue has spread far will one rise.”
B10.4.4 In the autumn, the seventh month,
Chǔ Zǐ led the Zhūhóu to attack Wú.
Sòng Dàzǐ and Zhèng Bó returned first,
with Sòng Huá Fèisuì and the Zhèng Dàfū following them.
He sent Qū Shēn to besiege Zhūfāng.
In the eighth month, on the day jiǎshēn,
he conquered it,
seized Qí Qìng Fēng, and completely exterminated his clan.
When he was about to execute Qìng Fēng,
Jiāo Jǔ said:
“I have heard that only one without flaws can execute others.
Qìng Fēng only disobeyed orders,
which is why he is here;
will he be willing to submit to execution?
If this is spread among the Zhūhóu,
what use is it?”
Wáng did not listen.
He made him carry an axe and halberd on his back
to be paraded before the Zhūhóu,
making him say:
“Let no one be like Qí Qìng Fēng, who murdered his ruler,
weakened his orphan heir,
and forced a covenant upon his Dàfū!”
Qìng Fēng said:
“Let no one be like the Shùzǐ of Chǔ Gòng Wáng, Wéi, who murdered his ruler
—his brother's son Jūn—and took his place,
and then forced a covenant upon the Zhūhóu!”
Wáng sent someone to kill him quickly.
He then used the Zhūhóu's forces to destroy Lài.
Lài Zǐ had his hands bound behind his back and held a jade disk in his mouth;
his officers bared their shoulders,
and he was followed by a carriage carrying a coffin,
as he went to the central army.
Wáng asked Jiāo Jǔ about this.
He replied:
“Chéng Wáng conquered Xǔ,
and Xǔ Xī Gōng acted in this way.
The King personally untied his bonds,
received his jade disk,
and burned his coffin.”
Wáng followed this advice.
He moved Lài to Yān.
Chǔ Zǐ wanted to move Xǔ to Lài,
so he sent Dòu Wéiguī and Gōngzǐ Qìjí to build a city there and then return.
Shēn Wúyǔ said:
“The source of Chǔ’s disaster will be here.
He summoned the Zhūhóu and they came;
he attacked a state and was victorious;
he built a city, and throughout the border no one resisted.
Wáng's heart's desires are not thwarted.
Can the people live with this?
If the people cannot dwell in peace,
who can endure it?
When Wáng's commands cannot be endured,
that is when disaster and disorder arise.”
B10.4.5 In the ninth month,
Zēng was taken;
this refers to its being easy.
Jǔ was in disorder.
Zhù Qiū Gōng had been established but did not soothe Zēng.
Zēng rebelled and came,
therefore it is called ‘taking’.
In all cases of conquering a city,
when troops are not used, it is called ‘taking’.
B10.4.6 Zhèng Zǐchǎn instituted the Qiūfù.
The people of the state slandered him,
saying:
“His father died on the road,
and he himself acts like a scorpion's tail,
issuing commands to the state;
what will become of the state?”
Zǐkuān told him of this.
Zǐchǎn said:
“What harm is there?
If it benefits the altars of soil and grain,
I will devote my life and death to it.
Moreover, I have heard that one who does good does not change his measures,
and thus can have success.
