The people's whims cannot be indulged,
and measures cannot be changed.
The Shī says:
‘Ritual and righteousness are without error;
why worry about what people say?’
I will not change.”
Hún Hǎn said:
“Will the Guó clan be the first to perish?
When a Jūnzǐ creates laws in a time of scarcity,
their defect will still be greed.
If he creates laws based on greed,
what will be the defect?
Among the Jī who are in the ranks,
will Cài, Cáo, and Téng be the first to perish?
They are pressed but lack ritual.
Zhèng will perish before Wèi;
it is pressed but lacks law.
When government does not follow the law
but is controlled by the mind,
and every person has their own mind,
what authority can there be?”
B10.4.7 In the winter,
Wú attacked Chǔ,
entering Jí,
Lì, and Má,
in retaliation for the campaign at Zhūfāng.
Chǔ Shěn Yǐnshè rushed to the rescue at Xiàruì;
Zhēnyǐn Yíjiù built a wall at Zhōnglí,
Wěi Qǐjiāng built a wall at Cháo,
and Rán Dān built a wall at Zhōulái.
The Dōngguó was flooded,
so it could not be walled.
Péngshēng withdrew the army from Lài.
B10.4.8 Early on,
Mùzǐ left the Shūsūn clan.
When he reached Gēngzōng,
he met a woman,
and had her privately prepare food for him and stayed the night there.
She asked about his journey,
and he told her the reason.
She wept and saw him off.
He went to Qí,
married into the Guó clan,
and fathered Mèng Bǐng and Zhòng Rén.
He dreamed that Heaven was pressing down on him.
Unable to withstand it,
he looked around and saw a person
who was dark-skinned and hunchbacked,
with deep-set eyes and a mouth like a boar.
He called out to him, saying:
“Niú!
Help me!”
Then he overcame it.
In the morning, he summoned all his followers,
but none looked like that person.
And he said:
“Remember this!”
When Xuānbó fled to Qí,
Mùzǐ sent him food.
Xuānbó said:
“Because of my late father, Lǔ
will preserve our house;
they will surely summon you.
If they summon you,
what will it be like?”
He replied:
“I have long desired it.”
The people of Lǔ summoned him,
and he returned without giving notice.
After he was established,
the woman of Gēngzōng where he had stayed presented him with a pheasant.
He asked about her family,
and she replied:
“My son is grown;
he is able to carry a pheasant and follow me.”
He summoned and saw him;
he was the person from the dream.
Before asking his name,
he called out to him:
“Niú!”
The boy said:
“Yes.”
He summoned all his followers to look at him,
and then made him an attendant.
He was favored,
and as he grew up, he was put in charge of affairs.
Gōngsūn Míng had known Shūsūn in Qí.
When Shūsūn returned,
he had not yet fetched Guó Jiāng.
Zǐmíng took her for himself.
Therefore, Shūsūn was angry,
and only after her son was grown did he send to fetch her.
While he was hunting at Qiūyóu,
he fell ill.
Shù Niú wanted to cause disorder in the household and take it for himself.
He tried to force an alliance with Mèng,
but Mèng would not agree.
Shūsūn made a bell for Mèng,
and said:
“You have not yet reached maturity;
feast the grandees to inaugurate it.”
Once everything was prepared,
he sent Shù Niú to request a date.
Niú went in,
but did not announce it;
he came out
and designated the date.
When the guests arrived,
Shūsūn heard the sound of the bell.
Niú said:
“Mèng has guests of the northern woman.”
Shūsūn was angry
and was about to go there,
but Niú stopped him.
When the guests left,
Shūsūn had Mèng seized and killed outside.
Niú then tried to force an alliance with Zhòng,
but he would not agree.
Zhòng and the Duke's charioteer Lái Shū were looking at the palace.
The Duke gave Zhòng a ring,
and sent Niú inside to show it to Shūsūn.
Niú went in,
but did not show it;
he came out
and told Zhòng to wear it.
Niú said to Shūsūn:
“What did you see in Zhòng?”
Shūsūn said:
“What was it?”
Niú said:
“Though you did not see him,
he has already presented himself;
the Duke gave him a ring, and he is wearing it.”
Shūsūn then drove him away,
and he fled to Qí.
When the illness became critical,
he ordered Zhòng to be summoned.
Niú agreed but did not summon him.
Dù Xiè saw Shūsūn,
who told him of his hunger and thirst,
and gave him a halberd.
Dù Xiè replied:
“I came because I sought this;
why should I leave now?”
Shù Niú said:
“The master is gravely ill
and does not wish to see anyone.”
He had the food placed in a side room and withdrew.
Niú did not bring it in,
but set out empty vessels and ordered them removed.
On the day guǐchǒu of the twelfth month,
Shūsūn did not eat;
on yǐmǎo,
he died.
Niú established Zhāozǐ and assisted him.
The Duke sent Dù Xiè to bury Shūsūn.
Shù Niú bribed Shūzhòng Zhāozǐ and Nán Yí
to speak ill of Dù Xiè to Jìsūn and have him removed.
Dù Xiè intended to use the state carriage for the burial
and fully observe the rites for a minister.
Nán Yí said to Jìsūn:
“Shūsūn never rode in the state carriage;
why use it for the burial?
Moreover, the chief minister does not have a state carriage;
if an assistant minister is buried with one,
is that not improper?”
Jìsūn said:
“Indeed.”
He ordered Dù Xiè to set aside the carriage.
Dù Xiè would not agree,
saying:
“The master received orders at court and went on a mission to the King;
the King, remembering old merits, bestowed the state carriage upon him.
He reported back and presented it to the Ruler.
The Ruler did not dare to go against the King's command and bestowed it back upon him,
and had the three officials record it.
You, sir, as the Sītú,
recorded the name;
the master, as Sīmǎ,
together with the Gōngzhèng, recorded the garments;
Mèngsūn, as Sīkōng, recorded the merits.
Now that he is dead, if we do not use it,
that is discarding the Ruler's command.
If the records are in the public office but we do not use it,
that is abandoning the three officials.
As for the ritual robes,
he did not dare wear them while alive;
if they are not used now that he is dead,
what purpose will they serve?”
Thereupon he was allowed to use them for the burial.
Jìsūn planned to abolish the Middle Army.
Shù Niú said:
“The master originally wished to abolish it.”
A10.5 The Annals of Duke Zhāo, Year Five
A10.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
in the royal first month,
the Middle Army was abolished.
A10.5.2 Chǔ killed its grandee Qū Shēn.
A10.5.3 The Duke went to Jìn.
A10.5.4 In the summer,
Móuyí of Jǔ came as a refugee with Móulóu, Fáng,
and Zī.
A10.5.5 In the autumn, in the seventh month,
the Duke arrived from Jìn.
A10.5.6 On the day wùchén,
Shū Gōng led an army and defeated the Jǔ army at Fènquán.
A10.5.7 The Earl of Qín died.
A10.5.8 In the winter,
the Viscount of Chǔ,
the Marquis of Cài,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Baron of Xǔ,
the Viscount of Dùn,
the Viscount of Shěn,
the people of Xú,
and the people of Yuè invaded Wú.
B10.5 The Zǔo Commentary on Duke Zhāo, Year Five
B10.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
in the royal first month,
the Central Army was disbanded,
which was done to degrade the ducal house.
The Central Army was dismantled at the residence of the Shī clan
and the process was completed at the residence of the Zāng clan.
Formerly, when the Central Army was first created,
the ducal house was divided into three parts,
and each of the three families had one of them.
The Jì clan took all the levies from their portion;
the Shūsūn clan treated the sons and younger brothers of the people as their own servants;
and the Mèng clan took half of the levies from theirs.
When it came to its disbandment,
the ducal house was divided into four parts;
the Jì clan selected two parts,
while the other two masters each took one.
They all took all the levies from their portions
and presented a contribution to the Duke.
A letter was sent through Dù Xiè to report this at the funeral hall,
saying:
"You, sir, originally wished to dismantle the Central Army.
Since it has now been dismantled,
we therefore report it to you."
Dù Xiè said:
"The master precisely did not wish to dismantle it;
therefore he made a covenant at Xīhóng
and an imprecation at Wǔfù zhī Qú."
He took the letter and threw it away,
then led the officers in wailing for him.
Shūzhòngzǐ said to Jìsūn:
"Dài received a command from Master Shūsūn, which said:
'Bury the one who died in his prime from the West Gate.'"
Jìsūn gave the order to Dù Xiè.
Dù Xiè said:
"The funeral of a minister starts from the court;
such is the ritual of Lǔ.
You, sir, are in charge of the state's government;
you have not changed the rituals, yet you would move this one?
The various officials fear death
and do not dare to act on their own."
After the burial was over, he went into exile.
Zhòng arrived from Qí,
and Jìsūn wished to establish him as the heir.
Nán Yí said:
"If the Shūsūn clan is strong,
then the Jì clan will be weak.
Their house is indeed in disorder;
if you do not involve yourself in it,
would that not be acceptable?"
Nán Yí sent the people of the capital to assist Shù Niú in attacking him in the courtyard of the Great Treasury.
The palace attendants shot at him;
he was hit in the eye and died.
Shù Niú took thirty cities on the eastern border to give to Nán Yí.
Zhāozǐ took his position,
and assembled the members of his house,
saying:
"Shù Niú brought calamity to the Shūsūn clan,
caused great disorder to follow,
killed the legitimate heir and established a concubine's son.
Furthermore, he carved up the cities,
intending to use them to seek pardon for his crimes.
No crime is greater than this.
He must be killed immediately!"
Shù Niú was afraid
and fled to Qí.
The sons of Mèng and Zhòng killed him outside the Sāiguān pass.
They threw his head onto the thorns of Níngfēng.
Zhòngní said:
"The fact that Shūsūn Zhāozǐ did not reward those who had done him private service
is truly exceptional.
Zhōu Rèn had a saying:
'One who governs does not reward private service
and does not punish out of private grudges.'
The *Shī* says:
'When one's virtuous conduct is great,
the four states will follow it.'"
Formerly,
when Mùzǐ was born,
Zhuāngshú used the *Zhōu Yì* to divine it.
He encountered *Míngyí* changing to *Qiān* and showed it to the diviner Bǔ Chǔqiū.
Chǔqiū said:
"This child will go abroad
and return to perform your sacrifices.
Because of a slanderer he will be admitted;
his name will be Niú;
and in the end, he will die of starvation.
*Míngyí*
represents the sun.
The number of the sun is ten,
thus there are ten times of day,
which also correspond to ten positions.
From the King downward,
the second is the Duke, and the third is the Minister.
The sun rises through their midst;
the time of the morning meal is the second position,
and the time of dawn is the third position.
*Míngyí* changing to *Qiān*
signifies light that is not yet fully bright;
does it not correspond to the dawn?
Therefore it says
'he will perform your sacrifices'.
The sun in *Qiān*
corresponds to a bird;
therefore it says
'the brightness is hidden in flight'.
The light is not yet fully bright,
so it says
'it droops its wings'.
It symbolizes the movement of the sun,
so it says
'the superior man is on the move'.
Corresponding to the third position at dawn,
so it says
'for three days he does not eat'.
*Lí*
is fire;
*Gèn*
is mountain.
*Lí* being fire,
the fire burns the mountain,
and the mountain is destroyed.
Among people, this corresponds to speech.
Destroyed speech is slander;
therefore it says:
'There is a place to go.
The host has something to say.'
The words spoken must be slander.
Pure *Lí* represents an ox.
When the world is in disorder, slander prevails;
the one who prevails will come through *Lí*,
therefore it says
'his name will be Niú'.
In *Qiān*, there is insufficiency;
in flight, one does not soar;
in drooping, one is not steep;
in wings, one is not broad.
Therefore it says,
'Will he be your successor?'
You, sir,
are a secondary minister,
but your lineage will somewhat fail to reach the end."
B10.5.2 The Viscount of Chǔ believed Qū Shēn was colluding with Wú,
so he killed him.
He appointed Qū Shēng as Mò'áo,
and sent him with the Chancellor Zǐdàng to Jìn to fetch a bride.
They passed through Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng hosted Zǐdàng at Fàn,
and hosted Qū Shēng at Tùshì.
The Marquis of Jìn escorted the lady to Xíngqiū.
Zǐchǎn assisted the Earl of Zhèng to meet the Marquis of Jìn at Xíngqiū.
B10.5.3 The Duke went to Jìn.
From the welcome in the suburbs to the presentation of gifts,
he did not fail in any point of ceremony.
The Marquis of Jìn said to Nǚ Shūqí:
"Is the Marquis of Lǔ not excellent at ritual?"
He replied: "How does the Marquis of Lǔ know ritual?"
The Marquis said:
"Why?
From the welcome in the suburbs to the presentation of gifts,
there was nothing in the ceremonies that he contravened; for what reason do you say he does not know it?"
He replied: "Those are ceremonies;
they cannot be called ritual.
Ritual
is that by which one preserves one's state,
carries out one's administrative orders,
and does not lose one's people.
Now administrative orders are in the hands of the private families,
and he cannot reclaim them.
He has Zǐjiā Jī,
but cannot use him.
He has violated the covenants with the great states
and oppressed small states.
He benefits from others' difficulties
and is unaware of his own vulnerable situation.
The ducal house is divided into four,
and the people eat from others.
Their thoughts are not on the Duke,
and he does not plan for the end.
Being a ruler of a state,
when calamity is about to reach his person,
he does not worry about his position.
The substance and details of ritual are found in these things,
yet he fussily practices ceremonies with excessive urgency.
To say he is excellent at ritual,
is that not far from the truth?"
The superior man said that Shū Hóu on this occasion truly knew ritual.
B10.5.4 Hán Xuānzǐ of Jìn went to Chǔ to escort the lady,
and Shū Xiàng served as his assistant.
Zǐpí and Zǐdàshū of Zhèng hosted them at Suǒshì.
Dàshū said to Shū Xiàng:
"The King of Chǔ is excessively arrogant;
you should be on your guard against him!"
Shū Xiàng said:
"His extravagance is already excessive;
it is a disaster for his own person,
how can it reach others?
If we offer our silks and tokens,
and are cautious in our dignified demeanor;
if we maintain it with trustworthiness,
and practice it with ritual propriety;
if we are respectful at the beginning and mindful of the end,
in the end, nothing will fail to be reciprocated.
If we follow without losing decorum,
and show respect without losing dignity;
if we guide him with instructive words,
and present him with old laws,
and verify them with the former kings,
and measure them by the standards of the two states,
even if he is extravagant,
what can he do to us?"
They reached Chǔ.
The Viscount of Chǔ held court for his grandees,
and said:
"Jìn
is our enemy.
If I can have my way with them,
I shall have no worries about anything else.
Now, those who have come
are a high minister and a high grandee.
If I make Hán Qǐ a gatekeeper,
and make Yángshé Xì a palace eunuch,
it would be enough to humiliate Jìn,
and I would have my way.
Is this possible?"
None of the grandees replied.
Wěi Qǐqiáng said:
"It is possible.
If you have the preparations for it,
for what reason would it be impossible?
To humiliate an ordinary man requires preparation,
how much more so to humiliate a state?
For this reason, the sage kings strove to practice ritual propriety,
and did not seek to humiliate others.
In court visits and missions, there are guī tablets;
in offerings and sightings, there are zhāng tablets;
small states report on their duties,
great states inspect achievements.
Low tables are set out but not leaned upon;
cups are filled but not drunk;
at banquets, there are fine gifts;
at meals, there are accompanying tripods;
upon entering, there are greetings in the outskirts;
upon departing, there are parting gifts;
this is the perfection of ritual.
When a state falls,
it is because it has lost the Way,
then disaster and disorder arise.
In the campaign of Chéngpú,
Jìn had no preparations against Chǔ,
and so was defeated at Bì.
In the campaign of Bì,
Chǔ had no preparations against Jìn,
and so was defeated at Yān.
Since Yān,
Jìn has not lost its preparedness,
and has added ritual propriety to it,
and reinforced it with harmony;
therefore Chǔ has been unable to retaliate,
and has sought closeness with them.
Having obtained a marriage alliance,
yet you wish to humiliate them,
to invite enmity and hostility;
what preparations do you have for this,
and who will take the lead in this?
If there are such people,
then humiliating them is fine.
If there are none,
Your Lordship should consider it.
As for Jìn serving Your Lordship,
I, your servant, say it is satisfactory:
they sought the lords and they came in crowds;
they sought a marriage and presented a daughter,
their lord personally escorted her,
and a high minister and a high grandee delivered her.
If you still wish to humiliate them,
Your Lordship must also have preparations.
Otherwise,
what then?
Below Hán Qǐ,
there are Zhào Chéng, Zhōngháng Wú, Wèi Shū, Fàn Yāng, and Zhì Yíng;
below Yángshé Xì,
there are Qí Wǔ, Zhāng Tì, Jí Tán, Nǚ Qí,
Liáng Bǐng, Zhāng Gé, Fǔ Lù, and Miáo Bènhuáng,
all are the elite of the lords.
Hán Xiāng is the grandee of the ducal clan,
Hán Xū has received orders and is serving as an envoy;
Jī Xiāng, Xíng Dài, Shū Qín,
Shū Jiāo, and Zǐ Yǔ,
are all from great houses.
The Hán family levies taxes from seven cities,
all of which are established districts.
The four branches of the Yángshé family
are all powerful houses.
If the people of Jìn lose Hán Qǐ and Yáng Xì,
five ministers
and eight grandees will assist Hán Xū and Yáng Shí;
relying on their ten houses and nine districts,
with nine hundred war chariots,
and the remaining forty districts,
leaving behind four thousand to guard,
they will exert their martial wrath
to avenge their great humiliation.
Bó Huá will plan it,
Zhōngháng Bó and Wèi Shū will lead them;
it is certain they will succeed.
Your Lordship will exchange kinship for resentment,
truly lacking ritual to invite enemies,
and yet not having preparations;
sending your ministers to provide them as prey
to satisfy Your Lordship's heart—
why would that not be possible?"
The King said:
"It is my mistake;
let the grandees not be humiliated."
He generously treated Hán Zǐ with ritual propriety.
The King wanted to overawe Shū Xiàng with things he did not know,
but he could not,
and also treated him with generous ritual propriety.
When Hán Qǐ returned,
the Earl of Zhèng greeted him at Yǔ.
He declined and did not dare to see him;
this was ritual propriety.
B10.5.5 Rǎn Hǔ of Zhèng went to Qí,
to marry into the Zǐwěi clan.
Yàn Zǐ saw him frequently.
Chén Huánzǐ asked the reason.
He replied:
"One who can employ good men
is a master of the people."
B10.5.6 In the summer,
Móu Yí of Jǔ came to flee with Móulóu, Fáng, and Zī.
Móu Yí was not a high minister, yet he was recorded,
because of the value of the territory.
The people of Jǔ appealed to Jìn;
the Marquis of Jìn wanted to detain the Duke.
Fàn Xiànzǐ said:
"This cannot be.
If someone comes to court and you seize him,
that is entrapment;
if you do not punish with an army,
but use entrapment to achieve it,
that is laziness.
To be the leader of the alliance and commit these two acts,
would that not be improper?
Please let him return,
and later punish him with an army."
So he let the Duke return.
In the autumn, the seventh month,
the Duke arrived from Jìn.
B10.5.7 The people of Jǔ came to attack,
but did not make preparations.
On the day wùchén,
Shū Gōng defeated them at Fénquán,
while Jǔ had not yet deployed its ranks.
B10.5.8 In the winter, the tenth month,
the Viscount of Chǔ led the lords and the Eastern Yí to attack Wú,
to retaliate for the campaigns of Jí, Lì, and Má.
Wěi Shè met them at Xiàruì with the army of Fányáng.
Cháng Shòuguò, a grandee of Yuè, led an army to meet the Viscount of Chǔ at Suǒ.
Hearing that the Wú army had come out,
Wěi Qǐqiáng led an army to follow them,
but because they were hurried and did not make preparations,
the people of Wú defeated them at Què’àn.
The Viscount of Chǔ reached Luóruì by post-horse.
The Viscount of Wú sent his younger brother Juéyóu to present gifts to the army;
the people of Chǔ seized him,
intending to use his blood to consecrate a drum.
The King sent someone to question him,
saying:
"Did your divination for coming here say it was auspicious?"
He replied:
"Auspicious.
My ruler heard that Your Lordship was going to exercise his troops in our humble territory,
and divined it with the state tortoise,
saying:
'I shall immediately send someone to present gifts to the army,
requesting to go and observe whether the King's anger is swift or slow,
so that we may make preparations;
may we be able to know this!'
The tortoise shell's cracks reported it as auspicious,
saying:
'We can know it.'
If Your Lordship had joyfully and kindly received the envoy,
it would have increased the relaxation and idleness of my humble territory,
and we would have forgotten our deaths;
our destruction would have been imminent.
Now Your Lordship is roused with thunderous and lightning-like fury,
cruelly seizing the envoy
to consecrate the drum;
thus Wú knows what to prepare for."
"Although our humble state is weak,
if we repair and complete our defenses early,
perhaps we can give our army rest.
To have preparation for both difficulty and ease
can be called auspicious.
Furthermore, it is the state altars of Wú that are being divined upon;
how could it be for one person alone?
If you use your servant to smear the blood of a victim on the war drums,
and our humble state knows to prepare
so as to guard against the unforeseen,
for that to be auspicious,
what could be greater?
Regarding the state's protective tortoises,
for what matter would they not be used for divination?
One result is good, another is bad.
Who can withstand it?
The omen of Chéngpú
had its recompense at Bì.
In this current campaign,
how could there not be a desire for recompense?"
Thereupon, he did not kill him.
The Chǔ army crossed at Luónuì,
Shěn Yǐn Chì met with the Viscount of Chǔ,
and they camped at Làishān.
Wěi Shè led the army of Fányáng to first enter Nánhuái,
and the Chǔ army followed them
as far as Rǔqīng.
Wú could not be entered.
The Viscount of Chǔ then reviewed his troops at Shānjī Mountain.
In this campaign,
Wú had prepared its defenses early,
so Chǔ returned without success,
going back with Jué Yóu.
The Viscount of Chǔ feared Wú,
and sent Shěn Yǐn Shè to await orders at Cháo,
and Wěi Qǐ Qiáng to await orders at Yúlóu,
which was in accordance with ritual.
B10.5.9 The younger brother of the Earl of Qín returned to Qín
because Duke Jǐng had died.
A10.6 The Classic of the Sixth Year of Duke Zhāo
A10.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
in the royal first month,
Yì Gū, Earl of Qǐ, died.
A10.6.2 Duke Jǐng of Qín was buried.
A10.6.3 In the summer,
Jì Sūn Sù went to Jìn.
A10.6.4 Duke Wén of Qǐ was buried.
A10.6.5 Huá Hé Bǐ of Sòng fled to Wèi.
A10.6.6 In the autumn, the ninth month,
the great rain sacrifice was performed.
A10.6.7 Wěi Bà of Chǔ led an army to attack Wú.
A10.6.8 In the winter,
Shū Gōng went to Chǔ.
A10.6.9 The Marquis of Qí attacked Běiyàn.
B10.6 The Commentary on the Sixth Year of Duke Zhāo
B10.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
in the royal first month,
Duke Wén of Qǐ died.
Condolences were offered as among covenanted allies,
which was in accordance with ritual.
B10.6.2 Great officers went to Qín
for the burial of Duke Jǐng,
which was in accordance with ritual.
B10.6.3 In the third month,
the people of Zhèng cast the penal books.
Shū Xiàng sent a letter to Zǐ Chǎn,
which said:
"At first I had expectations for you,
but now it is over.
Anciently, the former kings deliberated on matters to make regulations
and did not create penal laws,
fearing that the people would have a contentious mind.
Yet as they still could not be restrained,
therefore they fenced them with righteousness,
corrected them with administration,
guided them with ritual,
guarded them with good faith,
and upheld them with benevolence.
They established emoluments and ranks
to encourage their following;
they strictly applied punishments and penalties
to awe them against excess.
Fearing that this was not enough,
they therefore instructed them with loyalty,
urged them with conduct,
taught them with diligence,
employed them with harmony,
oversaw them with respect,
governed them with strength,
and decided for them with firmness.
Still, they sought sagacious and wise superiors, clear-sighted and observant officials,
loyal and trustworthy heads, and kind and generous teachers.
Only then could the people be employed
without calamity or disorder arising.
When the people know there are laws,
they lose their awe for those above.
They all have a contentious mind
and appeal to the written books,
hoping to succeed by a lucky stroke;
then it can no longer be managed.
When the Xià dynasty had disordered governance,
they created the 'Punishments of Yǔ';
when the Shāng dynasty had disordered governance,
they created the 'Punishments of Tāng';
when the Zhōu dynasty had disordered governance,
they created the 'Nine Punishments'.
The rise of these three sets of laws
all occurred in declining ages.
Now you, sir, assist the state of Zhèng;
you have made boundaries and ditches,
established policies that invite slander,
created the three-fold laws,
and cast the penal books.
Intending thereby to pacify the people,
is that not indeed difficult?
The Book of Odes says:
'Model yourself on the virtue of King Wén,
and daily pacify the four quarters.'
It also says:
'Model yourself on King Wén,
and the myriad states will have confidence.'
In such a case,
what need is there for penal laws?
Once the people know the points of contention,
they will abandon ritual and appeal to the books.
Even for the tip of a needle or a knife,
they will contend to the end.
Chaotic lawsuits will become more numerous,
and bribery will be practiced everywhere.
By the end of your generation,
will Zhèng not be ruined?
I, Bì, have heard:
'When a state is about to perish,
it must have many regulations.'
Is this not what it refers to?"
Zǐ Chǎn sent a reply saying:
"As for your words, sir, I, Qiáo, am untalented
and cannot reach to the sons and grandsons;
I do this to save the present age.
Since I cannot follow your command,
how would I dare to forget your great kindness!"
Shì Wén Bó said:
"The fire star has appeared;
will Zhèng have a fire?
Before the fire star had emerged,
they used fire to cast the vessels of punishment
and stored the laws of contention within them.
If the fire takes this as an image,
how could there not be a fire?"
B10.6.4 In the summer,
Jì Sūn Sù went to Jìn
to give thanks for the fields of Jǔ.
The Marquis of Jìn entertained him
with extra sacrificial baskets.
Wǔ Zǐ withdrew
and sent a messenger to report, saying:
"When a small state serves a large state,
if it escapes punishment,
it does not dare to seek gifts.
To receive a gift does not exceed three offerings.
Now there are extra platters;
your humble servant cannot bear them;
would this not be a transgression?"
Hán Xuān Zǐ said:
"Our lowly ruler did this to show his joy."
He replied:
"Our lowly ruler would not yet dare to do so,
how much less your humble servant,
who is your Lord's subordinate.
How would I dare to hear of an extra gift?"
He firmly requested the removal of the extras,
and only then completed the ceremony.
The people of Jìn considered him to understand ritual, and they valued material goods.
B10.6.5 Liǔ, a servant of Sòng, was favored;
the Crown Prince Zuǒ hated him.
Huá Hé Bǐ said:
"I will kill him."
Liǔ heard of this,
and thereupon dug a pit, used a sacrificial victim, buried a document,
and reported to the Duke, saying:
"Hé Bǐ is going to bring in the clans of the exiled,
and has already made a covenant at the north suburb."
The Duke sent someone to watch him,
and there he was,
and so he drove out Huà Hé-bǐ.
Hé-bǐ fled to Wèi.
Thereupon Huà Hái wanted to replace the Yòu Shī,
so he allied with the eunuch Sìrén Liǔ,
who followed and provided evidence for it,
saying:
“I have heard of this for a long time.”
The Duke made him replace him.
He visited the Zuǒ Shī,
and the Zuǒ Shī said:
“You, sir, will surely perish.
You have lost your ancestral lineage;
what do you have to do with others?
What do others have to do with you?
The *Shī* says:
‘The lineage head is the city wall;
do not let the wall be destroyed;
do not let loneliness cause fear.’
You should be afraid!”
B10.6.6 In the sixth month, on the day bǐngxū,
a fire occurred in Zhèng.
B10.6.7 The Prince of Chǔ, Qìjí, went to Jìn,
to return the visit of Hán Zǐ.
Passing through Zhèng,
Zhèng’s Hǎn Hǔ, Gōngsūn Qiáo, and Yóu Jí
followed the Zhèng Bó to greet him at Zhā,
but he declined and did not dare to see them.
They insisted,
and he saw them.
He saw them as if he were seeing the King.
He used his eight chariot horses for a private meeting.
He saw Zǐpí as a Shàngqīng,
using six horses;
he saw Zǐchǎn using four horses;
he saw Zǐtàishū using two horses.
He forbade grazing, gathering fuel, or cutting wood;
they did not enter the fields,
did not chop trees,
did not pick cultivated plants,
did not remove thatch from houses,
and did not forcefully beg.
He swore an oath, saying:
“If anyone violates these orders,
a gentleman shall be dismissed,
and a commoner shall be degraded!”
At his lodgings, he did not commit violence;
the host was not troubled by the guest.
Going and coming back in this manner,
the three ministers of Zhèng all knew he would become King.
When Hán Xuānzǐ went to Chǔ,
the people of Chǔ did not welcome him.
When Prince Qìjí reached the border of Jìn,
the Marquis of Jìn was also going to not welcome him.
Shū Xiàng said:
“Chǔ is perverse;
we are upright.
Why should we imitate perversity?
The *Shī* says:
‘That which you teach,
the people will all imitate.’
Let them follow us, that is all;
why use and imitate the perversity of others?
The *Shū* says:
‘The sage makes the pattern.’
Would it not be better to take good people as a pattern
than to take the perversity of others as a pattern?
If an ordinary man does good,
the people still take him as a pattern;
how much more so for the ruler of a state?”
The Marquis of Jìn was pleased
and thus welcomed him.
B10.6.8 In the autumn, in the ninth month,
the great sacrifice for rain was held,
because of a drought.
B10.6.9 Xú Yíchǔ paid a visit to Chǔ;
the Viscount of Chǔ seized him;
he escaped and returned.
Fearing he would rebel,
he sent Wěi Xiè to attack Xú.
The people of Wú rescued them.
The Lìngyǐn Zǐdàng led the army to attack Wú,
stationed the army at Yùzhāng,
and then halted at Gānxī.
The people of Wú defeated his army at Fángzhōng
and captured the Gōngjiùyǐn Qìjí.
Zǐdàng shifted the blame to Wěi Xiè and killed him.
B10.6.10 In the winter,
Shū Gōng went to Chǔ
to pay a visit and offer condolences for the defeat.
B10.6.11 In the eleventh month,
the Marquis of Qí went to Jìn
to request an attack on Běi Yàn.
Shì Gài and Shì Yǎng welcomed him at the Hé River;
this was in accordance with ritual.
The Marquis of Jìn granted it.
In the twelfth month,
the Marquis of Qí then attacked Běi Yàn,
intending to restore Jiǎn Gōng.
Yànzǐ said:
“He will not enter.
Yàn already has a ruler,
and the people are not divided.
Our ruler is greedy for bribes,
and those around him are flatterers;
to undertake a great matter without good faith
has never been possible.”
A10.7 The Annals of the Seventh Year of Zhāo Gōng
A10.7.1 In the spring of the seventh year,
in the royal first month,
peace was made with Qí.
A10.7.2 In the third month,
the Duke went to Chǔ.
A10.7.3 Shūsūn Ruò went to Qí to preside over a covenant.
A10.7.4 In the summer, in the fourth month, on the first day of the month, jiǎchén,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A10.7.5 In the autumn, in the eighth month, on the day wùchén,
È, the Marquis of Wèi, died.
A10.7.6 In the ninth month,
the Duke arrived from Chǔ.
A10.7.7 In the winter, in the eleventh month, on the day guǐwèi,
Jìsūn Sù died.
A10.7.8 In the twelfth month, on the day guǐhài,
Xiāng Gōng of Wèi was buried.
B10.7 The Commentary on the Seventh Year of Zhāo Gōng
B10.7.1 In the spring of the seventh year,
in the royal first month,
peace was made with Qí;
Qí had requested it.
On the day guǐsì,
the Marquis of Qí halted at Guó.
The people of Yàn sued for peace,
saying:
“Our humble city knows its crime;
how could we dare not obey your commands?
We request to use the precious vessels of our former rulers to apologize for our offense.”
Gōngsūn Xī said:
“Accept their submission and withdraw,
then wait for a rift and act;
that will do.”
In the second month, on the day wùwǔ,
they made a covenant at Rúshàng.
The people of Yàn returned Yàn Jī
and gave bribes of jasper jars, jade boxes, and jade-eared cups.
They returned without having achieved their goal.
B10.7.2 When the Viscount of Chǔ was the Lìngyǐn,
he used the king’s banners for hunting.
The Yùyǐn Wúyǔ cut them down,
saying:
“In one state, there cannot be two kings;
who could endure that?”
When he ascended the throne,
he built the Zhānghuá Palace
and filled it by taking in fugitives.
A gatekeeper of Wúyǔ fled into it.
Wúyǔ seized him.
The officials would not allow it,
saying:
“To seize a person in the king’s palace
is a great crime.”
They seized him and reported it to the King.
The King was about to drink wine.
Wúyǔ declined, saying:
“The Son of Heaven manages the world;
the feudal lords rectify the borders;
this is the system of old.
Within the borders,
what is not the ruler’s land?
Of those who eat the products of the land,
who is not the ruler’s subject?
Therefore the *Shī* says:
‘Under the vast heaven,
there is no land that is not the king’s;
to the ends of the earth,
there are no people who are not the king’s subjects.’
Heaven has ten suns;
people have ten ranks.
The lower ranks serve the higher,
and the higher ranks provide for the spirits.
Thus the King has the Gōng as subjects;
the Gōng have the Dàfū as subjects;
the Dàfū have the Shì as subjects;
the Shì have the Zào as subjects;
the Zào have the Yú as subjects;
Yú are servants to Lì,
Lì are servants to Liáo,
Liáo are servants to Pǔ,
Pǔ are servants to Tái.
Horses have grooms,
cattle have herdsmen,
to attend to all matters.
Now the officials say:
"Why did you seize a man in the royal palace?"
Where else should he be seized?
The law of Zhōu Wén Wáng says:
"If there is a fugitive,
conduct a thorough search."
This is how he gained the world.
Our former ruler Wén Wáng
established the law of Pǔ Qū,
which says:
"One who hides the thief's equipment
is as guilty as the thief."
This is how you were enfeoffed.
If I follow the officials,
there would be no way to seize runaway servants.
If we let runaways go,
there would be no subordinates or attendants.
Would not the King's affairs be deficient?
Formerly, Wǔ Wáng enumerated the crimes of Zhòu to inform the feudal lords, saying:
"Zhòu is the master of the fugitives of the world,
a gathering place like a deep pool or a thicket."
Therefore, men fought to the death against him.
If the King, beginning to seek the feudal lords, follows the model of Zhòu,
would that not be impermissible?
If we take him according to the laws of the two Wén,
the thief is caught where he is."
The King said:
"Take him and use him as a servant as before.
The thief is a favorite,
so he cannot yet be dealt with."
He then pardoned him.
B10.7.3 Chǔ Zǐ completed the Zhāng Huá zhī Tái
and wished to celebrate its completion with the feudal lords.
The Grand Steward Wěi Qǐ Qiáng said:
"I can get the Lǔ Hóu."
Wěi Qǐ Qiáng came to summon the Duke,
who declined, saying:
"Formerly, our late ruler Chéng Gōng commanded our late Great Officer Yīng Qí, saying:
'I do not forget the friendship of the late rulers;
I will send Hèng Fù to oversee the state of Chǔ,
to settle and soothe its altars of soil and grain,
and to bring peace and tranquility to your people.'
Yīng Qí received this command at Shǔ.
Since receiving and upholding it,
we have not dared to lose or drop it,
but have presented it in our ancestral temple.
Recently, our late ruler Gòng Wáng craned his neck to gaze northward,
hoping for it day and month;
it has been handed down in order,
reaching four kings until today.
The fine favor has not yet arrived,
but only Xiāng Gōng deigned to attend our mourning.
I and my few ministers, with grieving hearts and lost plans,
had no leisure even for our altars of soil and grain,
how much less could we cherish thoughts of your virtue?
Now, if you, my lord, would move your jade footsteps
and deign to see our humble ruler,
gracing the state of Chǔ
to fulfill the service of Shǔ
and bestow your fine favor,
then our humble ruler would have already received your bounty;
what more from Shǔ could we dare to hope for?
The spirits of the late rulers would truly find joy and reliance in it,
not only our humble ruler.
If you do not come,
let me ask for the date of your departure,
and our humble ruler will bring hostage-gifts to meet you at Shǔ,
to request the bounty of the late rulers."
The Duke was about to go
when he dreamed that Xiāng Gōng performed the ancestral sacrifice for a journey.
Zǐ Shèn said:
"The Lord will not complete the journey.
When Xiāng Gōng went to Chǔ,
he dreamed that Zhōu Gōng performed the ancestral sacrifice for his journey.
Now that Xiāng Gōng himself performs the sacrifice,
the Lord should not go."
Zǐ Fú Huì Bó said:
"Go!
The former ruler had never been to Chǔ,
so Zhōu Gōng performed the sacrifice to guide him;
Xiāng Gōng has been to Chǔ,
and thus he performs the sacrifice to guide the Lord.
If you do not go,
where else will you go?"
In the third month,
the Duke went to Chǔ.
Zhèng Bó greeted him at Shī zhī Liáng.
Mèng Xī Zǐ acted as the second,
but he was unable to assist with the rituals.
Upon reaching Chǔ,
he was unable to respond to the greeting in the outskirts.
B10.7.4 In summer, the fourth month, on the day jiǎchén, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
Jìn Hóu asked Shì Wén Bó:
"Who will suffer from this solar eclipse?"
He replied:
"Lǔ and Wèi will suffer for it.
Wèi is large;
Lǔ is small."
The Duke said: "Why?"
He replied: "As it leaves the territory of Wèi and enters the territory of Lǔ,
it is there that the disaster occurs;
Lǔ will truly receive it.
The greatest misfortune will fall upon the ruler of Wèi,
while Lǔ will lose a high minister."
The Duke said:
"What is meant
by what the Shī calls:
'That sun was eclipsed;
how is it not bad?'"
He replied:
"It refers to bad government.
If a state has no government
and does not employ the good,
it brings upon itself the reprimand of disasters from the sun and moon.
Therefore, government cannot but be careful.
It should focus on three things:
first, selecting people;
second, following the people;
third, acting according to the season."
B10.7.5 The people of Jìn came to manage the fields of Qǐ.
Jì Sūn was going to give them Chéng.
Xiè Xī was guarding it for Mèng Sūn
and would not agree,
saying:
"People have a saying:
'Even with the wisdom of one who carries a pitcher,
not to yield one's office to others
is the ritual.'
You are following the Lord,
while I, the guarding official, lose a city.
Even you would have suspicions about me."
Jì Sūn said:
"The Lord being in Chǔ
is a grievance to Jìn.
If we also do not listen to Jìn,
Lǔ's crime will be heavy.
The Jìn army will surely come,
and I have no way to meet it.
It is better to give it to them.
We will wait for an opening with Jìn and then take it from Qǐ.
I will give you Táo.
When Chéng is returned,
who would dare to possess it?
This way, we get two Chéng.
Lǔ will have no worries,
and Mèng Sūn's cities will increase.
What distresses you about this?"
He declined because there were no mountains,
so Jì Sūn gave him Lái and Zuò.
He then moved to Táo.
The people of Jìn took Chéng for Qǐ.
B10.7.6 Chǔ Zǐ feasted the Duke at the Xīn Tái
and had the one with a long beard act as the assistant.
He presented the Duke with the Dà Qū bow.
Soon after, he regretted it.
Wěi Qǐ Qiáng heard of this
and saw the Duke.
The Duke told him about it,
and he bowed in congratulation.
The Duke said:
He replied:
"Qí and Jìn, Yuè have desired this for a long time.
Our humble ruler had no one suitable to give it to,
so he passed it to you.
You should prepare to defend against these three neighbors
and carefully guard this treasure.
How could I not congratulate you?"
The Duke was afraid
and thus returned it.
B10.7.7 Zǐ Chǎn of Zhèng went on a mission to Jìn.
Jìn Hóu was ill.
Hán Xuān Zǐ met the guest
and spoke privately to him,
saying:
"Our humble ruler has been ill in bed
for three months now.
We have offered sacrifices to all the spirits of the mountains and rivers,
but it only gets worse without healing.
Now he dreamed of a yellow bear entering the door of his bedchamber.
What kind of malicious ghost is this?"
He replied:
"With your ruler's intelligence
and you managing the great affairs of state,
what malice could there be?
Formerly, Yáo executed Gǔn at Yǔ Shān;
his spirit transformed into a yellow bear
and entered the Yǔ Yuān."
It was truly the Xiàjiāo,
which the three dynasties sacrificed to.
Jìn being the leader of the alliance,
perhaps they have not yet sacrificed to it!"
Hán Zǐ sacrificed at the Xiàjiāo.
When the Marquis of Jìn (Jìn Hóu) had a respite from illness,
he bestowed two square tripods from Jǔ upon Zǐchǎn.
Zǐchǎn, on behalf of Fēng Shī, returned the lands of Zhōu to Hán Xuānzǐ,
saying:
"In the past, the ruler considered the late Gōngsūn Duàn capable of fulfilling his duties,
and thus bestowed the lands of Zhōu upon him.
Now he has died young without further blessing,
and did not manage to enjoy the ruler's virtue for long.
His son does not dare to keep them,
nor does he dare to inform the ruler directly,
so he privately presents them to you."
Xuānzǐ declined.
Zǐchǎn said:
"The ancients had a saying:
'When the father splits the firewood,
the son might not be able to carry the load.'
Shī is afraid he cannot even handle the emoluments of his ancestors,
how much less could he handle the gift of a great state?
Even if you, sir, are in power and allow it,
if later people should have disputes over the borders,
our humble state would incur blame,
and the Fēng lineage would suffer great punishment.
By you taking Zhōu,
you exempt our humble state from blame,
and establish the Fēng lineage.
I venture to make this request."
Xuānzǐ accepted them,
and reported it to the Marquis of Jìn (Jìn Hóu).
The Marquis of Jìn gave them to Xuānzǐ.
Because Xuānzǐ had previously spoken [against taking them],
he felt uneasy about possessing them,
so he exchanged them for Yuán County with Lè Dàxīn.
The people of Zhèng were alarming each other because of Bó Yǒu,
saying:
"Bó Yǒu has arrived!"
Then they would all run,
not knowing where they were going.
In the second month of the year the penal laws were cast,
someone dreamed that Bó Yǒu was walking in armor
and said:
"On the Rénzǐ day,
I shall kill Dài.
Next year on the Rányín day,
I shall also kill Duàn."
When the Rénzǐ day arrived,
Sì Dài died,
and the people of the state became even more afraid.
In the month when peace was made between Qí and Yān,
on the Rányín day,
Gōngsūn Duàn died,
and the people of the state became yet more afraid.
The following month,
Zǐchǎn established Gōngsūn Xiè and Liáng Zhǐ [as heirs to the lineage] to soothe the spirit,
and then it stopped.
Zǐ Dàshū asked the reason,
and Zǐchǎn said:
"When a ghost has a place to return to,
it does not become a malevolent spirit.
I have provided a place for him to return."
Dàshū said: "What was the purpose of [establishing] Gōngsūn Xiè?"
Zǐchǎn said: "To please the people.
To lack righteousness in one's person and yet seek to please,
one must reverse some administrative actions
to gain favor.
Without favor,
there is no trust;
without trust,
the people will not follow."
When Zǐchǎn went to Jìn,
Zhào Jǐngzǐ asked him,
saying:
"Can Bó Yǒu still act as a ghost?"
Zǐchǎn said: "He can.
When a person is first born, the transformation is called the pò.
Once the pò is produced,
the yang element is called the hún.
If one uses the essence of things in great quantity,
then the hún and pò are strong.
Therefore, there is brightness of essence reaching even to the spiritual and divine.
Even an ordinary man or woman who dies a violent death
can have their hún and pò still cling to people
as a malevolent haunting.
How much more so for Liáng Xiāo,
a descendant of our former ruler Mù Gōng,
the grandson of Zǐliáng,
and the son of Zǐ’ěr?
He was a minister of our humble state
and his family had been in government for three generations.
Although Zhèng is not grand,
yet the proverb says:
'A tiny state,'
yet for three generations his family held the handle of its government.
His use of things was vast,
and his intake of essence was much.
His clan was also large,
and that which he could lean upon was substantial.
Having died a violent death,
that he can act as a ghost
is indeed appropriate!"
The kinsmen of Zǐpí drank wine without moderation;
therefore, the Mǎshī Shì and the Zǐpí Shì had mutual animosity.
In the month when the Qí army returned from Yān,
Hǎn Shuò killed Hǎn Tuí.
Hǎn Shuò fled to Jìn.
Hán Xuānzǐ asked Zǐchǎn about his rank.
Zǐchǎn said:
"A runaway servant of a ruler,
if he is lucky enough to be tolerated and escape death,
how would he dare to choose his rank?
When a minister flees,
he follows the rank of a Great Officer;
a criminal is demoted according to his crime;
this is the ancient regulation.
Shuò, in our humble state,
was a secondary Great Officer.
His office
was the Master of Horses (Mǎshī).
Having incurred guilt and fled,
let the person in power place him as he sees fit.
If he can avoid death,
the favor is already great;
how could he dare to request a rank?"
Xuānzǐ, because of Zǐchǎn's cleverness,
made him follow the rank of a favored Great Officer.
In the autumn, in the eighth month,
Wèi Xiāng Gōng died.
The Great Officers of Jìn said to Fàn Xiànzǐ:
"Wèi has served Jìn harmoniously,
yet Jìn has not treated it with ritual.
We protected its rebels and took its land;
therefore, the feudal lords have become alienated.
The Classic of Poetry (Shī) says:
'The wagtail is on the plain,
brothers are in urgent distress.'
It also says:
'The terrors of death and burial,
brothers feel great concern.'
When brothers are not in harmony,
they are not condoled with;
how much more so for distant people—
who would dare to submit to us?
Now if we also do not treat the successor of Wèi with ritual,
Wèi will surely rebel against us,
and this is cutting ourselves off from the feudal lords."
Xiànzǐ reported this to Hán Xuānzǐ.
Xuānzǐ was pleased
and sent Xiànzǐ to Wèi to offer condolences
and to return the lands of Qī.
Wèi Qí’è announced the funeral to Zhōu
and requested the king's command.
The King sent Shàn Jiǎngōng to Wèi to offer condolences
and to posthumously confer a command on Xiāng Gōng, saying:
"Uncle, you have ascended in reverence
to be by the sides of my former kings,
to assist in serving the Lord on High (Shàngdì).
How could I dare forget Gāo Yǔ and Yà Yǔ?"
In the ninth month,
the Duke (Gōng) arrived from Chǔ.
Mèng Xīzǐ was distressed that he was not able to perform rituals,
so he studied them,
following anyone who was capable in ritual.
When he was about to die,
he summoned his Great Officers
and said:
"Ritual
is the trunk of a person.
Without ritual,
there is no way to establish oneself.
I have heard there will be a man of attainment named Kǒng Qiū,
who is a descendant of a sage,
but whose lineage was extinguished in Sòng.
His ancestor Fùfù Hé had Sòng but gave it to Lì Gōng.
When it came to Zhèng Kǎofù,
he assisted Dài, Wǔ, and Xuān.
With three appointments, he became increasingly respectful.
Therefore, his tripod inscription said:
'At the first appointment, I bowed my head;
at the second appointment, I bent my back;
at the third appointment, I stooped low.
I walked along the wall,
and yet no one dared to insult me.
I cooked thick congee in this,
and thin congee in this,
to feed my mouth.'
His respectfulness was like this.
Zāngsūn Hé had a saying:
'If a sage who possesses bright virtue
does not come into his era,
his descendants will surely have a man of attainment.'
Now, perhaps that will be Kǒng Qiū!
If I should die,
you must entrust Shuō and Héjì to the Master,
making them serve him
and learn ritual from him,
so as to secure their positions."
Therefore Mèng Yìzǐ and Nángōng Jìngshū served Zhòngní as their teacher.
Zhòngní said:
“One who can rectify their faults
is a Jūnzǐ.
The *Shī* says:
‘The Jūnzǐ is the one to take as a model and to imitate,’
and Mèng Xīzǐ can indeed be modeled and imitated.”
B10.7.13 Duke Xiàn of Shàn abandoned his kinsmen and employed Jī.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the day xīnyǒu,
the clans of Xiāng and Qǐng killed Duke Xiàn and established Duke Chéng.
B10.7.14 In the eleventh month,
Jì Wǔzǐ died.
The Marquis of Jìn said to Bóxiá:
“As for my question regarding the solar eclipse,
the event followed what you said.
Can it be made a regular rule?”
He replied:
“It cannot.
The six things are not the same,
the hearts of the people are not one,
the order of affairs is not of the same kind,
official duties do not follow a single pattern,
they start the same but end differently—
how could there be a constant rule?
The *Shī* says:
‘Some dwell in ease and rest,
while others are haggard in service to the state,’
their ending in difference is like this.”
The Marquis said:
“What are called the six things?”
He replied:
“The year, the seasons, the days, the months, the stars, and the Chén.
These are what is meant.”
The Marquis said:
“Many have spoken to me of the Chén, but none agree.
What is meant by Chén?”
He replied:
“The conjunction of the sun and moon is called Chén;
therefore it is used to denote the days.”
B10.7.15 Lady Jiāng, the wife of Duke Xiāng of Wèi, had no son.
The favorite concubine Zhōu Ài gave birth to Mèng Zhí.
Kǒng Chéngzǐ dreamed that Kāngshū said to him:
“Establish Yuán.
I shall make Yǔ, the grandson of Jī, and Shǐ Gǒu assist him.”
Shǐ Zhāo also dreamed that Kāngshū said to him:
“I shall command your son Gǒu and Yǔ, the great-grandson of Kǒng Zhēngchú, to assist Yuán.”
Shǐ Zhāo saw Chéngzǐ
and told him of the dream;
the dreams coincided.
In the year when Hán Xuānzǐ of Jìn was in charge of government and paid visits to the feudal lords,
Zhōu Ài gave birth to a son,
and named him Yuán.
Mèng Zhí's feet were not good for walking.
Kǒng Chéngzǐ consulted the *Zhōu Yì* by milfoil divination,
saying:
“May Yuán enjoy the state of Wèi
and preside over its altars of soil and grain.”
He encountered *Zhūn*
He also said:
“May I establish Zhí,
and may he be able to bring excellence.”
He encountered *Zhūn* ䷂ changing into *Bǐ*
He showed this to Shǐ Zhāo.
Shǐ Zhāo said:
“‘Supreme success,’
what more is there to doubt?”
Chéngzǐ said: “Does it not refer to the eldest?”
He replied: “Kāngshū named him;
he can be considered the principal one.
Mèng is not a complete man;
he will not be ranked in the ancestral line,
and so cannot be considered the eldest.
Moreover, the line oracle says:
‘Advantageous to establish a lord.’
If the succession were already auspicious,
why ‘establish’?
To ‘establish’ implies he is not the natural successor.
Both hexagrams say this;
you should indeed establish him!
Kāngshū commanded it,
the two hexagrams announced it;
the divination coincides with the dream,
which is what King Wǔ used;
why not follow it?
One with weak feet stays at home.
A lord presides over the altars of soil and grain,
attends the sacrifices,
serves the people,
serves the ghosts and spirits,
and attends meetings and audiences;
how could he just stay at home?
Each follows what is advantageous for them;
is that not also acceptable?”
Therefore Kǒng Chéngzǐ established Duke Líng.
In the twelfth month, on the day guǐhài,
they buried Duke Xiāng of Wèi.
A10.8 *Annals of the Eighth Year of Duke Zhāo*
A10.8.1 In the spring of the eighth year,
Zhāo, the younger brother of the Marquis of Chén, killed the Heir Apparent of Chén, Yǎnshī.
A10.8.2 In summer, in the fourth month, on the day xīnchǒu,
Nì, the Marquis of Chén, died.
A10.8.3 Shū Gōng went to Jìn.
A10.8.4 The people of Chǔ seized the Messenger of Chén, Gān Zhēngshī, and killed him.
A10.8.5 Prince Liú of Chén fled to Zhèng.
A10.8.6 In autumn,
there was a grand hunt at Hóng.
A10.8.7 The people of Chén killed their Grand Master, Prince Guò.
A10.8.8 The great rain sacrifice was performed.
A10.8.9 In winter, in the tenth month, on the day rénwǔ,
the army of Chǔ extinguished Chén.
They seized Prince Zhāo of Chén
and banished him to Yuè.
They killed Kǒng Huàn of Chén.
A10.8.10 They buried Duke Āi of Chén.
B10.8 *Commentary on the Eighth Year of Duke Zhāo*
B10.8.1 In the spring of the eighth year,
a stone spoke in Wèiyú of Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn asked Shī Kuàng:
“For what reason does a stone speak?”
He replied:
“A stone cannot speak;
something must have possessed it.
Otherwise,
the hearing of the people is deluded.
Moreover, your servant has heard it said:
‘When actions are taken out of season,
and resentment and slander stir among the people,
then things that do not normally speak will speak.’
Now the palaces are lofty and extravagant,
the people’s strength is withered and exhausted,
resentment and slander arise together,
and no one can preserve their natural life.
That the stone speaks,
is it not indeed appropriate?”
At that time, the Marquis of Jìn was building the Palace of Sīqí.
Shūxiàng said:
“The words of Zǐyě are those of a Jūnzǐ!
The words of a Jūnzǐ
are trustworthy and have evidence;
therefore resentment is far from his person.
The words of a small man
are fallacious and have no evidence;
therefore resentment and blame reach him.
The *Shī* says:
‘Alas for those who cannot speak!
It is not their tongues that come out,
but their persons that are exhausted.
Blessed are those who can speak,
their clever words flow like a stream,
enabling their persons to dwell in peace.’
Does this not refer to such a case?
Once this palace is completed,
the feudal lords will surely rebel,
and the ruler will surely meet with misfortune.
The Master knew it.”
B10.8.2 Zhèng Jī, the primary wife of Duke Āi of Chén, gave birth to the Mourned Heir Apparent Yǎnshī.
The second wife gave birth to Prince Liú,
and the third wife gave birth to Prince Shèng.
The second wife was a favorite,
and Liú was favored;
he was entrusted to the Minister of Instruction Zhāo and Prince Guò.
Duke Āi had a debilitating illness.
In the third month, on the day jiǎshēn,
Prince Zhāo and Prince Guò killed the Mourned Heir Apparent Yǎnshī and established Prince Liú.
In summer, in the fourth month, on the day xīnhài,
Duke Āi hanged himself.
Gān Zhēngshī went to Chǔ to announce the death
and to report that a ruler had been established.
Prince Shèng appealed the matter to Chǔ.
The people of Chǔ seized and killed him.
Prince Liú fled to Zhèng.
The text records:
“Zhāo, the younger brother of the Marquis of Chén, killed the Heir Apparent of Chén, Yǎnshī,”
indicating the guilt lies with Zhāo.
“The people of Chǔ seized the Messenger of Chén, Gān Zhēngshī, and killed him,”
indicating the guilt does not lie with the Messenger.
B10.8.3 Shū Gōng went to Jìn
to offer congratulations on the Palace of Sīqí.
Yóu Jí assisted the Earl of Zhèng in going to Jìn,
also to offer congratulations on Sīqí.
Shǐ Zhào saw Zǐdàshū,
and said:
“How extreme is their mutual deception!
It is a matter for condolence,
and yet they offer congratulations.”
Zǐ Dàshū said:
"Why offer condolences?
It is not only we who should congratulate [ourselves];
the whole world should truly congratulate [us]."
B10.8.4 In the autumn,
a grand military hunt was held in Hóng.
From Gēnmóu to Shāng and Wèi,
there were a thousand leather-covered chariots.
B10.8.5 In the seventh month, on the day jiǎxū,
Zǐwěi of Qí died.
Zǐqí wished to manage his household.
On the day dīngchǒu,
they killed Liáng Yīng.
In the eighth month, on the day gēngxū,
they expelled Zǐchéng, Zǐgōng, and Zǐjū,
who all came as refugees,
and they established the steward of the Zǐliáng clan.
His followers said:
"The young master is grown,
yet he acts as minister for our house;
he wishes to annex us."
They handed out armor
and were about to attack him.
Chén Huánzǐ was on good terms with Zǐwěi
and also handed out armor
to assist them.
Someone informed Zǐqí,
but Zǐqí did not believe it;
then several people informed him.
As he was about to go,
several more people informed him on the road,
and so he went to the Chén family.
Huánzǐ was about to go out,
but hearing of this he returned,
meeting him in casual dress
and asking for his orders.
He replied:
"I heard the Qiáng clan handed out armor and is about to attack you;
have you heard this?"
He said:
"I have not heard it."
"Why do you not also hand out armor?
Wúyǔ asks to follow you."
Zǐqí said:
"Why would you do that?
They
are but children.
I teach them,
yet fear they will not succeed;
I have also given them favors and rank.
How would I face the ancestors?
Why do you not speak to them instead?
The *Zhōushū* says,
'Be kind to the unkind,
and encourage the unencouraged';
this was how Kāngshū governed so greatly."
Huánzǐ bowed his head to the ground and said:
"With Qǐng and Líng blessing you,
I still have hope."
Thus he reconciled them as before.
B10.8.6 Prince Zhāo of Chén shifted the blame to Prince Guò and killed him.
In the ninth month,
Prince Qìjí of Chǔ led an army escorting Sūn Wú to besiege Chén;
Dài È of Sòng joined him.
In winter, in the eleventh month, on the day rénwǔ,
they extinguished Chén.
The carriage favorite Yuán Kè killed horses and destroyed jades for the burial.
The people of Chǔ were going to kill him,
but he asked to be spared,
and then asked for a private moment.
Having gone privately into a tent,
he put a mourning band on his forehead and escaped.
Chuānfēng Xū was made the Duke of Chén,
with the King saying:
"In the campaign of Chéngjùn, he was not deceitful."
While attending a drinking party with the King,
the King said:
"In the campaign of Chéngjùn,
if you had known I would reach this,
would you have avoided me?"
He replied:
"Had I known my lord would reach this,
I would certainly have fought to the death according to ritual to bring peace to Chǔ."
The Marquis of Jìn asked Historiographer Zhào:
"Will Chén finally perish?"
He replied:
"Not yet."
The Duke said:
He replied:
"Chén is of the lineage of Zhuānxū;
when Jupiter was in Chúnhuǒ,
they were finally extinguished.
Chén will be like that.
Now Jupiter is at the Ford of Xīmù;
it will yet rise again.
Moreover, the Chén clan will gain power in Qí, and only then will Chén finally perish.
From Mù to Gǔsǒu, none disobeyed orders;
Shùn reinforced them with illustrious virtue
and deposited virtue in Suì.
Suì guarded it for generations.
When it came to Húgōng, he was not dissolute;
therefore Zhōu granted him a surname
and had him sacrifice to Emperor Yú.
I have heard that great virtue must be sacrificed to for a hundred generations.
The generations of Yú are not yet finished;
the continuation of the line will be in Qí;
the signs are already present."
A10.9 The Annals of Duke Zhāo, Year Nine
A10.9.1 In the spring of the ninth year,
Shū Gōng met the Viscount of Chǔ in Chén.
A10.9.2 Xǔ moved to Yí.
A10.9.3 In summer, the fourth month,
Chén suffered a fire.
A10.9.4 In autumn,
Zhòngsūn Jué went to Qí.
A10.9.5 In winter,
a park was built at Láng.
B10.9 The Commentary on Duke Zhāo, Year Nine
B10.9.1 In the spring of the ninth year,
Shū Gōng, Huá hài of Sòng, and Yóu Jí of Zhèng,
and Zhào Yǎn of Wèi met with the Viscount of Chǔ in Chén.
B10.9.2 In the second month, on the day gēngshēn,
Prince Qìjí of Chǔ moved Xǔ to Yí,
which was in fact Chéngfù.
He took the lands of Zhōulái and the north of the Huái to increase it,
and Wǔ Jǔ handed the land over to the Baron of Xǔ.
Rán Dān moved the people of Chéngfù to Chén,
increasing their territory with the land west of Yí and Pú.
He moved the people from outside Fāngchéng to Xǔ.
B10.9.3 The people of Gān in Zhōu and Yán Jiā of Jìn disputed the lands of Yán.
Liáng Bǐng and Zhāng Tì of Jìn led the Yīnróng to attack Yǐng.
The King sent Zhān Huánbó to present a statement to Jìn,
saying:
"Since the Xià, because of Hòujì,
Wèi, Dài, Ruì, Qí, and Bì
have been our western lands.
When King Wǔ conquered Shāng,
Púgū and Shāngyǎn
were our eastern lands;
Bā, Pú, Chǔ, and Dèng
were our southern lands;
Sùshèn, Yàn, and Bó
were our northern lands.
What nearby territory is not our fief?
When Wén, Wǔ,
Chéng, and Kāng established their brothers by the same mother
as a fence and screen for Zhōu,
it was also to prevent downfall;
how could they be like a child’s cap,
to be discarded once it is worn out?
Former kings settled the Táowù in the four remote regions
to ward off mountain spirits and demons;
thus the wicked of the Yǔn surname were settled in Guāzhōu.
When your uncle Duke Huì returned from Qín,
he enticed them to come
and let them press upon our Zhī clans
and enter our suburbs and outskirts;
thus the Róng took them.
That the Róng possess the central states,
whose fault is it?
Hòujì established and cultivated the world,
yet now the Róng control it;
is this not a difficult situation?
Uncle, consider it!
My relation to you, uncle,
is like clothing having a cap and crown,
like trees and water having a root and source,
or like people having a leader for counsel.
If you, uncle, tear the cap and destroy the crown,
pull up the root and block the source,
and willfully abandon the leader,
then although there are the Róng and Dí,
what will they care for me, the Solitary Man?"
Shūxiàng said to Xuānzǐ:
"When Duke Wén was hegemon,
did he change anything?
He supported and respected the Son of Heaven
and added to it with reverence.
Since the time of Duke Wén,
there has been a decline in virtue through the generations,
and the royal house of Zhōu has been treated with violence and contempt
to display arrogance.
Is it not fitting that the regional lords are double-minded?
Moreover, the King's words are upright;
you should consider them."
Xuānzǐ was pleased.
The King had a death among his in-laws,
so he sent Zhào Chéng to Zhōu to offer condolences,
and to return the Yán lands along with burial garments,
and to return the captives from Yǐng.
The King also sent Bīn Huá to seize the Grand Master of Gān, Xiāng, to appease Jìn,
and the people of Jìn treated him with courtesy and sent him back.
B10.9.4 In summer, the fourth month,
Chén suffered a fire disaster.
Bì Zào of Zhèng said:
"In five years, Chén shall be restored to its enfeoffment,
and after fifty-two years of being enfeoffed, it will finally perish."
Zǐchǎn asked for the reason.
He replied:
"Chén
belongs to the element of Water;
Fire
is the mate of Water.
And it is the place where Chǔ acts as protector.
Now the Fire star has appeared and burned Chén;
this drives out Chǔ and establishes Chén.
A mate is completed by the number five;
hence I say five years.
When the year-star has five times reached the Chún Huǒ constellation,
then Chén will eventually perish,
and Chǔ will conquer and possess it;
this is the Way of Heaven,
hence I say fifty-two years."
B10.9.5 Xún Yíng of Jìn went to Qí to meet a bride;
as he was returning,
in the sixth month,
he died at Xìyáng.
His body was laid in state in Jiàng,
but not yet buried.
The Lord of Jìn drank wine
and had music.
Tǔ Kuài, the steward of the royal kitchen, hurried in
and requested to assist the Duke’s messengers with the wine vessels;
this was granted.
He then poured wine to give to the musicians,
saying:
"You serve as the ears of the ruler;
you are to manage his hearing.
When the stars are in Zǐ or Mǎo,
these are called 'ill-omened days.'
The ruler cancels banquets and music,
and students leave their tasks,
because of these ill-omened days.
The ruler’s high ministers and assistants
are what are called his 'limbs.'
When a limb is lost,
what pain could be greater than that?
You did not hear of this and played music;
this is being un-hearing."
He then gave wine to the external favorite Bì Shū,
saying:
"You serve as the eyes of the ruler;
you are to manage his vision.
Clothing manifests ritual;
ritual is used to conduct affairs;
affairs have their specific objects;
objects have their proper appearance.
Now the ruler's appearance
does not match the objects;
yet you did not see it;
this is being un-seeing."
He also drank wine himself,
saying:
"Flavors are for circulating the Qì;
Qì is for solidifying the will;
the will is for determining speech;
speech is for issuing orders.
I manage the flavors.
The two attendants failed their offices,
and the ruler did not issue commands;
this is my crime."
The Duke was pleased
and cancelled the wine.
Initially,
the Duke had wanted to abolish the Zhì clan and establish his external favorite;
because of this, he repented and desisted.
In the autumn, the eighth month,
he appointed Xún Lì to assist the Lower Army to show his satisfaction.
B10.9.6 Mèng Xīzǐ went to Qí for a grand mission;
this was in accordance with ritual.
B10.9.7 In winter,
the Láng park was built.
It was recorded
because it was timely.
Jì Píngzǐ wanted it to be completed quickly;
Shúsūn Zhāozǐ said:
"The *Classic of Poetry* says:
'When planning the start, do not be urgent;
the common people will come like children.'
Why use speedy completion
to exhaust the people?
It is fine to have no park;
but without people,
is it acceptable?"
A10.10 *The Classic of Duke Zhāo, Year Ten*
A10.10.1 In the tenth year, spring,
the King's first month.
A10.10.2 In summer,
Luán Shī of Qí came as a refugee.
A10.10.3 In autumn, the seventh month,
Jìsūn Yìrú,
Shú Gōng,
and Zhòngsūn Jué led an army to attack Jǔ.
A10.10.4 On the day *wùzǐ*,
Duke Biāo of Jìn died.
A10.10.5 In the ninth month,
Shúsūn Ruò went to Jìn,
for the burial of Duke Píng of Jìn.
A10.10.6 In the twelfth month, on the day *jiǎzǐ*,
Duke Chéng of Sòng died.
B10.10 *The Commentary on Duke Zhāo, Year Ten*
B10.10.1 In the tenth year, spring,
the King's first month,
a star appeared from Wùnǚ.
Bì Zào of Zhèng said to Zǐchǎn:
"On the *wùzǐ* day of the seventh month,
the ruler of Jìn will die.
Currently, the year is in the Void of Zhuānxū;
the clans of Jiāng and Rèn truly guard that land.
They dwell at the start of that corner,
and an ominous star is there;
it announces it to Yìjiāng.
Yìjiāng was the ancestress of Jìn.
Heaven uses seven as a cycle.
Meeting the Duke on *wùzǐ* to ascend,
the star appeared here;
this is why I predict it."
B10.10.2 The Luán and Gāo clans of the Huì lineage of Qí were both fond of wine;
they trusted their inner quarters and caused much resentment.
They were more powerful than the Chén and Bào clans and hated them.
In summer,
someone told Chén Huánzǐ:
"Zǐqí and Zǐliáng are going to attack Chén and Bào."
They also told the Bào clan.
Huánzǐ put on his armor and went to the Bào clan.
He happened upon Zǐliáng, who was drunk and galloping,
and then saw Wénzǐ,
who had also put on his armor.
They sent someone to observe the two,
and they were both about to drink wine.
Huánzǐ said:
"Though they are untrustworthy,
if they hear I have put on armor,
they will certainly pursue me.
While they are drinking wine,
should we attack them first?"
Chén and Bào being in harmony,
they then attacked the Luán and Gāo clans.
Zǐliáng said:
"If we first secure the Duke,
where can Chén and Bào go?"
So they attacked Hǔmén.
Yàn Píngzhòng stood outside Hǔmén in his official robes.
The four clans called him,
but he did not go to any.
His followers asked:
"Shall we help Chén and Bào?"
He said:
"What good is there in that?"
"Shall we help Luán and Gāo?"
He said: "How would that be better?"
"Then shall we return home?"
He said:
"When the ruler is under attack,
where can one return?"
The Duke summoned him,
and then he entered.
The Duke divined about using Wáng Hēi to lead with the Línggū axe;
it was auspicious.
He asked to cut off three feet of it to use.
On the *gēngchén* day of the fifth month,
they fought at Jì.
Luán and Gāo were defeated.
They were defeated again at Zhuāng.
The people of the capital pursued them
and defeated them again at Lùmén.
Luán Shī and Gāo Qiáng fled to Jìn.
Chén and Bào divided their households.
Yànzǐ said to Huánzǐ:
"You must yield them to the Duke!
Yielding
is the master of virtue.
Yielding is called admirable virtue.
All who have blood and breath
have a heart for contention.
Therefore, profit must not be forcefully seized;
to think of righteousness is better.
Righteousness
is the root of profit.
Amassing profit produces evil.
Let there be no amassing for now!
Then you can nourish growth."
Huánzǐ returned all the public fiefs to the Duke,
and requested to retire in Jǔ.
Huánzǐ summoned Zǐshān,
and privately prepared tents, utensils, and clothing and shoes for his followers,
and then returned Jǐ.
Zǐshāng also did the same,
and returned his city.
Zǐzhōu also did the same,
and was given Fúyú.
He returned the cities of Zǐchéng, Zǐgōng, and Gōngsūn Jié,
and increased the stipends for all of them.
For all sons
and grandsons of the Duke who had no stipends,
he divided his own cities among them.
For the poor, needy, orphans, and widows of the state,
he privately gave them grain.
He said:
"The *Shī* says,
'Bestowing gifts throughout Zhōu.'
This refers to being able to bestow.
Duke Huán achieved hegemony because of this."
The Duke gave Huánzǐ the cities neighboring Jǔ,
but he declined.
Mù Mèng Jī requested Gāotáng for him,
and the Chén clan began to grow great.
B10.10.3 In the autumn, the seventh month,
Píngzǐ attacked Jǔ
and took Gěng.
He presented the captives
and for the first time used human sacrifice at the Bó altar.
Zàng Wǔzhòng was in Qí,
and hearing of this,
he said:
"Will Duke Zhōu even accept the sacrifices of Lǔ?
Duke Zhōu accepts righteousness,
but Lǔ has no righteousness.
The *Shī* says,
'Virtuous reputation is very bright,
watching the people without being frivolous.'
Frivolity has reached an extreme,
yet he uses it at once;
to whom will blessing come?"
B10.10.4 On the day of wùzǐ,
Duke Píng of Jìn died.
The Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn;
upon reaching the River,
the people of Jìn declined his visit.
Yóu Jí then proceeded to Jìn.
In the ninth month,
Shū sūn Ruò, Guó Ruò of Qí,
Huà Dìng of Sòng, Běigōng Xǐ of Wèi,
Hǎn Hǔ of Zhèng, and the men of Xǔ and Cáo,
and the men of Jǔ, Zhū, Téng, Xuē, Qǐ, and Xiǎo Zhū went to Jìn
for the burial of Duke Píng.
Zǐpí of Zhèng intended to take silks for the journey;
Zǐchǎn said:
"Why use silks for a funeral?
Using silks requires a hundred carriages;
a hundred carriages require a thousand men.
When a thousand men arrive,
you will not be able to proceed.
If you cannot proceed,
you must use them all up.
With how many thousands of men can a state avoid ruin?"
Zǐpí insisted on taking them.
After the burial,
the Grandees of the feudal lords wished to see the new ruler.
Shū sūn Zhāozǐ said: "It is not in accordance with ritual."
They did not listen.
Shù Xiàng declined them,
saying:
"The business of the Grandees is finished,
yet you again give a command to the Orphan.
The Orphan is in the depths of mourning clothes,
if he sees you in festive clothes,
then the funeral rites are not yet complete;
if he sees you in mourning clothes,
this would be to receive condolences once again.
What would the Grandees have him do?"
None had any words with which to request an audience.
Zǐpí used up all his silks.
Upon returning,
he said to Zǐyǔ:
"It is not that knowing is truly difficult;
the difficulty lies in the doing.
The Master knew it,
but I was insufficient.
The *Shū* says,
'Desires ruin measures,
self-indulgence ruins ritual.'
This refers to me.
The Master knows measure and ritual,
whereas I truly indulged my desires
and could not overcome myself."
Zhāozǐ arrived from Jìn,
and all the Grandees went to see him.
Gāo Qiáng saw him and then withdrew.
Zhāozǐ said to the various Grandees:
"As a son, one cannot but be cautious!
Formerly, when Qìng Fēng fled,
Zǐwěi received many cities
and gradually returned them to the ruler.
The ruler considered him loyal
and favored him greatly.
When he was about to die,
he fell ill in the Duke's palace
and was carried home in a carriage;
the ruler personally pushed it.
His son could not sustain this,
and that is why he is here.
Loyalty is a fine virtue,
yet if the son cannot sustain it,
the guilt still reaches him.
How can one not be cautious?
To lose the strength of another's efforts,
to abandon virtue and neglect the clan,
thus bringing it upon one's own person—
is this not harmful?
The *Shī* says,
'Not before my time,
not after my time.'
It must be referring to this!"
B10.10.5 In the winter, the twelfth month,
Duke Píng of Sòng died.
Previously,
Duke Yuán hated the eunuch Liǔ
and wanted to kill him.
During the mourning period,
Liǔ kindled charcoal at the Duke's station;
when the Duke was about to arrive,
he would remove it.
By the time of the burial,
he was favored once again.
A10.11 The Annals of the Eleventh Year of Duke Zhāo
A10.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
in the Royal second month,
Shū Gōng went to Sòng.
A10.11.2 The burial of Duke Píng of Sòng.
A10.11.3 In the summer, the fourth month, on the day of dīngsì,
the Viscount of Chǔ, Qián, enticed the Marquis of Cài, Bān, and killed him at Shēn.
A10.11.4 The Prince of Chǔ, Qìjí, led an army to besiege Cài.
A10.11.5 In the fifth month, on the day of jiǎshēn,
the Lady of the Guī clan died.
A10.11.6 A great hunt was held at Bǐpú.
A10.11.7 Zhòngsūn Jué met with the Viscount of Zhū
and made a covenant at Jìnxiáng.
A10.11.8 In the autumn,
Jìsūn Yìrú met with Hán Qǐ of Jìn,
Guó Ruò of Qí,
Huà Hài of Sòng,
Běigōng Tuó of Wèi,
Hǎn Hǔ of Zhèng,
and the men of Cáo
and Qǐ at Juéyìn.
A10.11.9 In the ninth month, on the day of jǐhài,
the burial of our little lord, Qí Guī.
A10.11.10 In the winter, the eleventh month, on the day of dīngyǒu,
the Chǔ army destroyed Cài;
they captured the Heir Apparent of Cài, Yǒu, and returned,
and used him as a sacrifice.
B10.11 The Commentary of the Eleventh Year of Duke Zhāo
B10.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
in the Royal second month,
Shū Gōng went to Sòng
for the burial of Duke Píng.
B10.11.2 King Jǐng asked Cháng Hóng,
"Among the feudal lords this year, who will truly have good fortune,
and who will truly have misfortune?"
He replied:
"Cài will have misfortune.
This is the year the Marquis of Cài, Bān, murdered his ruler;
the year star is in Shìwéi,
and it will not pass beyond this.
Chǔ will possess it,
yet it will be an obstruction.
When the star reaches Dàliáng,
Cài will be restored
and Chǔ will face misfortune.
This is the Way of Heaven."
The Viscount of Chǔ was in Shēn,
and he summoned Marquis Líng of Cài.
Marquis Líng was about to go,
but the grandees of Cài said:
"The King is greedy and untrustworthy,
and he bears resentment only toward Cài.
Now his gifts are heavy and his words are sweet;
he is luring us.
It is better not to go."
The Marquis of Cài would not listen.
In the third month, on the day bǐngshēn,
the Viscount of Chǔ hid armored men and feasted the Marquis of Cài in Shēn,
got him drunk and seized him.
In summer, in the fourth month, on the day dīngsì,
he killed him.
He mutilated seventy of his officers.
Prince Qìjí led an army to besiege Cài.
Hán Xuānzǐ asked Shúxiàng:
"Will Chǔ be successful?"
He replied: "They will be successful!
The Marquis of Cài committed a crime against his ruler,
and he could not harmonize his people.
Heaven will lend its hand to Chǔ to destroy him;
for what reason would they not succeed?
However, I, Xì, have heard
that using untrustworthiness to seek good fortune
cannot be done a second time.
The King of Chǔ escorted Sūn Wú to conduct a punitive expedition against Chén,
saying:
'I will stabilize your state.'
The people of Chén obeyed his orders,
but then he turned it into a district.
Now he has again lured Cài and killed its ruler
in order to besiege its state.
Although he may luckily succeed,
he will certainly suffer the consequences;
he cannot last long.
Jié conquered Yǒumín
and thereby lost his state.
Zhòu conquered the Dōngyí
and lost his life.
Chǔ is small and its status is low,
yet it is more frequently violent than those two kings.
Can it escape disaster?
When Heaven lends aid to the unrighteous,
it is not to bless them,
but to increase their wickedness and then send down punishment.
Moreover, it is like the five materials of Heaven:
when they are about to be used,
their strength is exhausted until they are worn out.
Thus there is no salvation,
and they cannot be revived."
B10.11.3 In the fifth month,
Qí Guī passed away.
A great military hunt was held at Bǐpú,
which was contrary to ritual propriety.
B10.11.4 Mèng Xīzǐ met with Duke Zhuāng of Zhū,
and they made a covenant at Jìnxiáng
to cultivate good relations, which was in accordance with ritual.
A man of Quánqiū had a daughter
who dreamed that she used her curtains to cover the temple of the Mèng clan.
She then fled to Xīzǐ,
and her companion followed her.
They made a covenant at the altar of the god of the soil at Qīngqiū,
saying:
"If we have sons,
let us not abandon each other!"
Xīzǐ made her assist as a secondary wife of the Wěi clan.
Returning from Jìnxiáng,
he stayed the night with the Wěi clan,
and the woman from Quánqiū gave birth to Yìzǐ and Nángōng Jìngshū.
Her companion had no son,
so she was made to nurture Jìngshū.
B10.11.5 The Chǔ army was in Cài.
Xún Wú of Jìn said to Hán Xuānzǐ:
"We could not save Chén,
and now we cannot save Cài;
states will become estranged.
The inability of Jìn is now plain to see.
To be the leader of the covenant and yet not care for states being destroyed—
what use is such a leader?"
In autumn,
they met at Juéyìn
to plan the rescue of Cài.
Zipí of Zhèng was about to go.
Zǐchǎn said:
"The journey will not be long,
for they cannot save Cài.
Cài is small and non-compliant,
while Chǔ is large and without virtue.
Heaven is going to abandon Cài to satisfy Chǔ,
filling it up before punishing it.
Cài will surely perish.
Moreover, those who can defend a state after losing their ruler are few.
In three years,
the King will surely meet with disaster!
Good and evil, once they complete their cycle, must return;
the King's evil has completed its cycle."
The people of Jìn sent Húfù to request Cài from Chǔ,
but it was refused.
B10.11.6 Viscount Shàn met Hán Xuānzǐ at Qī.
His gaze was downward and his speech was slow.
Shúxiàng said:
"Viscount Shàn is likely to die!
In the court there are fixed positions,
at meetings there are markers;
on clothes there are seams,
and on belts there are knots.
Words at meetings and in court must be heard at the proper positions,
which is how the order of business is manifested.
The gaze should not go beyond the belt knots and seams,
which is how the appearance is guided.
Speech gives the command,
and appearance clarifies it.
If these are lost, there is a deficiency.
Now Viscount Shàn is the Chief of the King's Officers,
yet he is giving orders at a meeting
with a gaze that does not rise to the belt
and a voice that does not carry beyond his step.
His gaze does not guide his appearance,
and his speech is not manifest.
Without guidance,
there is no reverence;
without manifestation,
there is no following.
He no longer has the spirit to maintain himself."
B10.11.7 In the ninth month,
Qí Guī was buried,
but the Duke was not sorrowful.
The officers of Jìn who attended the funeral
returned and told Shǐ Zhào.
Shǐ Zhào said:
"He will surely be sacrificed to in the suburbs of Lǔ."
The attendants asked:
"For what reason?"
He said:
"She was of the Guī surname.
Since he does not think of his kin,
the ancestors will not return to him."
Shúxiàng said:
"How the ducal house of Lǔ will be debased!
The ruler has a great mourning,
yet the state did not cancel the military hunt.
He is in the three-year mourning,
yet he does not have one day of sorrow.
When the state does not care for mourning,
it does not respect the ruler;
when the ruler has no appearance of sorrow,
he does not care for his kin.
