If the state does not respect the ruler
and the ruler does not care for his kin,
can the house avoid being debased?
He will likely lose his state."
B10.11.8 In winter, in the eleventh month,
the Viscount of Chǔ extinguished Cài
and sacrificed Crown Prince Yǐn at Mount Gāng.
Shēn Wúyǔ said:
"This is inauspicious.
The five types of sacrificial animals are not used for each other's purposes,
how much less can a feudal lord be used for sacrifice!
The King will surely regret this!"
B10.11.9 In the twelfth month,
Duke Chéng of Shàn died.
B10.11.10 The Viscount of Chǔ walled Chén, Cài, and Bùgēng.
He made Qìjí the Lord of Cài.
The King asked Shēn Wúyǔ:
"How will Qìjí be in Cài?"
He replied:
"No one knows a son better than a father,
and no one knows a minister better than a ruler.
Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng walled Lì and placed Zǐyuán there,
which led to Duke Zhāo failing to be established.
Duke Huán of Qí walled Gǔ and placed Guǎn Zhòng there,
and they rely on it to this day.
I have heard that the five great ones should not be on the borders,
and the five small ones should not be in the court.
Relatives should not be on the outside,
and strangers should not be on the inside.
Now Qìjí is on the outside,
and Zhèng Dān is on the inside.
Your Majesty should be somewhat cautious!"
The King said:
"If the state has large walled cities,
how is that?"
He replied:
"The cities of Jīng and Lì in Zhèng actually killed Mànbó;
Xiāo and Bó in Sòng actually killed Zǐyóu;
Qúqiū in Qí actually killed Wúzhī;
Pú and Qī in Wèi actually expelled Duke Xiàn.
If we look at it from this perspective,
then they are harmful to the state.
When the tip is too large, it will surely snap;
when the tail is too large, it cannot be wagged.
This is something Your Majesty knows."
A10.12 The Annals of the Twelfth Year of Duke Zhāo
A10.12.1 In the spring of the twelfth year,
Gāo Yǎn of Qí led an army to escort the Earl of Northern Yàn into Yáng.
A10.12.2 In the third month, on the day Rénshēn,
Jiā, the Earl of Zhèng, died.
A10.12.3 In summer,
the Duke of Sòng sent Huá Dìng on a mission of state.
A10.12.4 The Duke went to Jìn;
when he reached the Hé, he then returned.
A10.12.5 In the fifth month,
they buried Duke Jiǎn of Zhèng.
A10.12.6 Chǔ killed its Grand Officer Chéng Xióng.
A10.12.7 Autumn, seventh month.
A10.12.8 In winter, the tenth month,
Gōngzǐ Yìn fled to Qí.
A10.12.9 The Viscount of Chǔ attacked Xú.
A10.12.10 Jìn attacked Xiānyú.
B10.12 Commentary on the Twelfth Year of Duke Zhāo
B10.12.1 In the spring of the twelfth year,
Gāo Yǎn of Qí installed Kuǎn, the Earl of Běiyàn, in Táng,
because of his followers among the people there.
B10.12.2 In the third month,
Duke Jiǎn of Zhèng died.
As they were preparing the path for the funeral,
it reached the ancestral temple of the Yóu clan,
and they were about to demolish it.
Zǐ Dàshū had his road-clearing laborers stand with their tools
but without having them demolish it,
saying:
“When Zǐchǎn passes you
and asks why you did not demolish it,
you shall say:
‘We could not bear to destroy the temple.
Very well,
we shall demolish it now.’”
After this occurred,
Zǐchǎn then ordered them to bypass it.
There was a house belonging to the overseer of the graves that stood in the way;
if it were demolished,
the interment would be held in the morning;
if not demolished,
the interment would be held at midday.
Zǐ Dàshū requested to demolish it,
saying:
“What shall we do about the guests from the various lords?”
Zǐchǎn said:
“The guests from the various lords who can come to join our funeral,
how could they dread the midday?
If there is no harm to the guests,
and the people are not harmed,
for what reason should we not do it?”
Consequently, it was not demolished,
and the burial took place at midday.
The superior man said that in this matter Zǐchǎn understood ritual.
Ritual
consists in not destroying others to achieve one's own goals.
B10.12.3 In summer,
Huá Dìng of Sòng came on a mission
to establish relations with the succeeding ruler.
At the banquet for him,
the poem 'Liǎo Xiāo' was recited for him;
he did not understand it
and did not offer a reciprocal poem.
Zhāozǐ said:
“He will surely perish.
He does not cherish the conversation of the banquet,
he does not manifest the honor shown to him,
he does not recognize excellent virtue,
and he does not accept shared blessings;
how can he remain in his position?”
B10.12.4 The Marquis of Qí, the Marquis of Wèi, and the Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn,
to have an audience with the succeeding ruler.
The Duke went to Jìn;
when he reached the Hé,
he then returned.
Because of the campaign to take Gěng,
the people of Jǔ had complained to Jìn.
Jìn was in mourning for Duke Píng
and had not yet dealt with it,
so they declined the Duke's visit.
Gōngzǐ Yìn then went to Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn hosted a banquet for the various lords.
Zǐchǎn assisted the Earl of Zhèng;
he declined the banquet
and requested to finish the mourning period before receiving orders.
The people of Jìn granted this;
this was in accordance with ritual.
The Marquis of Jìn held a banquet with the Marquis of Qí;
Zhōngháng Mùzǐ assisted him.
In playing pitch-pot,
the Marquis of Jìn went first.
Mùzǐ said:
“There is wine like the Huái,
there is meat like an islet;
if our ruler hits this,
he shall be the leader of the various lords.”
He hit it.
The Marquis of Qí raised an arrow
and said:
“There is wine like the Shéng,
there is meat like a hill;
if I hit this,
I shall rise in turn with your ruler.”
He also hit it.
Bóxiá said to Mùzǐ:
“You have failed in your speech.
We were already the leaders of the various lords;
what does a pot have to do with it,
that you would use hitting it
to show excellence?
The ruler of Qí has belittled our ruler;
when he returns, he will not come back.”
Mùzǐ said:
“Our army's commanders are strong and resistant,
and the soldiers and chariots are competitive and diligent;
today is still like the past;
what can Qí do?”
Gōngsūn Sǒu hurried forward
and said:
“The day is late and the ruler is tired;
he can now leave!”
and he went out with the Marquis of Qí.
B10.12.5 The Viscount of Chǔ said that Chéng Hǔ
was a remnant of the Ruò'áo clan,
and so he killed him.
Someone slandered Chéng Hǔ to the Viscount of Chǔ;
Chéng Hǔ knew of it
and yet could not flee.
The text says
“Chǔ killed its Grand Officer Chéng Hǔ,”
because he cherished his favored position.
B10.12.6 In the sixth month,
they buried Duke Jiǎn of Zhèng.
B10.12.7 Xún Wú of Jìn feigned joining the Qí army;
he requested passage through Xiānyú,
and then entered Xīyáng.
In autumn, on the day Rénwǔ in the eighth month,
he destroyed Féi,
and returned with Miángāo, the Master of Féi.
B10.12.8 Yuán Bó Jiǎo of Zhōu mistreated his attendants,
causing Cáo to flee.
In winter, on the day Rénshēn, the first day of the tenth month,
the people of Yuán drove out Jiǎo,
and installed Gōngzǐ Guìxún.
Jiǎo fled to Jiāo.
B10.12.9 Duke Jiǎn of Gān had no son,
so his younger brother Guò was installed.
Guò intended to remove the clans of Chéng and Jǐng.
The clans of Chéng and Jǐng bribed Duke Xiàn of Liú;
on the day Bǐngshēn,
they killed Duke Dào of Gān
and installed Qiú, the grandson of Duke Chéng.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
they killed Guò, the son of Yǔ Pí, tutor to the Crown Prince Xiàn;
they killed Xiá Xīn in the market, along with the palace favorites Chuò, Wángsūn Mò, Liú Zhōujiū, Yīn Jì, and Lǎo Yángzǐ.
B10.12.10 Jì Píngzǐ was established,
but he was not courteous toward Nán Kuài.
Nán Kuài said to Zǐzhòng:
“I shall expel the Jì clan
and return their household to the Duke;
you shall take his position,
and I shall serve the Duke with the city of Fèi.”
Zǐzhòng agreed.
Nán Kuài spoke to Shūzhòng Mùzǐ
and told him the reason.
When Jì Dàozǐ died,
Shūsūn Zhāozǐ became a minister through a second appointment.
When Píngzǐ attacked Jǔ and conquered it,
he received a third appointment.
Shūzhòngzǐ wished to sow discord between the two families
and said to Píngzǐ:
“A third appointment surpassing one's father and brothers
is contrary to ritual.”
Píngzǐ said: “True.”
Therefore he sent Zhāozǐ.
Zhāozǐ said:
“The Shūsūn clan has had domestic troubles;
the legitimate heir was killed and a concubine's son installed,
which is how I, Ruò, came to this.
If I am to be destroyed because of those troubles,
then I have heard your command.
But if the ruler's command is not to be discarded,
then there are established ranks.”
Zhāozǐ went to court
and ordered the clerks, saying:
“I, Ruò, am going to litigate with the Jì clan;
record the statements without partiality.”
Jìsūn was afraid,
and shifted the blame to Shūzhòngzǐ.
Thus Shūzhòng Xiǎo, Nán Kuài, and Gōngzǐ Yìn plotted against the Jì clan.
Yìn told the Duke,
and then followed the Duke to Jìn.
Nán Kuǎi feared he would not succeed,
and with Bì he rebelled and fled to Qí.
Zǐzhòng was returning;
when he reached Wèi,
he heard of the disorder
and left his attendants behind to go ahead.
Reaching the outskirts,
he heard Bì had rebelled
and subsequently fled to Qí.
When Nán Kuǎi was about to rebel,
a person of his village who knew of it
passed by him and sighed,
saying:
“How sorrowful!
How deep and distant!
Deep thoughts but shallow plans,
personal proximity but distant ambitions,
a household minister plotting against the lord—
what a man!”
Nán Kuǎi divined it with stalks,
and encountered Kūn ䷁ changing to Bǐ ䷇, which said:
“A yellow skirt, supreme good fortune.”
He considered it very auspicious.
He showed it to Zǐfú Huìbó
and asked:
“If I wish to undertake an affair,
how is it?”
Huìbó said:
“I have once studied this.
In matters of loyalty and trustworthiness, it is possible;
if not,
it will surely fail.
External strength and internal gentleness
is loyalty;
harmony used to lead uprightness
is trustworthiness;
therefore it says,
‘A yellow skirt, supreme good fortune.’
Yellow
is the color of the center;
the skirt
is the ornament of the lower part;
supreme
is the chief of goodness.
If the center is not loyal,
one does not obtain its color;
if the lower part is not respectful,
one does not obtain its ornament;
if the affair is not good,
one does not obtain its ultimate.
Harmony between the external and internal constitutes loyalty;
leading an affair with trust constitutes respect;
providing for the three virtues constitutes goodness;
without these three, it is not fitting.
Furthermore, the Yì
cannot be used to divine for dangerous deeds.
What affair do you intend?
And can it be adorned?
Beauty in the center can become yellow;
beauty above becomes supreme;
beauty below then becomes the skirt.
Only when all three are complete can one divine.
There is still a deficiency;
although the divination is auspicious,
it is not yet so.”
When he was about to go to Bì,
he gave wine to the villagers.
Someone from the village sang to him:
“I have a garden,
does the wolfberry grow there?
Will you be the one to follow me,
or will the base ones be those who leave me?
Is it not shameful to turn one's back on a neighbor?
Enough, enough!
Is he not a man of our group?”
Píngzǐ wanted to have Zhāozǐ expel Shūzhòng Xiǎo.
Xiǎo heard of this
and did not dare to attend court.
Zhāozǐ ordered an official to tell Xiǎo to wait for government business at court,
saying:
“I will not become a reservoir of resentment.”
Chǔ Zǐ hunted at Zhōulái
and was stationed at Yǐngwěi.
He sent Dàng Hóu, Pān Zǐ, Sīmǎ Dū,
Xiāoyǐn Wǔ, and Língyǐn Xǐ to lead the army and besiege Xú to frighten Wú.
Chǔ Zǐ was stationed at Gānxī to act as their support.
It rained and snowed.
The Wáng wore a leather cap,
a Qín-style wool-lined robe,
a kingfisher-feather cloak,
and leopard-skin
shoes, and he went out holding a whip.
Pú Xīfù followed him.
Yòuyǐn Zǐgé paid an evening visit.
The Wáng saw him,
removed his cap and cloak,
set aside the whip,
and spoke with him,
saying:
“Long ago, our late ruler Xióng Yì, together with Lǚ Jí, Wángsūn Móu, Xièfù, and Qínfù, served Kāng Wáng together.
The four states all received shares,
but I alone had none.
Now I am sending someone to Zhōu
to ask for a tripod as my share;
will the Wáng give it to me?”
He replied: “He will give it to the Jūnwáng!
Long ago, our late ruler Xióng Yì was secluded in Jīngshān,
using a wood cart and tattered clothes to live in the wilderness,
trekking through mountains and forests to serve the Tiānzǐ,
with only peach-wood bows and thorn-wood arrows to contribute to the Wáng’s service.
Qí
was the Wáng’s maternal uncle;
Jìn, Lǔ, and Wèi were the Wáng’s maternal brothers.
For this reason, Chǔ had no share,
while they all did.
Now Zhōu and the four states serve the Jūnwáng
and will follow whatever command;
how could they begrudge a tripod?”
The Wáng said:
“Long ago, my great ancestor’s elder uncle Kūnwú
dwelt in old Xǔ.
Now the people of Zhèng are greedy for its fields
and do not give them to me.
If I ask for them,
will they give them to me?”
He replied:
“They will give them to the Jūnwáng!
Since Zhōu does not begrudge a tripod,
would Zhèng dare to begrudge the fields?”
The Wáng said:
“Formerly, the Zhūhóu kept a distance from us and feared Jìn.
Now I have built great walls at Chén, Cài, and Bùgēng,
each with a levy of a thousand chariots.
You shared the labor in this;
will the Zhūhóu fear me?”
He replied:
“They will fear the Jūnwáng!
Those four states
are individually enough to be feared.
Adding Chǔ to them,
how could they not fear the Jūnwáng!”
Gōngyǐn Lù requested:
“The Jūnwáng ordered the carving of the Guī to make the battle-axe handle;
I venture to ask for instructions.”
The Wáng went in to inspect it.
Xīfù said to Zǐgé:
“My master,
you are the hope of the state of Chǔ.
Now your words to the Wáng are like an echo;
what will become of the state?”
Zǐgé said:
“I have been whetting the blade and waiting;
when the Wáng comes out,
my blade will strike.”
The Wáng came out
and spoke again.
Zuǒshǐ Yǐ Xiāng hurried past.
The Wáng said:
“He is a good scribe;
regard him well!
He can read the Sānfén, Wǔdiǎn, Bāsuǒ, and Jiǔqiū.”
He replied:
“I have once asked him about them.
Long ago, Mù Wáng wished to indulge his heart
and travel throughout the world,
so that everywhere there would be his wheel tracks and horse prints.
Jìgōng Móufù composed the poem ‘Qǐzhāo’ to restrain the Wáng’s heart;
thus the Wáng was able to die in the Zhī Gōng.
I asked him about that poem, but he did not know it.
If one asks about things so remote,
how could he know them?”
The Wáng asked:
“Do you know it?”
He replied:
“I do.
The poem says:
‘Gentle is the Qǐzhāo,
to clearly manifest the sound of virtue.
Reflecting on our Wáng’s measures,
they are like jade, like gold.
Measuring the strength of the people,
and not having a heart of drunken satiation.’”
The Wáng bowed and went in.
He was served food but did not eat;
he lay down but did not sleep.
For several days, he could not overcome himself,
leading to his disaster.
Zhòngní said:
“There is an ancient record:
‘To overcome oneself and return to Lǐ
is benevolence.’
Truly excellent!
If Chǔ Líng Wáng could have been like this,
how could he have been disgraced at Gānxī?”
Jìn attacked Xiānyú,
because of the campaign against Féiyǐ.
Zhāo Gōng Shísān Nián Jīng
A10.13.1 In the thirteenth year, in spring,
Shū Gōng led an army to besiege Fèi.
A10.13.2 In summer, in the fourth month,
the Chǔ Gōngzǐ Bǐ returned to Chǔ from Jìn
and assassinated his ruler, Qián, at Gánxī.
A10.13.3 The Chǔ Gōngzǐ Qìjí killed Gōngzǐ Bǐ.
A10.13.4 In autumn,
the Gōng met with Liú Zǐ,
Jìn Hóu,
Qí Hóu,
Sòng Gōng,
Wèi Hóu,
Zhèng Bó,
Cáo Bó,
Jǔ Zǐ,
Zhū Zǐ,
Téng Zǐ,
Xuē Bó,
Qǐ Bó,
and Xiǎo Zhū Zǐ at Píngqiū.
A10.13.5 In the eighth month, on the day jiǎxū,
they made a covenant at Píngqiū.
The Gōng did not participate in the covenant.
A10.13.6 The people of Jìn seized Jì Sūn Yìrú to return with him.
A10.13.7 The Gōng arrived from the meeting.
A10.13.8 Cài Hóu Lú returned to Cài.
Chén Hóu Wú returned to Chén.
A10.13.9 In winter, in the tenth month,
they buried Cài Líng Gōng.
A10.13.10 The Gōng went to Jìn
and upon reaching the Hé, he returned.
A10.13.11 Wú extinguished Zhōulái.
B10.13 The Commentary on Zhāo Gōng's Thirteenth Year
B10.13.1 In the spring of the thirteenth year,
Shū Gōng besieged Fèi,
but could not overcome it
and was defeated there. Píngzǐ was angry
and ordered that whenever any people of Fèi were seen, they should be seized
to be made prisoners and captives.
Yě Qūfū said,
"This is wrong.
If you see the people of Fèi,
clothe those who are cold,
feed those who are hungry,
be a generous master to them,
and provide for their needs and distress;
then the people of Fèi will come to you as if returning home,
and the Nán Shì will be finished.
The people will rebel against them,
and with whom will they occupy the city?
If you intimidate them with power
and frighten them with anger,
the people will suffer and rebel;
it is to gather them for the enemy.
If all the lords acted like this,
and the people of Fèi had nowhere to return,
and did not feel close to the Nán Shì,
where would they go?"
Píngzǐ followed this,
and the people of Fèi rebelled against the Nán Shì.
B10.13.2 When the Chǔ Zǐ was Lìngyǐn,
he killed the Dà Sīmǎ Wěi Yǎn
and took his household.
When he ascended the throne,
he seized the fields of Wěi Jū;
he moved the people of Xǔ and took Xǔ Wéi as a hostage.
Cài Wěi was favored by the Wáng;
when the Wáng extinguished Cài,
his father died there;
the Wáng made him join the garrison and then left.
At the meeting of Shēn,
a Yuè Dàfū was executed there.
The Wáng seized Zhōngchuó from Dòu Wéiguī,
and also seized the city of Chéngrán,
making him the Jiāoyǐn.
Màn Chéngrán had formerly served Cài Gōng.
Therefore, the Wěi clan, as well as Wěi Jū, Xǔ Wéi, Cài Wěi, and Màn Chéngrán,
were all those whom the Wáng did not treat with ritual propriety.
Relying on the various clans who had lost their offices,
they encouraged the Yuè Dàfū Cháng Shòuguò to start a rebellion;
they besieged Gùchéng,
captured Xīzhōu,
walled it, and occupied it.
When Guān Qǐ died,
his son was in Cài
serving Cháo Wú
and said,
"If Cài is not restored now,
it will never be restored.
I ask to try it."
In the name of Cài Gōng, he summoned Zǐgàn and Zǐxī;
when they reached the suburbs,
he told them the true situation
and forced them to make a covenant,
then entered and surprised Cài.
Cài Gōng was about to eat when he saw them and fled.
Guān Cóng made Zǐgàn eat,
dug a pit,
used a sacrificial victim,
placed the text upon it,
and moved quickly.
He personally went through Cài
and said,
"Cài Gōng summoned the two gentlemen
intending to admit them;
he has made a covenant with them and sent them off,
and will lead an army to follow them."
The people of Cài gathered
and were about to seize him.
He defended himself, saying,
"The enemy you lost has formed an army;
if you kill me,
what benefit is there?"
Thereupon they released him.
Cháo Wú said,
"If you gentlemen can face death,
then you should oppose them
to wait for success.
If you seek peace and stability,
then you should join them
to achieve what they desire.
Moreover, if you oppose your superiors,
where can you go?"
The multitude said,
"We will join them!"
Thereupon they supported Cài Gōng,
summoned the two gentlemen, and made a covenant at Dèng,
relying on the people of Chén and Cài to restore their states.
The Chǔ Gōngzǐ Bǐ, Gōngzǐ Hēigōng, Gōngzǐ Qìjí, Màn Chéngrán, and Cài Cháo Wú led the armies of Chén, Cài, Bùgēng, Xǔ, and Yè;
following the followers of the four clans,
they entered Chǔ.
When they reached the suburbs,
Chén and Cài wanted to make a name for themselves,
so they requested to form a Wǔ Jūn.
Cài Gōng knew this
and said,
"We want speed,
and the laborers are weary;
I request only to make a fence."
So they made a fence for the army.
Cài Gōng sent Xū Wùmóu and Shǐ Pái to enter first;
through the Zhèng Púrén, they killed Tàizǐ Lù and Gōngzǐ Bàdí.
Gōngzǐ Bǐ became Wáng,
Gōngzǐ Hēigōng became Lìngyǐn,
and they halted at Yúpī.
Gōngzǐ Qìjí became Sīmǎ
and first cleared the Wáng's palace.
He sent Guān Cóng to follow the army at Gánxī
and then made an announcement to them,
saying,
"Those who return first will regain their places;
those who are last will have their noses cut off."
The army reached Zǐliáng and then collapsed.
When the Wáng heard of the deaths of the various Gōngzǐ,
he threw himself down from his carriage
and said,
"Do other people love their sons
as much as I do?"
His attendants said,
"Even more so.
When a common person grows old and has no son,
he knows he will be cast into a ditch or a ravine."
The Wáng said,
"I have killed many of other people's sons;
how could it not come to this?"
The Yòuyǐn Zǐgé said,
"I request that you wait in the suburbs
to listen to the people of the capital."
The Wáng said,
"The anger of the multitude must not be provoked."
Zǐgé said,
"Then enter a major city
and beg for troops from the lords."
The Wáng said,
"They have all rebelled."
Zǐgé said,
"Then flee to the other lords
to wait for the great states to plan for you, my ruler."
The Wáng said,
"Great blessings do not come twice;
I would only bring shame upon myself."
Rán Dān then returned to Chǔ.
The Wáng went along the Xià,
intending to enter Yān. Shēnhài, the son of Yùyǐn Wúyǔ, said:
"My father twice violated the King’s commands,
yet the King did not execute him.
What kindness could be greater than this?
The King’s present state is unbearable to see,
but his past kindness cannot be abandoned.
I shall follow the King."
He then sought the King
and encountered him at Jíwéi, returning home with him.
In the summer, in the fifth month, on the day guǐhài,
the King hanged himself at the house of the Yùyǐn Shēn Hài.
Shēn Hài buried him, having his two daughters follow him in death.
Guān Cóng said to Zǐgàn,
"If you do not kill Qìjí,
even if you gain the state,
you will still suffer calamity."
Zǐgàn said, "I cannot bear to do so."
Zǐyù said, "Others will bear to do it to you,
and I cannot bear to wait for that."
Then he left.
Every night the capital was terrified, saying,
"The King has entered!"
On the night of yǐmǎo,
Qìjí sent men to run about and cry out,
"The King has arrived!"
The people of the capital were greatly alarmed.
He sent Màn Chéngrán to run and tell Zǐgàn and Zǐxī,
"The King has arrived.
The people of the capital have killed the King’s Sīmǎ
and are coming here.
If you lords would plan for yourselves early,
you may avoid disgrace.
The anger of the masses is like water or fire,
and cannot be reasoned with."
There were others who came running and crying out,
saying,
"The masses have arrived!"
Both of the two lords committed suicide.
On the day bǐngchén,
Qìjí ascended the throne,
taking the name Xióng Jū.
He buried Zǐgàn at Zǐ,
who was actually Zǐáo.
He killed a prisoner,
dressed him in the King's robes,
and set him adrift on the Hàn River,
then retrieved and buried him
to pacify the people of the capital.
He appointed Zǐqí as Lìngyǐn.
The Chǔ army returned from Xú,
and the people of Wú defeated them at Yùzhāng,
capturing five of their commanders.
King Píng enfeoffed Chén and Cài,
restored the moved settlements,
returned all the assets,
granted relief and was lenient to the people,
pardoned crimes and promoted officials.
He summoned Guān Cóng,
and the King said,
"Whatever you desire, I shall grant."
He replied,
"My ancestors assisted in the beginning of divination."
So the King appointed him Bǔyǐn.
He sent Zhīrú Zǐgōng on a mission to Zhèng
and to return the lands of Chōu and Lì.
After finishing his business, he did not return them.
The people of Zhèng requested, saying,
"We have heard on the roads
that you would command our humble ruler with Chōu and Lì,
and we venture to ask for that command."
He replied,
"I have not yet heard such a command."
After he returned,
the King asked about Chōu and Lì.
He dressed in humble garments and replied,
saying,
"I mistakenly failed to deliver the command
and have not yet returned them."
The King took his hand
and said,
"Do not trouble yourself!
Just go home for now.
I have matters to attend to,
and I shall inform you of them."
In another year,
Yùyǐn Shēn Hài reported concerning the King's coffin,
and then they reburied him.
Previously,
King Líng performed divination, saying,
"May I obtain the world!"
It was not auspicious.
He threw down the tortoise shell,
cursed Heaven and cried out,
"This small thing you will not grant me,
so I shall surely take it myself."
The people suffered from the King's insatiability,
so they followed the rebellion as if returning home.
Previously,
King Gòng had no primary heir,
but had five favored sons,
and none was designated as the successor.
He performed a great sacrifice to all the spirits
and prayed, saying,
"I ask the spirits to choose from among these five
to let him preside over the state."
He displayed a jade disk to all the spirits,
saying,
"The one who bows right over the jade disk
is the one established by the spirits;
who would dare oppose him?"
Afterward,
he and Bā Jī secretly buried the jade disk in the courtyard of the Great Hall,
had the five sons fast,
and they entered in order of age to bow.
King Kāng stepped over it;
King Líng’s elbow was over it;
Zǐgàn and Zǐxī were both far from it.
King Píng was young;
he was carried in,
and he bowed twice;
both times he was right over the cord.
Dòu Wéiguī entrusted Chéngrán to him,
and said,
"Abandoning ritual and violating commands,
Chǔ will surely be in danger!"
When Zǐgàn returned to Chǔ,
Hán Xuānzǐ asked Shūxiàng,
"Will Zǐgàn succeed?"
He replied, "It will be difficult."
Xuānzǐ said,
"Those with the same hatred seek each other,
like merchants in a market;
why should it be difficult?"
He replied,
"If there is no one with whom he shares likes,
who will share his dislikes?
Taking a state has five difficulties:
being favored but having no men of talent,
is the first;
having men but having no leader with a foundation,
is the second;
having a leader but having no plans,
is the third;
having plans but having no people's support,
is the fourth;
having people but having no virtue,
is the fifth.
Zǐgàn has been in Jìn
for thirteen years.
Among the followers of Jìn and Chǔ,
we have heard of none who are prominent among his followers;
this can be called having no men.
His clan is wiped out and his relatives have alienated him;
this can be called having no leader.
Acting without an opportunity;
this can be called having no plans.
Being a refugee for his whole life;
this can be called having no people.
Fleeing without evidence of being loved;
this can be called having no virtue.
The King is cruel and has no scruples,
but the Chǔ lord Zǐgàn
faces five difficulties while trying to assassinate his former ruler;
who can help him succeed?
The one who will possess the state of Chǔ
will likely be Qìjí!
He governs Chén and Cài,
and the regions outside the walls are attached to him.
Harassment and wickedness do not arise,
robbers and thieves remain hidden,
private desires do not violate the law,
and the people have no resentment in their hearts.
The ancestral spirits have commanded it,
and the people of the state believe in him.
When there is chaos in the Mǐ clan,
the youngest must be the one established;
this is the custom of Chǔ.
He has obtained the spirits—
this is the first;
he has the people—
this is the second;
he has excellent virtue—
this is the third;
he has favor and high status—
this is the fourth;
he follows the custom—
this is the fifth.
With five advantages to overcome five difficulties,
who can harm him?
As for Zǐgàn’s office,
it was Yòuyǐn;
assessing his noble favor,
he was a son of a concubine;
according to what the spirits commanded,
he was far from it.
His nobility is gone,
his favor is abandoned.
The people have no affection for him,
the state has no one to join him;
how then shall he be established?"
Xuān Zǐ said:
"Were
Qí Huán and Jìn Wén not examples of this?"
In reply it was said:
"Qí Huán was
the son of Wèi Jī,
and was favored by Xī;
he had Bǎo Shūyá, Bīn Xūwú, and Xí Péng as his assistants;
he had Jǔ and Wèi as external supporters;
he had Guó and Gāo as internal supporters;
he followed what was good as if it were a flowing stream,
and he treated those below him with respectful dignity;
he did not amass bribes,
did not follow his desires,
was untiring in giving and bestowing,
and was never weary of seeking the good.
Therefore, he possessed the state;
was it not appropriate?
Our former lord, Wén Gōng,
was the son of Hú Jìjī,
and was favored by Xiàn;
he was fond of learning and was tireless;
when he was seventeen years old,
he already had five capable men.
He had the former high officials Zǐ Yú and Zǐ Fàn as his heart and mind,
he had Wèi Chú and Jiǎ Tuó as his arms and legs,
he had Qí, Sòng, Qín, and Chǔ as external supporters,
and he had Luán, Xì, Hú, and Xiān as internal supporters.
He was in exile for nineteen years,
and maintained his will with ever-increasing resolve.
Huì and Huái abandoned the people,
and the people followed and joined him.
Xiàn had no other close relatives,
and the people had no other hopes.
Heaven is currently assisting Jìn;
how could anyone replace Wén?
These two lords
were different from Zǐ Gān.
Gòng had favored sons,
and the state had internal masters;
he had bestowed nothing on the people,
and had no support from outside;
when he left Jìn, no one saw him off,
and when he returned to Chǔ, no one welcomed him.
How could he hope for the state?"
B10.13.3 When Jìn completed the Sī Qí palace,
the feudal lords who had come to court and were returning all had divided hearts.
Because of the seizure of Gěng, Jìn intended to lead the feudal lords to punish the offender.
Shū Xiàng said:
"The feudal lords cannot be left without a display of majesty."
Thereupon, he collectively summoned them to an assembly
and announced it to Wú.
In autumn,
the Marquis of Jìn met with the Viscount of Wú at Liáng.
The water route was impassable,
so the Viscount of Wú declined and then returned.
On the day bǐngyín of the seventh month,
they reviewed the troops south of Zhū.
There were four thousand armored chariots.
Yángshé Fù acted as Marshal
and then assembled the feudal lords at Píng Qiū.
Zǐ Chǎn and Zǐ Dàshū assisted the Earl of Zhèng to attend the assembly.
Zǐ Chǎn brought nine sets of tents and screens,
while Zǐ Dàshū brought forty.
Later, Zǐ Dàshū regretted it,
and at every lodging place,
he reduced them.
When they reached the assembly,
it was like that too.
They camped in the territory of Wèi.
Shū Fù sought goods from Wèi
and behaved excessively toward those gathering fodder and wood.
The people of Wèi sent Tú Bó to present Shū Xiàng with soup and a chest of silk,
saying:
"The feudal lords serve Jìn
and have not dared to have divided hearts; how much more so for Wèi, being under your lordship's protection—
how would we dare to have different intentions?
Those gathering fodder and wood were treated differently than in previous days;
we venture to request your intervention."
Shū Xiàng accepted the soup but returned the silk,
saying:
"Jìn has one Yángshé Fù,
who is insatiably greedy for goods
and will soon meet his end.
Regarding this expedition,
if you grant him these gifts in the name of your lord,
it will stop."
The guest followed this advice,
and before he had even withdrawn, Shū Fù stopped the harassment.
The people of Jìn intended to renew the alliance,
but the people of Qí would not agree.
The Marquis of Jìn sent Shū Xiàng to inform Liú Xiàn Gōng, saying:
"If the people of Qí do not join the alliance,
what should be done?"
He replied:
"An alliance is used to confirm trust.
If your lordship possesses trust,
and the feudal lords are not divided,
what is there to worry about?
Inform them with refined words,
and oversee them with a martial host.
Even if Qí does not grant it,
your lordship's merit will be great.
The Elder of the Son of Heaven requests to lead the Royal levies,
'With ten great chariots
to lead the way.'
Whether to be slow or fast is up to your lordship."
Shū Xiàng informed Qí,
saying:
"The feudal lords' request for an alliance
is already here.
If your lordship now finds it disadvantageous,
my unworthy lord makes this request."
In reply it was said:
"When the feudal lords punish those who are divided,
then there is a renewal of the alliance.
If all follow orders,
why renew the alliance?"
Shū Xiàng said:
"The ruin of a state
occurs when there is business but no set tasks,
and so business lacks constancy;
when there are tasks but no ritual,
and so constancy lacks order;
when there is ritual but no majesty,
and so order lacks reverence;
when there is majesty but it is not displayed,
and so reverence lacks clarity.
When clarity is lacking and reverence is discarded,
the hundred affairs cannot be completed,
which is the reason for downfall.
For this reason, the regulations of the enlightened kings
made the feudal lords send annual missions to record their tasks,
hold occasional audiences to discuss ritual,
hold second audiences and assemblies to display majesty,
and hold second assemblies and alliances to manifest clarity.
Recording tasks fosters friendship,
discussing ritual defines status,
displaying majesty impresses the masses,
and manifesting clarity honors the spirits.
From ancient times until now,
none have ever failed in this.
The way of survival or ruin
has always arisen from this.
Jìn's ritual duty is to lead the alliance,
and we fear there might be a lack of governance;
having prepared the sacrificial victims of Qí
and announced it to all the lords,
we seek to complete the matter.
If your lordship says,
'I must discard it,'
what room is there for Qí?
Only may your lordship consider it.
My unworthy lord has heard your command."
The people of Qí were afraid
and replied:
"A small state speaks of it,
and the great state regulates it;
how would we dare not to listen and follow?
We have now heard your command
and will respectfully and reverently proceed;
whether to be slow or fast is up to your lordship."
Shū Xiàng said:
"The feudal lords have grown distant,
and we cannot fail to show our strength to the masses."
On the day xīnwèi of the eighth month,
they reviewed the troops,
setting up the banners but not unfurling them.
On the day rénshēn,
they unfurled them again.
The feudal lords stood in awe of them.
The people of Zhū and the people of Jǔ complained to Jìn, saying:
"Lǔ attacks us morning and night;
we are nearly destroyed.
Our failure to be reverent
is because of Lǔ."
The Marquis of Jìn refused to see the Duke of Lǔ.
He sent Shū Xiàng to come and decline his presence, saying:
"The feudal lords will ally on the day jiǎxū;
my unworthy lord knows he cannot have you serve him,
so he requests that your lordship not trouble yourself."
Zǐ Fú Huì Bó replied:
"Your lordship believes the complaints of the barbarians
and thereby cuts off a brotherly state,
abandoning the descendant of Zhōu Gōng;
that is up to your lordship.
My unworthy lord has heard your command."
Shū Xiàng said:
"My unworthy lord has four thousand armored chariots here;
even if he proceeds without the right Way,
he must be feared.
How much more so when he follows the Way—
what enemy could he have?
Though an ox be thin,
if it falls upon a piglet,
could the piglet fail to fear for its life?"
The anxieties caused by Nán Kuài and Zǐ Zhòng,
how could they be disregarded?
If we rely on the multitudes of Jìn,
use the armies of the feudal lords,
and take advantage of the anger of Zhū, Jǔ, Qǐ, and Zēng,
to punish the crimes of Lǔ,
and strike amidst their two anxieties,
what could we seek that would not be achieved?"
The people of Lǔ were afraid
and obeyed the commands.
On the day jiǎxū,
they held a joint covenant at Píng Qiū,
and Qí submitted.
The feudal lords were ordered to arrive at the clearing by noon.
On the day guǐyǒu,
they retired from court.
Zǐ Chǎn ordered the outer servants to quickly pitch the tents in the clearing,
but Zǐ Dàshū stopped them,
making them wait until the next day.
When evening came,
Zǐ Chǎn heard that they had not yet been pitched,
and sent them to go quickly,
but by then there was no place left to pitch them.
When it came time for the covenant,
Zǐ Chǎn disputed the order of precedence for the tribute,
saying:
"In the past, the Son of Heaven ranked the tributes,
their weight according to the rank.
High rank meant heavy tribute;
this was the regulation of Zhōu.
Those of lower rank who provide heavy tribute
are those of the Royal Domain (Diàn fú).
The Earl of Zhèng
is a Nán (Baron),
yet he is made to follow the tribute of a Duke or Marquis.
We fear we cannot provide it,
and dare to make this request.
When the feudal lords still the weapons of war,
they take friendly relations as their business.
The commands of the messengers
arrive every month;
if there is no limit to the tribute,
and a small state has a deficiency,
that is how it incurs guilt.
The feudal lords renew their covenants
to preserve the small states.
If the contributions are without limit,
then our ruin is to be expected.
The regulation of our preservation or ruin
lies in today's decision."
They disputed from noon
until dusk,
and then the people of Jìn granted it.
After the covenant,
Zǐ Dàshū blamed him, saying:
"If the feudal lords were to punish us,
could we afford to treat them with such disrespect?"
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"The government of Jìn has many factions,
and they have no time for anything but their own double-dealing and sloth;
what time do they have to punish us?
If a state does not assert itself, it will be insulted;
then what kind of state would it be?"
The Duke did not participate in the covenant.
The people of Jìn arrested Jìsūn Yìrú,
covered him with a tent-cloth,
and had the Dí people guard him.
Sīduó Shè hid some silk in his robe
and carried a jar of ice-water,
crawling to him on his hands and knees.
The guards resisted him,
but he gave them the silk and was able to enter.
The people of Jìn took Píngzǐ back with them,
and Zǐfú Qiū followed him.
Zǐ Chǎn returned home,
and before he arrived,
he heard that Zǐ Pí had died.
He wept
and said:
"I am finished!
There is no longer any reason to do good.
Only that master truly knew me."
Zhòngní said of Zǐ Chǎn:
"In this journey,
he was sufficient to be the foundation of his state.
The Odes say:
'Joyous is the gentleman,
the foundation of the state.'
Zǐ Chǎn
was a gentleman who sought joy."
He also said:
"Bringing together the feudal lords
and regulating the matters of tribute
is in accordance with ritual."
B10.13.4 The people of Xiānyú heard that the Jìn army had been fully mobilized,
but they did not alert the borders
nor did they prepare their defenses.
Xún Wú of Jìn led the Upper Army from Zhù Yōng to invade Xiānyú,
reaching Zhōngrén.
They drove their chariots and competed in the assault,
returning with great spoils.
B10.13.5 When Chǔ destroyed Cài,
King Líng moved the people of Xǔ, Hú, Shěn,
Dào, Fáng, and Shēn to Jīng.
When King Píng ascended the throne,
after enfeoffing Chén and Cài,
he restored all of them to their lands;
this was in accordance with ritual.
Lú, the son of the Great Heir Yǐn, returned to Cài;
this was in accordance with ritual.
Wú, the son of the Great Heir Dào, returned to Chén;
this was in accordance with ritual.
B10.13.6 In the winter, in the tenth month,
they buried Duke Líng of Cài;
this was in accordance with ritual.
B10.13.7 The Duke went to Jìn.
Xún Wú said to Hán Xuānzǐ:
"When the feudal lords visit each other's courts,
it is to cultivate old friendships.
If we arrest their high minister and then receive their ruler in court,
there is a lack of friendship there;
it would be better to decline his visit."
Thereupon, they sent Shì Jǐngbó to decline the Duke's visit at the River.
B10.13.8 Wú destroyed Zhōulái.
The Chief Minister (Lìngyǐn) Zǐqí requested to attack Wú.
The King did not grant it,
saying:
"I have not yet comforted the people,
have not yet served the ghosts and spirits,
have not yet repaired the defenses,
and have not yet stabilized the state.
If I use the people's strength now,
a defeat could not be remedied.
Zhōulái being in the hands of Wú
is like it still being in Chǔ.
You should wait for a while."
B10.13.9 While Jìsūn was still in Jìn,
Zǐfú Huìbó said privately to Zhōngháng Mùzǐ:
"In Lǔ's service to Jìn,
why is it not even equal to that of the small barbarian states?
Lǔ
is a brother state,
its territory is still large,
and it can provide whatever is commanded.
If you cast it aside for the sake of the barbarians
and cause it to serve Qí or Chǔ,
how would that benefit Jìn?
Treating kin as kin, siding with the large states,
rewarding the compliant and punishing the defiant—
this is how one acts as the leader of the covenants.
You should consider this!
A proverb says:
'A servant has one master, but a master has many servants.'
Do we not have other great states to turn to?"
Mùzǐ told Hán Xuānzǐ,
and added:
"When Chǔ destroyed Chén and Cài,
we could not save them;
and now if we arrest our own kin for the sake of the barbarians,
what use will we be?"
Thereupon, they allowed Jìsūn to return.
Huìbó said:
"Our ruler does not yet know the nature of the crime,
for you gathered the feudal lords and then arrested their elder minister.
If there is still a crime,
he will accept the command of death.
But if you say he is without crime and graciously release him,
yet the feudal lords do not hear of it,
then this is like a fugitive escaping his sentence.
What kind of release would that be?
We request to follow the ruler's grace at the assembly."
Xuānzǐ was troubled by this
and said to Shūxiàng:
"Can you make Jìsūn return home?"
He replied:
"I cannot.
But Fù can."
Thereupon they sent Shūyú.
Shūyú saw Jìsūn
and said:
"Formerly, I (Fù) incurred guilt with the ruler of Jìn
and took refuge with the ruler of Lǔ.
If not for the gift of Wǔzǐ,
I would not have survived until today.
Although I have been allowed to return my bones to Jìn,
if you were treated as meat,
how could I not fully explain the situation?
If you are supposed to return but do not,
I have heard from the officials
that they will prepare a lodge for you in Xīhé;
what will you do then?"
And then he wept.
Píngzǐ was afraid
and returned home first.
Huìbó waited for the proper rituals to be completed.
A10.14 The Annals of the Fourteenth Year of Duke Zhāo.
A10.14.1 In the spring of the fourteenth year,
Yìrú arrived from Jìn.
In the third month, Cáo Bó Téng died.
Summer, the fourth month.
Autumn,
buried Cáo Wǔ Gōng.
In the eighth month,
Jǔ Zǐ Qùjí died.
Winter,
Jǔ killed its Gōngzǐ Yìhuī.
The Commentary on the 14th Year of Lord Zhāo
In the spring of the 14th year,
Yìrú arrived from Jìn;
this was to honor Jìn and
blame himself.
To honor Jìn and
blame oneself
is ritual.
When Nán Kuài was about to rebel,
he made a covenant with the people of Fèi.
Sītú Lǎo Qí and Lǜ Guǐ feigned a crippling illness
and sent a request to Nán Kuài, saying:
"We wish to receive the covenant, but our illness has flared up.
If, by your spiritual power, we do not die,
we request to wait for an interval to make the covenant."
He granted it.
The two men, taking advantage of the people's desire to rebel,
requested to assemble the masses for the covenant.
They then coerced Nán Kuài, saying:
"The various ministers have not forgotten their ruler;
they have feared you until now,
and for three years have followed your orders.
If you do not make a plan,
the people of Fèi will not be able to endure the treatment of their ruler,
and will no longer be able to fear you.
What desire of yours can you not satisfy?
We request to escort you."
He requested a period of five days.
He then fled to Qí.
He attended a drinking session with Jǐng Gōng.
The Gōng said:
"A rebel!"
He replied: "I wished to strengthen the Ducal House."
Zǐ Hán Xī said:
"For a household minister to wish to strengthen the Ducal House—
no crime is greater than this."
Sītú Lǎo Qí and Lǜ Guǐ came to return Fèi,
and the Qí Hóu sent Bào Wénzǐ to deliver it.
In summer,
Chǔ Zǐ sent Rán Dān to inspect the troops of the Upper Country at Zōngqiū,
and to comfort its people.
He distributed wealth to the poor,
relieved the destitute;
cared for the orphaned and young,
supported the elderly and sick;
gathered the solitary,
saved those in disaster and distress;
pardoned the widowed and alone,
forgave those with crimes and offenses;
investigated wickedness and evil,
promoted those who were long-neglected;
honored the new with ritual,
arranged the old in order;
rewarded the meritorious,
unified relatives;
employed the worthy,
and assigned officials according to their nature.
He sent Qū Bà to inspect the troops of the Eastern Country at Zhàolíng,
also acting in this manner.
He was friendly toward the borders.
Resting the people for five years,
and only then using the army,
is ritual.
In the autumn, the eighth month,
Jǔ Zhùqiū Gōng died.
Jiāo Gōng did not show grief.
The people of the state did not follow him
and wished to establish the younger brother of Jǔ Zhùqiū Gōng, Gēngyú.
Púyúhòu hated Gōngzǐ Yìhuī
and was friendly with Gēngyú;
Jiāo Gōng hated Gōngzǐ Duó
and was friendly with Yìhuī.
Gōngzǐ Duó relied on Púyúhòu to plot with him,
saying:
"If you kill Yìhuī,
I will drive out the ruler and bring in Gēngyú."
He agreed to it.
The Chǔ Lìngyǐn Zǐqí had rendered service to the King
but did not know moderation,
and aligned himself with the Yǎng clan,
and was insatiable in his demands.
The King was troubled by him.
In the ninth month, on the day jiǎwǔ,
Chǔ Zǐ killed Dòu Chéngrán,
and exterminated the Yǎng clan.
He had Dòu Xīn reside in Yún
so as not to forget the old merits.
In winter, the twelfth month,
Púyúhòu Zīfū killed Jǔ Gōngzǐ Yìhuī.
Jiāo Gōng fled to Qí.
Gōngzǐ Duó welcomed Gēngyú from Qí.
Qí Xí Dǎng and Gōngzǐ Chú escorted him,
and there were lands given as bribes.
Jìn Xíng Hóu and Yōngzǐ disputed over the fields of Chù,
and for a long time there was no resolution.
Shì Jǐngbó went to Chǔ,
and Shūyú acted as the judge.
Hán Xuānzǐ ordered him to decide the old lawsuit,
and the guilt lay with Yōngzǐ.
Yōngzǐ offered his daughter to Shūyú,
and Shūyú suppressed the crime and blamed Xíng Hóu.
Xíng Hóu was enraged,
and killed Shūyú and Yōngzǐ in the court.
Hán Xuānzǐ asked Shūxiàng about their crimes.
Shūxiàng said:
"The three men are equally guilty.
Exposing the living and pillorying the dead is acceptable.
Yōngzǐ knew his own guilt
but used a bribe to buy righteousness.
Fù sold the legal case.
Xíng Hóu took killing into his own hands.
Their crimes are one.
To do evil and snatch the beauty of others' virtue is hūn;
to be greedy and corrupt one's office is mò;
to kill people without fear is zéi.
The Xià Shū says:
'Hūn, mò, and zéi
are to be killed.
These are the punishments of Gāoyáo.'
I request to follow this."
Thereupon he executed Xíng Hóu and exposed the corpses of Yōngzǐ and Shūyú in the market.
Zhòngní said:
"Shūxiàng
was a remnant of the upright of antiquity.
In governing the state and establishing punishments,
he did not hide the faults of his relatives.
He enumerated Shūyú's evils three times
without any reduction.
Was this not due to righteousness?
He can be called upright!
At the meeting of Píngqiū,
he enumerated their bribes
to show leniency to the state of Wèi,
so Jìn was not violent.
He returned Jìsūn of Lǔ,
calling out his deceit,
to show leniency to the state of Lǔ,
so Jìn was not oppressive.
In the lawsuit of Xíng Hóu,
he spoke of his greed
to rectify the penal books,
so Jìn was not biased.
With three statements he removed three evils
and added three benefits.
To kill a relative and increase one's glory—
this is indeed righteousness!"
The Annals of the 15th Year of Lord Zhāo
In the spring of the 15th year,
in the King's first month,
Wú Zǐ Yímò died.
In the second month, on the day guǐyǒu,
the Great Sacrifice was held in the Wǔ Gōng temple.
As the flutes entered,
Shū Gōng died.
The music was stopped,
and the service was completed.
In summer,
Cài Cháo Wú fled to Zhèng.
In the sixth month, on the day dīngsì, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
In autumn,
Jìn Xún Wú led an army to attack Xiānyú.
In winter,
the Lord went to Jìn.
The Commentary on the 15th Year of Lord Zhāo
In the spring of the 15th year,
they were about to perform the dì sacrifice to Wǔ Gōng
and cautioned the various officials.
Zǐ Shèn said:
"On the day of the dì sacrifice, will there be calamity?
I see red and black vapors;
these are not signs of sacrifice
but the aura of mourning.
Will it happen when presiding over the ritual?"
In the second month, on the day guǐyǒu,
the dì sacrifice was performed.
Shū Gōng presided over the ceremony;
as the flute players entered, he died.
The music was stopped,
and the ceremony was completed;
this was in accordance with ritual propriety.
B10.15.2 Fèi Wújí of Chǔ was jealous of Cháo Wú’s presence in Cài
and wished to remove him.
He then said to him:
“The King trusts only you,
which is why he stationed you in Cài.
You are senior now,
yet you remain in a low position;
this is a disgrace.
You must seek [advancement],
and I will assist you in your request.”
He also said to those in positions above him:
“The King trusts only [Cháo] Wú,
which is why he stationed him in Cài.
None of you can compare to him,
yet you are above him;
is this not difficult?
If you do not plan against him,
you will surely encounter trouble.”
In summer,
the people of Cài expelled Cháo Wú,
and Cháo Wú fled to Zhèng.
The King was angry
and said:
“I trusted only [Cháo] Wú,
which is why I placed him in Cài.
Furthermore, without [Cháo] Wú,
I would not have reached this point.
For what reason did you remove him?”
Wújí replied:
“How could I not want [Cháo] Wú?
However, I knew beforehand that his character was different.
If [Cháo] Wú were in Cài,
Cài would surely take flight quickly.
Removing [Cháo] Wú
is the means to clip its wings.”
B10.15.3 In the sixth month, on the day yǐchǒu,
the King’s Crown Prince Shòu died.
B10.15.4 In autumn, in the eighth month on the day wùyín,
the King’s Queen Mù died.
B10.15.5 Xún Wú of Jìn led an army to attack Xiānyú
and besieged Gǔ.
Someone from Gǔ asked to surrender the city through rebellion,
but Mùzǐ would not permit it.
His attendants said:
“The soldiers would not have to work hard,
yet we could obtain the city;
for what reason should we not do it?”
Mùzǐ said:
“I have heard from Shū Xiàng:
‘When likes and dislikes do not err,
the people know where to turn,
and affairs will not fail.’
If someone rebelled with one of my cities,
it would be what I most hate;
if someone comes with their city to me,
why should I alone like it?
If I reward what I most hate,
what becomes of what I like?
If I do not reward it,
it is a loss of trust;
how then can I protect the people?
If strength allows, then advance;
if not, then retreat;
act by measuring your strength.
I cannot, out of a desire for a city, draw near to treachery,
for the loss would be even greater.”
He made the people of Gǔ execute the rebel and repair their defenses.
He besieged Gǔ for three months,
then someone from Gǔ asked to surrender.
He had the people be seen
and said:
“You still have the look of having food;
for now, repair your city.”
The military officers said:
“To capture a city and not take it,
to weary the people and stall the army;
how can you serve the ruler this way?”
Mùzǐ said:
“This is precisely how I serve the ruler.
To obtain one city and teach the people to be indolent,
what use would the city be?
If a city is used to buy indolence,
it is not as good as preserving what is old.
Buying indolence leads to no good end,
and abandoning the old is inauspicious.
If the people of Gǔ can serve their ruler,
I can also serve my ruler.
Leading with righteousness without fail,
with likes and dislikes not erring,
the city can be obtained while the people know where righteousness lies,
having a resolve unto death without double-mindedness;
is this not acceptable?”
When the people of Gǔ reported that their food was exhausted and their strength spent,
only then did he take it.
After conquering Gǔ and returning,
he did not execute a single person
and brought back the Viscount of Gǔ, Yuāndī.
B10.15.6 In winter,
the Duke went to Jìn,
on account of the meeting at Píngqiū.
B10.15.7 In the twelfth month,
Xún Lì of Jìn went to Zhōu
to bury Queen Mù,
with Jí Tán as the assistant.
After the burial
and the ending of mourning,
the King held a banquet for Wénbó,
using a wine vessel from Lǔ.
The King said:
“Elder [Xún Lì],
the feudal lords all have something with which to stabilize and support the Royal House,
but Jìn alone has nothing;
why is that?”
Wénbó bowed to Jí Tán.
He replied:
“When the feudal lords were enfeoffed,
they all received ritual vessels from the Royal House
to stabilize and support their states,
and thus they are able to present sacrificial vessels to the King.
Jìn dwells in deep mountains
and is neighbor to the Róng and Dí,
and being far from the Royal House,
the King’s spiritual influence did not reach it;
having no leisure but to appease the Róng,
how could it present vessels?”
The King said: “Uncle [Jí Tán],
have you forgotten it!
Your ancestor Táng Shū
was the younger brother of the same mother as King Chéng;
could he have returned with no share?
The drum of Mìxū and its grand carriage
were what King Wén used for the great hunt;
the armor of Quēgǒng
was what King Wǔ used to conquer Shāng;
Táng Shū received them
to dwell in Shēn and Xù
and to keep the Róng and Dí in order.
Later, the two carriages of Duke Xiāng,
the battle-axes, the black millet
sacrificial wine, the red bows, and the Tiger Guards,
Duke Wén received them
to hold the lands of Nányáng
and to pacify and campaign against the eastern Xià states;
if these were not shares, then what were they?
Now, when there is merit and it is not discarded,
when there are achievements and they are recorded,
supported with lands and fields,
comforted with ritual vessels,
distinguished with carriages and robes,
and made manifest with patterns and emblems,
so that descendants do not forget—
this is what is called blessing.
If the record of blessings is not consulted,
where is the ‘Uncle’ status?
Furthermore, in the past your high ancestor Sūn Bó Yǎn managed the records of Jìn,
making it the great task,
which is why you are called the Jí clan.
When the two sons of Xīn Yǒu went to Jìn,
thereupon there were the Dǒng historians.
You
are the descendant of the Keeper of Records;
for what reason have you forgotten it?”
Jí Tán could not reply.
When the guests went out,
the King said:
“Will Jí Tán have no descendants!
He recounts the records yet forgets his ancestors.”
Jí Tán returned
and told Shū Xiàng.
Shū Xiàng said:
“The King will probably not come to a good end!
I have heard:
‘That in which one finds joy, one will surely end.’
Now the King finds joy in sorrow;
if he ends in sorrow,
it cannot be called a proper end.
In one year the King has had two three-year mourning periods,
and yet he holds banquets for guests during mourning
and even seeks ritual vessels;
his finding joy in sorrow is extreme,
and it is contrary to ritual propriety.
The arrival of ritual vessels
arises from auspicious achievements,
not from mourning.
In a three-year mourning,
even the noble must complete the wearing of mourning dress;
this is ritual propriety.
Although the King did not complete it,
to have banquets and music so early
is also contrary to ritual propriety.
Rites
are the great canon of a king.
If one movement causes the loss of two rites,
then the great canon is gone.
Speech is used to examine the records,
and records are used to record the canon.
If one forgets the canon and speaks much,
or cites the records,
of what use will it be?"
A10.16 *The Classic of the Sixteenth Year of Duke Zhāogōng*
A10.16.1 In the spring of the sixteenth year,
the Marquis of Qí attacked Xú.
A10.16.2 The Viscount of Chǔ enticed the Viscount of the Róngmán and killed him.
A10.16.3 In the summer,
the Duke arrived from Jìn.
A10.16.4 In the autumn, in the eighth month on the day jǐhài,
the Marquis of Jìn, Yí, died.
A10.16.5 In the ninth month,
the great sacrifice for rain was performed.
A10.16.6 Jìsūn Yìrú went to Jìn.
A10.16.7 In the winter, in the tenth month,
Duke Zhāogōng of Jìn was buried.
B10.16 *The Tradition of the Sixteenth Year of Duke Zhāogōng*
B10.16.1 In the spring of the sixteenth year,
in the King’s first month,
the Duke was in Jìn,
and the people of Jìn detained the Duke.
This is not recorded in the Classic,
to conceal it out of respect for him.
B10.16.2 The Marquis of Qí attacked Xú.
The Viscount of Chǔ heard of the disorder of the Mán clan and that the Viscount of Mán had no hostages;
he sent Rán Dān to entice Jiā, the Viscount of the Róngmán,
and killed him,
subsequently taking the Mán clan.
Soon after, he again established the son there;
this was according to the rites.
In the second month, on the day bǐngshēn,
the army of Qí reached Púsuì,
and the people of Xú sued for peace.
The Viscount of Xú, along with the people of Tán and Jǔ, met with the Marquis of Qí,
made a covenant at Púsuì,
and bribed him with the tripod of Jiǎfǔ.
Shúsūn Zhāozǐ said:
"That the feudal lords have no hegemon
is harmful indeed!
The ruler of Qí follows no Way;
he raises an army to attack a distant land,
holds a meeting,
and returns after achieving success,
yet no one resists him.
Truly, there is no hegemon!
The *Shī* says:
'Since the ancestral Zhōu was destroyed,
there is no place to rest.
The upright Grand Officers are dispersed,
and no one knows my toil.'
Does it not refer to this?"
B10.16.3 In the second month,
Hán Qǐ of Jìn went on a diplomatic mission to Zhèng,
and the Earl of Zhèng entertained him.
Zǐchǎn cautioned his officials, saying:
"If you have a position at court,
let there be none who are not respectful and diligent!"
Kǒng Zhāng arrived late
and stood among the guests.
An executive officer turned him away;
he went behind the guests,
and was turned away again;
he then went among the hanging bells.
The guests followed him and laughed at him.
When the business was finished,
Fùzǐ remonstrated, saying:
"As for the people of a great state,
one must be cautious.
Soon we will be laughed at by them,
and will they not then insult us?
Even if we are all ritualistic,
they still look down on us.
If a state lacks rites,
how can it seek glory?
That Kǒng Zhāng lost his place
is a shame for you, my master."
Zǐchǎn angrily said:
"If the issuing of orders is not appropriate,
if the commands sent out are not trustworthy,
if punishments are biased,
if litigation is chaotic,
if there is irreverence at meetings and court,
if diplomatic missions are not obeyed,
if we incur insults from great states,
if we exhaust the people without success,
and if crimes occur without our knowledge,
these are the shame of Qiáo.
Kǒng Zhāng
is the descendant of Zǐkǒng, the elder grandson of the ruler,
and the heir of an executive officer;
he serves as a hereditary Grand Officer.
He has received orders to serve as an envoy
and has gone around the feudal lords.
He is respected by the people of the state
and known by the feudal lords.
He stands at court and sacrifices at home;
he has a salary from the state
and contributes taxes to the army.
He has duties for funerals and sacrifices,
and he receives and returns sacrificial meat.
His sacrifices are in the temple,
and he already has a fixed position.
Having been in his position for several generations
and having defended his profession for generations,
yet he forgets his place,
how can Qiáo be shamed by this?
If the conduct of perverse people is all blamed on the executive officers,
then the former kings would have had no punishments.
You should rather use something else to admonish me."
Xuānzǐ had a pair of rings,
one of which was with a merchant of Zhèng.
Xuānzǐ requested it from the Earl of Zhèng.
Zǐchǎn did not give it,
saying:
"It is not a ritual vessel kept in the government offices,
and my humble ruler does not know of it."
Zǐtàishū and Zǐyǔ said to Zǐchǎn:
"Lord Hán does not ask for much,
and we cannot be disloyal to the state of Jìn.
The state of Jìn and Lord Hán must not be treated lightly.
If slanderers should provoke trouble between us,
and ghosts and spirits assist them
to stir up his fierce anger,
how can regrets be of use?
Why do you, my master, begrudge one ring,
and thus incur the hatred of a great state?
Why not seek it and give it to him?"
Zǐchǎn said:
"It is not that I treat Jìn lightly or have double-heartedness;
I intend to serve them to the end.
That is why I do not give it,
for the sake of loyalty and trustworthiness.
Qiáo has heard that for a gentleman, it is not the lack of wealth that is a difficulty,
but the worry of standing without a good reputation.
Qiáo has heard that for governing a state, it is not the difficulty of being unable to serve the great or nurture the small,
but the worry of lacking rites to stabilize its position.
If the people of a great state give orders to a small state
and always obtain what they request,
how will we supply them?
If we provide once and refuse another,
the offense will be even greater.
If the requests of a great state
are not rejected using rites,
what satiety could there be?
If I were to act like a lowly border town,
then I would lose my position.
If Lord Hán receives an order to go on a mission
and requests a jade there,
his greed and excess are extreme;
is that not indeed a crime?
To give one jade and thus provoke two crimes,
while I also lose my position
and Lord Hán perfects his greed,
what use would that be?
Furthermore, if I were to use jade to buy a crime,
would that not be very foolish?"
Lord Hán bought it from the merchants,
and the price was already settled.
The merchant said:
"I must inform the ruler and the Grand Officers!"
Lord Hán requested of Zǐchǎn, saying:
"I, Qǐ, previously requested that ring;
the executive officer did not consider it right,
and I did not dare to ask again.
Now I have bought it from a merchant,
but the merchant says
it must be reported;
so I venture to make this request."
Zǐchǎn replied:
"Formerly, our late ruler Duke Huángōng and the merchants both came from Zhōu.
Together they worked and partnered to clear this land,
cutting down the mugwort, wormwood, pigweed, and goosefoot,
and dwelt here together.
For generations there have been oaths and covenants
to trust one another,
saying:
'You shall not rebel against me,
and I shall not force a sale,
nor shall there be any begging or seizing.
If you have profitable markets or precious goods,
I shall not interfere with them.'"
Relying on this pledge,
they have been able to preserve each other until now.
Now you have come to visit in friendship,
yet you say my humble state has forcibly taken a merchant's jade.
This is teaching my humble state to betray its covenant;
would that not be unacceptable?
If you obtain the jade
but lose the support of the feudal lords,
you surely will not do it.
If a great state issues a command
and its demands are limitless,
Zhèng is a border state,
and will also not do it.
If I, Qiáo, were to present the jade,
I would not know what end it would achieve.
I venture to state this privately."
Hánzǐ declined the jade,
saying,
"I, Qǐ, am not clever.
How could I dare seek the jade and thereby incur two crimes?
I venture to decline it."
In the fourth month of summer,
the six ministers of Zhèng gave a farewell banquet for Xuānzǐ in the outskirts.
Xuānzǐ said,
"Gentlemen, please each recite a poem,
so that I, Qǐ, may also know the intent of Zhèng."
Zǐchī recited "The Creeping Grass of the Wild."
Xuānzǐ said,
"Young man, excellent!
I have hope."
Zǐchǎn recited the Zhèng poem "The Lambskin Robe."
Xuānzǐ said,
"I, Qǐ, am not worthy of it."
Zǐdàshū recited "Lifting the Skirts."
Xuānzǐ said,
"I, Qǐ, am right here;
would I dare trouble you for someone else?"
Zǐdàshū bowed.
Xuānzǐ said,
"Excellent!
Your words are correct!
Without this matter,
how could we have reached an end?"
Zǐyóu recited "Wind and Rain."
Zǐqí recited "A Lady in the Same Carriage."
Zǐliǔ recited "Falling Leaves."
Xuānzǐ was pleased
and said,
"Zhèng is nearly there!
You gentlemen bestowed gifts on me, Qǐ, by your ruler's command.
The poems did not stray from the intent of Zhèng;
they were all intimate and friendly.
You gentlemen
are the masters of several generations;
you can be without fear."
Xuānzǐ presented horses to all of them
and recited "I Will Offer."
Zǐchǎn bowed
and had the five ministers all bow,
saying,
"You have quelled disorder.
How could we dare not bow to your virtue!"
Xuānzǐ privately visited Zǐchǎn with jade and horses,
saying,
"You commanded me, Qǐ, to give up that jade.
This was like giving me the jade and sparing me from death.
How could I dare not use these gifts to bow in thanks!"
B10.16.4 The Duke arrived from Jìn.
Zǐfú Zhāobó said to Jì Píngzǐ,
"The ducal house of Jìn is about to become lowly.
The ruler is young and weak;
the six ministers are powerful, extravagant, and arrogant.
They will continue in these habits;
habits become regular practice.
How can it not become lowly?"
Píngzǐ said,
"You are young.
How do you understand state affairs?"
B10.16.5 In the eighth month of autumn,
Duke Zhāo of Jìn died.
B10.16.6 In the ninth month,
the Great Rain Sacrifice was performed
because of drought.
There was a great drought in Zhèng.
They sent Tújī, Zhùkuǎn, and Shùfù to perform sacrifices at Sāng Shān.
They cut down the trees there,
but it did not rain.
Zǐchǎn said,
"Performing sacrifices at a mountain
is to nourish its forests;
yet they cut down its trees;
their crime is great."
He stripped them of their offices and lands.
B10.16.7 In the tenth month of winter,
Jì Píngzǐ went to Jìn
for the burial of Duke Zhāo.
Píngzǐ said,
"The words of Zǐfú Huí were indeed true.
The Zǐfú clan has a worthy son!"
A10.17 Annals of the Seventeenth Year of Duke Zhāo
A10.17.1 In the spring of the seventeenth year,
the Viscount of Xiǎozhū came to court.
A10.17.2 In the sixth month of summer, on the first day of the moon, jiǎxū,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A10.17.3 In autumn,
the Viscount of Tán came to court.
A10.17.4 In the eighth month,
Xún Wú of Jìn led an army and destroyed the Róng of Lùhún.
A10.17.5 In winter,
there was a comet in the Great Star constellation.
A10.17.6 The people of Chǔ and Wú fought at Cháng'àn.
B10.17 Commentary for the Seventeenth Year of Duke Zhāo
B10.17.1 In the spring of the seventeenth year,
Duke Mù of Xiǎozhū came to court,
and the Duke held a banquet for him.
Jì Píngzǐ recited "The Gathering of Legumes,"
and Duke Mù recited "Luxuriant is the Wormwood."
Zhāozǐ said,
"Without having a state to rely on,
how could he last long?"
B10.17.2 In the sixth month of summer, on the first day of the moon, jiǎxū,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
The invokers and scribes asked what offerings should be used.
Zhāozǐ said,
"When there is an eclipse of the sun,
the Son of Heaven does not have full meals,
and drums are beaten at the Altar of the Soil.
The feudal lords use offerings at the Altar of the Soil
and beat drums at the court.
This is the ritual."
Píngzǐ opposed this,
saying,
"Stop.
Only on the first day of the first month,
when evil influences have not yet arisen,
if there is a solar eclipse,
then are drums beaten and offerings used.
This is the ritual.
For other months, it is not so."
The Grand Scribe said,
"It is in this month.
When the sun passes the equinox but has not reached the solstice,
if the three luminaries suffer a calamity,
then all the officials reduce their regalia;
the ruler does not have full meals
and moves from his main hall for the duration of the eclipse;
musicians beat the drums,
invokers use offerings,
and scribes use prayers.
Therefore, the Book of Xià says:
'When the celestial bodies are not in harmony in Fáng,
the blind musicians beat the drums,
the junior officers gallop about,
and the common people run.'
This refers to the first day of this month.
This corresponds to the fourth month of the Xià calendar,
which is called the first month of summer."
Píngzǐ did not follow this.
Zhāozǐ withdrew
and said,
"That gentleman will have rebellious intentions;
he does not treat the ruler as a ruler."
B10.17.3 In autumn,
the Viscount of Tán came to court,
and the Duke held a banquet for him.
Zhāozǐ asked him,
saying,
"Why did Shǎohào name his officials after birds?"
The Viscount of Tán said,
"He was my ancestor;
I know it.
Formerly, the Huángdì clan used clouds to record events;
thus he established cloud-officers and named them after clouds.
Yándì used fire to record events;
thus he established fire-officers and named them after fire.
Gònggōng used water to record events;
thus he established water-officers and named them after water.
Tàihào used dragons to record events;
thus he established dragon-officers and named them after dragons.
When my high ancestor Shǎohào Zhì ascended,
phoenixes happened to arrive;
thus he recorded things by birds,
establishing bird-officers and naming them after birds:
The Fèngniǎo clan
were the masters of the calendar;
the Xuánniǎo clan
were those in charge of the equinoxes."
The Bózhào clan
were the overseers of arrivals;
the Qīngniǎo clan
were the overseers of beginnings;
the Dānniǎo clan
were the overseers of closings.
The Zhùjiū clan
were the Sītú;
the Jūjiū clan
were the Sīmǎ;
the Shījiū clan
were the Sīkōng;
the Shuǎngjiū clan
were the Sīkòu;
the Gǔjiū clan
were the Sīshì.
These five Jiū
were those who managed the people.
The five Zhì served as the five Gōngzhèng,
who made tools effective and standardized measures,
thereby stabilizing the people.
The nine Hù served as the nine Nóngzhèng,
who prevented the people from becoming profligate.
Since the time of Zhuānxū,
because they could no longer record by distant things,
they recorded by what was near.
They served as teachers to the people and named offices after human affairs
because they could no longer do as before.
Zhòngní heard of this,
visited Tán Zǐ and learned from him.
Afterward, he told others:
"I have heard that
'when the Son of Heaven loses his offices,
the learning of the offices is found among the four Yí,'
which is still true."
B10.17.4 Jìn Hóu sent Tú Kuài to Zhōu,
to request sacrifices at the Luò and Sāntú.
Cháng Hóng said to Liú Zǐ:
"The guest's expression is fierce;
it is not for a sacrifice,
he will surely attack the Róng!
The Lùhún clan is very harmonious with Chǔ;
this must be the reason.
You, my lord, should prepare for it!"
Thus he alerted the defenses against the Róng.
In the ninth month, on the day Dīngmǎo,
Xún Wú of Jìn led the army to cross from Jíjīn,
sending sacrificial scribes to first offer victims at the Luò.
The people of Lùhún did not know,
and the army followed them.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
they then destroyed Lùhún,
reproaching them for their double-dealing with Chǔ.
Lùhún Zǐ fled to Chǔ,
and his followers fled to Gānlù.
Zhōu made great gains.
Xuānzǐ dreamed that Wén Gōng took Xún Wú by the hand and gave him Lùhún;
therefore he sent Mùzǐ to lead the army
and present captives at the Temple of Wén Gōng.
B10.17.5 In winter,
a comet appeared in Dàchén,
reaching west to the Hàn.
Shēn Xū said:
"A comet is that by which the old is removed and the new is spread.
Heavenly affairs always show signs;
now it removes in Fire.
When Fire emerges, it will surely spread;
will the feudal lords suffer fire disasters?"
Zǐ Shèn said:
"In former years I saw it;
this is the sign.
Fire emerged and was seen;
this year Fire emerges and is brilliant.
It will surely hide when Fire sets.
It has resided in Fire for a long time;
could it be otherwise?
When Fire emerges,
it is the third month for the Xià,
the fourth month for the Shāng,
and the fifth month for the Zhōu.
The Xià numbering accords with Heaven.
If fire breaks out,
the four states will be affected:
Sòng, Wèi, Chén, or Zhèng!
Sòng
is the ruin of Dàchén;
Chén
is the ruin of Dàhào;
Zhèng
is the ruin of Zhùróng;
all are fire chambers.
The comet reached the Hàn;
the Hàn
is an omen of water.
Wèi
is the ruin of Zhuānxū,
thus called Dìqiū.
Its star is Great Water.
Water
is the conqueror of fire.
Will it break out on the day Bǐngzǐ or Rénwǔ?
These are where water and fire meet.
If fire sets and hides,
it must be on Rénwǔ,
not exceeding the month in which it appeared."
Bì Zào of Zhèng said to Zǐchǎn:
"Sòng, Wèi, Chén, and Zhèng will have fires on the same day.
If I am given the Guànjiǎ jade libation cups and jade ladles,
Zhèng will surely not have fire."
Zǐchǎn did not give them.
B10.17.6 Wú attacked Chǔ.
Yáng Gài was the Lìngyǐn.
He divined about the battle
and it was not auspicious.
Sīmǎ Zǐyú said:
"We have the upper stream;
why would it be inauspicious?
Furthermore, in Chǔ's tradition,
the Sīmǎ commands the tortoise.
I request to re-divine."
The command said:
"I, Fáng, with my subordinates will die for it;
let the Chǔ army follow us,
and may they greatly overcome them!"
It was auspicious.
They fought at Cháng'àn.
Zǐyú died first;
the Chǔ army followed
and greatly defeated the Wú army,
capturing their royal boat, the Yúhuáng.
They ordered the people of Suí and those who arrived later to guard it,
digging a trench around it
down to the springs,
filling the passage with charcoal,
and arraying themselves to await orders.
Gōngzǐ Guāng of Wú made a request to his followers,
saying:
"Losing the royal boat of the former kings
is not only the crime of Guāng;
you all share in it.
I ask to borrow your strength to retake it and save ourselves from death."
The followers agreed.
He sent three men with long whiskers to hide by the side of the boat,
saying:
"When I call 'Yúhuáng,'
then answer."
The army followed him by night.
He called three times,
and they all answered in turn.
The Chǔ people followed the sounds to kill them.
The Chǔ army fell into disorder,
and the Wú people greatly defeated them,
taking the Yúhuáng and returning with it.
A10.18 The Annals of Zhāo Gōng's Eighteenth Year
A10.18.1 In the spring of the eighteenth year,
in the King's third month,
Cáo Bó Xū died.
A10.18.2 In summer, the fifth month, on the day Rénwǔ,
Sòng, Wèi,
Chén, and Zhèng suffered disasters.
A10.18.3 In the sixth month,
the people of Zhū entered Yǔ.
A10.18.4 In autumn,
they buried Cáo Píng Gōng.
A10.18.5 In winter,
Xǔ moved to Báiyǔ.
B10.18 The Commentary for Zhāo Gōng's Eighteenth Year
B10.18.1 In the spring of the eighteenth year,
in the King's second month, on the day Yǐmǎo,
Máo Dé of Zhōu killed Máo Bó Guò
and replaced him.
Cháng Hóng said:
"Máo Dé will surely perish.
This is the day when Kūnwú reached the peak of ripeness,
by account of following extravagance.
Yet Máo Dé uses it to achieve extravagance in the royal capital;
if he does not perish,
what is he waiting for?"
B10.18.2 In the third month,
Cáo Píng Gōng died.
B10.18.3 In summer, the fifth month,
the Fire star first appeared at dusk.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
there was wind.
Zǐ Shèn said:
"This is called the Róng Wind,
which is the beginning of fire;
in seven days,
will the fire break out?"
On the day of Wùyín,
the wind was strong.
On the day of Rénwǔ,
it was even stronger.
Sòng, Wèi, Chén, and Zhèng all caught fire.
Zǐ Shèn climbed the storehouse of the Dàtíng clan to observe them
and said:
"It is Sòng, Wèi, Chén, and Zhèng."
A few days later, they all came to report the fires.
Bì Zào said:
"If my words are not followed,
Zhèng will catch fire again."
The people of Zhèng asked to follow his advice,
but Zǐchǎn would not allow it.
Zǐ Dàshū said:
"Treasures are used to protect the people;
if there is a fire,
the state will nearly perish.
If they can save it from ruin,
why should you begrudge them?"
Zǐchǎn said:
"The Way of Heaven is distant,
while the Way of Man is near;
it is not something one can reach.
How can one know it?
How does Zào know the Way of Heaven?
This is also just talkative speech;
might it not occasionally come true by chance?"
Consequently, he did not grant the request.
There was no further fire.
Before Zhèng was struck by the disaster,
Lǐ Xī told Zǐchǎn:
"There will be a great omen;
the people will be shaken,
and the state will nearly perish.
My life is coming to an end,
so I will not live to see it.
If the state moves,
might that be possible?"
Zǐchǎn said:
"Even if it were possible,
I am not sufficient to determine a move."
When the fire occurred,
Lǐ Xī had already died;
he was not yet buried.
Zǐchǎn had thirty men move his coffin.
When the fire broke out,
Zǐchǎn took leave of the princes and grandsons of Jìn at the East Gate,
ordered the Minister of Justice to send out the new guests,
and forbade the old guests from leaving the palace.
He ordered Zǐ Kuān and Zǐ Shàng to patrol the various screens and gates
up to the Great Palace.
He ordered Gōngsūn Dēng to move the great tortoise shell.
He ordered the invokers and scribes to move the ancestral tablets to the Zhōu temple
and report to the former lords.
He ordered the treasury and storehouse officials to each be vigilant in their duties.
Shāng Chénggōng alerted the palace stewards,
brought out the former palace ladies,
and placed them where the fire could not reach.
The Minister of War and Minister of Justice stationed themselves along the path of the fire
to inspect the areas being scorched.
The people from below the city walls were organized into squads to mount the walls.
The next day,
he ordered the rural Ministers of Justice to each protect their districts.
The people of the suburbs assisted the invokers and scribes
in performing purification rituals north of the capital,
exorcising the fire to Xuánmíng and Huílù,
and praying at the four city altars.
He recorded the burned houses and reduced their taxes,
and provided them with timber.
For three days there was ritual wailing,
and the state markets were closed.
He sent the messengers to inform the feudal lords.
Sòng and Wèi did the same.
Chén did not save its people from the fire,
and Xǔ did not offer condolences for the disaster;
the gentleman thereby knew that Chén and Xǔ would be the first to perish.
B10.18.4 In the sixth month,
while the people of Yǔ were weeding the rice fields,
the people of Zhū launched a surprise attack on Yǔ.
The people of Yǔ were about to close the gates,
but Yáng Luó of Zhū seized the lead at the gate,
and they entered,
capturing everyone before returning.
The Viscount of Yǔ said:
"I have nowhere to return to."
He followed his wife and children to Zhū.
Duke Zhuāng of Zhū sent back the Lady of Yǔ
but kept her daughter.
B10.18.5 In autumn,
Duke Píng of Cáo was buried.
Those who went saw Yuán Bólǔ of Zhōu there
and spoke with him;
he showed no delight in learning.
Upon returning, they spoke of this to Mǐnzǐ Mǎ.
Mǐnzǐ Mǎ said:
"Zhōu will surely fall into disorder!
There must be many such opinions
before they reach the high officials.
When high officials fear loss and are deluded,
and they further say:
'One can do without learning,
for not learning does no harm.'
If they do not learn because they believe it does no harm,
then they will act as they please.
Thus those below will insult those above and those above will neglect their duties;
can there be no disorder?
Learning
is like cultivation.
If one does not learn, they will wither;
the Yuán clan will surely perish!"
B10.18.6 In the seventh month,
because of the fire, Zǐchǎn of Zhèng
performed a great sacrifice to the Altar of the Soil,
performed exorcisms in the four directions,
and performed purification to remove the fire disaster;
this was in accordance with ritual.
Then he reviewed the troops and held a great hunt,
intending to clear the land for the hunt.
Zǐ Dàshū’s ancestral temple was south of the road,
and his living quarters were north of the road;
the courtyard was small.
After three days had passed,
the laborers were ordered to line up at the temple north of the southern road,
saying:
"Zǐchǎn is passing by you
and has ordered a quick clearing,
thus we must demolish your neighborhood."
When Zǐchǎn went to court,
he passed by and was angry with them.
The laborers were demolishing to the south.
When Zǐchǎn reached the intersection,
he had his followers stop them,
saying:
"Demolish to the north."
When the fire broke out,
Zǐchǎn handed out weapons and mounted the parapets.
Zǐ Dàshū said:
"Will Jìn not punish us?"
Zǐchǎn said:
"I have heard that
a small state is in danger if it forgets its defense,
