how much more so when there is a disaster?
That a state cannot be belittled
is because it has preparation."
Later,
the border officials of Jìn reprimanded Zhèng, saying:
"The state of Zhèng has a disaster;
the Lord of Jìn and his Grand Officers did not dare to live in peace.
They performed divinations and sacrifices to the distant mountains and rivers,
and did not spare sacrificial animals or jade.
That Zhèng has a disaster
is our ruler's grief.
Now you officials have sternly handed out weapons and mounted the parapets;
who do you intend to incriminate?
The border people are terrified
and did not dare not to report it."
Zǐchǎn replied:
"As you have said,
the disaster of our humble city
is the ruler's grief.
Our humble city lost its proper government,
so Heaven sent down this disaster.
We also feared that slanderous and evil people might plot in the interval
to entice greedy people
to repeatedly bring disadvantage to our humble city,
thereby doubling the ruler's grief.
If by good fortune we do not perish,
it can still be explained;
but if by misfortune we perish,
though the ruler grieves for it,
it will be too late.
Since Zhèng has other borders,
our sacrifices and appeals are directed toward Jìn.
Having served Jìn,
how could we dare to have double-mindedness?"
B10.18.7 Wángzǐ Shèng, the Left Minister of Chǔ, said to the Viscount of Chǔ:
"Xǔ is a rival
to Zhèng,
yet it resides in Chǔ's land
and is disrespectful to Zhèng.
Jìn and Zhèng are currently on good terms.
If Zhèng attacks Xǔ
and Jìn assists them,
Chǔ will lose land.
Why should the ruler not move Xǔ?
Xǔ is not devoted solely to Chǔ,
and Zhèng currently has good governance.
Xǔ says:
'It is our old state.'
Zhèng says:
'It is our captive city.'
Shè is in the state of Chǔ,
serving as a screen outside the Fāngchéng Mountains."
"The land cannot be easily changed,
the state cannot be made small,
Xǔ cannot be treated as captives,
enmity cannot be initiated;
may the Jūn consider it!"
Chǔzǐ was pleased.
In winter,
Chǔzǐ sent Wángzǐ Shèng to move Xǔ to Xī,
which was in fact Báiyǔ.
A10.19 Zhāo Gōng Nineteenth Year Classic
A10.19.1 In the spring of the nineteenth year,
Sòng Gōng invaded Zhū.
A10.19.2 In summer, in the fifth month on the day wùchén,
Xǔ Shìzǐ Zhǐ murdered his Jūn, Mǎi.
A10.19.3 On the day jǐmǎo,
there was an earthquake.
A10.19.4 In autumn,
Qí Gāo Fā led an army to invade Jǔ.
A10.19.5 In winter,
Xǔ Dào Gōng was buried.
B10.19 Zhāo Gōng Nineteenth Year Commentary
B10.19.1 In the spring of the nineteenth year,
Chǔ Gōngyǐn Chì moved Yīn to Xiàyīn,
and Lìngyǐn Zǐxiá walled Jiá.
Shúsūn Zhāozǐ said:
"Chǔ is no longer among the Zhūhóu;
it is merely seeking to preserve itself
to maintain its generations."
B10.19.2 When Chǔzǐ was in Cài,
the daughter of the border warden of Jùyáng fled to him,
and she gave birth to Dàzǐ Jiàn.
When he ascended the throne,
he appointed Wǔ Shē as his teacher
and Fèi Wújí as Shǎoshī.
Fèi had no favor there
and wished to slander the prince to the Wáng,
saying:
"Jiàn can now have a household."
The Wáng sought a bride for him in Qín.
Wújí went along to meet her
and urged the Wáng to take her for himself.
In the first month,
the Chǔ Fūrén of the Yíng Shì arrived from Qín.
B10.19.3 Yǔ Fūrén
was the daughter of Sòng Xiàng Xù;
therefore Xiàng Níng requested an army.
In the second month,
Sòng Gōng invaded Zhū
and besieged Chóng.
In the third month,
he took it
and then returned all the captives of Yǔ.
B10.19.4 In summer,
Xǔ Dào Gōng suffered from malaria.
On the day wùchén of the fifth month,
he died after drinking medicine from Dàzǐ Zhǐ.
The Dàzǐ fled to Jìn.
The record says,
"He murdered his Jūn."
The superior man says:
"In serving a Jūn with all one's heart and strength,
it is permissible to omit the medicine."
B10.19.5 The people of Zhū, Ní, and Xú met with Sòng Gōng.
On the day yǐhài,
they made a covenant at Chóng.
B10.19.6 Chǔzǐ prepared a naval force to invade Pú.
Fèi Wújí spoke to Chǔzǐ, saying:
"The hegemony of Jìn
is near the various Xià states,
while Chǔ is remote and rustic;
therefore we cannot compete with them.
If you build a large wall at Chéngfù
and station the Dàzǐ there
to open communication with the north,
while the Wáng secures the south,
then the world will be gained."
The Wáng was pleased
and followed this.
Therefore Dàzǐ Jiàn resided in Chéngfù.
Lìngyǐn Zǐxiá went on a mission to Qín
to express thanks for the Fūrén.
B10.19.7 In autumn,
Qí Gāo Fā led an army to invade Jǔ.
Jǔzǐ fled to Jǐzhāng.
He sent Sūn Shū to attack it.
Previously,
there was a woman in Jǔ
whose husband Jǔzǐ had killed;
she had become a widow.
When she was old,
she took refuge in Jǐzhāng
and spun thread there to measure the wall and then left it hanging.
When the army arrived,
she threw it outside.
Someone presented it to Zǐzhān;
Zǐzhān ordered the army to use ropes to climb the wall at night.
Sixty men had climbed up
when the ropes broke.
The army beat drums and shouted,
and those on the wall also shouted.
Jǔ Gòng Gōng was terrified,
opened the west gate, and went out.
On the day bǐngzǐ of the seventh month,
the Qí army entered Jǐ.
B10.19.8 In this year,
Zhèng Sì Yǎn died.
Zǐyóu had married the daughter of a Jìn Dàfū,
and she gave birth to Sī.
He was young;
his paternal elders established Zǐxiá.
Zǐ產 detested his character
and considered it improper;
he did not permit it,
yet he did not stop it.
The Sì Shì was alarmed.
Another day,
Sī reported this to his maternal uncle.
In winter,
the people of Jìn sent an envoy with gifts to Zhèng
to ask the reason for the establishment of Sì Qǐ.
The Sì Shì was afraid.
Sì Qǐ wanted to flee,
but Zǐchǎn would not let him go;
he requested a tortoise shell for divination,
but Zǐchǎn would not give it either.
The Dàfū planned a reply,
but Zǐchǎn, without waiting, replied to the guest:
"The state of Zhèng is unfortunate.
Several ministers of our Jūn have died of epidemics and untimely deaths,
and now we have also lost our late Dàfū Yǎn.
His son is young and weak.
One or two of his paternal elders, fearing the loss of the lineage head,
consulted privately within the clan
and established the elder relative.
Our Jūn and his ministers said:
'Indeed, Heaven has truly ruined and disordered this;
what do we know of it?'
The proverb says,
'Do not pass through the gate of disorder.'
When the people face weapons
and disorder, they still fear to pass it;
how much more would we dare to interfere with what Heaven has disordered?
Now that you, Dàfū, ask for the reason,
our Jūn truly does not dare to know;
who indeed could know?
At the meeting of Píngqiū,
your Jūn renewed the old covenant, saying,
'Let no one fail in their duties!'
If our Jūn's ministers,
upon their death,
must have their positions controlled by the Dàfū of Jìn,
then this would be a Xiànbǐ of Jìn;
what kind of state would it be?"
He declined the guest's gifts and sent back the envoy.
The people of Jìn dropped the matter.
B10.19.9 The people of Chǔ walled Zhōulái.
Shěnyǐn Xū said:
"The people of Chǔ will surely be defeated.
Formerly, when Wú destroyed Zhōulái,
Zǐqí requested to attack them.
The Wáng said,
'I have not yet comforted my people.'
Now it is the same,
yet they wall Zhōulái to provoke Wú;
how can they avoid defeat?"
An attendant said:
"The Wáng has been tireless in his generosity;
he has rested the people for five years.
This can be called comforting them."
Xū said:
"I have heard that those who comfort the people
practice economy within
and establish virtue without,
so that the people find joy in their nature
and have no enemies.
Now the palaces are built without limit,
the people are daily terrified,
exhausted even unto death in the ditches,
forgetting sleep and food;
this is not comforting them."
B10.19.10 There was a great flood in Zhèng.
Dragons fought in the Wěi Pool outside the Shímén Gate.
The people of the capital requested to perform a sacrifice to avert the calamity.
Zǐchǎn would not allow it,
saying:
"If we fight,
the dragons do not watch us.
When dragons fight,
"Why should I alone see them?
To perform a ritual of exorcism for them,
then that is their chamber.
I have no request for the dragons,
and the dragons also have no request for me."
So it was stopped.
B10.19.11 Lìngyǐn Zǐxiá spoke of Juéyóu to the Viscount of Chǔ,
saying:
"What crime has he?
The proverb says,
'If one is angry in the house, one shows it in the marketplace.'
That
describes Chǔ.
It is better to set aside your previous anger."
Thereupon, Juéyóu was sent back.
A10.20 The Annals of Duke Zhāo, Twentieth Year.
A10.20.1 In the spring of the twentieth year,
the King's first month.
A10.20.2 In the summer,
Gōngsūn Huì of Cáo went from Méng to flee to Sòng.
A10.20.3 In the autumn,
brigands killed Zhì, the elder brother of the Marquis of Wèi.
A10.20.4 In the tenth month of winter,
Huá Hài,
Xiàng Níng,
and Huá Dìng fled to Chén.
A10.20.5 On the xìnmǎo day of the eleventh month,
Lú, the Marquis of Cài, died.
B10.20 The Zuo Commentary on Duke Zhāo, Twentieth Year.
B10.20.1 In the spring of the twentieth year,
on the jǐchǒu day of the King's second month,
the sun reached its southernmost point.
Zǐshèn observed the atmospheric vapors
and said:
"This year there will be disorder in Sòng,
and the state will nearly be lost;
only after three years will it be quelled.
There will be a great mourning in Cài."
Shūsūn Zhāozǐ said:
"In that case, it will be the Dài
and Huán families.
They are extravagant and overbearing,
and their lack of ritual is extreme;
that is where disorder resides."
B10.20.2 Fèi Wújì said to the Viscount of Chǔ:
"Jiàn and Wǔ Shē are going to use the lands outside of Fāngchéng to rebel.
They consider themselves like Sòng
and Zhèng,
and Qí and Jìn are also assisting them in turn.
They intend to harm Chǔ,
and their plan is nearly complete."
The King believed him
and questioned Wǔ Shē.
Wǔ Shē replied:
"Your Lordship has already made many errors;
why do you believe in slander?"
The King arrested Wǔ Shē
and sent Fèn Yáng, the Sīmǎ of Chéngfù, to kill the Crown Prince.
Before he arrived,
he sent someone to let him escape.
In the third month,
Crown Prince Jiàn fled to Sòng.
The King summoned Fèn Yáng,
and Fèn Yáng had the people of Chéngfù bind him to bring him there.
The King said:
"The words came out of my mouth
and entered your ears;
who told Jiàn?"
He replied:
"I told him.
My Lord and King commanded me, saying,
'Serve Jiàn as you serve me.'
Your servant is not clever
and could not be careless and deceitful.
Having received the first command to return to his service,
I could not bear the later command;
therefore, I sent him away.
Afterwards I regretted it,
but it was already too late."
The King said:
"And yet you dared to come;
why?"
He replied:
"To fail my mission when sent
and to fail to come when summoned,
that would be a second transgression.
If I fled, there would be nowhere for me to enter."
The King said:
"Return,
and attend to the government as in former days."
Wújì said:
"The sons of Shē are talented;
if they are in Wú,
they will certainly trouble the state of Chǔ.
Why not summon them by promising to spare their father?
They are humane;
they will certainly come.
Otherwise,
they will become a threat."
The King sent someone to summon them,
saying:
"Come,
and I will spare your father."
Wǔ Shàng, the Governor of Táng, said to his younger brother Yuán:
"You go to Wú;
I will return and die.
I know my wisdom is insufficient;
I can die,
but you can seek vengeance.
Hearing a command to spare our father,
one cannot fail to rush to him;
when one's kin are about to be executed,
one cannot fail to seek vengeance.
To rush to die to spare one's father
is filial piety;
to act after weighing the outcome
is benevolence;
to choose a task and go to it
is wisdom;
to know death and not avoid it
is courage.
Our father cannot be abandoned;
our reputation cannot be discarded.
You must exert yourself!
Each following his path is better."
Wǔ Shàng returned.
Shē, hearing that Yuán did not come,
said:
"The King of Chǔ
and his high officials will surely eat their evening meal late!"
The people of Chǔ killed them both.
Yuán went to Wú
and spoke of the benefits of attacking Chǔ to Zhōu Yú.
Prince Guāng said:
"His clan has been executed,
and he wishes to turn back against his enemy;
his advice cannot be followed."
Yuán said:
"That man has other ambitions;
for the time being, I will seek a man of service for him,
and wait for him in the countryside."
He then introduced Zhuàn Shèzhū to him
and went to farm in the countryside.
B10.20.3 Duke Yuán of Sòng was untrustworthy and full of personal favors,
and he hated the Huá and Xiàng families.
Huá Dìng, Huá Hài, and Xiàng Níng plotted, saying:
"Fleeing is better than dying;
shall we strike first?"
Huá Hài feigned illness
to lure the various princes.
When the princes came to inquire after him,
he then seized them.
In the summer, on the bǐngshēn day of the sixth month,
they killed Prince Yín, Prince Yùróng,
Prince Zhū, Prince Gù,
Gōngsūn Yuán, and Gōngsūn Dīng,
and confined Xiàng Shèng and Xiàng Xíng in their granary.
The Duke went to the Huá residence to plead with them;
they did not grant his request,
and then they took him hostage.
On the guǐmǎo day,
they took Crown Prince Luán, his brother by the same mother Chén,
and Prince Dì as hostages.
The Duke also took Huá Hài's son Wúqī,
Xiàng Níng's son Luó, and Huá Dìng's son Qǐ,
and made a covenant with the Huá family,
taking them as hostages.
B10.20.4 Gōngmèng Zhì of Wèi treated Qí Bào with contempt,
seizing from him the office of Sīkòu and the lands of Juàn.
When there was a service to perform, he would return them;
when there was none, he would take them back.
Gōngmèng disliked Běigōng Xǐ
and Chǔshī Pǔ,
and wished to remove them.
Prince Zhāo was having an affair with the Duchess Xuān Jiāng,
was afraid,
and wished to cause an insurrection.
Therefore, Qí Bào, Běigōng Xǐ,
Chǔshī Pǔ, and Prince Zhāo started a rebellion.
Earlier,
Qí Bào had recommended Zōng Lǔ to Gōngmèng,
and he served as his chariot attendant.
When Qí was about to start the rebellion,
he said to him:
"The wickedness of Gōngmèng
is known to you;
do not ride with him,
for I am going to kill him."
He replied:
"I served Gōngmèng because of you,
and you used my name for your ends;
therefore, he did not keep me at a distance.
Although he is not good,
I also know it;
however, because of the benefit,
I could not leave him,
and this is my fault.
Now to hear of trouble and flee
would be to deceive you.
You proceed with your business;
I will die for him.
Having served you loyally,
I shall return to die for Gōngmèng,
and that will be acceptable."
On the day of Bǐngchén,
the Marquis of Wèi was in Píngshòu.
Gōngmèng had a sacrifice to perform outside the Gàihuò Gate.
The Qízi clan set up a curtain outside the gate
and hid armored soldiers there.
They sent Zhù Wā to place halberds in a cart of firewood to block the gate,
and they sent one chariot to follow Gōngmèng as he went out.
They had Huà Qí drive for Gōngmèng,
and Zōng Lǔ served as the third man on the chariot.
When they reached the middle of the gate,
the Qí clan used halberds to strike Gōngmèng.
Zōng Lǔ shielded him with his back;
his arm was severed,
and the blow hit Gōngmèng’s shoulder.
Both were killed.
The Marquis heard of the rebellion,
mounted a chariot,
and drove in from the Yuè Gate.
Qìng Bǐ drove for the Marquis,
and Gōngnán Chǔ was the third man.
He ordered Huà Yín to ride in the second chariot.
When they reached the palace,
Hóngliú Tuí joined the Marquis as the fourth rider.
The Marquis loaded the treasures and went out.
Chǔshī Zǐshēn met the Marquis at the crossroads of the horse road
and subsequently followed him.
As they passed the Qí clan’s residence,
he ordered Huà Yín to bare his chest
and hold a canopy to cover the opening in the chariot.
The Qí clan shot at the Marquis,
hitting Gōngnán Chǔ in the back,
and the Marquis finally escaped.
Huà Yín closed the outer city gate,
then climbed over it and followed the Marquis.
The Marquis went to Sǐniǎo.
Xī Zhūchú went out through a drain at night
and followed the Marquis on foot.
The Marquis of Qí sent Gōngsūn Qīng on a mission to Wèi.
After he had set out,
he heard of the rebellion in Wèi
and sent someone to ask where the mission should be presented.
The Marquis said:
"As long as I am still within the borders,
I am the ruler of Wèi."
So Gōngsūn Qīng proceeded to perform his duties
and followed him to Sǐniǎo.
He requested to carry out the mission.
The Marquis declined, saying:
"I, a fugitive and unworthy man,
have failed to guard the altars of the state
and am now out in the wilds;
there is no place for you, sir, to fulfill your ruler's command."
The guest said:
"My ruler commanded me in the court, saying,
'Attend upon the officials.'
I dare not neglect this."
The host said:
"If your ruler kindly considers the friendship with my predecessor,
shines upon my humble city,
and stabilizes its altars,
then the ancestral temple is still there."
Thereupon he stopped.
The Marquis of Wèi insisted on seeing him.
Not receiving a formal command for the mission,
the envoy met him with his fine horses,
because he had not yet formally delivered the mission.
The Marquis of Wèi used them as his team of horses.
The guest was about to take the night watch,
but the host declined, saying:
"The worries of a fugitive
should not extend to you, sir;
in the midst of the wilds,
it is not right to trouble your followers.
I venture to decline."
The guest said:
"I, the humble servant of my ruler,
am also a groom to you, my lord.
If I do not fulfill the duty of defending against external threats,
it would be like disregarding my own ruler.
I fear I will not escape punishment;
I ask to perform this to avoid death."
He personally held the bell
and joined the night watch fires all night long.
Qújǐ, the steward of the Qí clan, summoned Běigōng Zǐ.
The steward of the Běigōng clan, who had not been informed,
plotted to kill Qújǐ,
then attacked the Qí clan
and exterminated them.
On the day of Dīngsì, the last day of the month,
the Marquis entered the city
and made a covenant with Běigōng Xǐ on the banks of the Péng River.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day of Wùwǔ, the first day of the month,
he then made a covenant with the people of the capital.
In the eighth month, on the day of Xīnhài,
Prince Zhāo, Chǔshī Pǔ,
Zǐyù Xiāo, and Zǐgāo Fáng fled to Jìn.
In the intercalary month, on the day of Wùchén,
they killed Xuān Jiāng.
The Marquis of Wèi granted Běigōng Xǐ the posthumous title of Zhēnzǐ,
and granted Xī Zhūchú the title of Chéngzǐ,
and gave him the Qí clan's graveyard.
The Marquis of Wèi announced the restoration of peace to Qí,
and also spoke about Zǐshí.
The Marquis of Qí was about to drink wine
and gave rewards to all the grandees, saying:
"This is due to the teachings of you gentlemen."
Yuàn Héjì declined,
saying:
"If I share in the rewards of Qīng,
I must also share in his punishment.
In the Kānggào it says,
'Fathers, sons, and brothers
are not implicated in one another's crimes';
how much more so for the various ministers?
How could I dare to covet the ruler's gift
and thus offend the former kings?"
Qín Zhāng heard that Zōng Lǔ had died
and was going to offer condolences.
Zhòngní said:
"He was the accomplice of the rebel Qí Bào
and the assassin of Mèng Zhì;
why should you offer condolences?
A gentleman does not eat the fruits of wickedness,
does not accept rebellion,
does not let gain corrupt his integrity,
does not treat others with crookedness,
does not cover up unrighteousness,
and does not violate ritual propriety."
B10.20.5 During the rebellion of the Huà and Xiàng clans in Sòng,
Prince Chéng, Gōngsūn Jì, Yuè Shè, Sīmǎ Qiáng, Xiàng Yí, Xiàng Zhèng, Chǔ Jiàn, and Ní Jiǎ fled to Zhèng.
Their followers fought with the Huà clan at Guǐyán
and defeated Prince Chéng.
Prince Chéng went to Jìn.
Huà Hài and his wife
would always wash their hands and feed the princes they held as hostages before eating themselves.
The Duke and his lady would go to the Huà residence every day,
feed the princes, and then return.
Huà Hài was troubled by this
and wanted to return the princes.
Xiàng Níng said:
"It is only because of the lack of trust
that we took the sons as hostages.
If we return them now,
our death will be imminent."
The Duke requested of Huà Fèisuì
that he attack the Huà clan.
He replied:
"I dare not cherish my life,
but would we not be seeking to remove sorrow only to have it grow further?
That is why I am afraid,
but how could I dare not obey your command?"
The Duke said:
"For your sons, life and death are fated;
I cannot bear their disgrace."
In winter, the tenth month,
the Duke killed the hostages of the Huà and Xiàng clans and attacked them.
On the day of Wùchén,
Huà and Xiàng fled to Chén,
and Huà Dēng fled to Wú.
Xiàng Níng wanted to kill the Crown Prince.
Huà Hài said:
"Having offended the ruler and been expelled,
if we then kill his son,
who would take us in?
Moreover, there is merit in returning him."
He sent the Minor Minister of Justice Kēng to return him,
saying:
"Your years are advanced,
and you cannot serve others.
If you take the three princes as hostages,
you will surely be spared."
Once the princes had entered,
Huà Kēng was about to leave from the gate.
The Duke saw him at once,
took his hand,
and said:
"I know you are guiltless;
come in
and return to your position."
The Marquis of Qí had the itch,
which then turned into an intermittent fever,
and for a long time he did not recover.
Many guests from the feudal lords who had come to inquire about his illness were present.
Liáng Qiū Jù and Yì Kuǎn spoke to the Duke, saying:
“Our service to the ghosts and spirits has been abundant,
exceeding that of the former lords.
Now your Lordship is ill,
causing concern to the feudal lords;
this is the fault of the Invoker and the Scribe.
The feudal lords do not know this;
they might say we are irreverent.
Why does your Lordship not execute Invoker Zhù Gù and Scribe Shǐ Yīn to excuse yourself to the guests?”
The Duke was pleased
and told Yàn Zǐ.
Yàn Zǐ said:
“In the past, at the covenant of Sòng,
Qū Jiàn asked Zhào Wǔ about the virtue of Fàn Huì.
Zhào Wǔ said:
‘The affairs of that master’s house were well-ordered;
when he spoke in the state of Jìn Guó,
he exhausted his feelings without selfishness.
When his Invokers and Scribes performed sacrifices,
they presented the truth without shame;
in his household affairs there was no suspicion,
so his Invokers
and Scribes did not offer prayers for personal gain.’
Qū Jiàn told this to King Kāng Wáng.
King Kāng Wáng said:
‘Since spirits and men have no grievances against him,
it is fitting that this master brilliantly assisted five rulers to become leaders of the feudal lords.’ ”
The Duke said:
“Jù and Kuǎn say that I am able to serve the ghosts and spirits,
and therefore wish to execute the Invoker and Scribe;
but you cite these words—for what reason?”
He replied:
“If there is a virtuous ruler,
external and internal affairs are not neglected,
those above and below have no grievances,
and in his actions there are no contrary deeds.
His Invokers and Scribes present the truth,
having no shame in their hearts.
Therefore the ghosts and spirits accept the offerings,
the state receives blessings,
and the Invokers and Scribes share in them.
The reason they enjoy abundant happiness and long life
is that they serve a faithful ruler,
and their words are loyal and faithful to the ghosts and spirits.
But if they happen to encounter an excessive ruler,
who is depraved and wicked internally and externally,
so that those above and below are resentful and ill-affected,
and his actions are perverse and contrary,
following his desires to satisfy his private ends,
with high terraces and deep ponds,
striking bells and dancing girls,
cutting down the strength of the people,
and plundering their wealth
to fulfill his excesses,
showing no care for those who come after;
being violent, cruel, and licentious,
acting lawlessly and without measure,
having no restraint or fear,
not considering slander or vituperation,
and not dreading the ghosts and spirits;
when the spirits are angry and the people are in pain,
and there is no repentance in his heart;
if his Invokers
and Scribes present the truth,
that is to speak of his crimes;
if they cover his faults and recount imaginary beauties,
that is to be false and deceptive.
Whether they advance or retreat, they have no words to offer,
so they resort to emptiness to seek favor.
Therefore the ghosts and spirits do not accept the offerings of that state and send down calamities,
and the Invokers and Scribes share in them.
The reason they die young, in darkness, or are lonely and ill
is that they serve a violent ruler,
and their words are presumptuous and disrespectful to the ghosts and spirits.”
The Duke said:
“Then what is to be done?”
He replied:
“Nothing can be done.
The timber of the mountains and forests
is guarded by the forest-wardens;
the reeds and rushes of the marshes
are guarded by the marsh-guards;
the firewood of the fens
is guarded by the park-keepers;
the salt
and shells of the sea
are guarded by the coastal-officials.
People from the remote districts
enter to follow the government;
at the nearby gates,
their private goods are violently taxed;
the hereditary Great Officers
forcibly exchange their wealth.
The distribution of regulations has no limit,
and levies are gathered without measure;
the palaces are changed daily,
and licentious music is never-ending.
The concubines favored within
plunder at will in the markets;
the ministers favored without
issue false commands in the districts.
Private desires are nurtured and sought;
if not supplied, then punishment follows.
The people are embittered and ill,
and husbands and wives all curse.
If an invocation can be beneficial,
a curse can also be harmful.
From Liáo and Shè to the east,
and Gū and Yóu to the west,
the people are many indeed.
Although one might be good at invokers’ prayers,
how could he overcome the curses of millions of people?
If your Lordship wishes to execute the Invoker and Scribe,
you should first cultivate your virtue and only then can it be done.”
The Duke was pleased,
and ordered the officials to ease the administration,
destroy the barriers,
remove prohibitions,
lighten taxes,
and cancel debts.
In the twelfth month,
the Marquis of Qí hunted in Pèi
and summoned the Gamekeeper with a bow,
but he did not come forward.
The Duke ordered him to be seized.
He excused himself, saying:
“In the hunts of our former lords,
a banner was used to summon Great Officers,
a bow to summon Knights,
and a fur cap to summon the Gamekeeper.
I did not see the fur cap,
and therefore did not dare to come forward.”
Thereupon he was released.
Zhòng Ní said:
“Holding to one’s path is not as good as holding to one’s office.”
Superior men considered this right.
The Marquis of Qí returned from the hunt,
and Yàn Zǐ attended him at Chuán Tái.
Zǐ Yóu came driving fast to the place.
The Duke said:
“Only Liáng Qiū Jù is in harmony with me!”
Yàn Zǐ replied:
“Liáng Qiū Jù is merely the same as you;
how can he be in harmony?”
The Duke said:
“Are harmony and sameness different?”
He replied:
“They are different.
Harmony is like soup.
Water, fire, vinegar, meat-sauce, salt, and plums
are used to cook fish and meat.
They are boiled over firewood,
and the cook harmonizes them,
balancing them with flavors,
making up for what is insufficient
and reducing what is excessive.
The superior man eats it
to calm his mind.
It is the same with ruler and minister.
When there is something the ruler considers right but which has wrong aspects,
the minister presents the wrong aspects to make the right complete.
When there is something the ruler considers wrong but which has right aspects,
the minister presents the right aspects to remove the wrong.
Therefore the government is balanced and not violated,
and the people have no spirit of contention.
Thus the *Shī* says:
‘There is also the harmonious soup,
prepared and balanced.
In the presence of the ancestors we are silent,
and at that time there is no contention.’
The former kings balanced the five flavors and harmonized the five sounds
to calm their minds
and complete their governance.
Sound is also like flavor:
one breath,
two bodies,
three classes,
four items,
five sounds,
six pitch-pipes,
seven notes,
eight winds,
nine songs—
they are used to complete one another.
Clear and turbid, large
and small, short and long, fast and slow,
sad and joyful, hard and soft,
slow and rapid, high and low,
beginning and ending, dense and sparse—
they are used to balance one another.
The superior man listens to them
to calm his mind.
When the mind is calm,
virtue is in harmony.
Therefore the *Shī* says:
"Virtuous reputation without flaw."
Now Jù is not like this.
What the Lord calls "yes,"
Jù also calls "yes";
what the Lord calls "no,"
Jù also calls "no."
If one uses water to supplement water,
who could eat it?
If the qín and sè zithers played only one note,
who could listen to them?
The unacceptability of "identity" is like this."
While drinking and being merry,
the Duke said:
"If from antiquity there were no death,
how great would the joy be!"
Ànzi replied:
"If from antiquity there were no death,
then it would be the joy of those from antiquity,
and what would you have gained from it?
Formerly the Shuǎngjiū clan first resided in this land,
Jìzé followed them,
the Yǒuféng Bólíng followed them,
the Púgū clan followed them,
and only after did Tàigōng follow them.
If from antiquity there were no death,
the joy of the Shuǎngjiū clan
would not be what you desire."
B10.20.9 Zhèng Zǐchǎn fell ill,
and said to Zǐ Dàshū:
"When I die,
you will surely lead the government.
Only the virtuous can use leniency to submit the people;
for the next best, nothing is better than severity.
For fire is fierce,
and the people look upon it and fear it;
therefore few die from it.
Water is weak and soft,
and the people become familiar with it and toy with it;
then many die from it.
Therefore leniency is difficult."
After several months of illness, he passed away.
Dàshū took over the government,
but could not bear to be severe and used leniency.
The state of Zhèng had many bandits,
who robbed people in the marshes of Guànfú.
Dàshū regretted it,
and said:
"Had I followed the Master earlier,
I would not have come to this."
He raised infantry to attack the bandits of Guànfú,
killing them all,
and the banditry slightly subsided.
Zhòngní said:
"Excellent!
If the government is lenient, the people will be disrespectful;
if they are disrespectful, correct them with severity.
If the government is severe, the people will be harmed;
if they are harmed, apply leniency.
Use leniency to supplement severity,
and severity to supplement leniency;
thus the government is in harmony.
The *Shī* says:
'The people are indeed exhausted,
it is hoped they may have a little rest;
favor this Central Kingdom,
to bring peace to the four quarters,'
which is applying leniency.
'Do not follow the deceptive and compliant,
to warn those who are not good;
suppress the bandits and the cruel,
who never fear the light,'
which is correcting with severity.
'Be gentle with those far away and treat those near well,
to stabilize our King,'
which is leveling with harmony.
It also says:
'Neither competing nor rushing,
neither hard nor soft,
spreading the government smoothly and gently,
all blessings gather here,'
which is the ultimate harmony."
When Zǐchǎn died,
Zhòngní heard of it
and wept, saying:
"The legacy of love from antiquity."
A10.21 The Classic of the Twenty-First Year of Duke Zhào.
A10.21.1 In the spring of the twenty-first year,
in the Royal third month,
Duke Píng of Cài was buried.
A10.21.2 In the summer,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Yāng to come on a mission of state.
A10.21.3 Huá Hài,
Xiàng Níng,
and Huá Dìng of Sòng entered the Southern Ward of Sòng from Chén to rebel.
A10.21.4 In the autumn, on the seventh month, on the day rénwǔ, the first day of the moon,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A10.21.5 In the eighth month, on the day yǐhài,
Shū Zhé died.
A10.21.6 In the winter,
Marquis Zhū of Cài fled to Chǔ.
A10.21.7 The Duke went to Jìn,
and returned upon reaching the Hé River.
B10.21 The Commentary of the Twenty-First Year of Duke Zhào.
B10.21.1 In the spring of the twenty-first year,
the Celestial King was about to cast the Wúshè bell.
Líng Zhōuqiū said:
"Will the King not die of heart disease?
Now, music
is the duty of the Son of Heaven.
Sound
is the carriage of music;
and bells
are the vessels of sound.
The Son of Heaven examines the airs to create music,
uses vessels to store it,
and carriages to carry it out.
If the small are not too thin,
and the large are not too overwhelming,
then there is harmony with all things.
When things are in harmony, then excellence is achieved.
Therefore harmonious sounds enter the ear and are stored in the heart;
when the heart is satisfied, there is joy.
If the sound is too thin, it is not all-encompassing;
if it is too overwhelming, it cannot be contained;
thus the heart is distressed,
and distress indeed gives rise to illness.
Now the bell is too overwhelming,
the King's heart cannot endure it;
how can he last long?"
B10.21.2 In the third month,
Duke Píng of Cài was buried.
Crown Prince Zhū of Cài lost his proper place;
his position was among the lowly.
When the high officials who escorted the burial
returned,
they saw Zhāozǐ.
Zhāozǐ asked about the situation in Cài,
and they told him.
Zhāozǐ sighed and said:
"Cài will likely perish!
If it does not perish,
this ruler will surely not reach his end.
The *Shī* says:
'Not remiss in his position,
he is the one the people rest upon.'
Now the Marquis of Cài has just acceded to the throne,
yet he places himself among the lowly;
he will soon follow that position."
B10.21.3 In the summer,
Shì Yāng of Jìn came on a mission of state;
Shúsūn was in charge of the government.
Jìsūn wished to disparage him to Jìn
and ordered the officials to use the rituals of Qí's Bǎo Guó returning the city of Fèi for Shì Yāng.
Shì Yāng was angry
and said:
"Bǎo Guó's rank was low
and his state was small,
yet you make Yāng follow the ritual of his sacrificial animals;
this is to belittle my humble state.
I shall report this to my lord."
The people of Lǔ were afraid
and added four more sets of sacrificial animals,
making eleven sets in total.
B10.21.4 Huá Fèisuì of Sòng fathered Huá Chū, Huá Duōliáo, and Huá Dēng.
Chū was the Junior Minister of War,
and Duōliáo was an Attendant Officer.
They disliked each other,
so Duōliáo slandered Chū to the Duke, saying:
"Chū is about to bring back the exiles."
He said this repeatedly.
The Duke said:
"The Minister of War, for my sake,
lost his good son.
Death and exile are fated;
I cannot make him lose another son."
He replied:
"If your Lordship loves the Minister of War,
then regard it as if he were lost.
If death can be avoided,
what distance is too far?"
The Duke was afraid,
and sent an attendant to summon the Minister of War's attendant Yíliáo,
gave him wine to drink,
and made him inform the Minister of War.
The Sīmǎ sighed and said:
"It must be Duōliáo.
I have a slanderous son
whom I cannot bring myself to kill,
yet I do not die myself.
But the Ruler has a command;
what can be done?"
He then plotted with the Duke to expel Huá Chū,
intending to send him away after having him go to hunt at Mèngzhū.
The Duke gave him wine to drink,
rewarded him generously,
and extended gifts to his followers.
The Sīmǎ did the same.
Zhāng Gài was particularly suspicious of this and said:
"There must be a reason."
He had Zipí hold a sword over Yíliáo to interrogate him.
Yíliáo told everything.
Zhāng Gài wanted to kill Duōliáo.
Zipí said:
"The Sīmǎ is old;
that Huá Dēng was exiled was already extreme;
if I add further to his burden,
it would be better to flee."
In the fifth month, on the day bǐngshēn,
Zipí was about to see the Sīmǎ before departing
when he encountered Duōliáo driving the Sīmǎ to court.
Zhāng Gài could not contain his rage,
and together with Zipí, Jiù Rèn, and Zhèng Pián, he killed Duōliáo,
took the Sīmǎ hostage to rebel,
and summoned the exiles.
On the day rényín,
the Huá and Xiàng families entered.
Yuè Dàxīn, Fēng Qiān, and Huá Kēng resisted them at Héng.
The Huá clan occupied the Lú Gate
and rebelled in Nánlǐ.
In the sixth month, on the day gēngwǔ,
Sòng fortified the old rampart and the Sānglín Gate to defend them.
B10.21.5 In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day rénwǔ, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
The Duke asked Zǐ Shèn:
"What kind of occurrence is this?
What do misfortune and fortune bring?"
He replied: "At the two solstices and the two equinoxes,
an eclipse of the sun
does not cause disaster.
In the movement of the sun and moon,
at the equinoxes,
they share the same path;
at the solstices,
they pass each other.
In other months, it portends disaster,
as the Yáng cannot overcome,
so it usually leads to floods."
Thereupon, Shū Zhé wailed for the solar eclipse.
Zhāozǐ said:
"Zǐshū is about to die;
this is not something to be wailed for."
In the eighth month,
Shū Zhé died.
B10.21.6 In winter, in the tenth month,
Huá Dēng led the forces of Wú to rescue the Huá clan.
Wū Zhīmíng of Qí defended Sòng.
Pú, the cook, said:
"The Jūnjì says:
'The predecessor captures the opponent's spirit;
the successor waits for their decline.'
Why not attack them while they are weary and unsettled?
If they enter and consolidate,
the Huá clan's followers will be numerous,
and regret will come too late."
He followed this advice.
On the day bǐngyín,
the armies of Qí and Sòng defeated the army of Wú at Hóngkǒu,
capturing their two commanders, Gōngzǐ Kǔwén and Yǎnzhōu Yuán.
Huá Dēng led the remnants of his forces to defeat the Sòng army.
The Duke wanted to flee,
but Pú, the cook, said:
"I am a lowly man
who can offer my life,
but I cannot escort an exile.
I beg the Ruler to wait."
He then proclaimed:
"Those who raise the banners
are the Duke's followers."
The crowd followed him.
The Duke saw them from the Yáng Gate,
descended and went among them,
saying:
"That the state is lost and the ruler dead
is a shame for you gentlemen;
is it solely my fault?"
Wū Zhīmíng of Qí said:
"To use a small force, nothing is better than being ready to die;
to be ready to die, nothing is better than removing armor.
They have many long weapons;
I request that everyone use swords."
He followed this.
The Huá clan fled north,
and they pursued them again.
Pú, the cook, wrapped a head in a garment
and carried it on his shoulder as he ran,
shouting:
"I have taken Huá Dēng!"
Thus they defeated the Huá clan at Xīnlǐ.
Zhái Lǚxīn lived at Xīnlǐ;
after the battle,
he removed his armor before the Duke and returned home.
Huá Zhǒu lived at Gōnglǐ;
he also did the same.
In the eleventh month, on the day guǐwèi,
Gōngzǐ Chéng arrived with the army of Jìn.
Cáo Hànhú joined with Xún Wú of Jìn,
Yuàn Héjì of Qí,
and Gōngzǐ Cháo of Wèi to rescue Sòng.
On the day bǐngxū,
they fought the Huá clan at Zhěqiū.
Zhèng Pián wished to use a stork formation;
his charioteer wished to use a goose formation.
Zǐlù drove for Gōngzǐ Chéng,
and Zhuāng Jǐn was the chariot-right.
Gàn Chōu drove for Huá Bào, the border official of Lǚ,
and Zhāng Gài was the chariot-right.
They met,
and Chéng turned back.
Huá Bào said:
"It is Chéng!"
Chéng was angry
and turned back toward him.
When he was about to set his arrow,
Bào had already drawn his bow.
Bào said:
"May the spirit of Duke Píng
still assist me!"
Bào shot,
the arrow passing through the gap.
When Chéng was about to set his arrow,
Bào had drawn his bow again.
Chéng said: "To not take turns shooting
is base."
Bào withdrew his arrow,
and Chéng shot him,
killing him instantly.
Zhāng Gài drew his mace and jumped down;
Chéng shot him,
breaking his thigh.
He crawled and struck at Chéng,
breaking the crossbar of the chariot.
Chéng shot him again,
and he died.
Gàn Chōu requested an arrow;
Chéng said:
"I will speak for you to the Ruler."
He replied:
"Not dying with one's squad or chariot
is the greatest capital offense in the military.
If I violate the law and follow you,
how could the Ruler use me?
You, hasten it!"
Chéng then shot him,
killing him instantly.
They greatly defeated the Huá clan
and besieged them at Nánlǐ.
Huá Hài beat his breast and cried out,
seeing Huá Chū,
and said:
"I have become like the Luán clan!"
Chū said:
"Do not deceive me;
one perishes only after misfortune."
He sent Huá Dēng to Chǔ to beg for troops,
and Huá Chū, with fifteen chariots and seventy foot-soldiers, broke through the army and went out,
ate on the banks of the Suī River,
wept as he saw him off,
and then returned inside.
Wěi Yuè of Chǔ led an army to go and meet the Huá clan;
Grand Chamberlain Fàn remonstrated, saying:
"Among the feudal lords, only Sòng serves its ruler.
Now they are again struggling for the state;
if we abandon the ruler and help the ministers,
would that not be improper?"
The King said:
"You tell me this too late;
I have already promised them."
B10.21.7 Zhū, the Marquis of Cài, fled to Chǔ.
Fèi Wújì took bribes from Dōngguó
and said to the people of Cài:
"Zhū does not follow the orders of Chǔ;
the King will establish Dōngguó.
If you do not follow the King's wishes first,
Chǔ will certainly besiege Cài."
The people of Cài were afraid;
they expelled Zhū and established Dōngguó.
Zhū complained to Chǔ.
The Viscount of Chǔ was about to punish Cài.
Wú Jí said:
"Marquis Píng had an alliance with Chǔ,
therefore he was enfeoffed.
His son has double-minded intentions,
therefore depose him.
King Líng killed the Great Heir Yǐn;
his son shares the same hatred as you,
and he will surely be extremely grateful to you.
If you furthermore establish him,
would that not be acceptable?
Moreover, deposing or establishing lies with you, My Lord;
Cài will have no other intentions."
B10.21.8 The Duke went to Jìn
and reached the River.
Gǔ rebelled against Jìn.
Jìn was about to attack Xiān Yú,
therefore they declined the Duke's visit.
A10.22 Classic of the Twenty-second Year of Lord Zhāo
A10.22.1 In the spring of the twenty-second year,
the Marquis of Qí attacked Jǔ.
A10.22.2 Huà Hài,
Xiàng Níng,
and Huà Dìng of Sòng fled from Nán Lǐ in Sòng to Chǔ.
A10.22.3 A great hunt was held in Chāng Jiān.
A10.22.4 In summer, in the fourth month, on the day yǐchǒu,
the Heavenly King passed away.
A10.22.5 In the sixth month,
Shū Yǎng went to the capital
to bury King Jǐng.
A10.22.6 The Royal House was in disorder.
A10.22.7 The Master of Liú and
the Master of Dān resided in Huáng with King Měng.
A10.22.8 In autumn,
the Master of Liú and
the Master of Dān entered the Royal City with King Měng.
A10.22.9 In winter, in the tenth month,
Prince Měng died.
A10.22.10 In the twelfth month, on the first day of the month guǐyǒu,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
B10.22 Commentary on the Twenty-second Year of Lord Zhāo
B10.22.1 In the spring of the twenty-second year,
in the royal second month, on the day jiǎzǐ,
Běi Guō Qǐ of Qí led an army to attack Jǔ.
The Viscount of Jǔ was about to do battle.
Yuàn Yáng Mù Zhī remonstrated, saying:
"The leader of the Qí army is of low rank,
his demands will not be great.
It is better to submit to him;
a great state must not be angered."
He did not listen
and defeated the Qí army at Shòu Yú.
The Marquis of Qí attacked Jǔ.
The Viscount of Jǔ sued for peace.
Marshal Zào went to Jǔ to oversee the alliance;
the Viscount of Jǔ went to Qí to oversee the alliance,
and they allied outside the Jì Gate.
Thereupon, the people of Jǔ greatly detested their ruler.
B10.22.2 Wěi Yuè of Chǔ sent a messenger to announce to Sòng, saying:
"My ruler has heard that you have unworthy ministers who cause you grief,
and rather than letting them bring shame upon your ancestral house,
my ruler requests to receive and execute them."
He replied:
"I am not clever,
and could not please my elders,
thus causing you concern;
I bow in receipt of your humbling command.
However, ruler and ministers have been at war daily.
If you, My Lord, say,
'I must assist these ministers,'
I will also simply obey your command.
People have a saying:
'Only avoid passing through the gate of disorder.'
If you, My Lord, would kindly protect my humble city,
and not support those who are disloyal,
thereby encouraging rebels,
that is my hope.
May you, My Lord, consider it!"
The people of Chǔ were troubled by this.
The garrisons of the feudal lords consulted together, saying:
"If the Huà clan knows they are cornered and fight to the death,
and Chǔ is ashamed of having no success and fights fiercely,
it will not be to our advantage.
It is better to let them out,
and treat it as a success for Chǔ;
they will not be able to do anything further anyway.
Saving Sòng and removing its harm—
what more could one seek?"
So they firmly requested to let them leave.
The people of Sòng followed this advice.
On the day jǐsì,
Huà Hài, Xiàng Níng, Huà Dìng, Huà Chù, Huà Dēng, Huáng Yǎn Shāng, Shěng Zāng, and Shì Píng of Sòng fled to Chǔ.
The Duke of Sòng appointed Gōng sūn Jì as Grand Marshal,
Biān Áng as Grand Minister over the Masses,
Lè Qí as Marshal,
Zhòng Jǐ as Left Master,
Lè Dà Xīn as Right Master,
Lè Wǎn as Grand Minister of Justice,
in order to pacify the people of the state.
B10.22.3 Prince Cháo and Bīn Qǐ were favored by King Jǐng.
The King and Bīn Mèng liked him
and wished to establish him.
Bó Fén, a concubine's son of Lord Xiàn of Liú, served Duke Mù of Dān.
He detested Bīn Mèng's character
and wished to kill him;
he also detested Prince Cháo's words,
considering them disorderly,
and wished to remove him.
Bīn Mèng went to the suburbs
and saw a rooster pecking off its own tail.
He asked
the attendants, who said:
"It fears becoming a sacrificial animal itself."
He hurried back and told the King,
and furthermore said:
"The rooster probably fears being used by people!
Men are different from this.
Sacrifice actually employs people;
to sacrifice a person is indeed difficult,
but what is the harm in sacrificing oneself?"
The King did not respond.
In summer, in the fourth month,
the King hunted at the Northern Mountain,
making all the high officials follow him;
he intended to kill the Master of Dān and the Master of Liú.
The King had a heart ailment.
On the day yǐchǒu,
he passed away at the Róng Qí residence.
On the day wùchén,
Zhì, the Master of Liú, died.
He had no son,
and the Master of Dān established
Fén of Liú. In the fifth month, on the day gēngchén,
they had an audience with the King,
then attacked Bīn Qǐ,
killed him,
and made an alliance with the various princes at the Dān residence.
B10.22.4 When Jìn took Gǔ,
they presented the captives and then returned the Viscount of Gǔ there.
Gǔ again rebelled against Jìn in favor of Xiān Yú.
In the sixth month,
Xún Wú patrolled Dōng Yáng,
making the soldiers pretend to be grain-buyers carrying armor and resting outside the gates of Xī Yáng.
They then surprised Gǔ,
destroyed it,
returned with the Viscount of Gǔ, Yuān Dī,
and made Shè Tuó guard it.
B10.22.5 On the day dīngsì,
King Jǐng was buried.
Prince Cháo, relying on the former officials
and the various artisans who had lost their offices and ranks,
together with the kinsmen of Kings Líng and Jǐng, started a rebellion.
Leading the armored men of Jiāo, Yào, and Jiàn,
they drove out the Master of Liú.
On the day rénxū,
the Master of Liú fled to Yáng.
The Master of Dān met King Dào at the Zhuāng Palace and returned with him.
Prince Huán took the King by night and went to the Zhuāng Palace.
On the day guǐhài,
the Master of Dān went out.
Prince Huán plotted with Duke Zhuāng of Shào, saying:
"If we do not kill Dān Qí,
we will not succeed.
If we make a solemn alliance with him,
he will certainly come.
Many have succeeded by breaking an alliance."
They followed this.
Master Qǐng of Fán said:
"These are not proper words;
you will certainly not succeed."
They then followed the King to pursue the Master of Dān,
and reaching Lǐng,
they made a great alliance and returned.
They killed Zhì Huāng to please him.
The Master of Liú went to Liú,
and the Master of Dān fled.
On the day yǐchǒu,
he fled to Píng Zhì.
The various princes pursued him;
the Master of Dān killed Huán, Gū, Fā,
Ruò, Zōng, Yán, Dìng, and Chóu.
Prince Cháo fled to Jīng.
On the day bǐngyín,
they attacked it.
The people of Jīng fled to the mountains.
Liú Zǐ entered the Royal City.
On the day Xīnwèi,
Duke Jiǎn of Gǒng was crushingly defeated at Jīng.
On the day Yǐhài,
Duke Píng of Gān was also defeated there.
Shū Yǎng arrived from the capital
and reported on the chaos in the royal house.
Mǐn Mǎfù said:
“Zǐ Zhāo will surely not succeed.
Those with whom he is associated
are those whom Heaven has abandoned.”
Shàn Zǐ wished to report the emergency to Jìn.
In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day Wùyín,
they took the King to Píngzhì,
then to Pǔjū,
and halted at Huáng.
Liú Zǐ went to Liú.
Shàn Zǐ sent Prince Chǔ to defend the Royal City.
He made a covenant with the various artisans at Pínggōng.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
Xún Xī attacked Huáng.
He was greatly defeated,
and Xún Xī was captured.
On the day Rénchén,
they burned him in the market of the Royal City.
In the eighth month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
Sītú Chǒu, with the royal army, was crushingly defeated at Qiánchéng.
The various artisans rebelled.
On the day Jǐsì,
they attacked the palace of the Shàn clan
and were defeated.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
[the Shàn clan] in turn attacked them.
On the day Xīnwèi,
they attacked Dōngyǔ.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the day Dīngsì,
Jí Tán and Xún Luò of Jìn led the Róng of Jiǔzhōu and the armies of Jiāo, Xiá, Wēn, and Yuán
to escort the King back into the Royal City.
On the day Gēngshēn,
Shàn Zǐ and Liú Fén, with the royal army, were crushingly defeated at Jiāo;
the people of Qiánchéng defeated the Lùhún at Shè.
In the eleventh month, on the day Yǐyǒu,
Prince Měng died.
The mourning rites were not completed.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
King Jìng ascended the throne.
He took up residence at the house of the Zǐlǚ clan.
In the twelfth month, on the day Gēngxū,
Jí Tán, Xún Luò, Jiǎ Xīn,
and Sīmǎ Dū of Jìn led an army to station at Yīn,
at Hóushì,
at Xīquán,
and halted at Shè.
The royal army stationed at Fàn,
at Xiè,
and halted at Rènrén.
In the intercalary month,
Jī Yí, Yuè Zhēng, and Yòuháng Guǐ of Jìn crossed the river with their army and took Qiánchéng,
stationing to its southeast.
The royal army stationed at Jīngchǔ.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
they attacked Jīng
and destroyed its southwest part.
A10.23 *The Classic of Duke Zhāo, Twenty-third Year*.
A10.23.1 In the spring of the twenty-third year,
in the first month of the King’s calendar,
Shūsūn Ruò went to Jìn.
A10.23.2 On the day Guǐchǒu,
Shū Yǎng died.
A10.23.3 The people of Jìn seized our envoy, Shūsūn Ruò.
A10.23.4 The people of Jìn besieged Jiāo.
A10.23.5 In summer, in the sixth month,
Marquis Dōngguó of Cài died in Chǔ.
A10.23.6 In autumn, in the seventh month,
Gēngyú, the Viscount of Jǔ, came in flight to our state.
A10.23.7 On the day Wùchén,
Wú defeated the armies of Dùn,
Hú, Shěn,
Cài, Chén,
and Xǔ at Jīfù.
Viscount Kūn of Hú
and Viscount Chěng of Shěn were killed,
and Xià Niè of Chén was captured.
A10.23.8 The Heavenly King resided at Díquán.
The Yǐn clan established Prince Zhāo.
A10.23.9 In the eighth month, on the day Yǐwèi,
there was an earthquake.
A10.23.10 In winter,
the Duke was going to Jìn;
when he reached the Yellow River,
he fell ill
and thus returned.
B10.23 *The Commentary of Duke Zhāo, Twenty-third Year*.
B10.23.1 In the spring of the twenty-third year,
on the first day of the first month of the King’s calendar, Rényín,
the two armies besieged Jiāo.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
Jiāo and Xún collapsed.
On the day Dīngwèi,
the Jìn army was at Píngyīn,
and the royal army was at Zéyì.
The King sent a messenger to report during an interval;
on the day Gēngxū,
they returned.
B10.23.2 The people of Zhū fortified Yì.
Upon returning,
they were going to pass through Lígū.
Gōngsūn Chú said:
“Lǔ will surely resist us.”
He wished to return from Wǔchéng,
following the mountains southward.
Xú Chú, Qiū Ruò, and Máo Dì said:
“The road is low;
if it rains,
we will not get out,
and that means not returning.”
So they went by way of Lígū.
The people of Wǔchéng blocked their front
and cut through the trees behind them without severing them completely;
when the Zhū army passed,
they pushed the trees down to trip them up.
They then captured the Zhū army
and took Chú, Ruò, and Dì.
The people of Zhū complained to Jìn,
and the people of Jìn came to call Lǔ to account.
Shūsūn Ruò went to Jìn,
and the people of Jìn seized him.
The record says,
“The people of Jìn seized our envoy Shūsūn Ruò,”
which indicates he was an emissary.
The people of Jìn ordered him to sit in council with the grand masters of Zhū.
Shūsūn said:
“That a minister of a great state should be the match for the ruler of a small state
is indeed the system of Zhōu.
Furthermore, Zhū is a barbarian state.
My ruler's subordinate officer Zǐfú Huí is here;
I request that you let him be the match for them,
precisely because I do not dare to discard the system of Zhōu.”
Consequently, the joint sitting did not take place.
Hán Xuānzǐ let the people of Zhū take back their captives,
and intended to give Shūsūn to them.
Shūsūn heard of this;
he dismissed his followers and weapons and went to court.
Shì Mímóu said to Hán Xuānzǐ:
“If you do not consider this carefully
and give Shūsūn to his enemy,
Shūsūn will surely die for it.
If Lǔ loses Shūsūn,
it will surely mean the destruction of Zhū.
When the ruler of Zhū loses his state,
where will he turn?
Even if you regret it then,
how will it be in time?
The so-called leader of the alliance
punishes those who disobey orders.
If they all seize each other,
what use is a leader of the alliance?”
Thereupon he did not give him up.
He had them each reside in a separate guest house.
Shì Bó heard Shūsūn’s arguments
and reported them to Xuānzǐ,
and then all of Shūsūn's party were detained.
Shì Bó drove the carriage for Shūsūn,
with four followers,
passing the Zhū guest house on the way to the officer's quarters.
First they sent back the Viscount of Zhū.
Shì Bó said:
“Because of the difficulty of gathering fodder and fuel
and the fatigue of your followers,
we will lodge you in the capital city.”
Shūsūn stood at dawn
and waited for the appointed time.
Then they lodged him in Jī.
They housed Zǐfú Zhāobó in another city.
Fàn Xiànzǐ sought goods from Shūsūn,
sending someone to request a cap from him.
Shūsūn took the pattern for his cap
and gave him two caps,
saying:
“This is all there is.”
On Shūsūn’s behalf,
Shēn Fēng went to Jìn with goods.
Shūsūn said:
“See me,
and I will tell you how to distribute the goods.”
They met,
but Shūsūn did not come out again.
Those among the officials and people who had lived with Shū Sūn at Jī
asked for his barking dog,
but he did not give it.
When he was about to return home,
he killed it and gave it to them to eat.
Wherever Shū Sūn lodged,
even for a single day,
he would certainly repair the walls
and the roof,
and leave it as it was when he first arrived.
B10.23.3 In the summer, the fourth month, on the *yǐyǒu* day,
Dān-zǐ took Zī,
and Liú-zǐ took Qiángrén and Zhírén.
In the sixth month, on the *rénwǔ* day,
Wáng-zǐ Cháo entered Yǐn.
On the *guǐwèi* day,
Yǐn Yǔ lured Liú Tuó and killed him.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
Dān-zǐ followed the Bǎndào road,
and Liú-zǐ followed the Yǐndào road to attack Yǐn.
Dān-zǐ arrived first and was defeated;
Liú-zǐ returned.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
Shào-bó Huàn and Nángōng Jí used the people of Chéngzhōu to garrison Yǐn.
On the *gēngyín* day,
Dān-zǐ, Liú-zǐ, and Fán Qí escorted the King to Liú.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Wáng-zǐ Cháo entered Wángchéng
and took up a position in Zuǒxiàng.
In the autumn, the seventh month, on the *wùshēn* day,
Xún Luó escorted him into the Zhuānggōng palace.
Yǐn Xīn defeated the army of Liú at Táng.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
he defeated them again at Xún.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Yǐn Xīn took Xīwéi.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
he attacked Kuài,
and Kuài collapsed.
B10.23.4 Gēngyú, the Viscount of Jǔ, was cruel and fond of swords.
If he cast a sword,
he would certainly test it on someone.
The people of the state were distressed by this.
Moreover, he was about to rebel against Qí.
Wū Cún led the people of the state to drive him out.
As Gēngyú was about to leave,
he heard that Wū Cún was standing by the left side of the road holding a spear;
he was afraid
and was about to stop and wait for death.
Yuàn Yángmùzhī said:
"My Lord, pass him by!
It is enough for Wū Cún to be known for his strength;
why must he achieve fame by murdering his ruler?"
Consequently, he fled here.
The people of Qí restored Jiāogōng.
B10.23.5 The people of Wú attacked Zhōulái,
and Wěi Yuè of Chǔ led his army and the armies of the feudal lords in a forced march to save Zhōulái.
The people of Wú resisted them at Zhōnglí.
Zǐ Xiá died,
and the spirit of the Chǔ army was extinguished.
Gōngzǐ Guāng of Wú said:
"The feudal lords following Chǔ are many,
but they are all small states;
they fear Chǔ and cannot help themselves,
which is why they have come.
I have heard it said:
'In undertaking an affair, if majesty overcomes affection,
even if it is small,
it will certainly succeed.'
The rulers of Hú and Shěn are young and erratic;
the Grand Officer Niè of Chén is in his prime but stubborn;
Dùn, Xǔ, and Cài resent the administration of Chǔ.
The Chǔ Lìngyǐn has died,
and their army's spirit is extinguished.
The commanders are of low rank and many are favorites;
administrative orders are not unified.
Seven states share the same service but do not have the same heart;
the commanders are of low rank and cannot maintain order;
they have no great and majestic command;
Chǔ can be defeated.
If we divide our army and first attack Hú, Shěn, and Chén,
they will certainly flee first.
When these three states are defeated,
the hearts of the feudal lords' armies will be shaken.
When the feudal lords are in disorder,
Chǔ will certainly flee in great haste.
I request that those in front discard their preparations and show little majesty,
while those behind form thick ranks and put the troops in order."
The Viscount of Wú followed this.
On the *wùchén* day, the last day of the month,
they fought at Jīfù.
The Viscount of Wú used three thousand criminals to first attack Hú, Shěn, and Chén,
and the three states vied to engage them.
Wú formed three armies to follow behind:
the Central Army followed the King,
Guāng led the Right,
and Yǎnyú led the Left.
Some of the criminals of Wú fled while others stood their ground;
the three states fell into disorder,
the Wú army struck them,
and the three states were defeated.
They captured the rulers of Hú and Shěn and the Grand Officer of Chén.
They released the prisoners of Hú and Shěn and made them run to Xǔ, Cài, and Dùn,
saying:
"Our lords are dead!"
The army followed them with a great clamor;
the three states fled,
and the Chǔ army fled in great haste.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* records:
"Kūn, Viscount of Hú, and Chěng, Viscount of Shěn, were extinguished;
Niè of Chén was captured,"
which are terms for ruler and subject.
It does not mention "battle"
because Chǔ had not yet formed its ranks.
B10.23.6 In the eighth month, on the *dīngyǒu* day,
Nángōng Jí was struck by disaster.
Cháng Hóng said to Liú Wén-gōng:
"My Lord, you should exert yourself!
The power of the former kings can be restored.
When Zhōu was about to fall,
its three rivers were shaken.
Now the high minister of the Western King has also been shaken;
Heaven has abandoned him.
The Eastern King will certainly achieve a great victory."
B10.23.7 The mother of the Chǔ Crown Prince Jiàn was in Jū;
she called for the people of Wú and opened the gates for them.
In the winter, the tenth month, on the *jiǎshēn* day,
the Wú Crown Prince Zhū Fán entered Jū
and took the Chǔ lady and her treasures to return.
The Chǔ Sīmǎ Wěi Yuè pursued them
but did not catch them.
As he was about to die,
the multitude said:
"Please proceed to attack Wú to seek a turn of fortune."
Wěi Yuè said:
"Twice I have caused the defeat of the ruler's army;
if I die now, I will still be guilty.
Having lost the ruler's lady,
I cannot but die for it."
He then hanged himself at Wěishì.
B10.23.8 The Duke, for the sake of Shū Sūn, was going to Jìn.
When he reached the River,
he fell ill
and returned.
B10.23.9 Náng Wǎ of Chǔ became Lìngyǐn
and fortified Yǐng.
Shěn Yǐn Xù said:
"Zǐ Cháng will certainly lose Yǐng.
If one cannot defend,
a wall is of no benefit.
In ancient times,
the Son of Heaven's defense lay in the four Yi tribes;
when the Son of Heaven was weak,
his defense lay in the feudal lords.
The defense of a feudal lord lay in his four neighbors;
when a feudal lord was weak,
his defense lay in his four borders.
If one is careful about the four borders
and binds one's four supports,
the people are at ease in the fields,
and the three seasons' labors are successful.
When the people have no internal worries
and also no external fears,
why would a state use a wall?
Now, fearing Wú,
they fortify Yǐng;
the defense is already small.
If even the low cannot be maintained,
can they escape ruin?
Formerly, the Earl of Liáng dug moats around his public palace and his people dispersed;
when the people abandon their superior,
for what else
but ruin should they wait?
Now, if one regulates the boundaries,
cultivates the fields,
makes the strategic points strong,
shows affection to the people,
clarifies the watches and scouts,
keeps faith with neighboring states,
is careful in official duties,
observes the rites of diplomatic exchange,
is neither encroaching nor greedy,
neither weak nor aggressive,
and completes defensive preparations
to wait for the unforeseen,
then what is there to fear?
The *Odes* says:
'Always think of your ancestors,
and cultivate their virtues.'
Should we not also look to Ruò Áo and Fén Mào, down to Wǔ and Wén?
Their territory did not exceed a hundred *lǐ* square,
yet they were careful about their four borders
and still did not fortify Yǐng.
Now the territory is several thousand *lǐ* square,
yet Yǐng is fortified;
is this not difficult?"
A10.24 Classic of Duke Zhāo, Year 24
A10.24.1 In the twenty-fourth year, spring,
in the royal second month, on the day Bǐngxū,
Zhòngsūn Jué died.
A10.24.2 Ruò arrived from Jìn.
A10.24.3 Summer, fifth month, on the day Yǐwèi, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A10.24.4 Autumn, eighth month,
the great rain sacrifice was performed.
A10.24.5 On the day Dīngyǒu,
Yùlí, Earl of Qǐ, died.
A10.24.6 Winter,
Wú destroyed Cháo.
A10.24.7 Píng Gōng of Qǐ was buried.
B10.24 Commentary on the Twenty-fourth Year of Zhāo Gōng
B10.24.1 In the twenty-fourth year, spring,
in the royal first month, on the day Xīnchǒu,
Jiǎn Gōng of Shào and Nángōng Yín, taking Huán Gōng of Gān, had an audience with Prince Cháo.
Liú Zǐ said to Cháng Hóng,
“The Gān clan has gone there again.”
He replied, “What harm?
They share the same virtue and measure righteousness.
The ‘Dàshì’ says,
‘Zhòu had hundreds of millions of ordinary people,
yet they were of divided virtue;
I have ten governing ministers
of one heart and one virtue.’
This is how Zhōu rose.
May my lord strive for virtue
and not worry about a lack of followers.”
On the day Wùwǔ,
Prince Cháo entered Wù.
B10.24.2 Shì Mímóu of Jìn met Shūsūn at Jī.
Shūsūn had Liángqí Jìng wait inside the gate
and said,
“If I look to the left and cough,
then kill him.
If I look to the right and smile,
then stop.”
Shūsūn saw Shì Bó.
Shì Bó said,
“Because our ruler is the leader of the alliance,
he has detained you for a long time.
These meager gifts from our humble state
will be presented to your followers;
I have been sent to meet you.”
Shūsūn accepted the gifts and returned.
In the second month,
“Ruò arrived from Jìn,”
as a mark of respect for Jìn.
B10.24.3 In the third month, on the day Gēngxū,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Jǐngbó to inquire into the affairs of Zhōu.
Shì Bó stood at Qiánjì
and questioned the masses.
The people of Jìn then rejected Prince Cháo
and would not admit his envoys.
B10.24.4 Summer, fifth month, on the day Yǐwèi, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
Zǐ Shèn said,
“There will be floods.”
Zhāozǐ said,
“It will be a drought.
The sun has passed the equinox, yet the Yáng is still not victorious.
When it does conquer, it must be extreme;
how can there not be a drought?
Since the Yáng is not victorious,
it will build up.”
B10.24.5 In the sixth month, on the day Rénshēn,
the army of Prince Cháo attacked Xiá and Xìng;
both collapsed.
B10.24.6 The Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn,
Zǐ Tàishū assisted him,
and they saw Fàn Xiànzǐ.
Xiànzǐ said,
“What shall be done about the Royal House?”
He replied,
“This old man cannot even care for his own state;
how would I dare speak of the Royal House?
But people also have a saying,
‘A widow does not care for her weaving
but worries about the fall of Zōngzhōu,
for it will eventually reach her.’
Now the Royal House is truly in turmoil,
and our small state is afraid;
but it is the concern of the large states;
what do people like us know?
You, my lord, should plan for it early!
The ‘Shī’ says,
‘When the pitcher is empty,
it is the shame of the jar.’
The instability of the Royal House
is the shame of Jìn.”
Xiànzǐ was afraid
and planned with Xuānzǐ.
They then summoned a meeting of the feudal lords,
scheduling it for the following year.
B10.24.7 Autumn, eighth month,
the great rain sacrifice was performed,
because of a drought.
B10.24.8 Winter, tenth month, on the day Guǐyǒu,
Prince Cháo used the precious Jade Tablet of Chéngzhōu to submerge it in the Hé.
On the day Jiǎxū, the ferryman found it on the riverbank.
Yīn Bùnìng led the people of Wēn to invade the south,
captured the one who found the jade,
and took the jade.
When he was about to sell it,
it turned into stone.
When the King was settled, he presented it;
he was given Dōngzì.
B10.24.9 The Viscount of Chǔ organized a naval force to raid the borders of Wú.
Shěnyǐn Xù said,
“On this expedition,
Chǔ will surely lose cities.
To exhaust the people without comforting them,
and to hasten Wú without Wú having moved—
Wú will follow Chǔ's heels while the borders are unprepared.
How can cities,
how can they not be lost?”
The Great Officer of Yuè, Xū Àn, welcomed the King at the bend of Yùzhāng;
the Prince of Yuè, Cāng, presented the King with a boat.
Cāng and Shòumèng led troops to follow the King.
The King reached Yǔyáng and returned.
The people of Wú followed Chǔ's heels,
and the border people were unprepared;
they then destroyed Cháo and Zhōnglí and returned.
Shěnyǐn Xù said,
“The beginning of the fall of Yǐng is here.
With one movement of the King, the commanders of two clans were lost.
If things continue like this, how can Yǐng be reached?
The ‘Shī’ says,
‘Who produced the steps of calamity
that remain a hindrance to this day?’
That surely refers to the King!”
A10.25 Annals of the Twenty-fifth Year of Zhāo Gōng
A10.25.1 Twenty-fifth year, spring,
Shūsūn Ruò went to Sòng.
A10.25.2 Summer,
Shū Yì met Zhào Yāng of Jìn,
Lè Dàxīn of Sòng,
Běigōng Xǐ of Wèi,
Yóu Jí of Zhèng,
the people of Cáo,
the people of Zhū,
the people of Téng,
the people of Xuē,
and the people of Xiǎo Zhū at Huángfù.
A10.25.3 Mynas came to nest.
A10.25.4 Autumn, seventh month, the first Xīn day,
the great rain sacrifice;
on the last Xīn day,
another rain sacrifice.
A10.25.5 Ninth month, on the day Jǐhài,
the Duke fled to Qí
and stayed at Yángzhōu.
The Marquis of Qí consoled the Duke at Yějǐng.
A10.25.6 Winter, tenth month, on the day Wùchén,
Shūsūn Ruò died.
A10.25.7 Eleventh month, on the day Jǐhài,
Duke Zuǒ of Sòng died at Qūjí.
A10.25.8 Twelfth month,
the Marquis of Qí took Yùn.
B10.25 Commentary on the Twenty-fifth Year
B10.25.1 In the twenty-fifth year, spring,
Shūsūn Ruò went on a mission to Sòng,
and the Right Master of the Tóng Gate saw him.
In their conversation,
he disparaged the Great Officers of Sòng and belittled the Sīchéng clan.
Zhāozǐ told his followers,
“The Right Master will surely perish!
A gentleman values his own person
and then is able to extend that to others;
thus he has ritual propriety.
Now this man disparages his Great Officers and belittles his own clan;
this is belittling himself.
Can he have ritual propriety?
Without ritual propriety,
he must perish.”
Sòng Gōng entertained Zhāo Zǐ
and recited "Xīn Gōng."
Zhāo Zǐ recited "Chē Xiá."
The following day, there was a feast;
they drank wine
and were joyful.
Sòng Gōng had Zhāo Zǐ sit in the place of honor on the right,
and as they spoke, they both wept.
Yuè Qí assisted them,
and upon withdrawing, he told others:
"This year, the Lord and Shūsūn will likely both die!
I have heard it said:
'To grieve when there is joy and to find joy when there is grief
are both signs of a lost mind.'
The essence and brilliance of the mind
are what are called the hún and pò.
Once the hún and pò depart,
how can one last long?"
B10.25.2 The elder sister of Jì Gōngruò became the lady of Xiǎo Zhū;
she gave birth to Sòng Yuán Fūrén,
who gave birth to a daughter
whom she gave in marriage to Jì Píngzǐ.
Zhāo Zǐ went to Sòng on a mission of state
and also to escort the bride.
Gōngruò followed him
and told Cáo Shì not to give the daughter,
as Lǔ was about to expel him.
Cáo Shì told the Duke.
The Duke told Yuè Qí.
Yuè Qí said: "Give her to him.
If it is as he says, the ruler of Lǔ will surely go into exile.
The government has been in the Jì Shì for three generations,
and the ruler of Lǔ has lost control of the government through the reigns of four dukes.
That one who lacks the people could still fulfill his will—
such a thing has never been.
It is for this reason that a ruler of a state uses ritual to pacify his people.
The *Shī* says:
'As the people vanish,
the heart is filled with sorrow.'
The ruler of Lǔ has lost his people;
how can he fulfill his will?
If he remains quiet and awaits his fate, it may still be well,
but if he acts, he will surely have sorrow."
B10.25.3 In the summer,
a meeting was held at Huángfù
to deliberate on the royal house.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ ordered the high officers of the feudal lords to transport grain to the King and
provide garrison troops,
saying:
"Next year we shall restore the King."
Zǐ Dàshū met with Zhào Jiǎnzǐ,
and Jiǎnzǐ asked him about the ceremonies of bowing, yielding, and moving in court.
He replied: "These are etiquette,
not ritual."
Jiǎnzǐ said: "May I venture to ask
what is meant by ritual?"
He replied:
"I, Jí, heard it from the former high officer Zǐchǎn:
'Ritual is
the constant principle of Heaven,
the righteousness of Earth,
and the conduct of the people.'
The people take the constant principles of Heaven and Earth
as their model.
Modeling themselves on the brightness of Heaven
and following the nature of Earth,
they generate the six qì
and utilize the five elements.
These qì become the five flavors,
manifest as the five colors,
and are displayed as the five sounds.
When there is excess, there is confusion and disorder,
and the people lose their nature.
Therefore, ritual was established to maintain them:
creating the six domestic animals, the five sacrificial beasts, and the three victims
to maintain the five flavors;
creating the nine patterns, the six colors, and the five ornaments
to maintain the five colors;
creating the nine songs, the eight winds,
the seven notes, and the six pitches
to maintain the five sounds.
Establishing the roles of ruler and subject, superior and inferior,
to model the righteousness of Earth;
establishing the roles of husband and wife, outer and inner,
to regulate these two domains;
establishing the roles of father and son, elder and younger brothers,
paternal and maternal aunts and sisters, nephews and uncles,
marriage relatives, and in-laws,
to imitate the brightness of Heaven.
Establishing administration, labor, and public duties,
to follow the four seasons;
establishing punishments, penalties, and the awe of prisons,
to make the people fearful and cautious,
to resemble the thunder and lightning's power to kill;
establishing warmth, kindness, benevolence, and harmony,
to emulate Heaven's power of reproduction and growth.
People have likes and dislikes, joy and anger, grief and happiness,
which arise from the six qì.
Therefore, one carefully models and follows the appropriate categories
to regulate the six emotions.
For grief, there is weeping and crying;
for happiness, there is song and dance;
for joy, there is giving and sharing;
for anger, there is fighting and combat.
Joy arises from liking;
anger arises from disliking.
Therefore, one is careful in conduct and faithful in commands,
using fortune and misfortune, reward and punishment,
to regulate life and death.
Life
is a thing that is liked;
death
is a thing that is disliked.
Things that are liked
are joy;
things that are disliked
are grief.
When grief and joy are not misplaced,
one can be in harmony with the nature of Heaven and Earth,
and thus endure for a long time."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"How great indeed
is the magnitude of ritual!"
He replied: "Ritual
is the discipline of superior and inferior, the warp and woof of Heaven and Earth,
and that by which the people live.
Therefore, the former kings honored it.
Thus, those who can bend or straighten themselves to follow ritual
are called complete persons.
That it is great—
is it not appropriate?"
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"I, Yǎng,
request to keep these words for the rest of my life."
Yuè Dàxīn of Sòng said:
"I will not transport grain.
I am a guest to Zhōu;
why should a guest be made to serve?"
Shì Bó of Jìn said:
"Since the time of Jiàntǔ,
which service has Sòng not joined,
and which covenant has it not shared?
It is said:
'Jointly care for the royal house';
how can you avoid it?
You bear your lord's command
to attend a great matter,
yet if Sòng turns its back on the covenant,
will that not be unacceptable?"
The Yòushī did not dare to reply;
he received the tablets and withdrew.
Shì Bó told Jiǎnzǐ:
"The Yòushī of Sòng will surely perish.
Entrusted with his lord's command on a mission,
yet wishing to betray the covenant and offend the leader of the covenant—
there is no greater inauspiciousness than this."
B10.25.4 "Mynas came and nested,"
which was something not previously recorded.
Shī Jǐ said:
"How strange!
I have heard that in the times of Wén and Chéng,
there was a nursery rhyme
that said:
'The mynas, the mynas!
The Duke goes out and is humiliated.
The feathers of the mynas!
The Duke is in the wild fields;
someone goes to present him with horses.
The mynas hop and skip!
The Duke is at Qiánhóu;
he requests trousers and jackets.
The nests of the mynas!
Far away, so far away!
Chóufù dies from labor;
Sòngfù becomes arrogant.
The mynas, the mynas!
They go out singing and come back crying.'
There was such a nursery rhyme.
Now that the mynas have come to nest,
it is likely about to arrive!"
B10.25.5 In the autumn,
it is recorded that the Yú rain sacrifice was performed twice;
the drought was severe.
B10.25.6 Previously,
Jì Gōngniǎo had taken a wife from Bào Wénzǐ of Qí,
who gave birth to Jiǎ.
When Gōngniǎo died,
Jì Gōnghài, Gōngsī Zhǎn, and Gōngniǎo's servant Shēn Yègū managed the household.
When Jì Sì had an affair with the cook Tán
and became afraid,
she had her maidservant whip her
to show it to the wife of Qín Chuán,
Someone said:
“Gōngruò wanted to employ me,
but I would not agree, so he whipped me.”
He also complained to Gōngfǔ,
saying:
“Zhǎn and Yègū are going to waylay me.”
Qín Jī told Gōngzhī about this.
Gōngzhī and Gōngfǔ told Píngzǐ.
Píngzǐ detained Zhǎn in Biàn
and arrested Yègū,
intending to kill them.
Gōngruò wept and felt sorrow for them,
saying:
“To kill these two
is to kill me.”
He was about to petition for them,
but Píngzǐ ordered the attendant not to let him in;
by midday, he still had not
obtained the petition.
The officials followed the order,
and Gōngzhī had them killed quickly.
Therefore Gōngruò resented Píngzǐ.
In a cockfight between the Jì and Hòu families,
the Jì family put armor on their cock,
while the Hòu family made metal spurs for theirs.
Píngzǐ was angry;
he expanded his residence into the Hòu family’s property
and rebuked them.
Therefore Hòu Zhāobó also resented Píngzǐ.
Zāng Zhāobó’s younger cousin Huì made slanders against the Zāng family
and fled to the Jì family.
The Zāng family arrested him.
Píngzǐ was angry
and detained the elder of the Zāng family.
When the dì sacrifice was to be performed for Duke Xiāng,
there were only two dancers for the wàn dance,
as the multitude of dancers were at the Jì family’s.
Zāngsūn said:
“This is what is called being unable to use the ancestral temple of the former ruler.”
The Great Officers then resented Píngzǐ.
Gōngruò presented a bow to Gōngwéi,
and went out hunting with him in the outskirts,
plotting to remove the Jì family.
Gōngwéi told Gōngguǒ and Gōngbèn.
Gōngguǒ and Gōngbèn sent the attendant Liáozhá to tell the Duke.
The Duke was in bed;
he was about to strike him with a halberd,
so he ran away.
The Duke said:
“Seize him!”
but gave no actual command.
He was afraid and did not come out,
and for several months he did not appear.
The Duke was not angry.
He sent word again;
the Duke held a halberd to frighten him,
and he ran away.
He sent word yet again;
the Duke said:
“This is not something a person of low status can handle.”
Gōngguǒ spoke for himself;
the Duke told Zāngsūn,
but Zāngsūn considered it difficult.
He told Hòusūn,
and Hòusūn considered it possible
and encouraged him.
He told Zǐjiā Yìbó.
Yìbó said:
“Slanderers use the Ruler to seek luck.
If the matter is not successful,
the Ruler will bear the bad reputation;
it must not be done.
Having abandoned the people for several generations,
to seek success in this matter
cannot be certain.
Moreover, since the government rests with them,
it is difficult to plot against.”
The Duke dismissed him.
He declined, saying:
“I have heard the command;
if the word leaks out,
I shall not escape death.”
So he stayed in the Duke’s palace.
Shūsūn Zhāozǐ went to Kàn;
the Duke resided at Chángfǔ.
In the ninth month, on the day wùxū,
they attacked the Jì family,
killed Gōngzhī at the gate,
and then entered.
Píngzǐ climbed a tower and pleaded, saying:
“If the Ruler has not investigated my crimes
and has sent officials to punish me with weapons,
I request to wait by the Yí River to await investigation of my crimes.”
It was not granted.
He requested to be imprisoned in Fèi;
it was not granted.
He requested to flee with five chariots;
it was not granted.
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
“The Ruler should grant it!
Government has issued from him for a long time;
many common people have received food from him,
and those who follow him are numerous.
When the sun sets and evil arises,
it cannot be known.
The anger of the masses cannot be stored up;
if stored and not dealt with,
it will smolder.
When it smolders and accumulates,
the people will have other intentions.
When they have other intentions,
those with common goals will unite.
The Ruler will surely regret it!”
He did not listen.
Hòusūn said:
“He must be killed.”
The Duke sent Hòusūn to meet Mèng Yìzǐ.
The Shūsūn family’s Marshall, Zōnglì, said to his followers:
“What shall we do?”
No one replied.
He said again:
“I
am a family servant;
I do not dare to know the affairs of the state.
Generally, having the Jì family or not,
which is more beneficial to me?”
All said:
“Without the Jì family,
there would be no Shūsūn family.”
Zōnglì said:
“In that case, let us rescue them!”
He led the followers and went,
breaking into the northwest corner.
The Duke’s followers removed their armor, held their quiver covers, and squatted;
then they were driven away.
The Mèng family had people climb the northwest corner
to look toward the Jì family’s house.
They saw the banners of the Shūsūn family
and reported it.
The Mèng family seized Hòu Zhāobó
and killed him west of the South Gate,
then attacked the Duke’s followers.
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
“The ministers can pretend to kidnap the Ruler
and flee with the burden of guilt;
