the Ruler should stay.
If Yìrú serves the Ruler,
he will not dare not to change.”
The Duke said:
“I cannot bear it.”
He went to Mù with Zāngsūn to plan,
and then departed.
On the day jǐhài,
the Duke fled to Qí
and halted at Yángzhōu.
The Marquis of Qí was going to condole with the Duke at Píngyīn,
but the Duke arrived first at Yějǐng.
The Marquis of Qí said:
“It is my fault.
I sent officials to wait at Píngyīn
because it was closer.”
The record says:
“The Duke fled to Qí,
and halted at Yángzhōu.
The Marquis of Qí condoled with the Duke at Yějǐng,”
which was in accordance with ritual.
When one is about to ask something of another,
one first humbles oneself;
this is a good element of ritual.
The Marquis of Qí said:
“From the border of Jǔ westward,
I request to offer a thousand communities
to await your command.
I shall lead my poor forces to follow your servants,
listening only to your commands.
Your worries
are my worries.”
The Duke was pleased.
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
“Heaven’s favor does not come twice.
If Heaven were to bless the Ruler,
he would be no greater than the Duke of Zhōu.
Lǔ is enough.
If you lose Lǔ and become a vassal with a thousand communities,
with whom will you stand?
Moreover, the Ruler of Qí is untrustworthy;
it is better to go to Jìn early.”
He did not follow this.
Zāng Zhāobó led his followers to form a covenant,
the text of which said:
“We shall exert our strength with one heart,
sharing likes and dislikes.
Trusting whether there is guilt or not,
we shall follow the Duke devotedly
and have no communication between the outside and inside!”
By the Gōng’s order, it was shown to Zǐjiā Zǐ.
Zǐjiā Zǐ said,
“If it is like this,
I cannot participate in the covenant.
I, Jī, am not clever,
I cannot be of the same mind as you gentlemen,
and I believe you are all guilty.
Some wish to communicate between the outside and the inside,
and also wish to remove the Lord.
You gentlemen love exile and hate stability;
how can we be together?
You have led the Lord into distress;
what crime is greater than this?
To communicate between the outside and the inside and to remove the Lord—
the Lord is about to enter quickly.
If you do not communicate, what will you do?
And what will you hold then?”
Thus he did not participate in the covenant.
Zhāozǐ returned from Kàn
and saw Píngzǐ.
Píngzǐ bowed his head to the ground
and said,
“What will you do with me?”
Zhāozǐ said,
“Who among men does not die?
You have made a name for yourself by driving out your Lord;
your descendants will not forget it.
Is this not also distressing?
What shall be done with you?”
Píngzǐ said,
“If Yìrú could be allowed to serve the Lord again,
it would be what is called bringing the dead to life and putting flesh on bones.”
Zhāozǐ followed the Gōng to Qí
and spoke with the Gōng.
Zǐjiā Zǐ ordered that those who went to the Gōng’s residence be arrested.
The Gōng spoke with Zhāozǐ inside the tent,
saying,
“He intends to pacify the masses and reinstate the Gōng.”
The Gōng’s followers intended to kill Zhāozǐ
and lay in ambush on the road.
Zuǒshī Zhǎn informed the Gōng,
and the Gōng sent Zhāozǐ back by way of Zhù.
Píngzǐ had other intentions.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day xīnyǒu,
Zhāozǐ fasted in his private chamber
and ordered the Zhùzōng to pray for his death.
On the day wùchén,
he died.
Zuǒshī Zhǎn intended to take the Gōng back on horseback,
but the Gōng’s followers arrested him.
B10.25.7 On the day rénshēn,
Yǐn Wéngōng waded across at Gǒng
and burned Dōngzī,
but was not successful.
B10.25.8 In the eleventh month,
Sòng Yuángōng was about to go to Jìn for the sake of the Gōng.
He dreamed that the Dàzǐ Luán took the throne in the temple,
and that he himself and Pínggōng wore robes to assist him.
At dawn,
he summoned the Liùqīng.
The Gōng said,
“I, the lonely one, am not clever;
I have been unable to serve my elders,
and have caused you gentlemen concern;
this is my fault.
If, through the spiritual power of you gentlemen,
I may keep my head until I die,
regarding the piánfū which support the body,
I request that they do not reach the level of the former lords.”
Zhòng Jǐ replied,
“If the Lord, for the sake of the Shèjì,
privately lowers the level of his intimate banquets,
your ministers would not dare to know of it.
But as for the laws of Sòngguó
and the regulations for death and life,
the former lords have left orders.
We, your ministers, will guard them unto death
and dare not fail in our ranks.
If I fail in my duty,
the regular punishments allow no pardon.
I cannot bear such a death,
and the Lord’s command only brings disgrace.”
Sònggōng then set out.
On the day jǐhài,
he died in Qǔjí.
B10.25.9 In the twelfth month, on the day gēngchén,
Qíhóu besieged Yùn.
B10.25.10 Previously,
Zāng Zhāobó went to Jìn,
and Zāng Huì stole his precious tortoise shell, Lǒugòu,
using it to divine whether he should be faithful or treacherous.
The divination for treachery was auspicious.
An elder of the Zāng clan was about to go to Jìn to inquire after Zhāobó;
Huì asked to go.
Zhāobó asked about the affairs of the house,
and Huì answered everything.
When it came to the Nèizǐ and his full brother Shūsūn,
he did not answer.
When asked two or three times,
he still did not answer.
Upon returning
and reaching the outskirts,
Huì met him.
When Zhāobó asked,
it was just as before.
When they arrived,
Zhāobó stayed outside and investigated the matter
and found none of it was true.
He arrested Huì and was going to execute him,
but Huì escaped
and fled to Hòu.
Hòu Fángjiǎ made him the Jiǎzhèng there.
While reporting accounts to the Jì clan,
the Zāng clan sent five men with daggers and shields to lie in ambush at the Tóngrǔ gate.
When Huì came out,
they pursued him.
He fled back
and they arrested him outside the middle gate of the Jì clan residence.
Píngzǐ was angry and said, “For what reason do you enter my gate with weapons?”
He detained the Zāng clan elder.
There was ill will between the Jì and Zāng clans.
When Zhāobó followed the Gōng into exile,
Píngzǐ established Zāng Huì.
Huì said,
“Lǒugòu did not deceive me.”
B10.25.11 Chǔzǐ sent Wěi Shè to wall Zhōuqū
and restored the people of Jiā there.
He walled Qiūhuáng
and moved the people of Zī there.
He sent Xióngxiāng Méi to build the outer wall of Cháo
and Jìrán to build the outer wall of Juàn.
Zǐ Dàshū heard of this
and said,
“The Chǔwáng is about to die.
Making the people unsettled on their land,
the people will surely be distressed.
The distress will reach the King;
he cannot last long.”
A10.26 Classic of Zhāogōng, Year 26
A10.26.1 In the spring of the twenty-sixth year,
in the first month of the King’s calendar,
Sòng Yuángōng was buried.
A10.26.2 In the third month,
the Gōng arrived from Qí
and resided in Yùn.
A10.26.3 In the summer,
the Gōng besieged Chéng.
A10.26.4 In the autumn,
the Gōng met with Qíhóu,
Jǔzǐ,
Zhūzǐ,
and Qǐbó,
and made a covenant at Zhuànlíng.
A10.26.5 The Gōng arrived from the meeting
and resided in Yùn.
A10.26.6 In the ninth month, on the day gēngshēn,
the Chǔzǐ, Jū, died.
A10.26.7 In winter, the tenth month,
the Tiānwáng entered Chéngzhōu.
Yǐnshì,
Shàobó,
and Máobó
fled to Chǔ with Wángzǐ Zhāo.
B10.26 Commentary on Zhāogōng, Year 26
B10.26.1 In the spring of the twenty-sixth year,
in the first month of the King’s calendar, on the day gēngshēn,
Qíhóu took Yùn.
B10.26.2 The burial of Sòng Yuángōng
was like that of former lords;
this was ritual propriety.
B10.26.3 In the third month,
the Gōng arrived from Qí
and stayed in Yùn;
this signifies that it was Lǔ territory.
B10.26.4 In the summer,
Qíhóu was about to reinstate the Gōng
and ordered that no bribes from Lǔ be accepted.
Shēn Fēng followed Nǚ Jiǎ,
taking two bolts of silk,
each bundled like ear-plug gems,
and went to the Qí army.
He said to Gāo Yǐ, a man of Zǐyóu,
“If you can bribe Zǐyóu
so that you may become the successor of the Gāoshì,
I will give you five thousand yǔ of grain.”
Gāo Yǐ showed some brocade to Zǐyóu,
and Zǐyóu wanted it.
Yǐ said:
“The people of Lǔ bought it,
at one hundred liǎng for one bolt.
Because the roads were impassable,
they first sent the payment.”
Zǐyóu accepted it,
and spoke to the Qí Hóu, saying:
“Among the ministers, those who do not exert their full strength for the Lǔ Jūn
are not unable to serve their lord.
However, there is something strange in the evidence.
Sòng Yuán Gōng went to Jìn on behalf of the Lǔ Jūn
and died at Qūjí;
Shúsūn Zhāozǐ sought to reinstate his lord
and died without illness.
I do not know if Heaven has abandoned Lǔ,
or if the Lǔ Jūn has committed a crime against the spirits and therefore reached this state.
If Your Lordship waits at Qūjí,
and sends the ministers to follow the Lǔ Jūn to perform divination there.
If it is favorable,
the army will achieve success;
then if Your Lordship follows it up,
you will be matchless.
If there is no success,
Your Lordship will suffer no disgrace.”
The Qí Hóu followed this,
and sent Gōngzǐ Chú to lead the army and follow the Gōng.
The Chéng Dàfū, Gōngsūn Zhāo, said to Píngzǐ:
“To have a capital city
is to defend the state;
I request that we receive the army.”
He permitted it.
He requested to present hostages,
but was not permitted,
with the words:
“Your trustworthiness
is sufficient.”
He announced to the Qí army, saying:
“The Mèng Shì
is a worn-out house of Lǔ.
Their use of Chéng has already become excessive;
we cannot endure it,
and request to rest our shoulders with Qí.”
The Qí army surrounded Chéng.
The people of Chéng attacked those of the Qí army who were watering their horses at the Zī River,
saying:
“This will be used to satisfy the multitude.”
After Lǔ Chéng was prepared, they then reported, saying:
“We cannot overcome the multitude.”
The army and the Qí army fought at Chuībí.
Zǐyuān Jié of Qí pursued Xiè Shēngzǐ,
shot at him,
and hit the shield-boss;
the arrow passed from the breastplate through the carriage pole,
the head entering three inches.
Shēngzǐ shot his horse,
severing the breast-strap,
and it died.
He changed the team;
people thought it was Zōng Lì
and helped him.
Zǐjū said:
“He is a person of Qí.”
As he was about to strike Zǐjū,
Zǐjū shot him,
and he died.
His driver said:
“Do it again.”
Zǐjū said:
“A multitude can be intimidated,
but they must not be provoked to anger.”
Zǐnáng Dài pursued Yě Xiè
and shouted at him.
Xiè said:
“In the army there is no private anger;
revenge is a private matter;
I will resist you.”
He shouted at him again,
and Xiè also shouted back.
Rǎn Shù shot Chén Wǔzǐ,
hitting his hand;
he dropped his bow and cursed.
He reported this to Píngzǐ,
saying:
“There is a gentleman, fair-skinned with thick hair, beard, and eyebrows,
who is very sharp-tongued.”
Píngzǐ said:
“It must be Zǐqiáng;
did you perhaps resist him?”
He replied, saying: “I called him a gentleman;
how would I dare to resist him?”
Lín Yōng was ashamed to be the right-hand man for Yán Míng
and stepped down.
Yuàn Héjì took his ear.
Yán Míng left him.
Yuànzǐ's driver said:
“Look down!”
He looked back.
Yuànzǐ struck Lín Yōng,
cutting off his foot;
clattering, he mounted another chariot to return.
Yán Míng entered the Qí army three times,
calling out:
“Lín Yōng, mount!”
B10.26.5 In the fourth month,
Shànzǐ went to Jìn to report the emergency.
In the fifth month, on the day wùwǔ,
the people of Liú defeated the army of the Wángchéng at Shīshì.
On the day wùchén,
the people of the Wángchéng and the people of Liú fought at Shīgǔ,
and the Liú army was utterly defeated.
B10.26.6 In autumn,
they covenanted at Zhuānlíng,
planning to reinstate the Gōng.
B10.26.7 In the seventh month, on the day jǐsì,
Liúzǐ went out with the Wáng.
On the day gēngwǔ,
they halted at Qú.
The people of the Wángchéng burned Liú.
On the day bǐngzǐ,
the Wáng stayed overnight at Chǔshì.
On the day dīngchǒu,
the Wáng halted at Huángǔ.
On the day gēngchén,
the Wáng entered Xūmǐ.
On the day xīnsì,
the Wáng halted at Huá.
Zhī Luò and Zhào Yāng of Jìn led an army to reinstate the Wáng,
and sent Rǔ Kuān to guard Quēsài.
B10.26.8 In the ninth month,
Chǔ Píng Wáng died.
The Lìngyǐn Zǐcháng wanted to establish Zǐxī,
saying: “Dàzǐ Rén is weak,
and his mother was not the primary wife;
Wángzǐ Jiàn had actually betrothed her.
Zǐxī is older and loves goodness.
Establishing the elder is natural;
establishing the good brings order.
If the Wáng is natural and the state is ordered,
can one not strive for this?”
Zǐxī said angrily:
“This is to disorder the state and to slander the deceased Wáng.
The state has external aid
and must not be trifled with;
the Wáng has a primary heir
and he must not be replaced in disorder.
To destroy kinship, invite enmity, and disorder the succession
is inauspicious.
I would bear the blame for it.
Even if you bribed me with all under heaven,
I would all the more not follow it;
what benefit would it be for the state of Chǔ?
I must kill the Lìngyǐn!”
The Lìngyǐn was afraid,
and so established Zhāo Wáng.
B10.26.9 In winter, in the tenth month, on the day bǐngshēn,
the Wáng raised the army at Huá.
On the day xīnchǒu,
they were in Jiāo
and then halted at Shī.
In the eleventh month, on the day xīnyǒu,
the Jìn army conquered Gǒng.
Shàobó Yíng drove out Wángzǐ Cháo;
Wángzǐ Cháo and the members of the Shào Shì, Máobó Dé, Yǐnshì Gù, and Nángōng Yín fled to Chǔ bearing the archives of Zhōu.
Yīn Jì fled to Jǔ to rebel.
Shàobó met the Wáng at Shī
and covenanted with Liúzǐ and Shànzǐ.
They then encamped at Yǔzé
and halted at Dīshàng.
On the day guǐyǒu,
the Wáng entered Chéngzhōu.
On the day jiǎxū,
they covenanted at Xiānggōng.
The Jìn army ordered Chénggōng Bān to garrison Zhōu and then returned.
In the twelfth month, on the day guǐwèi,
the Wáng entered Zhuānggōng.
Wángzǐ Cháo sent word to inform the feudal lords, saying:
“Formerly Wǔ Wáng conquered Yīn,
Chéng Wáng pacified the four quarters,
and Kāng Wáng gave rest to the people.
They collectively established their younger brothers from the same mother
to serve as screens for Zhōu,
also saying:
‘I do not exclusively enjoy the achievements of Wén
and Wǔ;
and if later generations fall into confusion, failure, or overthrow and are submerged in difficulty,
then rescue them.’
Coming down to Yí Wáng,
the Wáng had faults in his own person,
and all the feudal lords ran together to their shrines
to pray for the Wáng's person.
Coming down to Lì Wáng,
the Wáng's heart was perverse and cruel,
the myriad people could not endure it,
and they settled the Wáng at Zhì.”
The feudal lords abandoned their positions
to interfere in the royal government.
Xuān Wáng had the ambition
to subsequently make the officials effective.
Coming to Yōu Wáng,
Heaven did not pity Zhōu;
the King was dim and unrighteous,
and thus erred in his position.
Xié Wáng usurped the mandate,
so the feudal lords replaced him
and established the royal heir,
moving the capital to Jiá Rǔ—
—this was the ability of the brothers to exert effort for the royal house.
Coming to Huì Wáng,
Heaven did not grant peace to Zhōu,
giving rise to Tuí’s treacherous heart,
which extended to Shū Dài.
Huì Wáng and Xiāng Wáng fled from the hardship,
leaving the royal capital.
Then Jìn and Zhèng together removed the unrighteous
to stabilize the royal family.
This was the ability of the brothers to take the lead in following the former kings' mandates.
In the sixth year of Dìng Wáng,
the people of Qín sent down a portent,
saying:
"Zhōu shall have a king with a birthmark,
who yet will be able to cultivate his duties;
the feudal lords will submit and offer tribute
for two generations of shared service.
When the royal house has an interruption in the kingship,
if the feudal lords do not plan for it,
they shall suffer the calamities of its disorder."
Coming to Líng Wáng,
he was born with
a birthmark.
The King was exceedingly divine and sage,
and bore no ill will toward the feudal lords.
Líng Wáng and
Jǐng Wáng were able to complete their reigns.
"Now the royal house is in disorder;
Shàn Qí and Liú Dí have ravaged and disordered the world,
acting entirely without righteousness.
They say,
'What constancy did the former kings have?
Only what my heart mandates shall be,
and who would dare punish it?'
Leading a crowd of pitiless people,
they carry out disorder in the royal house.
Their invasive desires are insatiable,
their schemes and demands are without limit.
They treat the ghosts and spirits with habitual contempt,
they neglect and cast aside the penal laws,
they double-cross and violate the solemn covenants,
they are arrogant and stubborn toward the dignified ceremonies,
and they falsely represent the former kings.
Jìn acts unrighteously,
acting as their regent and support,
desiring to indulge their boundlessness.
Hereby, I, this unworthy one, am shaken and cast out,
fleeing to the Jīng Mán,
with no place to settle.
If my several brothers, nephews, and uncles would uphold and follow the laws of Heaven,
and not assist the crafty and treacherous,
but follow the mandates of the former kings,
and not hasten Heaven's punishment,
but forgive and plan for this unworthy one,
that would be my wish.
I dare to fully lay out my inner thoughts and the constants of the former kings,
and may the feudal lords truly give deep thought to it."
"In the past, the mandate of the former kings said:
'If the Queen has no legitimate son,
then choose and establish the eldest.
If their ages are equal, use virtue;
if their virtue is equal, use divination.'
The King does not establish a favorite,
and the high officials are not selfish;
this is the system of antiquity.
Mù Hòu and the Crown Prince Shòu died early and passed from the world;
Shàn and Liú supported their private interest by establishing a younger son,
thereby interfering with the former kings.
Let the brothers and cousins take heed of this!"
Mǐn Mǎfù heard Zǐ Cháo's words
and said:
"Refined words are for the performance of ritual.
Zǐ Cháo violated Jǐng Wáng's mandate
and relied on the distance of Great Jìn
to give rein to his own ambitions.
This is an extreme lack of ritual;
what use are refined words?"
B10.26.10 A comet appeared in Qí,
and the Marquis of Qí sent for it to be exorcised.
Yànzǐ said:
"It is of no use;
it only invites deception.
The Way of Heaven does not flatter,
nor does it change its mandate;
how can one exorcise it?
Moreover, Heaven has comets
to remove filth.
If your Lordship has no filthy virtue,
why exorcise it?
If your virtue is filthy,
how would exorcising it diminish the harm?
The Classic of Poetry says:
'Only this Wén Wáng,
was careful and reverent.
Brightly he served the Lord on High,
and thus he drew in much blessing.
His virtue did not swerve,
and thus he received the states of the four quarters.'
If your Lordship does not deviate from virtue,
the states of the four quarters will come to you;
what cause for concern is there in a comet?
The Classic of Poetry says:
'We have nothing to mirror ourselves in
but the lords of Xià and Shāng.
Because they used disorder,
the people ended in flight and ruin.'
If virtue swerves into disorder,
the people will flee and be ruined;
what the invocators and scribes do
will be unable to provide any remedy."
The Duke was pleased
and then stopped.
B10.26.11 The Marquis of Qí was sitting with Yànzǐ in the Main Hall.
The Duke sighed and said:
"How beautiful is this chamber!
Who shall possess this?"
Yànzǐ said: "I venture to ask,
what do you mean?"
The Duke said: "I think it depends on virtue."
Yànzǐ replied:
"According to your Lordship's words,
it would be the Chén clan!
Although the Chén clan has no great virtue,
they have been generous to the people.
In the measures of dòu, qū, fǔ, and zhōng,
what they take from the public is meager,
and what they give to the people is generous.
Your Lordship collects heavily from them,
while the Chén clan gives heavily to them;
the people have turned to them.
The Classic of Poetry says:
'Though I have no virtue to give you,
let us sing and dance.'
With the generosity of the Chén clan,
the people sing and dance for them.
If later generations are slightly indolent,
and the Chén clan does not perish,
then the state will become their state."
The Duke said: "Excellent!
What can be done about this?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"Only ritual can stop it.
According to ritual,
private generosity does not reach the level of the state,
the people do not move away,
farmers do not shift their lands,
artisans and merchants do not change their trades,
scholars are not promoted excessively,
officials do not overreach,
and Grand Officers do not seize the public's profits."
The Duke said:
"I am unable to do this.
Only from now on do I know that ritual can be used to govern a state."
Yànzǐ replied: "That ritual can be used to govern a state has been true for a long time;
it exists alongside Heaven and Earth.
That the ruler commands and the minister is reverent,
the father is kind and the son is filial,
the elder brother is loving and the younger brother is respectful,
the husband is harmonious and the wife is gentle,
the mother-in-law is kind and the daughter-in-law is obedient—
this is ritual.
That the ruler commands without violation,
and the minister is reverent without duplicity;
the father is kind and teaches,
and the son is filial and remonstrates;
the elder brother is loving and friendly,
and the younger brother is respectful and submissive;
the husband is harmonious and righteous,
and the wife is gentle and correct;
the mother-in-law is kind and accommodating,
and the daughter-in-law is obedient and graceful—
these are the good things of ritual."
The Duke said: "Excellent!
I, the solitary man, have only now heard of this supremacy of ritual!"
Yànzǐ replied:
"Ritual is what the former kings received from Heaven and Earth for the sake of their people;
therefore, the former kings held it supreme."
A10.27 The Classic of the Twenty-seventh Year of Zhāo Gōng.
A10.27.1 In the spring of the twenty-seventh year,
the Duke went to Qí.
A10.27.2 The Duke arrived from Qí
and stayed in Yùn.
A10.27.3 In the summer, in the fourth month,
Wú assassinated its ruler Liáo.
A10.27.4 Chǔ killed its Grand Master Xì Wǎn.
A10.27.5 In autumn,
Shì Yāng of Jìn,
Yuè Qílí of Sòng,
Běigōng Xǐ of Wèi,
the people of Cáo,
the people of Zhū,
and the people of Téng met at Hù.
A10.27.6 In winter, in the tenth month,
Earl Wǔ of Cáo died.
A10.27.7 Zhū Kuài came in flight.
A10.27.8 The Duke went to Qí.
A10.27.9 The Duke arrived from Qí
and resided at Yùn.
B10.27 Commentary on the Twenty-seventh Year of Duke Zhāo.
B10.27.1 In the spring of the twenty-seventh year,
the Duke went to Qí.
The Duke arrived from Qí
and stayed at Yùn;
this indicates he was outside the capital.
B10.27.2 The Viscount of Wú wished to take advantage of the mourning in Chǔ to attack it;
he sent Prince Yǎnyú and Prince Zhúyōng to lead an army and besiege Qián;
he sent Jìzǐ of Yánzhōu-lái on a mission of state to the upper states
and subsequently to Jìn
to observe the feudal lords.
Yǒu-yǐn Rán and Wáng-yǐn Jùn of Chǔ led an army to rescue Qián;
the Left Marshal Shěn-yǐn Xū led the sons of the capital lords and the King's cavalry units to reinforce the army;
they encountered the Wú army at Qióng.
Chief Minister Zǐcháng went as far as Shāruì with a naval force and then returned.
Zuǒ-yǐn Xì Wǎn and Gōng-yǐn Shòu arrived at Qián with their army,
but the Wú army could not retreat.
Prince Guāng of Wú said,
"This is the time;
it must not be lost."
He told Zhuān Shèzhū,
"There is a saying in the upper states:
'Without seeking,
what can one gain?'
I
am the King's heir;
I wish to seek the throne.
If the matter succeeds,
even though Jìzǐ arrives,
he will not depose me."
Zhuān Shèzhū said,
"The King can be assassinated.
His mother is old and his son is young;
what can they do against me?"
Guāng said,
"I
shall be your very self."
In the summer, in the fourth month,
Guāng hid armored men in a cellar and held a banquet for the King.
The King had armored guards sit along the road as far as the gate.
At the gate, the steps, the doors, and the mats,
they were all the King's personal attendants,
flanking the way with long spears.
Those presenting the delicacies presented the carcasses and changed their clothes outside the gate.
Those carrying the delicacies entered by crawling on their knees,
while those holding spears flanked and supported them;
once they reached the meat,
it was handed over.
Guāng feigned a foot ailment
and entered the cellar.
Zhuān Shèzhū placed a sword inside a fish to present it;
he drew the sword and stabbed the King.
Spear points crossed in his chest,
but he succeeded in assassinating the King.
Hélú made Zhuān's son a high official.
When Jìzǐ arrived,
he said,
"If the former rulers do not lack sacrifices,
the people do not lack a master,
the altars of soil and grain have a protector,
and the state does not fall,
then he is my ruler.
Whom would I dare to resent?
I mourn the dead and serve the living
to await the mandate of Heaven.
It was not I who started the disorder;
to follow whoever is established
is the way of our ancestors."
He reported the completion of his mission, wailed at the tomb,
returned to his position, and waited.
Prince Yǎnyú of Wú fled to Xú,
and Prince Zhúyōng fled to Zhōngwú.
The Chǔ army heard of the disorder in Wú and returned.
B10.27.3 Xì Wǎn was upright and harmonious;
the people of the state were pleased with him.
Yān Jiāngshī was the Commander of the Right;
he allied with Fèi Wújí and hated Xì Wǎn.
Chief Minister Zǐcháng was greedy and believed slanders.
Wújí slandered Xì Wǎn to him,
saying to Zǐcháng,
"Zǐ'è wishes to invite you to drink wine."
He also said to Zǐ'è,
"The Chief Minister wishes to drink wine at your house."
Zǐ'è said,
"I
am a person of low status,
not worthy of the honor of the Chief Minister's visit.
If the Chief Minister insists on coming,
the favor is already extreme.
I have nothing with which to repay him;
what shall I do?"
Wújí said,
"The Chief Minister is fond of armor and weapons.
Bring some out,
and I will choose among them."
He took five sets of armor and five weapons and
said,
"Place them at the gate.
When the Chief Minister arrives,
he will certainly look at them
and then proceed with the repayment."
When the day of the feast came,
they were screened off to the left of the gate.
Wújí said to the Chief Minister,
"I almost brought disaster upon you.
Zǐ'è is going to do you harm;
armor is at the gate.
You must not go!
Moreover, in this campaign,
Wú could have achieved its goal.
Zǐ'è took a bribe and returned;
he also misled the other commanders
and made them withdraw their forces,
saying
'taking advantage of disorder is inauspicious.'
If Wú takes advantage of our mourning,
and we take advantage of their disorder,
is that not also acceptable?"
The Chief Minister sent someone to look at the Xì residence,
and indeed there was armor there.
He did not go,
and he summoned Yān Jiāngshī to tell him.
Jiāngshī withdrew
and then ordered an attack on the Xì clan
to burn them.
Zǐ'è heard of this
and subsequently committed suicide.
The people of the state would not set the fire;
an order was issued:
"Those who do not set fire to the Xì residence
will share in the same crime."
Someone took a bundle of reeds,
and someone took a handful of straw;
the people of the state threw them
but still did not set the fire.
The Chief Minister burned it anyway,
completely exterminating the Xì clan and their partisans,
and killing Yáng Lìngzhōng and his younger brothers Wán and Tuó, along with Jìn Chén and his sons and younger brothers.
The clan of Jìn Chén cried out in the capital,
saying,
"The Yān and Fèi clans consider themselves kings;
they focus on bringing disaster to the state of Chǔ,
weakening and isolating the Royal House,
and deceiving the King and the Chief Minister for their own profit.
The Chief Minister believes them completely;
what will happen to the state?"
The Chief Minister was troubled by this.
B10.27.4 In the autumn,
they met at Hù
to order the guarding of Zhōu
and to plan for the reinstatement of the Duke.
Sòng and Wèi both found it advantageous to reinstate the Duke
and firmly requested it.
Fàn Xiànzǐ took a bribe from Jìsūn
and said to Sīchéng Zǐliáng and Běigōng Zhēnzǐ,
"Jìsūn did not yet know his crime
when the ruler attacked him.
He requested to be imprisoned or to go into exile,
but in this he was not successful.
The ruler then failed to overcome him
and left of his own accord.
Could he have expelled the ruler without being prepared?
The restoration of the Jì clan
was Heaven's rescue of them.
It calmed the anger of the Duke's followers
and opened the heart of the Shúsūn clan.
Otherwise,
how could one be attacking others yet take off his armor and hold a quiver to stroll about?
That the Shúsūn clan feared the spread of the disaster
and identified themselves with the Jì clan
was the Way of Heaven.
The Lord of Lǔ defended Qí,
for three years without success.
The Jì clan has greatly won over the people,
the Huái Yí are with them,
they have ten years of preparations,
they have the support of Qí and Chǔ,
they have the assistance of Heaven,
they have the help of the people,
they have the heart for firm defense,
they have the influence of the various states,
yet they dare not declare it,
serving the Lord as if he were in the capital.
Therefore, Yǎng considers it difficult.
You two are both those who plan for the state,
and wish to restore the Lord of Lǔ,
which is Yǎng's wish as well.
I request to follow you two to besiege Lǔ.
If there is no success,
I will die for it."
The two men were afraid,
and both declined.
Then they declined the small states,
and reported back citing the difficulties.
B10.27.5 Mèng Yìzǐ and Yáng Hǔ attacked Yùn.
The people of Yùn were about to fight.
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
"The mandate of Heaven has not erred for a long time.
Those who caused the Lord to flee
must be this multitude.
Since Heaven has already brought calamity upon them,
and they seek to bless themselves,
is that not also difficult!
If there are still ghosts and spirits,
they will surely be defeated.
Alas!
There is no hope!
They will surely die here!"
The Duke sent Zǐjiāzǐ to Jìn.
The Duke's troops were defeated at Qiězhī.
B10.27.6 Regarding the calamity of Xì Wǎn of Chǔ,
the talk in the state had not ceased.
None of those who presented the sacrificial meat did not slander the Lìngyǐn.
Shěn Yǐnxū said to Zǐcháng:
"As for the Zuǒyǐn and Zhōngjiùyǐn,
no one knows their crimes,
yet you killed them,
thereby giving rise to slander and complaints,
which continue to this day.
I, Xū, am confused by this:
a benevolent person killing someone to cover up slander
still would not do it;
now you kill people to provoke slander,
and do not plan for it, is that not strange!
Now, Wújì
is a slanderer of Chǔ,
as everyone knows.
He removed Cháo Wú,
expelled Cài Hóu Zhū,
caused the death of Crown Prince Jiàn,
killed Liányǐn Shē,
and blocked the King's ears and eyes,
making him not perceptive.
Otherwise,
King Píng's warmth, kindness, respect, and frugality
surpassed King Chéng
and King Zhuāng,
and was in no way inferior.
The reason he did not
win over the feudal lords
was that those close to him were not reached.
Now you have again killed three innocent men,
giving rise to great slander,
which is almost reaching you.
If you do not plan for it,
what use will you be?
Yān Jiāngshī forged your orders
to exterminate three clans.
These three clans
were the fine people of the state,
and did not neglect their positions.
Wú has a new ruler,
and the borders are alarmed daily.
If Chǔ has a major crisis,
you will be in danger!
A wise person removes slanders to secure themselves;
now you cherish a slanderer to endanger yourself,
how extreme
is your confusion!"
Zǐcháng said:
"This is Wǎ's fault;
how dare I not plan well!"
In the ninth month, on the day jǐwèi,
Zǐcháng killed Fèi Wújì and Yān Jiāngshī,
and completely exterminated their clans,
to please the state.
The slanderous talk then stopped.
B10.27.7 In winter,
the Duke went to Qí,
and the Marquis of Qí requested to feast him.
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
"Standing in his court morning and evening,
what need is there for a feast?
Let it just be drinking wine."
So they drank wine.
They had the steward present the offerings,
and requested ease.
The daughter of Zǐzhòng was named Zhòng,
and was the wife of the Marquis of Qí.
She said:
"I request to let Zhòng see him."
Zǐjiāzǐ then went out with the Lord.
B10.27.8 In the twelfth month,
Jí Qín of Jìn delivered the garrisons of the feudal lords to Zhōu.
The people of Lǔ declined, citing their difficulties.
A10.28 The Classic of the 28th Year of Duke Zhāo
A10.28.1 In the spring of the twenty-eighth year,
in the royal third month,
Duke Dào of Cáo was buried.
A10.28.2 The Duke went to Jìn,
and halted at Qiánhóu.
A10.28.3 In summer, in the fourth month on the day bǐngxū,
Earl Níng of Zhèng died.
A10.28.4 In the sixth month,
Duke Dìng of Zhèng was buried.
A10.28.5 In autumn, in the seventh month on the day guǐsì,
the Viscount of Téng, Níng, died.
A10.28.6 In winter,
Duke Dào of Téng was buried.
B10.28 The Commentary of the 28th Year of Duke Zhāo
B10.28.1 In the spring of the twenty-eighth year,
the Duke went to Jìn,
and was about to go to Qiánhóu.
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
"When one has a request of others,
yet stays at their place of comfort,
who would pity him?
Better to arrive at the border."
He did not listen,
and sent someone to request to be received in Jìn.
The people of Jìn said:
"Heaven has brought calamity to the state of Lǔ,
and its Lord has been suffering in exile abroad.
The Lord has not even sent a single messenger to pay respects to us,
but has gone to seek comfort with his relatives.
Should we then be made to receive the Lord?"
They made the Duke return to the border,
and only then received him.
B10.28.2 Qí Shèng and Wù Zāng of Jìn exchanged wives.
Qí Yíng was going to arrest them,
and consulted with Sīmǎ Shūyóu.
Shūyóu said:
"The Books of Zhèng have it:
'Those who hate the upright and dislike the correct
indeed have many followers.'
Those without the Way have established themselves;
you fear you will not escape.
The Book of Songs says:
'When the people have many perversions,
do not create perversions yourself.'
Better to stop for now;
what do you think?"
Yíng said:
"The Qí clan has its own private punishment to administer,
what does the state have to do with it?"
He then arrested them.
Qí Shèng bribed Xún Lè,
and Xún Lè spoke for him to the Marquis of Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn arrested Qí Yíng.
Qí Yíng's ministers said:
"Since we are all going to die anyway,
we might as well let our lord hear of the deaths of Shèng and Zāng to feel some satisfaction."
They then killed them.
In summer, in the sixth month,
Jìn killed Qí Yíng and Yáng Shíwǒ.
Shíwǒ
was of Qí Yíng's faction,
and assisted in the disorder,
so they killed him,
and then exterminated the Qí clan
and the Yángshé clan.
Earlier,
Shūxiàng wanted to marry a woman from the clan of Shēngōng Wūchén.
His mother wanted him to marry from her own clan.
Shūxiàng said:
"My mother's sisters are many but their sons are few;
I have taken warning from my maternal relatives."
His mother said:
"The wife of Zǐlíng killed three husbands,
one ruler, and one son,
and caused the destruction of one state and two high ministers.
Can one not take warning from this?"
I have heard it said:
"Extreme beauty is sure to be accompanied by extreme evil."
This woman is the daughter of Yáo Zǐ, the junior concubine of Zhèng Mù,
and the younger sister of Zǐ Hé
as well.
Zǐ Hé died young
and without heirs,
and yet Heaven has concentrated beauty in her;
she will surely cause a great downfall because of this.
Long ago, the Yǒu Réng clan produced a daughter,
with hair as black as a crow's wing
and extremely beautiful,
her luster such that she could be used as a mirror.
She was named Xuán Qī.
The Music Master Yuè Zhèng Hòu Kuí took her as his wife,
and she gave birth to Bó Fēng.
He truly had the heart of a pig,
insatiably greedy
and boundlessly contentious and perverse;
he was called Fēng Shǐ.
Hòu Yì of Yǒu Qióng destroyed him,
and because of this, Hòu Kuí has no one to offer sacrifices to him.
Furthermore, the fall of the Sān Dài and the deposition of Gòng Zǐ
were all caused by such creatures.
Why would you take her?
Truly, an extraordinary beauty
is enough to move men's hearts.
If one does not possess virtue and righteousness,
then there will surely be calamity."
Shū Xiàng was afraid
and did not dare take her.
Píng Gōng forced him to take her,
and she gave birth to Bó Shí.
When Bó Shí was first born,
the mother of Zǐ Róng ran to inform his sisters-in-law,
saying:
"The elder sister-in-law has given birth to a boy."
The sisters-in-law went to see him.
Upon reaching the hall,
they heard his cry and turned back,
saying:
"That is the voice of a jackal or wolf.
A wolf-cub has wild ambitions.
If not for him,
no one would cause the downfall of the Yáng Shé clan."
Consequently, they did not look at him.
In the autumn,
Hán Xuān Zǐ of Jìn died.
Wèi Xiàn Zǐ took charge of the government
and divided the lands of the Qí clan into seven districts,
and the lands of the Yáng Shé clan into three districts.
Sī Mǎ Mí Móu became the Grand Master of Wū,
Jiǎ Xīn became the Grand Master of Qí,
Sī Mǎ Wū became the Grand Master of Píng Líng,
Wèi Wù became the Grand Master of Gěng Yáng,
Zhī Xú Wú became the Grand Master of Tú Shuǐ,
Hán Gù became the Grand Master of Mǎ Shǒu,
Mèng Bǐng became the Grand Master of Yú,
Yuè Xiāo became the Grand Master of Tóng Dī,
Zhào Cháo became the Grand Master of Píng Yáng,
and Liáo Ān became the Grand Master of Yáng Shì.
He said that Jiǎ Xīn
and Sī Mǎ Wū had performed meritorious service for the Royal House, so he promoted them.
He said that Zhī Xú Wú, Zhào Cháo, Hán Gù, and Wèi Wù
were sons of noble families who had not failed in their duties and could maintain their heritage.
As for the other four men,
they all received their districts before being granted an audience with Wèi Zǐ;
they were promoted based on their worthiness.
Wèi Zǐ said to Chéng Zhuān:
"I have given a district to Wù.
Will people think I am showing favoritism to my own kinsman?"
He replied:
"Why would they!
As for Wù’s character,
when far away, he does not forget his lord;
when near, he does not press his peers.
When in a position of profit, he thinks of righteousness; when in straits, he thinks of purity.
He has a steadfast mind and no licentious conduct.
Even though you gave him a district,
is it not entirely appropriate?
In the past, when Wǔ Wáng conquered Shāng
and gloriously possessed the world,
fifteen of the states were ruled by his brothers,
and forty states were ruled by members of the Jī clan;
in all these cases, he promoted his relatives.
Promotion has no other principle:
it is only where goodness resides;
whether relative or stranger, it is the same.
The Shī says:
'Only this Wén Wáng,
God measured his heart.
Calm was his virtuous reputation,
his virtue was able to shine bright.
Able to be bright and to be good,
able to be a leader and a ruler.
Ruling this great state,
able to be compliant and to be cooperative.
Aligning with Wén Wáng,
his virtue was without regret.
Having received God's blessing,
it extended to his grandsons and sons.'
When the heart can control righteousness, it is called 'measure';
when virtue is upright and responded to with harmony, it is called 'calm';
when illumination reaches the four quarters, it is called 'brightness';
when diligent giving is without selfishness, it is called 'goodness';
when teaching and instructing are untiring, it is called 'leadership';
when rewarding, celebrating, punishing, and overawing are carried out with authority, it is called 'rulership';
when compassionate harmony wins universal submission, it is called 'compliance';
when choosing the good and following it, it is called 'cooperation';
when ordering heaven and earth, it is called 'civilized.'
If these nine virtues do not fail,
one's actions will bring no regret.
Therefore, one inherits the Mandate of Heaven,
and descendants rely upon it.
Your promotion of these men
is close to the virtues of Wén Wáng;
how far-reaching its impact will be!"
As Jiǎ Xīn was about to go to his district,
he had an audience with Wèi Zǐ.
Wèi Zǐ said:
"Jiǎ Xīn, come forward!
In the past, when Shū Xiàng went to Zhèng,
Zōng Miè was ugly.
He wished to observe Shū Xiàng,
so he followed those sent to collect the vessels
and went there.
He stood below the hall,
and with just one word, he showed his excellence.
Shū Xiàng was about to drink wine,
and when he heard him,
he said:
'This must be Zōng Míng!'
He went down,
took him by the hand and led him up,
saying:
'In the past, the Jiǎ Dà Fū was ugly.
He married a beautiful wife,
and for three years she neither spoke nor laughed.
He drove her to Rú Gāo
and shot a pheasant.
He hit it,
and only then did his wife laugh and speak.
The Jiǎ Dà Fū said:
"Talent cannot be suppressed.
If I had not been able to shoot,
you would never have spoken or laughed!"
Now, you are not prominent in appearance,
and if you had not spoken,
I would almost have missed knowing you.
Such is the necessity of speaking out!'
Thereupon, they became like old friends.
Now you have performed service for the Royal House,
and that is why I have promoted you.
Go now!
Be reverent in your duties!
Do not let your efforts flag!"
When Zhòng Ní heard of Wèi Zǐ's promotions,
he considered them righteous,
saying:
"He did not neglect his relatives nearby,
nor did he fail to promote the worthy far away.
This can be called righteousness."
He also heard of his instructions to Jiǎ Xīn
and considered them loyal, saying:
"The Shī says:
'Ever strive to be in harmony with the Mandate,
and seek for yourself much happiness.'
This is loyalty.
Wèi Zǐ's promotions were righteous,
and his instructions were loyal.
Will he not long have descendants in the state of Jìn?"
In the winter,
the people of Gěng Yáng had a legal dispute
which Wèi Wù could not decide,
so he referred the case to his superior.
The senior branch of the clan involved offered a bribe of female musicians,
and Wèi Zǐ was about to accept them.
Wèi Wù said to Yán Méi
and Nǚ Kuān:
"Our master is known among the feudal lords for not taking bribes.
If he accepts this from the people of Gěng Yáng,
no bribery could be greater.
You must remonstrate with him!"
They both agreed.
They retired from the court
and waited in the courtyard.
When the meal was brought in,
he summoned them.
As the food was being set out,
they sighed three times.
After the meal was finished,
he had them sit down.
Wèi Zǐ said:
“I have heard from my elders
that the proverb says:
‘Only food makes one forget their worries.’
Sir, why did you sigh three times in the midst of eating?
In unison they replied:
“Someone gave these two humble men some wine,
so we did not have an evening meal.
When the food first arrived,
we feared it would be insufficient,
and so we sighed.
In the middle of the meal,
we blamed ourselves, saying:
‘How could food from the General be insufficient?’
And so we sighed again.
When the meal was over,
we wished to use the bellies of humble men to measure the heart of a gentleman,
and we were sated, nothing more.”
Xiànzǐ declined the request of the person from Gěngyáng.
A10.29 The Classic: Duke Zhāo, Twenty-ninth Year
A10.29.1 In the spring of the twenty-ninth year,
the Duke arrived from Qiánhóu
and stayed in Yùn.
The Marquis of Qí sent Gāo Zhāng to offer condolences to the Duke.
A10.29.2 The Duke went to Jìn
and halted at Qiánhóu.
A10.29.3 In summer, the fourth month, on the gēngzǐ day,
Shū Yì died.
A10.29.4 Autumn, the seventh month.
A10.29.5 In winter, the tenth month,
Yùn collapsed.
B10.29 The Commentary: Duke Zhāo, Twenty-ninth Year
B10.29.1 In the spring of the twenty-ninth year,
the Duke arrived from Qiánhóu
and stayed in Yùn.
The Marquis of Qí sent Gāo Zhāng to offer condolences to the Duke,
addressing him as "Master of the House."
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
“Qí holds you in low esteem, my lord;
you only bring humiliation upon yourself there.”
The Duke went to Qiánhóu.
B10.29.2 In the third month, on the jǐmǎo day,
those at the capital killed Shào Bó Yíng, Yǐn Shì Gù, and the son of Yuán Bó Lǔ.
When Yǐn Gù returned earlier,
a woman met him in the suburbs of Zhōu
and rebuked him,
saying:
“At home you encouraged people to cause calamity;
in flight, you return within a few days.
This man,
will he last more than three years?”
In summer, the fifth month, on the gēngyín day,
Prince Zhào Chē entered Dǎn to rebel;
Yīn Bùnìng defeated him.
B10.29.3 Every year, Píngzǐ would buy horses
and provide clothes and shoes for the attendants
and send them to Qiánhóu.
The Duke seized the men who brought the horses
and sold them,
and then did not return the horses.
The Marquis of Wèi came to present his chariot horses;
one was named Qǐfú,
it fell into a trench and died.
The Duke intended to make a coffin for it.
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
“The attendants are suffering;
I request that you use it to feed them.”
So they used a curtain to wrap it.
The Duke gave Gōngyǎn a lambskin robe
and sent him to present the Lóngfǔ gem to the Marquis of Qí;
he then presented the lambskin robe as well.
The Marquis of Qí was pleased
and gave him Yánggǔ.
When Gōngyǎn and Gōngwéi were born,
their mothers had gone out together.
Gōngyǎn was born first.
Gōngwéi's mother said:
“Since we came out together,
let us report the births together.”
After three days,
Gōngwéi was born.
His mother reported first,
and Gōngwéi became the elder brother.
While the Duke was secretly pleased at Yánggǔ,
he thought of his situation in Lǔ
and said:
“It was Wùrén who caused this calamity.
Moreover, the one born later became the elder brother;
the deception has lasted a long time.”
He then demoted him
and made Gōngyǎn the heir apparent.
B10.29.4 In autumn,
a dragon appeared in the suburbs of Jiàng.
Wèi Xiànzǐ asked Cài Mò:
“I have heard
that among creatures none are more wise than the dragon,
because it cannot be captured alive.
It is called wise;
is this true?”
He replied:
“It is humans who are actually ignorant,
not that the dragon is actually wise.
In ancient times, people reared dragons;
thus the state had the Huànlóng clan
and the Yùlóng clan.”
Xiànzǐ said:
“As for these two clans,
I have heard of them too,
but I do not know their origins.
What is the meaning of this?”
He replied:
“In the past, there was Liù Shū’ān.
He had a descendant named Dǒng Fù,
who really loved dragons.
He was able to seek out their cravings to feed them,
and many dragons went to him.
He then tamed and reared dragons
to serve Emperor Shùn.
The Emperor granted him the surname Dǒng
and the clan name Huànlóng.
He was enfeoffed at Zōngchuān;
the Zōngyí clan are his descendants.
Therefore, for generations, the clan of Emperor Shùn reared dragons.
Coming to Kǒngjiǎ of Xià,
he was compliant with the Emperor of Heaven.
The Emperor granted him teams of dragons to ride,
two each from the Hé and Hàn rivers,
each having a male and a female.
Kǒngjiǎ was unable to feed them
and had not found the Huànlóng clan.
After the Táotáng clan had declined,
among its descendants was Liú Lěi,
who learned how to tame dragons from the Huànlóng clan
to serve Kǒngjiǎ.
He was able to feed them,
and the Sovereign of Xià praised him,
granting him the clan name Yùlóng,
to replace the descendants of Shǐwéi.
One of the female dragons died,
and he secretly made it into mincemeat to feed the Sovereign of Xià.
The Sovereign of Xià feasted on it
and later sent someone to look for it.
In fear, Liú Lěi moved to Lǔ Xiàn;
the Fàn clan are his descendants.”
Xiànzǐ said:
“Why are there none today?”
He replied:
“As for creatures,
each creature has its official.
The officials cultivate their methods
and think of them morning and night.
If they neglect their duties for one day,
then death will come to them.
If they lose their office, they do not eat.
When the officials are dedicated to their work,
the creatures arrive.
If they are neglected and abandoned,
the creatures will hide away
and be stifled and not breed.
Thus there were officials of the Five Elements,
which are called the Five Officials.
They were ranked and received clan names and surnames,
were enfeoffed as high lords,
and were sacrificed to as noble spirits.
The five sacrifices of the altars of earth and grain
are what were honored and served.
The Wood Rector was called Jùmáng,
the Fire Rector was called Zhùróng,
the Metal Rector was called Rùshōu,
the Water Rector was called Xuánmíng,
and the Soil Rector was called Hòutǔ.
The dragon
is a water creature.
The water office has been abandoned,
and so dragons are not caught alive.
Otherwise,
the Zhōu Yì has records of them:
In the hexagram Qián changing to Gòu,
it says:
‘A submerged dragon: do not act’;
in its Tóngrén, it says:
‘A dragon appearing in the field’;
in its Dàyǒu, it says:
‘A flying dragon in the heavens’;
in its Guài, it says:
‘A dragon at its height will have cause for regret.’
Its *Kūn* hexagram says:
“A flight of dragons appears without a head;
auspicious.”
The change from *Kūn* to *Bō* says:
“Dragons battle in the wilderness.”
If they were not seen morning and evening,
who could describe them?”
Xiànzǐ said:
“As for the five sacrifices of the Altars of Soil and Grain,
to which clans do the five officials belong?”
He replied:
“Shǎohào Shì had four descendants,
named Zhòng, Gāi, Xiū, and Xī;
they were truly capable in metal, wood, and water.
Zhòng was made Gòumáng,
Gāi was made Rùshōu,
and Xiū and Xī were made Xuánmíng.
Generation after generation they did not fail their duties,
and so they aided the state of Qióngsāng.
These are three of the sacrifices.
Zhuānxū Shì had a son named Lí,
who became Zhùróng;
Gònggōng Shì had a son named Gòulóng,
who became Hòutǔ.
These are the other two sacrifices.
Hòutǔ is the Altar of Soil;
Jì
is the Director of Agriculture.
Lièshān Shì had a son named Zhù who was Jì,
and he was sacrificed to from the Xià dynasty and before.
Qì of Zhōu was also Jì,
and he has been sacrificed to since the Shāng dynasty.”
B10.29.5 In winter,
Zhào Yāng and Xún Yín of Jìn led an army to wall Rǔbīn,
and then levied from the state of Jìn one *gǔ* of iron
to cast the penal tripods,
inscribing upon them the penal laws drafted by Fàn Xuānzǐ.
Zhòngní said:
“Jìn is likely to perish!
It has lost its proper measure.
The state of Jìn should maintain the laws and measures received by Táng Shú
to regulate its people,
and the high ministers and grand masters should maintain them in order;
the people are thereby able to respect the noble,
and the noble are thereby able to maintain their positions.
When the noble and the lowly do not err against each other,
it is what is called ‘measure.’
Duke Wén therefore created the officials of fixed ranks
and established the laws of Bèilú
to become the leader of the covenant.
Now they have abandoned these measures
and cast the penal tripods.
Since the people look only to the tripods,
how will they respect the noble?
What position will the noble maintain?
When there is no order between noble and lowly,
how can it be a state?
Furthermore, the penal laws of Xuānzǐ
were from the hunt of Yí,
which are the chaotic regulations of the state of Jìn;
how can they be used as permanent law?”
Shǐ Mò of Cài said:
“The Fàn clan and the Zhōngháng clan are likely to perish!
Zhōngháng Yín is a lower minister,
yet he interferes with superior orders
and presumptuously makes penal vessels
to be the law of the state;
this is codifying wickedness.
And they have added the laws of the Fàn clan to it;
changing the old
will lead to ruin.
It will also reach the Zhào clan,
as Zhào Mèng participated in it.
However, he did so out of necessity;
if he practices virtue,
he may be spared.”
A10.30 *The Classic: Thirtieth Year of Duke Zhāo*
A10.30.1 In the spring of the thirtieth year,
in the royal first month,
the Duke was in Qiánhóu.
A10.30.2 In summer, in the sixth month, on the day *gēngchén*,
Duke Qùjí of Jìn died.
A10.30.3 In autumn, in the eighth month,
Duke Qǐng of Jìn was buried.
A10.30.4 In winter, in the twelfth month,
Wú destroyed Xú,
and Zhāngyǔ, Viscount of Xú, fled to Chǔ.
B10.30 *The Commentary: Thirtieth Year of Duke Zhāo*
B10.30.1 In the spring of the thirtieth year,
in the royal first month,
the Duke was in Qiánhóu.
That the text does not first mention Yùn and Qiánhóu
is because it did not treat him as the Duke,
and also to signify his fault.
B10.30.2 In summer, in the sixth month,
Duke Qǐng of Jìn died.
In autumn, in the eighth month,
he was buried.
Yóu Jí of Zhèng offered condolences
and escorted the funeral.
Wèi Xiànzǐ sent Shì Jǐngbó to question him,
saying:
“At the funeral of Duke Dào,
Zǐxī offered condolences
and Zǐjiǎo escorted the funeral.
Now, you have no second companion;
what is the reason?”
He replied:
“The reason the feudal lords turn to the ruler of Jìn
is ritual propriety.
Ritual propriety
refers to the small serving the great and the great cherishing the small.
Serving the great lies in providing for its timely commands;
cherishing the small lies in pitying what they lack.
Since our humble state resides among great states,
we provide our duties and tribute
as well as our preparations against unforeseen calamities;
how could we forget to provide for commands?
The regulations of the former kings were:
for the funeral of a feudal lord,
a serviceman offers condolences
and a grand master escorts the funeral;
only for matters of auspicious meetings, missions of tribute, or military affairs does one send a high minister.
In the funeral affairs of Jìn,
when our humble state has the leisure,
our former rulers have assisted in holding the funeral ropes.
If there is no leisure,
then even servicemen
and grand masters sometimes cannot be supplied in full number.
The kindness of a great state
is to celebrate when more is given
and not to punish when there is a deficiency,
clearly understanding the circumstances
and merely seeking sufficiency;
this is considered ritual propriety.
At the funeral of King Líng,
our former ruler Duke Jiǎn was in Chǔ,
and our former grand master Yìn Duàn went there—
he was a junior minister of our humble state.
The King’s officers did not punish us,
out of pity for what we lacked.
Now you, Grand Master, say:
‘Why do you not follow the old precedent?’
Old precedents include both the lavish and the frugal,
and I did not know which to follow.
If I followed the lavish,
then my ruler is young and weak
and therefore could not provide it.
If I follow the frugal,
then I, Jí, am here.
Only you, Grand Master, can consider it!”
The people of Jìn could not question him further.
B10.30.3 The Viscount of Wú made the people of Xú seize Yǎnyú
and made the people of Zhōngwú seize Zhúyōng,
and the two princes fled to Chǔ.
The Viscount of Chǔ gave them large fiefs
and settled their migration,
sending the Director of Horse Inspections, Dàxīn, to welcome the princes of Wú,
making them reside in Yǎng.
Yǒuyǐn Rán
and the Marshal of the Left, Shěnyǐn Xū, walled it for them;
taking fields from Chéngfù and Hú to give to them,
intending to harm Wú.
Zǐxī remonstrated, saying:
“Guāng of Wú has newly gained his state
and is close to his people;
he treats the people like his children
and shares in their hardships,
as he intends to make use of them.
If we were on good terms with his borders
and made them submissive,
we would still fear his arrival.
Now we further strengthen his enemies
to increase his anger;
is this not impermissible?
Wú
is a descendant of the Zhōu,
yet they were cast away on the seacoast,
not communicating with the Jī clans.
Now they have begun to grow large
and compare themselves to the various Huá states.
Guāng is moreover very refined
and intends to equate himself with the former kings.
I do not know whether Heaven will make him a scourge,
making him destroy the state of Wú to enfeoff a great different surname,
or whether it will ultimately grant blessings to Wú.
The end of this is not far off.
Why do we not for now rely on our spirits
and pacify our own clan
to await its outcome?
What use is there in broadcasting our actions ourselves?”
The King did not listen.
The Viscount of Wú was angry.
In the twelfth month of winter,
the Viscount of Wú seized the Viscount of Zhōngwú.
He then invaded Xú,
damming the Shān River to flood it.
On the day jǐmǎo,
he destroyed Xú.
Zhāngyǔ, the Viscount of Xú, cut his hair
and took his wife to meet the Viscount of Wú.
The Viscount of Wú consoled him and sent him away,
making his close attendants follow him;
he then fled to Chǔ.
Shěn Yǐnxū of Chǔ led an army to rescue Xú,
but they did not arrive in time.
They then built walls at Yí
and made the Viscount of Xú reside there.
B10.30.5 The Viscount of Wú asked Wǔ Yuán,
"Previously, when you spoke of invading Chǔ,
I knew it was possible,
but I feared you would make me go,
and I also disliked that another would have the merit that should be mine.
Now I shall have it for myself.
What do you think of invading Chǔ?"
He replied,
"The high officials of Chǔ are numerous and at odds;
none are willing to take responsibility for troubles.
If you form three divisions to weary them,
when one division arrives,
they will certainly all come out.
When they come out, we withdraw;
when they withdraw, we come out.
Chǔ will certainly be exhausted on the roads.
By repeatedly wearying them to tire them out
and using many schemes to mislead them,
once they are tired, follow up with the three armies,
and you will surely achieve a great victory."
Hélú followed this advice,
and from then on, Chǔ began to suffer.
A10.31 The Annals of the Thirty-First Year of Duke Zhāo
In the spring of the thirty-first year,
in the royal first month,
the Duke was in Qiánhóu.
Jìsūn Yìrú met Xún Lè of Jìn at Shìlì.
In the summer, in the fourth month on the day dīngsì,
Bó Gǔ of Xuē died.
The Marquis of Jìn sent Xún Lè to condole with the Duke in Qiánhóu.
In autumn,
Duke Xiàn of Xuē was buried.
In winter,
Hēigōng came as a fugitive from Làn.
In the twelfth month, on the first day of the month xìnhài,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
B10.31 The Commentary of the Thirty-First Year of Duke Zhāo
In the spring of the thirty-first year,
in the royal first month,
the Duke was in Qiánhóu,
which signifies that he could not attend to matters internal or external.
B10.31.2 The Marquis of Jìn intended to use an army to escort the Duke back.
Fàn Xiànzǐ said,
"If we summon Jìsūn and he does not come,
then his failure to act as a subject will be truly manifest,
and only then should we attack him;
how about that?"
The people of Jìn summoned Jìsūn.
Xiànzǐ sent a private messenger to him,
saying,
"You must come;
I will ensure you receive no blame."
Jìsūn Yìrú met Xún Lè of Jìn at Shìlì.
Xún Lè said,
"Our ruler has sent me, Lè, to say to you:
'For what reason did you expel your ruler?
To have a ruler and not serve him—
Zhōu has constant punishments for this.
You should consider it!'"
Jìsūn wore a headband of undyed hemp
and hempen clothes,
walked barefoot,
and prostrated himself as he replied,
"To serve the ruler
is what this servant was not permitted to do;
how would I dare flee the sentence of punishment?
If the ruler considers me to have committed a crime,
I request to be imprisoned in Bì
to await the ruler's investigation;
it is entirely up to the ruler.
If, for the sake of my ancestors,
you do not cut off the Jì family
but grant me death,
and if I am neither killed nor exiled,
it would be the ruler's grace,
and even in death I would not rot.
If I could follow the ruler and return,
then that would truly be my wish;
how could I dare have a different heart?"
In the summer, in the fourth month,
Jìsūn followed Zhì Bó to Qiánhóu.
Zǐjiāzǐ said,
"The ruler should return with him.
If you cannot endure one moment of shame,
will you remain in shame for the rest of your life?"
The Duke said,
"Very well."
The crowd said,
"Everything depends on this one word—
the ruler must certainly drive him away!"
Xún Lè conveyed the Marquis of Jìn’s command to condole with the Duke
and said,
"Our ruler has sent me, Lè, to demand an accounting from Yìrú on your behalf;
Yìrú does not dare flee from death;
the ruler should enter the state!"
The Duke said,
"The ruler has graciously looked upon the friendship with my predecessor,
which extends even to this fugitive.
If I am to return to sweep the ancestral temple and serve the ruler,
then I cannot see that man.
If I ever could see that man again,
may I be as the River!"
Xún Lè covered his ears and ran away,
saying,
"My ruler is only afraid of being at fault;
how would he dare meddle in the troubles of the state of Lǔ?
I request to report back to my ruler."
He withdrew and told Jìsūn,
"The ruler's anger has not yet subsided;
you should go back for now to perform the sacrifices."
Zǐjiāzǐ said,
"If the ruler enters the Lǔ army with just a single carriage,
Jìsūn will surely return with the ruler."
The Duke wanted to follow this advice.
The crowd of followers coerced the Duke,
and he was unable to return.
Bó Gǔ of Xuē died;
as he was part of the covenant,
it was thus recorded.
In autumn,
the people of Wú invaded Chǔ,
attacked Yí,
and invaded Qián and Liù.
Shěn Yǐnxū of Chǔ led an army to rescue Qián,
and the Wú army withdrew.
The Chǔ army moved the people of Qián to Nángāng and then returned.
The Wú army besieged Xián.
Left Marshal Xū and Right Marshal Jī led an army to rescue Xián.
When they reached Yùzhāng,
the Wú army withdrew.
— — This was the first use of Zǐxū's strategy.
In winter,
Hēigōng of Zhū came as a fugitive from Làn.
Though he was of low rank, his name was recorded
because of the importance of the land.
The superior man says:
"The matter of having one's name recorded must be approached with such caution!
There are cases where being named is worse than not being named.
If someone rebels with land,
even if he is of low rank,
the land must be recorded
and the person named;
he is forever marked as unrighteous,
and this cannot be erased.
Therefore, the superior man thinks of ritual in every movement
and of righteousness in every action;
he does not turn back for the sake of profit
and does not suffer from the distress of unrighteousness.
Some seek fame but do not get it,
while some wish to hide but their names become manifest;
this is to punish the unrighteous.
Qí Bào was the Minister of Crime in Wèi,
an inherited Great Officer;
he acted unrighteously,
and he was recorded as
'a robber.'
Shùqí of Zhū,
Móuyí of Jǔ,
and Hēigōng of Zhū left with their lands,
only seeking a livelihood
and not seeking fame.
Yet even though they were of low rank, they had to be named.
These two types of recording
are the means by which to punish recklessness and remove greed.
If one makes their own life difficult
to endanger great men in high positions,
and yet their name becomes manifest and clear,
then those who struggle in difficulties will rush to follow them.
If one steals a city and rebels against their ruler to seek great profit and is not named,
then greedy people will apply their strength there.
For this reason, the Spring and Autumn records Qí Bào as
'a robber,'
and the names of the three rebels."
In order to punish the unrighteous,
and enumerate the evils of those without ritual,
it is a record of goodness.
Therefore it is said:
The phrasing of the *Chūnqiū* is subtle yet clear,
euphemistic yet discriminating.
When those above can make it shine brightly,
good people are encouraged by it,
and the excessive are afraid of it.
For this reason, the gentleman values it."
B10.31.6 In the twelfth month, on the day of *Xīnhài*, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
That night,
Zhào Jiǎnzi dreamed of a young boy, naked, turning around and singing.
At dawn, he consulted the scribe Shǐ Mò,
saying:
"I had such a dream,
and now there is a solar eclipse;
why is this?"
He replied:
"Six years from now, in this month,
Wú will likely enter Yǐng,
but in the end they will not hold it.
They will enter Yǐng on a *Gēngchén* day;
the sun and moon will be at the tail of the Chén constellation.
On the day *Gēngwǔ*,
the sun first had a flaw.
Fire overcomes Metal;
therefore, they will not succeed."
A10.32 The Annals of the Thirty-Second Year of Duke Zhāo
A10.32.1 In the spring of the thirty-second year,
in the royal first month,
the Duke was in Gānhóu.
A10.32.2 We took Kàn.
A10.32.3 In the summer,
Wú attacked Yuè.
A10.32.4 In the autumn, the seventh month.
A10.32.5 In the winter,
Zhòngsūn Héjì met with Hán Bùxìn of Jìn,
Gāo Zhāng of Qí,
Zhòng Jǐ of Sòng,
Shìshū Shēn of Wèi,
Guó Cān of Zhèng,
the people of Cáo,
the people of Jǔ,
the people of Xuē,
the people of Qǐ,
and the people of Xiǎo Zhū to wall Chéngzhōu.
A10.32.6 In the twelfth month, on the day *Jǐwèi*,
the Duke passed away in Gānhóu.
B10.32 The Commentary on the Thirty-Second Year of Duke Zhāo
B10.32.1 In the spring of the thirty-second year,
in the royal first month,
the Duke was in Gānhóu;
this says that he could neither manage the outside nor the inside,
and furthermore could not employ his people.
B10.32.2 In the summer,
Wú attacked Yuè;
this was the first time they used military force against Yuè.
Shǐ Mò said:
"In less than forty years,
Yuè will likely possess Wú!
Yuè has the favorable position of the Year Star, and yet Wú attacks them;
Wú will surely receive its misfortune."
B10.32.3 In the autumn, in the eighth month,
the King sent Fù Xīn and Shí Zhāng to Jìn
to request the walling of Chéngzhōu.
The Son of Heaven said:
"Heaven has sent down disaster upon Zhōu,
causing my brothers to both have rebellious hearts,
thus becoming a source of worry for my Uncle.
My various close relatives, nephews, and uncles have not had leisure to rest
for ten years now.
For five years, they have labored in garrison duty.
I, the One Man, have not forgotten this for a single day,
being as full of anxiety as a farmer looking forward to the harvest,
waiting in fear for the right time.
If my Uncle would extend great favor
to restore the legacy of the two Wén,
to ease the worries of the Zhōu house,
and to seek the blessings of Kings Wén and Wǔ,
so as to strengthen your position as covenant leader
and spread your good name abroad,
then I, the One Man, would have my great wish fulfilled.
Formerly, King Chéng assembled the feudal lords to wall Chéngzhōu,
making it the Eastern Capital
to exalt civil virtue.
Now I wish to seek blessings and borrow the spiritual power of King Chéng
by repairing the walls of Chéngzhōu,
so that the garrison men may no longer labor
and the feudal lords may thereby find peace,
and the destructive pests may be driven far away;
this will be due to the strength of Jìn.
May this matter be entrusted to my Uncle;
let my Uncle truly give it serious thought,
so that I, the One Man, will have no cause for resentment among the people,
while my Uncle will have glorious generosity
and the former kings will reward him."
Fàn Xiànzǐ said to Wèi Xiànzǐ:
"Rather than garrisoning Zhōu,
it is better to wall it.
Since the Son of Heaven has truly spoken thus,
even if there are later incidents,
it will be fine for Jìn not to be involved in them.
By following the King's command and relieving the feudal lords,
the state of Jìn will have no worries.
If we do not devote ourselves to this,
then what else should we attend to?"
Wèi Xiànzǐ said:
"Very well."
He sent Bóyīn to reply, saying:
"The Son of Heaven has issued a command;
how would we dare not receive it and hurry to announce it to the feudal lords?
The timing and the proportional distribution of duties
are all contained herein."
In the winter, in the eleventh month,
Wèi Shū and Hán Bùxìn of Jìn went to the capital
and assembled the grand masters of the feudal lords at Díquán
to renew the alliance
and to order the walling of Chéngzhōu.
Wèizi faced south.
Biāoxī of Wèi said:
"Wèizi will surely suffer a great disaster.
Usurping the position to command a great undertaking
is not his responsibility.
The *Shī* says:
'Revere the wrath of Heaven,
and do not dare to take leisure;
revere the changes of Heaven,
and do not dare to drive about.'
How much more so should one not dare to usurp the position to manage a great undertaking?"
On the day *Jǐchǒu*,
Shì Mímóu planned the layout of Chéngzhōu,
calculating the measurements,
estimating heights and depths,
measuring thicknesses,
determining the dimensions of the moats and channels,
examining the quality of the soil,
discussing distances,
determining the timeframe for the work,
counting the laborers,
considering the materials needed,
and recording the dry provisions
in order to order the corvée labor from the feudal lords.
He assigned the corvée and allotted the measurements,
recording them and handing them to the commanders,
and reported the results to Liúzi.
Hán Jiǎnzi oversaw it
to make it a completed order.
B10.32.4 In the twelfth month,
the Duke fell ill;
he offered gifts to all the grand masters,
but the grand masters did not accept.
He gave Zǐjiāzi a pair of tiger-shaped jades,
one ring, one disc,
and light garments;
he accepted them.
Then the grand masters all accepted his gifts.
On the day *Jǐwèi*,
the Duke passed away.
Zǐjiāzi returned the gifts to the treasury official,
saying:
"I did not dare to disobey the ruler's command."
The grand masters all returned their gifts.
The record says,
"The Duke passed away in Gānhóu,"
indicating that he had lost his proper place.
Zhào Jiǎnzi asked Shǐ Mò:
"The Jì lineage drove out their ruler,
yet the people submit to them;
the feudal lords side with them;
and the ruler died abroad without anyone being punished for it
indeed."
He replied:
"In the birth of things, there are pairs, threes, fives, and there are companions and seconders.
Therefore, Heaven has the three luminaries,
Earth has the five elements,
the body has left and right sides,
each having a match.
The King has dukes,
and the feudal lords have ministers;
all have seconders.
Heaven brought forth the Jì lineage
to be the seconder to the Lord of Lǔ
for a long time now.
That the people submit to them,
is it not appropriate?
Generation after generation, the rulers of Lǔ followed their path of failure,
while generation after generation, the Jì lineage cultivated their diligence,
The people have forgotten the ruler.
Even if he dies abroad,
who would pity him?
Altars of soil and grain do not have constant offerings,
rulers and ministers do not have constant positions;
it has been so since ancient times.
Therefore, the *Shī* says:
"High banks become valleys,
deep valleys become hills."
The surnames of the three royal lineages have now become commoners;
this is what you, my lord, know.
In the hexagrams of the *Yì*,
when Thunder rides over *Qián*, it is called *Dà Zhuàng*
it is the Way of Heaven.
Formerly, Chéng Jì Yǒu
was the youngest son of Duke Huán
and the beloved son of Wén Jiāng.
When she first felt the fetus move, she consulted the oracle.
The diviner reported to her,
saying:
"He will be born with an excellent reputation;
his name will be Yǒu,
and he will be a support to the ducal house."
When he was born,
it was as the diviner had said:
there was a mark on his hand that read
"Yǒu."
So they named him that.
Later, he performed great services for Lǔ
and received Bì to be a high minister.
Coming to Wén Zǐ and Wǔ Zǐ,
they increased their legacy generation by generation
and did not abandon the old achievements.
When Duke Wén of Lǔ passed away,
Dōngmén Suì killed the legitimate heir and established a son of a concubine.
The rulers of Lǔ then lost their state power,
and the government resided with the Jì lineage.
Since then, there have been four dukes.
The people do not know their ruler;
how can he regain the state?
Therefore, a ruler must be careful with his emblems and titles
and not lend them to others."
A11.1 Classic of the First Year of Duke Dìng
A11.1.1 In the spring of the first year,
the King.
A11.1.2 In the third month,
the people of Jìn seized Zhòng Jǐ of Sòng at the capital.
A11.1.3 In the summer, in the sixth month, on the day guǐhài,
the funeral procession of the Duke arrived from Qián Hóu.
A11.1.4 On the day wùchén,
the Duke ascended the throne.
A11.1.5 In the autumn, in the seventh month, on the day guǐsì,
we buried our ruler, Duke Zhāo.
A11.1.6 In the ninth month,
a great prayer for rain was performed.
A11.1.7 The temple of Yáng was established.
A11.1.8 In the winter, in the tenth month,
falling frost killed the pulse crops.
B11.1 Zuo Commentary for the First Year of Duke Dìng
B11.1.1 In the spring of the first year,
in the royal first month, on the day xīnsì,
Wèi Shū of Jìn assembled the grandees of the feudal lords at Dí Quán,
intending to build the walls of Chéng Zhōu.
Viscount Wèi presided over the administration.
Biāo Xī of Wèi said:
"To establish the Son of Heaven,
and then to change one's position to issue orders,
is not righteous.
To violate righteousness in a great matter
will surely bring about a great disaster.
Jìn will not lose its grip on the feudal lords,
but will Viscount Wèi escape calamity?"
On this expedition,
Wèi Xiàn Zǐ assigned the labor to Hán Jiǎn Zǐ and Yuán Shòu Guò
and went hunting at Dà Lù,
where a fire broke out.
On his return,
he died at Nìng.
Fàn Xiàn Zǐ removed his cedar outer coffin
because he had gone hunting before reporting the completion of his mission.
Mèng Yì Zǐ joined in building the walls of Chéng Zhōu;
on the day gēngyín,
they began setting up the frameworks.
Zhòng Jǐ of Sòng would not accept his assigned task,
saying:
"Téng, Xuē, and Ní
are our laborers."
The Steward of Xuē said:
"Sòng acts without principles,
severing our small state from the Zhōu,
and making us follow Chǔ.
Therefore, we used to follow Sòng.
But Duke Wén of Jìn made the covenant of Jiàn Tǔ,
which said:
'All those of our covenant
shall each return to their former duties.'
Whether we follow Jiàn Tǔ
or follow Sòng,
we will only follow your command."
Zhòng Jǐ said:
"Jiàn Tǔ was indeed like that."
The Steward of Xuē said:
"The Great Ancestor of Xuē, Xī Zhòng, lived in Xuē
and served as the Master of Chariots for Xià.
Xī Zhòng moved to Pī.
Zhòng Huǐ lived in Xuē
and served as the Left Minister for Tāng.
If we return to our former duties,
we shall serve as royal officers;
for what reason should we labor for the feudal lords?"
Zhòng Jǐ said:
"The three dynasties each had different practices;
how can Xuē claim what is 'former'?
To labor for Sòng
is also its duty."
Shì Mí Móu said:
"The administrators of Jìn are new.
You, sir, should for now accept the task.
When you return,
I will examine the matter in the old records."
Zhòng Jǐ said:
"Even if you forget it,
will the spirits of the mountains and rivers forget it?"
Shì Bó grew angry
and said to Hán Jiǎn Zǐ:
"Xuē offers evidence from human history;
Sòng offers evidence from ghosts.
Sòng's offense is great.
Moreover, he has no arguments of his own
but tries to suppress me with spirits;
this is deceiving me.
'To open the door to favor and invite insults'—
this is what it means.
Zhòng Jǐ must be punished."
Thereupon they seized Zhòng Jǐ and took him back.
In the third month,
they delivered him to the capital.
The wall-building was completed in thirty days,
and then the garrisons of the feudal lords were sent home.
Gāo Zhāng of Qí arrived late
and did not act in concert with the feudal lords.
Nǚ Shū Kuān of Jìn said:
"Cháng Hóng of Zhōu and Gāo Zhāng of Qí will both not escape calamity.
Master Cháng violates Heaven;
Master Gāo violates men.
What Heaven destroys
cannot be propped up;
what the multitude does
cannot be opposed."
B11.1.2 In the summer,
Shúsūn Chéng Zǐ went to Qián Hóu to meet the funeral procession of the Duke.
Jìsūn said:
"Zǐjiā Zǐ often spoke to me,
and it never failed to hit upon my own intentions.
I wish to participate in the government with him.
You must stop him
and listen to his instructions."
Zǐjiā Zǐ would not see Shúsūn;
he changed his mat and wailed.
Shúsūn requested to see Zǐjiā Zǐ.
Zǐjiā Zǐ declined,
saying:
"I, Jī, was never granted an audience before,
yet I followed the ruler when he went out.
The ruler passed away without leaving a final command;
I, Jī, do not dare to see you."
Shúsūn sent someone to tell him:
"Gōng Yǎn and Gōng Wéi truly caused the various ministers to be unable to serve the ruler.
If Prince Sòng presides over the altars of soil and grain,
it would be the wish of the various ministers.
As for all those who followed the ruler out and can now enter again,
we will follow your instructions.
The Zǐjiā lineage has no heir yet;
Jìsūn wishes to conduct the government with you.
These are all the wishes of Jìsūn,
and he sent me, though I hardly dare, to inform you."
He replied:
"As for establishing a ruler,
there are ministers, grandees, and the divining tortoise present;
I, Jī, do not dare to concern myself with that.
As for those who followed the ruler:
those who went out for appearances' sake
may enter;
those who went out as enemies
may keep going."
"As for me, Jī,
the Lord knows of my departure
but does not yet know of my return.
I shall flee."
When the funeral reached Huài Tuí,
Gōng Zǐ Sòng entered first,
and those who followed the Lord all returned from Huài Tuí.
B11.1.3 In the sixth month, on Guǐhài,
the remains of the Duke arrived from Qiánhóu.
On Wùchén,
the Duke ascended the throne.
Jì Sūn sent laborers to the Gōng clan in Kàn
to dig a moat there.
Róng Guà’é said,
"In life you could not serve him,
and in death you separate him again
to display your own conduct?
Even if you can bear it,
some among later generations will surely find it shameful."
So he stopped.
Jì Sūn asked Róng Guà’é,
"I wish to give the Duke a posthumous title,
so that his descendants may know of him."
He replied,
"In life you could not serve him,
and in death you hate him;
is this to show your own sincerity?
What use would it be?"
So he stopped.
B11.1.4 In autumn, the seventh month, on Guǐsì,
they buried Zhāo Gōng to the south of the cemetery road.
When Kǒngzǐ was Sīkòu,
he dug a moat and joined it with the other graves.
B11.1.5 Because Zhāo Gōng went into exile,
Jì Píng Zǐ prayed at the shrine of Yàng Gōng.
In the ninth month,
he established the Shrine of Yàng.
B11.1.6 Gǒng Jiǎn Gōng of Zhōu discarded his kinsmen and favored the use of distant people.
A11.2 The Annals of the Second Year of Dìng Gōng
A11.2.1 In the spring of the second year,
in the Royal first month.
A11.2.2 In summer, the fifth month, on Rénchén,
the Zhì Gate and the two lookout towers caught fire.
A11.2.3 In autumn,
the people of Chǔ attacked Wú.
A11.2.4 In winter, the tenth month,
the Zhì Gate and the two lookout towers were rebuilt.
B11.2 The Commentary for the Second Year of Dìng Gōng
B11.2.1 In the second year, summer, the fourth month, on Xīnyǒu,
the various sons and younger brothers of the Gǒng clan murdered Jiǎn Gōng.
B11.2.2 Tóng revolted against Chǔ.
The Master of Wú sent the Shūjiǔ clan to entice the people of Chǔ,
saying,
"Approach us with your army,
and when we attack Tóng,
make it so they have no fear."
In autumn,
Náng Wǎ of Chǔ attacked Wú
and stationed the army at Yùzhāng.
The people of Wú showed boats at Yùzhāng
but secretly moved their army to Cháo.
In winter, the tenth month,
the Wú army attacked the Chǔ army at Yùzhāng
and defeated them.
They then besieged Cháo,
captured it,
and took Gōng Zǐ Fán of Chǔ prisoner.
B11.2.3 Zhū Zhuāng Gōng was drinking wine with Yí Shè Gū
and went out privately.
A gatekeeper asked for meat from him;
he seized the gatekeeper's staff and struck him with it.
A11.3 The Annals of the Third Year of Dìng Gōng
A11.3.1 In the spring of the third year,
the Royal first month,
the Duke went to Jìn;
reaching the River,
he then returned.
A11.3.2 In the second month, on Xīnmǎo,
Chuān, the Master of Zhū, died.
A11.3.3 In summer, the fourth month.
A11.3.4 In autumn,
they buried Zhū Zhuāng Gōng.
A11.3.5 In winter,
Zhòng Sūn Hé Jì and the Master of Zhū made a covenant at Bá.
B11.3 The Commentary for the Third Year of Dìng Gōng
B11.3.1 In the spring of the third year, the second month, on Xīnmǎo,
the Master of Zhū was at the gate tower
overlooking the court.
A gatekeeper sprinkled the court with a jar of water;
the Master of Zhū saw this from afar
and was angry.
The gatekeeper said,
"Yí Shè Gū urinated here."
He ordered him to be seized.
When he was not found,
