his anger increased;
he threw himself upon the couch
and fell into the brazier of coals.
He was burned
and subsequently died.
He was buried first with five chariots
and five sacrificial victims.
Zhuāng Gōng was irritable and loved cleanliness,
and thus it came to this.
B11.3.2 In autumn, the ninth month,
the people of Xiānyú defeated the Jìn army at Píngzhōng
and captured Guān Hǔ of Jìn,
who had relied on his bravery.
B11.3.3 In winter,
they made a covenant at Tán to restore good relations with Zhū.
B11.3.4 Cài Zhāo Hóu had two jade pendants and two fur robes made to go to Chǔ,
and presented one pendant and one robe to Zhāo Wáng.
Zhāo Wáng wore them
to entertain the Marquis of Cài.
The Marquis of Cài also wore the other set.
Zǐcháng wanted them,
but was not given them,
so he detained the Marquis for three years.
Táng Chéng Gōng went to Chǔ;
he had two Sùshuāng horses.
Zǐcháng wanted them,
but was not given them,
so he also detained him for three years.
Some people of Táng plotted together,
asking to replace those who had originally followed the Marquis;
this was granted.
They gave those who followed wine
and made them drunk,
stole the horses, and presented them to Zǐcháng.
Zǐcháng sent the Marquis of Táng home.
They bound themselves before the Sī Bài,
saying,
"Because of the Lord's plaything horses,
you hid your person
and abandoned the state.
We, your subjects, ask to offer our wives and children to compensate for the horses;
it must be so."
The Marquis of Táng said,
"It was my own fault.
You gentlemen, do not feel disgraced!"
He rewarded them all.
The people of Cài heard of this,
insisted on complying,
and presented the pendant to Zǐcháng.
Zǐcháng went to court,
and seeing the followers of the Marquis of Cài,
he ordered the officials,
"The Marquis of Cài has been here for a long time
because the offices have not provided for him.
If the ceremonies are not completed tomorrow,
you shall die."
The Marquis of Cài returned;
reaching the Hàn River,
he held a jade and submerged it,
saying,
"If I ever cross the Hàn to go south again,
let it be like this Great River!"
The Marquis of Cài went to Jìn,
offering his son Yuán and the sons of his grandees as hostages,
and requested to attack Chǔ.
A11.4 The Annals of the Fourth Year of Dìng Gōng
A11.4.1 In the spring of the fourth year,
the Royal second month, on Guǐsì,
Wú, the Marquis of Chén, died.
A11.4.2 In the third month,
the Duke met with Liú Zǐ,
the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Cài,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Viscount of Chén,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Baron of Xǔ,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
the Viscount of Dùn,
the Viscount of Hú,
the Viscount of Téng,
the Earl of Xuē,
the Earl of Qǐ,
the Viscount of Xiǎo Zhū,
and Guó Xià of Qí at Zhàolíng,
to invade Chǔ.
A11.4.3 In the summer, the fourth month, on the day gēngchén,
Gōngsūn Xìng of Cài led an army and extinguished Shěn.
He took Shěn Zǐ Jiā back with him
and killed him.
A11.4.4 In the fifth month,
the Duke and the feudal lords made a covenant at Gāoyòu.
A11.4.5 Bó Chéng of Qǐ died at the assembly.
A11.4.6 In the sixth month,
Duke Huì of Chén was buried.
A11.4.7 Xǔ moved to Róngchéng.
A11.4.8 In the autumn, the seventh month,
the Duke arrived from the assembly.
A11.4.9 Liú Juǎn died.
A11.4.10 Duke Dào of Qǐ was buried.
A11.4.11 The people of Chǔ besieged Cài.
A11.4.12 Shì Yāng of Jìn
and Kǒng Yǔ of Wèi led armies to attack Xiānyú.
A11.4.13 Duke Wén of Liú was buried.
A11.4.14 In the winter, the eleventh month, on the day gēngwǔ,
the Marquis of Cài, with the Viscount of Wú, fought the people of Chǔ at Báijǔ;
the Chǔ army was utterly defeated.
Náng Wǎ of Chǔ fled to Zhèng.
On the day gēngchén,
Wú entered Yǐng.
B11.4 The Commentary on the Fourth Year of Duke Dìng.
B11.4.1 In the spring of the fourth year, the third month,
Duke Wén of Liú assembled the feudal lords at Zhàolíng
to plan an attack on Chǔ.
Xún Yín of Jìn sought bribes from the Marquis of Cài,
but did not obtain them.
He said to Fàn Xiànzǐ:
"The state is currently in danger,
and the feudal lords are currently divided.
To use this to attack the enemy—
is that not difficult?
Rains and floods are currently falling,
and malarial fevers are currently rising.
Zhōngshān is not submissive.
To abandon a covenant and incur resentment
would cause no loss to Chǔ
but would lose us Zhōngshān.
It is better to dismiss the Marquis of Cài.
Ever since we reached Fāngchéng,
we have not been able to have our way with Chǔ;
we will only reap toil from it."
So they dismissed the Marquis of Cài.
The people of Jìn requested feathered banners from Zhèng;
the people of Zhèng gave them.
The next day,
some used them as flags at the assembly.
Because of this, Jìn lost the support of the feudal lords.
When they were about to assemble,
Zǐxíng Jìngzǐ of Wèi said to Duke Líng,
"Meetings and assemblies are difficult,
and when there is a clamor of troublesome talk, no one manages it.
Should you not have Zhù Tuó follow you?"
The Duke said,
"Excellent."
He then sent for Zǐyú.
Zǐyú declined,
saying,
"I extend my four limbs
to carry out my old duties,
yet I still fear being inadequate and troubling the penal statutes.
If I were to hold two offices simultaneously,
it would be inviting a great crime.
Furthermore, the invocators
are the constant servants of the Altars of Soil and Grain.
If the Altars do not move,
the invocator does not leave the borders;
such is the regulation of the office.
When the ruler travels with the army,
he purifies the Altars and smears the drums with blood,
and the invocator holds them and follows;
only then does he leave the borders.
For matters of festive amity,
the ruler goes and the army follows,
the ministers go and the brigades follow;
I have no business there."
The Duke said,
"Go!"
Upon reaching Gāoyòu,
Cài was about to be ranked ahead of Wèi.
The Marquis of Wèi sent Zhù Tuó to speak privately to Cháng Hóng, saying:
"I have heard it on the roads,
and do not know if it is true or not.
If I heard that Cài is to precede Wèi,
is it true?"
Cháng Hóng said,
"It is true. Cài Shù
was the elder brother of Kāngshù;
that he precedes Wèi,
is that not acceptable?"
Zǐyú said:
"If we view it from the perspective of the former kings,
then they honored virtue.
Long ago, King Wǔ overcame Shāng,
and King Chéng stabilized it.
They selected and established those of illustrious virtue
to serve as a defensive screen for Zhōu.
Thus the Duke of Zhōu assisted the Royal House
to govern the world,
making all within Zhōu harmonious.
He granted the Duke of Lǔ the Great Chariot and the Great Banner,
the jade huáng of the Xiàhòu clan,
and the Fánruò bow of Fèngfù.
He gave him six clans of the Yīn people:
the Tiáo, the Xú, the Xiāo, the Suǒ, the Chángsháo, and the Wěisháo clans.
He made him lead their lineage heads,
gather their branch clans,
and lead their kin
and subordinates, so as to take the Duke of Zhōu as a model.
Thus they took up their mandates in Zhōu.
This made them serve in Lǔ,
to manifest the illustrious virtue of the Duke of Zhōu.
He granted him lands and fields, the Péidūn, and the Invocators, Lineage Heads, Diviners, and Scribes,
along with the provision of objects, statutes and records,
officials, and ritual vessels.
Relying on the people of Shāngyǎn,
he charged him with the 'Bóqín' and enfeoffed him in the ruins of Shǎohào.
He granted Kāngshù the Great Chariot, the Shǎobó,
the red-and-green pennants, the felt banners, and the Dàlǚ bell.
He gave him seven clans of the Yīn people:
the Táo, the Shī, the Fán,
the Qí, the Fán, the Jī,
and the Zhōngkuí clans.
He defined the borders and territories
from Wǔfù in the south to the northern border of Pǔtián,
taking land from Yǒuyán to provide for the royal duties,
and taking from the eastern capital of Xiāngtǔ to participate in the King's eastern hunts.
Dānjì handed over the land,
Táoshū handed over the people,
and he was charged with the 'Kāng Gào' and enfeoffed in the ruins of Yīn.
In all cases, they opened the way with Shāng administration
and bounded them with Zhōu regulations.
He granted Tángshù the Great Chariot, the drum of Mìxū,
the Quēgǒng armor, and the Gūxiǎn bell.
He gave him the nine lineages of the Huái surname
and the five official departments.
He was charged with the 'Táng Gào' and enfeoffed in the ruins of Xià,
opened the way with Xià administration,
and bounded them with Róng regulations.
All three of these were younger brothers,
yet they had fine virtue,
and so were distinguished by the items granted to them.
If it were not so,
the elder brothers of King Wén, King Wǔ, King Chéng, and King Kāng were many,
yet they did not receive such grants;
it was only because seniority was not the primary concern.
When Guǎn Shù and Cài Shù incited Shāng
to cause discord in the Royal House,
the King then killed Guǎn Shù and exiled Cài Shù,
providing him with seven chariots and seventy followers.
His son Cài Zhòng reformed his conduct and pursued virtue.
The Duke of Zhōu promoted him
and made him his own high official.
He presented him to the King,
and the King charged him with Cài.
His charge says:
'The King said:
"Hú!
Do not be like your father in disobeying the King's commands!"'
How then can Cài be made to precede Wèi?
Of King Wǔ's eight brothers from the same mother,
the Duke of Zhōu was the Grand Steward,
Kāngshù was the Minister of Crime,
and Dānjì was the Minister of Works.
The other five brothers held no office;
could it be that seniority was the primary concern?
Cào
is of the lineage of King Wén,
while Jìn
is of the lineage of King Wǔ.
Cào was a Count of the Royal Domain,
and this was not due to honoring seniority.
Now you intend to honor it;
this is to go against the former kings.
When Duke Wén of Jìn made the covenant of Jiàntǔ,
Duke Chéng of Wèi was not present;
Yíshù,
his younger brother by the same mother,
still preceded Cài.
The text of the covenant says:
'The King spoke thus:
Zhòng of Jìn, Shēn of Lǔ, Wǔ of Wèi,
Jiǎwǔ of Cài, Jié of Zhèng, Pān of Qí,
Wángchén of Sòng, and Qī of Jǔ.'"
They are stored in the house of Zhōu;
they can be re-examined.
If you, my son, wish to restore the strategies of Wén and Wǔ
but do not rectify your virtue,
how will you manage?”
Cháng Hóng was pleased
and told Liú Zǐ.
He consulted with Fàn Xiànzǐ
and then placed the Wèi Hóu above the Zhèng Hóu in the covenant.
B11.4.2 Returning from Zhàolíng,
Zhèng Zǐ Dàshū died before he arrived.
Jìn Zhào Jiǎnzǐ presided over the mourning for him,
being very grieved,
and said:
“At the meeting of Huángfù,
the Master told me nine sayings,
saying:
‘Do not start disorder,
do not rely on wealth,
do not depend on favor,
do not violate the consensus,
do not be arrogant toward ritual,
do not be proud of ability,
do not repeat anger,
do not plot against virtue,
do not commit what is not righteous.’”
B11.4.3 The people of Shěn did not attend the meeting at Zhàolíng;
the people of Jìn sent Cài to attack them.
In summer,
Cài destroyed Shěn.
In autumn,
for the sake of Shěn,
Chǔ besieged Cài.
Wǔ Yuán became the Xíngrén of Wú to plot against Chǔ.
When Chǔ killed Xì Wǎn,
the members of the Bó lineage fled.
Pǐ, the grandson of Bó Zhōulí, became the Dàzǎi of Wú to plot against Chǔ.
Since Chǔ Zhāo Wáng ascended the throne,
there has not been a year without the armies of Wú.
The Cài Hóu took advantage of this
and sent his son Qián and the son of his Dàfū as hostages to Wú.
In winter,
the Cài Hóu, Wú Zǐ, and Táng Hóu attacked Chǔ.
They left their boats at Huáinèi,
and from Yùzhāng, they faced Chǔ across the Hàn.
Zuǒ Sīmǎ Xù said to Zǐcháng:
“Follow the Hàn and move up and down with them;
I will lead all the troops from outside Fāngchéng to destroy their boats,
then return to block Dàsuì, Zhíyuán, and Míng’è.
You cross the Hàn and attack them,
while I strike from behind;
we will certainly defeat them thoroughly.”
Having planned, they set out.
Wǔchéng Hēi said to Zǐcháng:
“Wú uses wood,
while we use leather;
it cannot last long;
it is better to fight quickly.”
Shǐ Huáng said to Zǐcháng:
“The people of Chǔ dislike you and like the Sīmǎ.
If the Sīmǎ destroys the Wú boats at the Huái,
blocks the mountain passes and enters,
he alone will conquer Wú.
You must fight quickly!
Otherwise,
you will not escape blame.”
So they crossed the Hàn and drew up in lines,
from Xiǎobié to Dàbié.
After three battles,
Zǐcháng knew things were not going well
and wanted to flee.
Shǐ Huáng said:
“You were comfortable
when seeking this position;
to flee when there is difficulty,
where will you go?
You must die for it,
and your previous sins will be fully pardoned.”
In the eleventh month, on the day Gēngwǔ,
the two armies drew up at Bǎijǔ.
Fúgài Wáng, the younger brother of Hélú, requested of Hélú:
“Wǎ of Chǔ is not benevolent;
his ministers have no will to die.
If we attack first,
his troops will surely flee;
and after that, the main army follows,
we will surely win.”
He did not permit it.
Fúgài Wáng said:
“What is called
‘a minister acts righteously without waiting for orders’
refers to this.
Today, if I die,
Chǔ can be entered.”
With his five thousand followers, he first attacked Zǐcháng's troops.
Zǐcháng's troops fled,
the Chǔ army fell into disorder,
and the Wú army defeated them soundly.
Zǐcháng fled to Zhèng.
Shǐ Huáng died with his war chariot.
Wú followed the Chǔ army
to Qīngfā,
and was about to attack.
Fúgài Wáng said:
“A cornered beast still fights,
how much more so for men?
If they know they cannot escape and fight to the death,
they will surely defeat us.
If we let those who cross first know they can escape,
those behind will long for it,
and there will be no more will to fight.
After half have crossed, then we can strike.”
They followed this,
and defeated them again.
The people of Chǔ were making food;
the people of Wú reached them,
and they fled.
After eating, they followed them
and defeated them at Yōngshì.
After five battles,
they reached Yǐng.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
Chǔ Zǐ took his younger sister Jìmǐ Bìwǒ and went out,
crossing the Jū River.
Zhēnyǐn Gù was in the same boat as the Wáng;
the Wáng had him hold burning torches to stampede the elephants against the Wú army.
On the day Gēngchén,
Wú entered Yǐng
and occupied the palaces according to rank.
Zǐshān occupied the palace of the Lìngyǐn;
Fúgài Wáng wanted to attack him;
fearing this, he left it,
and Fúgài Wáng entered it.
Zuǒ Sīmǎ Xù reached Xī and returned;
he defeated the Wú army at Yōngshì,
but was wounded.
Previously,
the Sīmǎ had been a subject of Hélú,
so he was ashamed to be captured.
He said to his followers:
“Who can save my head?”
Wú Gòubēi said:
“I am lowly,
can I do it?”
The Sīmǎ said: “I have truly neglected you,
you may do it!”
In three battles, all with wounds,
he said: “I can no longer be of use.”
Gòubēi spread out a garment,
cut off his head and wrapped it,
hid his body,
and escaped with the head.
Chǔ Zǐ crossed the Jū,
then the Jiāng,
and entered Yúnzhōng.
While the Wáng was sleeping,
robbers attacked him
and struck the Wáng with spears.
Wángsūn Yóuyú received it with his back,
getting hit in the shoulder.
The Wáng fled to Yùn.
Zhōng Jiàn carried Jìmǐ on his back to follow.
Yóuyú slowly recovered and followed.
Huái, the younger brother of Yùn Gōng Xīn, was going to assassinate the Wáng,
saying: “Píng Wáng killed my father;
if I kill his son,
is it not acceptable?”
Xīn said:
“When the ruler punishes a subject,
who dares to hold a grudge?
The ruler's command
is Heaven's will.
If one dies by Heaven's command,
against whom should one hold a grudge?
The Shī says:
‘The soft he does not eat,
the hard he does not spit out.
He does not insult the widower or the widow,
nor does he fear the strong and oppressive,’
Only the benevolent can do this.
To defy the strong and oppress the weak
is not courage;
to take advantage of someone's straits
is not benevolence;
to destroy the ancestral line and abolish sacrifices
is not filial piety;
to act without a good reputation
is not wisdom.
If you must commit these,
I will kill you.”
Dòuxīn and his younger brother Cháo fled with the Wáng to Suí.
The people of Wú followed them
and said to the people of Suí:
“The descendants of Zhōu in the Hànchuān
have been completely wiped out by Chǔ.
Heaven has moved their hearts
to inflict punishment on Chǔ,
yet you give him refuge.
What sin has the House of Zhōu committed?”
"If you, my Lord, look back to repay the house of Zhōu,
and extend your favor to my humble self,
to encourage the sincerity of Heaven,
it would be your grace.
The fields of Hànyáng,
you shall truly possess them."
The Viscount of Chǔ was in the north of the public palace;
the people of Wú were in its south.
Zǐqī resembled the King;
he helped the King escape
and acted as the King himself,
saying:
"If I am given to them,
the King will surely be spared."
The people of Suí divined about giving him up,
but it was inauspicious.
So they declined the Wú people, saying:
"Because Suí is small and remote
and is closely adjacent to Chǔ,
Chǔ has indeed preserved it.
For generations there have been alliance oaths,
which have not changed to this day.
If we abandon them in their difficulty,
how can we serve you, my Lord?
The trouble for your officers is not just one man;
if you gather the borders of Chǔ,
how would we dare not obey your command?"
The people of Wú then withdrew.
Lǘ Jīn had first served in the household of Zǐqī;
he had indeed made a binding agreement with the people of Suí.
The King summoned him to see him,
but he declined,
saying:
"I dare not take a prior agreement as a source of profit."
The King cut Zǐqī’s chest to make an alliance with the people of Suí.
Long ago, Wǔ Yuán and Shēn Bāoxū were friends.
When Wǔ Yuán fled,
he said to Shēn Bāoxū:
"I must overturn the state of Chǔ."
Shēn Bāoxū said: "Exert yourself!
If you can overturn it,
I can certainly restore it."
When King Zhāo was in Suí,
Shēn Bāoxū went to Qín to request troops,
saying: "Wú is like a gluttonous boar or a long snake,
repeatedly devouring the superior states;
the cruelty began with Chǔ.
Our ruler lost the defense of the altars of state
and is out among the grass and wilds.
He sent me, his humble minister, to report the emergency,
saying:
'The virtue of the barbarians is insatiable.
If they become your neighbors,
it will be a trouble for your borders.
While Wú is not yet settled,
you, my Lord, should take your share.
If Chǔ eventually perishes,
it will be your land, my Lord.
If by your numinous power you soothe it,
we will serve you for generations.'"
The Earl of Qín sent a messenger to decline,
saying:
"I have heard the command.
You, sir, should go to the guest house for now;
I will deliberate and then inform you."
He replied:
"Our ruler is out among the grass and wilds
and has not yet found a place to hide.
How could I, his humble minister, dare seek rest?"
He stood,
leaning against the courtyard wall and wailed,
day and night without ceasing his voice;
not a spoonful of drink entered his mouth for seven days.
Duke Āi of Qín composed the poem "Wú Yī" for him.
He kowtowed nine times and sat down.
The Qín army then set out.
A11.5 The Classic of Duke Dìng, Year Five.
A11.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
in the King's third month, on the day xīnhài, the first of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A11.5.2 In the summer,
grain was sent to Cài.
A11.5.3 Yúyuè entered Wú.
A11.5.4 In the sixth month, on the day bǐngshēn,
Jìsūn Yìrú died.
A11.5.5 In the autumn, in the seventh month, on the day rénzǐ,
Shúsūn Bùgǎn died.
A11.5.6 In the winter,
Shì Yāng of Jìn led an army to besiege Xiānyú.
B11.5 The Commentary of Duke Dìng, Year Five.
B11.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
the King’s men killed Zǐcháo in Chǔ.
B11.5.2 In the summer,
grain was sent to Cài
because of their frequent emergencies,
and pitying their lack of resources.
B11.5.3 Yuè entered Wú
because the Wú army was in Chǔ.
B11.5.4 In the sixth month,
Jì Píngzǐ traveled to Dōngyě.
On his return,
before arriving,
on the day bǐngshēn,
he died in Fáng.
Yáng Hǔ wanted to use the yúfán jade for the burial shroud,
but Zhòngliáng Huái would not allow it,
saying:
"If the stride changes, the jade changes."
Yáng Hǔ wanted to expel him
and told Gōngshān Bùniǔ.
Bùniǔ said:
"He is doing it for the lord;
why do you resent him?"
After the burial,
Huánzǐ traveled to Dōngyě
and reached Fèi.
Zǐxiè was the steward of Fèi;
he met and welcomed him in the outskirts,
and Huánzǐ treated him with respect.
He greeted Zhòngliáng Huái,
but Zhòngliáng Huái was not respectful.
Zǐxiè was angry
and said to Yáng Hǔ:
"Will you carry out your plan?"
B11.5.5 Shēn Bāoxū arrived with the Qín army.
Zǐpú and Zǐhǔ of Qín led five hundred chariots to rescue Chǔ.
Zǐpú said:
"We do not yet know the terrain of Wú."
He had the Chǔ people fight the Wú people first,
and joined them from Jì,
greatly defeating King Fúgài at Yí.
The Wú people captured Wěi Shè at Bǎijǔ;
his son led the fleeing troops to follow Zǐxī
and defeated the Wú army at Jūnxiáng.
In the autumn, in the seventh month,
Zǐqī and
Zǐpú destroyed Táng.
In the ninth month,
King Fúgài returned
to set himself up as king.
He fought with the King,
but was defeated,
and fled to Chǔ,
where he became the head of the Tángxī clan.
The Wú army defeated the Chǔ army at Yōngshì.
The Qín army again defeated the Wú army.
The Wú army stayed at Mí;
Zǐqī was going to set it on fire.
Zǐxī said:
"Our fathers and elder brothers have their bones exposed there
and we cannot collect them;
to burn them again
is not permissible."
Zǐqī said:
"The state is perishing;
if the dead have knowledge,
could they enjoy the old sacrifices?
Why should we fear burning them?"
They burned it
and fought again.
The Wú army was defeated,
and they fought again at the stream of Gōngxù.
The Wú army was greatly defeated,
and the Viscount of Wú then returned.
They had imprisoned Yīnyú Bá.
Yīnyú Bá asked to go first
and then escaped back.
Hòuzāng, the younger brother of Zhūliáng, Lord of Yè, was with his mother in Wú;
he returned without waiting for the King.
The Lord of Yè never looked him straight in the eye again.
B11.5.6 On the day yǐhài,
Yáng Hǔ imprisoned Jì Huánzǐ and Gōngfù Wénbó,
and expelled Zhòngliáng Huái.
In the winter, in the tenth month, on the day dīnghài,
he killed Gōnghé Miǎo.
On the day jǐchǒu,
he made an alliance with Huánzǐ within the Jì Gate.
On the day gēngyín,
they performed a great imprecation.
He expelled Gōngfù Chù and Qín Chuán;
both fled to Qí.
B11.5.7 The Viscount of Chǔ entered Yǐng.
Earlier,
when Dòu Xīn heard of the Wú people's dispute over the palace,
he said:
"I have heard it said:
'Without yielding,
there is no harmony;
without harmony,
one cannot campaign in distant lands.'"
If Wú contends for Chǔ,
there will certainly be disorder;
if there is disorder,
then they must return;
how then can they settle Chǔ?"
When the King fled to Suí,
he was about to cross the Chéngjiù River.
Lányǐn Wěi crossed with his family
but did not provide the King with a boat.
When peace was restored,
the King wanted to kill him.
Zǐxī said,
"Zǐcháng failed because he only thought of old grudges;
why should my lord imitate him?"
The King said,
"Very well."
He allowed him to return to his former position,
saying, "I do this to record my own former grievance."
The King rewarded Dòuxīn, Wángsūn Yóuyú,
Wángsūn Yǔ, Zhōngjiàn, Dòucháo,
Shēnbāoxū, Wángsūn Jiǎ, Sòngmù, and Dòuhuái.
Zǐxī said,
"I request that you omit Dòuhuái."
The King said,
"Great virtue extinguishing small grudges
is the proper Way."
Shēnbāoxū said,
"I acted for the lord,
not for myself.
Since the lord is settled,
what more should I seek?
Moreover, I blamed Zǐqí for his rewards;
should I then do the same as him?"
He then fled from the reward.
The King was about to give Jìmǐ in marriage,
but Jìmǐ declined, saying:
"The reason one is a woman
is to keep away from men.
Zhōngjiàn carried me on his back."
So he gave her as a wife to Zhōngjiàn
and appointed him as the Lèyǐn.
While the King was in Suí,
Zǐxī prepared the King's carriages and robes to maintain his royal state,
and established a temporary capital at Píxiè.
Having heard where the King was,
he then followed the King.
The King sent Yóuyú to build a wall at Jūn;
he returned to report.
Zǐxī asked him about the height and thickness of the wall,
but he did not know.
Zǐxī said,
"If you were incapable,
you should have declined.
If you do not know the height and thickness of the wall,
what can you know of its small or large details?"
He replied,
"I did decline, saying I was incapable,
but you sent me.
Each person has what they can and cannot do.
When the King encountered bandits in Yúnzhōng,
I received their halberd blows;
the scars are still there."
He bared his back and showed it to him,
saying,
"This is what I am capable of.
As for the administrative matters of Píxiè,
I am indeed not capable."
B11.5.8 Shì Yāng of Jìn besieged Xiānyú,
to avenge the defeat of Guānhǔ.
A11.6 The Classic of Duke Dìng, Year 6.
A11.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
in the royal first month, on the day guǐhài,
Yóu Sù of Zhèng led an army and extinguished Xǔ,
and returned with Sī, the Baron of Xǔ.
A11.6.2 In the second month,
the Duke invaded Zhèng.
A11.6.3 The Duke arrived from the invasion of Zhèng.
A11.6.4 In the summer,
Jìsūn Sī and
Zhòngsūn Héjì went to Jìn.
A11.6.5 In the autumn,
the people of Jìn seized Yuè Qílí, the envoy of Sòng.
A11.6.6 In the winter,
they walled the inner city.
A11.6.7 Jìsūn Sī and
Zhòngsūn Jì led an army and besieged Yùn.
B11.6 The Commentary of Duke Dìng, Year 6.
B11.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
Zhèng extinguished Xǔ,
taking advantage of Chǔ's defeat.
B11.6.2 In the second month,
the Duke invaded Zhèng,
took Kuāng,
and on behalf of Jìn punished Zhèng for its attack on Xūmí.
On the way there, they did not request passage through Wèi;
when they returned,
Yáng Hǔ made the Jì and Mèng heads enter through the south gate
and exit through the east gate,
and they lodged at Túnzé.
The Marquis of Wèi was angry
and sent Mí Zǐxiá to pursue them.
Gōngshū Wénzǐ was old;
he was carried in a cart to the Duke
and said:
"To blame others and then imitate them
is contrary to ritual.
During the troubles of Duke Zhāo,
you, my lord, were prepared to use the Shū cauldron of Wén,
the Zhāozhào jade of Chéng,
or the girdle mirror of Dìng;
if it could have led to his reinstatement,
you would have chosen one to use.
Your sons and the sons of several of your ministers,
if the feudal lords had been concerned for him,
you would have made them hostages.
This is what all your ministers heard.
Now, to cover over old virtues because of a small grievance,
is that not unacceptable?
Of the sons of Tàisì,
only Zhōugōng and Kāngshū were harmonious with each other;
yet to imitate petty men and discard this bond,
is that not a betrayal?
Heaven will increase the crimes of Yáng Hǔ to bring about his downfall;
why does my lord not just wait for it?"
What do you think?
Thereupon he stopped.
B11.6.3 In the summer,
Jì Huánzǐ went to Jìn
to present the captives from Zhèng.
Yáng Hǔ forced Mèng Yìzǐ to go and return the gifts for the ruler's wife;
the people of Jìn entertained them both.
Mèngsūn stood outside the room
and said to Fàn Xiànzǐ:
"If Yáng Hǔ cannot remain in Lǔ
and seeks rest in Jìn,
if you do not make him the Sīmǎ of the Central Army,
may the former lords be my witness!"
Xiànzǐ said,
"My ruler has offices
and will employ the right men;
what would I, Yāng, know of it?"
Xiànzǐ said to Jiǎnzǐ:
"The people of Lǔ are troubled by Yáng Hǔ.
Mèngsūn knows there is a rift
and believes he will surely go to Jìn;
therefore, he forcefully made this request for him
in order to block his entry."
B11.6.4 In the fourth month, on the day jǐchǒu,
Zhōnglěi, the Crown Prince of Wú, defeated the naval forces of Chǔ,
and captured Pān Zǐchén, Xiǎowéizǐ, and seven grandees.
The state of Chǔ was greatly alarmed
and feared destruction.
Zǐqī was further defeated with the land forces at Fányáng.
The Lìngyǐn Zǐxī said happily,
"Now it can be done."
Thereupon they moved the capital from Yǐng to Ruò
and reformed the administration of its government
to stabilize the state of Chǔ.
B11.6.5 Dān Piān of Zhōu led the followers of Prince Cháo
and, relying on the people of Zhèng, intended to cause disorder in Zhōu;
Zhèng thereupon attacked Féng, Huá,
Xūmí,
Fùshǔ,
Húrén,
and Quēwài.
In the sixth month,
Yán Méi of Jìn garrisoned Zhōu
and walled Xūmí.
B11.6.6 In the autumn, in the eighth month,
Yuè Qí of Sòng said to Duke Jǐng,
"Among the feudal lords, only we serve Jìn;
if an envoy is not sent now,
Jìn will surely feel resentment."
Yuè Qí told his steward Chén Yín.
Chén Yín said,
"He will certainly make you go."
Another day,
the Duke said to Yuè Qí,
"Only I am pleased with your words;
you must go!"
Chén Yín said,
"Establish an heir before you go,
so my household will not perish;
may my lord also consider that I went knowing the difficulty."
[Lè Qí] saw Hùn and departed.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ met him,
and toasted him with wine at Miánshàng;
[Lè Qí] presented sixty poplar shields to Jiǎnzǐ.
Chén Yín said:
"Formerly my master served the Fàn family;
now your master serves the Zhào family.
Furthermore, you are making a presentation;
to use poplar shields to purchase misfortune
is something that must not be done.
However, you will die in the state of Jìn,
while your descendants will surely achieve their ambitions in Sòng."
Fàn Xiànzǐ spoke to the Marquis of Jìn, saying:
"To cross the borders on a mission by the ruler's command,
and to drink wine privately before delivering the mission,
is disrespectful to both rulers.
It must not go unpunished."
Thereupon they seized Lè Qí.
B11.6.7 Yáng Hǔ again made a covenant with the Duke and the Sān Huán at the Zhōu Altar of the Land,
made a covenant with the people of the capital at the Bó Altar of the Land,
and swore oaths at the Crossroads of Wǔfù.
B11.6.8 Winter, the twelfth month,
the Heavenly King stayed at Gūyóu,
to avoid the rebellion of Dān Piān.
A11.7 *The Classic of the Seventh Year of Duke Dìng*
A11.7.1 In the seventh year, spring,
the King's first month.
A11.7.2 Summer, the fourth month.
A11.7.3 Autumn,
the Marquis of Qí
and the Earl of Zhèng made a covenant at Xián.
A11.7.4 The people of Qí seized the envoy of Wèi, Běigōng Jié, in order to invade Wèi.
A11.7.5 The Marquis of Qí
and the Marquis of Wèi made a covenant at Shā.
A11.7.6 A great rain sacrifice was performed.
A11.7.7 Guó Xià of Qí led an army to attack our western border.
A11.7.8 Ninth month,
a great rain sacrifice was performed.
A11.7.9 Winter, the tenth month.
B11.7 *The Commentary on the Seventh Year of Duke Dìng*
B11.7.1 In the seventh year, spring, the second month,
Dān Piān of Zhōu entered Yílì to rebel.
B11.7.2 The people of Qí returned Yùn and Yángguān,
and Yáng Hǔ resided there to conduct government.
B11.7.3 Summer, the fourth month,
Duke Wǔ of Shàn and Duke Huán of Liú defeated the Yǐn clan at Qiónggǔ.
B11.7.4 Autumn,
the Marquis of Qí
and the Earl of Zhèng made a covenant at Xián,
and summoned a meeting in Wèi.
The Marquis of Wèi wished to rebel against Jìn,
but the various grand masters would not allow it.
He sent Běigōng Jié to Qí
and privately said to the Marquis of Qí:
"Seize Jié and invade me."
The Marquis of Qí followed this,
and then they made a covenant at Suǒ.
B11.7.5 Guó Xià of Qí attacked us.
Yáng Hǔ drove the chariot for Jì Huánzǐ,
Gōngliǎn Chǔfù drove the chariot for Mèng Yìzǐ,
and they intended to make a night attack on the Qí army.
The Qí army heard of this;
they let their guard down and lay in ambush to wait for them.
Chǔfù said:
"Hǔ does not consider the misfortune he causes,
and he will surely die."
Shān Yí said:
"Hǔ is leading you two gentlemen into disaster;
without waiting for the officials,
I will surely kill you."
Hǔ was afraid
and so returned;
they were not defeated.
B11.7.6 Winter, the eleventh month, on the day wùwǔ,
the Master of Shàn and the Master of Liú met the King at the Qìng clan.
Jí Qín of Jìn escorted the King.
On the day jǐsì,
the King entered the Royal City,
took lodging with the Dǎng clan of the ducal house,
and afterwards held court at the Zhuāng Palace.
A11.8 *The Classic of the Eighth Year of Duke Dìng*
A11.8.1 In the eighth year, spring,
the King's first month,
the Duke invaded Qí.
A11.8.2 The Duke arrived from invading Qí.
A11.8.3 Second month,
the Duke invaded Qí.
A11.8.4 Third month,
the Duke arrived from invading Qí.
A11.8.5 Marquis Lù of Cáo died.
A11.8.6 Summer,
Guó Xià of Qí led an army to attack our western border.
A11.8.7 The Duke met the Jìn army at Wǎ.
A11.8.8 The Duke arrived from Wǎ.
A11.8.9 Autumn, the seventh month, on the day wùchén,
Marquis Liǔ of Chén died.
A11.8.10 Shì Yāng of Jìn led an army to invade Zhèng,
and then invaded Wèi.
A11.8.11 Duke Jìng of Cáo was buried.
A11.8.12 Ninth month,
Duke Huái of Chén was buried.
A11.8.13 Jìsūn Sī
and Zhòngsūn Héjì led an army to invade Wèi.
A11.8.14 Winter,
the Marquis of Wèi
and the Earl of Zhèng made a covenant at Qūpú.
A11.8.15 They performed the sequential sacrifices to the former dukes.
A11.8.16 Thieves stole the precious jade
and the Great Bow.
B11.8 *The Commentary on the Eighth Year of Duke Dìng*
B11.8.1 In the eighth year, spring,
the King's first month,
the Duke invaded Qí
and attacked the gate of Yángzhōu.
The soldiers were all sitting in ranks,
saying:
"Yán Gāo's bow is six jun."
They all took it and passed it around to look at it.
The people of Yángzhōu came out;
Yán Gāo snatched a weak bow from someone.
Jíquī Zǐchú struck at him,
and fell along with another man.
[Yán Gāo] lay flat
and shot at Zǐchú,
hitting him in the cheek
and killing him.
Yán Xī shot a man in the eyebrow,
and withdrew, saying:
"I have no courage;
I aimed for his eye."
The army withdrew,
and Rǎn Měng feigned a foot injury to go ahead.
His older brother Huì then called out, saying:
"Měng is protecting the rear!"
B11.8.2 In the third month, on the day jǐchǒu,
the Master of Shàn attacked Gǔchéng,
and the Master of Liú attacked Yílì.
On the day xīnmǎo,
the Master of Shàn attacked Jiǎnchéng,
and the Master of Liú attacked Yú,
in order to stabilize the Royal House.
B11.8.3 Zhào Yāng spoke to the Marquis of Jìn, saying:
"Of the feudal lords, only Sòng serves Jìn;
even when we are welcoming to their envoys,
we still fear they will not come.
Now that we have seized one,
this is cutting ourselves off from the feudal lords."
They were about to return Lè Qí,
but Shì Yāng said:
"Having detained him for three years,
if we return him without a reason,
Sòng will surely rebel against Jìn."
Xiànzǐ privately said to Zǐliáng:
"My ruler fears he may not be able to serve the ruler of Sòng,
and for this reason he detained you.
For now, have Hùn take your place."
Zǐliáng told this to Chén Yín.
Chén Yín said:
"Sòng is about to rebel against Jìn;
to do this would be to abandon Hùn.
It is better to wait."
Lè Qí returned
but died at Dàháng.
Shì Yāng said:
"Sòng will surely rebel;
it is better to detain his corpse to seek a settlement."
Thereupon they detained it in Zhōu.
B11.8.4 The Duke invaded Qí,
and attacked the outer walls of Lǐnqiū.
The defenders set fire to the battering rams;
someone soaked horse-hair blankets to save them,
and subsequently destroyed the walls.
The defenders came out,
and the army fled.
Yáng Hǔ pretended not to see Rǎn Měng,
and said:
"If Měng is here,
we will surely be defeated."
Měng pursued them,
but looking back and seeing no backup,
he feigned a fall.
Hǔ said:
"It is all just guest-like energy."
B11.8.5 Shàn Yuè had a son,
and intended to wait for an achievement to name him.
Having made a capture during the expedition to Yángzhōu,
he named him
"Yángzhōu."
B11.8.6 In summer,
Guó Xià of Qí and
Gāo Zhāng invaded our western border.
Shì Yǎng, Zhào Yǎng, and Xún Yín of Jìn came to our rescue.
The Duke met the Jìn army at Wǎ.
Fàn Xiànzǐ held a lamb,
while Zhào Jiǎnzǐ and Zhōngháng Wénzǐ both held geese.
From this point, Lǔ began to favor the lamb.
B11.8.7 The Jìn army was about to enter into a covenant with the Marquis of Wèi at Zhuānzé.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Who among the ministers dares to administer the covenant to the ruler of Wèi?"
Shè Tuó and Chéng Hé said:
"We can administer the covenant to him."
The people of Wèi requested to hold the bull’s ear.
Chéng Hé said:
"Wèi
is like our Wēn or Yuán;
how can it be treated like a feudal lord?"
When they were about to smear the blood,
Shè Tuó squeezed the hand of the Marquis of Wèi
until it reached the wrist.
The Marquis of Wèi was angry.
Wángsūn Jiǎ hurried forward
and said:
"A covenant is for trust and ritual.
With one such as the ruler of Wèi,
how would he dare not serve ritual alone and receive this covenant?"
The Marquis of Wèi wanted to rebel against Jìn,
but was concerned about his grand masters.
Wángsūn Jiǎ had them camp in the suburbs.
When the grand masters asked for the reason,
the Duke told them of the insult from Jìn,
and said:
"I have brought shame to the altars of land and grain.
Please change the divination for a successor;
I shall follow the result."
The grand masters said:
"This is the calamity of Wèi;
how could it be the ruler's fault?"
The Duke said: "There is another worry.
They told me,
'You must take your sons and the sons of the grand masters as hostages.'"
The grand masters said:
"If it is beneficial,
let the young princes go.
How would the sons of the ministers dare not all shoulder the halters and ropes to follow them?"
When they were about to depart,
Wángsūn Jiǎ said:
"If Wèi has a crisis,
the merchants and craftsmen have always been a source of trouble.
Only if they all go will it be acceptable."
The Duke informed the grand masters,
and so they were all to be sent.
When the day of departure arrived,
the Duke held an audience for the people of the state,
and had Jiǎ ask them,
saying:
"If Wèi rebels against Jìn,
and Jìn attacks us five times,
how much will we suffer?"
They all said:
"If they attack us five times,
we can still fight."
Jiǎ said: "In that case, if we rebel,
and only give hostages after we are distressed,
why should we wait?"
Thus they rebelled against Jìn.
The people of Jìn requested to change the covenant,
but he did not allow it.
B11.8.8 In autumn,
Shì Yǎng of Jìn met with Duke Huán of Chéng and invaded Zhèng,
besieging Chóngláo,
to retaliate for the battle of Yīquē.
Then they invaded Wèi.
B11.8.9 In the ninth month,
our army invaded Wèi,
because of Jìn.
B11.8.10 Jì Wù, Gōngchú Jí, and Gōngshān Bùniǔ
all failed to get their way with the Jì family;
Shúsūn Zhé was not favored by the Shúsūn family;
Shǔzhòng Zhì failed to get his way in Lǔ;
therefore, these five men joined with Yáng Hǔ.
Yáng Hǔ wanted to remove the Three Huán,
to replace the Jì family with Jì Wù,
to replace the Shúsūn family with Shúsūn Zhé,
and to replace the Mèng family himself.
In winter, the tenth month,
he performed the regular sacrifices to the former Dukes and prayed there.
On the day xīnmǎo,
he performed the Dì sacrifice to Duke Xī.
On the day rénchén,
he planned to feast the head of the Jì family at Pǔpǔ and kill him.
He warned the carriages of the capital,
saying:
"Arrive on the day guǐsì."
Gōngliàn Chùfù, the steward of Chéng, informed Mèngsūn,
saying:
"The Jì family is warning the carriages of the capital;
for what reason?"
Mèngsūn said:
"I have not heard of it."
Chùfù said:
"In that case, there is disorder,
and it will surely reach you.
Prepare for it beforehand."
He made an agreement with Mèngsūn for the day rénchén.
Yáng Hǔ led the van.
Lín Chǔ drove for Huánzǐ.
The foresters flanked them with spears and shields.
Yáng Yuè brought up the rear.
They were about to go to Pǔpǔ.
Huánzǐ whispered to Lín Chǔ,
saying: "Your ancestors were all good men of the Jì family;
you should continue this."
He replied:
"I only received my orders late.
Yáng Hǔ manages the government,
and the state of Lǔ submits to him.
To disobey him is to be sentenced to death,
and death is of no benefit to my master."
Huánzǐ said:
"How can it be too late?
Can you take me to the Mèng family?"
He replied: "I do not dare to love my life,
but I fear that my master will not escape."
Huánzǐ said: "Go!"
The Mèng family selected three hundred of the strongest grooms
to use for the building of a house outside the gate as if for the Duke’s appointment.
Lín Chǔ whipped the horses,
and upon reaching the crossroads, he galloped.
Yáng Yuè shot at him
but missed.
The builders closed the gates.
Someone shot at Yáng Yuè from between the gates
and killed him.
Yáng Hǔ seized the Duke and Wǔshū
to attack the Mèng family.
Gōngliàn Chùfù led the people of Chéng to enter from the Upper East Gate,
and fought with the Yáng faction inside the South Gate
but did not win;
they fought again at Jǐxià,
and the Yáng faction was defeated.
Yáng Hǔ removed his armor and went to the Duke’s palace,
took the precious jades and the Great Bow and went out,
stopping at the Crossroads of Wǔfù,
where he slept and ate.
His followers said:
"The pursuers are about to arrive."
Hǔ said:
"When the people of Lǔ hear that I have left,
they will be happy to have escaped death;
what leisure would they have to pursue me?"
The followers said:
"Look!
Hitch up quickly!
Gōngliàn Yáng is here."
Gōngliàn Yáng requested to pursue him,
but Mèngsūn did not allow it.
Yáng wanted to kill Huánzǐ,
but Mèngsūn feared this and sent him back.
Zǐyán Biàn poured a libation in the temple of the Jì family and went out.
Yáng Hǔ entered Huān and Yángguān to rebel.
B11.8.11 Sì Chuàn of Zhèng succeeded Zǐ Dàshū in the government.
A11.9 The Annals of Duke Dìng, Ninth Year
A11.9.1 In the ninth year, spring,
the King's first month.
A11.9.2 In summer, the fourth month, on the day wùshēn,
Chài, Earl of Zhèng, died.
A11.9.3 The precious jades
and the Great Bow were recovered.
A11.9.4 In the sixth month,
we buried Duke Xiàn of Zhèng.
A11.9.5 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí and the Marquis of Wèi...
The Marquis halted at Wǔshì.
A11.9.6 The Earl of Qín died.
A11.9.7 Winter,
they buried Duke Āi of Qín.
B11.9 *Commentary for the Ninth Year of Duke Dìng*
B11.9.1 Spring of the ninth year,
the Duke of Sòng sent Yuè Dàxīn to form a covenant with Jìn,
and to receive the corpse of Yuè Qí.
He declined,
pretending to be ill;
so the Duke sent Xiàng Cháo to Jìn to form the covenant,
and to receive the corpse of Zǐliáng.
Zǐmíng addressed the Yòushī of Tóngmén as he came out,
saying:
"I am still wearing mourning clothes,
yet you are striking bells,
why is that?"
The Yòushī said:
"It is because the mourning is not here."
Afterward, he told others:
"He wears mourning clothes yet fathers a child;
for what reason should I abandon my bells?"
Zǐmíng heard of this,
was angry,
and spoke to the Duke, saying:
"The Yòushī intends harm to the Dài clan.
He was unwilling to go to Jìn,
and is about to start a rebellion.
Otherwise,
he has no illness."
Thereupon, he expelled the Yòushī of Tóngmén.
B11.9.2 Sì Chuán of Zhèng killed Dèng Xī,
but used his *Zhúxíng*.
The noble man said of Zǐrán
"In this, he was not loyal.
If there is something that can benefit the state,
one may discard the person's wickedness.
In the third stanza of 'Jìng nǚ',
the red tube is taken.
In 'Gān máo',
and the line 'What shall I tell him?',
one takes his loyalty.
Therefore, one uses their way
and does not discard the person.
The *Shī* says:
'Luxuriant is the sweet pear tree,
do not prune it, do not chop it down,
for under it the Earl of Shào rested.'
Thinking of the person,
one even loves their tree,
how much more so when using their way but having no pity for the person!
Zǐrán had no means to encourage the capable."
B11.9.3 Summer,
Yáng Hǔ returned the precious jade and the great bow.
The record says
*dé* (obtained),
as they are implements.
Whenever implements are acquired, it is called
*dé* (obtained);
when the use of them is gained, it is called
*huò* (captured).
In the sixth month,
they attacked Yángguān.
Yáng Hǔ ordered the burning of Láimén.
The army was alarmed;
he broke through them and went out, fleeing to Qí,
where he requested an army to attack Lǔ,
saying:
"With three reinforcements,
I will certainly take it."
The Marquis of Qí was about to grant this.
Bào Wénzǐ remonstrated, saying:
"I was once a servant to the Shī clan;
Lǔ cannot yet be taken.
Superiors and inferiors are still in harmony,
the common people are still at peace,
they can serve great states,
and there are no natural disasters;
how can it be taken?
Yáng Hǔ wishes to exhaust the army of Qí;
when the army of Qí is weary,
many of the great ministers will surely die,
and he will then exert his deceitful schemes.
Now Yáng Hǔ was favored by the Jì clan,
yet he intended to kill Jìsūn,
to the detriment of the state of Lǔ,
and then sought refuge here.
He stays close to the wealthy but not to the benevolent;
why should my lord employ him?
My lord is wealthier than the Jì clan,
and Qí is greater than the state of Lǔ;
these are what Yáng Hǔ wishes to overthrow.
Lǔ has escaped his affliction,
but my lord now takes him in;
is that not a harm?"
The Marquis of Qí seized Yáng Hǔ
and was going to send him to the east.
Yáng Hǔ wished to go east,
so the Marquis imprisoned him in the western border.
He borrowed all the carts from the people of the town,
notched their axles,
bound them with hemp, and returned them.
He boarded a covered carriage,
lay down inside it, and escaped.
They pursued and captured him,
and imprisoned him in Qí.
Again he escaped using a covered carriage,
fled to Sòng,
and then fled to Jìn,
going to the Zhào clan.
Zhòngní said:
"The Zhào clan will likely have generations of disorder!"
B11.9.4 Autumn,
the Marquis of Qí attacked Yíyí of Jìn.
The father of Bì Wúcún was about to find him a wife;
he declined,
giving the opportunity to his younger brother,
saying:
"In this campaign,
if I do not die
and return,
I will certainly marry into the Gāo or Guó families."
He was the first to scale the wall,
then sought to come out from the gate,
but died under the eaves.
Dōngguō Shū offered to let others scale first;
Lí Mí followed him,
saying:
"You yield and go to the left,
I yield and go to the right;
let those scaling be exhausted before we descend."
Shū went to the left,
Mí descended first.
Shū was resting with Wáng Měng.
Měng said:
"I was the first to scale."
Shū gathered his armor
and said:
"Earlier there was difficulty,
and now there is difficulty again!"
Měng laughed and said:
"I follow you
like an outside horse has a breast-strap."
A thousand chariots of Jìn were in Zhōngmóu.
The Marquis of Wèi was about to go to Wǔshì;
he divined by turtle shell about passing it,
and the shell was scorched.
The Marquis of Wèi said:
"It is fine!
Wèi's chariots are equal to half of theirs,
and I myself am equal to half of theirs;
that makes us equal."
So they passed Zhōngmóu.
The people of Zhōngmóu wanted to attack them.
Chǔshī Pǔ of Wèi was an exile in Zhōngmóu;
he said:
"Though Wèi is small,
its ruler is present;
they cannot yet be defeated.
The army of Qí has captured cities and is arrogant,
and its commander is of low rank;
if we encounter them,
we will certainly defeat them.
It is better to go after Qí."
So they attacked the army of Qí
and defeated them.
The Marquis of Qí presented Zhuó, Mèi, and Xìng to Wèi.
The Marquis of Qí rewarded Lí Mí.
Lí Mí declined,
saying:
"There was one who scaled first;
I followed him.
He wore a white turban and a coat of leopard skin."
The Duke sent someone to look at Dōngguō Shū
and said:
"It is that master. I bestow this upon you."
The Duke rewarded Dōngguō Shū;
he declined,
saying:
"That man
was but a guest-traveler."
So he rewarded Lí Mí.
While the army of Qí was at Yíyí,
the Marquis of Qí said to the people of Yíyí:
"Whoever gets the body of Bì Wúcún,
five families will be exempted from service."
They then obtained his corpse.
The Duke gave it three sets of burial clothes,
and gave him a rhinoceros-hide chariot with a straight canopy,
and sent it back first.
He sat the pullers down,
had the army wail for him,
and personally pushed the carriage three times.
A11.10 *Classic of the Tenth Year of Duke Dìng*
A11.10.1 In the tenth year, spring,
in the royal third month,
we made peace with Qí.
A11.10.2 In summer,
the Duke met the Marquis of Qí at Jiágǔ.
A11.10.3 The Duke arrived from Jiágǔ.
A11.10.4 Zhào Yāng of Jìn led the army to besiege Wèi.
A11.10.5 The people of Qí came to return the fields of Yùn,
Huān, and Guīyīn.
A11.10.6 Shūsūn Zhōuchóu and
Zhòngsūn Héjì led the army to besiege Hòu.
A11.10.7 In autumn,
Shūsūn Zhōuchóu and
Zhòngsūn Héjì led the army to besiege Hòu.
A11.10.8 Lè Dàxīn of Sòng fled to Cáo.
A11.10.9 Gōngzǐ Dì of Sòng fled to Chén.
A11.10.10 In winter,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Marquis of Wèi, and
Yóu Sù of Zhèng met at Ānfǔ.
A11.10.11 Shūsūn Zhōuchóu went to Qí.
A11.10.12 Chén, the younger brother of the Duke of Sòng, along with Zhòng Tuó and
Shí Kōu, fled to Chén.
B11.10 The Tradition of Duke Dìng’s Tenth Year.
B11.10.1 In the spring of the tenth year,
we made peace with Qí.
B11.10.2 In summer,
the Duke met the Marquis of Qí at Zhùqí,
which was actually Jiágǔ.
Kǒng Qiū assisted.
Lí Mí said to the Marquis of Qí:
“Kǒng Qiū knows ritual but lacks courage.
If you have the people of Lái use weapons to seize the Lord of Lǔ by force,
you will certainly achieve your aim.”
The Marquis of Qí followed this.
Kǒng Qiū led the Duke in retreat,
saying:
“Soldiers, take up arms!
When two rulers meet in friendship,
for captives of the remote barbarians to cause disorder with weapons
is not the way for the Lord of Qí to command the feudal lords.
The remote regions do not plot against the Xià,
the barbarians do not disrupt the Huá,
captives do not interfere with a covenant,
and weapons do not press upon friendship; before the spirits, it is inauspicious;
in terms of virtue, it is a lapse of righteousness;
in terms of humanity, it is a loss of ritual;
My Lord will certainly not allow this.”
The Marquis of Qí heard this
and quickly sent them away.
When they were about to swear the covenant,
the people of Qí added to the text of the oath:
“If the army of Qí crosses the border and you do not follow me with three hundred armored chariots,
may it be as according to this oath!”
Kǒng Qiū had Zī Wúhuán bow and respond,
saying:
“And if you do not return to me our fields of Wènyáng,
and I am yet expected to obey your commands,
may it also be as according to this!”
The Marquis of Qí intended to hold a banquet for the Duke.
Kǒng Qiū said to Liángqiū Jù:
“As for the precedents of Qí and Lǔ,
how is it that you have not heard of them?
The business is already finished,
and yet you wish to hold a banquet;
this is only to trouble the officers.
Moreover, the sacrificial vessels do not leave the gates;
the finest music is not performed in the wilds.
If the banquet is fully prepared,
it is a desertion of ritual;
if it is not prepared,
it is like using grain husks and weeds.
Using husks and weeds
shames the ruler;
deserting ritual
brings an evil name.
Why do you not consider this?
Indeed, a banquet
is that by which virtue is made manifest.
If it does not manifest virtue,
it is better to stop.”
Thus, the banquet was not held.
B11.10.3 The people of Qí came to return the fields of Yùn,
Huān, and Guīyīn.
B11.10.4 Zhào Yāng of Jìn besieged Wèi,
in retaliation for Yīyí.
Earlier,
the Marquis of Wèi attacked Hándān Wǔ at Hánshì,
fortified its northwest and held it,
but at night they were extinguished.
When Jìn besieged Wèi,
Wǔ led seventy foot soldiers to the West Gate of Wèi,
killed someone inside the gate,
and said:
“I ask to repay the service of Hánshì.”
Shè Tuó said:
“That gentleman is indeed brave;
however, if I go,
they will certainly not dare to open the gate.”
He also led seventy foot soldiers to the gate at dawn;
stepping left and right,
they all arrived
and stood
like stakes.
Until midday the gate was not opened,
and then he retreated.
Upon returning from the campaign,
the people of Jìn punished those responsible for Wèi's rebellion,
saying:
“It was because of Shè Tuó and Chéng Hé.”
Thereupon they seized Shè Tuó
to seek peace with Wèi.
The people of Wèi did not agree.
The people of Jìn then killed Shè Tuó,
and Chéng Hé fled to Yàn.
The Noble Man said:
“This is what is called abandoning ritual;
it must be uneven.
The *Shī* says:
‘If a man is without ritual,
why does he not quickly die?’
Shè Tuó was indeed quick!”
B11.10.5 Earlier,
Shūsūn Chéngzǐ wanted to establish Wǔshū as heir.
Gōngruò Miǎo firmly remonstrated,
saying:
“It cannot be.”
Chéngzǐ established him and then died.
Gōngnán sent an assassin to shoot him,
but was unable to kill him.
Gōngnán became the Master of the Horse,
and had Gōngruò serve as the Steward of Hòu.
Once Wǔshū was established,
he ordered Hóu Fàn, the Master of the Horse of Hòu, to kill Gōngruò,
but he was unable.
His groom said:
“I will pass through the court with a sword;
Gōngruò will certainly say,
‘Whose sword is that?’
I will name you and tell him;
he will certainly look at it.
I will pretend to be clumsy and hand him the tip,
then he can be killed.”
They had him do so.
Gōngruò said:
“Do you want to treat me like the King of Wú?”
They then killed Gōngruò.
Hóu Fàn rebelled with Hòu.
Wǔshū and Yìzǐ besieged Hòu,
but did not overcome it.
In autumn,
the two gentlemen and the army of Qí besieged Hòu again,
but did not overcome it.
Shūsūn said to Sì Chì, the Master of Artisans of Hòu:
“Hòu is not only a worry for the Shūsūn clan,
but a calamity for the state;
what shall be done about it?”
He replied:
“My business lies in the four words of the final stanza of the *Yáng Shuǐ*.”
Shūsūn bowed his head.
Sì Chì said to Hóu Fàn:
“To live between Qí and Lǔ and have no business
is certainly impossible.
Why do you not seek service from Qí to govern the people?
Otherwise,
they will rebel.”
Hóu Fàn followed this advice.
The envoy of Qí arrived.
Sì Chì and the people of Hòu spread a rumor in Hòu, saying:
“Hóu Fàn is going to exchange Hòu for territory in Qí,
and the people of Qí are going to relocate the people of Hòu.”
The multitude was terrified.
Sì Chì said to Hóu Fàn:
“The talk of the multitude is strange.
You would be better off exchanging with Qí;
rather than dying,
though it is still Hòu,
you will find relief there;
why insist on this?
The people of Qí want to use this to pressure Lǔ,
so they will certainly give you double the land.
Moreover, why not lodge many armored men at your gate to prepare for the unexpected?”
Hóu Fàn said, "Agreed."
Thereupon he lodged many armored men there.
Hóu Fàn requested to transfer allegiance to Qí,
and the officials of Qí came to inspect Hòu.
As they were about to arrive,
Sì Chì sent men to run around shouting,
"The Qí army has arrived!"
The people of Hòu were greatly alarmed;
they donned the armor from Hóu Fàn’s gatehouse
to surround Hóu Fàn.
Sì Chì was about to shoot them,
but Hóu Fàn stopped him,
saying,
"Scheme for my escape."
Hóu Fàn requested to leave,
and they permitted it.
Sì Chì went first to Sù,
while Hóu Fàn brought up the rear.
Each time they passed through a gate,
the people of Hòu closed it.
When they reached the outer wall gate,
they stopped him,
saying,
"You are taking the armor of the Shūsūn clan out;
if the officials execute us for this,
we, your servants, fear death."
Sì Chì said,
"The armor of the Shūsūn clan has markings;
I would not dare take it out."
Hóu Fàn said to Sì Chì,
"Stay and count them with them."
Sì Chì stayed
and admitted the people of Lǔ.
Hóu Fàn fled to Qí.
The people of Qí then returned Hòu.
B11.10.6 Gōngzǐ Dì of Sòng favored Qú Fù Liè;
he divided his household into eleven parts
and gave five of them to him.
Gōngzǐ Dì had four white horses;
the Duke favored Xiàng Tuí,
and Tuí wanted them.
The Duke took them and dyed their tails and manes red to give to him.
Dì was angry
and sent his followers to whip Tuí and seize them.
Tuí was afraid
and was about to flee;
the Duke closed the door and wept for him
until his eyes were completely swollen.
Chén, his younger brother by the same mother, said,
"You divided your household to give to Liè,
but you alone disparage Tuí;
there is partiality in this.
If you perform the ritual for the ruler
by merely leaving the border,
the ruler will surely stop you."
Gōngzǐ Dì went into exile in Chén,
but the Duke did not stop him.
Chén pleaded on his behalf,
but the Duke would not listen.
Chén said,
"This is me deceiving my elder brother.
If I lead the people of the state out,
with whom will the ruler remain?"
In winter,
the younger brother Chén, along with Zhòng Tuó, Shí Kōu, and Gōngzǐ Dì, fled into exile in Chén.
B11.10.7 Wǔshū went on a mission to Qí;
the Marquis of Qí held a feast for him
and said,
"Sir Shūsūn!
If Hòu were on another border of your ruler,
how would I have known of it?
It happens to border my humble state;
therefore, I dared to help your ruler with his concern."
He replied,
"This was not my ruler's expectation.
That which is used to serve you
is for the sake of the borders and the altars of the land;
how could I dare trouble your officers with a domestic servant?
An unruly subject
is what all under heaven hate;
how could you, My Lord, consider this a gift to my ruler?"
A11.11 The Annals of the Eleventh Year of Duke Dìng
A11.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
Chén, the brother of the Duke of Sòng, along with Zhòng Tuó,
Shí Kōu,
and Gōngzǐ Dì, entered Xiāo from Chén to rebel.
A11.11.2 In summer, the fourth month.
A11.11.3 In autumn,
Lè Dàxīn of Sòng entered Xiāo from Cáo.
A11.11.4 In winter,
peace was made with Zhèng.
Shū Huán went to Zhèng to preside over the covenant.
B11.11 The Commentary on the Eleventh Year of Duke Dìng
B11.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
Chén, the younger brother of the Duke of Sòng, along with Zhòng Tuó,
Shí Kōu,
and Gōngzǐ Dì, entered Xiāo to rebel.
In autumn,
Lè Dàxīn followed them;
they became a great trouble for Sòng
because of the favoritism toward Xiàng Tuí.
B11.11.2 In winter,
peace was made with Zhèng,
which was the beginning of the rebellion against Jìn.
A11.12 The Annals of the Twelfth Year of Duke Dìng
A11.12.1 In the spring of the twelfth year,
Baron Dìng of Xuē died.
A11.12.2 In summer,
Duke Xiāng of Xuē was buried.
A11.12.3 Shūsūn Zhōuchóu led an army to dismantle the walls of Hòu.
A11.12.4 Gōngmèng Kōu of Wèi led an army to attack Cáo.
A11.12.5 Jìsūn Sī and
Zhòngsūn Héjì led an army to dismantle the walls of Fèi.
A11.12.6 In autumn,
the great rain sacrifice was performed.
A11.12.7 In winter, the tenth month, on the day guǐhài,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Qí and made a covenant at Huáng.
A11.12.8 In the eleventh month, on the day bǐngyín, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A11.12.9 The Duke arrived from Huáng.
A11.12.10 In the twelfth month,
the Duke besieged Chéng.
A11.12.11 The Duke arrived from the siege of Chéng.
B11.12 The Commentary on the Twelfth Year of Duke Dìng
B11.12.1 In the summer of the twelfth year,
Gōngmèng Kōu of Wèi attacked Cáo
and captured Jiāo.
Returning,
Huá Luó brought up the rear.
Before he had left,
he did not retreat from the ranks.
His charioteer said,
"To bring up the rear and yet stay in the ranks—
does that not show a lack of courage?"
Luó said,
"Rather than having a reputation for ferocity,
I would rather be considered without courage."
B11.12.2 Zhòng Yóu became the steward for the Jì clan
and was about to dismantle the three capital cities;
thereupon the Shūsūn clan dismantled the walls of Hòu.
When the Jì clan was about to dismantle Fèi,
Gōngshān Bùniǔ and Shūsūn Zhé led the people of Fèi to launch a surprise attack on Lǔ.
The Duke and the three heads of the clans entered the palace of the Jì clan
and ascended the terrace of Wǔzǐ.
The people of Fèi attacked it
but could not overcome it.
They reached the side of the Duke.
Zhòngní ordered Shēn Gùxū and Lè Qí to go down
and attack them.
The people of Fèi fled.
The people of the state pursued them
and defeated them at Gūmiè.
The two men fled to Qí,
and then Fèi was dismantled.
They were about to dismantle Chéng,
when Gōngliǎn Chǔfù said to Mèngsūn,
"If Chéng is dismantled,
the people of Qí will surely reach the northern gate.
Moreover, Chéng
is the protection of the Mèng clan.
Without Chéng,
there is no Mèng clan.
You should pretend not to know,
and I will not dismantle it."
In winter, the twelfth month,
the Duke besieged Chéng,
but could not overcome it.
A11.13 The Annals of the Thirteenth Year of Duke Dìng
A11.13.1 In the spring of the thirteenth year,
the Marquis of Qí
and the Marquis of Wèi halted at Chuíjiá.
A11.13.2 In summer,
they built the garden of Shéyuān.
A11.13.3 A great hunt was held at Bǐpú.
A11.13.4 Gōngmèng Kōu of Wèi led an army to attack Cáo.
Zhào Yāng of Jìn entered Jìnyáng to rebel.
In winter,
Xún Yín and
Shì Jíshè of Jìn entered Zhāogē to rebel.
Zhào Yāng of Jìn returned to Jìn.
Xuē assassinated its ruler, Bǐ.
The Commentary on the Thirteenth Year of Duke Dìng.
In the spring of the thirteenth year,
the Marquess of Qí and the Marquess of Wèi halted at Chuíjiā, which was actually Júshì. They sent an army to attack Jìn.
As they were about to cross the River,
the high officers all said it was impossible, but
Bǐng Yìzī said,
"It is possible.
If a sharp force attacks Hénèi,
the report will certainly take several days to reach Jiàng.
Jiàng cannot send troops across the River within three months,
and by then we will have already crossed the water."
They then attacked Hénèi.
The Marquess of Qí took away the high carriages of all the high officers;
only Bǐng Yìzī rode in a high carriage.
The Marquess of Qí wished to ride with the Marquess of Wèi;
he feasted with him, and when the carriage was prepared, it was a large war carriage
carrying armored men.
He sent someone to report,
"The Jìn army has arrived!"
The Marquess of Qí said,
"While your carriage is being prepared,
I beg to act as your protector."
He then put on armor and rode with him,
driving forward.
Someone reported,
"There is no Jìn army."
Then they stopped.
Zhào Yāng of Jìn said to Hándān Wǔ,
"Return to me the five hundred households of the Wèi tribute;
I will settle them in Jìnyáng."
Wǔ gave his promise.
He returned and told his kinsmen.
The kinsmen all said,
"It is impossible.
Wèi is using them to provide for Hándān,
and to place them in Jìnyáng
is to cut off the route to Wèi.
It would be better to invade Qí and then plan for it."
They did so,
but eventually returned them to Jìnyáng.
Zhào Mèng was angry;
he summoned Wǔ
and imprisoned him in Jìnyáng.
He ordered his followers to remove their swords before entering,
but Shè Bīn would not.
He then sent someone to tell the people of Hándān,
"I have a private punishment for Wǔ;
you gentlemen may establish whomever you wish."
Then he killed Wǔ.
Zhào Jì and Shè Bīn rebelled with Hándān.
In the summer, in the sixth month,
Jí Qín, Marshal of the Upper Army, besieged Hándān.
Hándān Wǔ was
the nephew of Xún Yín;
Xún Yín was
a relative by marriage of Fàn Jíshè;
and they were on good terms with one another.
Therefore, they did not participate in the siege of Hándān,
intending to start a revolt.
Dǒng Ānyú heard of this
and informed Zhào Mèng,
saying,
"Should we prepare first?"
Zhào Mèng said,
"The state of Jìn has a mandate
that whoever starts a calamity shall die;
it is acceptable to be the one who follows."
Ānyú said, "Rather than harming the people,
I would rather die alone.
I beg to use my death as an explanation."
Zhào Mèng would not allow it.
In the autumn, in the seventh month,
the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans attacked the palace of the Zhào clan.
Zhào Yāng fled to Jìnyáng,
and the people of Jìn besieged him.
Fàn Gāoyí was not favored by Fàn Jíshè
and wished to cause a revolt within the Fàn clan.
Liáng Yīngfù was favored by Zhī Wénzǐ,
and Wénzǐ wished to make him a high minister.
Hán Jiǎnzǐ and Zhōngháng Wénzǐ disliked each other;
Wèi Xiāngzǐ also disliked Fàn Zhāozǐ.
Therefore, the five men plotted;
they would expel Xún Yín
and replace him with Liáng Yīngfù;
they would expel Fàn Jíshè
and replace him with Fàn Gāoyí.
Xún Lì said to the Marquess of Jìn,
"Your Lordship commanded the great ministers
that whoever starts a calamity shall die;
the record of this covenant is by the River.
Now the three ministers have started a calamity,
yet you only expel Yāng;
the punishment is already unequal.
I beg that all of them be expelled."
In the winter, in the eleventh month,
Xún Lì, Hán Bùxìn, and Wèi Mànduō
supported the Duke to attack the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans,
but they did not overcome them.
The two men intended to attack the Duke.
Gāo Qiáng of Qí said,
"One who has broken his arm three times knows how to be a good physician.
Only attacking the ruler is impossible;
the people will not support it.
I am here because I attacked my ruler.
The three houses are not yet in harmony;
they can all be overcome.
If you overcome them,
with whom will the ruler side?
If you first attack the ruler,
that will make them harmonize."
They did not listen
and subsequently attacked the Duke.
The people of the capital assisted the Duke;
the two men were defeated,
and they were pursued and attacked.
On the day dīngwèi,
Xún Yín and Shì Jíshè fled to Zhāogē.
Hán and Wèi pleaded on behalf of the Zhào clan.
In the twelfth month, on the day xīnwèi,
Zhào Yāng entered Jiàng
and made a covenant in the ducal palace.
Initially,
Gōngshū Wénzǐ of Wèi attended court
and requested to feast Duke Líng.
Having withdrawn,
he saw Shǐ Qiú and told him.
Shǐ Qiú said,
"You will certainly face calamity!
You are wealthy while the ruler is greedy;
how can it not reach you?"
Wénzǐ said, "Indeed.
That I did not first tell you
is my fault.
The ruler has already granted my request;
what can be done about it?"
Shǐ Qiú said, "It is not harmful.
If you act as a proper subject,
you can be exempt.
One who is wealthy but can act as a proper subject
will certainly be exempt from disaster.
Treat those above and below equally.
Shù is arrogant;
he will likely perish!
Those who are wealthy and not arrogant are few;
I have seen only you.
As for those who are arrogant and do not perish,
there has never been such a case.
Shù will certainly be involved."
When Wénzǐ died,
the Marquess of Wèi began to dislike Gōngshū Shù
because of his wealth.
Gōngshū Shù also intended to remove the faction of the ruler's wife;
the wife slandered him, saying,
"Shù is about to start a revolt."
The Annals of the Fourteenth Year of Duke Dìng.
In the spring of the fourteenth year,
Gōngshū Shù of Wèi came as a refugee.
Zhào Yáng of Wèi fled to Sòng.
In the second month, on the day xīnsì,
Prince Jié of Chǔ and
Gōngsūn Tuórén of Chén led an army to destroy Dùn,
and returned with Zāng, the Viscount of Dùn.
In the summer,
Běigōng Jié of Wèi came as a refugee.
In the fifth month,
Yúyuè defeated Wú at Zuìlǐ.
Guāng, the Viscount of Wú, died.
The Duke met with the Marquess of Qí and
the Marquess of Wèi at Qiān.
The Duke arrived from the meeting.
In the autumn,
the Marquess of Qí and
the Duke of Sòng met at Táo.
The Heavenly King sent Shí Shàng to come and return the sacrificial meat.
Kuàikuì, the Heir Apparent of Wèi, fled to Sòng.
Gōngmèng Kū of Wèi fled to Zhèng.
A11.14.12 Chén, the younger brother of the Duke of Sòng, came from Xiāo as a refugee.
A11.14.13 A great hunt was held at Bǐpú.
A11.14.14 The Viscount of Zhū came to meet the Duke.
A11.14.15 Walls were built at Jǔfù and Xiāo.
B11.14 *The Commentary on the Fourteenth Year of Duke Dìng*
B11.14.1 In the spring of the fourteenth year,
the Marquis of Wèi expelled Gōngshū Shù and his faction;
for this reason, Zhào Yáng fled to Sòng,
and Shù came as a refugee.
B11.14.2 Liáng Yīngfù disliked Dǒng Ānyú
and said to Zhì Wénzǐ:
"If you do not kill Ānyú
and allow him to continue to manage the administration for the Zhào clan,
the Zhào clan will surely gain control of the state of Jìn.
Why not use the fact that he was the first to initiate the conflict to punish the Zhào clan?"
Wénzǐ sent a messenger to inform Zhào Mèng, saying:
"Although the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans truly committed rebellion,
it was Ānyú who provoked it;
thus Ānyú conspired in the rebellion.
There is a decree in the state of Jìn
that the one who initiates a disaster must die.
Since the two leaders have already submitted to their punishment,
I venture to inform you of this."
Zhào Mèng was distressed by this.
Ānyú said:
"If my death brings peace to the state of Jìn
and stability to the Zhào clan,
what use is there in living?
Who among men does not die?
For me, death is timely."
He then hanged himself and died.
Zhào Mèng exposed his corpse in the marketplace
and informed the Zhì clan, saying:
"Your Lordship commanded the execution of the criminal Ānyú.
He has already submitted to his punishment;
I venture to inform you."
Zhì Bó joined a covenant with Zhào Mèng,
and only then was the Zhào clan stabilized.
They sacrificed to Ānyú in the ancestral temple.
B11.14.3 Zāng, the Viscount of Dùn, wished to serve Jìn,
so he turned his back on Chǔ and severed the friendship with Chén.
In the second month,
Chǔ extinguished Dùn.
B11.14.4 In the summer,
Běigōng Jié of Wèi came as a refugee,
because of the affair of Gōngshū Shù.
B11.14.5 Wú attacked Yuè.
Gōujiàn, the Viscount of Yuè, resisted them
and drew up his forces at Zuìlǐ. Gōujiàn was concerned about the disciplined order of the Wú army,
and sent death-defying warriors to attack twice,
but the Wú army did not move.
He then sent criminals in three rows,
who held swords to their own necks
and spoke, saying:
"Our two lords have a conflict,
and we, your servants, have violated the discipline of flags and drums.
Being incompetent before your presence,
we do not dare to flee from punishment,
and venture to return to death."
Thereupon they cut their own throats.
The army fixed its eyes upon them,
and the Viscount of Yuè took advantage of this to attack them,
defeating them soundly.
Línggū Fú struck Hélǘ with a halberd.
Hélǘ was wounded in his toe
and lost one of his shoes.
The Wú army retreated,
and he died at Xíng,
seven lǐ away from Zuìlǐ.
Fūchāi made a man stand in the courtyard,
and whenever he went out or came in,
he would command him to say to him:
"Fūchāi!
Have you forgotten that the King of Yuè killed your father?"
He would then reply:
"Yes.
I dare not forget!"
Three years later, he took revenge on Yuè.
B11.14.6 The people of Jìn besieged Zhāogē.
The Duke met with the Marquis of Qí and the Marquis of Wèi between Pí and Shàngliáng
to plan the rescue of the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans.
Xīchéng Fù and Xiǎowáng Táojiǎ
led an army of the Dí to launch a surprise attack on Jìn.
They fought in the midst of Jiàng,
but failed to prevail and returned.
Shì Fù fled to Zhōu,
and Xiǎowáng Táojiǎ entered Zhāogē.
B11.14.7 In the autumn,
the Marquis of Qí
and the Duke of Sòng met at Táo,
for the sake of the Fàn clan.
B11.14.8 The Marquis of Wèi summoned Sòng Zhāo for the sake of his wife Nánzǐ.
They met at Táo.
The Heir Apparent Kuàikuì presented the city of Yú to Qí
and passed through the countryside of Sòng.
The country folk sang about him, saying:
"Since you have already satisfied your sow,
why not return our handsome boar?"
The Heir Apparent was ashamed of this
and said to Xìyáng Sù:
"Follow me to have an audience with the Shào Jūn.
When the Shào Jūn sees me,
I will look back,
and then you shall kill her."
Sù said:
"Yes."
Thereupon they had an audience with the lady.
The lady saw the Heir Apparent.
The Heir Apparent looked back three times,
but Sù did not advance.
The lady saw his expression
and ran away crying,
saying:
"Kuàikuì is going to kill me!"
The Marquis took her hand and ascended a tower.
The Heir Apparent fled to Sòng.
The Marquis expelled all of his faction;
therefore, Gōngmèng Kōu fled to Zhèng,
and from Zhèng to Qí.
The Heir Apparent told people:
"Xìyáng Sù brought disaster upon me."
Xìyáng Sù told people:
"The Heir Apparent brought disaster upon me.
The Heir Apparent was unprincipled
and ordered me to kill his mother.
If I had not agreed,
he would have killed me;
if I had killed the lady,
he would have used me as a scapegoat.
For this reason, I agreed but did not act,
so as to delay my death.
The proverb says,
'The people are preserved by trustworthiness';
I acted according to trustworthiness and righteousness."
B11.14.9 In the winter, the twelfth month,
the people of Jìn defeated the armies of the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans at Lù,
capturing Jí Qín and Gāo Qiáng.
They also defeated the army of Zhèng and the army of the Fàn clan at Bǎiquán.
A11.15 *The Annals of the Fifteenth Year of Duke Dìng*
A11.15.1 In the fifteenth year, in the spring,
in the King's first month,
the Viscount of Zhū came to court.
A11.15.2 Field mice ate the suburban sacrificial ox;
the ox died,
and the divination for a replacement ox was performed.
A11.15.3 In the second month, on the day xīnyǒu,
the Viscount of Chǔ extinguished Hú,
and returned with Bào, the Viscount of Hú.
A11.15.4 In the summer, the fifth month, on the day xīnhài,
the suburban sacrifice was performed.
A11.15.5 On the day rénshēn,
the Duke died in the Gāoqǐn palace.
A11.15.6 Hǎn Dá of Zhèng led an army to attack Sòng.
A11.15.7 The Marquis of Qí
and the Marquis of Wèi halted at Qúchú.
A11.15.8 The Viscount of Zhū came to attend the funeral.
A11.15.9 In the autumn, the seventh month, on the day rénshēn,
Lady Sì died.
A11.15.10 In the eighth month, on the first day of the month gēngchén,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A11.15.11 In the ninth month,
the Viscount of Téng came to join the burial.
A11.15.12 On the day dìngsì,
we buried our ruler, Duke Dìng.
It rained, and the burial could not be completed.
On the day wùwǔ,
when the sun was past its zenith,
the burial was finally completed.
A11.15.13 On the day xīnsì,
Dìng Sì was buried.
A11.15.14 In the winter,
the walls of Qī were built.
B11.15 *The Commentary on the Fifteenth Year of Duke Dìng*
B11.15.1 In the spring of the fifteenth year,
Zhū Yǐn Gōng came to court.
Zǐgòng observed this.
The Master of Zhū held the jade high,
and his expression was tilted upward;
the Duke received the jade low,
and his expression was bowed down.
Zǐgòng said:
“Observing from the perspective of ritual,
both of these rulers
face death or ruin.
For ritual
is the embodiment of life and death, preservation and ruin.
Whether moving left or right, turning about,
advancing or retreating, bowing or looking up—
it is from these that it is derived;
at court visits, sacrifices, funerals, and military campaigns, it is in these that it is observed.
Now in the first month they come to court,
yet both are out of measure,
and their minds are already lost.
If an auspicious event does not follow the embodiment of ritual,
how can they long endure?
Holding it high and looking up
is pride;
holding it low and bowing down
is decline.
Pride is close to disorder,
and decline is close to illness.
Our ruler is the host,
so he will likely be the first to perish!”
B11.15.2 When Wú entered Chǔ,
Húzǐ captured all those in Chǔ towns that were near Hú.
After Chǔ was settled,
Húzǐ Bào also failed to serve Chǔ,
saying:
“Survival and ruin are fated,
why serve Chǔ?
It only incurs great expense.”
In the second month,
Chǔ destroyed Hú.
B11.15.3 In summer, the fifth month, on the day Rénshēn,
the Duke passed away.
Zhòngní said:
“It is unfortunate for Sì that his words were accurate;
this will make Sì a man of many words.”
B11.15.4 Zhèng Hǎn Dá defeated the Sòng army at Lǎoqiū.
B11.15.5 Qí Hóu and
Wèi Hóu halted at Qúná,
planning to rescue Sòng.
B11.15.6 In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Rénshēn,
Sì Shì died.
She was not called “Lady,”
no announcement was made of her death,
and her tablet was not placed in the temple.
B11.15.7 Duke Dìng was buried;
it rained,
and the ceremonies could not be completed,
which was in accordance with ritual.
B11.15.8 Dìng Sì was buried;
she was not called “Lesser Consort”
because the mourning rites were not properly completed.
B11.15.9 In winter,
the walls of Qī were built;
this is recorded because the report was not made at the proper time.
A12.1 《Āi Gōng First Year: The Classic》
A12.1.1 In the first year, spring, the King’s first month,
the Duke ascended the throne.
A12.1.2 Chǔzǐ,
Chén Hóu,
Suí Hóu, and
Xǔ Nán besieged Cài.
A12.1.3 Field mice ate the bull for the suburban sacrifice;
another bull was selected by divination. In summer, the fourth month, on the day Xīnsì,
the suburban sacrifice was performed.
A12.1.4 In autumn,
Qí Hóu and
Wèi Hóu attacked Jìn.
A12.1.5 In winter,
Zhòngsūn Héjì led an army to attack Zhū.
B12.1 《Āi Gōng First Year: The Commentary》
B12.1.1 In the spring of the first year,
Chǔzǐ besieged Cài,
to retaliate for Bǎijǔ.
Every lǐ they built a wall,
ten feet wide and twice as high.
The troops camped day and night for nine days,
according to Zǐxī's original plan.
The men and women of Cài were sorted.
He settled them in the region between the Jiāng and
Rǔ rivers and then returned.
Thereupon Cài requested to move to Wú.
B12.1.2 Wú Wáng Fūchāi defeated Yuè at Fújiāo,
to retaliate for Zuìlǐ.
He then entered Yuè.
Yuèzǐ, with five thousand men in armor and shields, held Huìjī,
and sent Dàfū Zhòng to seek peace through the Wú Dàzǎi Pǐ.
Wúzǐ was going to grant it.
Wǔ Yuán said:
“It must not be allowed.
I have heard:
‘Nothing is better than to nurture virtue,
and nothing is better than to remove a disease completely.’
Long ago, Jiāo of Guò killed the ruler of Zhēnguàn to attack Zhēnxún,
and destroyed the Xià Hòu Xiāng.
Hòu Mǐn was then pregnant;
she escaped through a hole in the wall,
returned to Yǒuréng,
and there gave birth to Shàokāng.
Shàokāng became the Master of Herds for Réng,
and because Jiāo might find him, he was on his guard.
Jiāo sent Jiāo to search for him,
so he fled to Yǒuyú,
where he became the Master of Kitchens
to avoid harm.
Yú Sī then gave him his two daughters of the Yáo clan in marriage
and gave him the city of Lún.
He had ten square lǐ of land
and a brigade of five hundred men.
He was able to spread his virtue
and manifest his plans,
so as to gather the people of Xià
and soothe the officials.
He sent Nǚ Ài to spy on Jiāo,
and sent Jì Zhù to entice Yì.
He then destroyed Guò and Gē,
restored the work of Yǔ,
and performed the Xià sacrifices to the ancestors as counterparts of Heaven,
not losing the old heritage.
Now Wú is not as strong as Guò,
and Yuè is larger than Shàokāng's force.
If you now allow them to flourish,
will it not be difficult later?
Gǒujiàn is able to be close to his people and strives to bestow favors;
his favors are not lost on the people,
and in his closeness, he does not forget those who labor.
They share a border with us,
and for generations have been our enemies.
If having conquered them, we do not take them
but instead allow them to survive,
it is to go against Heaven and nurture a mortal enemy.
Even if you regret it later,
you will not be able to undo it.
The decline of the House of Jī
can be expected any day.
Situated among the Mán and Yí,
while nurturing a mortal enemy,
if you seek hegemony by this means,
it will surely not succeed.”
The King would not listen.
Wǔ Yuán withdrew and told others:
“In ten years Yuè will have born and gathered people,
and in another ten years they will have been trained and educated.
After twenty years,
will Wú not be turned into a pool of water?”
In the third month,
Yuè and Wú made peace.
Wú entered Yuè,
but this is not recorded
because Wú did not report a victory and Yuè did not report a defeat.
B12.1.3 In summer, the fourth month,
Qí Hóu and Wèi Hóu rescued Hándān
and besieged Wǔlù.
B12.1.4 When Wú entered Chǔ,
they sent a summons to Chén Huái Gōng.
Chén Huái Gōng assembled the people of the state and asked them,
saying:
“Those who wish to be with Chǔ, stand to the right;
those who wish to be with Wú, stand to the left.”
The people of Chén followed the ownership of their fields;
those without fields followed their kin.
Féng Huá stepped forward to face the Duke
and said:
“I have heard
that a state’s rise is due to good fortune,
and its ruin is due to calamity.
Now Wú has not yet attained good fortune,
and Chǔ has not yet met with calamity.
Chǔ must not yet be abandoned,
and Wú must not yet be followed.
Moreover, Jìn
is the leader of the covenants;
if we refuse Wú on the grounds of our alliance with Jìn,
