how would that be?”
The Duke said:
“The capital has been overcome and the ruler has fled;
if that is not calamity, what is?”
He replied:
“A state having such things happens often;
why should it not recover?
If a small state can recover,
how much more so a great state?
I have heard
that when a state rises,
it looks upon the people as if they were wounded;
this is its blessing.
When it perishes,
it treats the people as dirt and weeds;
this is its calamity.
Although Chǔ lacks virtue,
it does not yet cut down and kill its people.
Wú is daily exhausted by war,
exposing bones like tangled grass,
and yet no virtue is seen there.
Heaven is perhaps currently instructing Chǔ;
as for calamity reaching Wú,
what day will it not come?”
The Marquis of Chén followed this.
When Fūchāi conquered Yuè,
he then pursued the grievances of his late father.
In the autumn, in the eighth month,
Wú invaded Chén,
pursuing old grievances.
B12.1.5 The Marquis of Qí and the Marquis of Wèi met at Gānhóu,
to rescue the Fàn clan.
The army, along with the army of Qí, Kǒng Yǔ of Wèi, and the people of Xiānyú, attacked Jìn
and took Jípǔ.
B12.1.6 When the Wú army was in Chén,
all the Grand Officers of Chǔ were afraid
and said:
“Hélú was only able to use his people
to defeat us at Bǎijǔ.
Now we hear his successor is even more extreme;
what shall we do?”
Zixī said:
“If you gentlemen worry about not being in harmony with each other,
there is no need to worry about Wú.
Formerly, Hélú did not eat two kinds of meat at a meal,
did not sit on double mats,
did not have high platforms for his chambers,
did not have red-lacquered or carved vessels,
his palaces had no observation towers,
and his boats and carriages were not decorated;
for clothing and material use,
he chose those that were not costly.
In the capital,
when there were natural disasters or pestilences,
he personally visited the orphans and widows and shared in their lack and distress.
In the army,
only after the cooked food was distributed did he dare to eat;
whatever he tasted,
the soldiers and chariot-drivers shared in it.
He diligently showed compassion to his people
and shared their labor and ease,
thus the people were not exhausted by labor,
and in death, they knew they would not be neglected.
Our former Grand Officer Zicháng was the opposite of this,
which is why we were defeated.
Now I hear Fūchāi
has terraces, pavilions, ponds, and lakes at his resting places,
and has consorts, concubines, and ladies-in-waiting for his nights;
in a single day’s journey,
whatever he desires must be accomplished,
and toys and curios must follow him;
rare and exotic things are gathered,
and observation and music are his business;
he treats the people like enemies,
and uses them with increasing novelty.
He has already defeated himself;
how can he defeat us?”
B12.1.7 In the winter, the tenth month,
Zhào Yáng of Jìn attacked Zhāogē.
A12.2 The Classic of Duke Āi, Second Year.
A12.2.1 In the spring of the second year,
in the royal second month,
Jìsūn Sī,
Shúsūn Zhōuqiú,
and Zhòngsūn Héjì led an army to attack Zhū,
taking the fields east of the Huò and west of the Yǐ.
On the day guǐsì,
Shúsūn Zhōuqiú
and Zhòngsūn Héjì made a covenant with the Viscount of Zhū at Gǒuyì.
A12.2.2 In the summer, the fourth month, on the day bǐngzǐ,
Marquis Yuán of Wèi died.
A12.2.3 The Viscount of Téng came to court.
A12.2.4 Zhào Yáng of Jìn led an army to install the eldest son of Wèi, Kuàikuì, in Qī.
A12.2.5 In the autumn, the eighth month, on the day jiǎxū,
Zhào Yáng of Jìn led an army and Hán Dá of Zhèng led an army and fought at Tiě.
The Zhèng army was utterly defeated.
A12.2.6 In the winter, the tenth month,
they buried Duke Líng of Wèi.
A12.2.7 In the eleventh month,
Cài moved to Zhōulái.
Cài killed its Grand Officer Gōngzǐ Sì.
B12.2 The Commentary of Duke Āi, Second Year.
B12.2.1 In the spring of the second year,
they attacked Zhū,
intending to attack Jiǎo.
The people of Zhū loved their land,
so they bribed with the fields of Huò and Yǐ and received a covenant.
B12.2.2 Formerly,
the Marquis of Wèi was traveling in the outskirts;
Zǐnán was his driver.
The Duke said:
“I have no son,
I will establish you.”
He did not reply.
Another day the Duke spoke to him again,
and he replied:
“Yǐng is not sufficient to be burdened with the altars of the state;
may your Lordship change your plan.
Your Lordship’s wife is in the hall,
and the three heirs are below;
your command only brings disgrace.”
In the summer,
Duke Líng of Wèi died.
The lady said:
“The command was to make Gōngzǐ Yǐng the heir;
it was the ruler’s command.”
He replied:
“Yǐng is no different from the other sons,
and since the ruler died in my arms,
if there had been such a command,
Yǐng would surely have heard it.
Moreover, Zhé, the son of the exile, is here.”
So they established Zhé.
In the sixth month, on the day yǐyǒu,
Zhào Yáng of Jìn installed the heir of Wèi in Qī.
Losing their way at night,
Yáng Hǔ said:
“Keep the Hé River on the right and go south,
you will surely arrive there.”
He made the heir wear mourning clothes
and had eight men in mourning dress
pretend to be those coming from Wèi to meet him.
They announced themselves at the gate,
entered wailing,
and consequently resided there.
B12.2.3 In the autumn, the eighth month,
the people of Qí transported grain to the Fàn clan;
Zǐyáo and Zǐbān of Zhèng escorted it.
Shì Jíshè met them,
and Zhào Yáng opposed them,
meeting at Qī.
Yáng Hǔ said:
“Our chariots are few;
take the pennons of the war chariots and line them up first with the war chariots of the Hán and Sī clans.
The Hán and Sī will follow behind;
when they see our appearance,
they will surely have fear in their hearts.
At that point, engage them,
and we will surely defeat them soundly.”
They followed this.
They divined about the battle,
and the tortoise shell was scorched.
Lè Dīng said:
“The Shī says:
‘Then he began, then he planned,
then he consulted my tortoise shell.’
Since the plans agree,
it is acceptable to consult the tortoise using the previous omen.”
Jiǎn Zǐ made an oath, saying:
“The Fàn and Zhōngháng clans have rebelled against and changed Heaven's brilliance,
cutting down the common people,
desiring to usurp Jìn and destroy its ruler.
My ruler relies on Zhèng for protection.
Now Zhèng acts without the Way,
abandoning a ruler to help a minister.
You gentlemen, follow Heaven's brilliance,
obey the ruler’s command,
uphold virtue and righteousness,
and remove disgrace;
it all lies in this campaign.
For those who overcome the enemy, upper officials shall receive counties,
lower officials shall receive districts,
knights shall receive one hundred thousand mu of land,
commoners, artisans, and merchants shall advance to office,
and servants and grooms shall be freed.
Zhìfù is without guilt;
let the ruler consider it!
But if I have guilt,
let me be strangled and executed,
with a paulownia coffin three inches thick,
without inner or outer linings, using a plain chariot and an unadorned horse,
and do not enter the ancestral graveyard;
this is the punishment for a lower minister.”
On the day jiǎxū,
when they were about to battle,
Yóu Wúxù drove for Jiǎnzǐ,
and the Crown Prince of Wèi was the right-hand attendant.
They climbed up the hill of Tiě,
and looking out, they saw that the Zhèng army was numerous.
The Crown Prince was afraid
and threw himself under the carriage.
Zǐliáng handed the Crown Prince the mounting strap
and helped him mount the carriage,
saying:
"He is like a woman."
Jiǎnzǐ inspected the ranks
and said:
"Bì Wàn
was but a common man,
yet in seven battles he always made captures.
He came to possess a hundred chariots
and died in his own bed.
Gentlemen, exert yourselves!
Death does not lie with the enemy."
Fán Yǔ drove for Zhào Luó,
and Sòng Yǒng was the right-hand attendant.
Luó had no courage,
so they bound him to the carriage.
The officer questioned them,
and the driver replied:
"His malaria flared up and he is lying down."
The Crown Prince of Wèi prayed, saying:
"Great-grandson Kuàikuì dares to clearly announce to the August Ancestor Wén Wáng,
the Illustrious Ancestor Kāng Shū,
and the Accomplished Ancestor Xiāng Gōng:
Zhèng has victoriously followed the rebellion;
Jìn Wǔ is in distress
and cannot govern the chaos,
so he has sent Yāng to punish them.
Kuàikuì does not dare to take his ease;
he is prepared and holding his spear.
I dare to pray that no sinews be severed,
no bones be broken,
and no wounds be on the face,
so that the great matter may be accomplished,
and no shame be brought upon the three ancestors.
For the great mandate of life, I do not dare to ask,
but my jade pendants I do not dare to begrudge."
A man of Zhèng struck Jiǎnzǐ, hitting him in the shoulder.
He collapsed in the carriage,
and they captured his Fēng banner.
The Crown Prince rescued him with a halberd.
The Zhèng army fled north.
They captured the Grandee of Wēn, Zhào Luó.
The Crown Prince attacked them again,
and the Zhèng army was greatly defeated.
They captured a thousand chariots of Qí grain.
Zhào Mèng was pleased and said:
"It will do."
Fù Sǒu said:
"Even though we have overcome Zhèng,
the Zhì family is still there;
our worries have not yet ended."
Formerly,
the people of Zhōu gave land to the Fàn family.
Gōngsūn Máng collected taxes there,
and the Zhào family captured him and presented him to Jiǎnzǐ.
The officers requested to kill him.
Zhào Mèng said:
"He did it for his master;
what crime is that?"
He stopped them and gave him land.
When it came to the battle of Tiě,
with five hundred foot soldiers he attacked the Zhèng army by night,
took the Fēng banner from below the tent of Zǐyáo,
and presented it,
saying:
"I request to repay my master's virtue."
While pursuing the Zhèng army,
Yáo, Bān, and Gōngsūn Lín acted as the rear guard and shot arrows;
many in the front ranks died.
Zhào Mèng said:
"A state should not be considered small."
After the battle,
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"I leaned on the quiver and vomited blood,
but the sound of my drum did not falter.
Today, I was the best."
The Crown Prince said:
"I rescued my lord in the carriage
and repelled the enemy below.
I
am the best of the right-hand attendants."
Yóu Liáng said:
"My two traces were about to break,
but I was able to stop them.
I
am the best of drivers."
He drove the carriage over some wood,
and both traces broke.
B12.2.4 Xiè Yōng of Wú went to Cài to deliver engagement gifts,
and gradually introduced troops.
When the troops had all entered,
the people realized it.
The Marquis of Cài told his grandees
and killed Gōngzǐ Sì to please the Wú.
They wept and moved the tombs.
In winter,
Cài moved to Zhōulái.
A12.3 The Classic of Duke Āi, Third Year
A12.3.1 In the spring of the third year,
Guó Xià of Qí
and Shí Màngū of Wèi led an army to besiege Qī.
A12.3.2 In summer, the fourth month, on the day jiǎwǔ,
there was an earthquake.
A12.3.3 In the fifth month, on the day xīnmǎo,
the Temple of Huán
and the Temple of Xī were destroyed by fire.
A12.3.4 Jìsūn Sī
and Shúsūn Zhōuqiú led an army to wall Qǐyáng.
A12.3.5 Lè Kūn of Sòng led an army to attack Cáo.
A12.3.6 In autumn, the seventh month, on the day bǐngzǐ,
Jìsūn Sī died.
A12.3.7 The people of Cài banished their grandee Gōngsūn Liè to Wú.
A12.3.8 In winter, the tenth month, on the day guǐmǎo,
the Earl of Qín died.
A12.3.9 Shúsūn Zhōuqiú
and Zhòngsūn Héjì led an army to besiege Zhū.
B12.3 The Commentary of Duke Āi, Third Year
B12.3.1 In the spring of the third year,
Qí and Wèi besieged Qī,
and sought aid from Zhōngshān.
B12.3.2 In summer, the fifth month, on the day xīnmǎo,
the Sīduó caught fire.
The fire jumped over the Duke's palace,
and the temples of Huán and Xī were destroyed.
Those fighting the fire all said, "Protect the treasury."
Nángōng Jìngshū arrived
and ordered the men of Zhōu to bring out the royal documents
to wait in the palace,
saying:
"Arrange your duties;
if you are not present,
you shall die."
Zǐfú Jǐngbó arrived
and ordered the stewards to bring out the ritual books
to await orders.
Failure to provide them
carried the standard punishment.
The masters of the stable mounted the horses,
the masters of the chariots greased the axles,
all the various officials were at their posts,
the treasuries and storehouses were carefully guarded,
and the officials were solemn and ready.
They soaked the curtains
to follow the rising fire.
They covered the roofs of the public buildings with wet mats,
starting from the Grand Temple,
and both outside and inside they worked with diligence.
They helped where there was insufficient labor.
If any did not follow orders,
there were standard punishments,
without pardon.
Gōngfù Wénbó arrived
and ordered the masters of the stable to harness the ceremonial carriages.
Jì Huánzǐ arrived,
and escorted the Duke to stand outside the Xiàngwèi,
and ordered the firefighters to stop if someone was being injured,
saying that property could be replaced.
He ordered the storage of the Xiàngwèi laws,
saying:
"The old statutes must not be lost."
Fùfù Huái arrived
and said:
"To have officials manage things without preparation
is like trying to pick up spilled liquid."
Thereupon they removed the dried stalks from the screens
and cleared the paths around the Duke's palace.
Kǒngzǐ was in Chén
when he heard of the fire;
he said:
"It must be the temples of Huán and Xī!"
B12.3.3 The Liú family and the Fàn family had been related by marriage for generations.
Cháng Hóng served Duke Wén of Liú,
so the Zhōu court sided with the Fàn family.
Zhào Yāng used this as a reason for punishment.
In the sixth month, on the day guǐmǎo,
the people of Zhōu killed Cháng Hóng.
B12.3.4 In autumn,
Jì Sūn fell ill,
and ordered Zhèng Cháng, saying:
“Do not die!
As for the child of the Nán lady,
if it is a boy,
then report it and establish him [as successor];
if it is a girl,
then Féí will be acceptable.”
Jì Sūn died,
and Kāng Zǐ succeeded to the position.
After the burial,
Kāng Zǐ was in the court.
The Nán lady gave birth to a boy;
Zhèng Cháng carried him to the court
and reported, saying:
“The late master had testamentary words,
and he commanded his groom-servant, saying:
‘If the Nán lady gives birth to a boy,
then report it to the Ruler and the Great Officers and establish him.’
Now he is born,
it is a boy,
and I venture to report it.”
He then fled to Wèi.
Kāng Zǐ requested to withdraw.
The Duke sent Gòng Liú to inspect the matter,
and someone had already killed the child.
Thereupon they punished the killer.
They summoned Zhèng Cháng,
but Zhèng Cháng did not return.
B12.3.5 In the winter, the tenth month,
Zhào Yāng of Jìn besieged Cháogē,
and stationed his army to its south.
Xún Yín attacked its outer walls,
and sent his followers to enter from the north gate,
while he himself broke through the army and went out.
On the day guǐchǒu,
he fled to Hándān.
In the eleventh month,
Zhào Yāng killed Shì Gāo Yí,
because he detested the Fàn clan.
A12.4 The Classic of the Fourth Year of Duke Āi.
A12.4.1 In the spring of the fourth year,
in the royal second month, on the day gēngxū,
robbers killed Marquis Shēn of Cài.
A12.4.2 Gōngsūn Chén of Cài fled to Wú.
A12.4.3 Duke Huì of Qín was buried.
A12.4.4 The people of Sòng seized the Master of Xiǎo Zhū.
A12.4.5 In the summer,
Cài killed its Great Officers Gōngsūn Xìng and
Gōngsūn Huò.
A12.4.6 The people of Jìn seized Chì, the Master of the Róng Mán, and returned him to Chǔ.
A12.4.7 They walled the western outer wall.
A12.4.8 In the sixth month, on the day xīnjiǔ,
the Bóshè suffered a fire.
A12.4.9 In the autumn, the eighth month, on the day jiǎyín,
Master Jié of Téng died.
A12.4.10 In the winter, the twelfth month,
Duke Zhāo of Cài was buried.
A12.4.11 Duke Qǐng of Téng was buried.
B12.4 The Commentary of the Fourth Year of Duke Āi.
B12.4.1 In the spring of the fourth year,
Marquis Zhāo of Cài was about to go to Wú.
The Great Officers feared he would move the capital again,
so they supported Gōngsūn Pián to pursue and shoot him.
He entered a commoner’s house and died.
Guarding the door with two arrows,
the crowd dared not advance.
Wénzhī Kǎi arrived later
and said:
“Advance like a wall;
at most he can kill two people.”
Kǎi held a bow and led the way;
Pián shot him,
hitting his elbow;
Kǎi then killed him.
Therefore, they drove out Gōngsūn Chén and killed Gōngsūn Xìng and Gōngsūn Xū.
B12.4.2 In the summer,
after the people of Chǔ had conquered Yíhǔ,
they planned for the northern region.
Left Marshal Pān, Shēn Gōng Shòu Yú,
and Zhū Liáng, the Lord of Yè, summoned the people of Cài to Fùhán,
and summoned those from outside the Fāngchéng Wall to Zèngguān,
saying:
“Wú is about to sail up the Yangtze River to enter Yǐng,
and we must rush to its defense.”
Setting a one-night deadline,
they made a surprise attack on Liáng and Huò.
Shàn Fú Yú besieged the Mán clan;
the Mán clan collapsed.
Chì, the Master of the Mán, fled to the Yīndì region of Jìn.
The Marshal raised the people of Fēng and Xī along with the Dí Róng
to approach Shàng Luò.
The Left Army encamped at Tùhé,
and the Right Army encamped at Cāngyě.
They sent word to Shì Miè, the Mandated Great Officer of Yīndì, saying:
“Jìn and Chǔ have a covenant,
sharing the same likes and dislikes.
If you do not discard it,
it is our ruler’s wish.
Otherwise,
we will force our way through Shǎoxí to receive your orders.”
Shì Miè requested instructions from Zhào Mèng.
Zhào Mèng said:
“The state of Jìn is not yet at peace,
how can we incur the enmity of Chǔ?
You must quickly give him to them!”
Shì Miè then gathered the Róng of the Jiǔ Zhōu,
and intended to divide the land to give to the Mán Master and build a wall for him,
and was also about to perform divination for him.
The Mán Master listened to the divination,
whereupon Shì Miè seized him and his five Great Officers
to hand them over to the Chǔ army at Sānhù.
The Marshal assigned them cities and established their ancestral lines there
to entice the remaining people,
and then took them all as captives and returned.
B12.4.3 In the autumn, the seventh month,
Chén Qǐ and Xián Shī of Qí, and Nìng Guì of Wèi rescued the Fàn clan.
On the day gēngwǔ,
they besieged Wǔlù.
In the ninth month,
Zhào Yāng besieged Hándān.
In the winter, the eleventh month,
Hándān surrendered.
Xún Yín fled to Xiānyú,
and Zhào Jì fled to Lín.
In the twelfth month,
Xián Shī met them
and then demolished Lín.
Guó Xià attacked Jìn
and took Xíng, Rèn, Luán, Hào,
Nìzhì, Yīnrén, Yú, and Hǔkǒu,
met with the Xiānyú,
and settled Xún Yín in Bǎirén.
A12.5 The Classic of the Fifth Year of Duke Āi.
A12.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
they walled Pí.
A12.5.2 In the summer,
the Marquis of Qí attacked Sòng.
A12.5.3 Zhào Yāng of Jìn led an army to attack Wèi.
A12.5.4 In the autumn, the ninth month, on the day guǐyǒu,
Chǔjiǔ, the Marquis of Qí, died.
A12.5.5 In the winter,
Shū Huán went to Qí.
A12.5.6 In the intercalary month,
Duke Jǐng of Qí was buried.
B12.5 The Commentary of the Fifth Year of Duke Āi.
B12.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
Jìn besieged Bǎirén,
and Xún Yín and Shì Jíshè fled to Qí.
Previously,
Wáng Shēng, a servant of the Fàn clan, detested Zhāng Liǔshuò
and spoke of him to Zhāozǐ,
making him the commander of Bǎirén.
Zhāozǐ said:
“Is he not your enemy?”
He replied:
“Private enmity should not affect public matters;
love should not overlook faults,
and hatred should not discard goodness.
This is the constant path of righteousness.
How would I dare violate it?”
When the Fàn clan left,
Zhāng Liǔshuò said to his son:
“You follow our master,
and exert yourself!
I will stay here to die.
Wáng Shēng recommended me,
and I cannot fail his trust.”
He then died at Bǎirén.
B12.5.2 In the summer,
Zhào Yāng attacked Wèi
because of the Fàn clan affair,
and then besieged Zhōngmóu.
B12.5.3 The consort Yàn Jī of Qí gave birth to a son,
who died before reaching adulthood.
Among the various sons, Tú, the son of Yù Sì, was a favorite.
The grandees feared that he would be made the crown prince
and spoke to the Duke, saying:
“Your Lordship is advanced in years
and does not yet have a crown prince;
what is to be done?”
The Duke said:
“If you gentlemen let yourselves be caught between worries and anxieties,
then you will fall ill.
For now, just seek joy;
why worry about having no ruler?”
When the Duke fell ill,
he ordered Guó Huìzǐ and Gāo Zhāozǐ to establish Tú [as his successor]
and placed the other princes in Lái.
In autumn,
Duke Jǐng of Qí died.
In the tenth month of winter,
Young Lord Jiā, Young Lord Jū, and Young Lord Qián fled to Wèi,
while Young Lord Chú and Young Lord Yángshēng came here in flight.
The people of Lái sang of it, saying:
“Duke Jǐng has died, but he is not buried with them!
The affairs of the three armies are not planned with them!
Oh, the soldiers! Oh, the soldiers!
To which faction do they belong?”
B12.5.4 Sì Qín of Zhèng was wealthy and extravagant;
he was a favored grandee,
and he frequently displayed the chariots and robes of a high minister in his courtyard.
The people of Zhèng detested him and killed him.
Zǐsī said:
“The *Shī* says:
‘Unremitting in his position,
he is the one in whom the people find rest.’
Rare are those who do not keep to their proper position and yet can endure for long.
The ‘Eulogies of Shāng’ says:
‘Neither overstepping nor overflowing,
not daring to be idle or indifferent,
they are ordained with many blessings.’”
A12.6 The Classic of Duke Āi, Sixth Year
A12.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
the wall of Zhūxiá was built.
A12.6.2 Zhào Yāng of Jìn led an army to attack Xiānyú.
A12.6.3 Wú attacked Chén.
A12.6.4 In summer,
Guó Xià and Gāo Zhāng of Qí came here in flight.
A12.6.5 Shū Huán met with the people of Wú at Zā.
A12.6.6 In the seventh month of autumn, on the day *gēngyín*,
Zhěn, the Viscount of Chǔ, died.
A12.6.7 Yángshēng of Qí entered Qí.
A12.6.8 Chén Qǐ of Qí assassinated his ruler, Tú.
A12.6.9 In winter,
Zhòngsūn Héjì led an army to attack Zhū.
A12.6.10 Xiàng Cháo of Sòng led an army to attack Cáo.
B12.6 The Commentary of Duke Āi, Sixth Year
B12.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
Jìn attacked Xiānyú,
to deal with the rebellion of the Fàn lineage.
B12.6.2 Wú attacked Chén,
to renew an old grudge.
The Viscount of Chǔ said:
“My late lord had a covenant with Chén;
I cannot but rescue them.”
He then went to rescue Chén
and stationed his army at Chéngfù.
B12.6.3 Chén Qǐ of Qí feigned serving Gāo and Guó;
every time they went to court,
he would surely act as an attendant in their carriage.
Wherever he followed them,
he would surely say to the grandees:
“They are both arrogant
and are going to discard your mandates.
They all say:
‘If Gāo and Guó gain control over the ruler,
they will surely press us;
why not remove them?’
They are certainly going to plot against you;
you should plan against them early!
In planning against them,
nothing is better than to exterminate them completely.
Delay
is the lowest way to handle affairs.”
When they reached court,
he would then say:
“They [the grandees]
are like tigers and wolves.
Seeing me by your side,
the day they kill me is not far off;
I beg to take my place among them.”
He also said to the grandees:
“Those two men are a calamity!
Relying on their influence with the ruler, they want to plot against you gentlemen,
saying:
‘The many troubles of the state
arise from those of high rank and favor.
Only after removing them all will the ruler be settled.’
Since their plan is already formed,
why not, before they act,
get ahead of them?
If you wait until they act,
it will be too late for regret.”
The grandees followed him.
In the sixth month of summer, on the day *wùchén*,
Chén Qǐ, Bào Mù, and the grandees entered the Duke’s palace with armed men.
Zhāozǐ heard of it
and with Huìzǐ rode to the Duke.
They fought at Zhuāng
and were defeated.
The people of the capital pursued them;
Guó Xià fled to Jǔ,
and subsequently Gāo Zhāng, Yàn Yǔ, and Xián Shī came here in flight.
B12.6.4 In the seventh month of autumn,
the Viscount of Chǔ was at Chéngfù,
preparing to rescue Chén.
He divined about battle:
it was inauspicious.
He divined about retreating:
it was inauspicious.
The King said:
“Then it means death.
To have the Chǔ army defeated again
is not as good as death;
to abandon a covenant and flee from a foe
is also not as good as death.
Death is the same in either case;
let me die facing the foe!”
He ordered Young Lord Shēn to be King,
but he refused;
then he ordered Young Lord Jié,
but he also refused;
then he ordered Young Lord Qǐ;
after five refusals, he finally consented.
As they were about to battle,
the King fell ill.
On the day *gēngyín*,
King Zhāo attacked Dàmíng
and died at Chéngfù.
Zǐlǘ withdrew and
said:
“The Lord King passed over his own son and yielded the throne;
how could we ministers dare to forget our lord?
To follow the King’s command
is obedience;
to establish the King’s son
is also obedience.
These two forms of obedience must not be lost.”
He planned with Zǐxī and Zǐqī,
moved the army secretly and closed the fortifications,
went to meet Zhāng, the son of a woman from Yuè, and established him,
and only then returned.
In this year,
there were clouds like a flock of red birds
flying around the sun for three days.
The Viscount of Chǔ sent someone to ask the Dàshǐ of Zhōu about it.
The Dàshǐ of Zhōu said:
“It likely concerns the person of the King!
If you perform a propitiatory sacrifice,
the omen can be shifted to the Lìngyǐn or the Sīmǎ.”
The King said:
“To remove a disease from the heart and belly
and place it in the limbs—
what benefit would that be?
If I have not committed a great fault,
would Heaven cut me off prematurely?
If I have committed a crime and receive punishment,
how can I shift it?”
So he did not perform the sacrifice.
Earlier,
when King Zhāo was ill,
the divination said:
“The Hé River is causing the curse.”
The King did not sacrifice to it.
The grandees asked to sacrifice to it in the suburbs.
The King said:
“The Three Dynasties ordained the sacrifices
so that they do not go beyond the landmarks of their spiritual jurisdiction.
The Jiāng, the Hàn, the Jū, and the Zhāng
are the spiritual jurisdictions of Chǔ.
When fortune or calamity arrive,
they do not go beyond these.
Although I am not virtuous,
the Hé is not something against which I have committed a crime.”
So he did not sacrifice to it.
Kǒngzǐ said:
“King Zhāo of Chǔ knew the Great Way!
That he did not lose his state
is indeed fitting!”
Xià Shū says:
"Thinking of that Táo Táng,
who followed those heavenly constants
and possessed this region of Jì.
Now he has lost his proper conduct,
disordered the laws and discipline,
and thus he is destroyed and perishes."
It also says:
"Verily, what comes from here resides here."
If one follows the constants from oneself,
it is sufficient."
B12.6.5 In the eighth month,
Bǐng Yìzī of Qí came as a refugee.
B12.6.6 Chén Xīzǐ sent someone to summon Gōngzǐ Yángshēng.
Yángshēng drove a carriage to see Nánguō Qiěyú
and said:
"I once offered a horse to Jìsūn,
but it was not accepted into the superior teams.
Therefore, I offer this one again;
please ride it with me."
They went out of the Lái Mén and he told him the reason.
Kàn Zhǐ knew of it
and waited for them outside beforehand.
Gōngzǐ said: "The outcome of this matter is not yet known.
Return
and stay with Rén."
He warned him
and then set out.
At nightfall, they arrived in Qí,
and the people of the state knew of it.
Chén Xīzǐ had the mother of Zǐshì care for him;
she entered together with those bringing food.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the day Dīngmǎo,
they installed him.
When they were about to swear the covenant,
Bàozǐ went while drunk.
His officer, the chariot attendant Bào Diǎn, said:
"Whose command is this?"
Chénzǐ said: "I received the command from Bàozǐ."
He then falsely accused Bàozǐ, saying:
"It was your command!"
Bàozǐ said:
"Have you forgotten how the late Ruler acted as an ox for Rǔzǐ and broke his tooth,
and yet you betray him?"
Dào Gōng kowtowed
and said:
"Sir,
you are one who acts according to righteousness.
If I am acceptable,
there is no need to lose a Dàfū;
if I am unacceptable,
there is no need to lose a Gōngzǐ.
If it is righteous, I shall advance;
if not, I shall withdraw.
How would I dare not follow only your will?
That deposition and elevation do not cause disorder
is my wish."
Bàozǐ said:
"Who is not a son of the Ruler?"
and then accepted the covenant.
He sent Hú Jī to take Ān Rǔzǐ to Lài,
removed Yù Sì,
killed Wáng Jiǎ,
detained Jiāng Shuō,
and imprisoned Wáng Bào at the Hill of Gōudòu.
Dào Gōng sent Zhū Máo to tell Chénzǐ,
saying:
"Were it not for you,
I would not have reached this position.
However, a ruler is different from a vessel;
there cannot be two.
Having two vessels means no lack,
but having two rulers brings many troubles.
I venture to announce this to the Dàfū."
Chén Xīzǐ did not reply but wept
and said:
"Does the Ruler not trust his ministers at all?
Because of the distress of the state of Qí,
and because there was anxiety amidst the distress,
and because a young ruler could not be consulted,
we sought an older ruler,
hoping he might also tolerate the ministers!
Otherwise, what crime has Rǔzǐ committed?"
Zhū Máo reported back,
and Dào Gōng regretted it.
Zhū Máo said:
"Your Lordship should consult Chénzǐ on great matters,
but you may plan small matters yourself."
He sent Zhū Máo to move Rǔzǐ to Tái.
Before arriving,
they killed him under a field tent
and buried him at Shūmào Chún.
A12.7 The Āi Gōng Year Seven Jīng
A12.7.1 In the spring of the seventh year,
Huáng Yuàn of Sòng led an army to invade Zhèng.
A12.7.2 Wèi Mànduō of Jìn led an army to invade Wèi.
A12.7.3 In the summer,
the Gōng met with Wú at Zèng.
A12.7.4 In the autumn,
the Gōng attacked Zhū.
On the day Jǐyǒu of the eighth month,
he entered Zhū,
and brought back Zhū Zǐ Yì.
A12.7.5 The people of Sòng besieged Cáo.
In winter, Sì Hóng of Zhèng led an army to rescue Cáo.
B12.7 The Āi Gōng Year Seven Zhuàn
B12.7.1 In the spring of the seventh year,
the army of Sòng invaded Zhèng,
because Zhèng had rebelled against Jìn.
B12.7.2 The army of Jìn invaded Wèi,
because Wèi would not submit.
B12.7.3 In the summer,
the Gōng met with Wú at Zèng.
Wú came to demand one hundred Bǎiláo.
Zǐfú Jǐngbó replied:
"The former kings never had such a thing."
The people of Wú said:
"Sòng gave us one hundred Bǎiláo;
Lǔ cannot fall behind Sòng.
Furthermore, Lǔ provided more than ten Bǎiláo for the Dàfū of Jìn.
For the King of Wú to have one hundred Bǎiláo,
is it not also acceptable?"
Jǐngbó said:
"Fàn Yāng of Jìn was greedy and abandoned ritual.
He used a great state to intimidate our humble city,
so our humble city gave him eleven Bǎiláo.
If your ruler commands the feudal lords with ritual,
then there are established numbers.
If he also abandons ritual,
then there will be excess.
When Zhōu ruled as kings
and established rituals,
the highest offerings did not exceed twelve,
considering it the great number of Heaven.
Now, if you abandon the Zhōu rituals
and say there must be one hundred Bǎiláo,
it is entirely up to you Zhíshì."
The people of Wú would not listen.
Jǐngbó said:
"Wú is about to perish,
for it has abandoned Heaven and turned its back on its roots.
If we do not give it,
they will certainly vent their malice upon us."
So they gave it to them.
Tàizǎi Pǐ summoned Jì Kāngzǐ;
Kāngzǐ sent Zǐgòng to decline.
Tàizǎi Pǐ said: "The rulers of the states have traveled a long way,
yet the Dàfū does not step out of his gate;
what kind of ritual is this?"
He replied:
"How could it be considered ritual?
It is out of fear of a great state.
The great state does not command the feudal lords with ritual.
If it does not act with ritual,
how can its actions be measured?
Our ruler has already complied with the command.
How would his elder minister dare to abandon his state?
Tàibó wore the Duānwěi to practice the Zhōu rituals;
Zhòngyōng succeeded him,
cut his hair and tattooed his body,
using nakedness as adornment.
Was that ritual?
There was a reason for it."
Returning from Zèng,
they considered Wú to be incapable of doing anything significant.
B12.7.4 Jì Kāngzǐ wished to attack Zhū,
so he held a feast for the Dàfū to plan it.
Zǐfú Jǐngbó said:
"The means by which the small serve the great
is trustworthiness;
the means by which the great protect the small
is benevolence.
Turning one's back on a great state
is lack of trustworthiness;
attacking a small state
is lack of benevolence.
The people find protection in the walls;
the walls find protection in virtue.
One who loses these two virtues
is in danger.
What then can he protect?"
Mèngsūn said:
"What do you gentlemen think?
Should we dislike his worthiness and oppose him?"
He replied:
"Yǔ assembled the feudal lords at Túshān,
and there were ten thousand states that brought jade and silk.
Now of those that remain,
there are not even several dozen,
because the great do not treat the small with kindness,
and the small do not serve the great.
Knowing that danger is certain,
why not speak?
The virtue of Lǔ is like that of Zhū,
yet you attack them with a multitude;
is this acceptable?"
He left displeased.
In autumn,
[Lǔ] attacked Zhū,
and upon reaching Fànmén,
the sound of bells could still be heard.
The Great Officers remonstrated,
but he did not listen.
Máo Chéngzǐ requested to report this to Wú,
but it was not permitted,
saying:
"The sound of striking the night watch in Lǔ is heard in Zhū;
Wú is two thousand lǐ away,
and will not arrive within three months,
so how can they reach us?
Besides, are the resources within our borders not sufficient?"
Chéngzǐ rebelled with Máo,
and the army then entered Zhū,
occupying its ducal palace.
The various troops plundered by day,
and the people of Zhū sought protection at Yì.
The army plundered by night,
and they brought Zhūzǐ Yì back with them,
presenting him at the Bó Shè,
and imprisoning him in Fùxiá;
Fùxiá formerly belonged to Yì.
Máo Yíhóng of Zhū, with bundles of silk and cured hides, personally requested rescue from Wú,
saying: "Lǔ weakens Jìn and distances itself from Wú,
relying on its numbers
to turn its back on the Lord's covenant,
and avoiding the Lord's attendants,
in order to oppress our small state.
It is not that Zhū dares to love itself alone,
but we fear that the Lord's majesty will not be established.
If the Lord's majesty is not established,
it will be a cause of worry for the small states.
If you held a covenant in the summer at Zēngyǎn,
and they turn their backs on it in the autumn,
if they achieve their requests without opposition,
how will the feudal lords of the four directions serve the Lord?
Moreover, the levies of Lǔ are eight hundred chariots,
and they are your second;
the levies of Zhū are six hundred chariots,
and they are your private retainers.
To use your private retainers to support your second—
let the Lord consider it!"
The Master of Wú followed his advice.
B12.7.5 The people of Sòng besieged Cáo,
and Zhèng Huánzǐ Sī said:
"If the people of Sòng possess Cáo,
it will be a calamity for Zhèng;
it cannot go unrescued."
In winter,
the army of Zhèng rescued Cáo
and invaded Sòng.
Previously,
someone in Cáo dreamed of several gentlemen standing in the Shè palace,
and plotting to destroy Cáo.
Cáo Shū Zhènduó requested to wait for Gōngsūn Qiáng,
and they agreed.
In the morning they searched for him
in Cáo, but he was not there.
He cautioned his son, saying:
"When I die,
if you hear that Gōngsūn Qiáng is in charge of government,
you must leave."
When Cáo Bó Yáng ascended the throne,
he was fond of hunting and archery.
Gōngsūn Qiáng, a man of the countryside in Cáo, was fond of archery;
he caught a white goose,
presented it,
and spoke of the theories of hunting and archery,
which pleased the ruler.
Consequently, he was consulted on matters of government,
which pleased the ruler even more.
Having gained favor,
he was made Sīchéng to handle the government.
The son of the dreamer then left.
Qiáng spoke of theories of hegemony to Cáo Bó,
and Cáo Bó followed him,
then turned his back on Jìn and provoked Sòng.
The people of Sòng attacked them,
the people of Jìn did not rescue them,
and built five towns in their outskirts,
named Shǔqiū, Yīqiū,
Dàchéng, Zhōng, and Yú.
A12.8 The Annals of Duke Āi, Year Eight
A12.8.1 In the spring of the eighth year,
in the royal first month,
the Duke of Sòng entered Cáo
and returned with Cáo Bó Yáng.
A12.8.2 Wú attacked us.
A12.8.3 In summer,
the people of Qí took Huān and Chǎn.
They returned Zhūzǐ Yì to Zhū.
A12.8.5 Autumn, the seventh month.
A12.8.6 In winter, the twelfth month, on the day Guǐhài,
Qǐ Bó Guò died.
A12.8.7 The people of Qí returned Huān and Chǎn.
B12.8 The Commentary of Duke Āi, Year Eight
B12.8.1 In the spring of the eighth year,
the Duke of Sòng was about to return from attacking Cáo,
and Chǔshī Zǐféi brought up the rear.
The people of Cáo reviled him,
so he did not move.
The army waited for him.
When the Duke heard of this,
he was angry
and ordered them to turn back,
whereupon they destroyed Cáo,
captured Cáo Bó Yáng and Sīchéng Qiáng to bring them back,
and executed them.
B12.8.2 Because of Zhū,
Wú was about to attack Lǔ
and consulted Shūsūn Zhé.
Shūsūn Zhé replied:
"Lǔ has the name but not the substance;
if you attack it,
you will certainly achieve your ambition."
He withdrew and told Gōngshān Bùniǔ.
Gōngshān Bùniǔ said:
"This is not ritual propriety.
When a gentleman leaves his state,
he does not go to a hostile state.
If you are not yet a minister and there is an attack on it,
even if you are called to serve,
you may die for it.
If you have taken refuge there, you should stay concealed.
Furthermore, in a person's conduct,
one does not destroy one's home village because of those one dislikes.
Now you wish to overthrow your ancestral state because of a minor grievance—is that not difficult?
If they make you lead,
you must decline.
The King will probably use me."
Zǐzhāng hated this.
The King consulted Zǐxiè.
He replied:
"Although Lǔ has no allies to stand with,
it will certainly have those who will die with it;
the feudal lords will rescue it,
and you may not be able to achieve your ambition.
If Jìn, Qí, and Chǔ assist it,
these are four enemies.
Now Lǔ
is the lips to Qí and Jìn.
If the lips are gone, the teeth will be cold,
as the Lord knows;
why would they not rescue it?"
In the third month,
Wú attacked us,
and Zǐxiè led the way;
since the old road was dangerous,
they went by way of Wǔchéng.
Previously,
a person of Wǔchéng had a field near the border of Wú,
and he detained a person of Zēng who was soaking reeds,
saying:
"Why do you make my water muddy?"
When the army of Wú arrived,
the one who had been detained guided them to attack Wǔchéng,
and they conquered it.
Wáng Fàn had once been its governor,
and the father of Dàntái Zǐyǔ was on good terms with him;
the people of the state were afraid.
Yìzǐ said to Jǐngbó:
"What shall we do?"
He replied:
"If the army of Wú comes,
then we shall fight them;
what cause is there for worry?
Furthermore, they have come because they were summoned,
so what else do they seek?"
The army of Wú conquered Dōngyáng and advanced,
encamping at Wǔwǔ.
On the following day,
he lodged at Cánshì.
Gōng Bīn Gēng
and Gōng Jiǎ Shūzǐ fought at Yí;
[the Wú army] captured Shūzǐ and Xī Zhūchú
and presented them to the King.
The King said:
"These two were in the same chariot;
they must be men of ability.
One cannot yet hope for [the conquest of] this state."
On the following day,
he lodged at Gēngzōng
and then halted on the banks of the Sì River.
Wēi Hǔ wished to attack the King's quarters by night.
Seven hundred men of his private followers leaped three times in the courtyard of the tent;
three hundred soldiers were chosen,
and Yǒu Ruò was among them.
When they reached the inside of the Jì Gate,
someone said to Jì Sūn:
"This is not enough to harm Wú,
but it will kill many of the state's gentlemen.
It is better to stop."
So he stopped it.
The Viscount of Wú heard of this
and moved his quarters three times in a single night.
The people of Wú sought peace.
When they were about to make a covenant,
Jǐng Bó said:
"When the people of Chǔ besieged Sòng,
they exchanged children to eat them
and split bones for fuel to cook,
yet they still would not make a covenant under the city walls.
We have not yet reached such depletion,
yet we are making a covenant under the city walls;
this is to abandon the state.
Wú is lightly equipped and far from home;
they cannot remain for long
and will soon return.
Please wait for them a little longer."
He did not follow this.
Jǐng Bó loaded his belongings on a carriage
and went to the Lái Gate.
Then he requested the release of Zǐfú Hé to Wú;
the people of Wú permitted it,
and took Prince Gū Cáo in exchange for him,
after which he stopped.
The people of Wú made the covenant and returned.
B12.8.3 When Duke Dào of Qí came,
Jì Kāngzǐ gave him his younger sister in marriage.
When he ascended the throne, he sent for her.
Jì Fánghóu had an illicit affair with her.
The woman told of the circumstances,
so he did not dare to give her.
The Marquis of Qí was angry.
In summer, the fifth month,
Bào Mù of Qí led an army to invade us,
taking Huān and Chǎn.
B12.8.4 Someone slandered Hú Jī to the Marquis of Qí, saying:
"She is of the party of Ān Rǔzǐ."
In the sixth month,
the Marquis of Qí killed Hú Jī.
B12.8.5 The Marquis of Qí sent an envoy to Wú to request troops,
intending to use them to invade us,
and then he returned the Viscount of Zhū.
The Viscount of Zhū was again lawless.
The Viscount of Wú sent Grand Solicitor Zǐ Yú to punish him,
imprisoned him in a multi-storied tower,
and surrounded it with thorns.
He ordered the various Grand Officers to support Crown Prince Gé to conduct the government.
B12.8.6 In autumn,
peace was made with Qí.
In the ninth month,
Zàng Bīn Rú went to Qí to preside over the covenant.
Lǘ Qiū Míng of Qí came to preside over the covenant
and to take Jì Jī back with him;
she became a favorite.
Bào Mù again said to the various princes:
"Shall I make it so that you have a thousand chariots?"
A prince reported this.
The Duke said to Bào Zǐ:
"Someone has slandered you.
You should reside in Lù for a while to observe the situation.
If it is true,
then take your family and go;
if it is not true,
then return to your place."
As he went out the gate,
he was made to go with only one-third of his family;
halfway there,
he was made to go with only two chariots.
When he reached Lù,
he was bound and taken in,
and then killed.
B12.8.7 In winter, the twelfth month,
the people of Qí returned Huān and Chǎn,
because Jì Jī was a favorite.
A12.9 The Classic of the Ninth Year of Duke Āi
A12.9.1 In the ninth year, spring,
the royal second month,
Duke Xī of Qǐ was buried.
A12.9.2 Huáng Yuàn of Sòng led an army and captured the Zhèng army at Yōngqiū.
A12.9.3 In summer,
the people of Chǔ invaded Chén.
A12.9.4 In autumn,
the Duke of Sòng invaded Zhèng.
In winter, the tenth month.
B12.9 The Commentary of the Ninth Year of Duke Āi
B12.9.1 In the ninth year, spring,
the Marquis of Qí sent Gōngmèng Chuò to decline the troops from Wú.
The Viscount of Wú said:
"Last year I received your command;
now it is changed.
I do not know which to follow.
I shall proceed to receive the command from your lord."
B12.9.2 Xǔ Xiá, a favorite of Wǔ Zǐ Shèng of Zhèng, asked for a city,
but there was none to give him.
He asked to take one from outside.
He agreed,
so he besieged Yōngqiū of Sòng.
Huáng Yuàn of Sòng surrounded the Zhèng army;
every day he moved his camp
until the fortifications closed in.
The Zhèng army wailed.
Zǐ Yáo went to rescue them
but was heavily defeated.
On the day jiǎxū of the second month,
Sòng captured the Zhèng army at Yōngqiū;
he spared the lives of those who were capable,
and returned with Jiá Zhāng and Zhèng Luó.
B12.9.3 In summer,
the people of Chǔ invaded Chén,
because Chén had become aligned with Wú.
B12.9.4 The Duke of Sòng invaded Zhèng.
B12.9.5 In autumn,
Wú built the city of Hán
and connected the Jiāng and Huái rivers by a canal.
B12.9.6 Zhào Yāng of Jìn divined by tortoise shell about rescuing Zhèng.
He encountered "Water going to Fire."
He consulted the scribes Shǐ Zhào, Shǐ Mò, and Shǐ Guī.
Shǐ Guī said:
"This is called 'Submerged Yang.'
One may raise troops;
it is advantageous for invading the Jiāng,
but not advantageous for us against Shāng.
To invade Qí is permissible,
but to oppose Sòng is not auspicious."
Shǐ Mò said:
"Yíng
is the name of a water;
Zǐ
is the position of water.
When names and positions are equal,
they cannot be crossed.
Yándì was the Master of Fire;
the Jiāng clan are his descendants.
Water overcomes fire,
so to invade the Jiāng is permissible."
Shǐ Zhào said:
"This is called 'like a river in full flood,'
which cannot be swum across.
Zhèng is currently in the wrong;
it cannot be rescued.
To rescue Zhèng would be inauspicious.
I do not know anything else."
Yáng Hǔ divined it with the Zhōu Yì
and encountered the hexagram Tài changing to Xū.
He said: "Sòng is currently auspicious;
we cannot contend with them.
Wēizǐ Qǐ
was the eldest son of Dì Yǐ.
Sòng and Zhèng
are nephew and uncle.
Bliss
means emolument.
If the eldest son of Dì Yǐ gave his sister in marriage and obtained auspicious emolument,
how can we obtain anything auspicious?"
So they stopped.
B12.9.7 In winter,
the Viscount of Wú sent an envoy to alert [our] army to join in invading Qí.
A12.10 The Classic of the Tenth Year of Duke Āi
A12.10.1 In the tenth year, spring,
the royal second month,
Yì, the Viscount of Zhū, came as a fugitive.
A12.10.2 The Duke met with Wú to invade Qí.
On the day wùxū of the third month,
Yáng Shēng, the Marquis of Qí, died.
A12.10.4 In summer,
the people of Sòng invaded Zhèng.
A12.10.5 Zhào Yǎng of Jìn led an army to invade Qí.
A12.10.6 In the fifth month,
the Duke arrived from the expedition against Qí.
A12.10.7 Burial of Duke Dào of Qí.
A12.10.8 Gōngmèng Kū of Wèi returned from Qí to Wèi.
A12.10.9 Bó Yí, the Count of Xuē, died.
A12.10.10 In autumn,
burial of Duke Huì of Xuē.
A12.10.11 In winter,
Prince Jié of Chǔ led an army to attack Chén.
A12.10.12 Wú rescued Chén.
B12.10 *The Commentary on Duke Āi, Year Ten*
B12.10.1 In the spring of the tenth year,
Duke Yǐn of Zhū came as a refugee;
he was a nephew to Qí,
and thus subsequently fled to Qí.
B12.10.2 The Duke met with the Viscount of Wú, the Viscount of Zhū, and
the Viscount of Tán to attack the southern borders of Qí,
and the army was stationed at Xì.
B12.10.3 The people of Qí assassinated Duke Dào
and reported it to the army.
The Viscount of Wú wailed for three days outside the military gates.
Xú Chéng led a naval force intending to enter Qí from the sea;
the people of Qí defeated them,
and the Wú army then returned.
B12.10.4 In summer,
Zhào Yǎng led an army to attack Qí,
and the grandees requested to perform divination for it.
Zhào Mèng said:
"I performed divination here when raising the troops;
an affair is not commanded twice,
and divination does not repeat a lucky omen.
Advance!"
Thereupon they took Lí and Yuán,
destroyed the outer walls of Gāotáng,
invaded as far as Lài, and then returned.
B12.10.5 In autumn,
the Viscount of Wú sent an envoy to again alert the army.
B12.10.6 In winter,
Zǐqī of Chǔ attacked Chén,
and Jìzǐ of Yánzhōu Lái in Wú rescued Chén,
saying to Zǐqī:
"The two rulers do not strive for virtue
but use force to struggle for the feudal lords;
what crime have the people committed?
I request to withdraw
to let you gain the fame,
while you strive for virtue and pacify the people."
Thereupon he returned.
A12.11 *The Canon of Duke Āi, Year Eleven*
A12.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
Guó Shū of Qí led an army to attack us.
A12.11.2 In summer,
Yuán Pō of Chén fled to Zhèng.
A12.11.3 In the fifth month,
the Duke met with Wú to attack Qí.
On the day Jiǎxū,
Guó Shū of Qí led an army and fought with Wú at Àilíng;
the Qí army was disastrously defeated,
and Guó Shū of Qí was captured.
A12.11.4 In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
Yúmǔ, the Viscount of Téng, died.
A12.11.5 In winter, in the eleventh month,
burial of Duke Yǐn of Téng.
A12.11.6 Shìshū Qí of Wèi fled to Sòng.
B12.11 *The Commentary on Duke Āi, Year Eleven*
B12.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
because of the affair at Xì,
Guó Shū and Gāo Wúpī led an army to attack us
and reached Qīng.
Jìsūn said to his steward Rǎn Qiú:
"The Qí army is at Qīng;
it must be because of Lǔ.
What shall we do?"
Qiú said:
"One of you should stay to guard, and the other two should follow the Duke to resist them at the borders."
Jìsūn said:
"We cannot do that." Qiú said:
"Then stay within the boundaries."
Jìsūn told the other two,
but they would not agree.
Qiú said:
"If it is not possible,
then the ruler should not go out.
One of you lead the army
and fight with your backs to the city;
those who do not join the ranks
are not men of Lǔ.
The households of Lǔ are more numerous than the war chariots of Qí;
one household is more than enough to match a chariot.
Why do you worry?
It is natural that the two of them do not want to fight;
the administration lies with the Jì clan.
In your time,
if the people of Qí attack Lǔ and you cannot fight,
it will be your shame,
and you will no longer be ranked among the feudal lords."
Jìsūn sent him to follow the court
and wait at the Dǎng clan's ditch.
Wǔshū called and asked him about the battle.
He replied:
"The superior man has long-term plans;
what does a small person know?"
Yìzǐ pressed him for an answer,
and he replied:
"A small person considers his talents before speaking
and measures his strength before contributing."
Wǔshū said:
"This is saying that I am not a real man."
He withdrew and inspected the chariots.
Mèng Rǔzǐ Xiè led the Right Army,
Yán Yǔ was the charioteer,
and Bǐng Xiè was the spearman on the right.
Rǎn Qiú led the Left Army,
Guǎn Zhōufù was the charioteer,
and Fán Chí was the spearman on the right.
Jìsūn said:
"Xū is young."
Yǒuzǐ said:
"He will follow orders."
The Jì clan had seven thousand armored men;
Rǎn Yǒu took three hundred men from Wǔchéng as his own foot soldiers.
The old and young guarded the palace,
and he took up a position outside the Yú Gate.
After five days,
the Right Army followed.
Gōngshū Wùrén saw those guarding and wept,
saying:
"The duties are many,
the administration is heavy,
the superiors cannot plan,
and the officers cannot die—
how can the people be governed?
I have already spoken of it;
how can I not exert myself!"
The army fought with the Qí army in the outskirts.
The Qí army came from Jìqǔ;
the army would not cross the ditch.
Fán Chí said:
"It is not that they cannot;
they do not trust you.
I request three beats of the drum and then we cross."
They did so,
and the multitude followed him.
The army entered the Qí camp.
The Right Army fled,
and the people of Qí followed them.
Chén Guàn and Chén Zhuāng crossed the Sì River.
Mèngzhī Cè was the last to enter, acting as the rear guard;
he pulled out an arrow and whipped his horse,
saying:
"It was that my horse would not advance."
A squad leader of Lín Bùniǔ said:
"Shall we run?"
Bùniǔ said:
"Who is not equal to this?"
He said: "Then shall we stop?"
Bùniǔ said:
"How would that be worthy?"
He walked slowly and died.
The army captured eighty armored heads,
and the people of Qí could not reform their ranks.
A night scout said:
"The people of Qí have fled."
Rǎn Yǒu requested to follow them three times,
but Jìsūn would not permit it.
Mèng Rǔzǐ said to others:
"I am not as good as Yán Yǔ,
but I am worthier than Bǐng Xiè.
Zǐyǔ is sharp and quick;
I did not want to fight but was able to remain silent;
yet Xiè said,
'Drive on!'"
Gōngwéi and his favorite boy Wāng Qǐ rode together and both died;
both were given a funeral.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"They were able to grasp shield and spear to defend the altars of the land and grain;
they need not be treated as those who died young."
Rǎn Yǒu used a spear against the Qí army,
so he was able to enter their camp.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"It was righteous."
B12.11.2 In the summer,
Yuán Pō of Chén fled to Zhèng.
Initially,
Yuán Pō served as the Sītú;
he levied taxes on the fief lands to marry off the Duke's daughter;
there was a surplus,
which he used for his own grand vessels.
The people of the state drove him out,
so he fled.
On the way he grew thirsty;
his clansman Yuán Xuān offered him rice ale, millet gruel, and dried meat.
He was pleased and said:
“How is it so well-supplied?”
The other replied:
“When the vessels were completed, these were prepared.”
He said: “Why did you not remonstrate with me?”
The other replied: “I feared being the first to be dismissed.”
B12.11.3 For the sake of the battle at the suburbs,
the Duke met with the Master of Wú to invade Qí.
In the fifth month,
they captured Bó.
On the day Rénshēn,
they reached Yíng.
The Central Army followed the King,
Xūmén Cháo commanded the Upper Army,
Prince Gūcáo commanded the Lower Army,
and Zhǎnrú commanded the Right Army.
Guó Shū of Qí commanded the Central Army,
Gāo Wúpī commanded the Upper Army,
and Zōng Lóu commanded the Lower Army.
Chén Xīzǐ said to his younger brother Shū:
“If you die,
I will surely achieve my aims.”
Zōng Zǐyáng and Lǘqiū Míng encouraged each other.
Sāng Yǎnxū drove for Guó Zǐ.
Gōngsūn Xià said:
“Those two men will surely die.”
As they were about to fight,
Gōngsūn Xià ordered his followers to sing the “Yú Bìn.”
Chén Zǐxíng ordered his followers to prepare the mouth-jade.
Gōngsūn Huī ordered his followers, saying:
“The enemy is within eight feet,
and the hair of the Wú men is short.”
Dōngguō Shū said:
“After three battles I must die;
this is the third.”
He sent a messenger to inquire after Xián Duō with a qín zither,
saying:
“I shall not see you again.”
Chén Shū said:
“In this campaign,
I hear only the drums,
and not the gongs.”
On the day Jiǎxū,
they fought at Àilíng.
Zhǎnrú defeated the leader of the Gāo clan,
Guó Zǐ defeated Xūmén Cháo,
but the King's personal troops assisted them,
greatly defeating the Qí army,
capturing Guó Shū, Gōngsūn Xià,
Lǘqiū Míng, Chén Shū, and Dōngguō Shū,
along with eight hundred leather chariots
and three thousand armored heads,
which were presented to the Duke.
When about to fight,
the Master of Wú called for Shūsūn
and said:
“What is your duty?”
He replied:
“To follow the Sīmǎ.”
The King granted him armor, a sword, and a spear,
saying:
“Attend to the service of your lord,
be reverent and do not fail his command!”
Shūsūn was unable to answer.
Wèi Cì stepped forward
and said:
“Zhōu Qiú carries his armor and follows his lord.”
He then bowed.
The Duke sent Grand Historian Gù to return the head of Guó Zǐ,
placing it in a new basket,
wrapping it in dark red and light red silk,
and adding silk cords.
He placed a letter on top of it,
which said:
“If Heaven did not recognize what is not loyal,
why would it employ a lesser state?”
B12.11.4 As Wú was about to invade Qí,
the Master of Yuè led his followers to have an audience;
the King and the various officers all received gifts and bribes.
The people of Wú were all pleased,
but only Zǐxū was afraid,
saying:
“This is but the fattening of Wú!”
He remonstrated, saying:
“Yuè is to us
a disease of the heart and belly;
our lands are adjacent,
and they have designs on us.
Their submissiveness
is to seek the fulfillment of their desires;
it is better to deal with them early.
Gaining one’s way in Qí
is like acquiring stony fields—
they are of no use.
If Yuè is not turned into a marsh,
Wú will likely perish.
If one has a physician remove a disease
and says
‘You must leave some remnant of it,’
this has never happened.
The ‘Pángēng’ announcement says:
‘If there are those who are perverse and non-compliant,
then cut off their noses and exterminate them without leaving any offspring,
and let them not change the seed in this city.’
This is how Shāng flourished.
Now you, My Lord, disregard this
and seek to become great—
will it not be difficult?”
The King did not listen.
He sent Zǐxū on a mission to Qí;
Zǐxū entrusted his son to the Bǎo clan,
where he took the name Wángsūn.
Upon returning from the mission,
the King heard of this
and sent him the sword Shǔlòu to die by.
When about to die,
he said:
“Plant catalpa trees on my grave;
catalpa can be used for timber.
Wú will likely perish!
In three years,
it will begin to weaken.
To be full and then be destroyed
is the Way of Heaven.”
B12.11.5 In the autumn,
Jìsūn ordered the repair of defenses,
saying:
“For the small to defeat the great
is a calamity;
the day Qí arrives is not far off.”
B12.11.6 In the winter,
Tàishū Jí of Wèi fled to Sòng.
Initially,
Jí married the daughter of Zǐcháo of Sòng,
and her younger sister was favored.
When Zǐcháo fled,
Kǒng Wénzǐ made Jí divorce his wife
and married his own daughter to him.
Jí sent an attendant to entice the younger sister of his first wife and placed her in Lí,
building a palace for her,
as if she were a second wife.
Wénzǐ was angry
and wanted to attack him,
but Zhòngní stopped him.
He then took back his daughter.
Some person committed adultery in an outer district;
the people of the outer district seized his carriage to present it.
Ashamed of these two things,
he fled.
The people of Wèi established Yí
and had him take Kǒng Jǐ as his wife.
Jí served Xiàng Tuí
and presented him with beautiful pearls;
Xiàng Tuí gave him Chéngzhú.
The Duke of Sòng sought the pearls,
but Tuí would not give them,
and thus incurred guilt.
When the Huán clan fled,
the people of Chéngzhú attacked Tàishū Jí.
Duke Zhuāng of Wèi restored him
and had him reside in Cháo,
where he died.
He was laid in state in Yún
and buried in Shǎochì.
Initially,
Yìn, the son of Duke Dào of Jìn, was a fugitive in Wèi;
he made his daughter act as a servant while hunting.
Tàishū Yìzǐ stopped them and gave them wine to drink,
and subsequently betrothed her,
and they gave birth to Dàozǐ.
When Dàozǐ took office,
Xià Wù became a Grand Officer.
When Dàozǐ fled,
the people of Wèi executed Xià Wù.
When Kǒng Wénzǐ was about to attack Tàishū,
he consulted Zhòngní.
Zhòngní said:
“As for matters of the hú and guǐ vessels,
I have once studied them;
as for matters of armor and weapons,
I have not heard of them.”
He retired,
ordered his carriage and departed,
saying:
"A bird chooses its tree;
how can a tree choose its bird?"
Wénzǐ hurriedly stopped him
and said:
"How could Yǔ dare to measure his private interests?
I am inquiring about the difficulties of the state of Wèi."
When he was about to stop,
the people of Lǔ summoned him with gifts of silk,
and so he returned.
B12.11.7 Jì Sūn wished to impose a land tax,
and sent Rǎn Yǒu to consult Zhòng Ní.
Zhòng Ní said:
"Qiū does not know about this."
After three inquiries,
Rǎn Yǒu finally said:
"You are an elder of the state;
the state waits for you to act.
How is it that you will not speak?"
Zhòng Ní did not answer him,
but privately said to Rǎn Yǒu:
"The conduct of a gentleman
is measured by ritual:
in bestowal, he values generosity;
in managing affairs, he upholds the mean;
in collection, he follows lightness.
If it is like this,
then what Qiū provides is also sufficient.
If one does not measure by ritual,
but is greedy and insatiable,
then even with a land tax,
it will still be insufficient.
Moreover, if your master Jì Sūn wishes to act according to the law,
the statutes of Zhōu Gōng exist;
if he wishes to act recklessly,
then why consult me?"
Jì Sūn did not listen.
A12.12 The Annals of the Twelfth Year of Duke Āi
A12.12.1 In the spring of the twelfth year,
the land tax was employed.
A12.12.2 In the summer, in the fifth month on the day jiǎchén,
Mèngzǐ died.
A12.12.3 The Duke met with Wú at Tuógāo.
A12.12.4 In the autumn,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Wèi and
Huáng Yuàn of Sòng at Yún.
A12.12.5 Xiàng Cháo of Sòng led an army to invade Zhèng.
A12.12.6 In the winter, in the twelfth month,
there were locusts.
B12.12 The Commentary for the Twelfth Year of Duke Āi
B12.12.1 In the spring of the twelfth year,
in the royal first month,
the land tax was employed.
B12.12.2 In the summer, in the fifth month,
Mèngzǐ, the consort of Duke Zhāo, died.
Duke Zhāo had taken a wife from Wú,
so her surname was not recorded.
No announcement of her death was sent,
so she was not called "Lady."
No wailing was performed upon returning from the burial,
so it is not said that the "Lesser Lord" was buried.
Kǒngzǐ joined in the condolences
and went to the Jì family.
The Jì family did not wear mourning caps,
but laid aside their mourning sashes and bowed.
B12.12.3 The Duke met with Wú at Tuógāo;
the Viscount of Wú sent Grand Chancellor Pǐ to request a renewal of the covenant.
The Duke did not wish to do so
and sent Zǐgòng to respond, saying:
"A covenant
is that by which good faith is made complete.
Therefore, the heart governs it,
jade and silk serve it,
words bind it,
and the bright spirits are invoked to witness it.
My unworthy ruler believes that if there is a covenant,
it cannot be changed.
If it could still be changed,
what benefit would a daily covenant bring?
Now you say,
'We must renew the covenant.'
If it can be renewed,
it can also be allowed to grow cold."
Thereupon, the covenant was not renewed.
B12.12.4 Wú summoned Wèi to a meeting.
Previously,
the people of Wèi had killed the Wú envoy Qiě Yáo and were afraid;
they consulted with the envoy Zǐyǔ.
Zǐyǔ said:
"Wú is currently lawless;
they might insult our ruler.
It is better not to go."
Zǐmù said:
"Wú is currently lawless.
When a state is lawless,
it must vent its sickness upon others.
Although Wú is lawless,
it is still enough to bring disaster to Wèi.
Go!
When a tall tree falls,
nothing nearby escapes being struck;
when a state dog goes mad,
nothing escapes its bite.
How much more so for a great state!"
In the autumn,
the Marquis of Wèi met with Wú at Yún.
The Duke, the Marquis of Wèi, and Huáng Yuàn of Sòng made a covenant,
but in the end declined a covenant with Wú.
The people of Wú built a fence around the Marquis of Wèi's quarters.
Zǐfú Jǐngbó said to Zǐgòng:
"In a meeting of the feudal lords,
after the business is finished,
the presiding lord offers gifts,
and the host of the land provides provisions,
as they take their leave.
Now Wú does not practice ritual toward Wèi,
but fences in their ruler's quarters to distress him.
Why don't you go see Grand Chancellor
Pǐ?"
He then requested a bundle of silk and went.
The conversation turned to the Wèi matter,
and Grand Chancellor Pǐ said:
"My unworthy ruler wishes to serve the ruler of Wèi,
but the ruler of Wèi's arrival was delayed;
my ruler was afraid,
so he is detaining him."
Zǐgòng said:
"When the ruler of Wèi came,
he must have consulted with his people.
Some of his people wanted to come, and some did not;
therefore he was delayed.
Those who wanted to come
are your partisans;
those who did not want to come
are your enemies.
If you seize the ruler of Wèi,
you are casting down your partisans and exalting your enemies.
Those who would cast you down will have their wishes fulfilled.
Furthermore, if you assemble the feudal lords and then seize the ruler of Wèi,
who would not be afraid?
Casting down partisans, exalting enemies,
and making the feudal lords afraid—
perhaps it will be difficult to maintain hegemony!"
Grand Chancellor Pǐ was pleased
and released the Marquis of Wèi.
When the Marquis of Wèi returned,
he imitated the barbarian speech.
Zǐzhī was still young
and said:
"The ruler will surely not escape;
he will likely die among the barbarians!
He was seized and yet is pleased with their speech;
his following them is firm."
B12.12.5 In the winter, in the twelfth month,
there were locusts. Jì Sūn asked Zhòng Ní about it.
Zhòng Ní said:
"Qiū has heard
that after the Fire star hides, all hibernating insects are gone.
Now the Fire star still flows to the west;
the calendar officers have made an error."
B12.12.6 Between Sòng and Zhèng, there was a vacant land,
called Mízuò, Qǐngqiū, Yùchàng, Yán, Gē, and Xī.
Zǐchǎn made a settlement with the people of Sòng,
saying:
"Let neither side possess these."
When the clans of Sòng's Píng and Yuán fled from Xiāo to Zhèng,
the people of Zhèng walled Yán, Gē, and Xī for them.
In the ninth month,
Xiàng Cháo of Sòng attacked Zhèng,
took Xī,
killed the grandson of Duke Yuán,
and then besieged Yán.
In the twelfth month,
Hàn Dá of Zhèng went to the rescue of Yán.
On the day bǐngshēn,
he surrounded the army of Sòng.
A12.13 The Annals of the Thirteenth Year of Duke Āi
A12.13.1 In the spring of the thirteenth year,
Hàn Dá of Zhèng led an army and captured the Sòng army at Yán.
A12.13.2 In the summer,
Chéng, Viscount of Xǔ, died.
A12.13.3 The Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn and the Viscount of Wú at Huángchí.
A12.13.4 Prince Shēn of Chǔ led an army to invade Chén.
A12.13.5 Yúyuè invaded Wú.
A12.13.6 In the autumn,
the Duke arrived from the meeting.
A12.13.7 Jìn Wèi Mànduō led an army to invade Wèi.
A12.13.8 Burial of Xǔ Yuán Gōng.
A12.13.9 Ninth month,
locusts.
A12.13.10 Winter, eleventh month,
there was a comet in the east.
A12.13.11 Robbers killed Xià Qūfū of Chén.
A12.13.12 Twelfth month,
locusts.
B12.13 *The Zuǒ Commentary on the Thirteenth Year of Āi Gōng*
B12.13.1 In the spring of the thirteenth year,
Xiàng Tuí of Sòng went to rescue his army.
Zhèng Zǐ Shèng had it proclaimed:
“Whoever captures Huán Tuí shall have a reward.”
Tuí fled and returned home.
Consequently, they took the Sòng army at Yán,
capturing Chéng Huān and Gào Yán.
Six towns were laid waste.
B12.13.2 Summer, the Gōng met with Shàn Píng Gōng, Jìn Dìng Gōng, and Wú Fūchāi at Huángchí.
B12.13.3 In the sixth month, on the day Bǐngzǐ,
the Zǐ of Yuè attacked Wú,
forming two columns;
Chóu Wúyú and Ōu Yáng arrived at the suburbs first from the south.
Tàizǐ Yǒu, Wángzǐ Dì,
Wángsūn Míyōng, and Shòu Yúyáo observed them from above the Hóng.
Míyōng saw the banner of Gūmiè
and said:
“It is my father’s banner.
I cannot see my enemy and not kill him.”
The Tàizǐ said:
“If we fight and do not win,
the state will perish;
please wait.”
Míyōng would not listen,
gathered five thousand men,
and Wángzǐ Dì assisted him.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
they fought;
Míyōng captured Chóu Wúyú,
and Dì captured Ōu Yáng.
The Zǐ of Yuè arrived,
and Wángzǐ Dì defended.
On the day Bǐngxū,
they fought again
and greatly defeated the Wú army,
capturing Tàizǐ Yǒu,
Wángsūn Míyōng,
and Shòu Yúyáo.
On the day Dīnghài,
they entered Wú.
The people of Wú reported the defeat to the King.
The King loathed the news being heard,
so he personally cut the throats of seven men beneath his tent.
B12.13.4 Autumn, seventh month, on the day Xīnchǒu, the alliance was made;
Wú and Jìn disputed precedence.
The people of Wú said:
“In the house of Zhōu,
we are the seniors.”
The people of Jìn said:
“Among those of the Jī surname,
we are the Bó.”
Zhào Yāng called for Sīmǎ Yín and said:
“The day is late;
the great matter is not yet accomplished;
this is the fault of us two ministers.
Set up the drums and arrange the ranks;
if we two ministers die for it,
who is senior and who is junior will surely be known.”
He replied:
“Please watch them for a moment.”
He returned
and said:
“Those who eat meat do not have dark complexions.
Now the King of Wú has a dark complexion;
has his state been defeated?
Has his Tàizǐ died?
Moreover, the virtue of the Yí is shallow
and they cannot endure for long;
please wait for them a little.”
Then precedence was given to the people of Jìn.
The people of Wú were going to have the Gōng meet the Hóu of Jìn;
Zǐfú Jǐngbó replied to the messenger:
“When a King assembles the lords,
then the Bó leads the Hóu and governors to an audience with the King;
when a Bó assembles the lords,
then the Hóu lead those of the rank of Zǐ
and Nán to an audience with the Bó.
From the King downwards,
the jade and silks for audiences and visits are different.
Therefore, the duties and tribute of our humble state to Wú
are more abundant than to Jìn,
and have never been lacking,
because we regard you as the Bó.
Now that the lords are meeting,
if your ruler leads our ruler to see the ruler of Jìn,
then Jìn will have become the Bó.
Our humble state will change its duties and tribute:
Lǔ pays a levy to Wú of eight hundred chariots;
if we are treated as a Zǐ
or Nán,
then we will follow Zhū in being attached to Wú
and serve Jìn as Zhū does.
Moreover, your Excellency summoned the lords as a Bó,
and yet ends by treating them as a Hóu—
what benefit is there in that?”
The people of Wú then stopped.
Soon they regretted it
and were going to imprison Jǐngbó.
Jǐngbó said:
“Why not? I have already established my successor in Lǔ;
I will follow you with two chariots and six men;
I am at your command whether we go slowly or quickly.”
They then imprisoned him and returned.
When they reached Hùyǒu,
he said to the Tàizǎi:
“Lǔ is about to perform sacrifices to the Shàngdì and the former Gōng on the first shàngxīn day of the tenth month
and complete them on the jìxīn day.
Every generation has held these duties;
since the time of Xiāng,
they have not been changed.
If I am not at the meeting,
the invocators and priests will say,
‘Wú made it so.’
Moreover, they will say that Lǔ was not disrespectful,
yet you seized seven of its lowliest men—
what loss is that to Lǔ?”
Tàizǎi Pǐ spoke to the King, saying:
“It does no harm to Lǔ
and only harms our reputation;
it is better to send him back.”
So they sent Jǐngbó back.
Shēnshú Yí of Wú begged for grain from the Gōngsūn Yǒushān clan,
saying:
“The jade pendants are tangled,
and I have nothing to tie them to;
there is one vessel of fine wine,
and I and the old man in hempen clothes gaze at it.”
He replied:
“As for fine grain, there is none;
as for coarse grain, there is some.
If you climb Shǒushān and cry out
‘Gēngguǐ!’,
then I will answer.”
The King wanted to attack Sòng,
kill its men and imprison its women.
Tàizǎi Pǐ said:
“You could conquer them,
but you could not occupy the land.”
So they returned.
B12.13.5 Winter,
Wú and Yuè made peace.
A12.14 *The Annals of the Fourteenth Year of Āi Gōng*
A12.14.1 In the spring of the fourteenth year,
there was a hunt in the west and a lín was captured.
A12.14.2 Shè of Xiǎozhū came as a fugitive with Gùyì.
A12.14.3 Summer, fourth month,
Chén Héng of Qí seized his ruler
and placed him in Shūzhōu.
A12.14.4 On the day Gēngxū,
Shū Huán died.
A12.14.5 Fifth month, on the day Gēngshēn, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A12.14.6 Chén Zōngshù fled to Chǔ.
A12.14.7 Xiàng Tuí of Sòng entered Cáo and rebelled.
A12.14.8 Kuáng, Zǐ of Jǔ, died.
A12.14.9 Sixth month,
Xiàng Tuí of Sòng fled from Cáo to Wèi.
A12.14.10 Xiàng Cháo of Sòng came as a fugitive.
A12.14.11 The people of Qí assassinated their ruler, Rén, in Shūzhōu.
A12.14.12 Autumn,
Zhào Yāng of Jìn led an army to attack Wèi.
A12.14.13 Eighth month, on the day Xīnchǒu,
Zhòngsūn Héjì died.
A12.14.14 Winter,
Chén Zōngshù returned from Chǔ to Chén,
and the people of Chén killed him.
Chén Yuánmǎi fled to Chǔ.
A comet appeared.
There was a famine.
The Commentary on the Fourteenth Year of Duke Āi.
In the spring of the fourteenth year,
during a hunt in the west at Dàyě,
the charioteer of the Shūsūn clan, Zǐchú Shāng, captured a lín.
Thinking it to be an ill omen,
he gave it to the foresters.
Zhòngní saw it
and said,
“It is a lín,”
and then he took it.
Shè of Xiǎozhū fled with Jùyì to Lǔ,
saying,
“If Jìlù is made to pledge his word to me,
I will not require a formal covenant.”
They sent Zǐlù,
but Zǐlù declined.
Jì Kāngzǐ sent Rǎn Yǒu to say to him,
“A state of a thousand chariots
does not trust its own covenant
but trusts your word.
How would you be disgraced by this?”
He replied,
“If Lǔ has an affair against Xiǎozhū,
I would not dare to ask the cause,
and it would be acceptable to die beneath its city walls.
But this man is a rebellious subject,
and to fulfill his words
is to treat him as being in the right.
Yóu cannot do it.”
When Duke Jiǎn of Qí was in Lǔ,
Kàn Zhǐ was in favor with him.
When he ascended the throne,
he appointed him to conduct the government.
Chén Chéngzǐ was apprehensive of him
and repeatedly glared at him in court.
Zhūyù Yǎng spoke to the Duke, saying,
“Chén
and Kàn cannot both be maintained;
you, my lord, should choose between them.”
He did not listen.
While Zǐwǒ was attending the evening audience,
Chén Nì killed someone
and encountered him;
consequently, he was seized and taken inside.
The Chén clan was then in harmony;
they feigned an illness
and sent him lye for hair-washing,
providing wine and meat within it.
They feasted the guards of the prisoner,
who got drunk and were killed,
and he escaped.
Zǐwǒ held a covenant with the Chén clan members at the Chén ancestral temple.
Formerly,
Chén Bào wished to be a servant to Zǐwǒ
and asked a Gōngsūn to speak for him.
The Gōngsūn had a death in his family and stopped,
but afterwards he spoke of it, saying,
“There is one Chén Bào,
who is tall and hunched in his upper back,
with an upward gaze.
In serving a gentleman, he will certainly attain his will.
He wishes to be your servant.
I was wary of his character,
so I was slow to inform you.”
Zǐwǒ said, “What harm?
That depends on me.”
He made him a servant.
On another day,
he spoke with him about the government,
and being pleased,
consequently favored him.
He said to him,
“If I drive out the entire Chén clan and establish you,
what about it?”
He replied,
“I am distant from the Chén clan,
and moreover, those who are disobedient are but a few men;
why drive them all out?”
He then informed the Chén clan.
Zǐxíng said,
“He has the Duke’s favor;
if we do not act first,
he will surely bring disaster upon you.”
Zǐxíng stayed in the Duke’s palace.
In the summer, the fifth month, on the day Rénshēn,
Chéngzǐ and his brothers with four chariots went to the Duke.
Zǐwǒ was in a tent;
he came out
to meet them,
and they then entered
and closed the gates.
Attendants resisted them,
and Zǐxíng killed the attendants.
The Duke was drinking wine with women at the Tántái terrace;
Chéngzǐ moved him to the bedchamber.
The Duke grasped a halberd
and was about to strike him.
The Grand Historiographer Zǐyú said,
“It is not that it is unfavorable;
they are going to remove a harm.”
Chéngzǐ went out to lodge at the treasury;
hearing that the Duke was still angry,
he was about to leave,
saying,
“Where is there not a ruler?”
Zǐxíng drew his sword
and said,
“Hesitation
is the thief of affairs.
Who is not of the Chén clan?
If I do not kill you,
let it be as by the Chén ancestors!”
Thereupon he stopped.
Zǐwǒ returned,
assembled his followers,
and attacked the side gate and the main gate,
but failed in both,
and then went out.
The Chén clan pursued him;
he lost his way in Yǎnzhōng
and went to Fēngqiū.
The people of Fēngqiū seized him
and reported it;
they killed him at the outer wall of Guōguān.
Chéngzǐ was about to kill Dàlù Zǐfāng,
but Chén Nì pleaded for him and he was spared.
Taking a chariot on the road by the Duke’s order,
he reached Ér;
the crowd recognized him and made him go east.
Passing out of the Yōng gate,
Chén Bào offered him a chariot.
He would not accept it,
saying,
“Nì pleaded for me,
and Bào offered me a chariot;
I have personal obligations to them.
If I serve Zǐwǒ yet have personal obligations to his enemies,
how can I face the gentlemen of Lǔ and Wèi?”
Dōngguō Jiǎ fled to Wèi.
On the day Gēngchén,
Chén Héng seized the Duke at Shǔzhōu.
The Duke said,
“If I had followed Yǎng’s words earlier,
I would not have come to this.”
The favor shown to Huán Tuí of Sòng was harmful to the Duke.
The Duke made his wife frequently invite him to a feast
and intended to punish him.
Before he could do so,
Tuí first plotted against the Duke,
asking to exchange Ān for Bó.
The Duke said,
“That is not possible.
Bó
is our ancestral city.”
Thereupon he added seven towns to Ān
and requested to feast the Duke there,
setting the time at noon.
All the members of his household prepared and went.
The Duke became aware of it
and told Huáng Yě,
“I have raised Tuí,
and now he is going to bring disaster upon me.
I ask you to come to my rescue.”
The Sīmǎ Zǐzhòng said,
“A servant who is not submissive
is what the spirits detest,
how much more so humans?
I dare not but obey your command.
But it will not do without the Zuǒshī;
I ask to summon him in the ruler’s name.”
Whenever the Zuǒshī ate,
he struck a bell.
Hearing the sound of the bell,
the Duke said, “The master is about to eat.”
When he had finished eating,
they played music again.
The Duke said,
“It is time.”
He went in his carriage
and said,
“A tracker came and told me,
‘In the Fèng Marsh there is a stag with full antlers.’”
The Duke said,
“‘Even if Tuí does not come,
if I get the Zuǒshī,
I will hunt with him,’
what about it?”
The Lord was afraid to
tell you (Sīmǎ Niú),
but Yě said:
"I once spoke privately with him."
The Lord wanted speed,
so he sent a carriage to meet you."
He rode with him,
and when they arrived,
the Duke told him the reason.
He bowed
and could not rise.
The Sīmǎ said: "The Lord is speaking with you."
The Duke said:
"What makes it difficult for you
is Heaven above
and the former Lords below."
He replied:
"Tuí's irreverence
is a calamity for Sòng.
How could I dare not obey your command?"
The Sīmǎ requested a token of authority
to order his followers to attack the Huán clan.
Their senior kinsmen and old retainers said,
"It cannot be,"
but their new retainers said,
"We follow our Lord's command."
They then attacked them.
Zǐ Qí galloped to inform Sīmǎ Huán (Xiàng Tuí).
The Sīmǎ wanted to enter,
but Zǐ Chē stopped him,
saying:
"If you cannot serve your Lord
and then attack the state,
the people will not support you;
you will only find death."
Xiàng Tuí then entered Cáo to rebel.
In the sixth month,
the Lord sent Zuǒ Shī Cháo to attack him,
wanting to take grandees as hostages to gain entry there.
He could not,
so he also entered Cáo
and took hostages.
Tuí said:
"This is not right.
Having failed to serve the Lord
and having offended the people,
what shall we do?"
He then released them.
The people then rebelled against him.
Xiàng Tuí fled to Wèi.
Xiàng Cháo came to flee,
but the Duke of Sòng sent someone to stop him,
saying:
"I have a promise with you;
the sacrifices of the Xiàng clan must not be terminated."
He declined, saying:
"My crime is great;
it would be proper to exterminate the entire Huán clan.
If, for the sake of my ancestors,
you allow there to be successors,
that is your Lordship's kindness.
As for me,
I cannot return."
Sīmǎ Niú returned his fief and ritual jade and went to Qí.
When Xiàng Tuí left the territory of Wèi,
the Gōngwén clan attacked him,
seeking the Xiàhòu clan's semi-circular jade.
He gave them other jades
and fled to Qí.
Chén Chéngzǐ appointed him as a secondary minister.
Sīmǎ Niú again returned his fief
and went to Wú.
The people of Wú disliked him,
so he returned.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ summoned him,
and Chén Chéngzǐ also summoned him.
He died outside the outer gate of the capital of Lǔ.
The Kēng clan buried him at Qiūyú.
B12.14.5 On the day jiǎwǔ,
Chén Héng of Qí assassinated his ruler, Rén, at Shūzhōu.
Kǒng Qiū fasted for three days
and requested to attack Qí three times.
The Duke said:
"Lǔ has been weakened by Qí for a long time.
If you attack them,
how will it be?"
He replied:
"Chén Héng has assassinated his ruler;
half the people do not support him.
With the multitudes of Lǔ added to half of Qí,
we can overcome them."
The Duke said:
"Tell Jì Sūn."
Confucius declined
and withdrew, telling others:
"Because I follow in the rank of the grandees,
I did not dare not to speak."
B12.14.6 Previously,
Mèng Rúzǐ Xiè was going to pasture horses at Chéng.
The Governor of Chéng, Gōngsūn Sù, would not accept them,
saying:
"Mèng Sūn is the source of Chéng's distress;
no horses shall be pastured here."
Rúzǐ was angry
and attacked Chéng,
but his followers could not enter,
so he returned.
When an official of Chéng was sent on a mission,
Rúzǐ whipped him.
In autumn, in the eighth month, on the day xīnchǒu,
Mèng Yìzǐ died.
The people of Chéng hurried to the funeral
but were not admitted.
They bared their shoulders and wore mourning headbands,
wailing in the thoroughfares,
and asking to provide offerings,
but they were not permitted.
Fearful,
they did not return home.
A12.15 The Annals of the Fifteenth Year of Duke Āi
