A12.15.1 In the spring of the fifteenth year,
in the royal first month,
Chéng rebelled.
A12.15.2 In the summer, in the fifth month,
Gāo Wúpī of Qí fled to Běiyàn.
A12.15.3 The Earl of Zhèng attacked Sòng.
A12.15.4 In the autumn, in the eighth month,
a great rain sacrifice was performed.
A12.15.5 Zhào Yāng of Jìn led an army to attack Wèi.
A12.15.6 In the winter,
the Marquis of Jìn attacked Zhèng.
A12.15.7 Peace was made with Qí.
A12.15.8 Gōngmèng Kōu of Wèi fled to Qí.
B12.15 The Commentary on the Fifteenth Year of Duke Āi
B12.15.1 In the spring of the fifteenth year,
Chéng rebelled and joined Qí.
Wǔbó attacked Chéng
but could not overcome it,
so he walled Shū.
B12.15.2 In the summer,
Zǐxī and Zǐqī of Chǔ attacked Wú
and reached Tóngruì.
The Marquis of Chén sent Gōngsūn Zhēnzǐ to pay respects there,
but he reached Liáng and died.
They intended to enter with the corpse.
The Viscount of Wú sent Grand Counselor Pǐ to greet them
and decline, saying:
"Because the rains and floods are unseasonal,
I fear the grandee’s corpse might be lost,
which would increase my ruler's sorrow.
My ruler ventures to decline."
The chief assistant Yùyǐn Gài replied:
"My ruler heard that Chǔ was acting unrighteously,
repeatedly attacking the state of Wú
and destroying its people.
My ruler sent me, Gài, to serve as an envoy
to console your humble officials.
Unluckily,
the envoy encountered Heaven's sorrow,
his great life fell away,
and his days ended at Liáng.
We have observed the days of mourning and prepared the offerings,
moving the coffin and stopping day by day.
Now your Lord has commanded you to meet the envoy and say,
'Do not approach the gate with the corpse.'
This is to cast my ruler's command into the wild grass.
Moreover, I have heard it said:
'Serving the dead as one serves the living
is Ritual.'
Thus, there are rituals for when one dies during a mission
and uses the corpse to fulfill the duty,
as well as rituals for encountering a death during a mission.
If we do not use the corpse to fulfill the mission,
it would be returning simply because of a death;
would that not be impermissible?
Even when Ritual is used to restrain the people,
some still overstep it;
now the Grandee says
'Die and abandon it.'
This is to abandon Ritual.
How then can you be a leader of the feudal lords?
The men of old had a saying:
'Do not defile or maltreat the officers.'
This assistant will carry the corpse to fulfill the mission.
If my ruler's command reaches your presence,
even if we fall into a deep abyss,
that is Heaven's decree,
and not the fault of your Lord or those who cross the waters."
The people of Wú admitted him.
B12.15.3 In autumn,
Chén Guàn of Qí went to Chǔ.
Passing through Wèi,
Zhòng Yóu saw him
and said:
“Perhaps Heaven will use the Chén clan as an ax and hatchet;
once they have carved and destroyed the ducal house,
and others possess it,
it cannot be known;
whether Heaven will cause them to enjoy it to the end
also cannot be known.
If you treat Lǔ well to wait for the opportune time,
would that not be acceptable?
Why must you hate them?”
Zǐyù said:
“Indeed.
I have received my orders,
but you should have someone tell my younger brother.”
B12.15.4 In winter,
peace was made with Qí.
Zǐfú Jǐngbó went to Qí,
with Zǐgòng as his assistant.
They saw Gōngsūn Chéng,
and [Zǐgòng] said:
“All men serve others as ministers,
yet there are those who have hearts that turn against others;
moreover, although the people of Qí are in your service,
how can they be without divided loyalties?
You
are a descendant of Zhōu Gōng;
you enjoy many great benefits,
yet you still think of unrighteousness.
If the benefits cannot be obtained
and you lose your ancestral state,
what use will it be?”
Chéng said:
“Excellent!
I had not heard these instructions sooner.”
Chén Chéngzǐ provided lodging for the guests
and said:
“My ruler has sent me, Héng, to inform you:
‘My ruler wishes to serve your ruler as he serves the ruler of Wèi.’”
Jǐngbó bowed to Zǐgòng and signaled him to step forward.
Zǐgòng replied:
“That is my ruler's wish.
Formerly, when the people of Jìn attacked Wèi,
Qí, for the sake of Wèi,
attacked Guànshì of Jìn
and lost five hundred chariots.
Consequently, you gave Wèi territory
west of the Jì River,
and south of Zhuó, Mèi, and Xìng,
consisting of five hundred shūshè.
When the people of Wú brought disorder to our humble state,
Qí took advantage of its distress
to take Huān and Chǎn.
My ruler was chilled at heart because of this.
If he can see your ruler treating him as you treat the ruler of Wèi,
then that is indeed what he desires.”
Chéngzǐ was troubled by this;
thus he returned to peace.
Gōngsūn Sù entered Yíng with his troops and armor.
B12.15.5 Kǒng Yǔ of Wèi married the elder sister of the Crown Prince Kuàikuì,
and she gave birth to Kuǐ.
Hún Liángfū, a servant of the Kǒng family, was tall and handsome.
When Kǒng Wénzǐ died,
he had an illicit affair with the inner chamber.
The Crown Prince was in Qī,
and Kǒng Jī sent him there.
The Crown Prince spoke with him, saying:
“If you enable me to enter and gain the state,
you shall wear the ceremonial robes and ride in a high carriage,
and for three death-penalty offenses you shall not be held responsible.”
He made a covenant with him
and requested help from Bó Jī.
In the intercalary month,
Liángfū and the Crown Prince entered
and lodged in the outer garden of the Kǒng family.
At dusk,
the two wore women’s clothing and rode in a carriage,
with the eunuch Luó driving,
and went to the Kǒng residence.
Luán Níng, the elder of the Kǒng family, asked about them.
They announced themselves as female relatives and entered.
They then entered
and went to Bó Jī’s quarters.
After they had eaten,
Kǒng Bó Jī took up a spear and led the way.
The Crown Prince and five others in armor,
followed by a carriage carrying a boar, followed her.
They cornered Kǒng Kuǐ in the privy
and forced him to make a covenant,
then abducted him and ascended the terrace.
Luán Níng was about to drink wine;
the meat was not yet roasted.
Hearing of the disturbance,
he sent word to Jìzǐ;
he summoned Zhào Huò to prepare the carriage,
finished his cup, ate the meat,
and escorted the Lord of Wèi, Zhé, as he fled to Lǔ.
As Jìzǐ was about to enter,
he met Zǐgāo who was coming out,
who said: “The gates are already closed.”
Jìzǐ said: “I will go there for a while.”
Zǐgāo said: “It is too late;
do not involve yourself in the danger!”
Jìzǐ said:
“Having eaten his bread,
I will not avoid his danger.”
Zǐgāo then left, and Zǐlù entered.
When he reached the gate, Gōngsūn Gǎn was guarding it
and said: “There is no use in entering.”
Jìzǐ said:
“This is Gōngsūn;
he seeks profit
and flees from danger.
Yóu is not like that;
since I benefit from his salary,
I must rescue him from his troubles.”
A messenger came out,
so he entered
and said:
“What use does the Crown Prince have for Kǒng Kuǐ?
Even if you kill him,
there will surely be someone to succeed him.”
And he added:
“The Crown Prince has no courage;
if I set fire to the terrace
and it is half burned, he will certainly release Kǒng Shū.”
The Crown Prince heard this
and was afraid.
He sent down Shí Qǐ and Yú Yǎn to oppose Zǐlù.
They struck him with spears
and severed his cap-string.
Zǐlù said:
“A superior man dies,
but his cap does not fall off.”
He tied the cap-string and died.
Kǒngzǐ heard of the disorder in Wèi
and said:
“Chái will return,
but Yóu has died.”
Kǒng Kuǐ established Lord Zhuāng.
Lord Zhuāng disliked the former administration
and wished to remove all of them.
He first said to the Sītú Mán Chéng:
“I have suffered abroad for a long time;
you, sir, should please try it as well.”
He returned and told Chǔshī Bǐ,
wishing to attack the Lord with him,
but it did not happen.
A12.16 The Classic of the Sixteenth Year of Duke Āi
A12.16.1 In the spring of the sixteenth year,
in the first month of the King, on the day jǐmǎo,
the Heir Apparent of Wèi, Kuàikuì, entered Wèi from Qī.
Zhé, the Lord of Wèi, fled to Lǔ.
A12.16.2 In the second month,
Zǐhuánchéng of Wèi fled to Sòng.
A12.16.3 In the summer, in the fourth month, on the day jǐchǒu,
Kǒng Qiū died.
B12.16 The Commentary for the Sixteenth Year of Duke Āi
B12.16.1 In the spring of the sixteenth year,
Mán Chéng and Chǔshī Bǐ fled to Sòng.
B12.16.2 The Lord of Wèi sent Yān Wǔzǐ to report to Zhōu, saying:
“Kuàikuì committed a crime against his lord and father, and his lord and mother,
and fled to Jìn.
Jìn, for the sake of the Royal House,
did not abandon its brothers
and settled him on the banks of the River.
Heaven guided his heart,
and he has succeeded in guarding the fief.
I, your humble servant Xì, venture to inform the officials.”
The King sent Duke Píng of Shàn to reply,
saying:
“Xì has come to inform me, the Lone One, with this auspicious decree.
Go and say to my Uncle:
I praise the completion of your succession,
and your restoration to your rank and emolument.
Be reverent!
Just now Heaven’s favor is upon you.
If you are not reverent and not favorable,
how can your regret be overtaken?”
B12.16.3 In the summer, in the fourth month, on the day jǐchǒu,
Kǒng Qiū died.
The Duke pronounced a threnody for him, saying:
“Compassionate Heaven has no pity;
it did not spare this one elder,
leaving me, the Lone One, unprotected in my position,
solitary and in distress.
Alas, how sorrowful, Nífù!
There is no one to set a rule for me.”
Zǐgòng said:
“Will the Lord perhaps not die in Lǔ?”
The Master’s words said:
“When ritual is lost, there is confusion;
when names are lost, there is error.”
To lose one's purpose is confusion;
to lose one's position is error.
To be unable to employ a person while they are alive,
and then to deliver a eulogy for them when they die,
is not ritual;
to address them as ‘The One Man,’
is not a correct name.
You, my lord, have lost both.”
B12.16.4 In the sixth month,
the Marquis of Wèi (Wèi Hóu) entertained Kǒng Kuí with wine at Píngyáng
and rewarded him heavily.
All the Great Officers had contributions there.
He escorted him while he was drunk
and sent him away at midnight.
He carried Bó Jī in a carriage from Píngyáng and departed;
upon reaching the West Gate,
he ordered the secondary carriage to return the ancestral tablet to Xīpǔ.
Zǐ Bó Jì Zǐ had originally been a retainer of the Kǒng family,
but had recently entered the service of the Duke.
He requested to pursue them,
encountered the one carrying the tablet,
killed him, and took his carriage.
Xǔ Gōng Wéi was returning with the tablet
and encountered him.
[Xǔ Gōng Wéi] said:
“In competing for brilliance with an unkind person,
there is no way not to win.”
He insisted that [Zǐ Bó Jì Zǐ] shoot first.
[Zǐ Bó Jì Zǐ] shot three times,
all of which landed far from Xǔ Wéi.
Xǔ Wéi then shot him
and killed him.
Someone followed with his carriage
and found the tablet in a bag.
Kǒng Kuí fled to Sòng.
B12.16.5 When the Crown Prince Jiàn of Chǔ (Chǔ Dàizǐ Jiàn) encountered slander,
he fled from Chéngfù to Sòng;
he also avoided the turmoil of the Huá family by going to Zhèng.
The people of Zhèng treated him very well.
He then went to Jìn,
and plotted with the people of Jìn to surprise Zhèng,
then he requested to return there.
The people of Zhèng restored him to his former status.
The people of Jìn sent a spy to Zǐmù,
requesting to proceed and setting a date.
Zǐmù acted tyrannically in his private fief,
and the people of the fief complained of him.
The people of Zhèng investigated it
and captured the Jìn spy,
whereupon they killed Zǐmù.
His son was named Shèng,
who was in Wú;
Zǐxī wished to summon him.
Shè Gōng said:
“I have heard that Shèng is deceitful and prone to chaos;
will he not be a harm?”
Zǐxī said:
“I have heard that Shèng is trustworthy and brave;
he will not act disadvantageously.
If we settle him on the borders,
we can make him a shield for the defenses.”
Shè Gōng said:
“To be comprehensive in benevolence is called trust;
to follow righteousness is called bravery.
I have heard that Shèng is fond of repeating his promises
and seeks men willing to die;
perhaps he has private ambitions!
Repeating promises
is not trust;
expecting death
is not bravery.
You will surely regret it.”
He did not follow the advice.
He summoned him
and made him reside at the border
as Bái Gōng.
He requested to attack Zhèng.
Zǐxī said:
“Chǔ has not yet attained balance.
Otherwise,
I would not forget.”
On another day,
he requested again;
it was granted,
but the army had not yet been raised.
The people of Jìn attacked Zhèng,
and Chǔ went to its rescue
and made a covenant with it.
Shèng was angry
and said:
“The people of Zhèng are here,
and my enemy is not far.”
Shèng sharpened his sword himself.
Píng, the son of Zǐqī, saw him
and said:
“Why does the King’s grandson sharpen his sword himself?”
He said:
“I, Shèng, am known for being straightforward;
if I do not tell you,
would I be straightforward?
I intend to use it to kill your father.”
Píng told this to Zǐxī.
Zǐxī said:
“Shèng is like an egg;
I have protected him with my wings and raised him.
In the state of Chǔ,
once I die,
as for the Lìngyǐn and Sīmǎ,
who could it be but Shèng?”
Shèng heard this
and said:
“How mad the Lìngyǐn is!
If he gets to die a natural death,
then it won't be by my hand.”
Zǐxī did not repent.
Shèng said to Shí Qǐ:
“With the King and the two ministers,
if we have five hundred men to face them,
it will be enough.”
Qǐ said:
“They cannot be obtained.”
[Shèng] said:
“South of the market there is a man named Xióng Yíliáo;
if we get him,
he can stand against five hundred men.”
He then followed Bái Gōng to see him.
He spoke with him,
and he was pleased.
When told the reason,
he declined.
He threatened him with a sword,
but he did not move.
Shèng said:
“He who is not swayed by profit,
not intimidated by power,
and does not leak others' words to seek favor—
leave him.”
The people of Wú attacked Shèn,
and Bái Gōng defeated them.
He requested to present the military equipment,
which was granted,
and he then started the rebellion.
In the autumn, the seventh month,
he killed Zǐxī and Zǐqī in the court,
and kidnapped King Huì (Huì Wáng).
Zǐxī covered his face with his sleeve and died.
Zǐqī said:
“Formerly I served my lord with strength;
I cannot fail to maintain it until the end.”
He uprooted a camphor tree to kill people and then died.
Shí Qǐ said:
“Burn the storehouses and assassinate the King.
Otherwise,
we will not succeed.”
Bái Gōng said:
“That cannot be done.
To assassinate the King
is inauspicious;
to burn the storehouses
leaves no resources;
how then would we defend ourselves?”
Qǐ said:
“Possessing the state of Chǔ and governing its people,
and serving the spirits with reverence,
you can obtain good fortune,
and moreover there will be resources;
what is there to worry about?”
He did not follow the advice.
Shè Gōng was in Cài;
those outside the Fāngchéng Mountains all said:
“You can enter now.”
Zǐgāo said:
“I have heard
that those who seek luck through danger
have insatiable desires;
and if one is partial and overbearing, people will certainly desert him.”
Only after hearing that they had killed Guǎn Xiū of Qí
did he enter.
Bái Gōng wished to make Zǐlǘ the King;
Zǐlǘ would not agree,
so he threatened him with weapons.
Zǐlǘ said:
“If the King’s grandson were to pacify the state of Chǔ,
correct the royal house,
and thereafter provide protection,
that is my [Qǐ’s] wish;
how could I dare not obey?
If you intend to act for your own profit to topple the royal house
and disregard the state of Chǔ,
I would die before complying.”
He was subsequently killed,
and the King was taken to the Gāofǔ.
Shí Qǐ guarded the gate.
Yǔ Gōng Yáng tunneled into the palace
and carried the King on his back to the palace of Lady Zhāo (Zhāo Fūrén).
Shè Gōng also arrived,
and upon reaching the North Gate,
someone met him
and said:
"Why does my lord not wear a helmet?
The people of the capital gaze upon my lord as they gaze upon their own loving parents.
If a rebel's arrow should wound my lord,
it would sever the hopes of the people.
Why not wear a helmet?"
Thereupon, he put on a helmet and advanced.
He met another person, who said:
"Why does my lord wear a helmet?
The people of the capital gaze upon my lord as they gaze upon a harvest year,
hoping for it day after day.
If they see my lord's face,
they will find relief.
Knowing they will not die,
they will indeed have hearts full of courage,
and will even raise banners for my lord to follow through the capital;
but to hide your face and sever the hopes of the people,
is this not excessive?"
Thereupon, he removed his helmet and advanced.
He met Zhēn Yǐn Gù leading his subordinates,
intending to join Bái Gōng.
Zǐ Gāo said:
"Were it not for the two of you,
Chǔ would no longer be a state.
If you abandon virtue to follow a rebel,
can you truly preserve yourselves?"
They then followed Shè Gōng.
He employed them along with the people of the capital to attack Bái Gōng,
and Bái Gōng fled to the mountains and hanged himself.
His followers hid his body.
They captured Shí Qǐ alive and questioned him about Bái Gōng's death.
He replied:
"I know the place of his death,
but my elder instructed me not to speak of it."
They said:
"If you do not speak, we shall boil you."
Shí Qǐ said:
"In this matter, success would have meant becoming a Qīng,
and failure means being boiled;
this is indeed my proper lot,
so what harm is there?"
Thereupon, they boiled Shí Qǐ.
Wáng Sūn Yàn fled to the Kuíhuángshì.
Shěn Zhūliáng held both offices,
and once the state was at peace,
he then made Níng the Lìngyǐn
and made Kuān the Sīmǎ,
while he himself retired in Shè.
B12.16.6 The Marquis of Wèi divined a dream.
A favored person had requested wine from Tàshū Xīzǐ
but did not receive it.
He colluded with a diviner
to tell the Marquis:
"My lord has a high minister in the southwest corner;
if he is not removed,
I fear there will be harm."
Thereupon, the Marquis expelled Tàshū Yí.
Yí fled to Jìn.
B12.16.7 The Marquis of Wèi said to Hún Liángfū:
"I have succeeded the former ruler but have not obtained his ritual vessels.
What should be done?"
Liángfū spoke on behalf of the torchbearer
and said:
"Jí and the exiled ruler are both my lord's sons;
it is permissible to summon them and choose based on talent.
If they lack talent,
the vessels can be obtained."
A servant informed the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince had five men carry a boar and follow him;
they kidnapped the Marquis and forced him into a covenant,
and further requested the death of Liángfū.
The Marquis said:
Said:
"I request that he be killed only after he has committed three crimes."
The Marquis said:
"Agreed!"
B12.17 *Commentary on the Seventeenth Year of Duke Āi*
B12.17.1 In the spring of the seventeenth year,
the Marquis of Wèi made a tiger-skin tent at Jièpǔ.
When it was completed,
he sought someone with a fine reputation to share the first meal there with him.
The Crown Prince requested to use Liángfū.
Liángfū rode in a middle-class chariot with two stallions,
wearing purple clothes and fox fur.
Upon arriving,
he bared his fur coat
and ate without removing his sword.
The Crown Prince had him led away,
enumerated his three crimes, and killed him.
B12.17.2 In the third month,
the Viscount of Yuè attacked Wú.
The Viscount of Wú resisted him at Lìzé,
and they were arrayed across the water.
The Viscount of Yuè formed "hooking troops" on the left and right,
and at night ordered some to move to the left and some to the right
to advance while drumming and shouting;
the Wú army divided to resist them.
The Viscount of Yuè secretly crossed the water with his three armies
and drummed against Wú's central army.
The Wú army fell into great chaos
and was subsequently defeated.
B12.17.3 Zhào Yāng of Jìn sent a message to Wèi,
saying:
"When my lord was in Jìn,
Zhìfù served as the host.
I request that either my lord or the Crown Prince come
to absolve Zhìfù of blame.
Otherwise,
my ruler will say it was Zhìfù's doing."
The Marquis of Wèi declined due to difficulties,
and the Crown Prince further provoked him.
In the summer, in the sixth month,
Zhào Yāng besieged Wèi.
Guó Guān and Chén Guàn of Qí came to rescue Wèi
and captured a challenger from the Jìn army.
Zǐyù had him dressed and presented,
saying: "Lord Guó truly holds the power of Qí,
and he ordered Guàn, saying:
'Do not avoid the Jìn army!'
How would I dare disobey his command?
Why did you deign to trouble yourself?"
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"I divined about attacking Wèi,
but I did not divine about fighting Qí."
Thereupon, he returned.
B12.17.4 During the rebellion of Bái Gōng of Chǔ,
the people of Chén relied on their gathering forces to invade Chǔ.
Once Chǔ was at peace,
it intended to take Chén's wheat.
The Viscount of Chǔ asked the Grand Master Zǐgǔ and Shè Gōng Zhūliáng about a commander.
Zǐgǔ said:
"The Right Commander Chāijū and the Left Scribe Lǎo
both assisted the Lìngyǐn and Sīmǎ in attacking Chén;
they can be employed."
Zǐ Gāo said:
"The leaders are of low rank,
and the people will be negligent toward them;
I fear they will not follow orders."
Zǐgǔ said:
"Guān Dīngfù
was a captive from Ruò,
yet King Wǔ made him a military leader;
thus he conquered Zhōu and Liǎo,
subdued Suí and Táng,
and greatly opened up the various Man tribes.
Péng Zhòngshuǎng
was a captive from Shēn,
yet King Wén made him Lìngyǐn;
he established counties at Shēn
and Xī,
made Chén and Cài pay court,
and established the borders at the Rǔ River.
Provided they are fit for the task,
what does low rank matter?"
Zǐ Gāo said:
"Heaven's mandate is not deceptive.
The Lìngyǐn had a grievance against Chén;
if Heaven wishes to destroy them,
it must be the Lìngyǐn's son who is granted this task.
Why does my lord not set the others aside?
I fear the Right Commander and Left Scribe have the lowliness of those two captives
but lack their excellent virtue."
The King divined on it,
and Jí, the Intendant of Wǔchéng, was auspicious.
He was sent to lead the army to take Chén's wheat.
The people of Chén resisted him,
were defeated,
and Chén was subsequently besieged.
In the autumn, on the jǐmǎo day of the seventh month,
Gōngsūn Cháo of Chǔ led the army and destroyed Chén.
The King and Shè Gōng individually divined for Zǐliáng to be Lìngyǐn.
Shěnyǐn Zhū said:
"It is auspicious,
but it exceeds his ambitions."
Shè Gōng said:
"A prince serving as a minister of state—
if it exceeds that, what would he do next?"
On another day,
they divined again for Zǐguó and made him Lìngyǐn.
B12.17.5 The Marquis of Wèi dreamed in the North Palace;
he saw a person climbing the Kūnwú Tower,
with disheveled hair and facing north, shouting:
"Climbing these ruins of Kūnwú,
where the long-vined melons grow.
I am Hún Liángfū,
crying out to Heaven of my innocence."
The Marquis personally divined it with milfoil,
and Xūmí Shè interpreted it:
He said:
"No harm."
He gave him a city,
but he stationed someone there and fled, running to Sòng.
The Marquis of Wèi performed a divination,
and its oracle said:
"Like a fish with a red tail,
swimming across the current and wandering.
There is a great state on the borders;
it will destroy it,
and you will perish.
Close the doors and block the holes,
then leap over from the back."
In the winter, in the tenth month,
Jìn again attacked Wèi,
entered its outer walls,
and was about to enter the city.
Jiǎn Zǐ said:
"Stop!
Shū Xiàng had a saying:
'Those who rely on disorder to destroy states shall have no descendants.'"
The people of Wèi expelled Zhuāng Gōng and made peace with Jìn.
Jìn established Bānshī, the grandson of Xiāng Gōng, and returned.
In the eleventh month,
the Marquis of Wèi entered from Juàn,
and Bānshī left.
Previously,
the Duke climbed the wall to look out
and saw Róngzhōu.
He asked about it,
and was told what it was.
The Duke said:
"I
am of the Jī surname;
what are the Róng doing here?"
He razed it.
The Duke kept the artisans working for a long time.
The Duke wanted to expel Shí Pǔ,
but before he could, trouble broke out.
On the day Xīnsì,
Shí Pǔ attacked the Duke by means of the artisans.
The Duke closed the doors and pleaded,
but was not permitted.
He leaped over the northern side and fell,
breaking his thigh.
The people of Róngzhōu attacked him.
Crown Prince Jí and Prince Qīng leaped over to follow the Duke,
and the people of Róngzhōu killed them.
The Duke entered the house of Jǐ Shì of Róngzhōu.
Previously,
the Duke had seen from the wall that the wife of Jǐ Shì had beautiful hair;
he had it shaved off
to make a hairpiece for Lǚ Jiāng.
After he had entered,
he showed them a jade disk
and said:
"Save my life,
and I will give you the jade disk."
Jǐ Shì said:
"If I kill you,
where else would the jade disk go?"
They then killed him
and took the jade disk.
The people of Wèi brought back Bānshī and established him.
In the twelfth month,
the people of Qí attacked Wèi.
The people of Wèi requested peace.
They established Prince Qǐ
and took Bānshī back with them,
leaving him in Lù.
The Duke met with the Marquis of Qí to form a covenant at Méng,
with Mèng Wǔ Bó assisting.
The Marquis of Qí bowed his head to the ground,
and the Duke bowed.
The people of Qí were angry.
Wǔ Bó said:
"Except for the Son of Heaven,
our ruler has no one to whom he bows his head."
Wǔ Bó asked Gāo Chái:
"When the lords formed a covenant,
who held the bull's ear?"
Jì Gāo said:
"At the campaign of Zēngyǎn,
it was Prince Gūcáo of Wú;
at the campaign of Fāyáng,
it was Shí Tuí of Wèi."
Wǔ Bó said:
"Then I am but a pig."
In Sòng, Huáng Yuàn's son Jūn had a friend named Tián Bǐng,
and he seized the city of his elder brother Chán Bān to give it to him.
Chán Bān was resentful and left;
he told Zǐyí Kè, a minister of Huán the Marshal.
Zǐyí Kè went to Sòng
and told the Duke's wife:
"Jūn is about to bring in the Huán clan."
The Duke asked Zǐzhòng about it.
Previously,
Zǐzhòng had intended to make Fēiwǒ, the son of Qǐ Sì, his heir.
Jūn said:
"You must establish Bó;
he is a man of fine talent."
Zǐzhòng was angry
and did not follow this,
so he replied:
"The Minister of the Right is old,
and I do not know Jūn's intentions."
The Duke arrested him.
Huáng Yuàn fled to Jìn,
but they summoned him back.
Commentary on the Eighteenth Year of Duke Āi
In the spring of the eighteenth year,
Sòng killed Huáng Yuàn.
When the Duke learned the truth of the matter,
he restored the Huáng clan
and made Huáng Huǎn the Minister of the Right.
The people of Bā attacked Chǔ
and besieged Yōu.
Previously,
when Zǐ Guó, the Marshal of the Right, performed a divination,
Guān Zhān said:
"It is as desired."
Therefore, he was given the command.
When the Bā army arrived,
they were about to divine for a commander.
The King said:
"It is better to follow the previous result;
why divine again?"
He sent him to lead the army and set out.
When he asked for assistance,
the King said:
"The Master of the Bedchamber and the Master of Works are those who served the former kings diligently."
In the third month,
Gōngsūn Níng of Chǔ, Wú Yóuyú,
and Wěi Gù defeated the Bā army at Yōu;
therefore, Zǐ Guó was enfeoffed at Xī.
The noble man says:
"King Huì knew the meaning of the oracle.
The Books of Xià say:
'The official diviner can only determine the intent
and then command the great tortoise';
surely this is what it means!
The Record says:
'The sage does not trouble the milfoil and the tortoise';
King Huì surely possessed this quality."
In the summer,
Shí Pǔ of Wèi expelled his ruler Qǐ,
and Qǐ fled to Qí.
The Marquis of Wèi, Zhé, returned from Qí,
expelled Shí Pǔ,
and restored Shí Tuí and Tàishū Yí.
Commentary on the Nineteenth Year of Duke Āi
In the spring of the nineteenth year,
the people of Yuè invaded Chǔ
in order to deceive Wú.
In the summer,
Prince Qìng and Gōngsūn Kuān of Chǔ pursued the Yuè army
as far as Míng,
but did not catch them
and so returned.
In the autumn,
Shěn Zhūliáng of Chǔ attacked the Eastern Yí;
the men and women of the three Yí tribes and the Chǔ army formed a covenant at Āo.
In the winter,
Shū Qīng went to the capital
because King Jìng had passed away.
Commentary on the Twentieth Year of Duke Āi
In the spring of the twentieth year,
the people of Qí came to request a meeting.
In the summer,
they met at Lǐnqiū;
for the sake of Zhèng,
they planned to attack Jìn.
The people of Zhèng declined the assistance of the feudal lords.
In the autumn,
the army returned.
Prince Qìngjì of Wú repeatedly remonstrated with the Master of Wú,
saying:
"If you do not change,
you will surely perish."
He would not listen.
Qìngjì went to live in Ài
and then went to Chǔ.
Hearing that Yuè was about to attack Wú,
in the winter,
he requested to return and make peace with Yuè,
and so he returned.
He wished to remove the disloyal ones to please Yuè.
The people of Wú killed him.
In the eleventh month,
Yuè besieged Wú,
and Zhào Mèng reduced his diet for mourning.
Chǔ Lóng said:
"The three-year mourning
is the ultimate expression of intimacy;
yet the master has reduced his diet even further—
could there be another reason?"
Zhào Mèng said:
"In the campaign of Huángchí,
my late predecessor and the King of Wú made a pledge,
saying:
'Our likes and dislikes shall be shared.'
Now that Yuè is besieging Wú,
the successor cannot abandon the former undertaking yet oppose it;
however, it is not something Jìn can reach.
Therefore, I consider this a submission of condolences."
Chǔ Lóng said:
"If you let the King of Wú know this,
how would it be?"
Zhào Mèng said: "Is that possible?"
Lóng said:
"Please let me try it."
He then went, first arriving at the army of Yuè,
and said:
"Wú has encroached upon the Great State many times.
Having heard that your ruler is personally punishing them,
none among the people of the various Xià states is not delighted,
only fearing that your ruler's will might not be followed.
I request to enter and observe it."
They permitted it.
He spoke to the King of Wú, saying:
"The elder of my humble ruler, Wúxù, has sent his accompanying minister Lóng
to venture to express apologies for his lack of assistance:
In the campaign of Huángchí,
the former minister of your ruler, Zhìfù, was able to receive the alliance of Qí,
saying,
'Our likes and dislikes shall be shared.'
Now that your ruler is in difficulty,
Wúxù does not dare to fear the labor of helping,
but it is not something the state of Jìn can reach.
He has sent me, his accompanying minister, to venture to set this forth."
The King bowed his head to the ground and said:
"I, the unworthy one,
was unable to serve Yuè,
causing distress to the Great Officers.
I am humbled to receive your command."
He gave him a basket of pearls
and sent him to inquire of Zhào Mèng,
saying:
"Gōujiàn is about to let me live in sorrow;
I shall not even obtain death."
The King said:
"A drowning man must be laughed at;
I have a question.
Why was Shǐ Àn able to be a gentleman?"
He replied: "Àn, when advancing, was not met with dislike;
when retreating, there were no slandering words."
The King said: "Rightly so!"
B12.21 Commentaries on the 21st Year of Duke Āi
B12.21.1 In the summer of the twenty-first year, in the fifth month,
the people of Yuè arrived for the first time.
B12.21.2 In the autumn, in the eighth month,
the Duke and the Marquis of Qí and the Master of Zhū made a covenant at Gù.
The people of Qí demanded a bow with the head to the ground;
because of this, they sang of it, saying:
"The marsh of the people of Lǔ,
for several years they did not realize,
making me step high.
Only their Confucian books
were the cause of worry for the two states."
On this journey,
the Duke first arrived at Yánggǔ.
Lǘqiū Xī of Qí said:
"The Ruler has deigned to lift his jade toes
to be in my humble ruler's army.
The various ministers will send couriers to inform my humble ruler.
By the time they return,
would the Ruler not be weary?
Since the servants' quarters are not yet arranged,
I request to clear a lodge at Zhōudào."
The Duke declined, saying:
"How could I dare to trouble the servants?"
B12.22 Commentaries on the 22nd Year of Duke Āi
B12.22.1 In the summer of the twenty-second year, in the fourth month,
Duke Yǐn of Zhū fled from Qí to Yuè,
saying:
"Wú acted without the Way;
they seized the father and established the son."
The people of Yuè returned him to his state,
and Heir Apparent Gé fled to Yuè.
B12.22.2 In the winter, in the eleventh month, on the day Dīngmǎo,
Yuè destroyed Wú.
They requested to have the King of Wú reside in Yǒngdōng.
He declined, saying:
"I am old;
how can I serve another ruler?"
He then hanged himself.
The people of Yuè returned with his body.
B12.23 Commentaries on the 23rd Year of Duke Āi
B12.23.1 In the spring of the twenty-third year,
Sòng Jǐng Cáo died.
Jì Kāng Zǐ sent Rǎn Yǒu to offer condolences
and to attend the burial,
saying:
"My humble city has the affairs of the altars of grain and soil,
and Féiyǔ is occupied with his duties there;
therefore he cannot help hold the funeral ropes.
He has sent me to seek to follow the attendants,
saying:
'Because of Féiyǔ's position as a distant nephew,
there are some meager horses produced by his ancestors,
and he has sent me to seek to present them to the Lady’s steward;
perhaps they can be called banner-decorating horses!'"
B12.23.2 In the summer, in the sixth month,
Xún Yáo of Jìn attacked Qí,
and Gāo Wúpī led the army to resist him.
Zhì Bó observed the Qí army;
his horse took fright,
and he then drove it forward,
saying:
"The people of Qí know my banner;
they would say I turned back out of fear."
He reached the ramparts and then returned.
When they were about to battle,
Zhǎng Wǔ Zǐ requested to perform divination.
Zhì Bó said:
"The Ruler informed the Son of Heaven,
and performed divination with the guardian tortoise in the ancestral temple;
it was auspicious.
Why should I perform divination again?
Moreover, the people of Qí took our Yīngqiū.
The Ruler commanded Yáo;
I do not dare to flaunt military might,
but to deal with the matter of Yīngqiū.
To punish the crime with words is sufficient;
why must there be divination?"
On the day Rénchén,
they battled at Líqiū,
and the Qí army was utterly defeated.
Zhì Bó personally captured Yán Gēng.
B12.23.3 In the autumn, in the eighth month,
Shū Qīng went to Yuè;
this was the first mission to Yuè.
Yuè Zhū Yāng came on a friendly mission
to reciprocate Shū Qīng's visit.
B12.24 Commentaries on the 24th Year of Duke Āi
B12.24.1 In the summer of the twenty-fourth year, in the fourth month,
the Marquis of Jìn was about to attack Qí
and sent word to request troops,
saying:
"In the past, Zāng Wén Zhòng used the army of Chǔ to attack Qí
and took Gǔ;
Xuān Shū used the army of Jìn to attack Qí
and took Wènyáng.
My humble ruler wishes to seek blessings from the Duke of Zhōu,
and desires to seek divine efficacy from the Zāng clan."
Zāng Shí led the army to join them
and took Lǐnqū.
The military officers ordered repairs,
intending to advance.
Lái Zhāng said:
"The Ruler is lowly and the government is tyrannical.
Last year they overcame the enemy,
and now they have again conquered a city.
Heaven's bounty is great;
how can they advance further?
These are false words.
The campaign will soon be disbanded."
The Jìn army then returned.
They provided Zāng Shí with cattle for provisions;
the Grand Scribe expressed thanks,
saying:
"Because my humble ruler is on the march,
the ritual gifts are not of the proper measure;
I venture to express my apologies."
B12.24.2 The Master of Zhū was again without the Way;
the people of Yuè seized him and returned with him,
and established Gōngzǐ Hé.
Hé was also without the Way.
B12.24.3 The mother of Gōngzǐ Jīng was favored;
the Duke intended to make her his Lady
and sent the Master of Ceremonies Xùn Xià to present the ritual.
He replied:
"There is no such ritual."
The Duke was angry and said:
"You are the head of the clan matters;
establishing a Lady
is a great ritual of the state.
For what reason is there no such ritual?"
He replied:
"The Duke of Zhōu and Duke Wǔ took wives from Xuē;
Duke Xiào and Duke Huì took wives from Shāng;
from Duke Huán downward, they took wives from Qí.
Such rituals indeed exist.
If you make a concubine a Lady,
then there is certainly no such ritual for that."
The Duke eventually established her,
and made Jīng the Heir Apparent.
The people of the state then began to dislike him.
B12.24.4 In the intercalary month,
the Duke went to Yuè
and met the Heir Apparent Shì of Yǐng,
who intended to give his daughter in marriage to the Duke and grant him much land.
Gōngsūn Yǒushān sent word to Jìsūn.
Jìsūn was afraid,
and sent someone to offer bribes through the Great Manager Pǐ,
and thus it was stopped.
B12.25 The Commentary on the Twenty-Fifth Year of Duke Āi
B12.25.1 In the summer of the twenty-fifth year, in the fifth month, on the day gēngchén,
the Lord of Wèi fled to Sòng.
The Lord of Wèi built the Língtái at Jípǔ
and drank wine there with the Great Officers.
Chǔshī Shēngzǐ ascended to the mats while wearing stockings,
and the Duke was angry.
Shēngzǐ excused himself, saying:
"Your servant has an illness
that is different from others;
if you were to see it,
my Lord would vomit,
and for this reason, I did not dare."
The Duke became even angrier.
The Great Officers pleaded for him,
but the Duke would not allow it.
Chǔshī went out.
The Duke gestured with his hand as if holding a halberd
and said:
"I will surely cut off your feet!"
Chǔshī heard this.
He rode with the Sīkòu Hài
and said:
"Today we are lucky to be able to flee."
When the Duke had entered,
he seized the city of the Nán clan
and took away the administrative power of Sīkòu Hài.
The Duke ordered an attendant to drive the carriage of Gōngwén Yìzǐ into a pond.
Previously,
the people of Wèi had eliminated the Xià Dīng clan
and gave their wealth and family to Péngfēng Mízǐ.
Mízǐ served wine to the Duke
and presented the daughter of Xià Wù,
who became a favorite
and was made the Consort.
Her younger brother Qī,
who was the grand-nephew of Tàishū Jí,
had been raised by the Duke since youth
and was made the Sītú.
When the Consort's favor declined,
Qī committed an offense.
The Duke kept the three types of craftsmen working for a long time.
The Duke ordered the actor Jiǎo to insult Quán Mí during an oath,
yet he closely trusted and favored him.
Therefore, Chǔshī Bǐ,
Gōngsūn Mímóu,
Gōngwén Yào,
Sīkòu Hài,
and Sītú Qī, using the three types of craftsmen and Quán Mí, rose in rebellion.
They all held sharp weapons;
those without them held axes.
They sent Quán Mí to enter the Duke's palace,
and they attacked the Duke while shouting from the palace of Heir Apparent Jí.
Juànzǐ Shì asked to resist them,
but Mí pulled his hand
and said:
"You are indeed brave,
but what will you do for the Lord?
Do you not see the former lords?
Where is there any desire that the Lord has not satisfied?
Moreover, the Lord has been abroad before;
why should he not return?
For now, it is impossible;
it is hard to oppose the anger of the masses.
If we rest, it will be easier to find an opening."
Then they went out.
They were going to go to Pǔ,
but Mí said:
"Jìn is not trustworthy;
it is not possible."
They were going to go to Juàn,
but Mí said:
"Qí and
Jìn are contending over us; it is not possible."
They were going to go to Líng,
but Mí said:
"Lǔ is not worth being with.
Please go to Chéngxú
to keep in touch with Yuè.
Yuè has a ruler."
So they went to Chéngxú.
Mí said:
"The rebels of Wèi are unpredictable;
please hurry,
and let it start with me."
Then he loaded the treasures and returned.
The Duke formed a band of crippled soldiers
and used the Invoker-Scribe Huī to invade Wèi.
The people of Wèi were distressed by this.
Yìzǐ knew of it
and saw Zǐzhī,
requesting to expel Huī.
Wénzǐ said:
"He is without guilt."
Yìzǐ said:
"He loves to monopolize profit and is reckless;
when he sees the Lord entering,
he will be the first to lead the way.
If you expel him,
he will surely go out of the South Gate
and go to the place where the Lord is.
Since Yuè has newly gained the support of the feudal lords,
he will surely request an army from them."
Huī was in the court;
they sent an officer to send him away from his house.
Huī went out;
it was as expected;
they did not let him back in.
After five days,
they lodged him in an outer neighborhood.
He subsequently gained favor
and was sent to Yuè to request an army.
B12.25.2 In the sixth month,
the Duke arrived from Yuè.
Jì Kāngzǐ and Mèng Wǔbó met him at Wǔwǔ.
Guō Zhòng was the charioteer;
he saw the two men
and said:
"There have been many evil words;
Lord, please settle them all."
The Duke held a banquet at Wǔwǔ.
Wǔbó offered a toast;
he disliked Guō Zhòng
and said:
"Why are you so fat?"
Jìsūn said:
"Please, let us have Zhì drink!
Because the state of Lǔ is so close to its enemies,
your servant was for this reason unable to follow the Lord,
but was able to escape the hardships of the great journey;
and yet you call Zhòng fat?"
The Duke said:
"This man has eaten his words many times;
how can he not be fat?"
The drinking of wine was not joyful,
and the Duke and the Great Officers began to have ill will.
B12.26 The Commentary on the Twenty-Sixth Year of Duke Āi
B12.26.1 In the summer of the twenty-sixth year, in the fifth month,
Shūsūn Shū led an army to meet Gāorú of Yuè,
Shéyōng, and Lè Fá of Sòng to reinstate the Lord of Wèi.
Wénzǐ wished to reinstate him.
Yìzǐ said:
"The Lord is stubborn and cruel;
wait for him a little,
he will surely be a poison to the people,
and then they will be in harmony with you."
The army invaded the outer districts
and made a great capture.
They went out to resist it
but were greatly defeated.
They dug up the grave of Chǔshī Dìngzǐ
and burned the remains above Píngzhuāng.
Wénzǐ sent Wángsūn Qí to have a private talk with Gāorú,
saying:
"Will you completely destroy Wèi,
or just reinstate the Lord?"
Gāorú said:
"My ruler's command is nothing else
but to reinstate the Lord of Wèi."
Wénzǐ gathered the masses and asked them,
saying:
"The Lord is using barbarians to attack the state;
the state is almost lost.
Please let us reinstate him."
The masses said:
"Do not reinstate him."
Wénzǐ said:
"If Mímóu flees, there will be benefit;
please let me go out from the North Gate."
The masses said: "Do not go out."
They heavily bribed the people of Yuè,
opened the gates and guarded the battlements to reinstate the Duke,
but the Duke did not dare to enter.
The army returned.
They established Duke Dào,
and the Nán clan assisted him.
They gave Chéngxú to the people of Yuè.
The Duke said:
"Qī was the one who did this."
He ordered that anyone who had a grievance against the Consort should take revenge on her.
Sītú Qī went on a mission to Yuè;
the Duke attacked him and seized his silks.
Qī told the King;
the King ordered him to take them back,
and Qī took them back with a crowd.
The Duke was angry
and killed Qī's nephew who had been made the Heir Apparent,
and finally died in Yuè.
B12.26.2 Duke Jǐng of Sòng had no son.
He took Dé and Qǐ, the sons of Gōngsūn Zhōu, and raised them in the ducal palace,
but had not yet established an heir.
At that time, Huáng Huǎn served as the Right Master,
Huáng Fēiwǒ as the Grand Marshal,
Huáng Huái as the Minister of State,
Líng Bùhuǎn as the Left Master,
Lè Fà as the Minister of Works,
and Lè Zhūchú as the Grand Minister of Crime.
These six ministers from the three clans submitted to and heard the administration,
but reached the Duke through the Dàyǐn.
The Dàyǐn often failed to report to the Duke
and instead used his own desires, claiming them to be the Duke's commands to issue orders.
The people of the capital hated him.
The Minister of Works wished to remove the Dàyǐn,
but the Left Master said:
"Let him be,
and let him fill up the measure of his crimes.
When one is heavy but has no foundation,
can he avoid ruin?"
In the winter, the tenth month,
the Duke went on an excursion to Kōngzé.
On the day xīnsì,
he died in Liánzhōng.
The Dàyǐn raised one thousand armored men from Kōngzé,
escorted the Duke from Kōngtóng to enter the Wò Palace,
and sent for the six ministers,
saying:
"I hear there is an army below;
the Duke requests the six ministers to devise a plan."
When the six ministers arrived,
he coerced them with the armored men, saying:
"The Duke is ill and ailing;
he requests you gentlemen to take an oath."
They then swore an oath in the courtyard of the Lesser Bedchamber,
saying: "Do nothing disadvantageous to the ducal house!"
The Dàyǐn then installed Qǐ
and escorted the funeral preparations to the Grand Palace;
it was only after three days that the people of the capital knew of it.
Lè Fà, the Minister of Works, sent word to be proclaimed in the capital, saying:
"The Dàyǐn has deluded and bewitched his lord
and monopolized the benefits.
Now the lord has died without being ill,
and after his death, it was hidden;
this is due to nothing else
but the crime of the Dàyǐn."
Dé dreamed that Qǐ was sleeping with his head to the north outside the Lú Gate,
while he himself became a crow and perched upon him;
his beak was upon the South Gate,
and his tail was upon the Tóng Gate.
He said: "My dream is beautiful;
I must be established."
The Dàyǐn plotted, saying:
"I was not present at the oath;
will they not perhaps expel me?
Let us swear another oath!"
He had the Invoker prepare the text of the covenant.
The six ministers were at Tángyú
and were about to swear the oath.
The Invoker Xiāng used the text of the covenant to inform Huáng Fēiwǒ.
Huáng Fēiwǒ, through Zǐlù, Dé the Gate-Keeper,
and the Left Master, plotted, saying:
"The people are with us;
shall we expel him?"
They all returned and distributed armor,
sending men to go through the capital,
saying:
"The Dàyǐn has deluded and bewitched his lord
to oppress and maltreat the ducal house;
those who are with us
are those who would save the lord."
The multitude said:
"We are with you!"
The Dàyǐn went through the capital, saying:
"The Dài clan and the Huáng clan are going to disadvantage the ducal house;
those who are with me
need not worry about not being wealthy."
The multitude said:
"We know no difference!"
The Dài clan and the Huáng clan wished to attack the Duke's palace,
but Lè Dé said:
"You must not.
He is guilty because he oppressed the Duke;
if we attack the Duke's palace,
we will be even more so."
They sent the people of the capital to descend upon the Dàyǐn,
and the Dàyǐn escorted Qǐ to flee to Chǔ.
Thereupon, Dé was established.
The Minister of Works became the Senior Minister,
and they swore an oath, saying:
"The three clans shall govern together,
and none shall harm the others!"
B12.26.3 Duke Chū of Wèi sent a bow from Chéngchú to inquire after Zǐgòng,
and moreover said:
"Shall I enter again?"
Zǐgòng bowed his head to the ground and received the bow,
replying:
"Your servant does not know."
He spoke privately to the messenger, saying:
"Formerly, Duke Chéng went into exile in Chén;
Nìng Wǔzǐ and Sūn Zhuāngzǐ made the covenant of Wǎnpú, and then the lord entered.
Duke Xiàn went into exile in Qí;
Zǐxiān and Zǐzhǎn made the covenant of Yíyí, and then the lord entered.
Now the lord is in exile for the second time;
internally, I do not hear of the kin of Duke Xiàn,
and externally, I do not hear of the ministers of Duke Chéng;
thus, Cì does not know the means by which he may enter.
The *Classic of Poetry* says:
'None are strong but for the men,
and the four quarters will follow them.'
If one obtains the right men,
the four quarters will take them as masters,
so what difficulty would there be for a state?"
The Commentary on the Twenty-seventh Year of Duke Āi
B12.27.1 In the spring of the twenty-seventh year,
the Viscount of Yuè sent Shéyōng on a mission of state
and spoke of the Zhū fields,
enfeoffing them at Táishàng.
In the second month,
they swore a covenant at Píngyáng,
and the three gentlemen all followed.
Kāngzǐ was troubled by this
and spoke regarding Zǐgòng,
saying:
"If he were here,
I would not have come to this!"
Wǔbó said:
"It is so.
Why not summon him?"
He said:
"I certainly intend to summon him."
Wénzǐ said:
"Another day, please remember this."
B12.27.2 In the summer, the fourth month, on the day jǐhài,
Jì Kāngzǐ died.
The Duke offered condolences
and reduced the ritual.
B12.27.3 Xún Yáo of Jìn led an army to attack Zhèng,
camping at Tóngqiū.
Sì Hóng of Zhèng requested help from Qí.
The Qí army was about to set out
when Chén Chéngzǐ ordered the orphans to attend court for three days.
He prepared a carriage with two horses
and attached five towns to it.
He summoned Jìn, the son of Yán Zhuójù,
and said:
"In the campaign of Xí,
your father died.
Because of the state's many difficulties,
I have not yet looked after you.
Now the lord commands you with these towns;
wear your robes and attend court,
so as not to let your father's former labors go to waste!"
Then he went to save Zhèng.
When they arrived at Liúshū,
they were seven lǐ away from Gǔ,
and the people of Gǔ did not know of it.
When they reached the Pú River,
it rained,
and they did not cross.
Zǐsī said:
"A great state is within the eaves of our humble city,
and for this reason we reported our emergency.
Now if the army does not proceed,
I fear it will be too late."
Chéngzǐ put on a raincoat and grasped a halberd,
standing upon the slope;
those horses that did not move forward, he helped to whip them.
Zhī Bó heard of this
and then retreated,
saying:
"I divined to attack Zhèng,
but did not divine to oppose Qí."
He sent word to Chéngzǐ, saying:
"Great Officer Chénzǐ,
you are descended from Chén.
That the sacrifices of Chén are no more
is the crime of Zhèng;
therefore, my ruler sent Yáo to investigate the grievance of Chén.
I thought you, Great Officer, would also be concerned for Chén.
If you find it profitable to overturn your own roots,
what does it matter to Yáo?"
Chéngzǐ said angrily:
"Those who frequently insult others do not last;
how can Zhī Bó endure for long!"
Zhōngháng Wénzǐ informed Chéngzǐ, saying:
"Someone from the Jìn army informed Yín
that they intend to use a thousand light chariots to crush the gates of the Qí army;
then we could be completely destroyed."
Chéngzǐ said:
"My ruler commanded Héng, saying:
'Do not be concerned that we are few;
do not fear the many.'"
Even if there were more than a thousand chariots,
would I dare to avoid it?
I shall report your command to my ruler."
Wénzǐ said:
"Now I know why I will perish.
In the plans of a gentleman,
the beginning, the middle, and the end are all considered,
and only then does he proceed.
Now I have proceeded while being ignorant of all three;
is this not difficult?"
B12.27.4 The Duke was distressed by the extravagance of the Sānhuán
and wished to use the other lords to remove them;
the Sānhuán were also distressed by the Duke's recklessness,
thus there were many rifts between the ruler and his ministers.
The Duke was traveling at Língbǎn
and met Mèng Wǔbó at the crossroads of the Mèng clan;
he said: "I have a question for you:
Will I live to reach a natural death?"
He replied:
"Your servant has no way of knowing that."
He asked three times,
but he ultimately declined and did not answer.
The Duke wished to use Yuè to attack Lǔ and remove the Sānhuán.
In the autumn, in the eighth month on the day jiǎxū,
the Duke went to the house of Gōngsūn Yǒuxíngshì.
Thence he fled to Zhū,
and then finally went to Yuè.
The people of the capital executed Gōngsūn Yǒushānshì.
B12.27.5 In the fourth year of Duke Dào,
Xún Yáo of Jìn led an army to besiege Zhèng.
Before they arrived,
Sì Hóng of Zhèng said:
"Zhìbó is stubborn and likes to win;
if we submit to him early,
then it can be managed."
They first fortified Nánlǐ to await him.
Zhìbó entered Nánlǐ
and attacked the Jiédié Gate.
The people of Zhèng captured Xī Kuíléi
and bribed him with the governance of Zhì;
he kept his mouth shut and died.
As they were about to attack the gate,
"Enter it!"
The reply was:
"The master is here."
Zhìbó said:
"Ugly and without courage,
how can you be a son?"
The reply was:
"By being able to endure shame,
perhaps I will not harm the Zhào clan!"
Zhìbó did not change his ways;
Zhào Xiāngzǐ because of this hated Zhìbó
and eventually destroyed him.
Zhìbó was greedy and stubborn;
therefore Hán
and Wèi turned against him and destroyed him.
